# ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

I gratefully acknowledge how much I owe to the pioneering work of Paul Müller-Walde, Ettore Verga, and Jean Paul Richter. <note>These individuals were key 19th and early 20th-century scholars who first began the monumental task of transcribing and organizing Leonardo’s scattered notebooks.</note>

I am also grateful to Sir Kenneth Clark, the Librarian of the Royal Library at Windsor, and the Secretary to the Syndics <term>Syndics: A board of directors or trustees, in this case, those who manage the business affairs of Cambridge University Press.</term> of the Cambridge University Press for their permission to reprint the translation of the passages concerning the "Nature of the Winds" from the *Catalogue of the Drawings of Leonardo da Vinci at Windsor*.

I owe special thanks to the Librarian of the Royal Library for his kindness in allowing me to select as many illustrations as I wished from the matchless collection of Leonardo's drawings at Windsor. It is largely because of this generosity that both the picture plates and the text of this volume serve as a guide to the almost infinite variety of Leonardo’s interests. I am also very grateful to the authorities of the Department of Prints and Drawings at the British Museum for granting me similar access to their collection. Finally, my thanks go to the staff of the London Library for their many years of courtesy, and to Mr. A. C. Fifield and the indexer, Mr. John Crow, both of whom read my proofs <note>original: "proofs" — preliminary versions of the printed pages kept for correction.</note> and offered many helpful suggestions.

### INTRODUCTORY NOTE

October 10, 1517.
In one of the outlying parts [of Amboise], Monsignor <note>This refers to Cardinal Luis of Aragon, for whom the author served as secretary.</note> and the rest of us went to see Mr. Leonardo da Vinci <note>original: "Messer Lunardo Vinci"</note>, the Florentine. . . . This gentleman has written about anatomy in great detail, showing through illustrations the limbs, muscles, nerves, veins, ligaments, intestines, and whatever else there is to discuss in the bodies of men and women, in a way that has never yet been done by anyone else. All of this we have seen with our own eyes; and he said that he had dissected more than thirty bodies, both of men and women, of all ages. He has also written about the nature of water, various <note>original: "divers"</note> machines, and other matters, which he has recorded in an infinite number of volumes, all in the common language <note>original: "vulgar tongue" — meaning Italian, the language of the people, rather than the scholarly Latin.</note>. If these should be published, they will be useful and very enjoyable.

> (Excerpt from *The Journey of Cardinal Luis of Aragon through Germany, the
> Netherlands, France, and Northern Italy, 1517–1518*, written by Antonio de
> Beatis. Edited by Ludwig Pastor and published at Freiburg im Breisgau <note>A city in Germany.</note>, 1905.)

<summary>This page contains a contemporary account by Antonio de Beatis describing a visit to Leonardo da Vinci in 1517, highlighting Leonardo's extensive anatomical dissections and his numerous unpublished notebooks.</summary>
<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, Antonio de Beatis, anatomy, Amboise, Cardinal Luis of Aragon, notebooks, scientific observation, 16th century</keywords>

# PREFACE

## I

IN THE year 1906, with the audacity of youth, I ventured to apply a comprehensive title to what was actually a relatively small selection from the contents of *Leonardo da Vinci’s Notebooks*.¹ I have now attempted to fulfill the promise of my title with some degree of completeness. More than half a century ago, when the work of transcribing Leonardo’s manuscripts first began, a controversy arose among scholars as to whether the best method of publication was by individual manuscripts or collectively with an attempt at classification. Time has a way of proving most controversies pointless, and in this instance, it has shown that both sides were essentially right. The publication of the transcripts of the original manuscripts, along with facsimiles, has served as the foundation for all subsequent study. However, some classification of the material has been found necessary because of the extraordinary diversity of subjects treated within the same manuscript in the majority of cases. Leonardo himself admitted as much in a prefatory note to the manuscript now in the British Museum (Arundel 263), and the actions of Pompeo Leoni—who compiled the *Codice Atlantico* from other manuscripts using scissors and paste—have only made the confusion worse. I have therefore arranged the subject matter under various main headings, but beyond this I have made no change to the order; the passages in each section appear in the same sequence as they do in the manuscripts, with those from Milan coming first, followed by those in Paris, London, and Windsor. In the few cases, however, where all or substantially all of a manuscript falls within the same section, I have given it priority—for example, in 'Anatomy', 'Flight', 'Painting', and 'Optics'.

About a dozen pictures are all that can be attributed to Leonardo

---

¹ *Leonardo da Vinci's Notebooks*, Edward MacCurdy, M.A., crown 8 vo, 14 illustrations, pp. xiv, 289. London: Duckworth & Co., 1906.

--- Page 20 ---
with any degree of certainty or even probability, and the testimony of contemporary records, however credulously interpreted, does not do more than double or triple that number. How he occupied his time would be a mystery if not for the existence of the vast collection of drawings, and particularly of the notebooks. These number more than five thousand pages, the contents of which I have attempted to classify under some fifty headings. This classification is, as I know, rough and imperfect, which the almost infinite variety of the contents rendered nearly inevitable. For, of this man who produced a few works of art most divinely well, it may be said that he took all knowledge as his province, and that in his individual achievement he symbolizes the diversity of an era as fully as can be said of any man at any period in the world’s history. To one who has studied them intermittently for more than a quarter of a century, these manuscripts—the product of how many thousand hours of intellectual activity!—are the records of the working of perhaps the mightiest machine that has ever been a human brain: fragments of a larger purpose, charted, defined, and explored, but never fulfilled, of which the treatises containing the sum of his researches in anatomy, physiology, and geology form component parts—fragments of a vast encyclopedia of human knowledge.

What thinker has ever possessed the cosmic vision so persistently? He sought to establish the essential unity of structure in all living things: the earth as an organism with veins and arteries, and the body of a man as a model for that of the world. The perceptions of his brain are hardly, if at all, restricted by the limitations of time and place. At rare times, however, the personal note emerges, and moods of exultation or depression flash out their meaning in a phrase. The mood of the seer finds expression in fable or allegory, or in the series of ‘the Prophecies,’ revealing the depth of his biting humor and his power of analyzing the motives that guide human conduct, or in speculation regarding the results that would follow the possible extension of man’s power—in which time has confirmed his foresight and his foreboding.

The manuscripts are a nearly inexhaustible quarry in which the student of every phase of Leonardo’s mental activity will find material. They are of peculiar value for the biographer, both in their revelation of personality and in the manner in which they react on contemporary

--- Page 21 ---
record. Thus they tend to confirm Vasari in his more picturesque statements. He has told how Leonardo, when he passed the places where birds were sold, would often take them from their cages, pay the price demanded, and restore their liberty by letting them fly into the air. "The goldfinch," wrote Leonardo, "will carry spurge to its little ones imprisoned in a cage—death rather than loss of liberty." The meaning of the note becomes clear from the fact that certain varieties of the spurge form a violent poison. His account of how Leonardo collected lizards, hedgehogs, newts, serpents, and all sorts of strange creatures, and from these constructed the head of a hideous monster—when in his youth he received a commission to paint something on a shield which should cause terror to the beholder—is directly confirmed by the painter’s own instruction on "how to make an imaginary animal appear real." The method was that each part should have a basis in reality: for example, the body of a serpent, the head of a mastiff or setter, the eyes of a cat, the ears of a porcupine, the nose of a greyhound, the eyebrows of a lion, the temples of an old cock, and the neck of a turtle. So also with reference to Leonardo’s activities as master of pageants at the Court of Milan, the automatic lion which, according to Vasari, formed part of the pageant on the occasion of the entry of the French King—which advanced a few steps and opened its chest to show it filled with lilies—is drawn in different positions on a page of the Anatomy MSS. at Windsor.

The letters and fragments of letters are also of primary importance for the biographer. They express the whole range of emotions, from the proud confidence of the first letter to Ludovico and that to the Commissioners of the Cathedral of Piacenza, through the brief appeals of the later days in Milan when "the horse" was ready for casting and foreign subsidies had exhausted the Treasury, to those written in the depression of the Roman period, when his hopes of employment had been frustrated and he had been denounced to the Pope for his practice of anatomy, while his nerves were reacting helplessly to the misbehavior of an apprentice.

Of the real ultimate value of the results of Leonardo’s various scientific researches and investigations, I have no right to attempt to speak. They can be judged only by specialists, and whenever a section is reviewed in this way, the result from the time of Dr. William Hunter onwards has been to confirm the impression of their great worth, es-

--- Page 22 ---
establishing him as a thinker with very precise powers of analysis as well as a productive investigator whose work shows a firm grasp of the principles of experimental science. For example, among the anatomical investigations recorded in the Windsor Manuscripts is that of the spinal cord and intestines of the frog. ‘The frog,’ he says, ‘remains alive for several hours when the head, the heart, and all the intestines have been removed. And if you prick the said cord, it instantly twitches and dies’ (Quaderni V 21 r.). On the back of the same sheet is written: ‘the frog dies instantly when the spinal cord is pierced; and before this, it lived without a head, without a heart, or any bowels, intestines, or skin; and here, therefore, it would seem, lies the foundation of movement and life.’

The originality of his methods of anatomical investigation is illustrated by the details he provides regarding the making of wax casts in order to discover the true shape of the ventricles of the brain:
> ‘Make two air holes in the horns of the great ventricles and insert melted wax by means of a syringe, making a hole in the ventricle of the memoria; through this hole, fill the three ventricles of the brain. Afterwards, when the wax has set, remove the brain and you will see the shape of the three ventricles exactly. But first, insert thin tubes into the air holes so that the air within these ventricles may escape and thus make room for the wax entering the ventricles’ (Quaderni V 7 r.).

Leonardo, as the learned editors of the Quaderni d’Anatomia inform us, was the first to make casts of the cerebral ventricles, and several hundred years passed before the idea occurred to any other anatomist.

It is on the edge of this unexplored knowledge that his gift of expression often lingers and teases us with its beauty.
> ‘Every weight tends to fall toward the center by the shortest path’ (C 28 v.) is the core of Newton’s law of gravitation. ‘The earth is moved from its position by the weight of a tiny bird resting upon it. The surface of the sphere of water is moved by a tiny drop of water falling upon it’ (B.M. 19 r.). Is this also the language of mechanics?

In the section of his treatise on ‘Painting,’ in which he compares painting with the other arts, he has no divided loyalty; but in ‘the Prophecies,’ he has expressed his sense of the potential of literature, though somewhat cryptically: ‘Feathers

--- Page 23 ---
shall raise men toward heaven just as they do birds; that is, by letters written with their quills.’

Although disclaiming for himself any title to the rank of literary artist, he displays a remarkable power of clear expression, so that his language seems to mirror his thought exactly and his phrases captivate by their simplicity. This literary quality permeates his humor, which is occasionally brief and cutting, for example: ‘that venerable snail, the sun’; ‘Man has great power of speech, but the greater part of it is empty and deceitful. Animals have little, but that little is useful and true; and a small, certain thing is better than a great falsehood.’ The latter sentence might appropriately serve as a preface to ‘A Bestiary’ in Manuscript H, where it is stated that the great elephant possesses by nature qualities that rarely occur among men, namely integrity, prudence, and a sense of justice and religious observance. Perhaps something of the same mood can be discerned in the instruction that leather bags—intended to prevent an aviator from harming himself if he happens to fall from a height of six *braccia* onto water or land—should be tied in the manner of rosary beads; or when, after referring to the damage caused to great things by the firing of a cannon, he speaks of spiders’ webs being completely destroyed. So too, where under the heading ‘Of local movement of flexible dry things’ he discusses the movement of dust when a table is struck—of the dust that is separated into various small mounds, descending from the *hypotenuse* of these mounds, entering beneath their base and rising around the *axis* of the mound’s peak, moving in such a way as to look like a right-angled triangle. One finds oneself wondering when, if ever, the table was dusted, and reflecting on how much his powers of observation would have been limited by marriage.

I have not considered it necessary to transcribe the numerous pages of Latin declensions and conjugations or the various portions of a Latin-Italian glossary found in Manuscript H of the ‘Institut’. It has been suggested that they were compiled for the instruction of Maximilian and Francesco Sforza, who were born in January 1493 and February 1495, and whose features are familiar as they kneel in chubby complacency in the Zenale altar-piece in the Brera; the elder of whom is the boy seen sitting and reading Cicero in the fascinating fresco by a Milanese painter now in the Wallace Collection. It is some-

<header>PREFACE</header>

## PREFACE

It is somewhat <note>The OCR "what" likely replaces "somewhat."</note> difficult to imagine Leonardo in the role of a private tutor to the Sforza princes <note>The Sforza family was the ruling dynasty of Milan; Leonardo worked for Duke Ludovico Sforza for many years.</note> even though he performed various functions at the court. However, it is quite possible that these lists—though written in his usual "left-handed writing" <note>This refers to Leonardo's famous mirror-image writing, which he wrote from right to left.</note>—were compiled for the purpose of teaching. The fact that his allegories about animals (which are mostly compiled from Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author of a massive natural history encyclopedia.</note> and medieval bestiaries <note>term: bestiaries; medieval books describing various real and mythical animals, often with moral lessons.</note>) are also found in Manuscript H suggests a possibility: if the Latin grammar and glossary were written for the instruction of the Sforza princes, then Leonardo’s book of beasts may have been put together for their education as a sort of "antidote." In this way, the harshness of learning Latin grammar could be varied by such rare and refreshing fruit as the story of the *amphisbaena*—a four-footed beast that resembled the "Pushmipullyou" of Hugh Lofting’s *Dolittle* books in having a head at each end. However, unlike the creature in the modern story, both heads of the *amphisbaena* discharged poison. Leonardo’s imagination is perhaps seen in its most complete freedom in a fragment of a fantastic tale written in the form of letters in the *Codice Atlantico* <note>original: "Codice Atlantico"; The Atlantic Codex, a twelve-volume set of Leonardo's drawings and writings.</note>. The giant described there is of such stature that when he shook his head, he dislodged showers of men who were clinging to his hairs—a fantasy curiously suggestive of the actions of *Gulliver in Lilliput*.

The problem of how to interpret the letters claiming to be written from Armenia has been a long-debated <note>original: "vexed"</note> question ever since Dr. Jean Paul Richter first made their existence known. The evidence, I think, tends to confirm the view that they are a record of fact and that Leonardo was indeed in the East for a time. I do not believe this interpretation is made impossible—as Dr. Verga seems to suggest—by the fact that Leonardo used the classical naming system <note>original: "nomenclature"</note> of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, an ancient Greek-Roman geographer and astronomer whose works were rediscovered in the Renaissance.</note> in these letters. The references to books found in Leonardo’s manuscripts show that he was in the habit of studying all available classical and medieval authorities on the subjects that interested him. Ptolemy was one of the primary sources he used to satisfy his curiosity regarding the distant and dimly recorded places and peoples of the earth. Pliny, Strabo <note>An ancient Greek geographer.</note>, and even Sir John Mandeville <note>The supposed author of a famous, though largely fictional, book of travels.</note> also appear in his list of sources. Ptolemy's system of naming supplied the terms Leonardo would have inevitably used to express his first ideas of distant places. The same consideration must certainly have influenced the minds of many contemporary travelers. Geography was one of the sciences in which the knowledge of classical literature may be said to...

<summary>The author discusses Leonardo’s potential role as a tutor for the Sforza family, his creative writing about giants and mythical beasts, and the scholarly debate over whether Leonardo actually traveled to Armenia.</summary>
<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, Sforza family, bestiaries, mirror writing, Codice Atlantico, Armenia travel controversy, Ptolemy, geography</keywords>

--- Page 25 ---
have lain like a dead hand. Leonardo’s debt to Ptolemy was great. In a passage in his treatise on anatomy in which he described how his system of dissection of the various parts of man is to be so coordinated that the result may reveal the structure or mechanism of the whole body, he pays a tribute to Ptolemy as a master of systematic arrangement whom he is proud to follow: ‘therefore there shall be revealed to you here in fifteen entire figures the cosmography of the “minor mondo” [the Microcosmos or ‘lesser world’] in the same order as was used by Ptolemy before me in his cosmography’. Might his debt to Ptolemy not have been much the same in the one case as in the other—in the one the arrangement, in the other the naming of places, and perhaps the initial interest in those locations?

The manuscripts are the repository of much practical wisdom designed to improve the social interactions of life and revealing itself in various unexpected ways. A social reformer might profitably stand by the precept: ‘Let the street be as wide as the average height of the houses’. The evils of absentee landlordism and those resulting from the accumulation of huge estates—‘field added to field, so that they may be placed alone in the middle of the earth’—are both warded off in the sentence, ‘Happy is that estate which is seen by the eye of its lord’. Riches had lost some of their chief attractions for the man who could write this: ‘Small rooms or dwellings set the mind on the right path, large ones cause it to go astray’; and, ‘Wine is good but water is preferable at the table’.

The golden mean in all things—failing this, renunciation. ‘You must do without, you must do without.’ ‘Neither promise yourself things nor do things’, he wrote, ‘if you see that when deprived of them they will cause you physical suffering’. The sentence serves to recall a remark once made by Dr. Jowett on the subject of smoking: ‘Do not create for yourself any new necessities’.

This practical sense is always noticeable when he is discussing the subject of art. In his ‘Botany for Painters’ he pauses while defining the laws of branch structure to address the painter who, as he recognizes, is bound to be unfamiliar with these laws, and to assure him that he may escape the criticism of those who have studied them if he is eager to represent everything according to Nature. So also in discussing the flight of birds (C.A. 214 r. a) he turns for a parallel to the movement of the fish’s tail; and this, he says, may be proved with a pair

of oars. When describing the variation in a bird’s weight as it spreads its wings or pulls them in (E 43 v.), he adds, "and the butterflies experiment with this during their descents." At times, however, the operation of this practical sense is overshadowed by his insistence on fundamental laws. For example: "To provide the exact science of the movement of birds in the air, it is first necessary to provide the science of the winds, which we shall prove through the movements of water. This science is itself observable through the senses; it will serve as a ladder to reach the knowledge of flying things in the air and the wind" (E 54 r.).

His anatomical drawings, along with his studies for paintings, provide examples of his incredibly close and exact powers of observation. The lines seem to possess the spontaneity and inevitability of life itself. This same power, when translated into words, is visible in his descriptions of Nature in her changing moods. These descriptions have the effect of studies taken with a camera at close range. For example, he speaks of:
* The waves made by the wind in May running over cornfields without the ears of corn moving from their place; 
* Reeds that are scarcely visible in the light but stand out clearly between light and shade (L 87 r.); 
* Waves that intersect like the scales of a fir cone, reflecting the image of the sun with the greatest brilliance because the radiance of so many reflections is blended together (B.M. 25 r.); 
* Water hitting a larger waterfall and turning like the wheel of a mill (F 81 r.). 

A statement in the <term>Leicester Manuscript</term> <note>original: "Codex Leicester"; a collection of scientific writings by Leonardo</note> (13 r.) describes the surface of tiny, shadowed waves shaping themselves into lines that meet at an angle, as if formed by sand; he notes this as proof of the water's shallowness. This could serve as an exact description of the waves in Botticelli’s *Birth of Venus*, as well as in some of his illustrations for Dante. 

Botticelli—who frequented Verrocchio’s studio <note>Andrea del Verrocchio was a leading Florentine sculptor and painter who taught both Leonardo and Botticelli</note> when Leonardo was an apprentice there—is the only one of his Florentine contemporaries whose work Leonardo cited in his writings on art. While Leonardo's teaching might help interpret Botticelli’s methods, it also bridges the nearly bottomless gap where the followers of classicism gather, anticipating the free composition and subtle atmospheric effects of the later period of naturalism. His rule that the mind should seek inspiration for various inventions by looking at the patterns of different stains on a wall suggests the greatest

The most delicate, fleeting effects of Anton Mauve, or of Courbet at the time when he painted his ‘Duck Shooter’, are brought before us by such a sentence as the following: ‘No opaque body is without shadow or light except where there is a mist lying over the ground when it is covered with snow, or it will be the same when it snows in the country’ (Quaderni II 6 r.).

Similarly, the spirit of Whistler’s creations is evoked in the directions under the heading, ‘How to represent white figures’ (MS. 2038 Bib. Nat. 20 r.); and Turner’s most characteristic effects are recalled by the ethereal simplicity and directness of Leonardo’s description of the phenomena of sunrise:

> ‘At the first hour of the day, the atmosphere in the south near the horizon has a dim haze of rose-flushed clouds; towards the west it grows darker, and towards the east the damp vapor of the horizon appears brighter than the actual horizon itself, and the white of the houses in the east is scarcely to be discerned; while in the south, the farther distant they are, the more they assume a dark rose-flushed hue, and even more so in the west; and with the shadows it is the opposite, for these disappear before the white’ (C.A. 176 r. b.).

Who, having witnessed the sequence of the effects of sunrise from the vantage point afforded by a hilltop, can doubt Leonardo’s description to be a record of what he had actually seen?

‘Pre-imagining—the imagining of things that are to be. Post-imagining—the imagining of things that are past.’ So, in a passage in the Windsor Manuscripts, Leonardo defines with singular grace two fields of thought over which his spirit ranged with a freedom limited only by the necessity of interpreting natural phenomena. The Leicester Manuscript contains the sum of his researches in the natural history of the earth; in the records that time has written in the rocks and the high deposits of the mountain ranges, of the period when, as he says, ‘above the plains of Italy where now birds fly in flocks, fishes were accustomed to wander in large shoals.’ ‘Sufficient for us,’ he states, ‘is the testimony of things produced in the salt waters and now found again in the high mountains far from the seas.’ Elsewhere in the same manuscript, he refers to the discovery of a prehistoric ship found during the digging of a well on the country estate of one of Ludovic Sforza’s retinue, and the decision taken to change the position of the well in

...order to leave it intact. In a passage in the <term>Arundel Manuscript</term> <note>A collection of Leonardo’s notes now held in the British Library.</note>, he addresses—as if it were a once-living instrument of nature’s creative power—the form of a great fish. Its bones, now stripped and bare as it lies in a winding hollow of the hills in <term>Lombardy</term> <note>A region in northern Italy.</note>, have become like a protective armor and support for the mountain that rests above it. These lines seem filled with the same kind of awe that must have inspired the first scientist in the <term>Dordogne</term> region when a lucky chance led him to enter the prehistoric caves of <term>Les Eyzies</term>.

However, it is in the realm of "pre-imagining"—the "imagining of things that are to be"—that the manuscripts reveal his creative thought most impressively. It is almost unbelievable that a single mind could anticipate the growth of knowledge in such diverse areas as the circulation of the blood, the theory that the earth revolves around the sun (heliocentrism), the law of inertia, and the *<term>dark chamber</term>* <note>original: "camera obscura"; an optical device that led to the invention of photography.</note>, yet the evidence for it exists.

In a fragment of a torn letter apparently written to <term>Ludovic Sforza</term> <note>Also known as Ludovico "Il Moro," the Duke of Milan and Leonardo’s patron.</note> during the troubled later years of his rule in <term>Milan</term>, <term>Leonardo</term> reveals how disastrous the demands of the time were for him as an artist. The same could be said for the conditions across Europe during much of the <term>Great War</term> <note>The common name for World War I (1914–1918).</note>: the arts were silenced, and altarpieces and frescoes were hidden in bomb-proof shelters or protected with sandbags. Amidst this silence, however, <term>Leonardo</term> was a unique exception among the great names of art. In war as in peace, the course of events proved what the historian <term>Sirèn</term> once said: "no one can be indifferent to Leonardo." All the most characteristic developments of the <term>Great War</term>—those that distinguished it from all previous wars—the use of the bombing airplane, poison gas, the tank, and the submarine—all provide examples of his foresight. He predicted the construction of each, not with the cryptic words of a prophet, but with the scientific and mechanical precision natural to someone who served as a military engineer. He held this office in the <term>Romagna</term> region under <term>Caesar Borgia</term> during Borgia’s brief time in power, and he had offered his services in a similar role to <term>Ludovic Sforza</term>. It may seem like a mystery that such inventions came from the brain of a man who condemned warfare as "most bestial madness" <note>original: "bestialissima pazzia"</note>. The clue to solving this mystery, however, is found in a passage in one of the...

# PREFACE

Leonardo’s manuscripts in the <term>Bibliothèque Nationale</term> <note>The National Library of France in Paris.</note> (Manuscript 2037, folio 10 r.) contain references to the difference between offensive and defensive warfare. In these notes, he emphasizes that preparing for war is a necessary safeguard for everything that life holds most dear: "When besieged by ambitious tyrants, I find a means of offense and defense in order to preserve the chief gift of Nature, which is liberty." He continues by speaking first about the positioning of walls and then about how a people may support and maintain their good and just lords.

He also envisioned the scientific possibilities of using poison gas in naval warfare. He provided a formula for its creation and described how a mask could be made to act as a preventative measure. It is impossible to lightly assume that Leonardo—who wrote, "It is an infinitely atrocious thing to take away the life of a man"—would have regarded the use of poison gas against a civilian population as permissible under any circumstances.

The prototype of the tank or armored car appears in one of Leonardo’s drawings in the <term>British Museum</term>. He thus foreshadowed its use in breaking through enemy lines: "These take the place of elephants. One may <term>tilt</term> <note>original: "tilt"; to charge or joust in combat.</note> with them. One may hold bellows in them to spread terror among the horses of the enemy, and one may put <term>carabiniers</term> <note>Soldiers armed with carbines, a type of short-barreled firearm.</note> in them to break up every company" (Manuscript B, folio 83 v.).

In this, as in his attempts to construct a flying machine, he was hampered by a lack of knowledge regarding a suitable power source for propelling such a device. He studied the laws of flight and the conditions under which it existed in Nature with inexhaustible zeal; his scientific deductions from these studies go far toward creating the model for the modern airplane. He thought of flight as humanity's natural entry into a long-awaited inheritance of the air. Apparently, he did not foresee that human nature was such that these wings would inevitably become the wings of war. Had he envisioned that the extension of human power would enable people to rain death from the skies, his attitude might conceivably have been like that of the artist in <term>Samuel Johnson’s</term> *Rasselas* <note>An apologue (moral fable) written in 1759.</note>. In that story, it is related that an artist, having mastered the art of flying by inventing wings modeled on those of a bat, refused to reveal his secret. "If men were all virtuous," he said, "I should with great <term>alacrity</term> <note>Eagerness or cheerful readiness.</note> teach them all to fly. But what would be the security of the good, if the bad could at will invade them from the sky? Against an enemy sailing through..."

the clouds, neither walls nor mountains and seas could afford any security. A flight of northern savages might hover in the wind and land at once with irresistible violence upon the capital of a fruitful region that was rolling beneath them. Even this [the Amharic] valley, the retreat of princes . . . might be violated.’

The conjecture that such would in fact have been Leonardo’s attitude is further strengthened by the nature of his remarks on the subject of the unrestricted use of the submarine. The passage in the *Leicester Manuscript* (22 v.) is as follows:

‘How by an appliance many are able to remain for some time under water. How and why I do not describe my method of remaining under water for as long a time as I can remain without food; and this I do not publish or divulge, on account of the evil nature of men, who would carry out assassinations at the bottom of the seas by breaking the ships in their lowest parts and sinking them together with the crews who are in them.’

‘To preserve the chief gift of Nature, which is liberty’—this, if not the motive underlying all his study of mechanisms of warfare, was undoubtedly a controlling factor; for in the world as he envisioned it, there is sovereign liberty for the individual to think and devise.

As the long labor of preparation of this edition of Leonardo’s writings draws to an end, a letter comes to me from the United States telling me of the fact that the Faculty of Princeton University has drawn up a list of ten names of men of all time who have done most to advance human knowledge. The names are: Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Galileo, Leonardo, Pasteur, Shakespeare, Newton, Darwin, and Einstein. No such list is ever likely to win general agreement, for the lack of a common standard of values. It may at any rate be claimed for this one that each name is cut deep in the rock of achievement. In thinking of some of the names, the strange prescience which has caused Leonardo to be styled ‘the forerunner’ recurs inevitably to the mind. Just as, independently of the researches of Galileo, he wrote ‘the sun does not move,’ so he enunciated the root principle of Newton’s law of gravitation in the words: ‘every weight tends to fall towards the center by the shortest way’; so also in several passages, the nature of which is indicated by such a sentence as the following: ‘write of the quality of time as distinct from its mathematical divisions,’ he would seem to have been pointing

--- Page 31 ---
along the road which in our own times has been traveled by Einstein.

Where his energy shows itself most inexhaustible is in the investigation of the working of the elemental forces, as in the sections, ‘Movement and Weight’ and ‘Water’. Just as water may be seen winding in wonder-working coils through his landscape backgrounds, so with infinite zeal he set himself to study how the elements are situated one within the other, why water moves and why its motion ceases, how it rises into the air through the heat of the sun, and afterwards falls as rain: the artist’s love of beauty transforming the scientist’s purpose even while he is in the act of wresting underlying principles from its infinite variety.

Certain results of these investigations formed that volume on ‘The Nature of Water’ which was one of those seen in the manor house at Cloux near Amboise, where Leonardo passed the last three years of his life, and where in October 1517 he was visited by a Cardinal of Aragon and his retinue. To the fortunate circumstance of the Cardinal’s secretary Antonio de Beatis having kept a diary in which he set down particulars of the visit, we owe our knowledge of the fact that the Leonardo manuscripts there formed ‘an infinite number of volumes . . . which if they should be published will be profitable and very enjoyable’.

## II

THE early biographers of Leonardo da Vinci cultivated the picturesque with an almost poetic license. Their narratives, which together constitute what Pater has termed the *légende*, are as inadequate to reveal his work and personality as the fables of Vulcan’s forge and the like are unsatisfying as an origin for Etna’s fire. Moreover, in the different aspects which Etna has assumed to the imagination—seeming at first a caprice of the gods and a thing of rhapsody, and subsequently (as the direction of thought changed) a field for the scientific study of the forces of Nature—there is presented a contrast no less sharply defined, and in its main features somewhat closely corresponding to that presented by the personality of Leonardo as shown in the earliest biographies and in the light of modern research. For the capricious, volatile prodigy of youthful genius which the *légende* has bequeathed, the latter has substituted a figure less romantic, less alluringly inexplicable, but of even

--- Page 32 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo da Vinci’s transition from artistic practice to scientific inquiry, picking up from the description of how his perception changed from a "caprice of the gods" to a field for rigorous study.</meta>

# PREFACE

...more varied and astonishing gifts. His greatness as an artist has remained unchanged, but modern research has revealed the methodical effort that led to his achievements. It has shown how he studied the anatomy of the human body, horses, rocks, and trees, so that he could better paint and sculpt. By doing so, his work was based on things he truly understood; no muscle or leaf would be a mere cliché, but instead drawn directly from the riches of nature. He believed the artist should be "the son, not the grandson, of Nature."

This habit of scientific investigation, which began as a secondary aid to his art, grew to dominate his work so much that it gradually drew him away from artistic practice and toward the study of scientific laws—not just those of art, but those governing all of nature. The results of these studies remained hidden in manuscripts whose contents have only been fully understood within the last fifty years. Through a strange appropriateness, he is associated in every era with the primary interests of that time. His versatility in the arts made him seem like the personification of the Renaissance spirit. As a painter, sculptor, architect, engineer, and musician, he inspired wonder and admiration in those who lived during his time. 

But to his contemporaries, his studies across all of nature—which anticipated the future direction of the Renaissance—were so poorly understood that they seemed like mere trifles, <term>whims</term> <note>original: 'ghiribizzi'</note>, to be mentioned apologetically, if mentioned at all, as evidence of the unpredictable nature of genius. They often expressed regret for the time he "wasted" on science that could have been spent on painting. Modern scholars <note>original: 'savants'</note> have decoded these trifles and, in doing so, have assessed the value of Leonardo’s discoveries and observations in the field of exact science. They have hailed him as one of the greatest scholars—not because his efforts reached completion in his lifetime, but because he anticipated and predicted what the progress of science would establish centuries later. Furthermore, these predictions were not based on fantasy but were the result of a lifetime spent studying natural phenomena and closely analyzing their laws. Anatomist, mathematician, chemist, geologist, botanist, astronomer, and geographer—the use of each of these titles is fully justified by the contents of his manuscripts now held in Milan, Paris, Windsor, and London.

To correctly judge the value of his research across these various scientific fields would require an almost encyclopedic breadth of knowledge.

It highlights his philosophy that art should be rooted in a deep, direct understanding of nature's laws.</summary>
<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, Renaissance, scientific method, manuscripts, ghiribizzi, anatomy, natural philosophy, history of science</keywords>

<header>PREFACE</header>

Regarding these matters, Leonardo himself, through his manuscripts, should be considered his own best biographer, despite the mysterious shortness of some of his notes and conclusions. We cannot claim that he was the original discoverer of every principle he anticipated, many of which were only formally proven later. The records of Milan's intellectual life under the Sforza family <note>The ruling family of Milan during Leonardo's time.</note> are so incomplete—having been lost during the many invasions that later struck the city—that it is almost impossible to be certain on this point. However, we must acknowledge the influence of his interactions with other scholars working in similar fields of research. 

We are told that, later in his life, he was friends with Marc Antonio della Torre, the Professor of Anatomy at the University of Pavia, and that they helped each other with their research. He was also a friend of the mathematician Fra Luca Pacioli and drew the diagrams for Pacioli's book, *On the Divine Proportion* <note>original: "De Divina Proportione"</note>. The two were companions for some time during the autumn and winter of 1499 after fleeing Milan together during the French invasion. Many notes throughout his manuscripts show that he was tireless in his search for knowledge. He sought information from every possible source, whether by borrowing books and essays or by reaching out to other people interested in the same subjects. 

He learned nothing from the astrologers found at the court of Ludovico Sforza—such as Ambrogio da Rosate and others. He considered their supposed "wisdom" to be as worthless as that of alchemists or those searching for <term>perpetual motion</term> <note>The impossible idea of a machine that runs forever without an energy source.</note>. His study of the stars and planets was completely different from theirs, both in how he did it and what he hoped to find. His scientific instruments were remarkably advanced, sometimes even appearing modern in their design. A line in his collection of drawings and writings known as the *Atlantic Codex* <note>original: "Codice Atlantico"</note>, "make glasses to see the moon large" <note>original: "fa occhiali da vedere la luna grande"</note>, refers, however, only to the use of magnifying lenses; the invention of the telescope did not actually happen until the next century.

At the beginning of the 1500s, almost everyone still believed in the <term>Ptolemaic theory</term> <note>An ancient Greek theory stating that the Earth is the stationary center of the universe.</note>. Leonardo initially accepted this view; in his early writings, he described the Earth as stationary, with the sun and moon orbiting around it. However, his thinking eventually progressed further toward modern scientific discovery. On a page of mathematical notes currently held at Windsor Castle, he wrote in large letters: "The sun does not move" <note>original: "il sole no si muove"</note>.

<summary>This page explores Leonardo da Vinci's scientific collaborations and his rejection of pseudo-sciences like astrology in favor of empirical observation. It highlights his transition from believing the Earth was the center of the universe to realizing the sun's stationary position.</summary>

<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, Milan, Sforza, Marc Antonio della Torre, Fra Luca Pacioli, On the Divine Proportion, astrology, Atlantic Codex, Ptolemaic theory, astronomy, heliocentrism</keywords>

--- Page 34 ---
He has been described as the forerunner of Francis Bacon, James Watt, Sir Isaac Newton, and William Harvey. It cannot be said that he anticipated the specific discoveries associated with their names. It may, however, be claimed that he anticipated the methods of investigation which, when followed to their logical conclusion, could not help but lead to these discoveries.

The great anatomist Vesalius, after giving up his Chair of Anatomy in 1561 to become the court physician at Madrid, spoke of himself as still looking forward to studying ‘that true bible, as we consider it, of the human body and of the nature of man.’ Sir Michael Foster takes these words as the keynote of Vesalius’s life’s work: ‘the true bible to read is nature itself, things as they are, not the printed pages of Galen or anyone else; science comes from observation, not from authority.’ In his method, Leonardo was the forerunner of Vesalius, and consequently of William Harvey, whose great work was the result of Vesalius’s teaching. No passage in his writings constitutes an anticipation of Harvey’s discovery. He knew that the blood moved, just as he also knew that the sun did not move, but the law of the circulation of the blood was as far beyond the stage his deductions had reached as was the discovery of Copernicus. It was his work to establish, even before the birth of Vesalius, that ‘science comes from observation, not from authority.’ Yet he was no mere amateur. He knew the authorities. He quotes in his manuscripts from Mundinus’s *Anatomia*, and he must have known the work of Galen, for which Mundinus served as an introduction. At a time when the Church ‘taught the sacredness of the human corpse, and was ready to punish as a sacrilege the use of the anatomist’s scalpel,’ Leonardo practiced dissection; and he suffered as a result of his boldness, since it was after the malicious reporting of these experiments that the withdrawal of papal favor led to his departure from Rome in 1515. The anatomical drawings are a rich harvest of such boldness. The cloak of authority was cast aside; the primary need was for actual investigation, and these drawings are a record of it. He would agree, he says, that it would be better for the student to watch an anatomical demonstration than to see his drawings, ‘if only it were possible to observe all the details shown in these drawings in a single body; in which, with all your ability, you will not see or acquire a knowledge of more than—

--- Page 35 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo da Vinci’s anatomical studies, following the mention of his departure from Rome in 1515 due to his dissections of human corpses.</meta>

<page-num>29</page-num>

-># PREFACE<-

"...some few veins. Meanwhile, in order to obtain an exact and complete knowledge of these, I have dissected more than ten human bodies. In the process, I destroyed all the various members and removed even the very smallest particles of the flesh surrounding these veins, without causing any bleeding <note>original: "effusion of blood"</note> other than the imperceptible leakage of the capillary veins."

After examining these drawings, the great anatomist Dr. William Hunter wrote that he was fully of the opinion that "Leonardo was the best anatomist in the world at that time."

Samuel Taylor Coleridge called Shakespeare "myriad-minded" <note>meaning a mind capable of infinite variety and vast range</note>. If the Baconian contention <note>the theory that Francis Bacon was the true author of Shakespeare's plays</note> were ever proven, the result would offer a parallel to the "myriad-mindedness" of Leonardo. Giovanni Morelli speaks of him as "perhaps the most richly gifted by nature among all the sons of men." Equally emphatic is the tribute of King Francis I, as recorded by Benvenuto Cellini: "He did not believe that any other man had come into the world who had attained such great knowledge as Leonardo; and that was not only as a sculptor, painter, and architect, but beyond that, he was a profound philosopher."

Regarding this undefined, uncollected knowledge, the tone of early biographers is one of pure wonder. To us, his personality seems to outspan the limits of his age and project itself into modern times through its sheer vitality, taking its place among the intuitive influences of modern thought. To those early biographers, however, his personality seemed to stretch back into the age of legend, gathering a sense of mystery and carefree grace <note>original: "insouciance"</note>. Leonardo was a figure whose physical beauty could never be praised enough. He wandered through the courts of princes, improvising songs and carrying a lute as a gift from one patron to another. He played the instrument with such skill that his music alone—out of all the arts he mastered—would have been a "magic key" <note>original: "open sesame"</note> to win him a welcome. Indeed, he seems more like a resident of Provence at the end of the twelfth century <note>a reference to the era of the troubadours, or traveling poet-musicians</note> than a contemporary and fellow citizen of the political strategist Machiavelli and the preacher Savonarola. 

Instead of the typical period of long, difficult apprenticeship we expect from Giorgio Vasari’s biographies, Leonardo seems to have possessed a "Pallas-like maturity" <note>referring to the goddess Pallas Athena, who was born fully grown and armored from the head of Zeus</note> at birth. According to legend, the angel he painted while still an apprentice caused his master <note>Andrea del Verrocchio</note> to give up his brush in shame that a mere child had surpassed him. In the same way, we are told that a monster he painted on a shield filled his own father with terror. Unsatisfied with this mastery...

<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, William Hunter, Coleridge, Francis I, anatomy, dissection, myriad-minded, Pallas Athena, Vasari, Verrocchio</keywords>

--- Page 36 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo da Vinci’s reputation among early biographers and his transition from an artist to a philosopher-scientist.</meta>

<page-num>30</page-num>

-># PREFACE<-

He sought to understand the secrets <note>original: "arcana"</note> of Nature through the arts, and a mere biographer could not say where that quest had led him. However, various hints—more expressive than words and harder to disprove—help us to theorize. Leonardo’s mocking references to the supposed wisdom of alchemists, astrologers, and sorcerers <note>original: "necromancers"</note> remained hidden in his manuscripts at that time, and were not available to contradict such assumptions.

The personality described in early biographies is essentially what Jules Michelet expressed in the phrase, "Leonardo, this Italian brother of Faust" <note>original French: "Léonard, ce frère italien de Faust"</note>. It tells us that he chose to know rather than to be, and that curiosity led him through forbidden doors. This represents, in fact, the popular medieval conception of scientific study. Much of modern artistic appreciation is essentially a milder restatement of this same viewpoint. While critical research from the time of Carlo Amoretti onward has corrected some errors, the general outlook remains the same as that of Giorgio Vasari and the Anonymous Florentine <note>original: "Anonimo Fiorentino," an unidentified 16th-century author of a manuscript on Florentine artists</note>. John Ruskin’s claim—that Leonardo "degraded his better instincts through caricature and remained until the end of his life a slave to an archaic smile" <note>the "archaic smile" refers to a specific, stylized expression found in early Greek sculpture, which Ruskin felt Leonardo obsessively repeated</note>—agrees with the opinion of the people of Wittenberg, who mourned Faust’s use of the unholy arts that had made him the lover of Helen of Troy. The true comparison, however, lies not with Faust but with Johann Wolfgang von Goethe. There is perhaps as great a psychological similarity between Leonardo and Goethe as has ever existed between two men of supreme genius.

In both men, the purely artistic and creative abilities became secondary, mastered by the clarity <note>original: "sanity"</note> of their philosophical minds.

In both alike, the restless workings of the human spirit desiring to *know* ranged over various mediums of artistic expression, shaped them for its own uses, and finally moved on. They looked beyond art to the thought itself, dissatisfied with what—even at its most perfect—was only a faint reflection of the natural world <note>original: "phenomena"</note> they wished to observe. The two parts of Goethe’s *Faust* symbolize this gradual change of purpose and may perhaps serve to represent Leonardo’s two spheres of activity. Verrocchio’s workshop <note>original: "bottega"</note> and all the influences of the 15th-century <note>original: "Quattrocento"</note> Florentine art world provided his mentorship and training, just as the medieval folk legends <note>original: "chap-book legends"</note> and the newly arisen literature of the Romantic School did for the poet of Weimar <note>Goethe</note>. The result in each case was clear, serene, and majestic, for the elements which had gone to the—

making it had been fused and melted in the fiery heat of genius. Yet the man behind the artist remains unsatisfied. He never shares in the artist’s achievement with the same degree of absorption that characterized Raphael and Giovanni Bellini. He possesses something of the detachment of Faust. There is something within him that art’s appeal to the senses never sparked into life, and never compelled to speak to any of its moments the ultimate password of Hedonism: "Stay, you are so beautiful." All the attractions of the medieval folk legend were revealed in the first part of the Faust drama; then, since this plea remained unspoken, the thinker attempts the problem. There are no well-worn paths as before in this new method of approach. There is no clear transparency of organized effort. Titanic energy struggles painfully amid the chaos of dimly perceived primeval forces. The result—and even the effort itself—according to much critical opinion, was an artistic mistake.

The same judgment was passed on Leonardo’s work as a philosopher and scientist by his earliest biographers. Yet in each case, the thinker is closer to the truth. Faust is redeemed from the hell of medieval tradition through the service of humanity. It was the restrictive chain of medieval tradition upon thought that Leonardo labored to unbind. It was his goal to expand the limits of man’s knowledge of himself, of his physical structure, of his surroundings, of all the forms of life around him, of the way the earth and sea were built, and of the stars in the heavens. To this end, he labored at the patient explanation of natural things, steadily and with proud confidence of purpose. "I wish," he says, "to work miracles: I may have fewer possessions than other men who are more peaceful, and than those who wish to grow rich in a day."

Incomplete and relatively unproductive as his investigation of natural phenomena was, it was nevertheless actual investigation, and it achieved results.

We may cite as an example the passages in the manuscript formerly at Holkham Hall, in which the fact that fossil shells are found in the higher mountain ridges of Lombardy is used through a process of deductive reasoning to show how the waters once covered the earth. He counters the hypothetical argument that the presence of these shells should be attributed to the Great Flood by considering the speed of the cockle’s progress. It is a creature that possesses no faster power of movement when out of

--- Page 40 ---
water than the snail. It cannot swim, but makes a furrow in the sand by means of its sides, and travels in this furrow a distance of three to four braccia daily; by such a method of progression, it could not have traveled in forty days from the Adriatic to Monferrato in Lombardy, a distance of two hundred and fifty miles. Neither is it a case of dead shells having been carried there by the force of the waves, for the living ones are recognizable by the shells being in pairs. Many other passages in the manuscripts might be cited to show by what varied paths he anticipated the modern methods of scientific investigation. The words which Pater uses of the Renaissance of the fifteenth century—"in many things great rather by what it designed or aspired to do than by what it actually achieved"—applicable to Leonardo in respect to his work as an artist, are not a bit less applicable in reference to his work in science. Painting and sculpture filled only two of the facets of a mind which, like a crystal, took the light from whatever direction light came. However, just as it was in these arts that he accomplished most, so those of his writings that treat of them are on the whole the most practical. In science, for the most part, he heralded the work of others; in respect to his writings on art, we may apply to him the words which Dürer uses of himself in a similar connection: "what he set down with the pen he did with the hand." It is this very factor of experience working in the mind which at times causes an abrupt contrast in the transition from the general principle to the discussion of the means by which it should be realized. His work may perhaps be considered to lose some of its literary value as a result, but it acquires an almost unique interest among treatises on art through its combination of the two standpoints of theory and practice. Of this, one of the most striking instances occurs in a passage which is only to be found in the revision of the treatise on "Painting" in the Vatican (Ludwig, chapter 180). Leonardo there sums up, concisely and profoundly, what should be the painter’s purpose: "a good painter has two chief objects to paint: man and the intention of his soul; the former is easy, the latter hard"; after which follows the eminently reasonable, if perhaps unexpected, explanation, "because he has to represent it by the attitudes and movements of the limbs"; and the knowledge of these, he proceeds to say, should be acquired by observing the mute, because their movements are more natural than those of any other class of persons. This very practical direction on how to

--- Page 41 ---
approach towards the realization of an apparently abstract aim is entirely characteristic of his intention. The supreme misfortune, he says, is when theory outstrips performance. This essential practicality of mind brought about the result that in the more abstract portions of this branch of his writings, his passion for first principles is most apparent. The sun, the origin of light and shade, is recognized as the first artist, and we are told that "the first picture consisted merely of a line which surrounded the shadow of a man cast by the sun upon a wall"; and the comparison of poetry and painting resolves itself into a consideration of the relative importance of the senses to which the two arts appeal.

It is perhaps in the passages indicating the manner in which particular scenes and actions should be represented in art that Leonardo’s powers as a writer find their most impressive expression. His natural inclination impelled him toward the contemplation of the vast and awe-inspiring in Nature; but in these terse, vivid, and analytical descriptions, the consideration of the ultimate purpose operates throughout to restrain and coordinate his thoughts. The descriptive passage titled "The way to represent a battle," in which the effect is built up entirely through fidelity to detail, constitutes an absolute triumph of realism. There can be no possibility of a difference of opinion regarding how Leonardo viewed warfare. It was a grim necessity, and he was himself busy on occasions designing its instruments; but he had no illusions as to its real nature, characterizing it elsewhere as "most bestial madness" (*bestialissima pazzia*). Here, however, he never allows his pen to digress from the work of simple description. To generalize would be alien to his purpose, which is to show how to portray a battle in progress. Consequently, he shows what is actually happening amid the clouds of dust and smoke and the rain of gunshot and falling arrows; he describes tersely, graphically, and relentlessly the passions and agonies of the combatants as shown in their faces and their actions, the bitterness of the deaths of the vanquished, the fury and exhaustion of the victors, and the mad terror of the horses, since these should find a place in the work of anyone who would represent war; "and see to it," he says in conclusion, "that you make no level spot of ground that is not trampled over with blood." The passage enables us in part to realize what he set himself to represent in the painting of the Battle of Anghiari. It is, however, far more

--- Page 42 ---
than a mere note for a picture. It possesses an interest and value apart either from this fact or from the mastery in the art of writing which it reveals. Its ultimate value is moral and educational. He refrains from generalizing but compels the reader to do so in his place. His description is of the same spirit that has animated the creations of Tolstoy and Verestchagin. Like them, Leonardo seeks to make war impossible by showing it stripped of all its pageantry and decorations, in its naked and hideous reality.

The passages which describe a tempest and a deluge, and their representation in painting, possess the same vigorous realism and accuracy of detail, and contain some of Leonardo’s most eloquent and vivid writing; and among the other notes connected with pictures, we may cite the one for the ‘Last Supper’, describing the actions of the disciples, which, although of a far slighter form than any of the passages already mentioned, yet possesses a restrained but very distinct dramatic power. These same qualities may be discerned perhaps even more effectively in one of the very rare comments on public events found in his writings. After Ludovic Sforza’s attempt to regain possession of Lombardy had ended with his defeat and capture at the battle of Novara in April 1500, Leonardo wrote among notes on various matters, ‘The Duke has lost his State, his possessions, and his liberty, and he has seen none of his works finished’. (*Il Duce perse lo Stato e la roba e la libertà, e nessuna sua opera si fini per lui.*) Leonardo was a homeless wanderer as a result of the events mentioned, and one of the works of which the Duke had not witnessed the completion was the statue on which Leonardo had been engaged intermittently for sixteen years, the model of which had served as a target for the French soldiers; but this terse, unemotional comment is the only reference to these occurrences found in his writings. There is a certain poignant brevity and concentration in the sentence, which is sufficient even to recall some of the most inevitable lines of Dante.

It is within the narrow limits of the short sentence and the apothegm that Leonardo’s command of language is most brilliant. In some of these, the thought expressed is so joined to the words as to hardly permit translation. ‘*Sì come una giornata bene spesa dà lieto dormire così una vita bene usata dà lieto morire*’ must lose something of its grace in any version. ...phenomena of Nature so simply as to cause us almost to doubt whether they are intended to do more than this. "All the flowers which see the sun ripen their seed, and not the others—that is, those which see only the reflection of the sun"—this is perhaps written as an observation of Nature without any thought of a deeper meaning; but it is hard to believe that a similar restriction applies to the sentence: "tears come from the heart, not from the brain," even though it is found in a manuscript that treats the subject of anatomy.

It would seem that it was natural to him as a writer to use words symbolically and figuratively, thus employing obvious and revealed things as metaphors. Of this habit of veiled speech, the section of his imaginative writings known as "the Prophecies" provides the most impressive and sustained series of examples. A few of these are, as their name implies, a forecast of future conditions; many attack the vices and abuses of his own time. In the brief, contrasting form of their composition, Leonardo apparently created his own unique model.

There are questions more personal than any of those which arise from the consideration of his achievements in these various arts and sciences; questions which the mere number of these external interests tends to hide in relative obscurity. This causes us to regard Leonardo almost as a result of historical forces rather than as an individual—to see in him, as it were, an embodiment of the various intellectual tendencies of the Renaissance, as though the achievements were the man himself. His figure crosses the stage of life in triumph, playing many parts to perfection. But enough of these. Let us try to come nearer, to get past the cloak of his activities, and attempt to "pluck the heart out of this mystery." <note>A famous quote from William Shakespeare's play *Hamlet*, meaning to discover someone's true essence or secrets.</note> As a means toward this end, let us consider his attitude regarding certain problems of life.

His writings teach the highest morality, though more as a logical process of the mind than as a revelation from an external authority <note>Meaning he arrived at his moral conclusions through reason rather than through religious scripture.</note>. He maintains such a complete silence on the subject of religious doctrine that he leaves very little evidence for us to guess at his faith or lack of faith. The statement by Vasari <note>Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574) wrote *The Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects*, the foundational text for art history.</note>—that he did not conform to any religion, perhaps deeming it better to be a philosopher than a Christian—was omitted in the second edition of the *Lives*. In temperament, <term>Leonardo</term> <note>Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519), the quintessential Renaissance polymath.</note> shares something with certain figures who preceded the <term>Reformation</term> <note>The 16th-century religious movement that led to the establishment of Protestant churches.</note>. Whenever reason and authority clashed, he chose the side of free thought. "Whoever," he wrote, "relies on authority in a discussion uses their memory rather than their intellect."

His mindset was <term>anti-clerical</term> <note>Opposed to the power or influence of the clergy in social and political matters.</note>. His anger at the abuses and corruption of the Church was expressed in satire as sharp and direct as that of <term>Erasmus</term> <note>Desiderius Erasmus, a Dutch humanist who famously criticized the Catholic Church's failings.</note>. His contempt for the vices of the priesthood, their promotion of superstition, and the business of selling miracles and pardons—vividly described in the section of his writings known as "the <term>Prophecies</term>" <note>A collection of Leonardo's riddles and allegorical forecasts.</note>—likely earned him the label of heretic from those he criticized. However, his dispute was not with the foundations of faith itself, but with what he saw as its corruption in practice by its followers. His own work focused on <term>scientific inquiry</term>; yet when his research results seemed to conflict with religious truth, he would set the issue aside, denying any intent of hostility. Nature cannot break her own laws. Scientific processes are certain, but there are areas where we cannot follow them. "Our body is subject to the heavens, and the heavens are subject to the spirit." Thus, at the end of a passage describing life's natural origins, he adds, "I do not speak against the sacred books, for they contain the ultimate truth." These words seem like a protest against pointless arguments over such matters. While he is cautious about stating religious formulas, the influence of faith is visible throughout his life.

The urgent need to live life fully is the constant theme of his <term>moral sayings</term> <note>Aphorisms or proverbs regarding ethics and human behavior.</note>:

> "A life well spent is long."
>
> "You, O God, sell us all good things at the price of labor."
>
> "Just as a well-spent day brings happy sleep, so a life well used brings a happy death."

This view of the end is steady. Death follows life just as sleep ends the day; if we work well during the day, sleep is peaceful. During the course of the day, there is...

There is so much to be done, such opportunity to construct and to observe, and so much knowledge to be gained about this world in which we spend our days, that there is scarcely time remaining to stand in fear and wonder at the thought of what monsters the coming shadow may hold within it. It is better to make use of today than to waste it by questioning tomorrow. Our duty in life is clear and we must follow it. When he speaks of what comes after, it is with that hesitation common to everyone—unless speaking of it has become a habit through custom—for to everyone, whatever their belief may be, there still remains something unknowable in the conditions of that transition.

In one of the most beautiful passages of his writings—a fragment on time, the destroyer—Leonardo describes Helen in her old age looking into her mirror and seeing there the wrinkles which time had imprinted on her face, and then weeping, and wondering why she had been twice carried away. Beautiful as the description is, the hand that wrote it is pre-eminently that of the scientist; we seem to see the anatomist at work with the scalpel, so minute is the observation revealed therein regarding the effect of age and of the relentless approach of death upon the human frame.

'In her the painter had anatomized Time’s ruin.'

And yet, as modern scholarship in the person of the late Gerolamo Calvi has recently shown, Leonardo was not the original author of the passage. He amplified it and transformed it into a richer harmony by placing the address to Time the destroyer at the beginning as well as at the end, but the description of Helen he found in Ovid's *Metamorphoses* (Book xv, lines 232-6).

This fact illustrates the difficulty of interpreting the contents of the Notebooks. They contain material, some of which is not original, and some of this is undoubtedly still unidentified.

The frequent recurrence in his writings and in his drawings and grotesques of the physical signs of decay and death suggests no morbid preference, such as that shown by the painters of the *danse macabre*. It forms a balanced part of his study and 'patient exposition' of the origin and development of the entire structure of man. In the results as we may read them, there is no intrusion of a personal tone. His attitude is always that of an observer, looking with curious eyes, noting all the phenomena of physical change, but yet all the while pre-

--- Page 46 ---
38
PREFACE

maintaining a strange impassivity. In none of his works or manuscripts does he ever suggest possessing any of that regret over the passing of time which resonates through Giorgione’s sun-drenched idylls. Indeed, he expressly dissociates himself from all such lamentation. Time, he maintains, lasts long enough for those who use it. The mere fact that death is inevitable forbids regret. Therefore, it cannot be an evil. He speaks of it as taking away the memory of evil and compares it to the sleep that follows the day. The thought of this sleep brings silence; when on rare occasions that silence is broken, he stands with Shakespeare and Montaigne, revealing, as they do when they address the same question, a quiet confidence, serene and proud.

The author of *Virginibus Puerisque*, discoursing whimsically upon the occurrences and attributes of romantic passion, professes his utter inability to understand how any member of his own sex, with at most two exceptions, could ever have been found worthy to be its object. "It might be all very well," he says, "if the Apollo Belvedere should suddenly glow all over into life and step forward from his pedestal with that god-like air of his. But of the misbegotten changelings who call themselves men and prattle intolerably over dinner tables, I never saw one who seemed worthy to inspire love—no, nor read of any except Leonardo da Vinci and perhaps Goethe in his youth."

The suggestion regarding the Apollo Belvedere is in entire harmony with the association of the names that follow. For if it had ever happened, as is conjectured in Heine’s fantasy, that the gods of Greece—after their worship ceased, having fallen on days of adversity and been forced into lowlier roles—had walked the earth as men, surely no lives of which we have a record would have fallen more naturally to Apollo’s lot than those of Goethe and Leonardo.

It would be futile to attempt to find better examples, yet these provide only a whimsical support at best for Stevenson’s argument. They offer far more proof of his amazing boldness in attempting to view the realm of sentiment from the feminine perspective.

He ranks these two names together in isolation from the rest of their sex—and specifically in regard to that condition in which the records of their lives reveal the least resemblance. Goethe was as susceptible and almost as fickle as Jupiter himself. The story of his heart is a romance with many chapters, each enshrining a new name, and all end—

--- Page 47 ---
ending abruptly at the stage where the poet remembers—sometimes rather late—the supreme demands of his art.

But in Leonardo’s case, there is no reason to believe that any such chapter was ever started. None of his biographers link his name with any woman in a romantic way, nor do his own writings provide any such sign. They show that he lived only for the things of the mind. He seems to have deliberately renounced any thought of sharing in the tenderness of human relationships. He viewed it as foreign to the artist’s highest purpose: he felt he had to be solitary in order to live entirely for his art. His concept of the mental conditions necessary for creating great art assumes something of that isolation expressed in Walter Pater’s phrase: "each mind keeping as a solitary prisoner its own dream of a world."

The praise of solitude has always been a productive theme, though much of the passion of its followers has resulted in little more than an echo of the monkish rhyme, "O blessed solitude, O sole happiness." Insofar as the praise of solitude is a criticism of the world and one’s fellow men, expressing a desire to avoid them and their activities, it is a useless thing or worse. Solitude is unnatural, and only the use one makes of it can justify the condition. Perhaps even then the dream will never be born! It is certain that if it is, we must suffer the labor pains alone!

Concentration of the mind comes through solitude; and in this, according to Leonardo, lies its value to the artist. (*Se tu sarai solo tu sarai tutto tuo.*) "If you are alone, you belong entirely to yourself. If you are accompanied by even one companion, you belong only half to yourself, or even less in proportion to the thoughtlessness of his behavior. . . . If you must have companionship, choose it from your studio; it may then help you to gain the advantages that come from different methods of study."

Such companionship in the studio implies a level of equal achievement that he could never have encountered himself after leaving the circle of Verrocchio and the art world of Florence. His own lesser companions in the studio were his pupils and servants, and the only one of these whom he allowed any degree of personal intimacy was Francesco de’ Melzi, who seems to have been to him in the final years of his life almost like a son to a father.

--- Page 48 ---
Behind all his strength lay springs of tenderness; though in life these were confined within the narrow limits by which his spirit intended his work to be more surely accomplished, they are manifest in his art, revealing the repression of his life. His paintings are now so few that we should look chiefly to his drawings for support of this statement, and among these primarily, perhaps, to the many studies for Madonna pictures and the sketches of children made in connection with them; also, however, to the two versions of the composition of the Madonna and Child with St. Anne. The differences between the version in Burlington House and the one in the Louvre show the artist's gradual growth of purpose. One motive, however, is found in both: namely, that the Madonna is represented as so entirely absorbed in her Child that she is completely unconscious of anything else. With the exception of the Madonna della Seggiola, and perhaps certain others of Raphael's Madonnas, there is no Madonna picture in Italian art in which the conception is more human or the ecstasy of motherhood is rendered with greater tenderness. Thus "art consoles for life"; and the same may be said in Leonardo's case of Nature, perhaps even more truly than of art—if indeed any thought of consolation can be allowed in connection with a life so confident and full! For a man's work is his ultimate self. Such human hopes as begin and end in the individual are puny even in their highest fulfillment, and the processes of Nature, whatever their final end, seem eternal in contrast with their transience.

He interpreted man's highest aim to consist in seeking to know and to hand on the lamp of knowledge.
