# A RECORD OF THE MANUSCRIPTS

In the opening lines of the volume of manuscript notes "begun at Florence in the house of Piero di Braccio Martelli, on the 22nd day of March, 1508," now in the British Museum (Arundel MSS. 263), Leonardo explains the method of its composition. The passage may serve to summarize the impression made by the entire mass of Leonardo’s manuscripts. "This," he says, "will be a collection without order, made up of many sheets which I have copied here, hoping afterwards to arrange them in order in their proper places according to the subjects of which they treat; and I believe that before I am at the end of this I shall have to repeat the same thing several times; and therefore, O reader, do not blame me, because the subjects are many, and the memory cannot retain them and say 'this I will not write because I have already written it.' And if I wished to avoid falling into this mistake it would be necessary, in order to prevent repetition, that on every occasion when I wished to transcribe a passage I should always read over all the preceding portion, and this especially because long periods of time elapse between one time of writing and another." Certain pages in the volume of manuscript in the British Museum would indeed seem to be of a much earlier date than this introductory sentence, and the whole body of the manuscripts, as may be shown by the time-references contained in them, extend over a period of some forty years, from Leonardo’s early manhood to his old age. He commenced them during the time of his first residence in Florence, and was still adding to them when at Amboise.

The contents of this "collection without order" are so diversified as to render almost impossible any attempt at formal classification. In addition to the numerous fragments of letters, the personal records, the notes relating to his work as an artist, and the fragments of imaginative composition which are to be found there, it presents by far the most complete record of his mental activity, and this may be said without exaggeration to have extended into practically all the avenues of hu-

--- Page 50 ---
human knowledge. These manuscripts serve in a sense to show the mind in its workshop, busy with research, making conjectures, and recording phenomena, tempering the vast forces of Nature to its uses as far as a human instrument can.

He planned many treatises intended to embody the results of these researches. Notes in the manuscripts themselves record the various stages of their composition. Some still exist in a more or less complete form. Regarding the fragments of others, the order of their arrangement is now only a matter of guesswork. In the manuscripts at Windsor, which treat mainly of anatomy, a note dated April 2nd, 1489, speaks of writing the book "about the human figure." The manuscript given to the Ambrosian Library by Cardinal Federico Borromeo, now MS. C of the Institut de France, which is a treatise on light and shade, contains a note stating that "on the 23rd day of April 1490, I commenced this book and recommenced the horse"—the latter reference being to the equestrian statue of Francesco Sforza. In August 1499, a note in the Codice Atlantico states that he was then writing "upon movement and weight." These dates are, however, of relatively less importance, because each of these subjects occupied his thoughts over a long period of years. The first two formed a part of the artist’s complete equipment as Leonardo conceived it; the third found practical expression in his undertakings in canalization and engineering in Lombardy, Tuscany, Romagna, and elsewhere. In connection with the former of these two divisions of his activities, one may cite the treatise on the nature of water formerly in the possession of the Earl of Leicester; the same subject is also treated among others in MS. F of the Institut, which, according to a note, was commenced at Milan on September 12th, 1508.

The manuscripts as a whole are picturesquely described in the diary of a certain Antonio de Beatis, the secretary of the Cardinal of Aragon, who with his patron visited Leonardo at Amboise in October 1517. The many wanderings of the painter’s life were then over, and he was living with Francesco Melzi and his servant Battista de Villanis in the manor house of Cloux, the gift of Francis I. The diary relates that he showed his guests three pictures: the St. John, the Madonna with St. Anne, and the portrait of a Florentine lady, painted at the request of Giuliano de’ Medici, which cannot now be identified. It further states that paralysis had attacked his right hand, and that therefore he could

If these were to be published, they would be profitable and very enjoyable."

This description of the manuscripts—the only one provided by an eyewitness during Leonardo’s lifetime—suggests that most, if not all, of them were in Leonardo's possession when he moved to France and were at Clos Lucé <note>original: "Cloux"</note> at the time of his death.

The manuscripts then passed into the possession of Francesco Melzi. In his will, dated April 23, 1518, Leonardo bequeathed them to him "in return for the services and favors done for him in the past." He left Melzi "each and every book which the said testator currently possesses, along with the other instruments and portraits belonging to his art and profession as a painter." Melzi returned to Milan shortly after Leonardo’s death, taking the manuscripts with him. Four years later, a man named Alberto Bendedeo, writing from Milan to Alfonso d'Este, stated that he believed the Melzi whom Leonardo had made his heir possessed "those of his notebooks that dealt with anatomy and many other beautiful things."

Giorgio Vasari visited Milan in 1566. He states that Melzi, whom he met and who was then "a beautiful and gentle old man," possessed a large portion of Leonardo’s papers on the anatomy of the human body and kept them as carefully as if they were religious relics. By this time, some of the manuscripts had already passed into other hands; Vasari refers to some that dealt with painting and methods of drawing and coloring as being in the possession of a certain Milanese painter...

...whose name he does not mention. The care that had been taken of the manuscripts in Melzi’s possession ended at his death, which occurred in 1570. Some years later, Melzi’s heirs placed no restrictions on the actions of a certain Lelio Gavardi di Asola, a tutor in the Melzi family. Gavardi took thirteen of the manuscript volumes with him to Florence for the purpose of selling them to the Grand Duke, Francesco. However, the duke’s death prevented this plan from being realized, and Gavardi subsequently took the volumes with him to Pisa.

Giovanni Ambrogio Mazzenta, a Milanese who was then studying law at the University of Pisa, protested to Gavardi regarding his conduct. He was so successful that, upon Mazzenta’s return to Milan in 1587, he took the volumes with him to restore them to the Melzi family. When he attempted to perform this duty, however, Dr. Orazio Melzi was so astonished by his concern <note>original: "solicitude"</note> in the matter that he gave Mazzenta all thirteen volumes as a gift. Melzi further told him that there were many other drawings by Leonardo lying neglected in the attics of his villa at Vaprio. In 1590, Giovanni Ambrogio Mazzenta joined the Barnabite Order <note>A Catholic religious order founded in the 1530s</note>, and he gave the volumes to his brothers. The brothers seemed to have talked somewhat freely about the incident; consequently, according to Ambrogio Mazzenta’s account, many people became eager to obtain similar treasures. Orazio Melzi then began giving away drawings, clay models, anatomical studies, and other precious relics from Leonardo’s studio for free.

Among the others who acquired works by Leonardo in this way was the sculptor Pompeo Leoni, who was employed in the service of the King of Spain. Leoni later persuaded Orazio Melzi—by promising to obtain official honors and professional advancement <note>original: "preferment"</note> for him—to appeal to Guido Mazzenta, who then possessed the manuscripts. Melzi asked him to return Leonardo’s volumes so that Leoni might present them to King Philip II. Melzi’s pleas were successful in recovering seven volumes, and three of the others later passed into Pompeo Leoni’s possession after the death of one of the Mazzenta brothers. Of the remaining three, according to Mazzenta’s account, one was given to Cardinal Federico Borromeo and passed into the Ambrosian Library, which he founded in 1603. Another was given to the painter Ambrogio Figini, who later bequeathed...

Apparently, the collector’s instinct proved stronger in Pompeo Leoni than his original intentions. He was later in Madrid, where he was employed in creating bronzes for the royal tombs in the Escorial <note>original: "Escurial"; a massive historic residence of the King of Spain.</note>, but there is no evidence to show that he ever gave any of Leonardo’s manuscripts to King Philip II. The <term>Codice Atlantico</term> remained in his possession until his death in 1610; it then passed to his heir, Polidoro Calchi, who sold it in 1625 to Count Galeazzo Arconati. Two of Leonardo’s manuscripts in Pompeo Leoni’s possession were included among the belongings sold after his death in Madrid, and were then bought by Don Juan de Espina. It seems probable that other manuscripts in Leoni’s possession were inherited by his heir Calchi and passed from him to Count Arconati, because in 1636, Arconati presented twelve volumes of Leonardo’s manuscripts to the Ambrosian Library at Milan. Leonardo’s manuscripts were increased by the gift of Count Orazio Archinti.

Of the list of twelve manuscripts described in Count Arconati’s deed of gift to the Ambrosian Library, the second was later lost, and the fifth was removed from the Library—it being, as the description shows, identical to the Leonardo manuscript which, around the year 1750, was bought from a certain Gaetano Caccia of Novara by Carlo Trivulzio and is now owned by Prince Trivulzio in Milan. The remaining ten manuscripts from the Arconati donation, together with the two from Cardinal Federico Borromeo and Count Archinti respectively, remained in the Ambrosian Library until 1796. There was also with them at that time a manuscript of ten sheets which dealt with the eye; its origin is unknown, but it is speculated that it had been substituted for the manuscript now in Prince Trivulzio's collection. These thirteen manuscripts were all moved to Paris in 1796 following the decree of Bonaparte as General-in-Chief of the Army of Italy on May 19th, 1796 (30 Floreal, Year IV). This decree provided for the appointment of an agent to select such paintings and other works of art as might be worthy of being sent to France. The words of the decree authorizing and justifying the removal catch one's attention by the naivety of their arrogance. "All men of genius," it stated, "all who have attained distinction in the republic of letters are French, whatever the country of their birth." (Tous les hommes de génie, tous ceux qui ont obtenu un rang distingué dans la république des lettres, sont Français, quelque soit le pays qui les aît vus naître.)

The Codice Atlantico was in the Bibliothèque Nationale in Paris in August 1796. The other twelve volumes of the manuscripts were deposited in the Institut de France. In 1815, the Austrian Ambassador, representing Lombardy, applied for the return of all the Leonardo manuscripts. The request was granted regarding the Codice Atlantico, which was then restored to the Ambrosian Library in Milan, but the twelve volumes in the library of the Institut de France were apparently overlooked, and they have remained there ever since.

This manuscript is identical to Number 3 in the Arconati donation, which is described as having at the end a small "little volume" <note>original: "volumetto"</note> of eighteen pages containing various mathematical figures and drawings of birds. This "little volume" seems in fact to have been treated somewhat as Venturi <note>Giovanni Battista Venturi (1746–1822) was an Italian physicist and historian of science who published the first extracts of Leonardo's scientific writings.</note> suggests by Count Guglielmo Libri. Libri frequently had access to the manuscripts in the Institute of France <note>original: "Institut de France"</note> in the early part of the last century, and he apparently removed <note>original: "abstracted"</note> it at some time before 1848, the date its loss was discovered. In 1868, it was sold by Libri to Count Giacomo Manzoni of Lugo, and in 1892 it was acquired from Count Manzoni’s heirs by Mr. Sabachnikoff. It has since been presented to the Royal Library at Turin.

Two other manuscripts by Leonardo, consisting of sixty-eight and twenty-six pages respectively, are now in the National Library <note>original: "Bibliothèque Nationale"</note> (Numbers 2038 and 2037). These must have originally been part of Manuscripts A and B from the Institute of France. They match both in the dimensions of their pages and in the subjects they cover. Furthermore, their total page numbers, when added to those of Manuscripts A and B respectively, almost equal the full count of leaves these two manuscripts possessed in 1636, as described in the list of the Arconati donation.

These two manuscripts in the National Library were formerly in the collection of the late Earl of Ashburnham, who purchased them in 1875 from Count Libri—from whom, as we have seen, Count Manzoni had also purchased the "little volume" *On the Flight of Birds*. The damage <note>original: "mutilation"</note> to Manuscripts A and B of the Institute of France and the removal of the "little volume" were first discovered in the year 1848. It is impossible to avoid the conclusion that the theft in each case was the work of Count Libri. The two manuscripts of the National Library have been included in the edition of the manuscripts of the Institute of France published in facsimile, with a transcript and French translation by Mr. Ravaisson-Mollien, in six volumes (Paris, 1880–91).

The *Codex Atlanticus* <note>original: "Codice Atlantico"</note> has also been published in facsimile, with a transcript, under the direction of the Academy of the Lincei <note>original: "Accademia dei Lincei"</note> at Rome

Joseph Addison, in his *Remarks on Several Parts of Italy* describing his visit to Milan in 1701, mentions the Ambrosian Library as containing “a manuscript by Leonardo da Vinci <note>original: Leonardus Vincius</note>, which King James I could not obtain, though he offered three thousand Spanish pistoles <note>A gold coin used in Europe at the time.</note> for it”; and the monarch in question is also stated to have been James I in the fuller record of the Arconati donation. The Duke of Feria was Governor of Milan from 1610 to 1633, during a part of the reign of both monarchs.

Apparently, however, the manuscripts only passed into the possession of Count Arconati in 1625, the year of the death of James I, and this makes it probable that the monarch referred to was actually Charles I. But the question of which king it was has relatively little importance; regarding the inscription, it may perhaps be well to recall the famous remark of Dr. Samuel Johnson that “in tombstone <term>lapidary: inscriptions carved into stone</term> inscriptions, a man is not testifying under oath.” The only conclusion that can fairly be drawn from this instance is that the manuscripts by Leonardo now in the Royal Collection at Windsor did not form part of the Arconati Collection. This is also confirmed by the testimony of Lord Arundel, as recounted by John Evelyn. That some of the Leonardo manuscripts at Windsor were once in the possession of Lord Arundel is established by the existence of an engraving of one of the drawings by Wenceslaus Hollar, whom Lord Arundel brought from Prague and established in London. It is inscribed, “Leonardo da Vinci drew this once in this way. W. Hollar made this from the Arundel Collection” <note>original: Leonardus da Vinci sic olim delineavit. W. Hollar fecit ex collectione Arundeliana</note>.

That some of these Windsor manuscripts were also formerly in the collection of Pompeo Leoni is clearly shown by the fact that one of the volumes is inscribed, “Drawings of Leonardo da Vinci, restored by Pompeo Leoni” <note>original: Disegni di Leonardo da Vinci Restaurati da Pompeo Leoni</note>.

Two of the manuscripts in Pompeo Leoni’s collection, as already stated, were purchased in Madrid after his death by Don Juan de Espina. Mr. Alfred Marks—from whose important contributions to this subject in the *Athenaeum* of February 23rd and July 6th, 1878, many of these facts are derived—has shown that for at least one of these volumes, the Earl of Arundel was in negotiations <term>in treaty: in the process of negotiating a purchase</term> with Don Juan de Espina. In a note by Endymion Porter dated 1629, printed by Mr. Sainsbury in his *Original Unpublished Papers illustrative of the Life of Rubens*, it says: "...of such things as my Lord Ambassador Sir Francis Cottington is to send out of Spain for my Lord of Arundel; and not to forget the book of drawings by Leonardo da Vinci which is in Don Juan de Espina's hands" (p. 294). Don Juan seems for a time to have proved stubborn, for Lord Arundel wrote on January 19th, 1636, to Lord Aston, who was then ambassador to Spain: "I beg you to be mindful of Don Juan de Espina's book, if his foolish mood changes" (p. 299). There the record breaks off. But as Mr. Marks truly observes, there can be little doubt that eventually a change did take place in Don Juan’s "foolish mood." At whatever date this happened, the volume passed into Lord Arundel’s possession. The earl may either have been negotiating for himself or for the King. If the former was the case, the book may presumably have passed into the Royal Collection at any time after 1646, when, upon the death of Lord Arundel, his collections were partially dispersed. If it was not acquired previously, the volume may have been bought in Holland by an agent of Charles II.

The earliest record of any of Leonardo’s manuscripts or drawings being in the royal possession occurs in an inventory found by Richter in the Manuscript Department of the British Museum, which states that some drawings by Leonardo da Vinci, marked with a cross, were delivered for Her Majesty’s use in the year 1728.

Richter also cites a note in an inventory at Windsor Castle written at the beginning of the last century, in which a drawing by Leonardo is referred to as not having been in the volume compiled by Pompeo Leoni, but in one of the volumes in the Buonfigluolo Collection bought at Venice. Nothing apparently is known about the collection referred to here, but the note is important as it tends to prove that the manuscripts by Leonardo now at Windsor were not all acquired at the same time, and did not all form part of Pompeo Leoni’s collection.

The volume of manuscript now in the British Museum (Arundel MSS. 263) was certainly once in the possession of Lord Arundel. Nothing is known of its history prior to this, and whether or not it belonged to Pompeo Leoni, or was acquired by purchase from Don Juan de Espina, it would be useless to attempt to guess. Lord Arundel had numerous agents in various parts of Europe, who were em-

<meta>This text continues from the previous page, describing the Earl of Arundel's activities in Europe.</meta>

...employed in collecting antiquities and works of art. It should be noted, however, that the Earl himself acquired the majority of his manuscript collection in Nuremberg in 1636. These documents had previously belonged to Wilibald Pirkheimer, the Renaissance scholar <note>original: humanist</note> who was a friend of Erasmus and Dürer. If the opportunity had arisen, Pirkheimer would certainly have acquired any manuscript by Leonardo; but to assume he did so would be to assume that some of the manuscripts passed into other hands during Leonardo's lifetime. While this is not impossible, it is at least improbable.

The only other manuscripts by Leonardo now known to exist—with the exception of a few separate sheets of sketches and diagrams with explanatory text—are three small notebooks in the Forster Library at South Kensington, and a seventy-two-page volume that was long in the possession of the Earls of Leicester at Holkham Hall. This volume was recently sold to Mr. Pierpont Morgan and is believed to be now in New York. The former (the notebooks) were acquired in Vienna for a small sum by the first Earl of Lytton, who presented them to Mr. Forster. The latter (the Holkham volume), according to a note on its title page, once belonged to the painter Giuseppe Ghezzi, who was living in Rome at the beginning of the 18th century. It was presumably acquired by the first Earl of Leicester (of the Holkham line), who spent several years in Rome prior to 1775 and acquired many art treasures there. Its earlier history is unknown. This volume—a treatise on the nature of water—is very likely the one referred to by Rafaelle du Fresne in the biographical sketch of Leonardo that appears in his edition of the *Treatise on Painting* <note>original: *Trattato della Pittura*</note>, published in Paris in 1651. There, it is stated that "the project of the Martesana canal <note>A major canal in Milan that Leonardo helped design and improve</note> was the occasion for his writing a book on the nature, weight, and motion of water, filled with a great number of drawings of various wheels and engines for mills to regulate the flow of water and raise it to a height."

Regarding the manuscripts at Windsor, which primarily deal with anatomy, two volumes containing facsimiles (60 leaves with about 400 drawings), transcripts, and translations have been published by Piumati and Sabachnikoff: *On Anatomy, Folios A* <note>original: *Dell' Anatomia Fogli A*</note> (Paris, 1898) and *Folios B* <note>original: *Fogli B*</note> (Turin, 1901). Additionally, the *Anatomy Notebooks* <note>original: *Quaderni d'Anatomia*</note>—six volumes containing 129 leaves with about 1,050 drawings—were published by Vangenstan, Fonahn, and Hopstock (Oslo, 1911–16). As Leonardo’s fame as a writer has chiefly rested upon the *Treatise on Painting*, it may not be out of place here to attempt to state the relation which this work bears to the original manuscripts.

The *Treatise* was first published by Rafaelle du Fresne in Paris in 1651, with a French translation by Roland Fréard, sieur de Chambrai, also being issued in the same year. Du Fresne derived his text from two old copies of MS. 834 in the Barberini Library, which manuscript has now presumably been transferred to the Vatican, along with the other contents of that library. One of these copies had been made by the Cavaliere Cassiano del Pozzo, who had given it in 1640 to M. Chanteloup, by whom it was presented to du Fresne for the preparation of his edition; the other was lent to him for the same purpose by M. Thevenot.

Another edition of the *Treatise* was issued in 1817 by Guglielmo Manzi, who used as his text a manuscript in the Vatican Library (Cod. Vat. [Urbinas], 1270), which had formerly belonged to the library of the Dukes of Urbino. This manuscript is by far the more complete of the two, as five out of the eight books it contains were missing from the version followed by du Fresne. There are, however, many omissions in Manzi’s edition, and the only adequate critical edition of the Vatican manuscript is that published by H. Ludwig (*Leonardo da Vinci: Das Buch von der Malerei* [Volumes 15–18 of *Quellenschriften für Kunstgeschichte*, etc., Edited by R. Eitelberger v. Edelberg], Vienna, 1882, Stuttgart, 1885). This contains the complete text, together with a German translation and commentary, and also an analysis of the differences that exist between the manuscripts in the Vatican and Leonardo’s own manuscripts.

The Vatican manuscript probably dates from the beginning of the sixteenth century. It has been attributed to some immediate pupil of Leonardo’s, preferably either Francesco Melzi or Salai, but there is no evidence that can be held to prove this view. Its close connection with Leonardo is, however, indisputable. Whether this be the original

--- Page 61 ---
Whether it was organized into a specific form or not, the compilation was undoubtedly made before the manuscripts were dispersed. About a quarter of the total number of paragraphs (two hundred and twenty-five out of nine hundred and forty-four) are identical to passages in the surviving manuscripts. Many others, which cannot currently be found in any form within the manuscripts, nevertheless clearly show their origin. These provide sufficient proof—even if it were not already evident from the troubled history of the various volumes—that some of the manuscripts have now been lost. It appears that, just as with Leonardo’s work as a painter, time has spared only fragments of his writing. The compiler of the *Treatise on Painting* had access to manuscripts, and probably also to sources of information regarding the artist’s intentions, of which we have no record. He presumably followed what he believed to be the plan of the artist’s work. Nevertheless, Leonardo cannot be considered directly or even indirectly responsible for the arrangement and divisions of this treatise, and it is somewhat difficult to attribute the entirety of the contents to him. Certain passages read more like a pupil’s repetition of a theme explained by the master.

Did Leonardo himself ever give his work a definite shape? Did he write a treatise on painting, or only parts of one? In Fra Luca Pacioli’s dedication to Ludovic Sforza in the *De Divina Proportione*, dated February 9th, 1498, he speaks of Leonardo as having finished ‘the Book on Painting and human movements.’ Dr. Ludwig, who apparently accepts this statement, suggests that the treatise was in the possession of Ludovic and was likely lost during the French invasion of Milan.

On this same occasion, according to both Vasari and Lomazzo, a treatise by Leonardo on the anatomy of the horse also perished; he had written it during his studies for the Sforza statue.

Vasari, as we have seen, mentions some writings by Leonardo ‘which treat of painting and of the methods of drawing and coloring’ as being at that time in the possession of a Milanese painter. This painter had recently visited him in Florence to discuss their publication and had taken them to Rome to carry out his plan, though Vasari could not say what the result was. These writings are described as being ‘in characters written with the left hand, backwards,’ and therefore they cannot possibly be the same as either the Barberini or the Vatican manuscripts.

--- Page 62 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the origins of Leonardo da Vinci's writings, specifically debating whether the *Treatise on Painting* was ever a completed book or merely a collection of notes organized by later compilers.</meta>

<page-num>54</page-num>

### RECORD OF THE MANUSCRIPTS

Since Vasari <note>original: "Vasari"; Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574) was an Italian painter and historian famous for his biographies of Renaissance artists</note> wrote his accounts during the lifetime of Francesco Melzi <note>Leonardo’s devoted pupil and heir who inherited his notebooks</note>, it is reasonable to conclude that this particular manuscript had been separated from the others early on. Therefore, it did not form part of the main body of manuscripts that Melzi inherited upon Leonardo’s death—manuscripts which Vasari notes Melzi cherished as if they were sacred relics. 

As to whether this manuscript was the same work mentioned by Friar Luca Pacioli <note>original: "Fra Luca Pacioli"; a famous mathematician and friend of Leonardo</note>, there is not enough evidence to form a definitive opinion. Furthermore, the Friar’s testimony should not be taken too literally. In the dedication of his book *On the Divine Proportion* <note>original: "De Divina Proportione"</note>, Pacioli writes that "its entire bronze mass amounts to about 200,000 pounds" <note>original: "tutta la sua ennea massa a libre circa 200000 ascende"</note>. These words would naturally suggest that the great statue of Francesco Sforza <note>a massive equestrian monument Leonardo worked on for years</note> was actually cast in bronze; however, the weight of evidence, including Leonardo’s own letters, proves that this never happened. In the same way, regarding the *Treatise on Painting*, Pacioli may have spoken of rough drafts and fragments as if they were a completed, finished work.

The work itself was constantly evolving in the mind of the author. It was shaped and rewritten countless times as Leonardo's goals changed and expanded. Each new field of study he entered revealed once again the deep kinship between art and nature. It is certain that he never wrote "the end" <note>original: "finis"</note>. It is quite possible that he never paused his investigations long enough to arrange and categorize what he had written—perhaps he left all of that for a more convenient time. We should remember that genius is not often inclined to be "synthetic" <note>meaning the ability to combine various parts into a single, organized whole</note>.

Regarding whether this was the work to which Fra Luca Pacioli referred, there is a risk in interpreting the passage too literally. The words of the dedication of the *De Divina Proportione*—"having seen his eternal work of bronze," etc.—would naturally suggest that the statue was actually cast in bronze; however, the evidence is so contradictory that, in the case of the Treatise, it is almost impossible to speak with any degree of certainty.

The only certain fact is that he never succeeded in completing the cast of the Sforza horse, on which he worked for a period of time long enough to have finished it.

## PREFACE

**IF INDEED** I lack the power to quote from authors as they do, it is a far greater and more worthy thing to read by the light of experience, which is the teacher of their masters. They strut about puffed up and pompous, dressed up and adorned not with their own labors but by those of others, and they will not even allow me my own. And if they despise me for being an inventor, how much more should blame be given to them, who are not inventors but merely trumpeters and reciters of the works of others?

---

Those who are inventors and interpreters between Nature and Man, when compared with the reciters and trumpeters of the works of others, are to be considered just as an object in front of a mirror is compared to its image seen in the mirror: the one being something in itself, the other nothing. These are people whose debt to nature is small, for it seems only by chance that they wear human form, and but for this, one might class them with herds of beasts.

Seeing that I cannot choose any subject of great usefulness or pleasure, because my predecessors have already taken as their own all useful and necessary themes, I will act like one who, because of his poverty, is the last to arrive at the fair; unable to provide for himself otherwise, he chooses all the things which others have already looked over and rejected as being of little value. With these despised and discarded wares—the leftovers of many buyers—I will load my modest pack and go on my way, distributing them not in the great cities, but among the humble villages, taking such reward as fits the things I offer.

I am fully aware that the fact that I am not a man of letters may cause certain arrogant persons to think they have reason to criticize me...

# PROEM

...criticize me, claiming that I am a man ignorant of book-learning <term>original: "book-learning"; here meaning formal academic education in Latin and classical texts</term>. Foolish people! Do they not know that I might reply to them as Marius did to the Roman Patricians <note>Gaius Marius (c. 157–86 BC) was a Roman general and "new man" who rose to power through merit rather than noble birth; he famously mocked aristocrats who had only book-learning but no military experience</note>: "They who themselves go about adorned in the labor of others will not allow me my own"? They will say that because of my lack of formal education, I cannot properly express the subjects I wish to treat. Do they not know that my subjects require experience <note>The author emphasizes "experience" (direct observation and experimentation) as the only valid foundation for science and art</note> rather than the words of others for their explanation? And since experience has been the teacher of whoever has written well, I take her as my mistress, and to her in all points I make my appeal.

Many will believe that they can with good reason criticize me, alleging that my proofs are contrary to the authority of certain men who are held in great reverence by their inexperienced judgments. They do not take into account that my conclusions were arrived at as a result of simple and plain experience, which is the true teacher.

These rules enable you to discern the true from the false, and thus to set before yourselves only things that are possible and characterized by moderation; they forbid you to use a cloak of ignorance, which will result in you achieving nothing and abandoning yourself to melancholy in despair.

The natural desire of good men is knowledge.

I know that many will call this a useless work, and they will be those of whom Demetrius <note>Demetrius the Cynic, a 1st-century philosopher known for his blunt honesty and contempt for superficiality</note> said that he took no more account of the wind that produced the words in their mouths than of the wind that came out of their backsides—men whose only desire is for material riches and luxury, and who are entirely destitute of the desire for wisdom, which is the sustenance and the only true riches of the soul. For as the soul is more worthy than the body, so much more are the soul’s riches more worthy than those of the body. And often when I see one of these men take this work in hand, I wonder whether he will not put it to his nose like an ape and ask me whether it is something to eat.

# PROEM

I know well that, because I am not a man of book-learning, some will think they can reasonably criticize me by claiming that I lack literary skill. Foolish people! Do they not know that I might answer them as Marius did the Roman patricians, by saying: "Those who deck themselves out in the labors of others will not allow me my own"? They will say that, because I have not learned from books, I cannot properly express what I wish to treat of. But they do not know that my subjects require experience rather than the words of others; and experience has been the mistress of those who wrote well, and so, as a mistress, I will cite her in all cases.

Many will believe that they can reasonably censure me, alleging that my proofs are contrary to the authority of certain men who are held in great reverence by their inexperienced judgments, not taking into account that my conclusions were arrived at as a result of simple and pure experience, which is the true mistress.

These rules enable you to discern the true from the false, and thus to set before yourselves only things that are possible and characterized by moderation; and they forbid you to use a cloak of ignorance, which will result in your attaining no result and, in despair, abandoning yourself to melancholy.

The natural desire of good men is knowledge.

I know that many will call this a useless work, and they will be those of whom Democritus said that he took no more account of the wind that produced the words in their mouths than of the wind that came out of their hindquarters: men whose only desire is for material riches and luxury and who are entirely destitute of the desire for wisdom, the sustenance and only true riches of the soul. For as the soul is much worthier than the body, so much more worthy are the soul's riches than those of the body. And often when I see one of these men take this work in hand, I wonder whether he will not put it to his nose like an ape and ask me whether it is something to eat.

Begun in Florence in the house of Piero di Braccio Martelli, on the 22nd day of March, 1508. This will be a collection without order, made up of many sheets which I have copied here, hoping afterwards to arrange them in order in their proper places according to the subjects of which they treat; and I believe that before I am at the end of this I shall have to repeat the same thing several times, and therefore, O reader, blame me not, because the subjects are many and the memory cannot retain them and say "I will not write this because I have already written it." And if I wished to avoid falling into this mistake it would be necessary, in order to prevent repetition, that on every occasion when I wanted to transcribe a passage I should always read over all the preceding portion, and this especially because long periods of time elapse between one time of writing and another.

## I
# Philosophy

->'Nature is full of infinite causes which were never demonstrated in experience.'<-

WE HAVE no lack of systems or devices to measure and to divide up these poor days of ours; in which it should be our pleasure that they are not squandered or allowed to pass away in vain, and without the reward of honor, leaving no record of themselves in the minds of men; so that this poor life of ours may not be spent in vain.

Our judgment does not calculate in their exact and proper order things which have happened at different periods of time; for many things which happened many years ago will seem closely related to the present, and many things that are recent will seem ancient, reaching back to the far-off period of our youth. And so it is with the eye regarding distant things, which, when illuminated by the sun, seem near to the eye, while many things which are near seem far off.

Supreme happiness will be the greatest cause of misery, and the perfection of wisdom the occasion of folly.

Every part is inclined to unite with the whole, so that it may thereby escape from its own incompleteness.

The soul desires to dwell with the body because without the members of that body it can neither act nor feel.

¹ Gerolamo Calvi has shown in an article in the *Historical Lombard Archive* <note>original: "Archivio Storico Lombardo"</note>, Year 49 (1916) Issue 3, that the source of this passage is found in Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, Book 15, lines 232–236:

The passage as it appears in the *Codice Atlantico* <note>The "Atlantic Codex," Leonardo’s largest collection of drawings and writings</note> serves to show how Leonardo, in borrowing these lines, enriched the Roman poet’s thought with the melody of music by introducing the address to time and envious age as both a prelude and a finale:

> "O time, consumer of things, and O envious antiquity, you destroy all things and consume all things with the hard teeth of old age, little by little, with a lingering death! Helen, when she looked at herself in the mirror and saw the withered wrinkles of her face made by old age, cried and thought to herself: why was I snatched away twice? Elena quando si specchiava... O tempo, consumatore delle cose..."</note>

Immediately below this passage, Leonardo wrote these words: "this book belongs to Michele di Francesco Bernabini and his family." It is a reasonable conclusion that this refers to the copy of Ovid from which the lines were taken. Further below, in handwriting from the same period, is a fragment: "Tell, tell me how things are passing over there, and whether Caterina wishes to make..."

Caterina was the name of Leonardo’s mother. He wrote the name just as his thoughts had been turning to the poet’s description of the changes that time had made in Helen’s beauty. From this has arisen the conjecture—though it is nothing more!—that the sentence refers to her and that he was making some provision for her in her old age.

There is no result in nature without a cause; understand the cause, and you will have no need for the experiment. <margin>Codex Atlanticus 147 verso a</margin>

Experience is never at fault; it is only your judgment that is in error by promising itself results from experience that are not caused by our experiments. When a process is started, whatever follows from it must necessarily be a natural development of that beginning, unless it has been subject to a contrary influence. If it is affected by any contrary influence, the result which ought to follow from the original beginning will be found to be influenced by this opposition, to a greater or lesser degree, depending on whether the said influence is more or less powerful than the original beginning. <margin>Codex Atlanticus 154 recto b</margin>

Experience is not at fault; it is only our judgment that is in error in expecting things from experience which are not within her power.

Men are wrong to cry out against experience and, with bitter reproaches, accuse her of deceitfulness. Leave experience alone, and instead turn your complaints against your own ignorance, which causes you to be so carried away by your vain and foolish <note>original: "insensate"</note> desires as to expect things from experience which are not within her power!

Men are wrong to cry out against innocent experience, often accusing her of deceit and false demonstrations! <margin>Codex Atlanticus 154 recto c</margin>

O mathematicians, shed light on this error.

The spirit has no voice, for where there is a voice, there is a body; and where there is a body, there is an occupation of space which prevents the eye from seeing things situated beyond that space. C.A. 289 v. b
Nothingness has no center, and its boundaries are nothingness.

My opponent says that nothingness and a vacuum are one and the same thing, having indeed two separate names by which they are called, but not existing separately in nature.

The reply is that whenever a vacuum exists, the space which surrounds it will also exist, but nothingness exists apart from the occupation of space. It follows that nothingness and a vacuum are not the same, for the one is infinitely divisible, and nothingness cannot be divided because nothing can be less than it is; and if you were to take a part from it, this part would be equal to the whole, and the whole to the part.

### CORNELIUS CELSUS ¹

Tr. 3 a
The chief good is wisdom; the chief evil is the suffering of the body. Seeing, therefore, that we are made up of two things—namely, soul and body, of which the first is the superior and the body is the inferior—wisdom belongs to the better part, and the chief evil belongs to the worse part and is the worst. The best thing in the soul is wisdom, just as the worst thing in the body is pain. Therefore, as the chief evil is bodily pain, so wisdom is the chief good of the soul—that is, of the wise man—and nothing else can be compared to it.

The lover is drawn by the thing loved, just as the senses are by what they perceive; the lover unites with it, and they become one and the same thing. The work is the first thing born of this union; if the thing loved is base, the lover becomes base. When the thing taken into union is in harmony with that which receives it, rejoicing follows.

Many times one and the same thing is pulled by two forces: namely, necessity and power.

Water falls as rain; the earth absorbs it out of a necessity for moisture; and the sun draws it upward, not out of necessity, but by its power.

The soul can never be infected by the corruption of the body, but acts within the body like the wind that creates the sound of an organ; if one of the pipes becomes damaged, no good result can be produced because of its defect.

If you kept your body in accordance with virtue, your desires would not be of this world.

You grow in reputation like bread in the hands of children.

There cannot be any sound where there is no movement or striking of the air. There cannot be any striking of the air where there is no instrument. There cannot be any instrument without a physical body. This being the case, a spirit cannot have sound, form, or force; and if it should take on a body, it cannot penetrate or enter where the doors are shut. And if anyone should say that by collecting and compressing air, a spirit may take on bodies of various shapes, and by such an instrument may speak and move with force, my reply to this would be that where there are neither nerves nor bones, there cannot be any force exerted in any movement made by imaginary spirits. Avoid the teachings of those theorists whose arguments are not confirmed by experience.

### OF WHAT FORCE IS

I define force as a spiritual power, incorporeal and invisible, which, with a brief life, is produced in those bodies that are taken out of their natural state and condition as a result of external violence.

I have said spiritual because in this force there is an active, incorporeal life; and I call it invisible because the body in which it is created does not increase in either weight or size; and of brief dura-

## THE CONFIGURATION OF THE ELEMENTS

Regarding the configuration of the elements, and first against those who deny the opinion of Plato, claiming that if these elements surround one another in the shapes Plato attributed to them, a vacuum would be created between them—which is not true. I prove this here, but first of all it is necessary to set forth certain conclusions.

It is not necessary for any of the elements that surround one another to be of equal thickness throughout their entire extent, between the part that surrounds and the part that is surrounded. We see that the sphere of water is clearly of different degrees of thickness from its surface to its base, and that it would not only cover the earth if it had the shape of a cube—that is, of eight angles, as Plato would have it—but it covers the earth even though it has the innumerable angles of rocks covered by the water and various protrusions and hollows, without creating any vacuum between the water and the earth. Moreover, regarding the air which clothes the sphere of water along with the mountains and valleys that rise above this sphere, no vacuum is left between the earth and the air. So, whoever has said that a vacuum is produced there has spoken foolishly.

To Plato, one would answer that the surfaces of the figures the elements would have according to him could not exist.

Every flexible and liquid element necessarily has a spherical surface. This is proved by the sphere of water, but first certain concepts and conclusions must be set forth. That thing is higher which is more remote from the center of the world, and that is lower which is nearer this center. Water does not move of its own accord unless it descends, and in moving itself, it descends. These four concepts, paired two by two, serve to prove to me that water which does not move of its own accord has a surface equidistant to the center of the world—speaking not of drops or other small quantities that attract one another as steel attracts its filings, but of great masses.

## OF THE SOUL

The movement of earth against earth pressing down upon it causes a slight movement of the parts struck.

Water struck by water creates circles at a great distance around the spot where it is struck; the voice in the air travels further, in fire further still; the mind ranges over the universe, but being finite, it does not extend into infinity.

The water which rises in the mountains is the blood which keeps the mountain alive. If one of its veins is opened, either internally or at the side, nature—which assists its organisms—overflowing with an increased desire to overcome the scarcity of moisture thus poured out, is generous there with diligent aid; this also happens at the place where a man has received a blow. For one sees then how, as help arrives, the blood increases under the skin in the form of a swelling in order to open the infected part. Similarly, when life is severed at the highest peak (of the mountain), nature sends her fluid from its lowest foundations up to the greatest height of the severed passage; and as this is poured out there, she does not leave it bereft of vital fluid until the end of its life.

Every wrong shall be set right.

## FLAX AND DEATH

Flax is dedicated to death and human corruption: to death by the nets in lakes for birds, beasts, and fish; to corruption by the linen cloths in which the dead are wrapped when they are buried, for in these cloths they undergo corruption.

And moreover, this flax does not become separated from its stalks until it begins to soften and decay; and it is this material which one should use to make garlands and decorations for funeral processions.

Truth alone was the daughter of time.

Small rooms or dwellings set the mind on the right path; large ones cause it to go astray.

Just as eating against one's inclination is harmful to health, so study without desire spoils the memory, and it retains nothing that it takes in.

Do not call that riches which may be lost; virtue is our true wealth and the true reward of its possessor. It cannot be lost; it will not abandon us unless life itself leaves us first. As for property and material wealth, you should always hold these in fear; quite often they leave their possessor in disgrace, mocked for having lost possession of them.

That which is termed "nothingness" is found only in time and speech. In time, it is found between the past and the future and retains nothing of the present; in speech, it likewise occurs when the things being spoken of do not exist or are impossible.

### [*Of the end of the world*]

The watery element remaining pent up within the raised banks of the rivers and the shores of the sea, it will happen with the upheaval of the earth that as the encircling air must bind and surround the complicated structure of the earth, its mass—which was between the water and the fiery element—will be left tightly hemmed in and deprived of the necessary supply of water.

The rivers will remain without their waters; the fertile earth will no longer put forth her budding branches; the fields will no longer be adorned with waving grain. All the animals will perish, failing to find fresh grass for fodder; and the ravenous lions, wolves, and other beasts that live by prey will lack sustenance; and it will come to pass after many desperate struggles that men will be forced to abandon their lives, and the human race will cease to exist.

And in this way, the fertile, fruitful earth, being deserted, will be left arid and sterile; and through the pent-up moisture of the water enclosed within its womb and by the activity of its nature, it will partly follow its law of growth until, having passed through the cold and thin air, it will be forced to end its course in the element of fire. Then its surface will remain burnt to a cinder, and this will be the end of all terrestrial nature.

### [*A disputation*]

*Against.*—Why nature did not ordain that one animal should not live by the death of another.

*For.*—Nature, being capricious and taking pleasure in creating and producing a continuous succession of lives and forms because she knows that they serve to increase her terrestrial substance, is more ready and swift in creating than time is in destroying; and therefore she has ordained that many animals shall serve as food for one another; and as this does not satisfy her desire, she frequently sends forth certain foul and pestilential vapors and continual plagues upon the vast accumulations and herds of animals, and especially upon hu-

--- Page 83 ---
human beings who increase very rapidly because other animals do not feed upon them; and if the causes are removed, the results will cease.

Against.—Therefore, this earth seeks to lose its life while desiring continual reproduction for the reason presented and demonstrated to you. Effects often resemble their causes. Animals serve as a model for the life of the world.

For.—Behold now the hope and desire of going back to one’s own country or returning to primal chaos, like that of the moth to the light, or of the man who, with perpetual longing, always looks forward with joy to each new spring and each new summer, and to the new months and the new years, feeling that the things he longs for are too slow in coming; and who does not perceive that he is longing for his own destruction. But this longing is, in its quintessence, the spirit of the elements, which, finding itself imprisoned within the life of the human body, desires continually to return to its source.

And I would have you know that this same longing is, in its quintessence, inherent in nature, and that man is a model of the world.

Therefore, the end of nothingness and the beginning of the line are in contact with one another, but they are not joined together; and in such contact is the point which divides the continuation of nothingness from the line.

It follows that the point is less than nothing, and if all the parts of nothingness are equal to one, we may further conclude that all points are also equal to one single point, and one point is equal to all.

And from this it follows that many points imagined in continuous contact do not constitute a line, and consequently, many lines in continuous contact along their sides do not make a surface, nor do many surfaces in continuous contact make a body, because among us, bodies are not formed of incorporeal things.

The point is that which has no center because it is all center, and nothing can be smaller.

The contact of a liquid with a solid is a surface common to both the liquid and the solid, and lighter liquids have the same relationship with heavier ones.

All points are equal to one, and one is equal to all.

--- Page 84 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of the mathematical and physical nature of boundaries (points and surfaces) and begins to apply these geometric principles to the concept of time.</meta>

Nothingness <note>original: "nulla"; here referring to a vacuum or the absolute absence of matter</note> has a surface in common with a physical thing, and the thing has a surface in common with nothingness. The surface of a thing is not actually a part of that thing. It follows, therefore, that the surface of nothingness is not part of that nothingness. It must be, then, that a mere surface is the common boundary of two things that are in contact. Thus, the surface of water does not form part of the water, nor, consequently, does it form part of the atmosphere, and no other bodies are placed between them. What is it, therefore, that separates the atmosphere from the water? There must be a common boundary which is neither air nor water and is without physical substance, because any body placed between two other bodies would prevent them from touching. This does not happen with water and air, because they are in contact without any medium <note>original: "interposition of any medium"; meaning no third substance is between them</note> between them.

<margin>British Museum Manuscript 159, Verso</margin>
Therefore, they are joined together, and you cannot raise or move the air without moving the water, nor will you be able to lift a flat object from another without drawing it back through the air. Therefore, a surface is the common boundary of two bodies which are not a single continuous piece; it does not form part of either one or the other. If the surface formed part of a body, it would have a thickness <note>original: "divisible bulk"</note> that could be divided, whereas a surface is not divisible, and "nothingness" <note>the dimensionless boundary</note> divides these bodies from one another.

### OF TIME AS A CONTINUOUS QUANTITY

Although time is counted among continuous quantities, because it is invisible and lacks physical substance, it does not fully fall under the category of geometric terms. Geometry is divided into shapes and bodies of infinite variety, as can constantly be seen in visible and physical things. However, time matches these geometric terms only in its first principles: namely, the **point** and the **line**. 

The **point**, when viewed in terms of time, should be compared to the **instant**. The **line** resembles the length of a duration <note>original: "quantity of time"</note>. Just as points are the beginning and end of a line, instants form the end and the beginning of any given space of time. And if a line is divisible to infinity, it is not impossible for a space of time to be divided in the same way. And if the divided parts of a line may

## DISCOURSE

Heat and cold result from the closeness or distance of the sun.

Heat and cold produce the movement of the elements.

No element has, by itself, inherent weight <term>original: "gravity"</term> or lightness <term>original: "levity"</term>.

Weight and lightness (without an external increase) arise from the movement of the element within itself through its expansion <term>original: "rarefaction"</term> and contraction <term>original: "condensation"</term>. We see this happen in the atmosphere during the creation of clouds, caused by the moisture that is spread through it.

When weight and lightness are increased, they move along a perpendicular line from one element to another. These physical events have as much more power as they have more "life," and they have as much more "life" as they have more movement. <note>The author often uses "life" to describe the kinetic energy or vital force driving natural processes.</note>

Movement originates from the fact that a thinner (less dense) substance can neither resist nor support a denser substance above it.

Lightness is born of weight, and weight is born of lightness. In the very instant of their creation, they repay the gift of their birth: they grow more in power as they grow in "life," and they have more life in proportion to their movement. In that same instant, they also destroy one another in a mutual cycle of destruction <note>original: "vendetta"</note>.

This is proven as follows: lightness is not created unless it is joined with weight, nor is weight produced unless it continues into lightness. Lightness has no existence unless it is beneath weight, and weight is nothing unless it is above lightness. So it is with the elements. For example, if a quantity of air lay beneath water, it follows that the water immediately acquires weight; not because the water itself has changed from its original condition, but because it does not meet with the necessary amount of resistance. It therefore descends into the position occupied—

occupied by the air which was beneath it, and the air fills up the vacuum which the gravity so created has left in it.

Every continuous quantity is infinitely divisible; therefore, the division of this quantity will never result in a point defined as the end of a line. It follows that the breadth and depth of a natural line are divisible to infinity.

<margin>B.M. 204 v.</margin>
It is asked whether all infinites are equal or whether one is greater than the other. The answer is that every infinite is eternal, and eternal things are equal in their permanence but not in the length of their existence. For that which functioned first began to divide and has experienced a longer existence, but the periods yet to come are equal.

No element possesses inherent gravity or levity unless it moves. The earth is in contact with the water and with the air and has, in itself, neither gravity nor levity. It has no awareness of the water or air surrounding it except by the accident that arises from their movement. We learn this from the leaves of plants growing upon the earth when it is in contact with water or air, for they do not bend except by the movement of the air or water.

From the foregoing, we should say that gravity is an event created by the movement of the lower elements within the higher.

Levity is an event created when a thinner element is drawn beneath a less thin one, which then moves because it is unable to resist and consequently acquires weight; this weight is created as soon as the element lacks the power of resistance. When this resistance is overcome by weight, it does not change without a change of substance; and in changing, it acquires the name of levity.

Levity is not produced except alongside gravity, nor gravity without levity. This may be demonstrated: for if air is suspended under water by blowing through a pipe, then this air will acquire levity from being beneath the water, and the water will acquire gravity from having beneath it the air, which is a body thinner and lighter than itself.

Therefore, levity is born of weight and weight of lightness; they give birth to one another while simultaneously repaying the gift of their existence, and at the same instant, they destroy one another as the avengers of their own death.

## EXAMPLE OF THE CENTER OF THE WORLD

<margin>British Museum MS 267 r.</margin>
Suppose the earth, together with its water, were drawn to the position of the moon, and that the element of air fills the vacuum in space which the earth left behind when it moved. If a vase full of air were then dropped from the air, it is certain that this vase—after many wavering movements, falling and rebounding <note>original: "reflex"</note>—would come to a stop at approximately the center of the elements. The center of the elements would remain in the air that is within the vase, and it would not touch the vase itself. Or, suppose the earth were hollowed out like a ball full of wind; you would then be certain that this center is not in the earth itself, but in the air contained <note>original: "clothed"</note> by the earth.

## OF NECROMANCY

But of all human discourses, that which affirms a belief in necromancy must be considered the most foolish. Necromancy is the sister of alchemy, which produces simple and natural things; however, necromancy is much more worthy of blame than alchemy because it never gives birth to anything at all except things like itself—that is to say, lies. This is not the case with alchemy, which works with the simple products of nature, performing functions that nature herself cannot execute because she lacks the organic instruments to do the work that man performs with his hands (by which he has made glass, etc.). But this necromancy—a mere banner or flying flag blown by the wind—is the guide of the foolish masses, who provide a continual witness by their shouting to the limitless effects of such an art. And they have filled entire books asserting that enchantments and spirits can work and speak without tongues, and can speak without any organic instrument—without which speech is impossible—and can carry the heaviest weights, and bring storms and rain, and that men can be changed into cats and wolves and other beasts, although those who affirm such things are the first to become beasts themselves.

And undoubtedly, if this necromancy did exist, as is believed by shallow minds, there is nothing on earth that would have so much power either to harm or to benefit man. That is, if it were true that by such an art one had the power to disturb the tranquil clarity of the air and transform it into the darkness of night; to create flashes of light and tempests with dreadful claps of thunder and lightning bolts rushing through the darkness; and with violent storms to overthrow high—

---

<note>¹ The phrase is one used by Benjamin Jowett regarding smoking. His advice was: ‘Do not create for yourself any new necessities.’</note>

--- Page 90 ---
<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s critique of necromancy from the previous page, shifting from the imagined powers of magic to the logical proof of why spirits cannot exist within the physical world, ultimately advocating for the certainties of mathematics.</meta>

<page-num>82</page-num>
<header>PHILOSOPHY</header>

...buildings and uproot forests, and with these to encounter armies and break and overthrow them, and—more important even than this—to make the devastating tempests, and thereby rob the farmers <note>original: "husbandmen"</note> of the reward of their labors. For what method of warfare can there be which can inflict such damage upon the enemy as the exercise of the power to deprive him of his crops? What sea battle could there be which should compare with that which he would wage who has command of the winds and can create ruinous tempests that would submerge every fleet whatsoever? In truth, whoever has control of such irresistible forces will be lord over all nations, and no human skill will be able to resist his destructive power. The buried treasures, the jewels that lie in the depths of the earth will all become manifest to him; no lock, no fortress, however impregnable, will avail to save anyone against the will of such a <term>necromancer</term> (one who claims to communicate with the dead or command supernatural forces). He will cause himself to be carried through the air from East to West, and through all the uttermost parts of the universe. But why do I thus go on adding instance after instance? What is there which could not be brought to pass by a <term>mechanician</term> (an engineer or master of mechanics) such as this? Almost nothing, except escaping from death.

We have therefore determined in part the harm and the usefulness that belong to such an art if it is real; and if it is real, why has it not remained among men who desire so much—not having regard for any deity—merely because there are an infinite number of persons who, in order to satisfy one of their appetites, would destroy God and the whole universe?

<margin>Fogli B. 31 v.</margin> <note>original: "Fogli" refers to the individual sheets of Leonardo's notebooks.</note>
If then it has never remained among men, although so necessary to them, it never existed, and never can exist, as follows from the definition of a <term>spirit</term> (an entity without a physical body), which is invisible and <term>incorporeal</term> (lacking a physical body). For within the elements there are no <term>incorporeal</term> things, because where there is no body there is a <term>vacuum</term> (a space entirely empty of matter), and the <term>vacuum</term> does not exist within the elements, because it would be instantly filled up by the element. 

<margin>Quaderni I. 7 r.</margin> <note>original: "Quaderni" refers to Leonardo's bound notebooks.</note>
Therefore, O students, study <term>mathematics</term> (the science of logic, number, and space) and do not build without foundations. 

Mental things which have not passed through the understanding are vain and give birth to no truth other than what is harmful. And because such discourses spring from poverty of intellect, those who make...

...such people are always poor, and if they were born rich, they will die poor in their old age. For nature, it seems, takes vengeance on those who would attempt to perform miracles; they end up with less than other men who live more quietly. Those who wish to grow rich in a single day shall live a long time in great poverty. This happens—and will happen for all eternity—to alchemists (the would-be creators of gold and silver), to engineers who think they can make stagnant <note>original: "dead"</note> water move itself with perpetual motion, and to those supreme fools: the <term>necromancer</term> (one who claims to speak with the dead) and the enchanter. <margin>Notebooks I 13 verso <note>original: "Quaderni I 13 v."</note></margin>

### [*The certainty of mathematics*]

Anyone who criticizes the supreme certainty of mathematics feeds on confusion and will never be able to silence the contradictions of the sophistical sciences, which cause a perpetual noise <note>original: "clamour"</note>.

Those who summarize <note>original: "abbreviators"</note> works do harm to both knowledge and love. For love of anything is the child of knowledge; love is more intense <note>original: "fervent"</note> as knowledge becomes more certain. This certainty arises from a complete understanding of all the parts that, when united, compose the whole of the thing being loved.

Of what use, I ask, is someone who—in order to shorten his account of a subject he claims to know fully—leaves out the majority of the parts that make up the whole?

Truly, impatience—the mother of folly—is what praises brevity. It is as if such people did not have a lifetime long enough to acquire complete knowledge of even one particular subject, such as the human body. And yet they think they can comprehend the mind of God, which embraces the entire universe, weighing and dissecting it as though they were performing an <term>anatomy</term> (a structural dissection). O human stupidity! Do you not see that you have spent your whole life with yourself, and yet you are not aware of what is most obvious: your own foolishness? 

And so, like a crowd of <term>sophists</term> (those who use clever but flawed reasoning), you think to deceive yourself and others by despising the mathematical sciences, which contain true information about the subjects they address! Or perhaps you would rather wander among "miracles" and give your opinions on subjects that the human mind is incapable of understanding and which cannot be proven by any natural example. It seems to you that you have performed miracles when...

<summary>Leonardo critiques the pursuit of alchemy and "miracles," contrasting the failures of such "fools" with the absolute certainty found in mathematics. He argues that true understanding requires deep, patient study of all parts of a subject rather than lazy summaries.</summary>
<keywords>mathematics, alchemy, perpetual motion, knowledge and love, human folly, sophistry, anatomy, brevity</keywords>

You have spoiled the work of some ingenious mind, and you do not perceive that you are falling into the same error as he who strips a tree of its adornment of branches laden with leaves intermingled with fragrant flowers or fruits, in order to demonstrate the suitability of the tree for making planks. This is just as Justinus did, the creator of an epitome of the histories of Trogus Pompeius, who had written an elaborate account of all the great deeds of his ancestors which lent themselves to picturesque description; for by doing so, Justinus composed a bald work fit only for such impatient minds as believe themselves to be wasting time when they spend it usefully in the study of the works of nature and of human affairs.

Let such people as these remain in the company of beasts, and let their courtiers be dogs and other animals eager for prey, and let them keep company with them; forever pursuing whatever flees from them, they hunt the inoffensive animals who, in the season of the snowdrifts, are driven by hunger to approach your doors to beg alms from you as from a guardian.

If you are, as you have described yourself, the king of the animals—though it would be better for you to call yourself king of the beasts, since you are the greatest of them all!—why do you not help them so that they may later be able to give you their young to gratify your palate, for the sake of which you have tried to make yourself a tomb for all the animals? I might say even more, if speaking the entire truth were permitted to me.

But let us not leave this subject without referring to one supreme form of wickedness which hardly exists among the animals, among whom there are none that devour their own species except for a lack of reason (for there are insane individuals among them as among human beings, though not in such great numbers). Nor does this happen except among the voracious animals, such as the lion species and among leopards, panthers, lynxes, cats, and creatures like these, which sometimes eat their young. But you not only eat your children, but you eat father, mother, brothers, and friends; and even this not being enough for you, you make raids on foreign islands and capture men of other races, and then, after mutilating them in a shameful manner, you fatten them up and cram them down your throat. Say, does not nature bring forth a sufficiency of

85
PHILOSOPHY

...simple things to produce satiety? Or if you cannot content yourself with simple things, can you not, by blending these together, make an infinite number of compounds as did Platina and other authors who have written for epicures?

And if any be found virtuous and good, do not drive them away from you, but do them honor lest they flee from you and take refuge in hermitages and caves or other solitary places in order to escape from your deceits. If any such person be found, pay him reverence; for as these are like gods upon the earth, they deserve statues, images, and honors. But I would impress upon you that their images are not to be eaten by you, as happens in a certain district of India; for there, when in the judgment of the priests these images have worked some miracle, they cut them in pieces—being made of wood—and distribute them to all the people of the locality, not without payment.

And each of them then grates his portion very fine and spreads it over the first food he eats; and so they consider that symbolically, by faith, they have eaten their saint, and they believe that he will then guard them from all dangers. What do you think, O Man, of your species? Are you as wise as you set yourself up to be? Are acts such as these things that men should do, Justinus?

Let no one read me who is not a mathematician in my basic principles.

Every action of nature is made by the shortest possible way.

You, O God, sell to us all good things at the price of labor.

PHILOSOPHY

## GIOVANNI ANTONIO DI GIOVANNI AMBROSIO
## DA BOLATE ¹

He who allows time to slip away and does not grow in virtue—the more one thinks about him, the sadder one becomes.

No man has a capacity for virtue who sacrifices honor for profit. Fortune is powerless to help one who does not exert himself. That man becomes happy who follows Christ.

There is no perfect gift without great suffering. Our triumphs and our ceremonies pass away; gluttony, sloth, and weakening luxury have banished every virtue from the world; so that, as if wandering from its course, our nature is subdued by habit. Now and from this point on, it is proper that you cure yourself of laziness. The Master has said that sitting on down cushions or lying under quilts will not bring you to fame.

He who has frittered life away without fame leaves no more trace of himself upon the earth than smoke does in the air or foam on the water.

Nothing grows in a spot where there is neither sentient, fibrous, nor rational life. Feathers grow upon birds and change every year; hair grows upon animals and changes every year, except for certain parts such as the hair of the beard in lions, cats, and similar creatures. Grass grows in the fields, leaves upon the trees, and every year these are largely renewed. So then we may say that the earth has a spirit of growth, and that its flesh is the soil; its bones are the successive layers of the rocks which form the mountains; its cartilage is the tufa stone; its blood is the springs of its waters. The lake of blood that lies around the heart is the ocean. Its breathing is the increase and decrease of the blood in its pulses, and just so in the earth is the ebb and flow of the sea. And the vital heat of the world is fire, which is spread throughout the earth; and the dwelling place of its creative spirit is in the fires, which in various parts of the earth are breathed out in thermal baths, sulfur mines, and in volcanoes, such as Mount Etna in Sicily, and in many other places.

# PHILOSOPHY

Falsehood is so utterly vile that even if it were used to praise the great works of God, it would offend His divinity. Truth is of such excellence that if it praises even the lowliest things, they become ennobled.

Without doubt, truth stands in relation to falsehood as light does to darkness. Truth is in itself of such excellence that even when it treats humble and lowly matters, it still immeasurably outweighs the sophistries <note>original: "sophistries"; clever but false arguments intended to deceive</note> and falsehoods that are spread throughout grand and high-sounding discourses. For although we have established falsehood as a "fifth element" <note>In traditional philosophy, the four elements were earth, water, air, and fire; the "fifth element" or quintessence was the pure substance of the heavens. The author suggests humans have made lying a fundamental part of their reality.</note> in our mental state, it remains that the truth of things is the primary food for all superior intellects—though certainly not for wandering or unstable wits.

But as for you who live in dreams: specious <note>original: "specious"; seeming right or true, but actually wrong</note> reasonings and the kind of feints and tricks that *palla* <note>original: "palla"; an Italian ball game (ancestor to tennis) involving deceptive movements</note> players might use please you more—provided they deal with vast and uncertain things—than do those things which are certain, natural, and make no such grand claims.
