<insert>*[Precepts for the study of the foot]*</insert>
You will make these two feet with the same contours turned in the same direction, and do not pay any regard to the fact that one remains the right and the other the left, because by making them this way they will be easier to understand.
First you will make all these bones separated from one another, arranged in such a way that each part of each bone may be seen, or may be turned toward the side of that bone from which it is separated, and to which it should be reunited when you join all the bones of these feet together in their original state.
And this demonstration is made in order to be better able to recognize the true shape of each bone in itself; and you will do the same with each demonstration of each limb, in whatever direction it may be turned. ->Fogli <term>A 1 r.</term><-

<insert>*[Method for the study of the arm and the forearm]*</insert>
You will first have these bones sawn lengthwise and then across, so that one can see where the bones are thick or thin; then represent them whole and separated, as shown above, but from four perspectives so that one can understand their true shape; then proceed to clothe them by degrees with their nerves, veins, and muscles.

<insert>*[Method for the study of the parts of the human body]*</insert>
The true knowledge of the shape of any body will be arrived at by seeing it from different perspectives. Consequently, in order to convey a

--- Page 102 ---
<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s detailed instructions for anatomical study, specifically focusing on the systematic illustration of limbs and his observations on the mechanics of the arm and the voice.</meta>

# ANATOMY

To provide a clear understanding of the true shape of any human limb—man being the highest of all animals—I will follow the rule mentioned before. I will create four demonstrations for the four sides of each limb. For the bones, I will create five demonstrations, cutting them in half to show the hollow of each; one will show the marrow, while the other will show the spongy, empty, or solid parts.

### [On the bones of the arm]

The arm, which contains the two bones located between the hand and the elbow, will be slightly shorter when the palm of the hand is turned toward the ground than when it is turned toward the sky, assuming the person is standing with their arm extended. This happens because these two bones <note>These are the radius and the ulna.</note>, in turning the palm toward the ground, cross each other. The bone that starts on the right side of the elbow moves toward the left side of the palm, and the bone that starts on the left side of the elbow ends on the right side of the palm.

<margin>Sheet A 1, back <note>original: Fogli A I v.</note></margin>
The arm is composed of thirty pieces of bone: three in the arm itself <note>The humerus, radius, and ulna.</note> and twenty-seven in the hand.

### [On the attachment of the muscles]

<margin>Sheet A 2, front <note>original: Fogli A 2 r.</note></margin>
The muscles mentioned above are only firmly attached at the ends of their casings and at the tips of their tendons. The Creator <note>original: the Master</note> has designed them this way so that the muscles remain free and ready to grow thicker, shorter, thinner, or longer, depending on the needs of the body part they are moving.

Begin your study of anatomy with the head and finish it with the soles of the feet.

### [Mechanism of voice production]

This is the rule for seeing how the sound of the voice is produced in the front of the windpipe <note>original: trachea</note>. This can be understood by removing the windpipe along with the human lungs. If the lungs are filled with air and then squeezed rapidly, one will immediately be able to see how the pipe called the trachea produces sound. This can also be clearly seen and heard in the neck of a swan or a goose, which often continues to make sound even after it is dead.

One cannot swallow and breathe—or make a sound—at the same time.

<summary>Leonardo explains his systematic method for illustrating bones and muscles, describes the rotational mechanics of the forearm, and proposes an experimental method to understand how the lungs and trachea produce the human voice.</summary>

One cannot breathe through the nose and through the mouth at the same time; and this is demonstrated if one should attempt to play one whistle or flute with the nose and another with the mouth simultaneously.

## WHY THE VOICE BECOMES THIN IN THE ELDERLY

Fogli A 3 r.
The voice becomes thin in the elderly because all the passages of the trachea become constricted, just as the other internal organs do.

Fogli A 3 v.
The pieces of bone of which a man’s foot is composed number twenty-seven, taking into account the two which are beneath the base of the big toe.

## THE NATURE OF THE VEINS

The origin of the sea is the opposite of that of the blood, for the sea receives into itself all the rivers, which are entirely caused by the water vapors that have ascended into the air; whereas the sea of the blood is the source of all the veins.

## ON THE NUMBER OF THE VEINS

The vein is a single whole, which is divided into as many main branches as there are principal places it must nourish, and these branches are subdivided an infinite number of times.

[Movements of the neck]
The neck has four movements, of which the first consists of raising and the second of lowering the face, the third of turning right or left, and the fourth of tilting the head toward the right or left shoulder. ### REASON WHY TWO MUSCLES ARE JOINED TOGETHER

It often happens that two muscles are joined together even though they serve two different limbs. This is done so that if one muscle is injured or disabled, the other can partially take the place of the one that is missing. <gloss>Fogli A 11 verso <note>original: "v." refers to "verso," the back side of a leaf or page in a manuscript.</note></gloss>

## HOW THE MUSCLES ARE ATTACHED TO THE JOINTS OF THE BONES

The end of each muscle transforms into a tendon, which binds the joint of the bone to which this muscle is attached.

## ON THE NUMBER OF TENDONS AND MUSCLES

The number of tendons—which overlap one another in layers and together cover and bind the bone joint they are joined to—is equal to the number of muscles that meet at that same joint.

<margin>Sheets <note>original Italian: "Fogli"</note> A 15 recto <note>The "recto" or front side of the leaf.</note></margin>
Suppose the connection of muscle *b* is made with the thigh bone and specifically with muscle *a*. Or, perhaps muscle *b* and muscle *a* are joined together and unite to attach themselves to this thigh bone. This third arrangement <note>Leonardo is likely referring to a combined attachment structure</note> is more effective for moving the thigh and more secure; if muscle *a* were cut or otherwise injured, muscle *b* could still move the thigh by itself. This would be impossible if the bone separated muscle *b* from muscle *a*.

[<insert>Action of muscles in breathing</insert>]
<margin>Sheets <note>original Italian: "Fogli"</note> A 15 verso <note>The "verso" or back side of the leaf.</note></margin>
These muscles move both voluntarily and involuntarily, as they are the ones that open and close the lungs. When they open, they pause their usual function of contracting. The ribs, which were previously drawn up and compressed by the contraction of these muscles, are then released and return to their natural spacing as the chest expands. Because nature allows no vacuum <note>original: "no vacuum in nature"; a reference to the classical scientific belief *horror vacui*, or nature's abhorrence of a vacuum</note>, the lungs—which touch the ribs from the inside—must follow this expansion. Therefore, the lungs open like a pair of bellows, drawing in air to fill the space created.

### [Relation between size and function of muscles]

<margin>Sheets <note>original Italian: "Fogli"</note> A 16 recto <note>The "recto" or front side of the leaf.</note></margin>

### [Function of muscles in breathing]

## A TREATISE ON MAN ACCORDING TO THE INSTRUMENTAL METHOD AND ITS CONTRARY
<note>Leonardo uses "instrumental" to refer to the mechanical or functional study of the body's "instruments" or organs.</note>

Almost universally, muscles do not move the limb to which they are attached. Instead, they move the limb where the tendon originating from the muscle is joined—with the exception of the muscle that raises and moves the ribs <note>original: "side"</note> to assist in breathing.

All these muscles serve to raise the ribs. As they raise the ribs, they expand the chest; as the chest expands, the lungs are also stretched. This expansion of the lungs draws in air, which enters through the mouth as the lungs enlarge.

## ON THE DEMONSTRATION OF HOW THE SPINE IS STABILIZED IN THE NECK

In this demonstration of the neck, one should illustrate as many muscle and tendon shapes as there are functional movements of the neck. The first point noted here is how the strength of the ribs keeps the cervical spine <note>original: "spine of the neck"</note> straight. The tendons that extend up to this spine serve a dual purpose: they support the spine using the ribs, and they support the ribs using the spine.

This doubling of forces located at the opposite ends of the tendon works in the same way that a bowstring works with the ends of a bow <note>original: "arch"</note>.

This convergence of muscles on the spine keeps it upright, just as a ship’s rigging <note>original: "ropes"</note> supports its mast. Furthermore, those same ropes bound to the mast also help support the sides of the ship to which they are attached.

### ON THE METHOD OF REPRESENTING THE CAUSES OF THE MOVEMENTS OF ANY LIMB

First, depict the motor muscles of the bone called the humerus; then, depict the motor muscles in the humerus that cause the arm to straighten or bend. ### ON THE MUSCLES THAT ORIGINATE IN THE RIBS REPRESENTED ABOVE

For a long time, and not without reason, I have doubted whether the muscles that originate beneath the shoulder blades above the third, fourth, and fifth right ribs—and the same also on the left side—are designed for the purpose of keeping the spinal column of the neck straight, to which they attach themselves with their tendons; or whether, in fact, these muscles, as they contract, pull themselves and the ribs toward the nape of the neck by means of the aforementioned tendons attached to the spinal column. Reason leads me to believe that these muscles are intended to support the spinal column so that it does not bend while supporting the heavy head of a man as it lowers or is raised. The muscles of the shoulders or of the pit of the throat do not assist in this, seeing as a man relaxes those originating in the shoulders or the pit of the throat when he raises his shoulders toward his ears, thereby taking away the force from those muscles. By this loosening and contracting, the movement of the neck will not be impeded, nor will the resistance of the spinal column in supporting the head. I am further confirmed in this same opinion by the powerful shape of the ribs where these muscles are located, which is extremely well-adapted to resist any weight or force that would pull.

And if this tendon had to raise the rib in order to facilitate and increase breathing, nature would have placed this cord not at the slant *a b*, but at the greater slant *a c*. And read the propositions set forth below and in the margin, which are relevant to this purpose. <margin>Fogli A 16 v.</margin>

### [*Muscles of hand, leg and foot. Dated note: 1510*]

When you represent the hand, represent with it the arm as far as the elbow, and with this arm the tendons and muscles that move this arm from the elbow. And do the same in the demonstration of the foot.

### [*Precepts for the study of the foot*]

### [*Considerations upon the origin of the muscles of the foot*]

Mondinus says that the muscles which raise the toes of the feet are to be found in the outer part of the thigh; and then he adds that the back of the foot has no muscles because nature has wished to make it light so that it should be easy to move, as it would be heavier if it had a good deal of flesh; and here experience shows that the muscles *a b c d* move the second segments of the toe bones, and that the muscles of the leg *r S t* move the tips of the toes. Here then it is necessary to inquire why necessity has not made them all start in the foot or all in the leg; or why those of the leg which move the tips of the toes should not start in the foot instead of having to make a long journey in order to reach these tips of the toes; and similarly, why those that move the second joints of the toes should not start in the leg.

### [*Precepts*]

Set down first the two bones of the leg from the knee to the foot, then show the first muscles that start upon the said bones, and pro-

### *[By way of note]*

You will create nothing but confusion in your demonstration of the muscles and their positions, origins, and endings, unless you first create a demonstration of the thin muscles using threads <note>Leonardo used strings or "threads" in his drawings to represent the "line of force" or the central axis of a muscle's pull, making the mechanics easier to see.</note>. In this way, you will be able to represent them one above another as nature has placed them. Then, you will be able to name them according to the part of the body <note>original: "member"</note> they serve—for example, the mover of the tip of the big toe, or of the middle bone, or the first bone, and so on.

After you have provided these details, you will show at the side the exact shape, size, and position of each muscle. But remember to place the threads that represent the muscles in the same positions as the central lines of each muscle; in this way, these threads will show the shape of the leg and their distance from each other during rapid movement and while at rest.

### *[The extensor and flexor muscles of the foot]*

The muscles which are only used to move the foot as it rises forward are labeled *m* and *n*, which start in the leg from the knee downward; and those which bend it toward the outside of the ankle are the muscles *f* and *n*. Therefore, *n* is common to both of these movements.

### *[Atrophy of the muscles]*
I have dissected <note>original: "stripped of skin"</note> the body of a person who had been so wasted by illness that their muscles were worn away and reduced to a kind of thin membrane <term>pellicle: a thin skin or film</term>. This occurred in such a way that the tendons, instead of being converted into muscle, were transformed into loose skin; and when the bones were covered with this skin, their natural size was only slightly increased.

### *[Topography of the muscles and motor and sensory nerves of the lower limb]*
You will first show the bones separated and slightly out of position, so that it is possible to better distinguish the shape of each individual bone. Afterward, join them together in such a way that they do not differ from the first demonstration, except in the areas where they touch. Having done this, you will make a third demonstration of those muscles that bind the bones together. 

Afterward, you will make a fourth illustration of the nerves which convey sensation <note>sensory nerves</note>. Then follows the fifth, showing the nerves that move or give direction to the first joints of the toes <note>motor nerves</note>. In the sixth, you will show the muscles on the top of the feet where the sensory nerves are located. The seventh will be that of the veins which supply these muscles of the foot. The eighth will be that of the nerves that move the tips of the toes. The ninth will show the veins and arteries that are positioned between the flesh and the skin. The tenth and last will be the completed foot with all its sensory functions. Finally, you will be able to make an eleventh demonstration in the form of a transparent foot, in which one is able to see all the previously mentioned structures at once.

### *[Precepts for the study of the leg]*
First, however, make the demonstration of the sensory nerves of the leg and their branching <term>ramification: the arrangement of branching parts</term> from four different views, so that one may see exactly where these nerves originate. Then, make a representation of a young, soft foot with fewer visible muscles.

All the nerves in the front of the legs serve the tips of the toes, as is shown with the great toe.

Eleventh, the foot in its final beauty.

## HOW THE FIVE SENSES ARE THE SERVANTS OF THE SOUL

The soul apparently resides in the seat of judgment, and judgment apparently resides in the place where all the senses meet, which is called the "common sense." It is not distributed throughout the entire body as many have believed, but is contained entirely in this one part. For if it were distributed throughout the whole body and every part of it, it would not have been necessary for the sensory organs to converge at one specific spot; instead, it would have been enough for the eye to perform its function of perception on its own surface, rather than transmitting the images of things seen to the common sense by way of the optic nerves. This is because the soul—for the reason already stated—would perceive them directly upon the surface of the eye.

Similarly, regarding the sense of hearing, it would be sufficient for a sound merely to echo in the arched cavities of the petrous bone within the ear, without there being another passage from this bone to the common sense, through which the said sound might report to the common judgment.

The sense of smell is also clearly forced by necessity to have recourse to this same judgment.

The sense of touch passes through the perforated tendons and is transmitted

--- Page 119 ---
to this sense; these tendons proceed to spread out with infinite branches into the skin which encloses the body’s members and the organs. The perforating tendons carry impulse and sensation to the subject limbs; these tendons, passing between the muscles and the sinews, dictate their movement to them, and these obey, and in the act of obeying they contract, because the swelling reduces their length and draws with it the nerves, which are interwoven among the parts of the limbs; and being spread throughout the tips of the fingers, they transmit to the sense the impression of what they touch.

The nerves with their muscles serve the tendons just as soldiers serve their leaders, and the tendons serve the common sense as the leaders serve their captain, and this common sense serves the soul as the captain serves his lord.

So therefore the articulation of the bones obeys the nerve, and the nerve the muscle, and the muscle the tendon, and the tendon the common sense, and the common sense is the seat of the soul, and the memory is its advisor, and its faculty of receiving impressions serves as its standard of reference.

How the sense waits on the soul, and not the soul on the sense, and how where the sense that should minister to the soul is lacking, the soul in such a life lacks any concept of the function of this sense, as is seen in the case of a mute or one born blind.

How the nerves sometimes work of themselves, without the command of other agents or of the soul:

This appears clearly, for you will see how paralytics or those who are shivering or benumbed by cold move their trembling limbs, such as the head or the hands, without permission of the soul; which soul, with all its powers, cannot prevent these limbs from trembling. The same happens in the case of epilepsy or with severed limbs, such as the tails of lizards.

### FUNCTION OF LIVER, BILE, AND INTESTINES

The liver is the distributor and dispenser of vital nourishment to man.

The bile is the attendant or servant of the liver which sweeps away

and cleans up all the waste and excesses left after the food has been distributed to the limbs by the liver.

The intestines. Regarding these, you will understand their windings well if you inflate them. And remember that after you have depicted them from four perspectives arranged in this way, you should then depict them from four other perspectives, expanded in such a manner that from their spaces and openings you can understand the whole—that is, the variations in their thickness.

[Chyle. Mesentery]
Through the branching of the chyle vein in the mesentery, nourishment is drawn from the decomposition of the food in the intestines; and ultimately, it returns through the final branches of the artery to these intestines, where this blood, being then dead, decomposes and acquires the same stench that comes from the feces.

The mesentery is a thick, fibrous, and fatty membrane in the branches of which are twelve principal veins, and it is joined to the lower part of the diaphragm.

See whether the mesentery has arteries or not.

In this mesentery are planted the roots of all the veins, which unite at the gateway of the liver and purify the blood within the liver; it then enters the chyle vein, and this vein goes to the heart and further purifies the blood, which penetrates into the arteries as spirituous blood.

### ON THE FORCE OF THE MUSCLES

If any muscle whatsoever is stretched lengthwise, a slight force will break its fleshy tissue; and if the sensory nerves are stretched lengthwise, a slight power tears them from the muscles where their branching weaves them together, spreads, and exhausts itself; and one sees the same process occur with the fibrous covering of the veins and arteries which are mingled with these muscles. What, therefore, is the cause of such great strength in the arms and legs as is seen in the actions of any animal whatsoever? One can say nothing other than that it is the skin which clothes them; and that when the sensory nerves cause the muscles to swell, these muscles contract and pull after them the tendons into which their ends are converted; and in this proc-

--- Page 121 ---
ess of thickening, they fill out the skin and make it tight and hard; and it cannot be stretched out unless the muscles become thinner; and since they do not become thinner, they cause resistance and strengthen the aforementioned skin, in which the swollen muscles perform the function of a wedge.

### *[Of the neck]*

And in addition to this, you should describe the distances placed between the nerves themselves, both regarding their depth and breadth, and the differences in the heights and depths of their origins; and you will do the same with the muscles, veins, and arteries; and this will be extremely useful to those who have to dress wounds.

### *[Umbilical vein]*

Note if there are four umbilical veins in both males and females.

By the umbilical vein, the life and the body of every four-footed animal is composed, except for those that start from the egg, such as frogs, tortoises, green lizards, chameleons, and the like.

I believe that these four nerves are those of the kidneys or arteries.

I have found that they belong to the larger veins of the kidneys.

The navel is the gateway through which our body is formed by means of the umbilical vein.

### [*Reason for the position of veins in the knee*]
Nature has placed the principal veins of the leg in the middle of the thickness of the knee joint, because during the process of bending this joint, the veins are less compressed than if they were situated in front of or behind the knee.

### [*Relation of nerves to muscles*]
There are as many branches of the nerves as there are muscles, and there can be neither more nor less, because these muscles can only be contracted or extended by means of these nerves, from which the muscles receive their sensation. And there are as many tendons that move the limbs as there are muscles.

[Instructions for anatomical drawings and demonstrations]

[Changes of the arteries in old age]

As veins grow old, they lose the straightness of their branching paths and become increasingly flexible or winding, with thicker walls, as old age advances with the years.

You will find almost universally that the paths of the veins and the paths of the nerves follow the same route, directing themselves to the same muscles and branching in the same manner within each of these muscles. Furthermore, each vein and nerve passes alongside the artery between one muscle and another, and they branch into these muscles with equal distribution.

[Expansibility of the vessels]

The veins are capable of stretching and expanding; evidence of this is found in the fact that I have seen someone who accidentally wounded a common vein and immediately bound it up again with a tight bandage. Within a few days, a blood-colored tumor as large as a goose’s egg grew there, full of blood, and it remained so for several years. I have also found in the case of an elderly man that the mesenteric veins had narrowed the passage of the blood and doubled in length.

[Changes of the arteries, hepatic veins, and abdominal organs in the elderly]

The artery and the vein which, in the elderly, extend between the spleen and the liver, acquire such a great thickness of tissue that it restricts the passage of the blood coming from the mesenteric veins. This is the blood that passes through to the liver, the heart, the two major veins, and consequently through the entire body. Aside from the thickening of the tissue, these veins grow in length and twist.

themselves in the manner of a snake, and the liver loses the fluid of the blood that was carried there by this vein; consequently, this liver becomes dried up and grows like frozen bran in both color and substance, so that when it is subjected to even the slightest friction, this substance falls away in tiny flakes like sawdust and leaves the veins and arteries exposed.

And the veins of the gallbladder and of the navel, which entered into this liver through the portal of the liver, all remain deprived of the substance of this liver, in the manner of maize or Indian millet when their grains have been removed.

The colon and the other intestines in the elderly become much constricted, and I have found stones there in the veins which pass beneath the collarbone, which were as large as chestnuts, with the color and shape of truffles or of iron dross or clinkers; these stones were extremely hard, as such clinkers are, and had formed sacs which were hanging from the said veins like goitres.

And this old man, a few hours before his death, told me that he had lived a hundred years, and that he felt no bodily ailment other than weakness; and thus, while sitting upon a bed in the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova at Florence, without any movement or sign of anything being wrong, he passed away from this life.

And I performed an autopsy in order to ascertain the cause of so peaceful a death, and found that it proceeded from weakness through the failure of blood and of the artery that feeds the heart and the other lower members, which I found to be very parched, shrunk, and withered. I wrote down the results of this autopsy very carefully and with great ease, for the body was devoid of either fat or moisture, which form the chief hindrance to the knowledge of its parts.

The other autopsy was on a child of two years, and here I found everything to be the opposite of what it was in the case of the old man.

The elderly who enjoy good health die through lack of sustenance. This is brought about by the passage to the mesaraic veins becoming continually restricted by the thickening of the walls of these veins; and the process continues until it affects the capillary veins, which are the first to close up altogether. From this it comes to pass that the elderly dread the cold more than the young, and that those who are very

### *[Heart and vessels proceeding from the heart, and comparison with the roots and ramifications of plants]*

The plant never springs from the branches, for the plant exists before the branches, and the heart exists before the veins.

All the veins and arteries proceed from the heart; and the reason is that the maximum thickness found in these veins and arteries is at the junction they make with the heart; and the farther away they are from the heart, the thinner they become and they are divided into more minute branches. And if you should say that the veins start in the protuberance of the liver because they have their branches in this protuberance, just as the roots of plants have in the earth, the reply to this comparison is that plants do not have their origin in their roots, but that the roots and the other branches have their origin in the lower part of these plants, which is between the air and the earth; and all the parts of the plant above and below are always smaller than this part which borders upon the earth; therefore it is evident that the whole plant has its origin from this thickness, and, in

### [*Changes in the inner lining of the blood vessels in the elderly*]
One might ask why the veins in the elderly grow so long, why those that used to be straight become twisted <note>original: "bent"</note>, and why the vessel walls <note>original: "skin"</note> thicken so much that they close up and stop the flow of blood. This is what causes the death of the elderly, even when they have no specific disease.

I believe that a thing that is closer to its source of nourishment grows more. For this reason, since these veins act as a sleeve or casing for the blood that nourishes the body, they themselves are nourished even more because they are so close to the blood.

Because this healthy blood becomes corrupted away from the bowels, the elderly pass away without fever when they reach a great age.

And this also explains why the bowels in the elderly are significantly narrowed.

## ON THE REASON FOR THE HEAT OF THE BLOOD

The heat is produced by the movement of the heart, and this reveals itself because the heat increases more in proportion to how much more swiftly the heart moves, as is shown by the pulse of those suffering from fever, which is moved by the beating of the heart.

[Drawing of heart—below:—]
Marvelous instrument, invented by the supreme Master.

[Mechanism of action of the heart]
Heart open in the receptacle of the spirits, that is, in the artery; and at M it takes or rather gives the blood to the artery, and through the mouth, B, it refreshes itself with air from the lung, and through c it fills the auricles of the heart s.
N Firm muscle is drawn back, and it is the primary cause of the movement of the heart; and as it draws back it thickens, and as it thickens it becomes shortened and draws back with it all the lower and upper muscles, and closes the door M, and shortens the space that lies between the base and the apex of the heart, and consequently comes to empty it and to draw to itself the fresh air.

Of the heart. This moves of its own accord and does not stop unless forever.

--- Page 128 ---
On the lung. This is moved by other parts, specifically by the primary mover, which is the heart. As the heart constricts, it pulls the veins along with it, through which it returns heated air to the lung and expands it. This lung can close either voluntarily or through distraction—that is, forgetfulness caused by deep thought. By this process, the heart draws back from the lung the heated air it had previously given it; however, this action cannot be repeated many times, for if the lung did not refresh itself with new air, the person would eventually suffocate.

Testicles, witnesses of coition. These contain within themselves ardor; that is, they increase the spirit and ferocity of animals. Experience shows us this clearly in castrated animals, such as the bull, the boar, the ram, and the rooster—all very fierce animals which, after being deprived of these testicles, remain very cowardly. Thus, one sees a ram drive a herd of wethers before it, and a rooster put a number of capons to flight; I have seen the same thing happen with a hen, and also with oxen.

*Della verga.* This communicates with human intelligence and sometimes possesses intelligence of its own. Although a man’s will may desire to stimulate it, it remains obstinate and follows its own course, moving sometimes on its own without permission or thought from the man, whether he is asleep or awake, doing what it desires. Often the man is asleep while it is awake, and many times the man is awake while it is asleep; many times the man wishes it to perform and it does not wish to; many times it wishes to and the man forbids it. It seems, therefore, that this creature often has a life and intelligence separate from the man, and it would appear that the man is wrong to be ashamed to give it a name or to display it, seeking instead to constantly cover and conceal what he ought to adorn and display with ceremony as an attendant.

No lower organ in the human body is able to suspend its action voluntarily except for the lung. You see the heart, which carries out its function on its own, as do the stomach and the other intestines joined to it, and similarly the liver, the gall, the spleen, the testicles, the kidneys, and the bladder.

--- Page 129 ---
In fact, man does not differ from animals except in what is incidental, and it is in this that he shows himself to be a divine being; for where nature finishes producing its species, there man begins—using natural things and the aid of this nature—to create an infinite number of species. And as these are not necessary to those who govern themselves rightly as the animals do, it is not in the animals' nature to seek after them.

[*Passage of the urine from the kidneys into the bladder by means of the ureters*]

The authorities say that the uretary ducts do not enter directly to carry the urine to the bladder, but that they enter between layers of skin through paths that do not align with each other; and they say that the more the bladder fills, the more these paths become contracted. They claim nature has done this simply so that when the bladder is full, it should not turn the urine back to where it came from. In this way, by finding the paths between membrane and membrane—penetrating the interior through narrow passages that are not opposite the opening of the first membrane—the more the bladder fills, the more it presses one membrane against the other; consequently, the urine has no way to spread out and turn back. This proof, however, does not hold, seeing that if the urine were to rise higher in the bladder than its entrance (which is near the middle of its height), it would follow that this entrance would suddenly close and no more urine would be able to pass into the bladder. The quantity would never exceed half the capacity of the bladder; the remainder of the bladder would therefore be superfluous, and nature does not create anything superfluous. We may say, therefore, by the fifth section of the sixth book concerning waters, that the urine enters the bladder by a long and winding path, and when the bladder is full, the uretary ducts remain full of urine. The urine that is in the bladder cannot rise higher than the surface of the urine in the ducts when the man is upright; but if he remains lying down, it can turn back through...

When the man is upside down, the entrance of the urine is closed.

### *[The reason for the arrangement of the human intestine in relation to nutrition]*

Animals without legs have a straight intestine, which is why it always remains lying down; for an animal without feet cannot raise itself, and if it should raise itself, it returns immediately to a level position. But in the case of a man, this would not be appropriate because he holds himself quite upright; the stomach would suddenly empty itself if the twisted nature of the intestines did not check the descent of the food. Furthermore, if the bowel were straight, every part of the food would not come into contact with the intestinal walls as it does in the twisted intestines.

And consequently, much nutritive substance would remain in the waste products <note>original: "superfluous parts"</note> of this food, which would not be able to be absorbed <note>original: "sucked"</note> by the tissue of these bowels and transported into the mesenteric veins <term>mesaraic veins</term>.

### *[Defecation: Intestinal movements in relation to the diaphragm]*

When one uses the transverse muscles of the body to press out the waste products from the intestines, these muscles would not perform their function well or powerfully unless the lungs were filled with air.

All the muscles of the body are enveloped in extremely thin cartilage, and then they change into thicker cartilage, and in that their substance ends.

### [*Action of the transversal muscles of the abdomen upon defecation*]

The transversal muscles squeeze the intestines but the longitudinal ones do not, because if it were so, when the man holds himself bent and relaxes these muscles, he would not have the force to perform the duty of squeezing them; but the transversal muscles never relax as the man bends, but rather become stretched.

->*[Instructions for the demonstration of the muscles of the thorax]*<-

The demonstration of the region of the ribs requires first the plain sides bare with open spaces; afterward, the muscles which are joined to their sides, by which they are linked together; then the muscles that interlace above them, which serve for the movements of expansion and contraction of these sides; in addition to this, the other muscles crossed above the aforementioned muscles at different angles, serving various movements.

->*[Reason for the movement of the ribs]*<-

Concerning the maximum raising and lowering of the shoulders, which restricts the movement of the sides. Because the maximum raising and lowering of the shoulders—by means of the neck muscles which are based in the vertebrae of the spine—prevents the downward movement of the ribs when these shoulders are raised; and as these shoulders are lowered, the upward movement of these sides is prevented.

Nature has provided for this fact by means of the muscles of the diaphragm, which lower the diaphragm at its concave center; and when it is raised again, this results from the compressed gas enclosed in the intestines, which gas is produced by the fact that excrement gives off vapors as it dries; and if the raised shoulders keep the ribs high by means of muscle *b*, then the diaphragm, by merely moving itself by means of its muscles, performs the function of opening and closing the lung; and the compressed intestines together with the

--- Page 134 ---
condensed air which is generated in them pushes the diaphragm back upwards; this diaphragm presses the lung and expels the air.

[*Muscles of the anterior wall of the thorax and of the abdomen*]
The muscle *a* contains the breast within itself, and descends as flesh as far as the seventh rib by the side of the Adam’s apple; then, having been converted into a membrane, it proceeds to form a covering over all the lower part of the belly and ends by joining itself to the pubic bone; and this muscle of the breast is composed of several muscles which all start in the thorax, and converge and end in the area of the muscles of the humerus.
*a d c* ends in the shoulder bone and starts in the middle of the thorax, and below it does not go so far as to cover *b*, shown above, except by its cartilage, with which it covers all the lower part of the belly, and it ends in the flank and in the pubic bone. Fogli B 16 v.

[*Lung*]
When the lung has sent out the air and is thus diminished in volume by an amount corresponding to the amount of air which emerged from it, one ought then to consider from where the space of the cavity of the diminished lung attracts to itself the air which fills up its expansion, because in nature there is no vacuum.
And one also asks, since after the lung has been expanded it drives out the air from its receptacle, by what path this air escapes and where it is received after it has escaped.

[*Mechanism of respiration. Action of intercostal muscles*]
The lung is always full of a quantity of air, even when it has driven out that air which is necessary for its exhalation; and when it is refreshed by new air, it presses on the sides of the chest, dilates them a little, and pushes them outwards; for as may be seen and felt by placing the hand upon the chest during breathing, the chest expands and contracts, and even more so when one heaves a deep sigh. For nature has willed that this force should be created in the ribs of the chest and not in the membrane that encloses the substance of the lung, lest by an excessive intake of air to form some unusually deep sigh, this membrane might break and burst.

<header>ANATOMY 127</header>

[*Function of the diaphragm*]
The <term>diaphragm</term>—the large membrane located below the base of the <term>lung</term>—is not moved or pushed in any part by the growth of the <term>lung</term> itself. This is because the <term>lung</term> increases in width rather than length. However, it is possible for the <term>diaphragm</term> to be driven downward by the air that makes room for the <term>lung</term>'s expansion. In this case, the air would push the <term>diaphragm</term>, which in turn pushes the <term>liver</term>; the <term>liver</term> then pushes the <term>stomach</term> (for which it serves as a cover), leading to the compression of all the <term>intestines</term>. This continual movement helps speed up the evacuation of the <term>intestines</term>, especially when a person is exercising with great vigor.

[*Cause of the formation of gas in the intestines*]
Regarding the gas produced in the <term>intestines</term>, we may say it is caused by the waste matter <note>original: "superfluous quantity"</note> that collects in the <term>rectum</term>. This matter becomes drier as its moisture evaporates; this vapor, acting like air, stretches the <term>bowels</term> and causes pain when it is trapped within the <term>colon</term>.

[*Latitudinal increase of the lung in breathing. How its expansion acts upon the functions of the stomach*]
When the <term>lung</term> fills with air, it expands sideways <note>original: "latitudinal"</note> rather than in length, as can be seen by inflating the <term>lung</term> of a pig. The air located between the uninflated <term>lung</term> and the surrounding <term>ribs</term> is displaced as the <term>lung</term> expands. This air escapes into the space below, between the <term>lung</term> and the <term>diaphragm</term>, causing the <term>diaphragm</term> to bulge downward against the <term>stomach</term>. When the <term>stomach</term> is pressed in this way, it pushes its contents forward into the <term>intestines</term>.

[*Action of the expansion of the lungs upon the pericardium and function of the pericardial fluid*]
Furthermore, this air pressed between the <term>lung</term> and the <term>diaphragm</term> bears against the <term>pericardium</term> <note>original: "case which encloses the heart"</note>. The small amount of <term>pericardial fluid</term> at the bottom of this case is forced upward, bathing the entire <term>heart</term>. By doing this continually, the fluid moistens the heated <term>heart</term> <note>The author refers to the Renaissance belief that the heart was a source of vital heat that needed cooling</note> and prevents it from becoming dried out by its constant movement.

The entire body originates from the heart regarding its initial creation; the blood, therefore, as well as the veins and nerves do the same, even though these nerves clearly seem to all start from the spinal cord and to be far from the heart, and the spinal cord appears to be of the same substance as the brain from which it is derived.

### [*Precepts for the study of tendons*]

Note which are the primary tendons <note>original: "cords"</note> and those which would cause the greatest injury to the animal if they were severed, as well as those which are of less importance; you should do this for every limb.

### [*Precepts for the demonstration of the bones and muscles of the leg*]

Observe the proportions of the bones relative to one another, and what purpose each one serves.

### [*Notes concerning the muscles which become uncovered and hide themselves in their movement*]

Different muscles become visible during the various movements of animals, and different muscles are those which hide themselves during such a variety of movement. Regarding this, it is necessary to write an extensive treatise for the purpose of identifying areas that have been injured by wounds, and also for the benefit of sculptors and painters.

### [*Origin of the movements of the legs and feet*]

All movements of the leg originate from the muscles of the thigh; these movements are the cause of the leg bending, straightening from a bent position, and turning to the right or left. 

However, the movements of the feet are caused by the muscles that originate in the lower leg. Regarding the movements of the toes, some originate in the leg and some in the foot.

### [*Insertion of the motor muscles of the leg*]

Some of the motor muscles <note>original: "motive muscles"</note> of the leg begin in the hip and some in the thigh; you must record the true position of all of them. <term>Sheets <note>original: "Fogli"</note> B 20 recto <note>the front side of the page</note></term>

### [*Postures for stopping while running*]

When a man wishes to stop his run and offset his <term>impetus</term><note>original: "impetus"; here meaning momentum or the force of motion.</note>, necessity causes him to lean back and take short, quick steps.

### [*Mechanics of certain movements of the human body and the foundation of human statics*]

The center of gravity of a man who raises one of his feet from the ground rests directly above the center of the sole of the foot that remains planted.

### [*The mechanics of climbing*]

A man climbing stairs places as much of his weight forward and to the side of the upper foot as he uses to balance the lower leg; as a result, the effort of the lower leg is limited only to moving itself.

The first thing a man does when he ascends by steps is to release the leg he wishes to raise from the weight of the <term>bust</term><note>original: "bust"; Leonardo uses this to refer to the torso or upper body.</note> resting upon it. In addition to this, he loads the opposite leg with the entire remaining mass of his body along with the other leg. Then, he raises the leg and places his foot upon the step where he wishes to climb. Having done this, he shifts the rest of the weight of the torso and leg back to the higher foot, rests his hand upon his thigh, pushes his head forward, and moves toward the point of the higher foot. He swiftly raises the heel of the lower foot and, using the momentum acquired, lifts himself up. At the same time, he extends the arm he was resting on his knee; this extension of the arm pushes the torso and head upward, thereby straightening the curve of the back. <margin>Fogli B 21 v.</margin>

### [Change of the vessels in the elderly]

I have found in the elderly how the vein which proceeds from the portal of the liver crosses behind the stomach and branches out in the spleen; in the young, these branches and veins are straight and full of blood, while in the old they are twisted, flattened, wrinkled, and emptied of blood.

### [Changes in the liver in old age]

And thus the liver, which in youth is usually of a deep color and of uniform consistency, is pale in the old, without any redness of blood; the veins remain empty amidst the substance of this liver. This substance may be compared, because of its thin texture, to bran soaked in a small quantity of water, which readily disintegrates when washed, leaving the veins that branch within it freed from all the substance of the liver.

The colon in the elderly becomes as slender as the middle finger of the hand, whereas in the young it is equal to the maximum width of the arm.

The net which sits between the sifac and the intestines, in the case of the elderly, uncovers all these intestines by itself and withdraws between the bottom of the stomach and the upper part of the bowels.

[*Spinal marrow and nerves*]

These two layers <note>original: "crusts"</note> which clothe the spinal marrow are the same as those that clothe the brain—that is, the **pia mater** <note>Latin: "tender mother"; the delicate innermost membrane</note> and the **dura mater** <note>Latin: "tough mother"; the thick, protective outer membrane</note>.

The vertebrae of the neck have been sawn through and removed from the center in front, revealing the position of the spinal marrow and showing how it resides and branches out <note>original: "ramifies"</note> beyond these vertebrae.

[*Anatomical and functional relations between nerves and muscles*]

The substance of the spinal marrow extends for a certain distance into the origins of the nerves, and then follows the hollow nerve as far as its final branches. Through this passage, it conveys sensation to each muscle. Every muscle is composed of many other very minute muscles, just as there are fibers <note>original: "threads"</note> into which a muscle can be separated. Each of these tiny muscles is wrapped in almost invisible membranes, which are actually the final branches of the aforementioned nerves. These fibers obey the sensory impulses in order to contract the muscle as they withdraw, and to cause it to expand again with every demand of the sensation that passes through the hollow center <note>original: "vacuity"</note> of the nerve.

But to return to the spinal marrow: this is wrapped in two membranes. Only one of these clothes the inner core <note>original: "pith-like substance"</note> of the spinal marrow; as it emerges from the hollow of the vertebrae, it is transformed into nerve. The other membrane clothes the nerve, along with its principal branches, and branches out together with every nerve branch. This forms the second cover of the spinal marrow, positioning itself between the bone of the vertebrae and the spinal marrow's first membrane.

The spinal marrow is the source of the nerves that provide voluntary movement to the limbs.

The *pia mater* and the *dura mater* clothe all the nerves that originate from the spinal marrow.

[*Precepts for the demonstration of the nerves of the arm*]

You will create a drawing of the branching nerves with all their muscles attached.

And then you will create this branching system with the muscles attached to both the nerves and to the bones that form the entire arm.

Here, each nerve of the arm is joined with all four nerves that issue from the spinal marrow.

## ORDER OF ANATOMY

First, depict the bones—that is to say, the arms—and show the motive power proceeding from the shoulder to the elbow in all its lines; then from the elbow to the forearm; then from the forearm to the hand, and from the hand to the fingers.
And in the forearm, you should show the movements of the fingers as they open; and in your demonstration, you will present these on their own.

--- Page 146 ---
In the second demonstration, you will cover these muscles with the second movements of the fingers; and you will do this stage by stage so as not to cause confusion. But first, place upon the bones those muscles which attach themselves to these bones without the confusion of other muscles; and with these, you will place the nerves and veins that nourish them, having first created the map of the veins and nerves over the bare bones.

[*On the nature of the teeth and their position and distance from the axis of their movements*]

A tooth has less gripping power the further it is from the center of its movement. If the center of the movement of the teeth were *a*, the axis of the jaw, I say that in proportion as these teeth are more distant from this center *a*, they have less power in their grip; therefore, *d e* is less powerful in its grip than the teeth *b c*. From this follows the corollary which states: that tooth is more powerful which is nearer to the center or axis of its movement; that is, the grip of the teeth *b c* is more powerful than that of the teeth *d e*. (Nature made them less able to penetrate into food and gave them blunter points which possess greater power.) Therefore, the teeth *b c* will have points that are more blunt as they are moved by greater power; and for this reason, the teeth *b c* will be blunter in proportion to the teeth *d e* when they are nearer the axis *a* of the jaws *a d* and *a e*. For this reason, nature has made the molars with large crowns to enable them to grind food rather than penetrate or cut it; and in front, she has made the teeth sharp and penetrating, not suitable for grinding food, and has placed the eye teeth between the molars and the incisors.

[*Reaction of the pupil to the stimulus of light, dilation and constriction*]

In nocturnal animals, the pupil varies from a large to a larger size according to the great or greater darkness of the night.

In these nocturnal animals, the pupil also varies from a small to a smaller size according to the great or greater brightness of the day.

From what has been said, one concludes that these nocturnal animals always possess the same degree of visual faculty throughout all the variations of brightness or darkness that can occur during the day and night.

--- Page 147 ---
The visual faculty exists entirely within the whole pupil and entirely within each of its parts.

It follows that half of the pupil sees an object in its entirety, just as if the pupil were whole.

In proportion to the size of the pupil, it will see its object with greater scale and clarity; conversely, as the pupil is smaller, it will see the object as much smaller and more obscure.

It follows that if one eye is closed, the power of sight is diminished by half; this may be proven with luminous bodies such as the sun, the moon, and the stars, and also with a lamp or fire.

This reduction in brightness may be observed without closing one of the eyes; instead of closing it, you must place your hand or finger in front of one of the pupils between the air and the eye. You will then see with both pupils a stretch of air that has the same boundaries as the air seen by a single pupil alone, yet that which is seen by one pupil will be just as much darker than that which is seen by two pupils. The reason for this is as the diagram shows.

### *[Precepts for the topographical demonstration of the muscles of the back]*

You will establish the rule and the measurement of each muscle, and you will provide the reason for all their functions, the manner in which they perform them, and what moves them.

You will first create the spine of the back; then proceed to clothe it in stages, one above the other, with each of these muscles. Place the nerves, arteries, and veins of each muscle by themselves, and additionally note how many vertebrae they are joined to, which intestines are opposite them, and what bones and other organic instruments are present.

The higher parts of the thin person are more prominent in those who have well-developed muscles, and similarly with fat people; however, the difference between the shape of the muscles in those who are fat compared to those who have well-developed muscles will be described below.

--- Page 148 ---
### OF THE FUNCTION OF THE INTERCOSTAL MUSCLES

The three muscles which draw up the ribs we call the drawing muscles.

To the four muscles c d e f, being created for the expansion of the chest, we give the name of the expanding muscles.

The intercostals are the minute muscles positioned between the ribs which serve for the expansion and contraction of these ribs; and these two diametrically opposite movements are ordained for the purpose of drawing in and breathing out the air in the lung, which is enclosed within the region of the ribs. The expansion of these ribs proceeds from the external muscles of the ribs, which are arranged in the slant m n with the help of the three muscles o p q; as these draw the ribs upward with great force, they extend their capacity in the manner that one sees occurring with the ventricles of the heart. But since the ribs must turn downwards, they would not be able to descend on their own if a person remained lying down, were it not for the internal muscles; these have a slant opposite to the external muscles, which extends along the line f n.

### OF THE POWER OF THE INTERCOSTAL MUSCLES

The function of the external intercostal muscles is to raise and expand the ribs, and they possess admirable power in their position; seeing that they are established with their uppermost ends upon the same spine where the floating ribs begin, and their slant descends towards the navel.

### [Of fingers and toes]

Each protuberance formed by the joints of the toes and fingers has a corresponding hollow in the adjacent toes and fingers which receives this roundness within itself. Nature has done this in order not to make their width misshapen; for if the said protuberances were in direct contact with one another, the feet would become very wide. One of two results would also be necessary: either the fingers would all be of the same length, or one would have two joints and the other only one, as will be demonstrated in its proper place concerning the bones.

# HOW THE BODY OF THE ANIMAL CONTINUALLY DIES AND IS RENEWED

The body of anything whatsoever that receives nourishment continually dies and is continually renewed. For nourishment cannot enter except in those places where the preceding nourishment is exhausted, and if it is exhausted, it no longer has life. Unless, therefore, you supply nourishment equivalent to that which has departed, life fails in its vigor; and if you deprive it of this nourishment, life is completely destroyed. But if you supply it with just as much as is destroyed day by day, then it renews its life just as much as it is consumed; like the light of this candle formed by the nourishment given to it by the fat of this candle, which light is also continually renewed by the swiftest support from beneath, in proportion as the upper part is consumed and dies, and in dying becomes changed from radiant light to murky smoke. And this death extends for as long as the smoke continues; and the period of duration of the smoke is the same as that of what feeds it, and in an instant the whole light dies and is entirely regenerated by the movement of that which nourishes it; and its life receives from it also its ebb and flow, as the flicker of its point serves to show us. The same process also comes to pass in the bodies of animals by means of the beating of the heart, whereby a wave of blood is produced in all the veins, and these are continually either enlarging or contracting, because the expansion occurs when they receive the excessive quantity of blood, and the contraction is due to the departure of the excess of blood they have received; and this the beating of the pulse teaches us, when we touch the aforementioned veins with the fingers in any part whatsoever of the living body.

But to return to our purpose, I say that the flesh of animals is made anew by the blood which is continually produced by that which nourishes them, and that this flesh is destroyed and returns by the mesaraic arteries and passes into the intestines, where it putrefies in a foul and fetid death, as they show us in their deposits and steam like the smoke and fire which were given as a comparison. <note>Fogli B 28 r.</note>

## OF THE MUSCLES WHICH MOVE THE TONGUE

No part of the body requires as many muscles as the tongue—twenty-four of these are already known, in addition to the others I have discovered; and of all the parts moved by voluntary action, this one exceeds all the rest in the variety of its movements.
And if you should say that this variety is rather a characteristic of the eye, which receives all the infinite variations of form and color from the objects placed before it, or of the sense of smell with its infinite mixture of odors, or of the ear with its sounds, we may reply that the tongue also perceives an infinite number of flavors, both simple and complex. However, this is not our current focus, for our intention is to treat only the specific movement of each body part.
Consider carefully how, through the movement of the tongue and with the help of the lips and teeth, the pronunciation of all the names of things is made known to us; and how, by means of this instrument, the simple and compound words of a language reach our ears. Consider also how these words, if there were a name for every effect of nature, would approach infinity in number, along with all the countless things that are active and within the power of nature. These would not be expressed in one language only, but in a great number of languages, and these too would tend toward infinite variety because they vary continually from century to century, and from one country to another, through the intermingling of peoples who are constantly being mixed together by wars or other misfortunes. These same languages are liable to be forgotten, and they are mortal like all other created things; and if we grant that our world is everlasting, we must then say that these languages have been, and must still be, of infinite variety throughout the infinite number of centuries that constitute infinite time.
This is not true of any other sense; for the other senses are concerned only with the things that nature is continually producing, and she does not change the ordinary types of things she creates in the same way that things created by man are changed from time to time. Indeed, man is nature’s primary instrument, because nature is concerned only with the production of elementary things, but man produces from these elementary things an infinite...

--- Page 151 ---
<header>ANATOMY</header>
<page-num>143</page-num>

number of compounds, although he has no power to create any natural thing except another like himself, that is, his children. And of this the old alchemists will serve as my witnesses, who have never, either by chance or deliberate experiment, succeeded in creating the smallest thing which can be created by nature; and indeed, this generation deserves unmeasured praise for the usefulness of the things which they have invented for the use of men, and would deserve it even more if they had not been the inventors of harmful things like poisons and other similar things which destroy life or the intellect. But they are not exempt from blame in that, through much study and experiment, they are seeking to create not the lowliest of nature's products, but the most excellent, namely gold, which is begotten of the sun inasmuch as it has more resemblance to it than to anything else that exists, and no created thing is more enduring than this gold. It is immune from destruction by fire, which has power over all the rest of created things, reducing them to ashes, glass, or smoke. If, however, mindless greed should drive you into such error, why do you not go to the mines where nature produces this gold, and there become her disciple? She will completely cure you of your folly by showing you that nothing which you employ in your furnace will be numbered among the things which she employs in order to produce this gold. For there is no mercury there, no sulfur of any kind, no fire nor other heat than that of nature giving life to our world; and she will show you the veins of gold spreading through the stone—the blue lapis lazuli, whose color is unaffected by the power of the fire.

<margin>Fogli B 28 v.</margin>
And consider carefully this branching of the gold, and you will see that its extremities are continually expanding in slow movement, transforming into gold whatever they come in contact with; and note that therein is a living organism which it is not within your power to produce.

## OF THE MUSCLES WHICH MOVE THE LIPS OF THE MOUTH

The muscles which move the lips of the mouth are more numerous in man than in any other animal; and this arrangement is a necessity for him on account of the many tasks in which these lips are continually employing themselves, as in the four letters of the alphabet *b f*

### WHICH MUSCLE IS IT THAT TIGHTENS THE MOUTH SO MUCH THAT ITS SIDES DRAW CLOSE TOGETHER?

The muscles that tighten the mouth, thereby reducing its length, are in the lips themselves; or rather, these lips are the actual muscles that close themselves. It is true that the muscle alters the position of the lip beneath the other muscles joined to it, of which one pair are those that stretch it and move it into laughter. The muscle that contracts it is the same muscle of which the lower lip is formed, which restrains it by drawing its ends toward its center; and the same process occurs simultaneously with the upper lip. There are other muscles that bring the lips to a point and others that flatten them; others are those that cause them to curl back, others that straighten them, others that twist them completely awry, and others that bring them back to their original position. Thus, there are always as many muscles as there are various positions of these lips, and just as many others that serve to reverse these positions; and it is my purpose here to describe and represent these in full, proving these movements by means of my mathematical principles.

### ON THE MOVEMENTS OF THE MUSCLES OF THE MOUTH ALONG WITH ITS LATERAL MUSCLES

There are many occasions when the muscles forming the lips of the mouth move the lateral muscles joined to them, and there are an equal number of occasions when these lateral muscles move the lips of this mouth, returning the mouth to a position it cannot regain on its own; for the function of a muscle is to pull and not to push, except in the case of the genitals and the tongue. But if the contracting of the mouth draws back its lateral muscles equally, this mouth will not regain its lost length by itself unless the said lateral muscles return to their place; and if these lateral muscles extend the length of the mouth to create laughter, it is necessary for these lateral muscles to be pulled back by the contraction of the mouth when laughter ceases.

--- Page 153 ---
## [Umbilical cord and vein]

These four nerves do not contain any blood in themselves; but when they enter the navel, they are transformed into a thick vein which then extends to the gate of the liver and branches out through its lower part, where each of its lowest branches ends and does not extend any higher.

Of the aforementioned four umbilical veins, the outer pair form the <term>sifac</term>, the membrane adjacent to the peritoneum, and then bend downwards and end in the first branch of the vein and the larger artery, which lies over the spine of the back.

The outer branch of the umbilical vein is enclosed between the first and second membranes with which the child is frequently born.

## [Origin of the umbilical vein; its relation with the artery and its course]

This umbilical vein is the origin of all the veins of the creature produced in the <term>matrix</term>, and it does not originate from any vein of the pregnant woman, because each of these veins is entirely separate and divided from the veins of the pregnant woman. The veins and arteries are found together in pairs; it is extremely rare for one to be found without the other accompanying it. The artery is almost always found above the vein because the blood of the artery is the passage for the <term>vital spirit</term>, and the blood of the veins is that which nourishes the creature. Of these branches represented, those that are raised up are intended for the nourishment of the third thin membrane of the <term>matrix</term>, and the lower veins, positioned obliquely, are those that feed the last membrane which is adjacent to the animal enclosed by it. Both the one and the other of these membranes often emerge, together with the creature, out of the mother's <term>matrix</term>; this occurs when the animal is unable to break them, for then it emerges enveloped. This is easily done because these two extremely thin membranes, as stated above, are not connected in any way to the said <term>matrix</term>, which is also equipped with two membranes of considerable thickness, fleshy and covered with nerves.

--- Page 154 ---
## CONCERNING THE NERVES THAT COMMUNICATE SENSATION TO THE INTERCOSTAL MUSCLES (MESOPLEURI)

The small muscles situated diagonally which descend from the upper part of the spine and end toward the Adam’s apple derive their name from the pleura, and they are placed between one rib and another merely in order to contract the intervening spaces; and the nerves which communicate sensation to these muscles have their origin in the spinal cord which passes through the backbone, and the lowest point at which they begin in the spinal cord is where the spine borders upon the kidneys.

## OF SPIRITS

We have just now stated that the definition of a spirit is a power united to a body, because by itself it can neither offer resistance nor perform any kind of local movement; and if you say that it does in itself offer resistance, this cannot be the case within the elements, because if the spirit is a quantity without a body, this quantity is what is called a vacuum, and the vacuum does not exist in nature; and assuming that one were formed, it would be instantly filled up by the rushing in of that element within which such a vacuum had been created. So by the definition of weight which says that gravity is an accidental power created by one element being drawn or forced toward another, it follows that any element, though without weight when within the same element, acquires weight in the element above it, which is lighter than itself; so one sees that one part of water has neither gravity nor levity in the rest of the water, but if you draw it up into the air then it will acquire weight, and if you draw the air under the water then the water, finding itself above this air, acquires weight, which weight it cannot support by itself, and consequently its descent is inevitable, and therefore it falls into the water, at the very spot which had been left a vacuum by this water. The same thing would happen to a spirit if it were among the elements, for it would continually create a vacuum in whatever element it happened to find itself; and for this reason it would be neces-

--- Page 155 ---
...sarily in perpetual flight towards the sky until it had passed out of these elements.

## WHETHER THE SPIRIT HAS A BODY AMONG THE ELEMENTS

We have proved how the spirit cannot exist by itself among the elements without a body, nor can it move by its own voluntary movement except to rise upwards. We now proceed to say that such a spirit, in taking a body of air, must of necessity spread itself through this air; for if it remained concentrated, it would be separated from the air and would fall, thereby creating a vacuum, as is stated above. Therefore, if it is to be able to remain suspended in the air, it is necessary that it should spread itself over a certain quantity of air. If it becomes mingled with the air, two difficulties follow: first, that it thins that quantity of air with which it is mingled, and consequently this air, becoming rarefied, flies upwards of its own accord and will not remain among the air that is heavier than itself; and second, that as this ethereal essence is spread out, its parts become separated and its nature becomes modified, and it thereby loses something of its former power. To these is also added a third difficulty, which is that this body of air assumed by the spirit is exposed to the penetrating force of the winds, which are incessantly severing and tearing in pieces the connected portions of the air, spinning them round and whirling them amid the rest of the air. Therefore, the spirit which was spread through this air would be dismembered or rent in pieces and broken, along with the tearing apart of the air within which it was spread.

## WHETHER THE SPIRIT, HAVING ASSUMED A BODY OF AIR, CAN MOVE BY ITSELF OR NOT

It is impossible that the spirit diffused within a quantity of air can have the power to move this air; and this is shown by the previous section, which states that the spirit thins that quantity of air into which it has entered. This air, consequently, will rise above the other air, and this will be a movement made by the air through its own lightness, and not through the voluntary movement of the spirit. Furthermore, if this air meets the wind, according to the third part of this section, this air will be moved by the wind and not by the spirit which is diffused within it.

--- Page 156 ---
<page-num>148</page-num>
<header>ANATOMY</header>

## WHETHER THE SPIRIT CAN SPEAK OR NOT

To prove whether or not the spirit can speak, it is necessary first to define what voice is and how it is produced. We may define it as follows: the voice is the movement of air in friction against a solid body, or of a solid body in friction against the air, which is the same thing. This friction of a solid with a thin substance condenses the latter, making it capable of resistance. Moreover, when a thin substance in swift motion contacts a similar substance moving slowly, they condense each other at their point of contact, creating a noise or a tremendous uproar. The sound or murmur caused by one thin substance moving through another at a moderate pace is like a large flame that creates noises within the air. The loudest uproar made by one thin substance against another occurs when one moving swiftly penetrates another that is stationary—for instance, the flame of fire issuing from a cloud, which strikes the air and thus produces thunderbolts.

We may say, therefore, that the spirit cannot produce a voice without the movement of air. There is no air within the spirit, and it cannot expel air from itself if it does not possess it. If it wishes to move the air in which it is diffused, it would be necessary for the spirit to multiply itself, and this it cannot do unless it has physical volume. According to the fourth part, it is stated that no thin body can move unless it has a fixed point from which to initiate its motion, especially in the case of an element moving within its own element. Such an element does not move on its own except by uniform evaporation at the center of the evaporating object, as happens with a sponge squeezed in the hand while held under water; the water flows away from it in every direction with equal movement through the openings between the fingers of the hand in which it is squeezed.

### [The heart is a muscle nourished like others by arteries and veins]

The heart itself is not the source <note>original: beginning</note> of life. Instead, it is a vessel formed of thick muscle, given life and nourishment by the artery and vein just like other muscles. It is true that the blood and the artery which empties <note>original: purges itself</note> into it are the life and nourishment of the other muscles. The heart is of such density that fire can hardly damage it; this is seen in the case of men who have been burned, in whom—after the bones have been reduced to ash—the heart within still bleeds. Nature has given it this great resistance to heat so that it may be able to withstand the intense heat generated in the left side of the heart by the arterial blood, which becomes refined <note>original: attenuated</note> in this ventricle.

The variation of the voice comes from the expansion <note>original: dilatation</note> and contraction of the rings that make up the trachea. The expansion is produced by the muscles that connect to these rings; I believe the contraction is produced by the rings themselves, because they are made of cartilage which bends on its own to return to its original shape.

### [Origin of all the veins of the bulging part of the heart]

The source <note>original: root</note> of all the veins is in the bulging <note>original: gibbous</note> part of the heart—that is, the outer layer <note>original: skin</note> of the blood. This is evident because the veins are thicker there than anywhere else, and they go on branching an infinite number of times through every limb of the creature.

### [*Veins from the liver to the spleen and their function*]

Regarding the two thick veins that go from the liver to the spleen, which originate from the larger veins of the spine, I believe that these are collectors of excess blood. This blood, being evacuated every day by the mesaraic veins, is deposited in the bowels, causing the same stench when it reaches there that arises from the dead in tombs, which is the stench of excrement.

### [*Process for examination of the brain and the basilar nerves*]

You will take apart the substance of the brain as far as the borders of the dura mater, which is positioned between this basilar bone and the substance of the brain. Then, note all the places where this dura mater penetrates the basilar bone, along with the nerves covered by it together with the pia mater. You will acquire this knowledge with certainty whenever, through diligent effort, you lift this pia mater little by little, starting from the extremities and noting from one part to another the positions of the previously mentioned perforations. Begin first at the right or left side, representing this in its entirety; then you will follow with the opposite part, which will inform you as to whether the previous part is correctly positioned or not. It will also lead you to an understanding of whether the right part is similar to the left part; and if you find that it varies, you will look again in the other.

### [*Preparation of the hemorrhoidal veins*]

## ON THE FOOD WHICH CAUSES DECAY

<margin>Folio B 36 v.</margin>
I maintain that the ends of the mesenteric <term>original: mesaraic; the veins that absorb nutrients from the intestines</term> veins, which draw in the nutrients from the food contained in the intestines, are expanded by the natural heat of the human body. This occurs because heat separates and expands, while cold assembles and constricts. However, this heat alone would not be sufficient if it were not joined by the foul gas <note>original: "stench"</note> formed by the decay <note>original: "corruption"</note> of the blood returned by the arteries to these intestines. In these intestines, that blood acts no differently than it does in buried corpses. This gas expands the intestines and penetrates into every crevice, swelling and puffing out the body like a barrel. If you were to argue that this gas arose only from the heat in the body, you would find that not to be the case with inflated bodies covered in snow. The power of this decay is much more active and multiplies much more than the power of heat does.

## DEMONSTRATION OF THE MALE BLADDER

### [*Kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra*]
