[*Entry of the urine into the bladder*]
The urine, after departing from the kidneys, penetrates the ureteral passages, and from these passes into the bladder near the center of its height, entering it by means of small perforations made diagonally between one membrane and another. This slanting perforation was not made because nature doubted whether this urine could return to the kidneys, because this is impossible according to the fourth rule concerning channels (*de’ condotti*), where it is stated: "Water which descends from a height through a thin stream and penetrates beneath the surface of a body of water cannot be pushed back by a reverse movement, unless there is as much thickness in the body of water as there is in the descending stream, nor any greater height of water in the body than the depth of the descending stream." And if you were to say that the more the bladder fills, the more it closes, one would reply to this that if such perforations were pressed together by the urine closing these walls, it would prevent the entrance of the rest of the descending urine; this cannot happen according to the previously mentioned fourth rule, which states that the thin, elevated urine is more powerful than the low and wide body of urine in the bladder.

You will make this demonstration.

### *[Description of the region of the mouth]*

In this region, the lips act as muscles, moving the side (<term>lateral</term>) muscles along with them.

In turn, these lateral muscles move the lips.

It is necessary to first take note of the bones of the face: in which part they arise and from where the nerves originate that first open and then close the lips of the mouth. We must also see where the muscles are attached that these nerves penetrate.

### *[Nerves and muscles of the mouth and their functions in various movements]*

The nerve marked *n m* in the lower lip and the nerve *o p* in the upper lip are the reason the mouth closes, assisted by the muscles that form the lips.

As the muscles of the lips compress toward their center, they pull the side muscles toward them. Conversely, as the side muscles contract and pull back, they draw the lips back, causing the mouth to widen.

The maximum contraction of the mouth makes its width half of what it is when fully extended. This same proportion applies to the maximum width of the nostrils and the distance between the tear ducts of the eyes.

The lips perform two tightening movements: the first presses and strains the lips against each other; the second compresses or shortens the width of the mouth. However, the pressure of one lip against the other does not extend past the back molars. When these muscles are pulled, they have such great power that, even while keeping the teeth slightly apart...

### [*Which muscles are those that tighten the mouth across?*]

The muscles that tighten the mouth across, as shown above, are the lips themselves, which draw the sides of the mouth toward the center; and this is demonstrated to us by the fourth rule of this subject, which says: the skin forming the covering of the muscles that pull always points with its wrinkles toward the spot where the cause of the movement is located; and by the fifth rule: no muscle uses its power by pushing, but always by drawing toward itself the parts that are joined to it; therefore, the center of the muscles called the lips of the mouth draws the extremities of this mouth toward itself along with part of the cheeks, and for this reason, the mouth is always filled with wrinkles during this function.

### *[Cavities of the face and their relation]*

The cavity of the eye socket, the cavity of the bone that supports the cheek, and those of the nose and the mouth are of equal depth, and they end below the seat of the senses¹ in a vertical line.

Each of these cavities is as deep as the third part of a man’s face—that is, the distance from the chin to the hairline.

### *[The different kinds of teeth and their function]*

The six upper molars have three roots each: two roots on the outer side of the jaw and one on the inner side. The last two of these emerge at about four years of age.

Next come four premolars with two roots each, one on the inside and one on the outside of the jaw; these are followed by the two *maestre* (canines) with only one root; and in front are the four teeth that do the cutting, which have only one root.

### [*How nature gives animals the power of motion*]

### ON MACHINES

Why nature cannot give the power of movement to animals without mechanical instruments, as is demonstrated by me in this book on the actions of movement which nature has created in animals. For this reason, I have established the rules of the four powers of nature, without which nothing through her can provide local movement to these animals. We shall, therefore, first describe this local movement and how it produces and is produced by each of the other three powers. Then we shall describe natural weight; for although no weight can truly be said to be anything other than accidental, it has pleased us to name it thus to distinguish it from force. Force, in all its operations, shares the nature of weight and is for this reason called accidental weight; this is the force produced by the third power of nature, that is, the inherent or natural power. The fourth and last power will be called percussion, which is the end or the restraint of movement. And we shall

Begin by stating that every local, imperceptible movement is produced by a perceptible mover, just as in a clock the counterweight is raised by a person who is its mover. Moreover, the elements repel or attract each other, for one sees water expelling air from itself, and fire entering as heat under the bottom of a boiler and afterwards escaping in the bubbles on the surface of the boiling water. And again, the flame draws the air to itself, and the heat of the sun draws up the water in the form of moist vapor which afterwards falls down in thick, heavy rain. Percussion, however, is the immense power of things which is generated within the elements. Quaderni I 1 r.

->[*Description of the human body in process of dissection*]<-

## THE ORDER OF THE BOOK

This plan of mine of the human body will be unfolded to you just as though you had the natural man before you. The reason is that if you wish to know the parts of a man thoroughly after he has been dissected, you must either turn him or your eye so that you are examining from different aspects—from below, from above, and from the sides—turning him over and studying the origin of each limb; in such a way, the natural anatomy has satisfied your desire for knowledge. But you must understand that such knowledge as this will not continue to satisfy you on account of the very great confusion which must arise from the mixture of membranes with veins, arteries, nerves, tendons, muscles, bones, and the blood, which of itself stains every part with the same color; the veins through which this blood is discharged are not perceptible because of their smallness. The integrity of the membranes is broken during the process of investigating the parts which they enclose, and the fact that their transparent substance is stained with blood prevents the proper identification of the parts which these cover on account of the similarity of the blood-stained color; for you cannot attain any knowledge of the one without confusing and destroying the other.

Therefore, it becomes necessary to perform several dissections: you will need three in order to have a complete knowledge of the veins and arteries, destroying all the rest with very great care; and three others for a knowledge of the membranes, 'panniculi', and three for the tendons.

Therefore, there shall be revealed to you here in fifteen entire figures the "geography" of the **little world** <note>original: "minor mondo"; this refers to the "microcosm," the Renaissance idea that the human body is a smaller reflection of the entire universe.</note> in the same order used by Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy was an ancient Greek-Egyptian astronomer and geographer whose works defined how the world was mapped in the Renaissance.</note> before me in his *Cosmography*. I shall divide the members as he divided the whole world—into provinces—and then I shall define the functions of the parts in every direction, placing before your eyes the perception of the whole figure and the capacity of man, specifically how he achieves movement through his various parts.

And how I wish it might please our Creator that I were able to reveal the nature of man and his customs as clearly as I describe his physical figure!

I would remind you that the dissection of the nerves will not reveal the position of their **branching** <note>original: "ramification"</note> nor which muscles they enter if you use bodies dissected in either flowing water or in lime water. *[Dissection of the human hand]*

## OF THE HAND FROM WITHIN

When you begin the hand from the inside, first separate all the bones a little from each other so that you may be able quickly to recognize the true shape of each bone from the palmar side of the hand, and also the real number and position of each; and have some sawn through down the center of their thickness—that is, lengthwise—so as to show which is hollow and which is solid. And having done this, place the bones together at their true contact points and represent the whole hand from the inside, wide open. Then set down the complete figures of the first ligaments of the bones. The next demonstration should be of the muscles which bind together the wrist and the rest of the hand. The fifth shall represent the tendons which move the first joints of the fingers. The sixth, the tendons which move the second joints of the fingers. The seventh, those which move the third joints of these fingers. The eighth shall represent the nerves which give them the sense of touch. The ninth, the veins and the arteries. The tenth shall show the whole hand complete with its skin and its measurements; and measurements should also be made of the bones. And whatever you do for this side of the hand, you should do the same for the other three sides: that is, from the palmar or underside, from the dorsal side, and from the sides of the extensor and the flexor muscles.

And thus, in the chapter on the hand, you will make forty demonstrations; and you should do the same with each limb.

And in this way, you will attain complete knowledge.

You should afterwards write a discourse concerning the hands of various animals in order to show in what way they vary—as with the bear, in which the ligaments of the tendons of the toes are joined above the neck of the foot.

### [Nothing is superfluous or lacking in nature]

Nothing is redundant and nothing is missing in any species of animal or product of nature, unless the defect arises from the means that produced it.

### WHETHER OR NOT THE AIR ESCAPING FROM THE TRACHEA COMPRESSES ITSELF DURING ITS PASSAGE

All the air that enters the trachea remains equal in volume throughout every stage of its branching; this is similar to the branches grown during a plant's seasonal development, where every year the combined thickness of all the new branches equals the thickness of the plant's main stem.

However, the trachea narrows at the larynx in order to compress the air, which acts like a living force as it travels from the lung to create various types of voices. This compression also serves to pressure and expand the different passages and ventricles of the brain. If the trachea were as wide at its upper end as it is in the throat, the air would be unable to condense and perform the functions necessary for life and for man—namely speaking, singing, and the like. Furthermore, the air that is suddenly expelled from the lung during deep sighs is driven by the abdominal wall, which squeezes the intestines; these, in turn, raise the diaphragm, which presses against the lung.

--- Page 172 ---
# WHETHER THE HEART CHANGES POSITION AT DEATH OR NOT

The change the heart undergoes at death is similar to the change it experiences during the expulsion of its blood, though it is somewhat less. This is demonstrated when one observes the pigs in Tuscany, where they pierce the hearts of the pigs using an instrument called a borer, which is typically used for drawing wine out of casks. Thus, after turning the pig over and tying it securely, they pierce its right side and its heart at the same time with the borer, thrusting it in a straight line. If this borer pierces the heart while it is expanded, the heart, as it expels the blood, becomes contracted and draws the wound upward along with the point of the borer; the more it raises the point of the borer on the inside, the more it lowers the handle of the borer on the outside. Afterward, when the heart expands and moves this wound downward, the part of the borer that is outside makes a movement opposite to that of the part within, which moves in unison with the movement of the heart. It does this many times, so that at the end of life, the part of the borer that is outside remains in the middle of the two extremes where the last opposing movements of the heart occurred while it was alive. When the heart becomes completely cold, it shrinks somewhat and contracts as much as it had expanded when warm, because heat causes a body to increase or diminish as it enters or leaves it; I have seen this many times and have observed such measurements by allowing the instrument to remain in the heart until the animal was butchered.

The distance from the greatest to the smallest movement of the heart in this animal is about the thickness of a finger, and in the end, the heart remains with its tip out of its usual position by about half the thickness of a finger. Be careful not to make a mistake in taking this measurement, because sometimes the handle of this borer will not show any change whether the heart is living or dead; this occurs when the heart receives its wound halfway through the process of its contraction, which is the position in which it remains when it is dead. Sometimes this handle shows a greater change, and this occurs when the heart receives its wound during its period of greatest or least length; thus, it will produce as many variations in distance as there are variations in the length or shortness of the heart at the moment it is wounded.

Above this, the handle will show greater or lesser changes depending on how far the point of the borer penetrates into the heart. If the iron point pierces through the heart entirely, it makes a smaller movement from its center of motion—that is, from the insertion point—than it would if the iron had only wounded the front wall of the heart. I will not dwell further on this point because a complete study of these movements has been compiled in the twentieth book on the forces of the lever <note>Leonardo frequently applied principles of physics and mechanics to the human body.</note>. 

If you should consider that, once the heart has been pierced, the length of the borer could not follow the movement mentioned above because it is blocked by the front wall of the heart, you must understand that as the heart expands and dilates, it pulls or pushes the point of this iron along with its motion. The iron located in the front wall enlarges the wound both upward and downward—or to put it more accurately, it moves the wound. Since the roundness of the thick part of the iron does not enlarge the hole (because it does not cut), it carries the front wound of the heart along with it. This compresses the part of the heart in contact with the tool, first at the upper part of the wound and then at the lower part. Such stretching and compression are easily performed by the heart when it is warm because it is less dense.

And you who say that it is better to look at an anatomical demonstration than to see these drawings, you would be right, if it were possible to observe all the details shown in these drawings in a single figure, in which, despite all your ability, you will not see nor acquire a knowledge of more than a few veins; whereas, in order to obtain an exact and complete knowledge of these, I have dissected more than ten human bodies, destroying all the various members, and removing even the very smallest particles of the flesh that surrounded these veins, without causing any spilling of blood other than the imperceptible bleeding of the capillary veins. And as one single body did not suffice for such a long time, it was necessary to proceed by stages with as many bodies as would render my knowledge complete; and this I repeated twice over in order to discover the differences.

But though possessed of an interest in the subject, you may perhaps be deterred by natural disgust, or, if this does not restrain you, then perhaps by the fear of passing the night hours in the company of these corpses, quartered and flayed and horrible to behold; and if this does not deter you, then perhaps you may lack the skill in drawing essential for such representation; and even if you possess this skill, it may not be combined with a knowledge of perspective, while, if it is so combined, you may not be versed in the methods of geometrical demonstration or the method of estimating the forces and strength of muscles, or perhaps you may be found wanting in patience so that you will not be diligent.

<margin>Quaderni I 13 v.</margin>
Concerning these things, whether or not they have all been found in me, the hundred and twenty books that I have composed will give their verdict ‘yes’ or ‘no’. In these I have not been hindered either by greed or negligence, but only by lack of time. Farewell.

Why the heart does not beat nor the lung breathe during the time that the child is in the womb, which is filled with water; for if it should draw a breath, it would instantly be drowned. But the breathing and the beating of its mother’s heart works in the life of the child, which is joined to her by means of the umbilical cord, just as it works in her other limbs.

Therefore, during every harmonic or, as you may say, musical tempo, the heart makes three movements, as is described below; of these tempos, an hour contains one thousand and eighty. The heart, therefore, moves three thousand five hundred and forty times in each hour in the process of opening and shutting. And it is this frequency of movement which warms the thick muscles of the heart, and this heat warms the blood that continually beats within it. It heats it more in the left ventricle, where the walls are very thick, than in the right ventricle with the thin wall. And this heat makes the blood grow thinner and turns it to vapor and changes it into air, and would change it to elemental fire, if it were not that the lung provides help at this crisis with the coolness of its air.

But the lung cannot send air into the heart, nor is this necessary since, as has been said, air is generated in the heart; and this air, as it becomes mingled with the warm, thick moisture, evaporates through the ends of the capillary veins at the surface of the skin in the form of perspiration. Moreover, the air which is breathed in by the lung enters continually dry and cold, and issues forth moist and warm. But the arteries, which are joined by continual contact to the network of branches of the trachea spreading through the lung, are what catch the coolness of the air as it enters into this lung. [Balance of heart in man and animals]

And if you say that the left external wall (of the heart) has been

made thick in order that it might acquire greater weight, so that it should act as a counterpoise to the right ventricle, which holds a great weight of blood, you have not reflected that this balancing was not necessary, seeing that all land animals except man have the heart in a recumbent position; and the heart of man also lies this way when he is lying in his bed. But you would not be weighing the matter well in your conclusion, because the heart has two supports which descend from the collar bone, from which—according to the fourth book of ‘De Ponderibus’—the heart is unable to balance itself if there is not a single support above; and these two supports are the Arteria Aorta and the Vena cava. Furthermore, if the heart is deprived of the weight of the blood as it contracts and places it in deposit in its upper ventricles, the centre of gravity of the heart would then be on the right side of the heart, and thus its left side would be lightened. But this theory of balancing is not a true one, as was said above, because animals which lie down or which stand on four feet have the heart lying just as they are themselves, and with these, no balancing of the heart is required.

And in the case of the bat, which always positions itself upside down when it sleeps, how does the heart balance with the right and left ventricle?

### WHY THE PRINCIPAL VALVES OF THE RIGHT VENTRICLE ARE MADE WITH SO LITTLE MEMBRANE AND SUCH A NETWORK OF CORDAE

This was ordained by nature so that as the right ventricle begins to close, the escape of the blood from its huge capacity should not suddenly cease, because a portion of that blood had to be given to the lung, and it would not be given if the valve had blocked the exit. But this ventricle closed itself when the lung had received its quantity of blood, and so from the right ventricle it was able to press through the pores of the median wall into the left ventricle; and at the same time the right auricle became the depository for the excess blood which it passes to the lung, and this suddenly gives it to the opening of this right ventricle, restoring itself through the blood with which the liver supplies it.

### HOW MUCH BLOOD IS THE LIVER ABLE TO GIVE TO THE HEART THROUGH ITS OPENING?

It restores as much as it consumes; that is a very small amount, because in an hour the heart opens about two thousand times. There is great weight involved.

The right ventricle was made heavier than the left one so that the heart may maintain a slanting position; and when the blood rises out of the left ventricle and lightens it, this blood moves from there toward the left side along with its center of gravity when it is in the upper ventricles.

The heart has four ventricles: specifically, two upper ones called auricles of the heart, and two lower than these called the right and left ventricles.

### [Definitions]

Definition of the instruments.
A discourse on the nerves, muscles, tendons, ‘panniculi’ (membranes), and ligaments.

The function of the nerves is to convey sensation; they are the drivers of the soul, for they originate from its seat and command the muscles to move the limbs according to the will of this soul.

The muscles, as the servants of the nerves, pull the sinews toward themselves, which are joined to these limbs in a similar manner.

The tendons are mechanical instruments which have no sensation of their own but carry out as much work as is assigned to them.

The membranes (panniculi) are joined to the flesh, being positioned between the flesh and the nerve, and they are most frequently joined to the cartilage.

The ligaments are joined to the tendons and have the nature of membranes (panniculi) which bind the joints of the bones together and are converted into cartilage. There are as many of them at every joint as there are tendons moving the joint and tendons opposite to these coming to the same joint; these ligaments join and mingle together, helping, strengthening, and connecting one with another.

--- Page 179 ---
171
ANATOMY

The cartilage is a hard substance, like, let us say, hardened tendon or softened bone, and its position is always between the bone and the tendon because it partakes of both substances; it is flexible and unbreakable, with its flexibility acting like a spring.

Pellicles are certain muscular parts made up of flesh, tendons, and nerves, the union of which forms a composition capable of being extended in any direction; flesh is a mixture made up of muscles, tendon, nerve, blood, and artery.

Bone is a hard substance, inflexible and adapted for resistance; it is without sensation and terminates in the cartilages that form its extremities. Its marrow is composed of sponge, blood, and soft fat coated over with a very thin tissue. The sponge-like substance is a mixture of bone, fat, and blood.

The membranes (panniculi) are of three kinds: those made up of tendons, those made up of nerves, and those made up of nerves and tendons; the mixed membrane is woven of tendon, nerve, muscle, vein, and artery.

The membranes between the tendons and the cartilages are formed so as to unite tendon with cartilage in a large and continuous joint, so that it may not break through excessive force. When the muscle itself thickens, it does not pull the tendon or any limb toward itself; instead, the muscle is pulled by the tendon toward the membrane and the cartilage, as happens with the muscles inside the ventricles of the heart when they shut their openings. However, the muscles of the other limbs are pulled toward the bone where they are attached, and they pull their tendon behind them along with the limb that is joined to that tendon.

Tears come from the heart and not from the brain.

Quaderni II 18 v.
Define all the parts of which the body is composed, commencing with the skin and its outer coating, which often detaches itself through the action of the sun.

There are six things which take part in the composition of movements: namely bone, cartilage, membrane, tendon, muscle, and nerve; consequently, these six are in the heart.

Trace the recurrent nerves as far as the heart, and observe whether these nerves provide movement to the heart or whether the heart moves on its own. If its movement comes from the recurrent nerves which originate in the brain, then you will demonstrate how the soul is seated in the ventricles of the brain, and how the vital powers originate from the left ventricle of the heart. --- Page 183 ---
movement of the heart originates in itself, then you will say that the seat of the soul is in the heart, as is the seat of the vital powers. Therefore, you should pay close attention to these recurrent nerves and similarly to the other nerves, because the movement of all muscles springs from these nerves, which spread into the muscles through their branches. There are many times when the heart draws into itself some of the air found in the lung and returns it after it has been heated, without the lung having gathered any new air from outside.

It is proved that it must necessarily be as set forth here: the heart, which moves by itself, only moves by opening and shutting. This opening and shutting creates motion along the line that lies between the apex and the base or crown of the heart. It cannot open without drawing air into itself from the lung, which it immediately blows back into the lung. Afterward, it will be seen that the lung is restored by a vigorous movement of sudden deep breathing from the fresh intake of cold air; this occurs when a fixed focus of the mind causes one to forget to breathe.

In closing itself, the heart—with its nerves and muscles—pulls behind it the powerful vessels that extend from the heart to join with the lung. This is the primary cause of the lung's expansion, because it cannot expand unless the vacuum within increases, and the vacuum cannot increase unless it refills itself; finding air to be the most suitable substance for restoring this vacuum, the lung refills itself with it. Afterward, as the heart contracts, it begins to reopen; as it reopens, it relaxes the stretched nerves and vessels of the lung. It follows that the lung closes itself up again, and at the same time, it fills the increasing vacuum of the heart with the air it exhales. Part of this air is sent out through the mouth as superfluous air for which there is no room in either the lung or the heart.
Quaderni IV 7 r.

## [Tonsils]

The two tonsils are formed on opposite sides of the base of the tongue and are shaped like two small cushions placed between the jawbone and the base of the tongue to create a space between them. This allows one side to accommodate the rounded lateral shape of the tongue's convex curve when it bends, while its own convex part can wipe food away from the angle of the jaw around the sides of the base of the tongue.

Twenty-eight muscles are located in the roots of the tongue.

## [Of tongues]
## [Leonine and bovine species]

This is the underside of the tongue [drawing], and its surface is rough in many animals, especially in the leonine species—such as lions, panthers, leopards, lynxes, cats, and the like. These have the surface of their tongues very rough, as if they were covered with very small, somewhat flexible nails; when they lick their skin, these nails penetrate down to the roots of the hair and, acting like combs, they remove the tiny parasites that feed upon them.

I once saw a lamb being licked by a lion in our city of Florence, where there are always twenty-five to thirty of them and they breed. With only a few strokes of his tongue, the lion stripped off the entire fleece covering the lamb, and having thus made it bare, he ate it. The tongues of the bovine species are also rough.

## [Pronunciation of vowels]

The membrane positioned between the passage where air travels partly through the nose and partly through the mouth is the only one a person uses to pronounce the letter *a*—that is, the membrane *a n*. Even if the tongue and lips do what they can, they will never prevent the air streaming out from the trachea from forming the sound *a* while in this cavity *a n*. Furthermore, *u* is formed in the same place with the help of the lips, which tighten and push forward.

--- Page 185 ---
themselves out a little; and the more these lips thrust themselves out, the better they pronounce the letter *u*. It is true that the epiglottis rises somewhat toward the palate.

And if it were not for it doing so, the *u* would be changed into *o*, and this *o* . . .

And whether, when *a o u* are pronounced distinctly and rapidly, it is necessary that in pronouncing them continuously without any interval of time, the opening of the lips should go on continually contracting—that is, that in pronouncing *a* they should be wide apart, closer together in pronouncing *o*, and much closer still in pronouncing *u*.

It is proved how all the vowels are pronounced with the back part of the movable palate which covers the epiglottis; and moreover, such pronunciation comes from the position of the lips, by means of which a passage is formed for the air as it streams out, carrying with it the created sound of the voice. Even when the lips are closed, this sound streams out through the nostrils, but when issuing through such a passage, it will never become a demonstrator of any of these letters.

From such an experiment, one may conclude with certainty that the trachea does not create any vowel sound, but that its function only extends to the creation of the aforementioned voice, and especially in *a o u*.

### [*The muscles of the tongue*]

The tongue is found to have twenty-four muscles which correspond to the six muscles of which the mass of the tongue that moves in the mouth is composed.

The present task is to discover in what way these twenty-four muscles are divided or apportioned in the service of the tongue in its necessary movements, which are many and varied; and in addition to this, it must be seen in what manner the nerves descend to it from the base of the brain, and in what manner they pass into this tongue, distributing themselves and breaking into ramifications. And it must further be noted how and in what manner the said twenty-four muscles convert themselves into six in the formation they make in the tongue. # ANATOMY

...nourish them, and how the arteries provide them with vital spirits <note>original: "spiritus"; in this period, these were believed to be subtle fluids that carried life and sensation through the body</note>, (and how the nerves give them sensation).

Furthermore, you shall describe and illustrate how the process of varying, modulating, and articulating the voice in singing is a simple function of the rings of the trachea <term>trachea: the windpipe</term> moved by the recurrent nerves <note>original: "reversive nerves"; these are the nerves that control the larynx</note>. In this case, no part of the tongue is used.

This is proven by what I have demonstrated before: that organ pipes do not become deeper or sharper by changing the mouthpiece <note>original: "fistula"; the part of the instrument where the sound is generated</note>—that is, by making that opening wider or narrower. Instead, the pitch changes only by making the pipe itself wide or narrow, or long or short. This is seen in the expansion or compression of the slide trumpet <note>original: "winding trumpet"</note>. Also, in a pipe of fixed width or length, the sound varies according to the force with which the air is blown into it. This degree of variation is not found in objects that are struck with greater or less force, as observed when bells are struck by very small or very large clappers. The same thing occurs with pieces of artillery <note>cannons</note> that are similar in width but differ in length; in this case, the shorter piece makes a louder and deeper noise than the longer one. I will not go into further detail on this because it is fully treated in the book about musical instruments <note>original: "harmonical instruments"</note>. For this reason, I will resume my discussion regarding the functions of the tongue where I left off.

The tongue works in the pronunciation and articulation of syllables, which are the building blocks of all words. The tongue is also used to move food around during the process of chewing <note>original: "mastication"</note> and to clean the inside of the mouth and the teeth. Its principal movements are seven: stretching out, drawing together <note>contracting</note>, drawing back, thickening, shortening, spreading out, and pointing. Of these seven movements, three are composite because one cannot occur without another necessarily occurring with it. This is the case with the first and second—stretching out and drawing together—for you cannot stretch out a substance that is capable of being expanded without it also contracting and narrowing on all its sides. A similar result occurs in the third and fourth movements, which are the opposite of the first two: namely, thickening and shortening.

After these come the fifth and sixth movements. Together, they form a third category consisting of three distinct motions: spreading out, pointing, and shortening.

   Although human ingenuity <note>original: "subtlety"</note> creates various inventions that achieve the same goal through different means, it will never devise an invention more beautiful, simple, or direct than those of nature. In her inventions, nothing is lacking and nothing is unnecessary. Nature requires no counterbalancing weights when she creates limbs designed for movement in animal bodies. Instead, she places within them the soul of the body that forms them—that is, the mother's soul, which first constructs the shape of the human within the womb and, in due time, awakens the soul that will inhabit it. 

   Initially, this soul remains asleep under the guardianship of the mother’s soul, which nourishes it and gives it life through the umbilical vein and all its vital organs <note>original: "spiritual members"; in Renaissance anatomy, these were the organs responsible for distributing life-giving "spirits" throughout the body</note>. This continues as long as the umbilical cord is joined to it by the placenta <term>secundines: the fetal membranes and placenta</term> and the vascular connections <term>cotyledons: the functional units of the placenta where the exchange of nutrients occurs</term> by which the child is attached to the mother. This explains why any wish, intense desire, fright, or mental suffering experienced by the mother is felt more powerfully by the child than by the mother; indeed, there are many cases where a child loses its life because of such experiences.

   This discussion does not strictly belong here, but it is necessary when examining the structure of living bodies. I leave the rest of the definition of the soul to the wisdom of the friars—those fathers of the people who, through divine inspiration, understand all mysteries. I do not speak against the sacred books, for they represent the supreme truth.

One shall perform an experiment in the anatomy of animals by pumping air into their lungs and compressing them, thereby narrowing and widening the tube <note>original: "fistula"; here referring to the trachea or windpipe</note> which produces their voice.

There is a question regarding the membranes <term>pannicles: small layers of tissue or membranes</term> that keep the blood within the antechamber of the heart at the base of the aorta. It is worth considering whether nature could have functioned without them or not, since one can clearly see how the three walls or hinges where these membranous valves of the heart are located are the very things that—by their swelling—shut this blood out from the heart when the heart reopens on the side below these valves.

Nature carries out this final closing so that the great force the heart uses in the left ventricle—as it reopens to draw in the blood that filters through the narrow gaps in the wall dividing it from the right ventricle <note>Leonardo believed blood passed through the septum, the wall between the heart's chambers</note>—does not, in creating a vacuum, pull back the most delicate membranes of these heart valves.

The circulation of the blood in the antechamber of the heart at the base of the aorta serves two purposes. The first is that this circulation, moving in many directions, causes great internal friction. This friction heats and lightens the blood, increasing and sustaining the vital spirits <note>original: "spiritus vitales"; in Renaissance medicine, these were refined substances in the blood that provided life and heat</note> which always maintain themselves through warmth and moisture. The second effect of this blood circulation is to close the open gates of the heart again with a complete sealing system during its first reflexive movement.

<margin>Notebook IV 11 recto</margin>
The heart beats as many times as this gate expels the blood; for this reason, those who have a fever become inflamed.

Between the cords <note>original: "cordae"</note> and threads of the muscles in the right ventricle, there are many tiny interwoven threads. These are similar in nature and shape to the small muscles that form the "worm" in the brain <note>original: "worm in the brain"; likely referring to the vermis of the cerebellum</note> and those that weave the "wonderful net" <note>original: "rete mirabile"; a complex network of blood vessels at the base of the brain</note>. These wind themselves around the most tiny and imperceptible nerves and are woven together with them. These muscles are themselves very capable of expanding and contracting, and they are located within the powerful rush of the blood as it passes in and out among them.

minute cords of the muscles before they are converted into the membranes (panniculi) of the valves.

Before you open the heart, inflate the ventricles of the heart starting from the aorta artery; then tie them up and consider their size. Afterwards, do the same with the right ventricle or the right ‘orecchio’ (auricle); by doing so, you will see its shape and its purpose, for it was created to expand and contract and thus cause the blood to swirl as it passes through its cells. These cells are full of winding passages divided by rounded walls without any angles, so that the motion of the blood, encountering no angular obstructions, may have an easier revolution in its eddying course. In this way, the blood warms itself with more heat in proportion to the rapidity of the heart's movement. Sometimes it attains such great heat that the heart is suffocated; I have already seen one case where the heart burst as a man was fleeing from his enemies, and he poured out perspiration mingled with blood through all the pores of his skin. This heat forms the *spiritus vitales* (vital spirits). Thus, heat gives life to all things; just as one sees the heat of the hen or the turkey-hen giving life and growth to the chickens, and as the returning sun causes all fruits to blossom and sprout. Quaderni IV 13 r.

## [*Division of the surface of the heart by vessels. Peeling the flesh off to find certain vessels*]

The surface of the heart is divided into three parts by three veins that descend from its base. Two of these veins mark the boundaries of the right ventricle and have two arteries in contact beneath them. As for the third vein, I have not yet seen whether it has an artery with it, and consequently, I am about to remove some of the surface flesh to satisfy my curiosity. However, the surface area of the heart enclosed within its arteries occupies half the circumference of the heart's thickness and forms the outer wall of the right ventricle.

# OF THE MOVEMENTS OF THE FINGERS OF THE HANDS

The movements of the fingers are chiefly those of extension and flexing <note>original: "bending"</note>. Extension and flexing are done in various ways. Sometimes they bend as a single unit at the first joint. At other times, they bend or straighten halfway at the second joint. At other times, they bend along their whole length, using all three joints at the same time. 

If the first two joints are prevented from bending, the third joint will bend more easily than before. However, the third joint can never bend by itself if the other joints are free; instead, all three joints must bend together. In addition to the movements mentioned above, there are four other primary movements: two move upwards and downwards, and the other two move from side to side. Each of these is produced by a single tendon. From these, an infinite number of other movements follow, which are always produced by two tendons; and if one of

### OF THE MUSCLES

Nature has provided man with functional muscles that pull the sinews, and these are able to move the limbs according to the will and desire of the common sense, in the same manner as officials stationed by their lord throughout various provinces and cities to represent and carry out his will in those places. And an official who, on more than one occasion, has carried out the commission given to him by the word of his lord will then sometimes do something on his own that does not proceed from the lord's will. Thus, one often sees with the fingers how, after having very obediently learned to play things upon an instrument as commanded by the judgment, they will afterwards play them without the judgment accompanying the action. ### OF THE NERVES

The hand that holds a stone feels a portion of the pain when that stone is struck with a hammer, just as the stone itself would feel it if it were a sentient body.

### OF THE BLOOD WITHIN THE CROWN OF THE HEAD

It would seem to be a simple proposition that if someone were to break the crown of a man's head, nothing would flow out from this fracture except for the blood that was already positioned between its edges. In nature, every heavy object seeks the lowest point; blood possesses weight, and it appears impossible that it could ever rise to a height on its own, as if it were a light or airy substance. 

One might argue that blood is forced upward by the expansion of the lungs. The theory suggests that when the lungs inhale and fill with air, they expand into the "lake of blood" <note>original: "lago del sangue." Leonardo likely refers to the heart or the central thoracic cavity where blood was thought to collect.</note>. Then, as the lungs deflate, they drive the blood out from this "lake" into the veins, causing them to swell. This argument claims that it is this swelling which causes blood to flow out from a fracture at the crown of the head. However, this opinion is immediately disproven by the fact that the veins are perfectly capable of expanding to serve as a convenient container for the increased volume of blood. The blood would not be forced to flow out of a head wound as if it had no other place to go.

### WHY THIS BLOOD ESCAPES THROUGH THE CROWN OF THE HEAD

The "spiritual parts" <note>In Renaissance science, "spirits" were considered subtle, vaporous substances—finer than liquid but more material than soul—that circulated through the body to provide life, heat, and movement.</note> have the power to move and carry material parts along with them in their course. We see that fire, by means of its "spiritual" heat, sends physical matter that has weight and body—such as soot—up through a chimney amidst steam and smoke. If you burn that soot, you will see it reduced to ashes, proving its physical weight. 

In the same way, the heat that is mingled with the blood evaporates through the fracture in the head. In its "desire" to return to its own element <note>Refers to the Aristotelian theory that fire naturally seeks to rise to the "Sphere of Fire" above the atmosphere.</note>, this heat carries with it the blood with which it is infused and intermingled. The reason smoke rises with such force and carries substances with it is that as the fire attaches itself to the wood, it is nourished and fed by a fine moisture; and as this moisture...

becomes thicker than can be consumed by the heat within the fire, the fire seeks to return to its element and carries the heated vapors with it. ### PAINTING

O painter skilled in <term>anatomy</term>, beware lest the excessive prominence of the bones, sinews, and muscles causes you to become a "wooden" painter through your desire to make your nude figures reveal all their emotions. If you wish to remedy this, you should consider how the muscles of old or thin people cover or clothe the bones; furthermore, note the principle by which these same muscles fill the surface spaces between them. Note which muscles never lose their prominence regardless of the degree of fatness, and which ones have tendons that become indistinguishable at the slightest hint of it. There are many cases where several muscles appear to become one due to an increase in fat, and many in which a single muscle divides into several when a person becomes thin or old. In this treatise, all their peculiarities shall be explained in their proper places, especially regarding the spaces between the joints of each limb. Furthermore, you should not fail to observe the variations of these muscles around the joints of any animal's limbs, caused by the diversity of each limb's movements; for the indication of these muscles is never completely lost on any side of these joints, regardless of the increase or decrease of the flesh that composes them.

And you should do the same for a child from its birth until the time of its decrepitude, through all the stages of its life, such as infancy,

### OF THE HEAD

The parts of the structure of the head are ten, namely five external and five internal.

The external parts are: hair and skin, muscular flesh, the large membrane, and the skull. The internal parts are these: the dura mater, the pia mater, and the brain; below, the pia mater and the dura mater return and enclose the brain between them; then there is the rete mirabile, and then the bone foundation of the brain, and from there the nerves proceed.

## [*Organs of the senses in man as compared with those of other animals*]

In studying the structure of the human body, I have found that among all animal types, humans have duller and less refined senses. The human body is formed with less sophisticated organs and parts that are less capable of receiving sensory power. I have observed in the <term>leonine species</term> <note>Lions and other members of the cat family.</note> how the sense of smell is part of the very substance of the brain; it descends into a very large cavity to meet the olfactory receptors, which enter through many cartilaginous passages that lead to the brain mentioned above.

The eyes of the lion species occupy a large portion of the head as their socket, allowing the optic nerves to connect directly with the brain. In humans, the opposite is seen to be the case: the eye sockets take up only a small part of the head, and the optic nerves are thin, long, and weak. Consequently, as one can see, human eyes work poorly by day and even worse at night. In contrast, the aforementioned animals see better at night than by day. The proof of this is that they hunt their prey at night and sleep during the day, as do nocturnal birds.

The "light" or pupil of the human eye gains or loses half its size as it expands or contracts. In nocturnal animals, however, this increase or decrease is more than a hundredfold. This can be seen in the eye of the owl, a nocturnal bird, by bringing a lit torch near it, or even better, by making it look at the sun. You will then see the pupil—which once occupied the entire eye—shrink to the size of a grain of millet. Through this shrinking, it becomes equal in size to the pupil of a human eye. At that point, bright objects appear to the owl in the same color as they do to a human. Furthermore, because the brain of this creature is smaller than a human's, its vision is even more concentrated. Because the owl's pupil expands a hundred times more than a human's at night, it perceives a hundred times more light than a human does; therefore, its power of sight is not defeated by the darkness of night. Meanwhile, the human pupil, which only doubles in size, sees only faint light—much like the bat, which does not fly when the darkness is too great.

## [*Differences between the human intestines and those of other animals*]

## PUPIL OF CAT

If the darkness of night is a hundred times more intense than that of evening, and the human eye doubles the size of its pupil in darkness, this darkness is reduced by half in that eye because it has doubled its visual power; therefore, fifty degrees of darkness remain. And if the eye of the owl has its pupil increased a hundred times in the aforementioned darkness, it increases its visual capacity a hundred times, so that one hundred degrees of visual capacity are acquired. Because equal forces do not overcome one another, the bird sees in the darkness with the pupil increased a hundredfold just as it does in the day with the pupil diminished by ninety-nine parts out of a hundred.

And if you were to say that this animal does not see light by day and for this reason it remains hidden, to this I reply that the bird only hides itself in the day in order to free itself from the harassment of birds which, in a great multitude, always surround it with a loud clamor; frequently they would be put to death if they did not hide themselves in the grottos and caverns of the high rocks.

Of the nocturnal animals, only the lion species changes the shape of its pupil as it enlarges or contracts: for when it is at its smallest stage, it is long in shape; when halfway, it is oval; and when it has attained its greatest expansion, it is circular in shape.

The continual passing of the blood in these veins makes them thicken and harden so that at last they close up and prevent the passage of the blood.

The spaces or hollows in the veins of animals and the long passage of the fluid that nourishes them harden and finally contract. In contrast, the hollows of the veins of the earth become enlarged through the long, continuous passage of water.

## MUSCLES OF ANIMALS

The hollows situated between the muscles should not be of such a kind that the skin looks as though it covers two sticks placed so that they touch each other, as in *c*; nor should they be in such a way as to look like two sticks at a small distance from each other with the skin hanging idly in a loose curve, as in *f*. Instead, the skin should be as in *i*, laid over the spongy fat that lies between the angles, such as in the angle *n m o*, which originates at the point where the muscles cease to touch. Because the skin cannot descend into such a sharp angle, nature has filled it with a small quantity of spongy or—as I prefer to call it—vesicular fat; that is, fat containing small cells full of air, which become compressed or expanded according to the increase or decrease in the volume of the muscles. In this case, the hollow *i* always has a deeper curve than the muscle itself.

Perform a dissection of different eyes and see which muscles open and close the aforementioned pupils of the eyes of animals.

## OF THE EYES OF ANIMALS

The eyes of all animals have pupils which have the power to increase or diminish on their own according to the greater or lesser light of the sun or another light source. In birds, however, the difference is greater, especially with nocturnal birds of the owl species, such as the long-eared, white, and brown owls. For with these, the pupil increases until it almost covers the entire eye or diminishes to the size of a grain of millet, preserving its round shape all the while. But in the lion species—such as panthers, leopards, lionesses, tigers, wolves, lynxes, Spanish cats, and others—the pupil, as it diminishes, changes from a perfect circle to an elliptical shape, as is seen in the margin. Man, however, having feebler vision than any other animal, is less

When the eye of the bird closes with its two coverings, it closes the secondina first; this closes it from the lachrymal gland as far as the angle of the eye, and the first covering closes it from the bottom upwards. ### REPRODUCTIVE POWER

The frog remains alive for several hours when the head, the heart, and all the intestines have been removed. And if you prick the aforementioned cord, it instantly twitches and dies.

All the nerves of animals derive from here: when this is pricked, the animal dies instantly.

# PHYSIOLOGY

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 80 recto, section b</margin>

Where there is life, there is heat; where there is vital heat, there is movement of the watery humours <note>original: "humours" — refers to the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, choler, and melancholy) believed in the Renaissance to control health and temperament</note>.

The common sense <note>original: "common sense" — in Renaissance psychology, this was a specific part of the brain where all five senses were thought to meet and be processed into a single perception</note> is that which judges the things given to it by the other senses.

[*The common sense is set in motion by the things given to it by the five senses.*]

These senses are moved by objects, and these objects send their images to the five senses. From the senses, these images are transferred to the organ of perception (<term>imprensiva</term>) <note>Leonardo used this term for a specific part of the brain's ventricles that receives sensory data</note> and from this to the common sense. Once they are judged there, they are transmitted to the memory, where they are retained more or less distinctly depending on their power.

[*The five senses are these: seeing, hearing, touch, taste, and smell.*]

Ancient thinkers have concluded that the faculty of judgment given to man is produced by an organ with which the other five senses are connected by means of the organ of perception (<term>imprensiva</term>). To this organ, they have given the name "common sense," and they say that this sense is located in the center of the head. They use the name "common sense" simply because it acts as the shared judge of the other five senses: seeing, hearing, touch, taste, and smell. 

The common sense is set in motion by the organ of perception (<term>imprensiva</term>), which is situated in the center between it and the senses. The organ of perception acts by using the images of things presented to it by the "superficial instruments"—that is, the senses—which are placed between external objects and the organ of perception. In the same way, the senses are acted upon by the objects themselves.

The images of surrounding things are transmitted to the senses, the senses transmit them to the organ of perception, and the organ of perception transmits them to the common sense. There, they are imprinted on the memory and are retained more or less distinctly according to the importance or power of the thing perceived. The sense that functions most swiftly is the one nearest to the organ of perception; this is the eye, the chief and leader of the others. We will treat only the eye and leave the others aside so as not to make our material too long.

Experience tells us that the eye perceives ten different qualities of objects: namely, light and darkness—one serving to reveal the other nine, the other to conceal them—color and substance, form and position, distance and nearness, movement and rest.

## OF THE GROWTH OF MAN

A man at three years of age will have reached half of his full height.
A woman of the same size as a man will weigh less than he does.
A dead woman lies face down in water, while a man lies the opposite way.

How radiating lines carry visual power with them as far as the point of impact:
Our mind or common sense, which philosophers claim resides in the center of the head, keeps its spiritual members at a great distance from itself. This is clearly seen in the lines of the visual rays which, after ending at an object, immediately transmit back to their source the characteristics of the form they have encountered.

Also—regarding the sense of touch which derives from the common sense—do we not see it extending its power as far as the tips of the fingers? For as soon as these tips have touched an object, the sense is immediately made aware of whether it is hot or cold, hard or soft, pointed or smooth.

## OF THE GAIT OF MAN

The gait of man is always modeled after the universal gait of four-footed animals; seeing as these move their feet crosswise, as a horse does when it trots, so a man moves his four limbs crosswise. That is, if he thrusts his right foot forward as he walks, he thrusts his left arm forward with it, and it always continues in this manner.

Men born in hot countries love the night because it cools them, and they hate the sunlight because it makes them hot again; for this reason, they are the color of the night, which is black; and in cold countries, everything is the opposite.

That cause which moves the water through its springs against the

--- Page 210 ---
natural course of its gravity is like that which moves the fluids in all the forms of living bodies.

The faculties are four: memory and intellect, appetite and desire.

The first two belong to reason; the others belong to the senses.

Of the five senses, sight, hearing, and smell may be partially suppressed—touch and taste, however, cannot.

The sense of smell carries that of taste with it in the dog and other gluttonous animals.

All spiritual powers, as they move further away from their primary or secondary cause, occupy more space and become less powerful.

Regarding the bending of the joints and the manner in which the flesh grows upon them during their contraction and extension: make a separate treatise of this most important study in the ‘Description of the movements of four-footed animals,’ among which is man, who also in infancy moves on four feet.

When a man is walking, he carries his head ahead of his feet. When a man walking traverses a level space, he leans forward at first and then leans just as far backward.

It is impossible to breathe through the nose and through the mouth at the same time. The proof of this is seen when anyone breathes with the mouth open, taking the air in through the mouth and exhaling it through the nose; for then one always hears the sound of the valve located near the uvula as it opens and shuts.

Male corpses float in water on their backs; female corpses float face downwards.

If, when going up a staircase, you rest your hands upon your knees, all the strain placed upon the arms is subtracted from the tendons below the knees.

We sustain our lives by the death of others.

In dead matter there remains a lifeless vitality which, upon being united

--- Page 211 ---
to the stomachs of living things, resumes a life of the senses and the intellect.

Every body is composed of those members and fluids which are necessary for its support; this necessity is well known and provided for by the soul, which has chosen such a body shape for a time as its habitation.

Consider the fish, which, on account of the continuous friction it necessarily creates with the water, is prepared—since its own life is a daughter of nature—to be delivered of a certain slimy discharge. This occurs through the porosity found to exist between the joints of the scales; this discharge separates from the fish with difficulty and performs the same function for the fish that pitch does for a ship.

# VI
# Natural History

> ->‘*Why is the fish in the water faster than the bird in the air when it ought to be the opposite, seeing that water is heavier and thicker than air, and the fish is heavier and has smaller wings than the bird?*’<-

LOBSTERS and crabs are empty during the waning of the moon, because there is little light for them to feed by; however, if one brings a light to them at night, they all hurry toward it. 
And when the moon is full, they see their food well and eat plenty of it.

Why is the fish in the water faster than the bird in the air when it ought to be the opposite, seeing that water is heavier and thicker than air, and the fish is heavier and has smaller wings than the bird? For this reason, the fish is not moved from its place by the swift currents of the water as the bird is by the fury of the winds in the air; and in addition to this, we may see the fish speeding upward on the very path down which water has fallen abruptly with very rapid movement, like lightning amid the incessant clouds, which seems a marvelous thing. And this results from the immense speed with which it moves, which so exceeds the movement of the water as to make the water seem motionless in comparison to the movement of the fish. The ratio of these movements is as one is to ten; the movement of the water being one and that of the fish ten, exceeding it therefore by nine. Therefore, although the fish has a power of ten, it is left with a power of nine; for as it leaps up the descent—its power being ten and the water taking away one from it—nine remains.

This happens because water is inherently thicker than air and consequently heavier, and therefore it is faster in filling up the

For this reason, the fish is swifter than the bird, in front of which the air is condensed. <term>C.A.</term> <note>original: Codex Atlanticus</note> 168 v. b

## HOW OXEN FEED ON TALL PLANTS

Oxen, in order to feed on the leaves of tall, slender plants such as young poplars and the like, are in the habit of rearing themselves up so that they stride with their legs across the base of the plant. They then press continually forward in such a way that the plant, being unable to bear up against the oppressive weight, is obliged to give way and bow down its lofty top. <term>C.A.</term> 297 r. b

[*With a drawing of a moth*]

The *pannicola* <term>pannicola</term> <note>Leonardo likely refers here to a dragonfly or similar four-winged insect, though the text calls it a "moth."</note> flies with four wings, and when those in front are raised, those behind are lowered.

But it is necessary for each pair to be, by itself, sufficient to sustain the animal's whole weight.

When one pair is raised, the other is lowered.

In order to observe flight with four wings, go to the moats and you will see the black *pannicole*. <term>C.A.</term> 377 v. b

## VII
# Human Proportions

> ->*'The span of a man’s outstretched arms is equal to his height.'*<-

[Proportions of the human figure]
From the chin to the hairline <note>original: "starting of the hair"</note> is a tenth part of the total height of the figure.
From the wrist <note>original: "junction of the palm of the hand"</note> to the tip of the middle finger is a tenth part.
From the chin to the top of the head is an eighth part.
And from the pit of the stomach to the top of the chest is a sixth part.
And from the base of the sternum <note>original: "fork of the ribs"</note> to the top of the head is a fourth part.
And from the chin to the nostrils is a third part of the face.
The measurement is the same from the nostrils to the eyebrows, and from the eyebrows to the hairline.
<margin>Codex Atlanticus 358 r. a</margin>
The foot is a sixth part of the height, and the forearm to the elbow is a fourth part. The width across the shoulders is also a fourth part.

There is as great a distance between the base of one ear and the base of the other as there is from the space between the eyebrows to the chin.
<margin>Manuscript A 62 v.</margin>
The size of the mouth in a well-proportioned face is equal to the distance between the parting of the lips and the bottom of the chin.

[With sketches of heads]
The dip or angle of the lower lip is midway between the bottom of the nose and the bottom of the chin.
The face itself forms a square, of which the width is measured from the outer corner <note>original: "extremity"</note> of one eye to the other, and the height is from the tip of the nose to the bottom of the lower lip; the remaining areas above and below this square have the same height as the square itself.

## VIII
### Medicine

> *‘Medicine is the restoring of conflicting elements; sickness is the discord of the elements infused in the living body.’*

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 270 r. c</margin>
‘You know that medicines, when used well, restore health to the sick. They will be used well when the doctor, alongside an understanding of the medicine’s nature, also understands what a human being is, what life is, and what the human constitution and health are. Understand these well and you will understand their opposites; and when that is the case, you will know well how to devise a remedy.’

#### TO BREAK A STONE IN THE BLADDER

Take the shell of a hazelnut <note>original: "filbert"</note>, date stones, saxifrage <note>a plant whose name literally means "stone-breaker," traditionally used in herbalism to treat kidney and bladder stones</note>, and nettle seed in equal quantities. Grind them into a fine powder and mix it with your food as you would a spice; or, if you prefer, take it in the form of a syrup made with warmed white wine.

# IX
## Optics

> "These are the miracles—forms already lost, mingled together in so short a space, which it can recreate and reconstitute by its expansion <note>original: "dilation"</note>."

**Why nature did not create a uniform power in the visual faculty:**
Nature has not created a uniform power in the visual faculty <note>the ability to see</note> but has given this faculty greater power the closer it is to its center. She has done this so as not to break the law given to all other powers, which possess more potency as they approach their center.

This is seen in the impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> of any body, and in the supports of the arms of a balance where the weight’s effect is lessened as it draws nearer to the center. It is seen in the case of columns, walls, and pillars; it is seen with heat and in all the other natural powers.

**Why nature made the pupil convex—that is, raised up like part of a ball:**
Nature has made the surface of the pupil situated in the eye convex in form so that surrounding objects may imprint their images at wider angles than could happen if the eye were flat.

### OF THE EYE

**Why the rays of luminous bodies appear larger the farther they are removed from their source:**
The rays of luminous bodies increase the more they proceed farther from their origins. This is proven thus: let *a* be the luminous body whose image is impressed in the pupil of the eye of the beholder, and let us say that *c* is the pupil upon which the impression is made. The same image is impressed also upon the thick part of the upper lid *b* and on the lower lid *o*, and from the upper...

<summary>Leonardo explains that the eye's visual power is strongest at its center, consistent with other natural laws of physics, and notes that the pupil's convex shape allows for a wider field of view.</summary>
<keywords>Optics, visual faculty, percussion, gravity, pupil, convex, luminous bodies, physics of light</keywords>

--- Page 226 ---
and lower lids, the second images are reflected in the pupil of the eye *c*. But regarding the pupil that receives the three aforementioned images—which are divided by the images of the eyelids (in this instance almost closed)—it seems that the images of the luminous bodies impressed on the thick parts of the eyelids are as though actually subdivided. These divisions are pyramidal because the gaps between the lids are also pyramidal. And since it appears to the pupil receiving these three images that the two images rebounding upon it from the lids are joined above and below to the central image representing the luminous body, it seems to this pupil that image *b* is at *a n*, and image *o* appears to be at *a m*, and that the two images are divided by the image of the luminous body *a*.

And since in closing the rims of the eyelids together it is necessary for the watery substance to continually keep the lids moistened as they rub against the eye, this moisture fills the angle produced by the contact made by the lids with the pupil of the eye. The surface of this watery substance is concave, as is proved in the fourth part of the eighth book on water, where it states that "the contact which water makes with its moist bank will always have a concave surface," and that "if this bank is dry, the surface of the water bordering it will be convex."

This angle, therefore, being created by the contact between the eyelid and the pupil, will have the surface of the aqueous humour filling this angle in a concave shape. And since every concave mirror shows the image of its object upside down within the pyramidal convergence of its rays, it follows that the weights or lids of the eyes reflected within this hollow, together with the image of the light, will show these lids inverted. This is the reason why, when the pupil is within the convergence of the pyramidal rays of the concave mirror, the pupil sees the pyramids formed by the rays from the spaces between the lids upside down.

And this is the true cause of the rays of luminous bodies which, the further they extend, seem to approach nearer to the eye. Such a demonstration, however, ought to be divided into its parts in order to make it more intelligible, setting out first its concepts and other propositions necessary for such proof.
