### Whether the images of objects are taken by the visual faculty to the surface of the eye or whether they pass within it:

The lenses of spectacles show us how the images of objects pause at the surface of these glasses and then, by bending <note>original: "bending themselves"; this refers to the refraction of light</note>, penetrate from this surface to the surface of the eye. From that surface, it is possible for the eye to see the shapes of the aforementioned objects.

This is proven to be possible because the surface of the eye is the common boundary between the air and the eye, in that it separates the vitreous humor <note>the clear gel that fills the space between the lens and the retina</note> from the air. If we were to argue that the images of objects stop only on the surfaces of the spectacles, one might say that in spectacles for the elderly <note>convex lenses used to correct farsightedness</note>, the object would appear much larger than it actually is; but without the glass placed between the eye and the object, the object would appear its natural size. Therefore, <insert>[the fact that the size changes]</insert> is clear proof that the convergence of the images of any object—which is intercepted by transparent bodies—will impress itself on the surface of these bodies. This creates a new convergence which then leads the images of these objects into the eye.

<sig>D 2 r.</sig>

### How the images of any object whatsoever which pass to the eye through some aperture imprint themselves on its pupil upside down and the understanding sees them upright:

The pupil of the eye, which receives images through a very small round hole, always receives the images of bodies situated beyond this hole upside down; yet the visual faculty <note>the mental power of sight</note> always sees them upright as they are. This happens because the images pass through the center of the crystalline sphere <note>Leonardo’s term for the lens of the eye</note> situated in the middle of the eye. In this center, the rays unite in a single point and then spread themselves out upon the opposite surface of this sphere without deviating from their course. The images arrange themselves on this surface according to the object that created them; from there, they are captured by the impression and transmitted to the "common sense" <note>original: "commune senso"; the Renaissance concept of a central place in the brain where all sensory data is processed</note> where they are judged. 

This may be proved as follows: let *a n* be the pupil of the eye *k h*, and let *p* be a small round hole made in paper with the fine point of a stylus, and let *m b* be the object placed beyond this opening. I maintain that the upper part of this object cannot reach the upper part of the pupil of the eye through the straight line *m a* because at *v* its...

<summary>Leonardo explains how spectacle lenses refract light toward the eye and proposes a theory for why we perceive images as upright even though they enter the pupil inverted, focusing on the role of the "crystalline sphere" (lens).</summary>
<keywords>optics, spectacles, refraction, vitreous humor, crystalline sphere, common sense, image inversion, pupil, visual perception</keywords>

--- Page 228 ---
passage is blocked by the placement of the paper. However, this upper extremity *m* passes in a straight path through the hole to *n*, the lower part of the pupil—or, one might say, of the crystalline sphere—and from there it directs its course toward the center of this sphere. It then rises to the upper part of the opposite side, and from there, as has been stated, it travels to the common sense.

### Why a mirror, in its images of objects, switches the right side to the left and the left to the right:

The image of every object is reversed in a mirror so that its right side is opposite the left side of the reflected object, and similarly, the left is opposite the right. This is necessarily the case because every natural action is performed by nature in the shortest way and the briefest time possible. Let *a b* be a face that sends its image to the mirror *c d*; this face will have another face in the mirror turned toward it, so that it will have the left eye *c* opposite the right eye *a*, and similarly, the right eye *d* will be opposite the left eye *b*.

And if an opponent should argue that the right eye of the image was opposite the right eye of the object, we might project lines from the right eye of the image to the right eye of the object, and similarly from the left to the left. These lines, *a d* and *b c*, are seen to intersect; and it is proven that in all cases where lines intersect, the right end of one is always opposite the left end of the other. This result is not produced by the shortest line, because the diagonal of a square is always longer than its side; and here *a d* is the diagonal of the square *a b c d*, of which *a c* is one of the sides. Thus, the necessary proof for such a result is concluded.

This effect in the mirror is as if someone were looking at you—someone, that is, who has their left eye opposite your right—and as if by a miracle, they were transposing left and right, as is the case with letters used in stamping and with wax that takes the impression of a cornelian seal.

## OF THE HUMAN EYE

The pupil of the eye changes to as many different sizes as there are differences in the degrees of brightness and darkness of the objects that appear before it:

--- Page 229 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on optics and the mechanics of vision, moving from mirror reflections and light paths to the biological function of the pupil and the comparative anatomy of the eyes in humans versus nocturnal animals.</meta>

<page-num>221</page-num>

# OPTICS

In this instance, nature has provided for the visual faculty when it is irritated by excessive light by contracting the pupil of the eye, and by enlarging this pupil—much like the drawstring of a purse—when the eye must endure varying degrees of darkness. In this, nature works like someone who, having too much light in their house, blocks up the window halfway (or more or less, according to necessity), and who, when night comes, throws open the whole window in order to see better within the dwelling. Nature is here establishing a continual equilibrium, perpetually adjusting and equalizing by making the pupil dilate or contract in proportion to the darkness or brightness that presents itself. You will see this process in the case of nocturnal animals such as cats, screech owls, long-eared owls, and the like, which have small pupils at midday and very large ones at night. This is the same for all land animals, as well as those of the air and water, but it is more extreme—beyond all comparison—with nocturnal animals.

If you wish to perform this experiment with a person, look intently at the pupil of their eye while you hold a lit candle a short distance away. Have them look at this light as you bring it closer to them little by little; you will then see that the nearer the light approaches, the more the pupil will contract.

### Whether the eye sees bright and dark things at the same time:

The <term>crystalline humor</term> <note>original: "crystalline humour"; this refers to the lens of the eye, which early anatomists believed was the primary organ of sight.</note> which dwells within the pupil is condensed on meeting with shining things and becomes rarefied on meeting with dark things. The truth of this is shown upon closing the eye, for then the retained images of bright things seem dark and those of dark things seem bright. This happens more with weak eyes than with those that are strong, and I will speak more fully of this in its proper place.

There follows the discourse concerning the eyes of nocturnal animals, which see better by night than by day. This occurs because the size of their eyes is greater than the size of their entire brain, especially in the case of long-eared and short-eared owls, white owls, little owls, horned owls, and similar creatures. This does not occur with humans, who have a larger brain in proportion to the size [of their eyes]...

<summary>This page explains the involuntary contraction and dilation of the pupil as a survival mechanism to regulate light, comparing human eyes to those of nocturnal animals like owls.</summary>
<keywords>pupil dilation, nocturnal animals, optics, anatomy of the eye, crystalline humor, light adaptation, owls</keywords>

--- Page 230 ---
of his eyes than any other animal that lives on land, and can see very little light after daytime.

There follows concerning the eye of nocturnal animals which see more by night than by day; this arises in great part from the fact that, as was said before, there is a much greater difference between the size of the pupil when dilated and contracted than there is in the case of animals which are active by day. For if the pupil of a man doubles its diameter at night—that is to say, it is increased to four times its daytime area—the diameter of the pupil of the horned owl or the long-eared owl is increased to ten times what it is by day, which is to say that the pupil is a hundred times as large as it is by day.

Furthermore, the ventricle situated in the brain of man called the *imprensiva* is more than ten times the size of the entire human eye, and of this, the pupil in which the sight originates is less than a thousandth part; yet in the case of the long-eared owl, the pupil at night is considerably larger than the ventricle of the *imprensiva* situated in its brain. From this it follows that the *imprensiva* in man is greater in proportion to the pupil, being in fact ten thousand times as great, whereas in the case of the horned owl they are almost equal.

And this *imprensiva* of man, in comparison with that of the long-eared owl, is like a large room that receives light through a small hole compared to a small room that is entirely open. For within the large room it will be night at midday, and in the small one which is open, it will be day at midnight when the weather is not overcast. And herewith may be shown the workings of the most powerful causes by means of the anatomy of the eyes and the *imprensiva* of these two animals, namely of man and of the horned owl.

That object will seem of greater radiance and size which is seen by a larger pupil. One may conduct an experiment of this with our eyes by making as small a hole as possible in a sheet of paper and then bringing it as near as possible to the eye; if you then look at a star through this hole, you are only making use of a small part of the pupil, which sees this star with a wide space of sky around it and sees it so small that hardly anything can be smaller. And if you make the hole near to the edge of the said paper, you will be able to see the same star with the

--- Page 231 ---
other eye at the same time, and it will appear large to you; thus, at that moment, you will see the same star twice with your two eyes—once small and the other time large. Furthermore, you will be able to see the entire body of the sun with only a moderate amount of radiance, for as its size is diminished, its radiance is reduced in proportion, as was explained above. From this it follows that large pupils (the *luce*) see very little in daylight because the excess of radiance hinders their vision.

The image of the sun is unique throughout the entire watery sphere that sees and is seen by this sun, yet it appears divided into as many parts as there are eyes of animals which, from different positions, behold the surface of the water.

What is set forth here is proven because, however far the eyes of navigators carried by ships may move through the universe, they behold the image of the sun simultaneously through all the waters of their hemisphere, in every movement made and from every perspective.

If the eye were as large as the sphere of water, it would see the image of the sun covering a great part of the ocean.

This is demonstrated because if you were to move across a bridge from which you can see the image of the sun in the water of its river, and you move yourself about twenty-five *braccia*, you will see the image of the sun move just as far across the surface of that water. And so, if one were to join together all the images seen during this movement, you would have a single image shaped like a fiery beam. Now, imagine yourself drawing a circle of which this beam is the diameter, and that this entire circle is filled with these images; without doubt, you would see one image with a diameter of twenty-five *braccia*. Now you must understand that if a pupil were to have a diameter of those same twenty-five *braccia*, it would, without moving itself, see an image of the sun in that same water which would encompass seventy-eight and four-sevenths *braccia*.

If, due to the great distance the eye was from the watery sphere, the watery sphere were to diminish to the size of an ordinary image of the sun—as is shown in *perspective*—you would see that the sphere of this water seen by the sun was a single image of this sun.

It is proven in *perspective* how things remote from the eye even

Things that are exceedingly large appear very small in size when far away. This can be seen without any complex demonstration if you simply raise your eyes to a star-filled sky. You will see many stars there that are many times larger than the earth, yet they appear tiny because of their immense distance. Furthermore, the light you perceive in them is not their own; it is merely an image of the sun reflected in them. <note>Leonardo da Vinci believed, as did some others of his time, that stars and planets did not generate their own light but reflected the sun like mirrors or spheres of water.</note> For these stars have no light of their own; instead, they have a surface similar to a sphere of water, suitable for receiving and reflecting the sun’s light.

## THE HUMAN EYE

The <term>pupil</term> <note>original: *luce*; the author uses this to refer to the pupil or the functional opening of the eye.</note> of the eye possesses the power of vision as a whole and within each of its individual parts. If an object smaller than the pupil is placed directly in front of the eye, it does not block the eye's view of distant objects. Even though such an object is solid, it effectively functions as if it were transparent [because the eye can see around it].

Here, an opponent might argue that the power of vision is concentrated into a single point. It would follow from this that any object placed in front of the pupil that is larger than this point would block the eye's entire field of vision. I reply to him that if it were true that the power of vision was reduced to a single point, the <term>convexity</term> <note>the outward curve</note> of the eye—which faces a vast portion of the universe—could not have such a curve unless every part of its surface was at an equal distance from that point. The surface would have to be shaped so that the images of objects meeting at that point corresponded perfectly in their angles and proportions to the actual bodies they represent.

To answer such a person, it is necessary to appeal to experience and then show that this experience is conclusive. First, regarding experience: if you place the thick end of a medium-sized sewing needle as close as possible to your pupil, you will see that it does not interfere with your perception of any object placed behind the needle, no matter how great the distance.

What I say is entirely supported by experience, and logic confirms it. If this visual faculty were reduced to a single point, every object, however small, placed in front of it would block the view of a—

If this faculty resides in the center of the crystalline lens, it captures images with its surface. These images are directed there from the surface of the pupil, where objects are mirrored or reflected from the surface of the <term>uvea</term> <note>the pigmented layer of the eye, including the iris and choroid</note>. The uvea surrounds and coats the vitreous humor, which has darkness behind its transparency—much like how the dark lead backing of a glass mirror allows objects to be reflected more clearly on the surface of the glass. However, if the visual faculty is located in the center of the crystalline sphere, all the objects transmitted to it from the surface of the pupil will appear in their true positions. They will not be reversed from right to left and will appear larger, as demonstrated in the study of perspective. If this crystalline sphere receives images reflected from the curve of the uvea, it will receive them upright, even though the uvea acts as a <term>concave mirror</term> <note>a mirror that curves inward; usually, these invert images, but the author argues the alignment prevents this here</note>. They will be upright because the center of the crystalline sphere is aligned with the center of the uvea’s sphere.

It is true that images from outside the eye pass through the center of the crystalline lens on their way to the uvea. Once they reach the uvea, they become inverted, just like images that reach the uvea without passing through this fluid. Therefore, if we assume the visual faculty resides at the end of the optic nerve, we can conclude that the objects captured by the crystalline sphere appear upright. This is because it takes the images that were inverted in the uvea and inverts them a second time. Consequently, the crystalline sphere presents the images as upright, even though they were received in an inverted state. To an expert in optics, one might argue that the surface of the crystalline sphere, when joined with the vitreous humor, does not change its basic nature; it acts as if the entire eye were filled with the same vitreous fluid. The images of the objects placed before the eye pass to the vitreous sphere through the opening of the pupil, and they intersect within this pupil in such a way that the vitreous sphere is struck on its left side by the right ray of the right sphere, and the same happens on the opposite side; afterwards it penetrates this vitreous sphere, and the rays contract and find themselves much closer together when they are on the opposite side of this sphere than when they first strike it.

And this process of contraction results from the fact that the rays of the images approach the perpendicular when they pass from a thin medium to a dense one, and because the albugineous humour is much thinner and more subtle here than the space enclosed by the surface of the vitreous sphere. Afterwards, the image ought to enlarge as it returns into this albugineous humour, but it does not follow this rule because it is forced to obey the nature of the vitreous sphere from which it originates rather than that of the albugineous humour through which it passes.

And this is why it forms a pyramid as it issues forth from the vitreous sphere and passes through the albugineous humour, and intersects its sides at point *f*; and passes to the visual faculty *g* at the end of the optic nerve *g s*.

### Of the intersection of the images of the objects received by the eye within the albugineous humour:

Experience, which shows that objects transmit their images or likenesses intersected within the eye in the albugineous humour, demonstrates what happens when the images of illuminated objects penetrate through some small round hole into a very dark room. You will then receive these images on a sheet of white paper placed inside this room somewhat near to this small hole, and you will see all the aforementioned objects on this paper with their true shapes and colors, but they will be smaller, and they will be upside down because of the said intersection.

These images, if they originate from a place lit by the sun, will actually seem painted upon this paper, which should be very thin and viewed from the back; and the said hole should be made in a very thin sheet.

### Why the point of a stylus, when placed across the pupil of the eye, casts a large shadow upon the object:

When the point of a stylus is placed crosswise before the pupil of the eye, with its thickness being considerably less than the diameter of the pupil, it will occupy more or less space against other objects in proportion to how near or remote it is from the eye; and this occupation of space will obscure, but will not prevent, the passage of the images of the aforementioned objects.

### Why the rays of luminous bodies increase in proportion to the space that lies between them and the eye:

The lengths of the rays created by luminous bodies increase as the distance between these bodies and the eye increases. It is necessary here first to define what the rays of luminous bodies are, and whether they originate in the eye that looks at these bodies or actually proceed from the luminous bodies themselves; and if we should conclude that they proceed from the eye, it is necessary to define why and in what manner.

### Why luminous bodies show their contours full of straight luminous rays:

The rays that reveal the contours of luminous bodies do not originate from these bodies, but from their images which imprint themselves upon the thickness of the eyelids of the eyes looking at these bodies. We learn this first by the inductive method, which teaches us that the eye, when wide open, does not show us such rays around luminous bodies, and that if the image of a star or other light passes to the eye through the smallest hole made in a paper placed before the eye, such luminous images will always be without rays. But the real proof is shown by the ninth principle of Perspective, where it is stated: the angle of incidence is always equal to the

--- Page 237 ---
angle of reflection—therefore, the rays, which seem as though they extend from the luminous body to make contact with the eye that beholds it, begin when the eye, being almost closed, looks through the narrow crack that exists between the eyelids at that luminous body. The image of this body is reflected in the thick parts of the lids which edge these coverings, and after making this impression, it is reflected onto the pupil of the eye. This pupil receives three images from the same luminous body: namely, two in the thick parts of the lids of the eye's coverings and one in the pupil. Because these three images are very near to one another, they seem to the eye to be continuous and joined to the image in the pupil.

And the proof that experience offers us to confirm this proposition is shown when you raise or lower your face while keeping the eye firmly fixed upon the luminous body; for as the face is raised, the eye will lose all the lower rays of this luminous body. This happens because *the image of this luminous body does not proceed to imprint itself in the thick part of the lower lid of this eye*; where the luminous body does not see the lid, it cannot imprint its image there, and where the falling ray does not strike, it does not produce the reflected ray, and for this reason the pupil does not receive it. And the same will happen when the face is lowered, for then the thick part of the upper covering of the eye neither sees nor is seen by that luminous body; for this reason, the image, as has been said, cannot imprint itself there, and consequently the eye cannot discern there what is not present. But it sees this image in the lower covering, and this lid sees and is seen by the luminous body, and thus we have proved our intent.

## ON THE IMAGES OF OBJECTS INFUSED THROUGHOUT THE AIR

Objects have their images infused throughout all the air that is visible to these objects; these images are present in their entirety throughout the aforementioned air and are present in every part of it.

### Why the eye does not know the boundary of any body:

The eye will never be capable of perceiving the true boundary of the shapes of any body when they appear against a distant background. This may be proved: let *a b* be the pupil of the eye and *c p* the body placed opposite the eye, of which we have noted that *c* is the upper extremity, and let *n m* be the background against which this extremity ought to be perceived by the eye. I maintain that it is not possible to determine in what part of this background the extremity of this body ends, and this is proved with the help of the third section of this treatise. There it is stated that the faculty of vision is not located in a single point, as the painters who have written on perspective would have us believe, but is distributed throughout the whole of the pupil into which the images of objects penetrate, and within the eye in a larger space than that occupied by this pupil. However, these images are perceived more clearly the closer they are to the center of this visual faculty located in that space, and less clearly the further they are removed from this center.

If, therefore, the visual faculty *a b* takes in the extremity of the object *c*, the center line of the visual faculty *r* sees *c* at the part of the background *f*, and the upper extremity of this visual faculty, which is *s*, sees *c* against the background *h*, and the lower part of the visual faculty sees *c* against the background *d*. Thus, the image goes on spreading itself through the whole background *d h*; and because of this, such an extremity is not known to the eye, because the sense of the visual faculty is spread through this entire faculty, which offers to the judgment a vague perception of this ex-

--- Page 239 ---
...tremity *c*, and more or less so depending on whether it is closer to or further from this center line of the visual faculty, and more or less so as it is further from or closer to the eye.

A stone thrown through the air leaves the impression of its movement in the eye that sees it, and drops of water do the same as they descend from the clouds when it rains.

## ON THE NATURE OF SIGHT

I maintain that sight is exercised by all animals through the medium of light; and if anyone should cite the sight of nocturnal animals as an argument against this, I would say that these animals are subject to the same law of nature in exactly the same way. For, as one may easily understand, the senses do not send out any actual power from themselves when they receive the images of things; on the contrary, the air between the object and the sense organ acts as a medium, incorporating the images of things within itself, and presents them to the sense organ through its own contact with it—provided that the objects project themselves to the eye or the nose by sound or smell through their incorporeal powers. In such cases, light is not necessary, nor is it used.

The forms of objects do not enter the air as images unless they are luminous; this being so, the eye cannot receive these images from air that does not contain them, but only touches their surface.

If you wish to speak of the many animals that hunt their prey by night, I answer that when the small amount of light sufficient for them to see their way fails them, they make use of their senses of hearing and smell, which are not hindered by the darkness and in which they are far superior to man. If you watch a cat in the daytime leaping among many pieces of pottery, you will see that they remain unbroken; but if it does the same at night, it will break a considerable number. Night birds do not fly unless the moon is shining, either fully or in part; rather, their feeding time is between the hour of sunset and the total darkness of the night.

No substance can be perceived without light and shade; light and shade are caused by light.

--- Page 240 ---
## OF THE EYE

Since the eye is the window of the soul, the soul is always in fear of being deprived of it, to such an extent that when anything moves in front of it which causes a man sudden fear, he does not use his hands to protect his heart—which supplies life to the head where the lord of the senses dwells—nor his hearing, nor his sense of smell or taste. Instead, the frightened sense, immediately unsatisfied with merely shutting the eyes and pressing their lids together with the utmost force, causes him to turn suddenly in the opposite direction; and still not feeling secure, he covers them with one hand and stretches out the other to form a screen against the object of his fear.

Preamble to perspective—concerning the functions of the eye:
Consider now, O Reader, what trust we can place in the ancients who have set out to define the nature of the soul and of life—things incapable of proof—while those things which may always be clearly known and proved by experience have for so many centuries either remained unknown or have been wrongly interpreted.

The eye, which so clearly offers proof of its functions, has even down to our own times been defined by countless writers in one way, but I find by experience that it acts in another.

All the images of the objects placed before the eye converge in shining lines on the surface of the eye; and these intersect on the surface of the eye at equal angles.

The atmosphere is entirely, and in every part of it, filled with the images of the bodies which are enclosed within it.

I find by experience that the black or almost black fringe of color (*colore crispo* or *rasposo*) which appears around the pupil serves no other purpose except to increase or diminish the size of this pupil; to increase it when the eye is looking toward a dark place, and to diminish it when it is looking at the light or at a luminous thing.

And you should perform the experiment of holding a light near to the eye; do this while you are looking into the darkness and then turn the eye toward this light, and you will be convinced by this experiment.

--- Page 241 ---
If the object in front of the eye sends its image to the eye, the eye also sends its image to the object; therefore, no portion of the object or the image proceeding from it is lost for any reason, either in the eye or the object. Consequently, we can more readily believe that it is the nature and power of this luminous atmosphere to attract and take into itself the images of the objects within it, rather than that it is the nature of the objects to transmit their images through the atmosphere.

If the object in front of the eye were to send its image to the eye, the eye would have to do the same to the object, which would suggest that these images were incorporeal powers. If this were the case, it would be necessary for each object to rapidly diminish in size; because every body appears as an image in the atmosphere in front of it—that is, the whole body in the entire atmosphere and the whole in every part, and all bodies in the entire atmosphere and all in every part—referring to that portion of the atmosphere capable of receiving the direct and radiating lines of the images transmitted by the objects. For this reason, then, it must be admitted that it is the nature of this atmosphere, situated among the objects, to draw to itself like a magnet the images of the objects among which it is located.

### A proof of how all objects placed in one position are present in the whole of it and in every part:

I maintain that if the front of a building, a piazza, or a field illuminated by the sun has a dwelling facing it, and you make a small round hole in a part of the front that does not face the sun, all the objects lit by the sun will transmit their images through this hole and will be visible inside the dwelling on the opposite wall, which should be made white. They will be there exactly, but inverted; and if you make similar holes in different parts of the same wall, you will produce the same effect in each.

Therefore, the images of the illuminated objects are present everywhere on this wall and in each of its smallest parts. The reason is this: we know clearly that this hole must provide some light to the dwelling, and the light passing through it is caused by one or many luminous bodies. If these bodies are of different colors and shapes, the rays forming their images will be of different colors and shapes, as will the representations on the wall. C.A. 135 v.

A proof of the way in which glasses assist the sight:
Let *a b* be the glasses and *c d* the eyes, and suppose these eyes have grown old. Previously, they used to see an object at *e* with great ease by turning their position significantly away from the line of the optic nerves; but now, due to age, the power of bending has weakened. Consequently, the eye cannot be turned without causing great pain, so that the person is forced by necessity to place the object farther away—that is, from *e* to *f*—and thus they see it better, but not in detail. However, through the placement of spectacles, the object is clearly discerned at the same distance it was when they were young, which is at *e*. This occurs because the object at *e* passes to the eye through various mediums—namely, thin and thick. The thin medium is the air between the spectacles and the object, and the thick medium is the thickness of the glass of the spectacles. Consequently, the line of direction bends within the thickness of the glass, and the line is diverted so that while seeing the object at *e*, the eye sees it as though it were at *f*. This offers the advantage that the position of the eye relative to its optic nerves is not strained, and it sees the object nearby, discerning it better at *e* than at *f*, especially the minute details.

I say that the power of vision extends by means of visual rays as far as the surface of bodies that are not transparent, and that the power possessed by these bodies extends up to the power of vision, and

--- Page 243 ---
that every similar body fills all the surrounding air with its image. Each body separately and all together do the same, and not only do they fill it with the likeness of their shape, but also with that of their power.

->Example<-

You see with the sun, when it is at the center of our hemisphere, how there are images of its form in all the parts where it reveals itself; and you see how in all these same places there are also the images of its radiance, and to these must also be added the image of the power of its heat. All these powers proceed from the same source by means of radiant lines which issue from its body and end in opaque objects, without the sun thereby undergoing any diminution.

The north star remains continually with the images of its power spread out, becoming incorporated not only in thin but in thick bodies, in those that are transparent and those that are opaque; yet it does not on this account suffer any loss of its shape.

->Confutation<-

Consider those mathematicians, then, who say that the eye has no spiritual power which extends to a distance from itself, arguing that if it were so, it could not function without a great diminution in the use of the power of vision, and that even if the eye were as large as the body of the earth, it would of necessity be consumed in beholding the stars. For this reason, they maintain that the eye takes in but does not send forth anything from itself.

->Example<-

What will these people say of musk, which always keeps a great quantity of the atmosphere charged with its odor, and which, if it were carried a thousand miles, would permeate a thousand miles of that volume of atmosphere without any diminution of itself?

Or will they say that the sound which the bell makes upon contact with the clapper—which daily fills the whole countryside with its sound—must of necessity consume this bell?

Certainly, it seems to me, there are such men as these—and that is all that need be said of them.

--- Page 244 ---
Is not that snake called the lamia seen daily by country folk attracting the nightingale to itself with a fixed gaze, just as a magnet attracts iron, while the bird hastens to her death with a mournful song?

It is also said that the wolf has the power to make men hoarse by its look.

The basilisk is said to have the power to deprive every living thing of life by its glance.

The ostrich and the spider are said to hatch their eggs simply by looking at them.

Maidens are said to have power in their eyes to attract the love of men to themselves.

The fish called the linno, which some name after St. Elmo and which is found off the coasts of Sardinia—is it not seen at night by fishermen, shedding light from its eyes over a great expanse of water as though they were two candles? And all those fish that come within the range of this radiance immediately rise to the surface of the water and turn over, dead.

If you take a light and place it in a lantern tinted green or other transparent colors, you will see by experiment that all the objects illuminated by this light seem to take their color from the lantern.

You may also have seen in churches how the light that comes through stained-glass windows assumes the color of the glass in those windows. If this does not convince you, watch the sun at its setting when it appears red through the mist, and see how it dyes red all the clouds that receive their light from the sun.

## Opinions

All these instances are given in order to prove how all things, or certainly many things, transmit the manifestation of their powers along with the image of their form without any harm to themselves; and this may also happen with the power of the eye.

--- Page 245 ---
## Contrary opinion

Furthermore, if anyone wished to argue that the eye was not designed to receive the images of objects—like the ear—without transmitting some power in exchange for them, this may be disproved by the example of a small hole made in a window shutter, which reflects all the images of the bodies opposite it; therefore, one might say that the eye functions in the same way.

## Refutation

If the small hole cited as an example reflects the images of objects in their color and form into the house—without sending forth anything except its shape and without any incorporeal power—and inverts them there, the eye would have to do the same, so that everything seen would appear inverted.

## Proof to the contrary

The circle of light which is in the middle of the white of the eye is naturally suited to perceive objects. This same circle contains a point that appears black, which is a hollowed nerve that leads inward to the seat of the faculties charged with the power of receiving impressions and forming judgment, and this penetrates to the <term>common sense</term>. Now, the objects positioned before the eyes act with the rays of their images in the manner of many archers who wish to shoot through the barrel of a carbine; for the one among them who is in a straight line with the direction of the carbine's barrel will be most likely to hit the bottom of that barrel with his arrow. Likewise, the objects opposite the eye will be more effectively transferred to the senses when they are more directly aligned with the piercing nerve.

The fluid within the light that surrounds the black center of the eye serves the same purpose as hounds in a hunt, for they are used to flush out the prey so that the hunters may then capture it. It is the same with this fluid, because it is a humor derived from the power of the <term>imprensiva</term> and it sees many things without grasping them; however, it suddenly turns the central beam—which proceeds along the line to the sense—toward the object, and this seizes the images and confines those that please it within the prison of the memory.

--- Page 246 ---
The reason why objects appear large as they reach the small surface of the eye is that the pupil acts as a concave mirror; for example, one can see with a glass ball filled with water that anything placed at the side, whether inside or outside, appears larger.

Nothing can be seen that does not transmit its image through the air.

Therefore, nothing that is spiritual or transparent can see anything positioned across from it, for this requires that it possess a dense, opaque instrument within itself; and being so constituted, it is not called a spirit.

Prove how nothing can be seen except through a small opening, through which the atmosphere passes, filled with the images of objects that intersect within the dense and opaque sides of the aforementioned openings. For this reason, nothing that lacks physical substance can discern either the shape or color of any object, since it is necessary for a dense, opaque instrument to exist so that, through its opening, the images of objects may take on their colors and shapes.

Since the images of objects are spread throughout all the air surrounding them, and are entirely present in every point of that air, it must be that the images of our hemisphere enter and pass together with those of all the heavenly bodies through the natural point in which they merge and become united, by mutually penetrating and intersecting each other; whereby the image of the moon in the east and the image of the sun in the west become united and blended together with our hemisphere at this natural point.

> O marvelous Necessity, you with supreme reason compel all effects to be the direct result of their causes, and by a supreme and irrevocable law, every natural action obeys you by the shortest possible process!

Who would believe that so small a space could contain the images of the entire universe? O mighty process! What talent can suffice to penetrate a nature such as this? What tongue will be able to reveal so great a wonder? Truly, none! This is what guides human discourse to the consideration of divine things.

--- Page 247 ---
Here the figures, here the colors, here all the images of every part of the universe are contracted to a point.

O, what a point is so marvelous!

O wonderful, O stupendous Necessity, you by your law constrain all effects to issue from their causes in the briefest possible way!

These are the miracles... forms already lost, mingled together in so small a space, which it can recreate and reconstitute by its expansion.

How it may be that from indistinct causes there may issue effects manifest and immediate, such as the images which have passed through the aforementioned natural point.

Write in your Anatomy what proportion exists between the diameters of all the lenses of the eye, and the distance from these to the crystalline lens.

The point is in itself an indivisible part, separated from and similar to all, and possessing the capacity of all; and all the indivisible parts are similar to the one and are such as may all be contained in that one, as is shown by experience in the points of the angles of the air-holes; for when the solar rays have passed through these, the angles become the termination and point of the primitive and derived pyramid.

This derived pyramid, although of less force, is nonetheless capable of traveling a long way, enlarging and expanding itself with the convergence of its rays much more than the primitive one.

And this same phenomenon may be seen in concave mirrors, for these, after receiving the solar rays according to their capacity, lead them in the fashion of a pyramid to the divisible part of the point; and although it is the smallest part of the sun, or rather of the solar rays which illuminate and warm the entire surface of the mirror, this point nevertheless contains within itself the whole sum and power, whether of heat or radiance, of which the entire surface of the mirror is capable. The derived pyramid, when equal in volume, is similar in all its powers to the primitive one, and when this equality is exceeded, it becomes weaker in proportion as its size surpasses the volume of the primitive.

### PERSPECTIVE AND MOVEMENT

<margin>A 26 v.</margin>
Every body that moves rapidly seems to color its path with the impression of its hue. The truth of this proposition is seen from experience; thus, when lightning moves among dark clouds, the speed of its winding flight makes its entire course resemble a luminous snake. In the same way, if you wave a lighted torch, its entire path will seem like a ring of flame. This is because the organ of perception acts more rapidly than the judgment.

#### Why the movement of water, although slower than that of a man, always seems swifter:

<margin>A 58 v.</margin>
The reason for this is that if you look at the movement of the water, your eye will not be able to fix on anything; its action is like that of things seen in your shadow when you are walking. For if the eye attempts to distinguish the nature of the shadow, the wisps of straw or other things contained within it appear to move rapidly, and it seems that these are much swifter to flee from the shadow than the shadow is to move forward.

<margin>c 6 r.</margin>
If the eye looks at the light of a candle at a distance of four hundred *braccia*, this light will appear to the eye looking at it to be increased a hundred times its true size; but if you place a stick in front of it that is somewhat larger than this light, this stick—which would appear two *braccia* wide—will hide it. This error, therefore, comes from the eye, which captures the luminous images not only with the center of its vision but also with the whole of its light, and I will define the reason for this in another place.

#### The eye will retain and preserve within itself the images of luminous things better than those of shaded things.

The reason is that the eye in itself is completely dark, and since like cannot be distinguished from like, the night or other dark things cannot be retained or recognized by the eye. Light is entirely the opposite, and the more it is divided, the more it tends to destroy and

### A rod or cord in rapid oscillation appears to be double.

This occurs when a knife is secured, and its tip is forcibly pulled to one side and released, so that it vibrates many times. The same thing happens with the string of a lute when one tests it to see if it is a good one. The double movement occurs because when the movement reaches the limit of the object's path, it is much swifter at this extremity. But this extremity stops and turns back when its momentum has been spent, and as the pause is made first at one and then at the other end of the movement, the eye must necessarily receive the impression of two images of the same moving object. But tell me why a defective lute string, as it vibrates, creates two or three images and sometimes four?

<margin>c 16 r.</margin>
<insert>[*The effect on the eye of sudden light*]</insert>

The eye that is accustomed to darkness is hurt upon suddenly seeing the light and therefore closes quickly, being unable to endure the brightness. This is due to the fact that the pupil, in order to recognize any object in the darkness to which it has grown accustomed, increases in size, employing all its power to transmit the image of things in shadow to the receptive part of the eye. And the light, suddenly penetrating, causes too large a portion of the pupil—which was in darkness—to be hurt by the radiance that bursts in upon it. This radiance is the exact opposite of the darkness to which the eye has already grown accustomed and habituated, and which seeks to maintain itself there, and will not let go without inflicting injury upon the eye.

One might also say that the pain caused to the eye in shadow by sudden light arises from the sudden contraction of the pupil, which does not occur except as the result of the sudden contact and friction of the sensitive parts of the eye. If you wish to see an instance of this, observe and note carefully the size of the pupil when someone is looking at a dark place, and then have a candle brought before it and moved rapidly toward the eye; you will see an instantaneous contraction of the pupil.

## PAINTING

First—The pupil of the eye contracts as the light reflected in it increases.

Second—The pupil of the eye expands as the brightness of day or of any other light reflected in it decreases.

Third—The eye sees and perceives objects of vision with greater intensity when the pupil is more dilated; and this is proven in the case of nocturnal animals such as cats and others, and birds such as the owl and similar creatures, in which the pupil undergoes a great variation from large to small in the dark and in the light.

How the rays that are seen around a luminous body when squinting the eyelids are produced in the eyes and not elsewhere:

Convex mirrors reflect the rays they receive from a light source <note>original: "luminous body"</note> into all the areas that can see the mirror from the same perspective that the light source "sees" it.

A light source sends three images of itself to the eye. One goes directly to the pupil; the other two strike the curved surface <note>original: "convexity"</note> of the eyelids. From there, they bounce back <note>original: "leap back"</note> in opposite directions to the opposite edges of the eyes. From those edges, they bounce back into the eyeball <term>luce</term> <note>original: "luce," literally "light," used here by the author to refer to the cornea or the receptive part of the eye</note>. They join with the first image from below and above, appearing with the brilliance that has been imprinted on the eyelids in the form of rays. This happens when the eye is squinted <note>original: "drawn together"</note>, as when one takes aim at a target.

This is proven: squint your eye as described, and you will see two groups of rays around the separate light source, one part pointing upward and the other downward. If you hold your finger up against the light, placing it horizontally <note>original: "crosswise"</note> slightly below the light source, and raise it slowly toward the light until you reach the bottom <note>original: "origin"</note> of the light, you will observe that the light source instantly loses all its upper rays. If you move your finger horizontally starting from above the light and slowly lower it until it meets the top <note>original: "summit"</note> of the light, you will then see that all the lower rays disappear. 

This proves our argument: if ***a*** is the light source, then ***a-o*** is the first ray from its center which goes straight to the pupil of the eye. The ray below, ***a-m***, strikes the curve of the eyelids below the eyelashes and creates several images. As soon as these are formed, they are reflected onto the lid ***n***, which forms the thick part of the eye's covering. From there, the image bounces back into the eyeball <note>original: "luce"</note>, along with all the images formed by the individual eyelashes. These rays appear somewhat long and distinct, spreading out toward their ends just like real eyelashes.

To conclude our point, let ***t-s*** be the space between the source of the light and your eye. If you block <note>original: "cut"</note> the ray ***a-m***, the ray will not make its impression on the curves of the lower eyelids. Therefore, the upper ray will stop at ***n*** and consequently disappear from the eyeball <note>original: "luce"</note>; for if the cause of the images (***m***) is removed, the effects of the rays (***m-n***) will <note>The sentence ends abruptly, implying the rays will also vanish.</note>

## OF THE FACULTY OF SIGHT

If all the images that come to the eye met at an <term>angle</term>, then by the definition of an <term>angle</term> they would meet at a <term>mathematical point</term>, which is proven to be indivisible; in that case, all things seen in the universe would appear as one, and that one would be indivisible, and there would be no more space from one star to another that could be measured within such an <term>angle</term>.

And if experience shows us all things separated by proportioned and definite spaces, then this power which imprints the images of objects is also itself divisible into as many larger and smaller parts as there are images of the things seen. We conclude, therefore, that the sense receives the images which are reflected on the surface of the eye and then judges them internally; therefore, they do not meet at a point, nor consequently at an <term>angle</term>.

Every surface of a <term>transparent body</term>, both inside and out, is formed and fitted to receive the images of its objects.

<margin>F 34 r.</margin>
In no part of <term>transparent bodies</term> enclosed by their surfaces is the power to receive or create an image lacking, but each part is well-suited to provide a passage for the images from the surface.

### A luminous body will appear smaller at the same distance if it loses more of its radiance.

This is demonstrated by an iron rod heated through part of its length in a dark place; although it is of uniform thickness, it appears to be considerably larger in the heated part, and more so as it becomes hotter. The reason for this is as follows:

<margin>F 37 r.</margin>
Every <term>luminous body</term> creates visible rays in the image which it transmits to the eye; and these rays are longer as the body has greater brilliance, and vice versa.

<margin>F 36 v. and 37 r.</margin>
There are many occasions when the images of a single light source <note>original: "luminous body"</note> will appear two or three times simultaneously in the same eye.

They will appear twice when the eye is partially closed—as it is when looking at light that is too intense—and when the head is tilted <note>original: "bending"</note>, as shown in figure *a*. In this case, two rays are created: one hits the moist edge <note>original: "humid circumference"</note> of the lower eyelid and reflects <note>original: "leaps back"</note> to the pupil, while the other ray goes directly to the pupil. The image will appear three times as shown in figure *b*: one reflection on the upper eyelid, one on the lower eyelid, and one in the center of the pupil. Even though these two or three images of light reach the same sensory perception <note>original: "sense"</note>, they appear as a single image. However, this image appears larger than it would normally, just as the brain <note>original: "sense"</note> perceives two separate images from two eyes as a single unified image.

<margin>F 39 v.</margin>
Regarding the pupils of all animals—both those of the land and those of the water—nature has designed them so that when they are affected by greater or lesser brightness, the pupil (the black portion of the eye) contracts or expands. This happens because an excess of brightness causes a change in the eye; the pupil closes up like a drawstring purse <note>original: "after the manner of a purse"</note>. Consequently, the intense brightness is reduced in both size and splendor in proportion to this contraction. When these pupils are in darkness, they become large and the perceived brightness is diminished; in this way, the pupils increase their size in response to the lack of light <note>original: "increase according to the increase of this brightness"</note>, and so the amount of objects seen by such a pupil is increased.

This explains why, when the light of a candle is moved further away from the eye, the pupil expands because the brightness has diminished, which in turn causes the perceived size <note>original: "figure"</note> of the light to increase.

The reflection <note>original: "image"</note> of the sun on the surface of water creates rays that shine over a great distance, both underwater and above it, as if the reflection itself were a real light source.

Why is it that when the image of a candle's light shrinks upon the eyeball as the candle is moved to a great distance, the spectator's judgment of its size does not decrease, except in its degree of brightness <note>original: "radiance"</note>?

<margin>F 63 v.</margin>

If you bring your eye near the surface of the sea or a pool located between your eye and the sun, you will find that the image of the sun on this surface appears very small. But if you move back to a distance of several miles from this sea, you will perceive a proportionate increase in the size of the sun's image. While the first image (up close) preserves the true shape and brilliance of the sun as mirrors do, the second (at a distance) keeps neither the shape nor the brilliance of the sun; instead, it becomes a figure with broken outlines <note>original: "contour lines"</note> and a lesser degree of brightness.

This distorted image with broken and confused outlines is formed by the blending of many images of the sun reflected to your eye by the many waves of the sea. The reduced brightness results from the fact that the shadowed and luminous images of the waves reach the eye all mingled together; consequently, their light is dimmed by their shadows.

This, however, cannot happen with the surface of a single wave when you have approached very near to it with your eye.

The eye does not diminish its light at any distance, because the image of the light which imprints itself on the surface of the eye illuminates the interior just as paper windows do; these diffuse the light they receive throughout the areas that face the paper, which previously could not see the source of the paper's illumination when the paper was not there. The sun also, when reflected in mirrors, causes the image to be reflected outward as though it were a real light without passing through; and if the lead backing were not behind the glass of the mirror, the image of the sun which imprints itself on the surface of the glass would pass through and cast its light inside or behind the mirror. And the eye acts in this same way, receiving the light of this image within and spreading it considerably throughout the visual faculty.

### *[Distant lights and reflection]*

Why, as the image of the light of a candle diminishes when it is moved to a great distance from the eye, the size of this light does not diminish, but it lacks only the power and brightness of its radiance.

A light that is smaller in quantity is also smaller in illuminating power, but because it does not change its position, it does not lose its original quantity of radiance in all the places where it formerly shone. This is proven: the light of the sun hitting the surface of water is reflected back and emits rays as though it were a physical light both inside and out, and actually illuminates the objects placed opposite it as well as those within.

### *[Presbyopia]*

Why, when men are somewhat advanced in years, they see better at a distance.

Sight is better at a distance than near at hand for men who are somewhat advanced in years because the same object transmits a smaller impression of itself to the eye when it is remote than when it is near.

Things near to the eye will seem of greater bulk than those far away.

Things seen with both eyes will seem rounder than those seen with one eye.

**[Man and owl]**
All things seen will appear larger at midnight than at midday, and larger in the morning than at midday.

This happens because the pupil of the eye is considerably smaller at midday than at any other time.

<margin>H 86 [38] r.</margin>
Because the eye or pupil of an owl is much larger in proportion to its body than that of a human, it sees more light at night than a person does. As a result, at midday it can see nothing unless its pupil grows smaller; in the same way, it sees things larger at night than by day.

The larger the pupil is, the larger the appearance of the objects it sees will be.

<margin>H 88 [40] r.</margin>
This is evident when we look at luminous objects, especially at heavenly bodies <note>stars and planets</note>. When the eye emerges from darkness and suddenly looks at these bodies, they will appear larger at first and then diminish. And if you look at these bodies through a small hole, you will see them as smaller because only a small part of the pupil is functioning in that act.

When the eye, emerging from darkness, suddenly sees a luminous body, it will appear much larger at the first glance than it does as the eye continues to look at it.

A luminous body will seem larger and more radiant when seen with both eyes than when seen with only one.

This luminous body will appear to be of a smaller size when it is seen by the eye through a smaller hole.

<margin>H 91 [43] v.</margin>
An elongated luminous body will appear rounder in shape when it is located at a greater distance from the eye.

<margin>H 109 [34 v.] r.</margin>
When the eye is positioned at night between a light source and the eye of a cat, the cat's eye will appear to glow like fire.

<margin>H 133 [10 r.] v.</margin>
Objects seen by the same eye will sometimes appear large and sometimes small.

An example of the enlargement and contraction of the pupil caused by the movement of the sun or another luminous body:

The darker the sky, the larger the stars will appear, and if you illuminate the atmosphere, these stars will appear smaller. This change results solely from the pupil, which expands and contracts according to the brightness of the atmosphere situated between the eye and the luminous body. Let the experiment be performed with a candle placed above your head while you are looking at a star; then proceed to lower this candle, little by little, until it is near the ray of light traveling from the star to the eye, and you will then see the star diminish so much that you will almost lose sight of it.

The pupil of the eye in the open air changes its size with every degree of the sun’s movement. And as its size changes, the same object will appear to be of different sizes when viewed, although it often happens that comparisons with surrounding objects prevent this change from being noticed when you look at a specific thing.

No opaque body of spherical shape seen with two eyes will ever appear perfectly round.

### *[The structure and anatomy of the eye]*

The pupil of the eye is situated in the center of the eyeball (*luce*), which is shaped like a segment of a sphere that contains the pupil at the center of its base. This eyeball, forming part of a sphere, receives all the images of objects and transmits them through the pupil to the interior where vision is formed.

In the anatomy of the eye, in order to see the interior clearly without spilling its aqueous humor, you should place the entire eye in egg white and boil it until it becomes solid. Then, cut the egg and the eye crosswise so that no part of the middle portion is poured out.

---

### *[Optical illusions. A brand of fire]*

The eye is moved just as much when a luminous object remains fixed as the object appears to move when the eye remains fixed.

What is stated in the first part is proven by previous experience, and I will prove the second part with the help of that same experience.

For when the eye is fixed and you move a burning torch in a circle or from below the eye upward, this torch will appear to be a line of fire rising from below; yet this torch cannot actually be in more than one part of that line at any single moment.

In the same way, if this torch remains fixed and the eye moves downward from above, it will appear to the eye that the torch is rising from below in a continuous line.

---

### *[Optical illusions. Brands of fire. Stars]*

If the eye looking at a star turns swiftly in the opposite direction, it will appear to the eye that the star forms itself into a curved line of fire.

[Diagram]

Let *a b c* be the eyeball (*luce*) of the eye looking at the star *d*; I maintain that if the eyeball moves the part *a* rapidly to *c*, then *b*, in coming to the position of *a*, will take on the appearance of a continuous line the color of the star. This occurs because the eye preserves the image of the shining object for a certain amount of time. Because this impression of the star's radiance lasts longer in the pupil than the duration of its movement, the impression persists throughout the movement across all positions that pass before the star.

When the eye moves from a position that has been fixed in relation to a near object, it will seem as though distant objects are moving very rapidly, while the near object remains stationary and the distant star appears to move along the eye's line of sight.

->[Diagram]<-

Let us say that the eye at point **a** has fixed its range of vision upon object **c**. While its vision remains fixed upon **c**, the eye itself actually moves from **a** to **b**. When the star **d** is seen through the lines of the eye other than the central ones <note>These are "peripheral" lines of vision.</note>, it will appear to move very swiftly. In the time it takes for the eye to travel from **a** to **b**, the star will appear to have moved across the entire span of the sky from **d** to **e**.

->[Diagram]<-

In proportion to how high an object is when it begins to descend, it will appear at the start of its movement as if it must fall closer to the observer’s eye than an object descending from a lower position.

->[Diagram]<-

This effect arises from the background of the moving object, which is the sky. The moving object stands out prominently against the sky; the lower the object is against this background, the more the eye perceives it against a more distant background. For instance, if the eye **p** sees the moving object at **e**, it sees it occupy the part of the sky at **d**, which seems almost directly above it. If it sees the moving object lower down at **h**, the eye sees it occupy the part of the sky at **a**. Because of the distance between **a** and **d**, it seems to the eye **p** that the object is more at the <term>zenith</term> <note>The point in the sky directly overhead.</note> when it is at **e** than when it is at **h**. That is, when falling from **d**, it seems to the observer that it ought to fall closer than when falling from **a**.

If the ratio of the movement of two moving objects is the same as the ratio of their distance from the eye in the same direction, the movements of these objects will always appear equal, even though they may be of almost infinite variety.

If half the diameter of the base of a pyramid measures three-quarters of its hypotenuse, nothing can remain stable upon that hypotenuse; but if the hypotenuse is longer than this, it will support anything.

Among things moving at the same speed, the one that is nearer will appear faster, and the one that is more remote will seem slower.

*[Diagram]*

Because everything that moves is seen against the background where its path ends, and a distant object moving at the same speed as a near object will occupy less of the background than the near object does in the same amount of time; for this reason, by occupying a greater space of the background, the near object appears faster in proportion to the greater area it has covered.

*[Spherical bodies]*

If a spherical body is equal in size to the pupil that sees it, then regardless of the variety of distances—provided the object can be clearly defined and the eye is able to discern it—it will never be seen as more or less than exactly half. This happens because its diameter and its edges always end within equal angles between parallel visual lines.

But if the pupil is smaller than the spherical body situated in front of it, it will never be able to see half of the sphere at any distance; it will see less of it the nearer it is, and more of it the further away it is.

An object smaller than the pupil placed before the eye will not block any distant object from the view of that pupil.

No spherical body smaller than the pupil will ever be seen by a single pupil without that pupil seeing more than half of it, regardless of the distance. It will see more of it the closer the object is, and less of it the further it is from the eye that sees it.

### [*Opposing movements seen at the same time*]

Furthermore, it is possible for the same pupil to see the same object making two opposite movements at the same time, without the pupil itself changing position.

### [*Diagram*]

What is described above is seen by the pupil when it looks through a small hole made in paper with the point of a needle. By keeping the eye close to the hole and placing a very fine straw between the eye and the hole, your eye will see the straw's true movement as you move it from right to left in the space between the hole and the eye—it appears in the actual position where the straw is moving. However, beyond this hole, the eye will see it moving in the opposite direction to its true movement. Thus, at one and the same time, the eye sees both the true and the false movements as distinct from one another. <meta>K 127 [47] r.</meta>

### THE PUPIL SEEING AN OBJECT TWICE

It is possible for the same pupil to see the same object twice, in two places at the same time.

->[Diagram]<-

The lower part *b* of the pupil *a b* sees the object *c* covering *d*, and the upper part *a* of the same pupil sees the same object *c* covering the wall *g f*, beyond the hole *e*, at the position *g*.

Therefore the object *c* is seen at the same time at *d* and *g*, and it is this that I wished to demonstrate.

As the light diminishes, the pupil of the eye that beholds this light expands. Therefore, the eye which looks through a pea-shooter has a larger pupil than the other, and sees the object larger and clearer than the other eye does. You may prove this if you look with both eyes at a white line against a black background, with one eye looking at it through a pea-shooter and the other through the luminous air.

When the eye in the luminous air looks at a place that is in shadow, this space will seem much darker than it actually is.

This happens simply because the eye which is in the air contracts its pupil more as the air reflecting into it is more luminous; and as the pupil becomes more contracted, the thing seen by it appears less luminous.

But when the eye enters into any shaded spot, the darkness of this shaded spot will immediately appear to diminish.

This takes place because as the pupil enters into the more shaded air, its size increases, and this increase causes the great darkness to seem to diminish.

Of concave mirrors of equal diameter, the one which has less concavity will unite a greater total of rays at the point where these rays strike and converge, and as a consequence, it will kindle a fire with greater speed and force.

It is impossible for the reflection of any object on water to be identical in shape to the object being reflected, due to the fact that the center of the eye is positioned above the surface of the water.

If the eye's seat of judgment lies within it, the direct lines of the images are refracted at its surface because they pass from a thin medium into a dense one.

If you stand underwater and look at something in the air, you will see that object out of its true position; the same will occur with an object in the water when viewed from the air.

The convergence of the lines created by the images of objects placed before the eye does not meet at a point within the eye by means of straight lines.

Here let us discuss physical movements, because spiritual movements have already been treated by others.

Physical movement performed with great speed will never hide from the eye an object located behind the moving body, provided that the moving body is near the eye and not significantly larger than the eye itself. An example would be the movement of certain instruments used by women for the convenience of gathering their threads, which are called "winders" (*arcolai*) by the Florentines and "turrets" (*bicocche*) by the Lombards. In their revolving motion, these move so swiftly that, because they are perforated, they do not obstruct the eye's view of anything behind them.

### *[Central line and other lines of eye]*

The eye has one central line, and all things that reach the eye along this line are seen distinctly.

Surrounding this line are an infinite number of other lines that attach to this center line; these possess less strength in proportion to how far they are removed from the central line.

### *[Phenomenon of sun shining on rain-drops]*

A falling raindrop, as seen by the eye, appears illuminated by the sun; in its descent, it seems continuous over a space large enough to display all the colors of the rainbow, and it appears larger or smaller depending on the distance.

[*A burning brand moved in a circle seems to be an unbroken circle*]
A firebrand <note>original: "firebrand"; a piece of burning wood used as a torch</note> whirled in a circle passes through an infinite number of adjacent positions, and therefore this circle appears solid in the air.
Quaderni IV 12 v.

Necessity has dictated that all the images of objects placed before the eye intersect in two places, of which one intersection is formed within the pupil and the other within the crystalline sphere <note>The "crystalline sphere" refers to the lens of the eye</note>; if this were not the case, the eye would not be able to see as many things as it does. This is proven because all the lines that intersect form this crossing at a single point. Since nothing of an object is visible except its surfaces—the edges of which are lines (according to the inverse definition of a surface)—and every smallest part of a line is equal to a point (because "smallest" refers to that thing which cannot be further reduced, which is the same as the definition of a point), it is therefore possible for the entire circumference of a circle to transmit its image through its point of intersection. This is shown in the fourth section of this treatise, which says: all the smallest parts of images penetrate one another without occupying the same space as one another.

These demonstrations serve as an example of the eye: no image, however small the object may be, enters the eye without being inverted; then, as it penetrates the crystalline sphere, it is inverted once more, and so the image within the eye becomes upright, matching the object outside the eye.

## ON THE INTERSECTION OF IMAGES IN THE PUPIL
## OF THE EYE

The intersections of images at the entrance of the pupil do not mingle with one another in the space where this intersection unites them; and this is evident because if the rays of the sun pass through two panes of glass in contact with one another, one being blue and the other yellow, the ray that penetrates them does not assume the hue of blue or yellow but of a most beautiful green. The same process would occur within the eye if images of yellow and green color were to mingle with each other at the intersection they make within themselves at the entrance of the pupil; but as this does not happen, such a mingling does not exist.

## ON THE NATURE OF THE RAYS FORMED BY THE IMAGES
## OF BODIES AND THEIR INTERSECTION

The straight line of the rays which transmit through the air the form and color of the bodies from which they proceed does not itself tint the air, nor can the rays tint one another where they touch at their intersection; instead, they only color the place where they cease to exist. This is because that place sees and is seen by the original source of these rays, and no other object surrounding that original source can be seen from the place where the ray is cut off and ended, leaving there the appearance it has carried. This is proved by the fourth principle on the color of bodies, which says the surface of every opaque body shares in the color of surrounding objects; so we conclude that the place which—by means of the ray carrying the image—sees and is seen by the source of this image is tinted by the color of that object.

### How innumerable rays from innumerable images can converge at a point:

Just as all lines pass through a single point without obstructing one another because they lack physical substance, so may all the images of surfaces pass. And as every given point faces every object opposite to it and

In proportion to how much smaller the opening is than the shaded body, the images transmitted through this opening will penetrate one another to a lesser degree. The images that pass through openings into a dark place intersect at a point that is closer to the opening as the width of that opening decreases. . . .

It is impossible for the images of bodies to be seen between the bodies themselves and the openings through which the images of these bodies penetrate; this is evident because these images do not become visible where the atmosphere is illuminated.

When images are duplicated by mutually penetrating one another, they always possess a double depth of tone.

## Acoustics

### THE CHARACTERISTICS OF THE ECHO

The sound of an echo is either continuous or intermittent; it occurs individually or is combined; it is of brief or long duration, and can be limited or endless in sound, occurring immediately or far away.

An echo is continuous when the surface that produces it is uniformly concave. The sound of the echo is intermittent when the place that produces it is broken and uneven. It is single when it is produced in one place only. It is combined when it is produced in several places simultaneously. It is either brief or long-lasting, such as when it winds around inside a struck bell, or in a cistern or other hollow space. It also occurs in clouds, where the sound recurs at fixed distances in regular intervals of time, growing steadily fainter; it is like a wave that spreads itself out in a circle over the sea.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 77 v. b</margin>
The sound often seems to come from the direction of the echo rather than from the place where the actual sound originated. A similar thing happened at Ghiera d’Adda <note>A region in Lombardy, Italy.</note> when a fire broke out; it caused twelve glowing <note>original: "lurid"</note> reflections upon twelve clouds in the air, and the true cause was not immediately perceived.

Consider whether the entire circle created in the air by a person’s voice carries the whole word spoken, since that part of this circle...

If you wish to argue the point and say that this light illuminates the aforementioned part of the dwelling not with its whole but with a part of itself, I will provide the example of one or two mirrors placed in different positions in that spot. Each part of such a mirror will contain within itself the whole of the aforementioned light; this shows, therefore, that this light is present in its entirety throughout the whole space and in its entirety in every part of this dwelling. It is the same with the voice within its circle.

## CONCERNING THE SOUND WHICH SEEMS TO REMAIN IN THE BELL AFTER THE STROKE

"That sound which remains or seems to remain in the bell after it has been struck is not in the bell itself but in the ear of the listener; the ear retains within itself the image of the bell's stroke which it has heard and only loses it by slow degrees, similar to the impression the sun creates in the eye, which is only lost and no longer seen by slow degrees."
