### THE NATURE OF THE EFFECT OF THE ROAR OF THE CANNON

The rumbling of a cannon is caused by the violent force <note>original: "impetuous fury"</note> of the flame being beaten back by the resistance of the air. This quantity of powder causes this effect because it ignites within the body of the cannon; finding itself in a place that lacks the capacity for it to expand, nature guides it to search violently for a place suitable for its increase. Breaking through or driving the weaker obstacle before it, the flame wins its way into the open air. Because the fire is more volatile than the air, the air is not capable of escaping with the same speed with which it is attacked. Since the air cannot make way with the velocity and swiftness with which the fire assails it, resistance is created; this resistance is the cause of the great roar and rumbling of the cannon.

However, if the cannon were fired against a violent oncoming wind, it would cause a louder roar due to the greater resistance of the air against the flame. Conversely, it would produce less of a rumble when fired in the same direction as the wind, because there would then be less resistance.

In marshy places or other wide expanses of air, the cannon will produce a louder report close at hand; yet it will be perceived that at a shorter distance, up in the mountains or in other places where the air is thin <note>original: "rarefied"</note>, if

<summary>This page discusses the physical properties of sound, explaining that sound stops when an object's vibration is physically dampened and attributing the roar of a cannon to the violent resistance of air against expanding fire.</summary>
<keywords>acoustics, vibration, ventriloquism, percussion, ballistics, air resistance, atmospheric density, gunpowder</keywords>

--- Page 273 ---
If the air is equally thick or thin and without the direct movement of winds, the roar will be equally perceptible all around its cause, and it will continue expanding from circle to circle just as the ripples in water do when caused by a stone thrown into it; and in a place where similar instruments are being used, the adjacent air will break or scatter all things with a weak power of resistance. All large vessels with wide mouths will be broken, as well as paper windows and similar things; the neighboring roofs will all be shaken on their supports; and this will take place even though many windows and doors stand open, and walls that are thin and without buttresses will become dangerous.

This happens because the air swells and expands, seeking to escape in every direction in which movement is possible. Doors, windows, trees, and things such as these will all be moved, and if you set an arrow lightly fastened with a small stone, it will be carried a distance of about six miles by the movement of the air.

### WHAT THING IS SOUND CAUSED BY THE BLOW?

The time in which a blow is produced is the shortest thing that can be achieved by man, and no body is so large that, when suspended, it does not make an instantaneous movement at a sudden blow; this movement beats back against the air, and the air sounds as it touches the moving object.

### WHETHER THE SOUND LIES IN THE HAMMER OR IN THE ANVIL

I say that because the anvil is not suspended, it cannot resound. The hammer resounds in the jump it makes after the blow; and if the anvil were to re-echo the sound made on it by every small hammer—just as a bell does with every different object that strikes it with the same pitch—then the anvil would do the same when struck by each different hammer. Therefore, as you hear different notes with hammers of different sizes, it follows that the note is in the hammer and not in the anvil.

Why the thing which is not suspended does not sound, and why, when it is suspended, every slight contact takes the sound away from it:

--- Page 274 ---
When a bell is struck, it creates a sudden vibration, and this sudden vibration causes it to instantly strike the surrounding air, which instantly resounds.

When it is obstructed by even slight contact, it does not vibrate or strike, and therefore the air does not resound.

If a bird suddenly beats the air, should it resound or not? I maintain that it does not, because as the air passes through the object that beats it, the air does not receive the blow, and consequently, it cannot produce sound.

## OF THE BOMBARD OR ARROW

Here, the movement of air sounds more powerfully than the resisting air.

## CONCERNING VIOLENCE

I say that every body moved or struck retains within itself for a time the nature of that blow or movement, and it retains it more or less in proportion to whether the power of the force of that blow or movement is greater or less.

### *Example*

Observe a blow given to a bell, and how long it preserves within itself the noise of the percussion.

Observe a stone projected from a bombard, and how long it preserves the nature of the movement.

The blow given to a thick body will retain its sound longer than one given to a thin body, and the sound of longest duration will be that which is made upon a body that is suspended and thin. The eye keeps within itself the images of luminous bodies for a certain interval of time.

It is possible to recognize by ear the distance of a clap of thunder, after first seeing its flash, by its resemblance to the sound of an echo.

The voice exists as a whole in the entirety and as a whole in every part of the wall surface where it strikes. And that part which is shaped in such a way as to be suited to reflect the percussion gives back the voice in as many different small portions of itself as there are different positions of the hearers.

# ACOUSTICS

<margin>Manuscript A, folio 19 r.</margin>
The ear receives the images <note>original: "species"; Leonardo often used this term to describe the formal qualities or "images" of sound and light as they travel through a medium</note> of sounds through straight, curved, and refracted <note>original: "broken"</note> lines, and no twists or turns in the ear's passages can prevent it from functioning.

<margin>Manuscript A, folio 19 v.</margin>
After the voice has struck an object, it will return to the ear at an angle of reflection equal to its angle of incidence. <note>Leonardo is describing the law of reflection: the angle at which sound hits a surface is the same angle at which it bounces off.</note> This is the line that carries the voice from its source to the place where the sound can reform itself <note>as an echo</note>. This voice acts in the same way as an object seen in a mirror: the image is present in the whole mirror and also in every part of it. 

Let us say, for example, that the mirror is marked **a b** and the object being seen is **c**. Just as **c** "sees" all the parts of the mirror, so all the parts of the mirror "see" **c**. Therefore, **c** is present in the whole mirror because it is in all its parts; and it is present in the parts because it can be seen in as many different spots as there are different positions for spectators.

Let us take the sun as an example: if you were to walk along the bank of a river and watch the sun’s reflection in the water, the sun would appear to move along with you for as long as you walk. This happens because the sun's image is present in the whole river and in every part of it.

<margin>Manuscript A, folio 22 v.</margin>

## CONCERNING A BLOW

A blow struck upon a bell leaves its impression <note>original: "likeness"</note> behind, imprinted just as the image of the sun remains in the eye or a scent remains in the air. However, we want to determine whether the impression of the blow remains in the bell or in the air; this can be discovered by placing your ear against the surface of the bell after it has been struck.

A blow struck upon one bell will cause a slight sound and vibration in another bell that is similar to it. Likewise, a string on a lute, as it sounds, produces movement and a response in another similar string of the same tone on a different lute. You can perceive this by placing a piece of straw upon the string that corresponds to the one that was played. <note>This describes the phenomenon of sympathetic resonance.</note>

## CONCERNING THE VOICE

The question is whether many tiny voices joined together will create as much sound as one large voice. I maintain that they will not; for if you were to take ten thousand buzzing flies all together, they would not carry as far as the voice of a man. Furthermore, if that man's voice were split up into ten... <note>The text ends abruptly here, likely continuing on the next page.</note>

## OF SOUND

Whether a sound that is twice as loud as another will be heard twice as far. I maintain that it will not, for if it were so, two men shouting would be heard twice as far as one; but experience does not confirm this.

If you cause your ship to stop, and place the end of a long tube in the water, and place the other end to your ear, you will hear ships at a great distance from you. You can also do the same by placing the end of the tube upon the ground, and you will then hear anyone passing at a distance from you.

[*Of the echo*]
The voice, after having proceeded from the man and having been reflected by the wall, will fly upwards. If there is a ledge above this wall with a right angle, the surface above will send the voice back toward its source.
How one should produce the sound of an echo which, whatever you may say, will be repeated to you in many voices:
[*Drawing*]
One hundred and fifty *braccia* from one wall to the other.
The voice which issues forth from the horn forms itself on the opposite wall and from there leaps back to the second, and from the second it returns to the first, like a ball that rebounds between two walls and diminishes its bounce; and so the voices grow weaker.

## OF THE SOUND MADE BY PERCUSSION

Sound cannot be heard at such close proximity to the ear that the eye does not first see the contact of the blow, and the reason is this: if we admit that the moment of the blow is instantaneous, that the nature of the blow does not produce its expansion upon the body which has been struck without taking time, and that no body struck can resound while the object...

--- Page 277 ---
that strikes is touching it, and that the sound cannot travel from the body struck to the ear without time, then you must admit that the thing which strikes is separated and divided from the thing struck before this thing struck can of itself have any resonance; and not having this, it cannot give it to the ear.

## OF REFLECTED MOVEMENTS

I wish to define why physical and spiritual movements, after the impact made by them upon an object, spring back at equal angles.

### OF PHYSICAL MOVEMENTS

I say that the sound of the echo is cast back to the ear after it has struck, just as the images of objects strike a mirror and are reflected from there to the eye. And in the same way as these images fall from the object to the mirror and from the mirror to the eye at equal angles, so the sound of the echo will strike and rebound within the hollow where it first struck, at equal angles to the ear.

## OF SOUNDS

Why the swift wind which passes through a reed makes a shrill sound:

The wind passing through the same reed will make a sound that is deeper or shriller in proportion to whether it is slower or swifter. And this is seen in the changes in the sounds made by trumpets or horns without holes, and also in the winds that howl in the cracks of doors or windows. This originates in the air, where the sound, having issued forth from the instrument, traverses the valley and proceeds to spread itself to a greater or lesser degree according to whether the air is driven by a greater or smaller force. This may be proved.

Why the reflected movement of a stone makes more noise in the air than its initial movement, even though the reflected movement is less powerful than the initial one, and whether this reflected movement makes a greater or lesser sound as the angle of its impact is more or less obtuse. But as regards the first question, the reflected movement is made by the composite

--- Page 278 ---
movement of this projectile, and the incidental movement is produced by the same motion of the same projectile; for this reason, the sound exists in the reflected movement of the projectile and not in the incidental movement. Regarding the second question, as the angle becomes more obtuse, the projectile is more inclined to revolve than when the impact occurs between acute angles.

### [Acoustics]

The sound caused by the wind or by a blow will grow fainter as it is further removed from its cause by time or distance.

The stroke given to a bell will continue to diminish as more time passes, and it remains the same whether the distance is far or near.

### [Of separated forces:—rivers, bells, ropes]

On dividing the force of rivers:

If the excessive size of rivers damages and destroys the sea coasts, then if such rivers cannot be diverted to other places, they should be divided into small streams.

->Comparison<-

If a ringing bell is heard at six miles and weighs six thousand pounds—six miles being eighteen thousand *braccia* . . . But not to lose myself in too many arguments, I maintain that if I were to break it up into tiny bells, it would not be heard even at an eighth of a mile, even if all the metal in the bells rang at the same time.

Similarly, if a rope supports a hundred thousand ounces and you separate it into a hundred thousand strands, each strand by itself will not support even one-eighth of an ounce. And so it follows with all divided powers.

How the sound of the voice dissipates <note>original: "is lost"</note> due to distance:
[*With diagram*]
At the distance between points *a* and *b*, two voices, *m* and *n*, are reduced by half. Consequently, although there are two "half-voices," together they are not as powerful as one whole voice, but merely as powerful as a half.

And even if an infinite number of these half-voices were present at such a distance, they would still only equal the volume of a single half-voice.

At that same distance, a voice, *f*, which is twice as loud as *n* or *m*, loses one-fourth of its power. It remains, therefore, as powerful as a voice and a half, surpassing the others by three times the power. Thus, at three times the distance (at point *g*), voice *f* will be as powerful as voices *m* and *n* were at the distance *a–b*.

<margin>L 80 r.</margin>
[*Voice over Distance*]
In a place where a single voice cannot be heard <note>original: "does not carry"</note>, no matter how many voices of the same volume are added together, they still will not be heard.

[*With drawing*]

## Astronomy

> 'The moon has a winter and a summer every month. It experiences greater cold and greater heat, and its equinoxes are colder than ours.'

<margin>C.A. 190 r. a</margin>
Construct lenses in order to see the moon magnified.

If you know the distance of an object, you will know the size of the visual pyramid if you take a cross-section of it on a wall near the eye, and then move the line so far from the eye that the size of the section doubles. Then note the distance between the first and the second section and ask yourself: if within such a space the diameter of the moon increases for me by that much compared to the first section, what will it do across the entire space between the eye and the moon? It will form the exact diameter of this moon.

If you were moving toward the sun along that line of water which lies between the sun and its image, you would be sailing along a continuous image that would be the length of your movement.

### How bodies project their form, heat, and power:

#### The nature of the sun:

If the moon is a mirror of our earth, when it is full the earth will be half dark and half illuminated, or perhaps more than half dark.

And regarding dark things, we cannot discern the shapes of the objects that are within their boundaries.

The opponent says that the light of the moon illuminates the portion of the earth seen by it, and for this reason—since the earth is surrounded by water—only the water reflects the light of the moon. Because the earth is not smooth or polished on its surface like the water, it does not transmit its own image to this water, and so it remains dark; thus, our water shines in the moon along with the darkness of the islands it surrounds.

The moon has a winter and a summer every month.

And it has greater cold and greater heat, and its equinoxes are colder than ours.

How it is possible for the multitude of images of the sun to pass through the indivisible point of the primary pyramid into the derivative pyramid:

The sun is composed of a very great number of indivisible parts; and although this sun possesses a physical body, its powers are incorporeal, consisting of heat and radiance. Since an incorporeal power has no physical substance, and having no substance it occupies no space, and occupying no space it does not block the aperture, the passage through this aperture back and forth is therefore permitted to every spirit at the same time.

It is possible that the solar rays, reduced through a pyramid to a point by a concave mirror, are doubled in warmth and radiance; as these rays are in the derivative pyramid, they are reflected back by a similar mirror to an equal distance from the point.

## OF THE CIRCLES OF THE MOON

I find that those circles which at night seem to surround the moon, varying in circumference and in their degree of redness, are caused by the different degrees of thickness of the vapors situated at different altitudes between the moon and our eyes. And the circle that is larger and less red is in the first part lower than the said vapors; the

## BURNING MIRROR [sketch]

<margin>Manuscript A, 54 recto</margin>
As many times as the point of the solar pyramid <note>original: "solar pyramid"—a term describing the cone of light rays focused by a lens or mirror</note> (when cut at any point) is contained within its own base, it is that many times hotter than that base.

## WHAT THE MOON IS

The moon does not shine by its own light, but it is well-suited to take on the characteristics of light, much like a mirror, water, or any other shiny body. It appears larger in the east and the west <note>The "Moon Illusion": the moon appears larger near the horizon than when it is high in the sky.</note> like the sun and the other planets; the reason for this is that every luminous body appears larger as it becomes more distant.

It can be easily understood that every planet and star is farther away from us when it is in the west <note>meaning on the horizon</note> than when it is directly overhead, by a distance of about three thousand five hundred miles, according to the proof provided in the diagram at the side of the page.¹ If you see the sun and moon reflected in water that is close by, the reflection will seem to be the same size in the water as the object appears in the sky. However, if you move away to a distance of a mile, the reflection will seem a hundred times larger. And if you see the sun reflected in the sea at the moment it sets, the image of the sun will appear to be more than ten miles long, because the reflection covers more than ten miles of the sea's surface. 

If you were standing on the moon, it would appear to you that the sun was reflected over as much of Earth's sea as it illuminates in its daily course. The land would appear amidst this water like the dark spots that are on the moon. Therefore, the moon presents the same appearance to mankind as our Earth would present to people living on the moon.

## ON THE NATURE OF THE MOON

<margin>A 64 r.</margin>
When all that we can see of the moon is illuminated, it gives us its maximum amount of light; at that time, due to the reflection of the sun's rays which strike it and rebound toward us, its ocean sends less moisture down to us, and the less light it gives, the more harmful it is.

## EXPLANATION OF WHY THE SUN SEEMS LARGER IN THE WEST

Certain mathematicians contend that the sun grows larger when it is setting because the eye sees it continually through atmosphere of greater density, alleging that objects seen through mist and in water appear larger.

To this I reply that this is not the case; for things seen through mist are similar in color to those at a distance, but because they do not undergo the same process of shrinking in perspective, they appear greater in size.

In the same way, nothing appears larger in calm water, and you may prove this by tracing an object upon a board placed under water.

<margin>A 64 v.</margin>
The real reason why the sun appears larger is that every luminous body appears larger the farther away it is.

## PRAISE OF THE SUN

If you look at the stars without their rays—as may be done by looking at them through a small hole made with the very tip of a fine needle and placed so as to almost touch the eye—you will perceive these stars to be so small that nothing appears smaller; and in truth, their great distance causes a natural reduction in size, although there are many stars there which are many times larger than the star which is our earth together with its water. Think, then, what this star of ours would look like at such a great distance, and then consider how many stars might be placed lengthwise and crosswise among these stars scattered throughout this dark expanse. I can never do anything but blame those many ancients who said that the sun was no larger

...than it appears—Epicurus was one of these. I believe this theory is based on the idea of a light placed in our atmosphere at an equal distance from the center [of the earth]; anyone who sees it finds it never looks smaller regardless of distance. I shall reserve the explanation of its size and power for the Fourth Book.

But I am very surprised that Socrates spoke so dismissively of that body, and that he said it resembled a burning stone; it is certain that whoever opposes him in such an error can hardly be wrong. I wish I had such a command of language that I could criticize those who would rather praise the worship of men than the worship of the sun. I do not see any body in the whole universe greater or more powerful than this, and its light illuminates all the heavenly bodies <term>celestial bodies</term> which are distributed throughout the universe.

All life force <term>vital principle</term> <note>original: "vital principle"; the animating force believed to give life to all creatures.</note> comes from it, since the heat found in living creatures proceeds from this life force. There is no other heat or light in the universe, as I shall show in the Fourth Book. Indeed, those who have wished to worship men as gods—such as Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, and the like—have made a very serious mistake, seeing that even if a man were as large as our earth, he would look like one of the smallest stars, appearing as only a speck in the universe; and seeing also that these men are mortal and subject to decay and rot in their tombs.

<margin>Folio 5 recto and 4 verso</margin>
*The Sphere* <note>original: "Spera"; likely referring to the common astronomical textbook "De sphaera mundi" by Johannes de Sacrobosco.</note>, and Marullus <note>original: "Marullo"; referring to the Renaissance poet Michele Marullo.</note>, and many others praise the Sun.

<margin>Folio 5 verso</margin>
The stars are visible at night and not by day because we are beneath a dense atmosphere which is full of a countless number of particles of moisture. Each of these is lit up when it is struck by the rays of the sun, and consequently, these innumerable glowing particles hide the stars. If it were not for this atmosphere, the sky would always show the stars against the darkness.

Epicurus perhaps noticed that the shadows of columns hitting opposite walls were equal in diameter to the column from which they originated. Because the shape of the shadow from beginning to end was a parallelogram, he thought he might conclude that the sun was also opposite to this parallelogram and, as a result, would be no larger [than it appears].

<summary>Leonardo defends the sun as the ultimate source of life and light, criticizing Socrates's dismissal of it and Epicurus's misunderstanding of its size based on the physics of shadows.</summary>
<keywords>Sun, Socrates, Epicurus, vital principle, atmosphere, shadows, astronomy, planetary worship</keywords>

--- Page 287 ---
than this column, not perceiving that such a reduction of the shadow would be imperceptible because of the sun's great distance.

If the sun were smaller than the earth, the stars in a large part of our hemisphere would be without light; this contradicts Epicurus, who says that the sun is only as large as it appears to be.

Epicurus says that the sun is as large as it shows itself; therefore, since it appears to be a foot wide, we must consider it to be that size.

It would follow that when the moon eclipsed the sun, the sun would not surpass it in size as it does; therefore, the moon being smaller than the sun, the moon would be less than a foot wide. Consequently, when our earth eclipsed the moon, the earth would be smaller by a finger’s breadth, seeing that if the sun is a foot across and our earth casts a pyramidal shadow toward the moon, it is inevitable that the luminous body which causes the shaded pyramid must be larger than the opaque body which casts this pyramid.

A calculation of how many times the sun will fit into its orbit in twenty-four hours:

Make a circle and set it to face south in the manner of sundials; place a rod in the middle of it so that its length points toward the center of the circle, and note the shadow cast by the sun from this rod upon the circumference of the circle. Let us say that the width of the shadow is the distance *a n* (as shown in the diagram). Now measure how many times this shadow fits into the circumference of the circle, and this will be the number of times that the solar body fits into its orbit in twenty-four hours. In this way, one may see whether Epicurus was right in saying that the sun is as large as it seems to be; for as the apparent diameter of the sun is about a foot, and as the sun would fit a thousand times into its orbit in twenty-four hours, the length of its orbit would be a thousand feet—that is, five hundred braccia, which is one-sixth of a mile. So then, the orbit of the sun between day and night would be the sixth part of a mile, and this venerable snail, the sun, would have traveled only twenty-five braccia an hour.

### THE ORDER OF PROVING THAT THE EARTH IS A STAR

First explain the mechanism of the eye, then show how the scintillation of each star originates in the eye, and why the scintillation of one star is greater than that of another. And how the rays of the stars originate in the eye. I affirm that if the scintillation of the stars were actually in the stars, as it appears to be, this scintillation would appear as widely extended as the body of the star; and since the star is larger than the earth, this movement, being made instantaneously, would quickly be found to cause the star to seem double in size. Observe afterwards how the surface of the air at the boundary of the fire, and the surface of the fire at its own boundary, is the medium through which the penetrating solar rays carry the likeness of the heavenly bodies, making them appear large at their rising and setting and small when they are in the center of the sky.

### AN EXPERIMENT TO SHOW HOW RAYS PENETRATE LIQUID BODIES

Make two vessels, each with parallel sides, one being four-fifths the size of the other and of equal height. Then fix one within the other as you see in the drawing, and cover the outside with color, leaving an opening the size of a lentil. Allow a ray of the sun to enter there, which then exits through another dark hole or through the window. Then observe whether the ray that passes through the water enclosed between the two vessels maintains the same direction it has outside or not; and from this, deduce your rule.

In order to see how the solar rays penetrate the curve of the sphere of the air, have two glass balls made, one twice as large as the other, and let them be as round as possible. Then cut them in half, place one inside the other, seal them in front, and fill them with water. Then let the solar ray pass through them as you did above, and observe whether the ray is bent or curved, and from this, deduce your rule. And in this way, you can perform an infinite number of experiments.

Observe, as you place your eye in the center of the ball, whether the light of a candle maintains its size or not.

## ON THE SUN

<margin>F 34 v.</margin>
Some claim that the sun is not hot because it is not the color of fire, but is much paler and clearer. To these people, we may reply that when molten bronze is at its hottest, it most resembles the sun in color; when it is less hot, it looks more like the color of fire.

<margin>F 38 v.</margin>

Why the image of the sun is present in the entire sphere of water that sees the sun, and yet is also present in every individual part of that water:

All the sky that views the portion of the water’s surface struck by the sun sees that water covered by the sun's image, and every part of the sky sees the whole image. 

A water surface without waves reflects light equally onto the places struck by the sun’s reflected rays.

The image of the sun is unique within the sphere of water visible to the sun. However, it reveals itself to the entire sky facing it. Every point in the sky sees its own version of the image; what is seen by one person in one position is seen differently by another person in another position, such that no single part of the sky sees the image in its entirety.

### Whether the friction of the heavens makes a sound or not:

Every sound is caused by the air striking a dense body, and if it is made by two heavy bodies against one another, it is by means of the air that surrounds them; and this friction wears away the bodies that are rubbed. It would follow, therefore, that the heavens, having no air between them during their friction, would not produce sound. Had this friction really existed, however, in the many centuries that these heavens have revolved, they would have been consumed by their own immense daily speed. And if they did make a sound, it would not be able to spread, because the sound of a percussion made underwater is barely heard, and it would be heard even less, or not at all, in the case of dense bodies. Furthermore, in the case of smooth bodies, friction does not create sound, and it would similarly happen that there would be no sound in the contact or friction of the heavens. And if these heavens are not smooth at the point of their friction, it follows that they are full of lumps and rough, and therefore their contact is not continuous; if this is the case, a vacuum is produced, which it has been concluded does not exist in nature. We arrive, therefore, at the conclusion that friction would have rubbed away the boundaries of each heaven, and because its movement is swifter toward the center than toward the poles, it would be more consumed in the center than at the poles; then there would no longer be friction, the sound would cease, and the dancers would stop, unless the heavens were turning one toward the east and the other toward the north.

### Whether stars have light from the sun or in themselves:

It is said that they have light in themselves, since if Venus and Mercury had no light of their own, when they come between our eye and the sun, they would darken as much of the sun as they cover from our eyes. This, however, is false, because it has been proved how a dark object placed against a luminous body is surrounded and entirely covered by the lateral rays of the remainder of this luminous body, and so it remains invisible. As is shown when the sun is seen through the branches of leafless trees in the far distance, these branches do not conceal any part of the sun from our eyes. The same thing happens with the above-mentioned planets, for though they are themselves without light...

### DARKNESS OF THE SUN, MOON, AND EARTH

The moon has its days and nights just as the earth does: night occurs on the part that does not shine, and day on the part that does.

Here, during the moon's night, the light reflected from the earth—specifically from its waters—grows dim. Conversely, the darkened water observes the darkness of the sun, and the moon's night lacks the reflection <note>original: "reverberation"</note> of solar rays that are usually reflected there from this earth.

### ON THE RAINBOW

Whether the rainbow is produced by the eye—that is, its curve—or by the sun by means of the cloud:

A mirror does not capture any images except those of visible objects, and images are not produced without these objects; therefore, if this arch is seen in a mirror, and the images that originate in this rainbow converge there, it follows that this arch is produced by the sun and by the cloud.

The rainbow is seen in fine rain by eyes that have the sun behind them and the cloud in front of them; a perpetually straight imaginary line that starts from the center of the sun and passes through the center of the eye will end in the center of the arch.

And this arch will never be seen by one eye in the same position as it is by the other eye; it will be seen in as many positions on the cloud where it is formed as there are eyes that see it.

Therefore, this arch is present throughout the cloud where it is produced, and is fully present in each of the positions where it may be found; thus, it will appear larger or smaller, as a half, a whole, double, or triple.

If two metal spheres transmit solar rays into a dark place, as the water is turned into vapor, it will make the solar spectrum long in shape.

This also occurs with water turned into vapor when a solar ray passes into a dark place with the sun behind it, and also with the light of torches or of the moon.

How the earth, in performing the function of the moon, has lost a considerable amount of its ancient light in our hemisphere due to the lowering of the waters, as is proved in Book Four, "Of the Earth and the Waters":

The earth is heavy within its own sphere, but even more so when it is placed in a lighter element.

Fire is light within its own sphere, and even more so when it is placed in a heavier element.

### THE SPOTS ON THE MOON

Some have said that vapors are given off from the moon like clouds and are positioned between the moon and our eyes. If this were the case, these spots would never be fixed in either position or shape; and when the moon was viewed from different locations, even if these spots did not change their position, they would change their shape, just as an object does when seen from different sides.

### OF THE SPOTS ON THE MOON

Others have said that the moon is composed of parts that are more or less transparent, as if one part were like alabaster and another like crystal or glass. It would then follow that when the sun's rays struck the less transparent part, the light would remain on...

...the surface; consequently, the denser part would be illuminated, while the transparent part would reveal the shadows of its dark depths. Thus, they define the nature of the moon, and this view has found favor with many philosophers, especially Aristotle. Nevertheless, it is false, because in the different phases that the moon and the sun frequently present to our eyes, we would see these spots vary—appearing dark at one time and light at another.

They would appear dark when the sun is in the west and the moon is in the center of the sky, because the transparent hollows would then be in shadow right up to their edges, since the sun could not cast its rays into the openings of those same hollows. They would appear bright at the full moon, when the moon in the east faces the sun in the west; for then the sun would illuminate even the lowest depths of these transparent parts. Consequently, as no shadow would be created, the moon would not reveal the spots mentioned above at such times. This would vary, more or less, according to the changing positions of the sun relative to the moon, and of the moon relative to our eyes, as I have said above.

It has also been said that the spots on the moon are created within the moon itself because it has varying levels of thinness or density. If this were true, then during lunar eclipses, solar rays could pierce through parts where the moon is thin. However, since we do not see this happen, the theory mentioned above is false.

Others say that the surface of the moon is smooth and polished and that, like a mirror, it reflects the earth. This theory is false because the earth, where it is not covered by water, presents different shapes from different points of view. Therefore, when the moon is in the east, it would reflect different spots than when it is overhead or in the west. In reality, the spots on the moon as seen during a full moon never change throughout its course across our hemisphere. 

A second reason is that an object reflected in a convex surface fills only a <term>small part of the mirror</term> <note>Convex mirrors, like the curved surface of the moon, shrink the image of the object being reflected</note>, as is proven in <term>perspective</term> <note>The mathematical study of how objects appear to the eye based on distance, light, and geometry</note>. The third reason is that when the moon is full, it only faces half the globe of the illuminated earth. In this reflection, the ocean and other waters would shine brightly, while the land would form dark spots amidst this brightness. Consequently, half of our earth would appear to be surrounded by the radiance of the sea.

### SOLAR RAYS

The solar rays pass through the cold region of the air and do not change their nature. They pass through glasses filled with cold water and lose nothing of their nature by doing so; and whatever transparent place they pass through, it is as though they passed through so much air.

And if you maintain that the cold rays of the sun are clothed with the heat of fire as they traverse its element, just as they assume the color of the glass they penetrate, it would follow that in penetrating the cold region they put on this mantle of cold after they have already put on the said mantle of heat; thus the cold would counteract the heat, and therefore the solar rays would reach us deprived of heat. As this is not confirmed by experience, such a method of reasoning—that the sun is cold—is useless.

But if you were to say that the cold through which the fiery rays of the sun pass somewhat modifies the excessive heat of these rays, it would follow from this that one would feel greater heat on the high peaks of the Caucasus, the mountain of Scythia, than in the valleys, because the mountain towers above the middle regions of the air, and no clouds are found there, nor anything that grows.

And if you say that these solar rays thrust toward us the element of fire through which they pass by local movement, this cannot be admitted because the local movement of such a volume of air cannot occur without the passage of a period of time, and this time is greater in proportion as the sun is closer to the horizon; for when there, it is 3,500 miles farther away from us than when it is at the center of our heaven. If it acted this way, it would cool the part of our horizon opposite to it, because it would carry away in its rays that part of the element of fire opposite to it which it penetrated.

--- Page 296 ---
If the smaller fire is attracted to and deflected by the larger fire, as one observes through experience, it must be that the sun draws the element of fire toward itself rather than banishing it and driving it toward us.

And the heat of fire does not descend unless it follows burning matter; in doing so, it is material and, consequently, visible.

How, if the moon is polished and spherical, the image of the sun upon it is powerfully luminous and occupies only a small part of its surface:

You will see the proof of this by taking a ball of burnished gold, placing it in the dark, and setting a light at some distance from it. Although this illuminates about half the ball, the eye only sees the light reflected on a small part of its surface, and all the rest of the surface reflects the darkness surrounding it. For this reason, the image of the light is apparent only there, and all the rest remains invisible because the eye is at a distance from the ball. The same thing would happen with the surface of the moon if it were polished, glittering, and solid, like bodies that have a reflecting surface.

Show how, if you were upon the moon or upon a star, our earth would appear to you to perform the same function for the sun as the moon does now. And show how the reflection of the sun in the sea cannot itself appear as a sun, as it does in a flat mirror.

My book attempts to show how the ocean, along with the other seas, makes our world act like a moon by means of the sunshine, and to more remote worlds, it appears as a star; and this I prove.

Moon cold and moist.

Water is cold and moist.

Our sea has the same influence on the moon as the moon has on us.

### PROOF THAT THE SUN IS INHERENTLY HOT AND NOT MERELY HOT BY INFLUENCE

That the sun is hot in itself by nature, and not merely through some external power or influence, is shown very clearly by the radiance of the solar body, which the human eye cannot endure to look upon. Furthermore, this is shown very clearly by rays reflected by concave mirrors; when their <term>percussion</term> <note>original: "percussion"; the point where concentrated light rays strike a surface</note> is of such brilliance that the eye cannot endure it, this strike of light will have a radiance resembling that of the sun in its own position. 

The truth of this is proved by the fact that if such a mirror has the specific concave surface required to produce this focused ray, no created thing will be able to withstand the heat of such a strike from a ray reflected from any mirror. And if you argue that the mirror itself is cold and yet reflects warm rays, I reply that the ray comes from the sun and must pass through the mirror while retaining the nature of its source, and it can pass through whatever medium it requires. . . .

The ray from the concave mirror, having passed across the windows of the furnaces where [metals] are cast . . . does not have great heat, nor does it any longer possess its whiteness.

### THE SOLAR RAYS

Where there is a finer and more <term>rarefied medium</term> <note>original: "rarefied medium"; a substance, such as air, that is thin or less dense, like the air at high altitudes</note>, the solar rays meet with less resistance. Where there is less resistance, the medium is less permeated by the nature of the agent <note>the sun</note>. Consequently, one may infer that where the air is more rarefied, the strike of the solar rays transmits less radiance and is, as a result, darker; the opposite is also true <note>denser air appears brighter because it provides more matter for the light to strike</note>.

### A proof of how the closer you are to the source of the sun’s rays, the larger the sun will appear when reflected upon the sea:

<margin>MS. 2038 Bib. Nat. 16 v.</margin>
If the sun produces its radiance from its center, reinforced by power from its entire body, it must follow that the further its rays travel from it, the more they continue to spread apart. This being the case, when your eye is near water that reflects the sun, you see only a very small portion of the sun’s rays carrying the reflected image of the sun upon the water's surface. However, if you are closer to the sun—as would be the case when the sun is at the meridian and the sea is to the west—you will see the sun reflected in the sea at a very great size. This is because, as you are closer to the sun, your eye captures the rays nearer to their point of origin, taking in more of them, and thus a greater radiance results. For this reason, it might be proved that the moon is another world similar to ours, and that the part of it which shines is a sea reflecting the sun, while the part which does not shine is land.

<margin>B.M. 19 r.</margin>
If you keep the details of the moon’s spots under observation, you will often find great differences in them, and I have proved this myself by making drawings of them. This happens because clouds rise from the waters of the moon and come between the sun and this water; with their shadows, they block the sun's rays from the water, and consequently, it remains dark because it cannot reflect the body of the sun.

## OF THE MOON

The moon has no light of its own, but the sun illuminates as much of it as it can "see." We see only as much of this illuminated part as faces us. Its night side receives as much brightness as our waters provide, as they reflect the sun's image onto it; this light is mirrored in all the waters that face both the sun and the moon.

The crust or surface of the water—which makes up the seas of both the moon and the Earth—is always wrinkled to some degree. This ruggedness causes the reflection of the sun to expand into countless images. These images are reflected in the hills, valleys, slopes, and crests of the innumerable <term>furrows</term> <note>original: "furrows"; here meaning waves or ripples in the water</note>. This creates as many different reflections in each wave as there are different vantage points for the eyes that see them. 

This could not happen if the sphere of water covering much of the moon were perfectly smooth. If it were, there would be only one image of the sun for every observer; its reflection would be distinct, and its radiance would always be spherical in shape, just as we see in the gilded balls placed on the tops of tall buildings. But if these gilded balls were grooved or composed of many small <term>globules</term> <note>tiny spheres</note> like mulberries (which are a dark fruit made of tiny round sections), then every part of that rounded mass visible to both the sun and the eye would reveal to the eye...

the radiance produced by the reflection of the sun. And thus, in the same body, many minute suns will be seen, and very often, on account of their great distance, they will blend with one another and seem continuous.

The lustre of the new moon is brighter and more powerful than when it is full; and this is due to the fact that the angle of its incidence is much more obtuse in the new moon than in the full moon, where the angles are extremely acute, and the waves of the moon reflect the sun both on their hollows and on their crests, while the sides remain dark. But at the sides of the moon, the troughs of the waves do not see the sun, for they only see the crests of these waves, and in consequence, the reflections are less frequent and more mingled with the shadows of the valleys. And this intermixture of shaded and luminous images, all blending together, comes to the eye with only a moderate amount of radiance, and at its edges it will be even darker, because the curve of the side of these waves will be insufficient to reflect the rays which it receives to the eye.

For which reason, the new moon by its nature reflects the solar rays more towards the eye through these last waves than through any other place, as is shown by the figure of the moon striking with the rays *a* on the wave *b* and reflected in *b d* where the eye *d* is situated. And this cannot happen at full moon, where the solar ray, being in the west, strikes the last rays of the moon in the east from *n* to *m*, and does not reflect towards the eye in the west; but leaps back to the east, slightly bending the direction of this solar ray; and so the angle of the incidence is very great.

The countless images which are reflected by the innumerable waves of the sea from the solar rays that strike upon these waves cause a continuous and far-reaching splendour upon the surface of the sea.

The moon is an opaque and solid body, and if, on the contrary, it were transparent, it would not receive the light of the sun.

You have to prove how the earth performs all those same functions towards the moon which the moon does towards the earth.

The moon does not shine with its reflected light as the sun does, because the moon does not receive the light of the sun on its surface.

# ASTRONOMY

The moon's light is not constant; rather, it appears in the crests and troughs of its watery waves. Because the sun's reflection in the moon is blurred by the shifting shadows above the waves that radiate light, its radiance is not as bright or clear as that of the sun.  
<note>original: B.M. 104 r. — British Museum, Codex Arundel, folio 104 recto (front of the page).</note>

To study the nature of the planets, make an opening in a roof and project the image of a single planet onto a base below. The reflected movement on this base will reveal the structure of that planet; however, you must arrange it so that the base only reflects one planet at a time.  
<note>original: B.M. 279 v. — British Museum, Codex Arundel, folio 279 verso (back of the page).</note>

The rotations of the celestial spheres, along with the <term>elements</term><note>The four classical elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note>, exert an equal force that pushes heavy objects away from themselves. For this reason, we must acknowledge that the centers of these spheres must meet and remain stationary.

Consequently, we must conclude that objects falling toward the center are being pushed from above rather than being pulled downward by the center itself. If it were possible to remove a portion of the earth and fill that space with air, you would see a stone thrown into that air become stationary at the center of the elements and the spheres.  
<note>original: Forster III 6 v. — Forster Codex III, folio 6 verso. Leonardo is exploring a theory of gravity based on external pressure rather than internal attraction.</note>

The center of the world cannot be the center of the universal circles formed by the paths of the glittering stars. In such a position, we cannot assume that the various parts of the earth—which surrounds and encloses this center—are of equal weight when measured at an equal distance from that center.

By nature, every heavy object is pushed toward the center because the center is the point furthest removed from these expelling, rotating forces.

I conclude: the center of gravity for the earth and the water is the center of the celestial spheres, but it is not the geometric center of the mass of this world.  
<note>original: Forster III 7 r.</note>

These heavy components, which were pushed down from the heavens above, have formed themselves into bodies that constantly "desire" to return to the heights.  
<note>original: Forster III 8 r. This reflects the ancient idea that elements seek their "natural place."</note>

**The sun does not move.**  
<note>original: Quaderni v 25 r. — "Il sole non si muove." This is one of Leonardo’s most famous scientific insights, anticipating the Copernican heliocentric view, though he likely meant it in the context of the sun being the stationary center of the planetary system.</note>

### OF THE MOON

No solid body is lighter than air.
Since we have proved that the part of the moon which shines consists of water, and that it serves the body of the sun as a mirror reflecting the radiance it receives from it; and that if this water were without waves it would appear small but with a radiance almost equal to that of the sun, it is now necessary to show whether the moon is a heavy or light body. Thus, if it were a heavy body—considering that in the progression upward from the earth, every stage of altitude brings an increase in lightness, just as water is lighter than earth and air is lighter than...

--- Page 303 ---
water and fire than air, and so continuing in succession—it would seem that if the moon had density, as it has, it would have weight; and that having weight, the space in which it is located would not be able to support it. Consequently, it would have to descend toward the center of the universe and join itself to the earth; or if not the moon itself, its waters at any rate would fall away and be lost to it, falling toward the center and leaving the moon stripped of them and devoid of radiance. The fact, however, that these events do not occur as might reasonably have been anticipated is a clear sign that the moon is clothed with her own elements—namely water, air, and fire—and so sustains itself by itself in that part of space, just as our earth does with its elements in this other part of space; and that heavy bodies perform the same function within its elements as other heavy bodies do in ours.

[Diagram] sun, moon, earth.

When the eye in the east sees the moon in the west near the setting sun, it sees it with its shaded part surrounded by the luminous part. Of this light, the side and upper portions are derived from the sun, and the lower portion from the western ocean, which still receives the solar rays and reflects them onto the lower seas of the moon. Moreover, it imparts as much radiance to the whole of the shaded part of the moon as the moon gives to the earth at midnight, and for this reason, it does not become absolutely dark. Because of this, some have believed that the moon has, in part, a light of its own in addition to that which is given to it by the sun, and that this light is due to the cause already mentioned—namely, that our seas are illuminated by the sun.

[Diagram] moon, solar body, earth.

Further, it might be said that the circle of radiance which the moon shows when it is in the west along with the sun is derived entirely from the sun, when its position with regard to the sun and the eye is as shown above.

Some might say that the air, which is an element of the moon, catches the light of the sun just as our atmosphere does, and that this is what completes the luminous circle on the body of the moon.

Some have believed that the moon has some light of its own, but this opinion is false, for they have based it upon that glimmer which is visible in the middle between the horns of the new moon, which ap-

And this difference in the background arises from the fact that the part of it which borders on the illuminated portion of the moon, by comparison with that brightness, appears darker than it actually is; and in the part above, where a portion of a luminous circle of uniform width appears, it happens that because the moon is brighter there than the medium or background upon which it is positioned, it appears brighter on 그 extremity than it actually is in comparison with this darkness. This brightness at such a time is derived from our ocean and the other inland seas, for they are at that time illuminated by the sun, which is then on the point of setting. # ASTRONOMY

...that the surface of the moon is furrowed; and this roughness only exists in liquid bodies when they are stirred by the wind. We have seen this with the sea, where the sun is reflected by tiny waves near to the eye, and stage by stage over a distance of more than forty miles, these illuminated waves appear to grow larger. Therefore, we conclude that the luminous part of the moon is water <note>Leonardo incorrectly believed the moon was covered in oceans similar to Earth.</note>. If this water were not in motion, it would not be luminous to the same degree. However, through the movement of this water being stirred up by winds, it becomes filled with waves. Every wave catches the light from the sun, and a great multitude of waves beyond number reflect the sun <note>original: "solar body"</note> an infinite number of times. The sun reflected this way will appear as bright as the sun itself; for as we see when the water does not move, it reflects the sun to the eye in the original splendor that it has by nature.

But the shadows are also beyond number, just like the waves, and these are interspersed between the waves. Their shapes blend with the images of the sun that appear upon the waves. Each shadow shape becomes blended with a luminous shape, and so they obscure the luminous rays and make them weak, as is clearly shown to us by the light of the moon. When the "sea" of the moon is stirred into a storm <note>original: "tempest"</note> by the winds, the waves are larger and the lights less frequent; the enlarged shadows intermingle more with the sparse images of the sun upon the waves, and for this reason, the moon becomes less luminous. 

But when the moon is in its circle and is positioned at about the center of our hemisphere, each wave shows the reflection of the sun both in the center of the valleys between the waves and on the summits of these waves. For this reason, the moon shows itself more luminous than ever, because the number of parts in the light is doubled.

The moon also appears strongly luminous a short time after its turn <note>This likely refers to the moon's phase cycle, specifically shortly after the New Moon.</note>. This is because the sun, which stands beyond the moon, strikes the summits of the waves. When these summits are near together and seem almost to clash against one another from our perspective, the shadows between the waves do not transmit their images to the eye or mingle with the luminous images. For this reason, the light of the moon is more powerful.

And what is proved of one luminous body holds true of all the rest.

Concerning the moon: all the objections of the opponent, who claims that there is no water on the moon.

Objection: Every body denser than the air is heavier than that air and cannot be supported by it without some other cause; and the higher it rises, the less resistance it meets from its medium. Therefore, if there were water on the moon, it would strip itself away from the moon and come down to cover our earth, because on the moon, the water would be positioned above its own air. The answer here is that if there is water on the moon, there is also earth there upon which this water rests, and consequently the other elements are there as well. Water is supported up there among the three other elements just as our water down here is supported among its accompanying elements. If, however, as the opponent maintains, the water had to fall from the moon, it would be more likely that the moon itself would have to fall, being a body heavier than water. Therefore, since it does not fall, it is clear proof that the water and earth up there are supported by their other elements, just as the heavy and light elements down here are supported in space that is lighter than themselves.

The opponent says that the light of the moon is inherently the same throughout, if not in its entirety; and that it appears more or less illuminated depending on whether the eye sees more or less of its shaded part—that is, whether it is further to the east or the west.

### XII
# Botany

> *‘All seeds have an umbilical cord, which breaks when the seed is ripe. Similarly, they have a womb and a fetal membrane, as is seen in herbs and all seeds that grow in pods.’*

When a tree has had part of its bark stripped off, nature, in order to provide for it, supplies a far greater quantity of nutritive moisture to the stripped portion than to any other part; so that, because of the initial scarcity mentioned, the bark there grows much more thickly than in any other place. This moisture has such power of movement that after reaching the spot where its help is needed, it rises up partly like a rebounding ball and creates various buds and sprouts, somewhat in the manner of boiling water.

Many trees planted in such a way that they touch will, by the second year, have learned how to do away with the bark growing between them and become grafted together; by this method, you will make the walls of gardens continuous, and in four years you will even have very wide boards.

When many grains or seeds are sown so that they touch and are then covered by a board filled with holes the size of the seeds and left to grow underneath it, the seeds will become fused together as they germinate and will form a beautiful clump. If you mix seeds of different kinds together, this clump will look like jasper.
C.A. 76 r. a

The branches of plants are found in two different positions: either opposite each other or not opposite. If they are opposite each other, the center stem is not bent; if they are not opposite, the center stem is bent.
C.A. 305 v. a

### [Of barking trees]

If you remove a ring of bark from the tree *d*, it will wither from the ring upward, while everything below the ring will remain alive.

If you make this ring incomplete and then skillfully graft the plant near the base, the skillfully treated part will be preserved while the rest will be ruined. B 17 v. <note>B 17 v. refers to Leonardo's Manuscript B, folio 17 verso (the back of the page).</note>

## ON THE BRANCHING OF PLANTS

Plants that spread out extensively have wider <note>original: "obtuse"</note> angles where their branches divide the closer they are to the ground—that is, the nearer they are to the thicker and older part of the tree. Conversely, in the newer parts of the tree, the angles of its branching <note>original: "ramifications"</note> are more acute <note>meaning sharper or narrower</note>. E 6 v.

Tree trunks have a lumpy <note>original: "bulbous"</note> surface caused by the roots that carry nutrients to the tree. These protrusions <note>original: "excrescences"</note> have bark with few cracks <note>original: "fissures"</note>. The spaces between them are hollows where the bark has dried out because nutrients do not reach those areas as easily. G 1 r. <note>G 1 r. refers to Manuscript G, folio 1 recto (the front of the page).</note>

When looking at translucent <note>original: "transparent"</note> leaves from below, the shadows appear the same as they do on the upper <note>original: "right"</note> side of the leaf. This is because the shadow is visible through the leaf on the underside just like the lit part is; however, the shine <note>original: "lustre"</note> or reflected highlights can never be seen through the leaf. G 3 v.

The lowest branches of trees with large leaves and heavy fruit—such as coconut palms, figs, and similar species—always bend toward the ground.

Branches always emerge from above the leaf. <note>Leonardo is observing the position of the axillary bud.</note> G 5 r.

Young trees have more translucent leaves and smoother bark than old ones. The walnut tree, in particular, is lighter in color in May than it is in September. G 8 r.

A plant that produces very small <note>original: "minute"</note> branches will grow in the straightest line. G 13 r.

## OF BRANCH STRUCTURE

The base of a branch will always have its central axis <note>original: "central line of its thickness"</note> aligned with the central axis of the main plant. G 14 r. <note>G 14 r. refers to Leonardo's Manuscript G, folio 14 recto.</note>

## OF THE BIRTH OF LEAVES UPON THEIR BRANCHES

The thickness of a branch does not decrease in the space between one leaf and the next, except by the width of the bud <note>original: "eye"</note> located just above the leaf; this reduction in thickness remains constant until the branch reaches the next leaf.

Nature has arranged the leaves on the youngest branches of many plants so that the sixth leaf is always positioned directly above the first, and this sequence continues regularly unless the pattern is obstructed.

This arrangement serves two purposes for the plant. First, because the new branch or fruit grows the following year from the bud <note>original: "eye"</note> located at the leaf’s attachment point, any water that wets the branch can flow down and be caught in the axil <term>axil</term> <note>the angle between the upper side of a leaf or stem and the supporting branch</note> where the leaf grows, thereby nourishing the bud. The second purpose is that when these buds grow into branches the following year, they will not overlap or shade one another; the first five branches emerge in five different directions, and the sixth emerges directly above the first, but at a sufficient distance away to avoid interference. G 16 v.

<insert>[Of branch structure]</insert>
Between one branching point <note>original: "ramification"</note> and the next, if there are no other smaller branches, the tree trunk or limb will be of uniform thickness. This happens because the entire volume of the sap <note>original: "humour"</note> that feeds the start of this section continues to feed it equally until it reaches the next division. This equal cause—the nourishment—produces an equal effect in growth. G 17 r.

Trees that divide into main trunks near the ground seldom grow branches in the space between those trunks; even if a branch does emerge there, it will have a short life and will not grow much because of the shadow cast by the neighboring trunks.

The principal branches of the trees that rise the highest are always nearer the center of the plant than any of its siblings or offshoots.

The small branches of the same year grow in all parts of the tree only in those places where there were its old ramifications, produced in the order of the birth of their leaves; that is to say, each is produced one above the other.

### DESCRIPTION OF THE ELM

This branching of the elm has the largest branch in front, and its smallest are the first and the second-to-last when the main branch is straight.

From the starting point of one leaf to the next is half of the greatest length of the leaf; a little less, because the leaves form an interval which is about a third of the width of the leaf.

The elm has the tips of its leaves nearer the end of the branch than its starting point, and in width they vary very little when looked at from the same side.

The leaf always turns its upper side toward the sky so that it may be better able to receive over its whole surface the dew which drops down with the slow movement of the atmosphere; and these leaves are arranged on the plants in such a way that one covers another as little as possible, but they lie alternately one above the other as is seen with the ivy which covers walls. And this alternation serves two ends: first, in order to leave spaces so that the air and the sun may penetrate between them; and the second purpose of it is so that the drops which fall from the first leaf may fall onto the fourth, or onto the sixth in the case of other trees.

### [*Structure of the walnut tree*]

The leaves of the <term>walnut tree</term> are distributed across the entire branch grown during that year. They are spaced farther apart and appear in greater numbers when the branch from which the <term>shoot</term> <note>original: "shoot" - a new growth or young stem</note> springs is younger. Conversely, they are closer together at their base and fewer in number when the shoot grows from an older branch.

Its fruits grow at the tips of its shoots, and its largest branches are located on the underside of the <term>bough</term> from which they grow. This occurs because the weight of its <term>sap</term> causes it to pull downward rather than upward; for this reason, the branches that grow from the top and reach toward the sky are small and thin. When a shoot points toward the sky, its leaves spread out from the tip with their points evenly distributed. If the shoot points toward the horizon, the leaves still remain spread out; this happens because leaves always turn their undersides toward the ground.

The branches are proportionately smaller the closer they are to the base of the bough that produces them.

---

<margin>G 29 r.</margin>
### [*The elder*]

Observe the lower branch of the <term>elder</term>, which has its leaves arranged in pairs placed crosswise one above the other. If the stem grows straight up toward the sky, this pattern never fails; the larger leaves grow on the thicker part of the stem, and the smaller leaves appear on the thinner part toward the top. 

But returning to the lower branch, I argue that the leaves—even those positioned crosswise to the ones on the upper branch—must necessarily twist out of their crosswise alignment. They are compelled by the natural law that causes leaves to turn their surfaces toward the sky to catch the night dew, and so they can no longer remain strictly crosswise.

## ON THE ORIGIN OF BRANCHES IN TREES

The way branches begin to grow from the main boughs follows the same pattern as the way leaves grow on the <term>shoots</term> <note>the new growth of a plant during a single season</note> of that same year. These leaves emerge in three different arrangements, one higher than the other. The first and most common is that the sixth leaf on the upper side is always born above the first leaf on the underside. <note>Leonardo is describing "phyllotaxis," the mathematical arrangement of leaves around a stem which ensures each leaf gets sunlight and water.</note> The second arrangement is where the upper two-thirds are positioned over the lower two-thirds; and the third way is that the upper third is positioned over the lower third.

## WHY THE GRAIN OF WOOD IS FREQUENTLY NOT STRAIGHT

When the branches that grow in the second year are not of equal thickness compared to those of the previous year, but instead grow unevenly on one side, the strength of the lower branch is diverted to nourish the higher growth, even if it is slightly off-center.

However, if these branches grow equally, the <term>veins</term> <note>original: "veins" - referring here to the grain of the wood</note> of their branch will be straight and evenly spaced at every stage of the plant's height.

There is no protrusion on a branch except where there was once a branch that failed to grow.

The lower shoots of a tree's branches grow more than the upper shoots; this happens simply because the sap that feeds them, being subject to gravity, flows downward more easily than upward. It is also because those that grow downward distance themselves from the shade found in the center of the tree.

The older the branches are, the greater the difference will be between their upper and lower shoots, and between those produced during the same year or period.

## ON THE SCARS OF TREES

The scars of trees increase in thickness more than is required by the sap that flows through and nourishes them.

After forming the angle where they separate from the trunk, the lower branches always bend downward so as not to press against the other branches that follow above them on the same trunk, and to be better able to reach the air that nourishes them.

The elm always produces greater length in the most recent branches of the year’s growth than it does in the branches from the same year that are lower down. Nature does this because the higher branches are the ones meant to increase the size of the tree, while those below tend to dry up because they remain in the shade; their growth would otherwise block the entry of sunlight and air among the tree's primary branches.

The main lower branches bend down more than the upper ones, both to maintain a sharper angle than the upper ones and because they are larger and older; they also do this to seek the air and escape the shade.

[Branch structure and the sun]

Universally, almost all upright parts of trees are found to bend somewhat, turning their convex side toward the south. Furthermore, the branches are longer, thicker, and more numerous toward the south.

--- Page 314 ---
than towards the north. This arises from the fact that the sun draws the sap towards that part of the tree's surface which is nearest to it. This is evident in trees that are frequently pollarded, for they renew their growth every three years. And one notices this unless the sun is screened off by other trees.

All the flowers that face the sun mature their seeds, and the others do not—that is, those that see only the reflection of the sun.

The cherry tree is of the same nature as the fir in that its branching occurs in tiers around its stem; and its branches grow in groups of four, five, or six opposite one another; and the total area of the tips of the branches forms an equilateral pyramid from its center upwards; whereas the walnut and the oak form a half-sphere from the center upwards.

## [Symmetry of nature—branching of trees and water]

All the branches of a tree at every stage of its height, when joined together, are equal to the thickness of its trunk.

All the branches of a body of water at every stage of its length, provided they move at an equal speed, are equal to the size of their parent stream.

## [Laws regarding the growth of plants]

Every year, when the branches of the trees have completed their growth, they have attained—when joined together—a thickness equal to the thickness of their trunk; and at each stage of their branching, you will find the thickness of the said trunk, as in *ik, gh, ef, cd, ab*. They will all be equal to each other if the tree has not been pollarded; otherwise, the rule will not hold.

If the plant *n* grows to the thickness of *m*, its branches will form the entire junction *ab* through the swelling of the branches both inside and out.

The branches of plants form a curve at the start of every tiny shoot, and as this other branch is produced, they bifurcate; and this bifurcation occurs in the middle of two angles, the greater of which will be on the side of the thicker branch, and this will be proportional unless some accident has marred it.

All the branches produced towards the center of the tree wither and

--- Page 315 ---
fall on account of the excess of shade; only such part of the system of branching endures as lies in the extremities of the tree.

### [Unity in nature—all seeds have the umbilical cord]

All seeds have the umbilical cord, which breaks when the seed is ripe. And in like manner they have a womb and a placenta, as is seen in herbs and all the seeds which grow in pods. But those which grow in shells, such as hazel-nuts, pistachio-nuts and the like, have a long umbilical cord, and this reveals itself in their early stages.

# XIII
## Geology

> '*When nature is about to create stones, it produces a kind of sticky paste which, as it dries, hardens into a solid mass along with whatever it has enclosed there; however, it does not change these objects into stone but preserves them within itself in the form in which it found them.*'

The false interpreters of nature assert that mercury is a common element in all metals; they forget that nature varies its components according to the variety of things it intends to produce in the world.

The currents of rivers move different kinds of matter which have varying degrees of weight; these materials are moved farther from their original position in proportion to how light they are, and will remain closer to the bottom in proportion to how heavy they are, and will be carried a greater distance when driven by water of greater power.

But when this power is no longer capable of overcoming the resistance of the gravel, this gravel becomes settled and blocks the direct movement of the water that brought it to this place. Then the water, as it strikes the gravel which has accumulated in this manner, rebounds sideways and strikes other spots it was not used to hitting, and washes away other deposits of soil down to their foundations. And so the places where the said river used to pass are deserted and become filled in again by a fresh deposit from the muddy waters, and these in due course become blocked up in these same places.

Concerning rivers greatly swollen by the collapse of mountains along their sides, which cause the formation of very large lakes at high altitudes:

The avalanches from the mountains falling down upon their bases

--- Page 317 ---
which have been worn away by the continuous currents of the rivers rushing precipitously at their feet with their swift waters, have closed up the mouths of the great valleys situated in the high places.

These are the reasons why the surface of the water is raised by the creation of lakes, and why new streams and rivers are formed in high places.

The ebb and flow of the sea is continually moving the earth with all its elements away from the center of the elements. This is proved by the first chapter of this treatise, which states that the center of the world takes account of that which is higher than it because no hollow lies deeper than it. The center of the world is in itself immovable, but the place in which it is found is in continual movement toward different directions. The center of the world changes its position continually, and of these changes some have a slower movement than others, for some changes occur every six hours and some take many thousand years.

But that of six hours proceeds from the ebb and flow of the sea; the other comes from the wearing away of the mountains through the movements of the water produced by the rains and the continual course of the rivers. The location changes in its relation to the center of the world and not the center to the location, because this center is immovable and its location is continually moving in a straight-line movement, and such movement will never be curved.

The rains wear away more of the bases of the mountains than they do the summits for two reasons; and the first is that the impact of the rain in falling from the same height is more powerful on the bases of the mountains than on their summits according to my seventh rule, which says that a heavy thing becomes faster the farther it descends through the air, and as it becomes faster, it becomes heavier. Therefore, as there is more space between the bases of the mountains and the cloud than between these clouds and the summit of the mountain, the rain, as has been said, is heavier and more powerful upon these bases of the mountains than on the summit of the same mountain, and so stage by stage its power to wear away is less as it has a shorter fall.

The second reason is that the greater mass of water is that which descends from the center of the mountain to its bases rather than from

Valleys widen as time passes, but their depth increases very little. This is because rains bring almost as much soil into the valley as the river washes away—in some places more, and in others less.

Massive rivers flow underground.

Rivers create larger deposits of soil when they are near populated areas than they do where there are no inhabitants. This is because, in populated places, the mountains and hills are being cultivated <note>original: "worked upon"</note>, and the rains wash away the soil that has been turned over more easily than they do the hard ground covered with weeds.

Mountain peaks are more permanent and enduring when they are covered with snow throughout the entire winter.

Between the density of water and stone, there is an almost infinite range of different weights. This earth increases bit by bit until it forms mud; then this mud becomes more solid until it becomes firm earth; it then goes on to become like the hardest stone, and is even transformed into metals.
