Beginning thus to hollow it out, they created a bed for the other surrounding waters; and in this way, throughout the entire length of their course, they gained breadth and depth, their waters constantly increasing until all this water was drained away. Of creatures which have their bones on the outside, such as cockles, snails, oysters, scallops, ‘bouoli’ and the like, which are of innumerable kinds:

When the floods of the rivers, which were cloudy with fine mud, deposited this silt upon the creatures that lived beneath the waters near the ocean shores, these creatures became embedded in this mud. Finding themselves entirely covered under a great weight of mud, they were forced to perish for lack of the creatures on which they were accustomed to feed.

In the course of time, the sea level became lower, and as the salt water flowed away, this mud was transformed into stone. Those shells that had lost their inhabitants were filled with mud in their place; and consequently, during the process of the surrounding mud changing into stone, the mud that was inside the frames of the half-opened shells—since it was joined to the rest of the mud through the opening of the shell—also changed into stone itself. Therefore, all the frames of these shells were left between two petrified substances: namely, that which surrounded them and that which they enclosed.

These are still to be found in many places, and almost all the petri-

fied shellfish in the mountain rocks still have their natural shells around them, especially those that were old enough to be preserved because of their hardness; meanwhile, the younger ones, which were already largely turned into chalk, were penetrated by the sticky and petrifying moisture.

## ON THE BONES OF FISHES FOUND WITHIN THOSE THAT HAVE BEEN PETRIFIED

All creatures that have their bones inside their skin, when covered by mud from the floods of rivers that have left their usual beds, are immediately enclosed in a mold by this mud. In the course of time, as the river channels become lower, these creatures remain embedded and shut within the mud. Once the flesh and organs have decayed and only the bones remain—and even these having lost their natural arrangement—they fall to the bottom of the mold formed by their own impression. As the mud is raised above the level of the stream, the water drains away so that the mud dries, becoming first a sticky paste and then changing into stone, enclosing whatever it finds within itself and filling every cavity. Finding the hollow part of the mold formed by these creatures, the sediment percolates gradually through the tiny crevices in the earth, through which the air inside escapes—that is, it escapes sideways, for it cannot escape upward since those crevices are filled by the moisture descending into the cavity, nor can it escape downward because the moisture that has already fallen has closed the crevices. There remain the openings at the side, from which this air, condensed and pressed down by the descending moisture, escapes at the same slow rate as the moisture descends. This paste, as it dries, becomes stone which is light in weight, preserving the exact shapes of the creatures that created the mold and enclosing their bones within it.

## SHELLS AND THE REASON FOR THEIR SHAPE

The creature that lives within the shell constructs its dwelling with joints, seams, roofing, and various other parts, just as man does.

...does in the house in which he dwells; and this creature expands the house and roof gradually in proportion as its body increases and as it is attached to the sides of these shells.

Consequently, the brightness and smoothness which these shells possess on the inner side is somewhat dulled at the point where they are attached to the creature that dwells there, and the hollow of it is roughened, ready to receive the knitting together of the muscles by means of which the creature draws itself in when it wishes to shut itself up within its house.

When nature is about to create stones, it produces a kind of sticky paste, which as it dries, forms itself into a solid mass together with whatever it has enclosed there; however, it does not change these things into stone but preserves them within itself in the form in which it found them. This is why leaves are found whole within the rocks which are formed at the bases of the mountains, together with a mixture of different kinds of things, just as they were left there by the river floods which occurred in the autumn seasons; and there the mud caused by the successive inundations has covered them over, and then this mud grows into one mass together with the aforementioned paste, and becomes changed into successive layers of stone which correspond with the layers of the mud.

# XIV
## Physical Geography

> ‘The earth wears away the mountains and fills up the valleys, and if it had the power, it would reduce the earth to a perfect sphere.’

The wave travels beneath the surface of the sea and leaves behind all the foam that is produced in front of it.

The area of the water's surface that lies between the waves as they approach the shore is polished and smooth; this happens because the largest wave is faster than the smaller waves that compose it on the general surface of the sea. This largest wave draws back the surface of the sea, and the initial foam of the wave descends as it opens at the point where the rest of the water is receding.

The shape of the foam that then remains behind in the wave is always triangular, and its angle is formed by the initial foam and the foam at the front of the path where the wave first descended.

The lowest parts of the world are the seas where all the rivers flow. A river never stops moving until it reaches the sea; therefore, the sea is the lowest part of the world.

Water does not move from place to place unless it is drawn by a lower elevation. Lowliness, therefore, acts as a magnet for water.

Make a sketch to show where the shells are located at Monte Mario.

## DOUBT

A question arises here: was the Great Flood in the time of Noah truly universal? Based on the following reasons, it would seem that it was not. The Bible states that the Flood was caused by forty days and forty nights of continuous, global rain, and that this water rose ten cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> above the highest mountain in the world. Consequently, if the rain had been universal, it would have formed a uniform covering around our spherical globe. Since every part of a sphere's surface is equally distant from its center, once the water reached this state, it would have been impossible for it to move. Water does not move on its own unless it is flowing downward to a lower point. 

How, then, did the waters of such a massive flood recede if it is proven they had no way to move? If the water did depart, where did it go, unless it went upward? At this point, natural laws cannot explain it. Therefore, to resolve this doubt, we must either rely on a miracle or suggest that all this water was evaporated by the heat of the sun. <term>C.A.</term> 155 r. b

### INSTANCES AND DEDUCTIONS AS TO THE EARTH'S INCREASE

Within a short time, they change into the earth's substance and increase its volume. After this, you will see the new seeds springing up and passing through the same cycle. Thus, you will always see successive generations completing their natural course and, by their death and decay, increasing the earth. And if you let ten...

The surface of the Red Sea is level with the Ocean.

The greatest river in the world is the Mediterranean, which is a river that moves from the source of the Nile to the Western Ocean.

Just as snow, as it falls in flakes upon various rounded objects, covers them with itself but with as many varying degrees of thickness as there are variations in the curves of this roundness, so the earth, carried by the floods of the rivers following the mass of the waters, descends upon the various rounded objects which are at the bottom of the waters and covers these with itself in the manner shown above.

### OF THE CENTRE OF THE OCEAN

The centre of the sphere of water is the true centre of the orb of our world, which is composed of land and water in the shape of a sphere. But if you wish to find the centre of the element of the earth, this is situated at a point equidistant from the surface of the ocean and not equidistant from the surface of the earth. For it is easy to understand that this globe of the earth has no perfect roundness whatever except in those parts where there are the sea or lakes or other surfaces of still water; and every part of the land which rises above the water is farther removed from the centre.

### OF THE MOVEMENT OF AIR AND WATER

This air which borders and continually moves upon this terrestrial machine is mixed with moisture similar to that of which the earth is composed, and the excess of this moisture falls back continually upon the earth once every twenty-four hours and then springs back raised.

a little by the heat of the sun and sustained by it as long as it remains in our hemisphere. Then, being abandoned by the sun at its departure and still possessing weight, it falls back to the earth. In summer this moisture is called dew, and in winter, as the cold condenses and freezes it, it is called hoar frost.

## HOW THE SEA CHANGES THE WEIGHT OF THE EARTH

The shells of oysters and other similar creatures born in the mud of the sea testify to us of the change in the earth around the center of our elements. This is proved as follows: mighty rivers always flow turbid because of the earth stirred up in them through the friction of their waters against their beds and banks; and this process of erosion uncovers the tops of the ridges formed by the layers of these shells, which are embedded in the mud of the sea where they were born when the salt waters covered them. These same ridges were from time to time covered over by varying thicknesses of mud brought down to the sea by rivers in floods of varying magnitude; in this way, these shells remained walled up and dead beneath this mud, which was raised to such a height that the bed of the sea emerged into the air.

And now these beds are at such a great height that they have become hills or lofty mountains, and the rivers that wear away the sides of these mountains lay bare the strata of the shells. Thus, the light surface of the earth is continually raised, the antipodes draw nearer to the center of the earth, and the ancient beds of the sea become chains of mountains.

The destruction of marshes will be brought about when turbid rivers flow into them. This is proved by the fact that where a river flows swiftly it washes away the soil, and where it slows down it leaves its deposit. Both for this reason and because water never travels as slowly in rivers as it does in the marshes of the valleys, the movement of the waters there is imperceptible. But in these marshes, the river must enter through a long, narrow, winding channel, and it must flow out over a large area.

--- Page 330 ---
of but little depth; and this is necessary because the water flowing in the river is thicker and more laden with earth in the lower than in the upper part; and the sluggish water of the marshes is also the same, but the variation between the lightness and heaviness of the upper and lower waters of the marshes far exceeds that in the currents of the rivers, in which the lightness of the upper part differs but little from the heaviness of the part below.

So the conclusion is that the marsh will be destroyed because it is receiving turbid water below, while above, on the opposite side of the same marsh, only clear water is flowing out; and consequently the bed of the marsh will of necessity be raised by means of the soil which is being continually discharged into it.

### How by running waters one should conduct the soil of the mountains into marshy valleys and so render them fertile and purify the surrounding air:

The ramifications of the canals which are led from the high hills according to their natural course are those which in their changes carry the soil from these hills to the low marshes, filling them up with earth and rendering them fertile.

Let *a* be the main stream which enters the marshes at *b f s*; let the canal start from the height of the hills *a c n*, from which suppose various branches to have fallen, changing it where it is all united into different places, and thus their fury tears away the soil and after they have run their course they deposit it in the low swamps; and thus you will be able to change the fall of the whole canal so much, abounding as it does in water, that you will have leveled the soil left uncovered from these marshes.

### Why pools are formed near the sea, and why their great floods are poured into the sea through so narrow a channel, upon the sides of which between the pool and the sea so great a bank is formed:

The storms of the sea cast up on the shore a great quantity of sand, and this is heaped up all along the shore both at the mouth of the pool and elsewhere; and as the storm ceases the mouth of the pool remains closed by the aforementioned matter thrown up by the sea. And as the water that the pool receives from the neighboring rivers cannot find any other exit, it proceeds to rise and acquire weight and power; and there-

--- Page 331 ---
before it either bursts through the bank positioned between it and the sea or flows over it, and with its outpouring wears away as much of the bank as it touches, pursuing its course until it has cleared from its path all the material that impeded its necessary dispersion.

Moreover, it only consumes what is necessary; at first, the opening is very large because the water flowing toward where the mouth should be is clear, and at the end, the course of the water becomes narrow because it has become thicker as it gains depth; and this is the reason why such an outlet from the pools to the sea is always narrow.

### OF THE WAVES

Sometimes the waves are swifter than the wind, and sometimes the wind is much swifter than the waves; ships on the sea prove this. The waves can be swifter than the wind by having been started by powerful winds, the wind then having ceased while the wave still preserved a great momentum.

One asks whether a river passing through a lake changes the uniform distance at which the surface of this lake stood from the center of the earth before this river passed through the said lake.

This is an interesting question; and one can show that this surface disturbs the uniformity of its distance from the center of the earth in order to provide a passage for the said river, according to the fourth rule, which shows that water does not move except to descend. And here it is necessary to understand whether the exit of the river has a width equal to that of the entrance; if this is so, it is necessary that the water have a uniform flow, according to the seventh rule, which shows that the movement of every river in an equal amount of time gives to every part of its length an equal weight of water. Now, if the river discharged water which required a drop of one *braccio* in a mile, and the width of the exit being, as has been said, equal to the width of the entrance, it would be necessary for all the river water passing through the lake to also have a drop of one *braccio* per mile; consequently, the water of this lake would have its surface at a varying distance from the center of the earth. But the water will follow this course...

That part of the lake water will have the slowest movement which

It follows from this that the Sea of Azov, which borders the River Don, is the highest part of the Mediterranean Sea. It is 3,500 miles away from the Straits of Gibraltar, as shown on navigators' charts, and it has a descent of 3,500 <term>braccia</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement based on the length of an arm, approximately 23 inches or 58 cm. ## OF THE WIND

Because wind eddies move upward, downward, and sideways, the local people cannot always tell which direction the wind is truly blowing. Those who live at the foot of hills near the sea shores do not know if the wind they feel is a local eddy or the main, direct wind.

When the wind strikes the sea coasts, the borders, or the sides of mountains, it rises toward the summit. There, it presses against the course of the other direct wind and then spreads out, bringing moisture to the opposite side. . . I 130 [82] v.

Why does thunder last for a longer time than the event that causes it? And why, immediately upon its creation, does lightning become visible to the eye, while thunder requires time to travel—like a wave—and makes the loudest noise when it meets with the most resistance? K 110 [30] v.

## WINDS AND THUNDERBOLTS

The winds which rise from the clouds continue in movement; the more they move, the higher they rise into the thinner air, because they are less impeded there. If they collide with each other, they rebound, and it is in these encounters that <term>thunderbolts</term> <note>In this context, Leonardo refers to the flash and discharge of lightning.</note> are produced.

If the wind originates at a low altitude, what is it that drives it more toward the east than toward the west? K 113 [33] r.

The center of the world <note>Leonardo refers to the Earth's center of gravity, which in the science of his time was considered the center of the universe.</note> continually changes its position within the body of the Earth, moving toward our hemisphere.

This is demonstrated by the aforementioned soil, which is continually stripped from the slopes <note>original: "declivities"</note> or sides of the mountains and carried to the seas. The more material is carried away from the mountains, the lighter they become; consequently, the areas where this soil is deposited by the ocean waves become heavier. Therefore, it is necessary that the Earth's center of gravity changes its position.

**[Surface of the earth and centre of gravity]**

Any part of the surface of a heavy body will move further from its center of gravity as it becomes lighter.

<margin>L 17 r.</margin>
Therefore, the land where rivers erode the slopes of the mountains and carry them to the sea is the place from which mass <note>original: "gravity"</note> is being removed. This part of the Earth will make itself lighter and, as a result, will move further away from the center of gravity of the Earth—that is, from the center of the universe, which is always aligned <note>original: "concentric"</note> with the Earth's center of gravity.

**[Changes in mountains and valleys]**

The summits of the mountains rise continually over the course of time.

The opposing sides of mountains always draw closer to one another.

Over time, the depths of the valleys located above the water level <note>original: "watery sphere"</note> constantly move closer to the center of the world.

During the same period of time, valleys sink much more than mountains rise.

The bases of the mountains are always drawing closer together.

<margin>L 76 r.</margin>
As a valley grows deeper, its sides are worn away in a shorter amount of time.

### [Water upon sand]

Why, since smooth sand is composed of grains uneven in shape and size, does the water flowing above them drive these grains with varying degrees of movement? Just as bodies that vary in weight and shape move differently in still air, so do air and water behave as they move among stationary bodies. This is why sand loses its smoothness due to the movement of the water passing over it. The moving water performs the same function upon the sand as the moving air does upon the water. And if you argue that the bed of flat sand creates waves and becomes uneven because of the unevenness of its granules, and that such unevenness could not exist on the surface of water—which is a struck and uniform body—I will maintain that the air is full of parts that move non-uniformly, and therefore the parts moved by contact with the air also move without uniformity.

The cause that makes water move in springs contrary to the natural pull of its gravity works in the same way as all the humours in every species of living body. Just as blood from below surges upward and then falls back if a vein bursts in the forehead, so the water rises from the lowest depths of the sea to the summits of the mountains; there, finding the springs burst open, it pours out through them and returns to the depths of the sea. Have you ever seen how the water that drips from the severed branches of a vine and falls back upon its roots penetrates them and so rises up again? It is the same with the water that falls back into the sea, for it penetrates through the pores of the earth and, having returned to the power of its mover, rises again with force, descends in its accustomed course, and then returns. Thus, adhering together and united in a continual revolution, it moves backward and forward; at times it all rises together with accidental movement, and at times it descends in natural liberty. Thus moving up and down, backward and forward, it never rests in quiet, either in its course or in its own substance: and as a mirror takes on the color of the objects that pass before it,

## OF THE SEA

If water becomes so salty because the earth is scorched by the sun, it should follow that when earth is boiled in water, this water would also become salty. Quaderni II 19 r.

[Influence of sun and moon on tides]

A force appears greater when it is applied against a lesser resistance. This conclusion is universal, and we may apply it to the ebb and flow of the tide to prove that the sun or moon exerts more influence on its object—that is, on the waters—when they are at a shallower depth. Consequently, the shallow waters of swamps ought to react more powerfully to the cause of the ebb and flow than the great depths of the ocean. Quaderni II 22 v.

[Filling of footprints in sand]

When a foot is pulled out of wet sand, the water rushes back right to the surface of the sand. This occurs because the water mixed with the sand is quicker to fill the vacuum left by the foot than the sand is. The air would be even quicker if it could enter; however, the wet sand always keeps the path closed through which the leg entered, and so prevents the air from entering to fill the vacuum. Quaderni IV 15 r.

To the west, the Sardonius range, as it proceeds westward, changes its name from Sardus to Rebi as it approaches Dalmatia. Then, continuing toward the west, it crosses Illyria (now called Slavonia) and changes the name Rebi to Albanus; continuing further westward, it changes again to the Ocra range.

To the north and south above Istria, it is named Caruancas (perhaps Carusadius?), and to the west above Italy, it unites with the Adula range where the <term>Danube</term> <note>original: "Rhine"</note> rises. This river flows for a course of fifteen hundred miles, covering about a thousand miles in a direct line; the spur of the Adula range changes into the names of the mountains already mentioned for just as far, or thereabouts.

To the north stands the Carpathian range, which encloses the width of the Danube valley. As I have stated, this valley stretches eastward for a distance of about a thousand miles and has a width of sometimes two hundred and sometimes three hundred miles. Through the midst of it flows the Danube, the greatest river of Europe in size. As it flows, the Danube leaves Austria and Albania to the south, and Bavaria, Poland, Hungary, Wallachia, and Bosnia to the north. The Danube—or the *Donau*, as it is called—then flows into the Black Sea. 

This sea used to extend almost as far as Austria and covered all the plains where the Danube flows today. The evidence for this is shown by the oysters, cockleshells, scallops, and bones of great fishes which are still found in many places on the high slopes of these mountains. This sea was created when the spurs of the Adula range, which extend to the east, joined with the spurs of the Taurus range, which extend to the west. Near Bithynia, the waters of this Black Sea discharged themselves into the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>, falling into the Aegean Sea—that is, the Mediterranean Sea. At that point, the spurs of the Adula range were severed from those of the Taurus range at the end of their long course; the Black Sea level then sank down and laid bare the valley of the Danube with the provinces named above. It also revealed the whole of Asia Minor north of the Taurus range, the plain stretching from the Caucasus to the Black Sea to the west, and the plain of the Tanais (the River Don) at the foot of the Ural Mountains.

So the Black Sea must have sunk about a thousand <term>braccia</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement; a Florentine *braccio* was approximately 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note> to uncover such vast plains. <margin>Codex Leicester, 1 verso.</margin>

In this work of yours, you must first prove that the shells found at a height of a thousand <term>braccia</term> <note>original: "braccia"; an Italian unit of length based on the arm, roughly 23 inches</note> were not carried there by the Deluge <note>The biblical Great Flood</note>. This is because they are found at a single, consistent level, yet there are mountains that rise significantly higher than this level. You must also investigate whether the Deluge was caused by rain or by the sea rising in a swirling flood. Then, you must show that neither by rain (which causes rivers to flood) nor by the swelling of the sea could these shells—being heavy objects—have been driven up the mountains by the sea or thrown there by rivers, as that would be contrary to the natural flow of the water.

<margin>Codex Leicester, 6 verso</margin>
When a river flows out from the mountains, it deposits a large quantity of big stones in its gravelly bed. These stones still retain some of their sharp angles and sides. As the river continues its course, it carries smaller stones with more worn-down angles, and so the large stones become smaller. Further on, it deposits first coarse and then fine gravel; after this, it deposits large and then small shingle <note>Small, rounded pebbles or stones</note>. This is followed by sand, which is coarse at first and then becomes finer. Thus, as the water continues its journey, turbid with shingle and sand, it reaches the sea.

This shingle is deposited along the seashores by the backwash of the salt waves, until finally the sand becomes so fine that it seems almost like water. This sediment does not remain on the shore but is pulled back with the wave because it is so light, being composed of rotting leaves and other extremely light materials. Consequently, as it is almost like water in its consistency, it drops down and settles at the bottom of the sea during calm weather. Because of its fineness, it becomes compressed and resists the waves that pass above it due to its smoothness. Shells are found within this material, and this is the "white earth" <note>likely referring to kaolin or potter's clay</note> used for making jugs.

### OF THE FLOOD AND OF MARINE SHELLS

Even if we grant that this Flood rose seven <term>cubits</term> <note>An ancient unit of measurement, roughly 18 to 22 inches</note> above the highest mountain, as was written by the person who measured it, these shells (which always live near the shores of the sea) should be found lying on the moun-

...mountain sides, and not at such a short distance above their bases, but all at the same level, layer upon layer.

If you also argue that the nature of these shells makes them stay near the seashore, and that as the sea rose in height, the shells left their former homes and followed the rising waters up to the highest level—to this I reply that the cockle is a creature incapable of moving faster than a snail when it is out of the water. <note>original: "that in forty days the shells cannot travel"; these words were crossed out in the original manuscript.</note> It may even be slower, since it does not swim, but instead digs a furrow in the sand. By supporting itself against the sides of this furrow, it travels between three and four <term>braccia</term> <note>An Italian unit of length based on the arm, roughly 23 inches</note> in a day. Therefore, with such a slow rate of motion, it could not have traveled from the Adriatic Sea as far as Monferrato in Lombardy—a distance of 250 miles—in forty days, as has been claimed by those who kept a record of that time.

And if you say that the waves carried them there, they could not move because of their weight unless they remained on the seabed. Even if you do not grant me this, you must at least admit that they would have remained on the peaks of the highest mountains and in the landlocked lakes within the mountains, such as Lake Como <note>original: "Lario"; the Latin name for Lake Como. Leonardo's manuscript lists "Lake Lario, Maggiore, and Como," seemingly listing the same lake twice.</note>, Lake Maggiore, and the lakes of Fiesole, Perugia, and others.

The water of the surrounding seas forms a sphere of water. The center of this sphere's surface is the center of the world, but it is not the center of its gravity. This is because the sea is of great depth in many places and shallow in others; because it is not of uniform thickness, it is not of uniform weight. However, because an object is considered "higher" the further it is from the center of the world, this surface—when not in motion—cannot remain higher in one part than in another. The highest part of the water always seeks to flow down and fill the parts of itself that are lower.

If the Flood occurred as has been said, rising above the mountains of our hemisphere, it would undoubtedly have made the gravity of our habitable side greater than that of the <term>antipodes</term> <note>The side of the Earth directly opposite to one's own</note>. As a consequence, it would have pulled our side closer to the center of the world than it was before, and the opposite side would have been pushed further away from this center. For this reason...

the aforesaid Flood submerged more than would have been submerged if such gravity had not been acquired by it on this side.

If you should say that the shells were empty and dead when carried by the waves, I reply that where the dead ones went, the living were not far distant; and in these mountains, all the living ones are found, for they are recognized by the shells being in pairs, and by their being in a row without any dead ones. A little higher up is the place where all the dead shells, separated from each other, have been cast up by the waves. Near there, the rivers plunged into the sea at great depth; like the Arno, which fell from the Gonfolina near Monte Lupo and there left gravel deposits, and these can still be seen welded together, forming one concrete mass out of various kinds of stones from different localities and of varying color and hardness. And a little farther on, where the river turns toward Castel Fiorentino, the hardening of the sand has formed tufa stone; and below this, it has deposited the mud in which the shells lived; and this has risen in layers according to how the floods of the muddy Arno were poured into this sea, and so from time to time the bed of the sea was raised.

This has caused these shells to be produced in pairs, as is shown in the cutting of Colle Gonzoli, made sheer by the river Arno which wears away its base; for in this cutting, the aforesaid layers of shells may be seen distinctly in the bluish clay, and various things from the sea may be found there.

And the earth of our hemisphere became raised up more than it was before as it gradually became lightened of the water that flowed away from it through the Straits of Gibraltar; and it was raised so much the more because the weight of the water which flowed away from it was added to that of the earth that was turned toward the other hemisphere.

And if the shells had been in the muddy water of a deluge, they would be found mixed up and separated from one another amid the mud, and not in regular rows in layers as we see them in our own times.

As for those who say that these shells are found to exist over a wide area because they were created far from the sea by the nature of the locality and the disposition of the heavens, which moves and influences the place toward such a creation of animal life, to these it may be answered—

--- Page 341 ---
that granted such an influence over these animals, it could not have happened that they were arranged in a single line except in the case of animals of the same species and age; and not the old with the young, nor one with an outer covering and another without its covering, nor one broken and another whole, nor one filled with sea sand and the fragments, great and small, of others inside the whole shells which stand gaping open; nor the claws of crabs without the rest of their bodies; nor with the shells of other species fastened onto them like animals crawling over them and leaving the mark of their track on the outside where it has eaten its way like a worm in wood; nor would there be found among them bones and fishes' teeth which some call arrows and others serpents' tongues; nor would so many parts of different animals be found joined together, unless they had been thrown up there upon the borders of the sea.

And the Flood would not have carried them there because things heavier than water do not float upon the surface of the water, and the aforementioned things could not be at such heights unless they had been carried there floating on the waves, and that is impossible on account of their weight.

Where the valleys have never been covered by the salt waters of the sea, there the shells are never found; as is plainly visible in the great valley of the Arno above Gonfolina, a rock which was once united with Monte Albano in the form of a very high bank. This kept the river dammed up in such a way that before it could empty itself into the sea—which was afterwards at the foot of this rock—it formed two large lakes. The first of these is where we now see the city of Florence flourish together with Prato and Pistoia; and Monte Albano followed the rest of the bank down to where Serravalle now stands. In the upper part of the Val d'Arno as far as Arezzo, a second lake was formed, and this emptied its waters into the above-mentioned lake. It was shut in at about where we now see Girone, and it filled all the valley above for a distance of forty miles. This valley received upon its base all the earth carried down by the turbid waters, and it is still to be seen at its maximum height at the foot of Prato Magno, for there the rivers have not worn it away.

Within this soil may be seen the deep cuttings of the rivers which

have passed there in their descent from the great mountain of Prato Magno; in which cuttings there are no visible traces of any shells or of marine earth.

This lake was joined to that of Perugia.

A great quantity of shells may be seen where the rivers empty themselves into the sea, because in such places the water is not very salty on account of the mixture of the fresh water which unites with it. A proof of this is to be seen where the Apennines once emptied their rivers into the waters of the Adriatic, for there among the mountains in most parts a great quantity of shells are visible together with bluish marine clay; and all the rocks which are broken away in such places are found to be full of shells.

We know that the Arno did the same when it fell from the rock of Gonfolina into the sea which was not very far below it, because in those times it must have stood higher than the top of San Miniato al Tedesco, since in the highest summits of this mountain one sees the rocks full of shells and oysters within its banks; the shells did not extend in the direction of Val di Nievole because the fresh waters of the Arno did not extend so far.

How the shells were not carried from the sea by the Deluge, because the waters which came from the earth to the sea, although they drew the sea towards the earth, were those which struck its base; because the water which comes from the earth has a stronger current than that of the sea, and as a consequence is more powerful and enters beneath the other water of the sea, and stirs up the bottom and carries with it all the movable objects which are to be found in it, such as the above-mentioned shells and other like things; and as the water which comes from the land is muddier than that of the sea, it is so much the more powerful and heavier than it. I do not see, therefore, in what way the said shells could have come to be so far inland unless they had been born there.

If you should tell me that the river Loire which passes through France spreads itself over more than eighty miles of country when the sea is increased, because the country forms a great plain and the sea rises about twenty braccia, and that shells are sometimes found in this plain at a distance of eighty miles from the sea, the reply is that the flow and ebb in our Mediterranean seas does not cause so much variation—

The sea level does not change much in the Gulf of Genoa; at Venice and in Africa, it varies only a little. Where the tide varies so little, it covers only a small portion of the land.

<margin>Leicester Codex, folio 9 recto</margin>

### A Refutation of those who claim that sea shells were carried many days' journey from the sea because of the Deluge.

I maintain that the Deluge <note>Leonardo refers to the biblical Great Flood of Noah.</note> could not have carried objects native to the sea up into the mountains unless the sea had risen so high that it flooded over the peaks of those very places. This could not have occurred because it would have created a vacuum; and if you were to say that the air would rush in to fill it, we have already concluded that a heavy substance cannot be supported by a light one. Therefore, we must necessarily conclude that this Deluge was caused by rainwater. If this was the case, all that rainwater flowed into the sea, and the sea does not flow up mountains. If the water ran toward the sea, it would have pushed the shells along the shore into the ocean rather than drawing them toward itself. 

And if you should argue that because the sea was raised by rainwater, it carried these shells to such heights, we have already stated that objects heavier than water cannot float upon its surface; they remain at the bottom and are not moved from there unless by the pressure of the waves. If you were to say it was the waves that carried them to these high places, we have proved that when waves are very deep, the water at the bottom moves in the opposite direction to the movement at the surface. This is demonstrated by the <term>turbidity</term> <note>original: "turbidity"; the cloudiness or muddiness of water caused by stirred-up sediment.</note> of the sea, which comes from the soil being washed away near the shores.

An object lighter than water moves with the surface wave and is left on the highest spot of the bank by the highest wave; however, an object heavier than water moves only when driven by the wave along the surface of the seabed. From these two conclusions (which will be fully proved in their proper places), we may conclude that surface waves cannot carry shells because shells are heavier than water. Consequently, shells would only be driven by the lower waves when the wind blows from the land; this is because when the wind blows from the land, the current at the bottom of the sea moves in the opposite direction to the prevailing wind. Furthermore, even this would not cause the shells to be carried up the mountains, because the water at the bottom, which moves...

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci uses principles of fluid dynamics to argue that the biblical flood could not have deposited sea shells on mountains, as heavy objects like shells remain at the seabed and move toward the sea rather than uphill.</summary>

in the opposite direction to the wind will be so much slower than the surface wave as it is deeper than the height of the wave. This is evident because if the surface wave is one braccio high and there are a hundred braccia of water below it, then without doubt the lower wave will be a hundred times slower than the upper wave, as is shown in the seventh proposition. The upper wave will never turn back on its base with any great force unless the depth of the water below the wave is equal to the height of the wave.

The tiny wave which may be seen on the high seas traveling against the direction of the wind will not pass over its base—that is, it will not touch it, but will dissolve upon contact with the surface wave. I maintain that such movement of water, changing from its surface to its base, resembles that which takes place on the surface between two banks; for if a third of the river's width moves toward the west, another third will move toward the east, and the remainder toward the west; and if there were another similar part there, it would return to the east. The lateral movements of rivers will become slower in proportion to their distance from the primary current. Regarding the friction created by water moving swiftly within other water—whether it divides immediately (that is, whether the edges of this body of water are worn away) or whether the layers follow one after another (that is, the swifter portion carrying the less swift with it)—I maintain that this is not the case; for if it carried more water with it than usual, it would grow to such a size during its long course that it would be carrying all the water of the river with it.

The reason why oysters are very seldom found dead on the seashores is because they usually live fastened to the rocks at the bottom of the sea and are incapable of movement, except for the half that is sensitive and light. The other valve is fixed to the stone, or if not fixed, nature has caused them to grow larger and thus become so heavy that the small amount of undulation occurring in the vast depths of the sea cannot easily dislodge them. But the valve that has the power of movement is very light and performs the same function for it as a lid does for a chest. And when the oyster feeds, its food walks into the house of its own accord, for it consists of certain animalculae which feed around the shells of dead ones and which, consequently, are found where there are a great many shells of dead oysters. Under the ground and down in the deep excavations of the stone quarries, timbers of worked beams are found which have already turned black. In Candia, in Lombardy, near to Alessandria della Paglia, while some men were engaged in digging a well for Messer <term>Messer</term> <note>A title of address for a gentleman, similar to "Mr." or "Sir."</note> Gualtieri, who has a house there, the skeleton of a very large ship was found at a depth of about ten <term>braccia</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement; one *braccio* is roughly 23 inches or 0.6 meters.</note> beneath the ground. And if you should argue that these shells were and are still being created in such places by the nature of the site and through the influence of the stars <note>original: "potency of the heavens"; referring to the then-popular belief in spontaneous generation caused by astrological forces.</note>, such an opinion cannot exist in minds possessed of any real reasoning power. How the northern foundations of certain Alps are not yet turned to stone; this is seen clearly where the rivers that cut through them flow toward the north. These rivers carve through the layers <note>original: "strata".</note> of solid rock in the mountain heights; but where they meet the plains, these layers consist entirely of potter’s clay. This is evident in the Val di Lamona <note>The Lamona river valley in the Romagna region of Italy.</note>, where the Lamona River does these same things to its banks as it emerges from the Apennines.

How the rivers have sawn through and separated the members of the great Alps from one another; this is revealed by the arrangement of the stratified rocks. From the summit of the mountain down to the river, one sees the layers on one side of the valley matching those on the other. The stratified rocks of the mountains are all made of layers of mud deposited one atop another by river floods. The varying thicknesses of these rock layers are created by different floods—that is, the larger and the smaller floods.

How between the various layers of stone, the tracks of worms are still to be found, which crawled about upon them when the mud was not yet dry. All marine clays still contain shells, and the shell is turned to stone along with the clay. This shows the stupidity and ignorance of those who imagine that these creatures were carried to such places far from the sea by the Great Flood <note>original: "Deluge".</note>.

How another set of ignorant people maintain that nature or the heavens created them in these places through celestial influences. It is as if they do not find the bones of fish in those same places, which take a long time to grow; as if one could not count on the shells...

### PHYSICAL GEOGRAPHY

In the past, the islands we see today were not yet surrounded by salt water. Nor had Africa yet revealed the vast earth of its great plains—stretching some three thousand miles—behind the Atlas Mountains. On the shore of this ancient sea stood the city of Memphis <note>An ancient capital of Egypt</note>; and above the plains of Italy, where flocks of birds fly today, schools of fish once swam in great numbers.

There are springs that suddenly burst forth or just as suddenly fail as a result of earthquakes or other unforeseen causes. This happened in a mountain in Savoy <note>A region in the western Alps</note>, where certain forests sank into the earth, leaving behind a very deep abyss. About four miles from that spot, the ground opened on a mountainside and suddenly discharged an immense flood of water. This flood swept through an entire valley of cultivated fields, vineyards, and houses, causing irreparable damage wherever it spread.

Many springs fail suddenly because of a collapse in a cavern trapped within the body of the earth; this blockage hinders the passage of the water.

Conversely, many springs emerge suddenly and become permanent. This happens when a river, over its long course, has worn away enough of a mountain to break into underground water channels. It may also occur, as I mentioned before, when a cave collapses and blocks a spring; the water is then forced upward within the cavern until it reaches a fissure in the rock, escapes, and creates a new river.

Many saltwater springs are found far from the sea. This occurs because the water has passed through a salt mine, like those in Hungary where salt is hewn out of immense quarries just as blocks of stone are.

Within rocks surrounded by salt water, and even within the salt water itself, springs of fresh water rise up in many places.

In many places, there are springs of water that rise for six hours and sink for six hours. I have personally seen one above Lake Como called the <term>Fonte Pliniana</term> <note>original: "Fonte Pliniana"; named after Pliny the Elder and Pliny the Younger, who both described this intermittent spring</note>, which increases and decreases in this way to such an extent that when it is flowing, it powers two mills; and when

A storm at sea is much more violent near the shore than on the open ocean; and this is because the recoil of the waves strikes the sea on one side while the wind strikes it on the other, and this causes the wave to be higher and more topped with spray.

How the flow and ebb of the tide is not uniform, for on the coast of Genoa there is none; at Venice it creates a variation of two braccia; between England and France, eighteen braccia. How the current that flows through the Straits of Sicily is very powerful because all the waters of the rivers which discharge themselves into the Adriatic pass through them.

When the surface of the water consists of small shaded waves which form themselves into lines that meet at an angle, this fact shows that the bed of the river is not far below, and it is also produced by the sand thrown off by the water as it passes through a confined space such as the arch of a bridge or something similar. When the lines of its surface form a curved or crescent-shaped figure, this is a sign of its lack of depth, for it is caused by the sand carried by the stronger current into the weaker—that is, by the less sluggish into the more sluggish—since both of them have very little speed or depth. When the surface of the water appears as a straight line or is just slightly bent with tiny waves, and these have very little sheen or brightness, there is very little depth there; and this is caused by two currents, one slower than the other, which join together again below the island that divides them further upstream; for these have caused the sand which each carried with it to settle, because it is deposited at the point of their junction, since their movement ended at this spot.

Why are the bones of great fishes and oysters and corals and various other shells and sea-snails found on the high tops of mountains that border the sea, in the same way in which they are found in the depths of the sea?

How the rocks and promontories <note>promontories: high points of land or rock that project into the sea</note> of the seas are being continually destroyed and worn away.

How the brightness of the atmosphere is caused by the water dissolved in it, which has formed into imperceptible particles. After capturing the light of the sun from the opposite side, these particles reflect the brightness that is visible in the air. The blue color that appears in the sky is caused by the darkness hidden behind this atmosphere.

Why the Adige <note>The Adige is a river in Northern Italy, the second longest after the Po.</note> rises every seven years and falls every seven years, and whether this is the cause of famine or abundance.

<margin>Leicester Codex, folio 20 recto</margin>
Why, following great pestilences, the rivers become deeper and run clear, even though they were previously wide, shallow, and always murky?

The sea is enclosed within the great valleys of the earth, and the earth serves as a basin <note>original: "cup"</note> for the sea. The shores of the seas are the rims of this basin; if they were removed, the sea would cover the entire earth. However, because every part of the dry land is higher than the highest level of the sea, the sea cannot overflow it; it simply remains within the earth that serves as its bed. 

Many people, however, ignorant of this fact, have arrogantly written that the surface of the sea is higher than the highest mountain. In this regard, even though they can see that the shore is higher than the water, those who claim it is a miracle for the water in the middle of the sea to be higher than its shore or the cliffs overhanging it are profoundly blind. This error arises because they imagine a straight line of indefinite length <note>In modern terms, a tangent line</note> extended above the middle of the sea. Such a line would indeed be higher than the shores, because the earth is a sphere and its surface forms a curve; the further a point on the surface is removed from the middle of that line, the further it recedes from it. The fact that the surface curves downward in this condition is what has deceived them; and it is this reasoning which will be brought forward...

For a long time the water of the Mediterranean flowed through the Red Sea, which is a hundred miles wide and fifteen hundred miles long, and completely full of reefs; and it has worn away the sides of Mount Sinai. This circumstance does not point to a flood from the Indian Ocean having struck these shores, but to a great deluge of water which carried with it all the rivers—which are very numerous around the Mediterranean—and also the ebb of the sea. On the shores of the Mediterranean, three hundred rivers are found discharging their waters, and there are some forty thousand two hundred harbors, and this sea is three thousand miles in length. Many times the swollen waters of the sea have been heaped up by its reflux, by western gales, and by the flooding of the Nile and of the rivers which flow into the Black Sea. That part of the flow and ebb of the sea will show greater variety from its greatest height to its lowest depth when it is nearest to its cause.

There is great variation between the ebb and flow of the sea in the vicinity of those places where the springs of water depart from the depths of the seas in order to supply a perpetual stream of water to the rivers, which afterwards descend from the high mountains.

There is a spring in Sicily that, as it rises during certain seasons of the year, throws out large quantities of chestnut leaves. Since chestnut trees do not grow in Sicily, however, this spring must have originated from an underground lake in Italy, passed beneath the sea, and afterward found an outlet in Sicily. <note>original: Richter points out that the chestnut is a common tree in Sicily and suggests that Leonardo may have written ‘Cicilia’ (Sicily) by mistake for Cilicia, a region in modern-day Turkey.</note>

In the Bosphorus, the Black Sea always flows into the Aegean, and never the Aegean into the Black Sea. The Don and the Danube do the same; consequently, the waters of the Black Sea are always higher than those of the Aegean. It follows that the higher waters always descend into the lower, and never the lower into the higher.

Some argue that the waters rising at the summits of high mountains are part of the seawater, which they believe is higher than the summits of the highest mountains. They use this to try to prove that the surface of the sea is lower than any part of the land standing above the water, or any part of the surface of a river flowing into that sea.

Others claim that the waters flowing from high mountain peaks descend from even higher mountains elsewhere in the world that are covered with snow which melts during the summer. However, this opinion is proven incorrect. All the outlets of the waters which flow from the mountain to the sea carry stones from the mountains with them to the sea; and by the backwash of the ocean surges against these mountains, these stones were thrown back toward the mountain; and as the waters moved toward the sea and returned from it, the stones turned with them, and as they were rolled back, their corners struck together, and those parts of them that offered the least resistance to the blow were worn away, creating stones without angles and of a round shape, such as are to be seen on the shores of Elba. And those stones remain larger which are carried the shortest distance from their native spot, and likewise, the stone becomes smaller as it is transported farther away from the aforementioned spot, for in the course of its progress it is changed to fine shingle, then to sand, and finally to mud. After the sea had receded from the aforementioned mountains, the salt deposit which it left behind, along with the other moisture from the earth, formed a compound with the shingle and sand so that the shingle was changed to rock and the sand to tufa.

And of this we may see an example in the Adda where it emerges from the mountains of Como, and in the Ticino, the Adige, the Oglio, and the Adriano from the Austrian Alps; and in the same way with the Arno from Monte Albano around Monte Lupo and Capraia, where the largest rocks are all formed of solidified shingle of different varieties of stone and of different colors.

<margin>Leic. 31 v.</margin>
The thing which is lighter will be carried farther by the rivers from the place where its waters snatched it away; and so that which is heavier will be moved a shorter distance from the place where it was separated. The impact of the water carries away more of the river bank when it strikes the bank at more equal angles; and conversely, it will carry away less when the angles are more unequal.

There are as many differences in the resistance made by water beneath that which is supported by it as there are differences in its heat or cold.

Given two rivers of equal volume of water at their entrances, their

the exits will be equal. That is to say, given an equal volume of water over an equal period of time, the amount leaving will equal the amount entering, even if the rivers vary in length, width, slope <note>original: "slant"</note>, and depth; even if one is winding <note>original: "twisted"</note> and the other straight; or if both are winding but with different curves; or if one has a uniform width while the other varies—and if both vary, their variations may be different. One may be of a uniform depth and the other of varying depth; and should both depths vary in themselves, their variations may not have any kind of likeness. Furthermore, the whole of one might be uniformly fast and the other uniformly slow, or the speed and slowness of one might be mixed—that is, running in some places and lingering in others, where the waters fall vertically <note>original: "perpendicularly"</note> and where they rise in a swirling flood. The fact that infinite varieties of currents in width, length, slope, and depth exist in these two rivers will not, therefore, prevent the equal entrance of one from being equal to its exit, nor the equal entrances of both from being equal in their exits.

If the Mediterranean Sea moves from its current location, it raises the sphere of the water and occupies new valleys; consequently, the center of gravity of this increase will be near the antipodes <term>antipodes</term> <note>the parts of the earth directly opposite to each other; the "other side" of the world</note>. Because of this, the weight increases on that side, while on this side, the weight of the water that has departed is lost. Although this space may be filled by the soil carried by rivers into the Mediterranean, the center of its gravity will be opposite to that of the sphere of water which has increased in the antipodes. Therefore, the weight on this side is not increased by the earth which was moved to replace the sea that was expelled, because this earth—that is, its center of gravity—remains in our hemisphere; nevertheless, it is still true that the total weight of the water here is diminished. Consequently, the center of the world will shift closer to our antipodes, lightening itself of the weight of the departed water; as a result, the summits of the mountains will rise further from this center. This will continue until the rivers that join the Nile, after much winding about through the great plain where the Mediterranean is divided, carry all the sediment <note>original: "soil that makes it turbid"</note> through the Straits of Gibraltar. In the course of time, they will deposit as much soil in the ocean beyond the Straits of Gibraltar as is currently found between Libya and

So then it is concluded that the more the soil is removed from us, the more it lightens our regions; as a consequence, the more it is removed from the center of the earth, the more the waters consume it and the more it becomes light again; and so it will continue until all the exposed earth is carried to the sea by the Nile or by the rivers that are poured into it.

And so the earth that is found in the rivers that now pour themselves into the Mediterranean will be carried by the Nile, together with the muddy water that remains in it, to the ocean.

So then the sea will return to cover the places where the roots and bases of the mountains formerly were, and it will cover the earth.

It is not denied that the Nile is always muddy as it enters the Egyptian sea, and that this muddy condition is due to the soil which this river continually carries away from the places through which it passes; and this soil never returns, nor does the sea receive it except to cast it back upon its shores; behold the ocean of sand beyond Mount Atlas, where it was once covered with salt water.

The water that is found in the highest mountains is not there because it has been drawn there by the heat of the sun, for but little of this heat passes downwards, as is seen below La Vernia, where the power of the sun is not sufficient to melt the ice during the greatest heat of summer, but it remains there in the hollows in which it has been lying since the winter. And on the northern slopes of the Alps, where the sun does not strike, the ice never melts, because the heat of the sun cannot penetrate the small thickness of the mountains; still less, therefore, will the vast space that lies between the summits of the great mountains and the depths of the watery sphere be penetrated by this heat of the sun, which would have to pass beneath the base of the mountain. If you should say that the earth's action is like that of a sponge which, when part of it is placed in water, sucks up the water so that it passes up to the top of the sponge, the answer is that even if the water itself rises to the top of the sponge, it cannot then pour any part of itself down from this top unless it is squeezed by

--- Page 358 ---
something else, whereas with the summits of the mountains one sees it is just the opposite, for there the water always flows away of its own accord without being squeezed by anything.

Perhaps you will say that water can only rise the same distance as it descends, and that the surface of the sea is higher than the summits of the highest mountains. The answer to this is that the exact opposite is the case, for the lowest part visible to the sky is the surface of the sea, since water does not move of itself unless to descend, and so descends when it moves; as therefore the rivers which stretch from the summits of the mountains to the sea are everywhere in movement, they are therefore everywhere descending, and when they come to the sea they stop and end their movement; for which reason one must conclude that they are stationary in the lowest reaches of the river. But if you should say that the farther the sea is away from the shore the more it rises up, and so it comes to equal the height of the high mountains; it is shown here that a thing is higher which is farther removed from the center of the earth, and if the element of water is spherical, the definition of spherical bodies is those in which every part of the surface is equidistant from the center. So therefore the shore of the sea is as high as its center, and whatever may be discerned from the shore is higher than any part of the sea; and the distance that there is from the summits of the high mountains to the center of the earth is greater than the distance from this center to the sea shore: this then is our conclusion.

And if you should say, as has been said, that the sun sucks up and draws the waters from the roots of the mountains to their summits, then as the heat draws the moisture to itself, the heat which is more powerful would draw to itself a greater amount of water than the less powerful. In summer, therefore, during the fiery heats, the springs of the waters would have to rise higher into the summits of the mountains than they do in winter; but we see it is the contrary, seeing that in summer the rivers lack a great part of their waters.

### OF THE ORIGIN OF RIVERS

The body of the earth, like the bodies of animals, is interwoven with a network of veins which are all joined together, and are formed for

--- Page 359 ---

# PHYSICAL GEOGRAPHY

<margin>Leicester Codex, Sheet 33 verso</margin>
The nutrition and life-giving force of this earth and its creatures originate in the depths of the sea. After many cycles, these waters return through the rivers formed by the high eruptions of these veins <note>The author compares the earth's internal water channels to the veins in a human body.</note>. If you wish to claim that winter rains or the melting of summer snow are the cause of rivers, one could point to the rivers that originate in the tropical regions of Africa. In those places it does not rain, and even less does it snow, because the excessive heat always evaporates all the clouds driven there by the winds into the air. 

And if you should say that these rivers—which swell in July and August—come from snow melting in May and June as the sun approaches the snowfields of the mountains of Scythia <note>Scythia was an ancient region in Eurasia, north of the Black Sea.</note>, and that the melted snow collects in certain valleys to form lakes, entering them through springs and underground caverns before emerging to form the source of the Nile, this is incorrect. Scythia lies at a lower elevation than the source of the Nile. Furthermore, Scythia is only four hundred miles from the Black Sea, whereas the source of the Nile is three thousand miles from the Mediterranean Sea <note>original: "Egyptian sea"</note> into which it pours its water.

In the western regions near Flanders, the sea rises and falls about twenty <term>braccia</term> <note>A "braccio" (plural: braccia) was an Italian unit of measurement roughly equal to the length of an arm, or about 23 inches.</note> every six hours; it rises twenty-two when the moon is favorable. However, twenty *braccia* is its usual variation, and as is clearly seen, this is not caused by the moon <note>The author incorrectly rejects the moon's influence on tides here, seeking a mechanical explanation based on water displacement.</note>. This variation in the rising and falling of the sea every six hours may occur because of the swelling of the waters poured into the Mediterranean by the many rivers from Africa, Asia, and Europe. These rivers pour their waters into this sea, which then gives them back to the ocean through the Strait of Gibraltar, between the promontories of Abyla and Calpe <note>Abyla and Calpe are the ancient names for the mountains flanking the Strait of Gibraltar, known as the Pillars of Hercules.</note>.

This ocean, as it extends between the island of England and other islands farther north, swells up and forms a bore <note>A "bore" is a large wave or surge caused by the meeting of two tides or a tide entering a narrow inlet.</note> at the mouths of certain gulfs. These gulfs—acting like smaller seas with surfaces separated from the central body of the earth—acquire weight. As this weight exceeds the force of the incoming waters that caused it, it forces the water to retreat with a momentum contrary to its approach. This creates a counter-momentum against the flow in the straits, especially against the Strait of Gibraltar, which remains in a swirling flood for as long as this process continues.

Layered rocks <note>original: "stratified rocks"</note> are created in the vast depths of the seas because the mud, which storms detach from the sea coasts, is carried out to the deep sea by the recoil of the waves. After these storms, the mud is deposited on the seabed. Since no storm can penetrate the sea at such a great depth below the surface, the mud lies there motionless and becomes petrified <note>meaning: turned into stone over time</note>. Sometimes it remains in the form of white clay which is used for making pots. Thus, with blocks set at different angles, the earth is composed of layers of many different thicknesses, corresponding to the intensity of the storms, whether greater or less.

### WHETHER THE EARTH IS LESS THAN THE WATER

Some assert as a fact that the dry land which is not covered by water is much smaller in area than the land covered by it. But since the diameter of the earth is seven thousand miles, one might conclude that because the water is almost universally quite shallow, its weight is incomparable to that of the earth. The answer to those people is that the water which evaporates into the atmosphere—becoming concentrated as it rises to the cold regions of the air—is very heavy and falls in great deluges and floods. Furthermore, how do we know whether the earth contains enormous caverns with reservoirs of water?

And consider the innumerable springs fed by as many streams of water as are seen in the formation of rivers. Take, for instance, the Caspian Sea, which is vast.

<meta>This page continues Leonardo's discussion on the physical properties of the Earth, specifically examining the relationship between the planet's geometric center and its center of gravity given the presence of water and uneven landmasses.</meta>

<lang>English</lang>
<page-num>353</page-num>
<header>PHYSICAL GEOGRAPHY</header>

The center of the sphere of water will always be concentric <note>meaning: sharing the same center</note> with the center of the world. However, the center of the water's weight will not be, because water is not spread over the earth with an equal thickness. The same is true regarding the center of gravity of the combined earth and waters; it does not align with the world's center in terms of its total gravity or its magnitude. 

If the earth were a perfect sphere on its own and contained no water within itself, then the water would clothe it with a uniform size and weight. In that case, the center of the world would remain the center of the water's sphere, magnitude, and weight. It would also remain the center of the earth’s sphere, magnitude, and gravity. 

However, the earth is a mixture, filled with internal "ramifications" <note>original: "ramifications of the waters"; Leonardo likely means the network of underground rivers and springs</note> of water. In some parts it is spread out, while in others it is compact; in some places it is soil, and in others rock. Consequently, this earth does not possess a center of sphericity <term>sphericity</term> or a center of gravity. This is especially true because there is land and water rising above the general sphere of the water <note>referring to mountains and landmasses above sea level</note>, which add weight to it as if it were the weight of the earth itself.

Consequently, from this one concludes that the gravity of the earth and water joined and mingled together usually has its center concentric with the center of the world. This center is also the center of the water’s spherical surface—but not the center of its weight, as I said above. This surface of the sphere of water is broken and divided by the land that borders the air.

If the earth were entirely submerged by water, even if it were of a varied and irregular shape, it would have the center of its natural gravity concentric with the center of the world and the surface of the water’s sphere. However, it would not align with the center of its natural or even its accidental gravity <note>original: "accidental gravity"; in Leonardo's physics, this refers to weight shifted by external circumstances or movement</note>.

Land that is not covered by water will be much heavier than land that is beneath the water <note>Leonardo is noting the effects of buoyancy: land underwater is "lighter" than dry land because of the water it displaces</note>.

The centers of heavy bodies are three, and they are situated differently. Sometimes they are joined together, at which point accidental gravity disappears. Sometimes two are together while the third is separated from them; this is where accidental gravity arises. And sometimes they are placed in three different positions, one from the other. These are:
1. The center of **magnitude** <note>the geometric center of the shape</note>.
2. The center of its **natural gravity** <note>the inherent balance point of the object’s material</note>.
3. The center of **accidental gravity** <note>the shifting balance point caused by external weight or movement</note>.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the Earth's centers of gravity and magnitude, arguing that the uneven distribution of land and water prevents the planet from being a perfectly balanced sphere. He defines three distinct "centers" that govern the physics of heavy bodies: magnitude, natural gravity, and accidental gravity.</summary>

### PHYSICAL GEOGRAPHY

The geometric center <note>original: "centre of the magnitude"</note> is the point that is equally distant from the opposite extremities of the body enclosing it, whether that body is uniform or not. It is sufficient for it to be situated at an equal distance from the opposite ends of a staff, or a cloth made of any material. These centers are joined together in a body of perfect roundness <term>sphericity</term> and uniform substance and density, because in such a case there are only two centers and they are <term>concentric</term> <note>meaning: they share the same central point</note>.

Necessity dictates that the mechanism of the earth is hollow of soil and full of water, much like a vessel filled with water.

This is supported by the theory of the tenfold proportion which the <term>four elements</term> <note>The classical elements: earth, water, air, and fire. Ancient science often claimed each element was ten times the volume of the one below it.</note> are said to have between them. This is seen in the air's relationship with the earth, where the proportion is thought to be a hundredfold. This is because the thickness of the air has been measured between the comets—which occupy the uppermost part of the air <note>In Leonardo's time, comets were often thought to be atmospheric phenomena rather than celestial bodies.</note>—and the surface of the sphere of water, which is at the lowest part of the sphere of air. 

Now, one might say that the amount of earth projecting above the surface of the water is equal to the volume missing from the water's surface toward the center of the world. That is, I consider the highest mountain on earth to be as far above the surface of the sea as the greatest depth of the sea is below that surface. It follows that if one were to fill the depths of the sea with the excess land from the mountains, the earth would become a perfect sphere and be entirely covered by water. 

However, as far as one can discern, this sphere of water—or "element"—would not be ten times as large as the sphere of the earth. In fact, far from being ten times larger, it would not even reach a one-to-one ratio. This is because the sphere of water would not even rise a mile above the earth’s sphere; it would not reach the height of the highest mountain. This would only happen if all the uncovered land were everywhere as high as the highest mountain.

Therefore, it is concluded that the rest of this water remains inside the body and the springs of the earth. It may have drained there over a wide area and lightened the spot from which it separated itself, as is represented opposite in diagram B.

In two ways the <term>gravity</term> of the earth can have its center sharing the same center as the world: that is, if it is either altogether submerged...

The center of gravity of the water and of the earth might be concentric with the center of the world if the earth were perfectly spherical. The center of the world would then be the center of the sphere of the earth, as well as the sphere of the water. But it would not produce land animals.

### OF THE EARTH IN ITSELF

The fact that the summits of the mountains project so far above the watery sphere may be due to the fact that a very large space of the earth which was filled with water—that is, the immense cavern—must have fallen in a considerable distance from its vault toward the center of the world. This occurred after it was pierced by the course of the springs, which continually wear away the spot through which they pass, containing within them some of the air from above; because water has no weight unless it sends a wave out of its level through the air, and it is this wave alone that has weight and falls and wears away the base. Now this great mass has the power of falling, being at the center of the world within the water: it balances itself with equal opposing weights around the center of the world, and lightens the earth from which it is divided; and it removed itself immediately from the center of the world and rose to the height, for so one sees the layers of the rocks, formed by the changes which the water has undergone, at the summits of the high mountains.

Subsidence of lands, as in the Dead Sea in Syria, namely Sodom and Gomorrah.

It must be that there is more water than land; and the part uncovered by the sea does not reveal it; it must be, therefore, that there is a great mass of water within the earth, in addition to that which is diffused through the lower parts of the atmosphere and runs through the rivers and springs.

I say that it is not necessary for the center of the world to be situated more in the earth than in the water, because the gravity of the earth and of the water, joined together in any manner whatever, rests with

--- Page 364 ---
weights of gravity situated oppositely around the center of the world; and the earth does not expect to have parts of itself equally distant from this center, but rather weights of equal heaviness placed opposite one another. In this case, the water being mingled with various branches of springs together with the earth, cannot provide weights equally distant from this center, but will instead have a surface equidistant from this center.

Now if it is as has been said, it is possible—the center of the world being situated in the water—that on some occasion, through the constant friction the water creates in the springs through which it passes, it may have so widened these springs that the part of the earth positioned between them, exhausting the tenacity of the rest, brings it about that the weight it has acquired by being above the water has detached itself from the remainder and fallen toward the center, making this point concentric with its center of gravity. Because of this, the rest of the earth, having made itself lighter by that part from which the said weight fell, will of necessity move away from the center of the world; and the earth and the mountains, lightened by this part, will emerge out of the sphere of the water and will also make themselves lighter by the weight of the water that rested upon them, and will rise even further toward the sky. The sphere of the water in this case does not change its position, because its water fills up the place from which the weight of that part of the earth that fell detached itself; and thus the sea remains as it was without a change in height. This may also be the reason why the marine shells and oysters seen in the high mountains, which were formerly beneath the salt waters, are now found at such a great height, together with the stratified rocks once formed of layers of mud carried by the rivers into the lakes, swamps, and seas; and in this process there is nothing contrary to reason.

Given a perfectly smooth surface, the water will not rest upon it; given a spherical surface, the water will instantly rest there, and this sphericity will be the sphere of the water.

The strata or layers of stone do not continue to any great distance underneath the roots of the mountains because they are made of earth used for making vessels and are full of shells; also, these go only a short distance below because one finds ordinary earth there.
