The revolving movements are driven toward the bank of the less powerful stream, which, as it burrows down with its two types of motion—namely, the straight and the revolving—hollows out the base of the banks. The upper parts, which were supported by these bases, fall headlong as their foundations crumble and are worn away again by this eddying motion.

When the currents of the waters are unequal, these waters circle around as they meet; the less powerful stream enters with the branches of its lower eddies beneath those of the upper eddies created by the more powerful stream.

When the water of greater power strikes the water of less power, the line of eddies describes a curve, entering in a convex shape into the body of the water of greater power.

C.A. 77 r. b
When the curving line of the eddies enters with its convexity into the water of less power, this water remains within its limits without moving; at this stage, it swells up, raises itself, and acquires weight. Because of the weight it has acquired, its power multiplies and it makes headway against the water that initially overcame it, so that the line of eddies curves in the opposite direction and becomes concave where it was formerly convex. Thus, the lesser water is often driven by the greater and the greater by the lesser, but the lesser is driven farther in proportion to its lack of power.¹

## WHY THE CURRENT FROM SPAIN IS ALWAYS GREATER TOWARD THE EAST THAN TOWARD THE WEST

The reason is that if you were to gather together the mouths of all the rivers that flow into the Mediterranean Sea, you would find that their total volume of water is greater than what this sea pours back through the straits into the ocean. You can see that Africa discharges into this sea those of its rivers that flow north, including the Nile—which waters three thousand miles of Africa—as well as the river Bragada <note>original: "Bragada"; likely the Medjerda River in modern-day Tunisia</note>, the Mauretanus <note>original: "Mauretanus"; likely referring to the rivers of ancient Mauretania in Northwest Africa</note>, and others like them. 

Europe pours into it the Don and the Danube, the Po and the Rhone, the Arno and the Tiber. It is clear, therefore, that these rivers, along with an infinite number of lesser-known rivers, create a greater breadth, depth, and current than can be found in the eighteen miles of the ocean straits <note>the Strait of Gibraltar</note> that divide Europe from Africa at their western ends. 

If you were to argue that the rivers emptying into the ocean behave differently, it is certain that almost all the aforementioned rivers originate in mountains near this ocean. If those mountains emptied the rivers directly into the ocean, no river in that vicinity would have a current as great as the Nile or the Danube. Furthermore, even if they were similar, consider that these rivers provide very little increase when emptying into the ocean to restore an eastward current. This is true unless the clouds always contain a greater volume of water than the rivers provide; when these clouds become constricted, they compress the air with swift movement within the surrounding air. It is like a hand squeezing a water-soaked sponge while it is submerged in other water, so that the water that is pushed away makes room for the rest.

Water moves within water as easily as air moves within air, although it is more... <unclear>t...</unclear> as seen in its ripples <note>original: "circles"</note>.

A current only exists in seas that connect with the ocean. The Caspian Sea and swamps have no current. While the Indian Ocean flows eastward, the western Mediterranean flows westward.
<margin>Codex Atlanticus 215 v. d</margin>

Write to Bartolomeo the Turk <note>likely an informant or traveler known to Leonardo</note> about the ebb and flow of the Black Sea, and ask whether he knows if there is the same ebb and flow in the Hyrcanian or Caspian Sea <note>Hyrcania was an ancient name for the region south of the Caspian Sea</note>.
<margin>Codex Atlanticus 260 r. a</margin>

### ON THE CONSUMPTION OR EVAPORATION OF THE WATER OF THE MEDITERRANEAN SEA

The Mediterranean Sea, a vast river positioned between Africa, Asia, and Europe, gathers within itself about three hundred principal rivers; in addition to these, it receives the rains that fall upon it over a span of three thousand miles. It returns its own waters and the others it has received back to the mighty ocean, and without doubt, it returns less to the sea than what it receives; for from it descend many springs that flow through the bowels of the earth and give life to this terrestrial machine. This is necessary because the surface of this Mediterranean is further from the center of the world than the surface of the ocean, as is proved by my second rule; furthermore, the heat of the sun is continually evaporating a portion of the water of the Mediterranean. Consequently, this sea gains very little increase from the aforementioned rains, and is only slightly diminished by the added water being poured into the ocean, or by it being evaporated by the heat of the sun or the path of the parching winds.

The watery sphere desires perfect roundness, and any part that projects above its general surface cannot last, but in a short time becomes level. If you should wish for the water to be drawn aside to allow space for the earth and uncover it, and for it to remain spherical in this way, it would be impossible; this is because the water flowing from Syria would be low, while at the island of Aritella—which is four hundred miles away from the Strait of Gibraltar—it would be the high sea. This island is three thousand four hundred miles away from the shores of Syria, and at this island the water is very shallow, and beyond it, little depth is to be found.

Amboise has a royal fountain which has no water.

## Why there is water in the high parts of the mountains:

From the Straits of Gibraltar to the Don River is three thousand five hundred miles; that is to say, a distance of one mile and one-sixth, allowing a descent of one *braccio* per mile for all water that moves at a moderate speed. ### BRIDGE OF PERA AT CONSTANTINOPLE

Width forty braccia, height above the water seventy braccia, length six hundred braccia—that is, four hundred over the sea and two hundred resting on land, thus forming its own abutments.¹

In Romagna, where all the dullards congregate, they use carts with four equal wheels, or they have two low ones in front and two high ones behind; and this is a great hindrance to movement because more weight rests upon the front wheels than upon those behind, as I have shown in the first part of the fifth book of ‘Concerning Elements’.

And these front wheels move less easily than the large ones, so that to increase the weight in front is to diminish the power of movement and thus double the difficulty.

[*Diagram*]

Here the larger wheel *a* has three times the leverage of the small wheel; consequently, the small one encounters three times as much resistance, and to add a hundred pounds necessitates adding two hundred more to the small wheel *a*; observe how this works.

## ON THE CUTTING OF ABYLA AND CALPE IN THE STRAITS OF CADIZ

The cutting of Abyla and Calpe in the Straits of Cadiz considerably reduces the rivers that descend from the Alps and flow to the north. This is proven by the fact that before this opening in the mountains of Cadiz was formed, the surface of the Mediterranean Sea was very high and exceeded the height of three-quarters of the Alps. Consequently, the penetration of the sea through the passages and veins of the earth was very high and abundant. After this cutting at Cadiz, the surface of the Mediterranean Sea was lowered, and the aforementioned high passages were emptied of their waters, causing the rivers to lose the abundance of their streams. B.M. 168 v.

[With drawings]

When two rivers intersect, the one with the slower current will be shallower.

When Rifredi *b* meets the sluggish Arno, the Arno raises its bed, and the current of Rifredi wears it away, creating a sudden depth. B.M. 271 r.

They do not know why the Arno never stays in its channel. It is because the rivers that enter it deposit soil at their confluence and take

## FOR THE SHRINE OF VENUS

You should construct steps on four sides to ascend to a plateau formed naturally on the summit of a rock. Let this rock be hollowed out, supported by pillars in front, and pierced beneath by a large portico where water falls into various basins of granite, porphyry, and serpentine within semicircular recesses. Let the water in these basins flow over continually. Facing this portico toward the north, let there be a lake with a small island in the center, and on this island, plant a thick and shady wood.

Let the water at the top of the pillars be poured down into vases.

# XVI

# Atmosphere

> "The air moves like a river and carries the clouds with it, just as running water carries all the things that float upon it."

SURFACE is the name given to the boundaries where bodies meet the air—or, I would rather say, where the air meets bodies. It is what is contained between the body and the air that surrounds it; and if the air makes contact with the body, there is no space to place another body there. Consequently, it may be concluded that a surface has no physical substance and therefore requires no physical space.

Surface is the name given to that which divides bodies from the air surrounding them; or, as you may prefer to say, that which divides or separates the air from the things located within it.

And if the atmosphere and the bodies enclosed within it are in perpetual contact and there is no space between them, the surface—being that which reveals the shape of the bodies—exists in its own right. And if the atmosphere and the body are touching each other, no space will remain there; so we conclude that the surface exists, but space does not. Consequently, this surface is equal to nothing, and all the nothingness of the world is equal to the smallest part, if such a part can exist. Therefore, we may say that surface, line, and point are equal to one another, and each is in itself equal to the other two joined together.

Surface is the name of that division which the body of the air makes with the bodies enclosed within it. It does not share the substance of the body by which it is surrounded, nor that of the body it surrounds; on the contrary, it is the actual contact these bodies make with each other.

Therefore, if these bodies are in continual contact, it is necessary that nothing should come between them, and consequently the surface,

--- Page 381 ---
which is enclosed there, is nothing. This surface has a name but no substance, because that which has substance occupies space. Not occupying space, it resembles nothingness, which has a name without substance; consequently, since a part of nothing has nothing except the name and not the substance, this part is equal to the whole. Thus, we conclude that the point and the line are equal to the surface.

### ELEMENT OF FIRE. MIDDLE REGION OF THE ATMOSPHERE

The atmosphere positioned between fire and water shares the qualities of both water and fire, but it shares more of one than the other depending on which it is closer to. It follows that the less it shares the qualities of each, the more remote it is from them. This remoteness occurs in the middle region of the atmosphere; therefore, this middle region is in the primary state of cold. From this, it follows that the part of the cloud in closest contact with the middle region becomes the coldest. Consequently, the warmth of the sphere of fire acting upon this cloud—which is the attractor and mover—has less power, and from this it follows that the movements of the moisture particles forming the clouds are slower. It follows then that as these moisture particles rise, the closer they come to the vicinity of this middle region, the slower their movement becomes; the movement of the moisture following them is swifter, and consequently it overtakes them. It often happens that it strikes from underneath and mingles with the moisture above, thus increasing its quantity and weight. The atmosphere, being unable to support it, gives way and allows it to descend; in doing so, it strikes all the drops that obstruct its path and incorporates many into itself. By acquiring weight, it acquires velocity in its descent. This is the reason why, after it has penetrated the entire cloud, its pace will become slower at every stage of its descent, and there will be many occasions when these particles will not reach the ground. If, however, these particles at their greatest height acquire so much gravity that their weight produces a swift descent, then without doubt this movement will increase their size, as this speed will cause them to overtake the drops which are—

--- Page 382 ---
scending below it and incorporate them into itself, and this will bring about an increase of weight at every stage of its descent.

The descent of the drops which strike together without wind will not be straight but at an angle.

This is proved by the fact that if two bodies strike one another in the air, the one which is smaller in bulk will be diverted more from its course.

And if two particles of dew or of quicksilver varying in size become joined together, each will be moved from its position, and the proportion of their movements will be according to their size.

The drop of that liquid is of the most perfect roundness which is of less . . . 

Why, if two spherical liquids unequal in quantity come into contact with each other, does the greater draw the lesser to itself and incorporate it immediately without destroying the perfection of its own roundness?

It is difficult to give an answer; but I will not for this reason refrain from stating my opinion. Water surrounded by atmosphere naturally desires to be united in its sphere, because in such a position it is deprived of gravity, which gravity is double; for the whole has a gravity which depends on the center of the elements, and there is a second gravity dependent on the center of this watery sphere. For if it were not so, it would form by itself only a half-sphere, which is that which stands from the center upwards; and I do not perceive that the human intellect has any means of acquiring perception of this except by saying, as one says of the action of the magnet when it draws iron, that such power is a hidden property of which there are an infinite number in nature.

But it may be asked why there is greater perfection in the small sphere of the liquid than in the large one. To this the reply is that the small drop has a lightness which more resembles the atmosphere that surrounds it than the large drop has, and because of this small difference, it is more sustained from its center downwards by this atmosphere than the large drop. And as a proof of this, one may take as an instance the small drops which are so small in shape as to be almost invisible by themselves, but which are visible when there are a large

--- Page 383 ---
quantity together; and these are the particles which go to form clouds and mist.

Why the atmosphere, when it has been submerged, rises enveloped in a sheet of water which settles on its surface in the shape of a hemisphere.

And if it is slimy water, it moves through the atmosphere in the form of a sphere.
[Drawing] Bubble or rather vesicle of water.

You will perform an experiment with these water bubbles which, when placed over a little water in a basin, produce images in the shape of a cross on the bottom of this basin by means of the solar rays.

Air and fire are capable of an infinite amount of compression, as is seen with mortars and thunderbolts.

The body of the air is filled with an infinite number of radiant pyramids formed by the objects situated within it; these pyramids, intersecting and interweaving without displacing one another, blend together in their separate courses throughout the whole of the surrounding air. They are of equal power, and all have as much capacity as each one, and each has as much as all; through them, the image of the body is carried entirely into the whole and entirely into a part, and each receives within itself, in its every smallest part, the whole cause.

The movement of the thunderbolt which originates in the cloud is curved because it bends from thickness to thinness, this thickness being caused by the fury of the aforementioned movement. Since this thunderbolt is unable to extend in the direction in which it began, it bends into the path that is freest and proceeds along it until it has created a second obstacle; following this rule, it continues on to the end.

Why flame does not occur except above some space where there is smoke, and why it does not strike except through its smoke. This happens because the flames, as they strike the air, divide into pyramids connected by ends which curve concavely and not convexly; air within water does the same.

# ATMOSPHERE

The fact that the atmosphere attracts to itself—like a magnet—all the images of the things surrounding it, including not only their physical shapes but also their essential nature, is clearly visible in the case of the sun. The sun is a hot and luminous body, and all the atmosphere exposed to its influence is filled in every part with light and heat; the air receives within itself the form of the source of this radiance, doing so even in its smallest parts. The North Star <note>original: "north star"</note> is shown to have a similar influence by the way it affects the needle of a compass, and each of the planets acts in the same way without losing any of its own substance <note>original: "diminution"</note>.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, 138 v. b</margin>
Among the products of the earth, the same phenomenon is found to occur with musk and other scents.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, 162 r. a</margin>
A cloud, carried by the warmth trapped within it, thrusts itself toward [ . . . . ] the disc of fire <note>The "disc of fire" likely refers to the sun or the "sphere of fire" theorized in Renaissance cosmology to exist above the atmosphere.</note>. When it reaches the cold region of the air, it is frozen on the outside but not on the inside, because the internal warmth that carried it upward protects it from the cold. This leads to three results: 

First is the evaporation of moisture; after being trapped by the cold, it separates and dissolves into vapor, which produces a raging wind. 

Second is the production of rain through the accumulation of moist vapor particles. The fast-moving particles, driven by heat, collide with those moving more slowly. As they encounter the part of the cloud that grows cold at its edges, these moisture particles bond together and gain weight, eventually falling to earth as large drops. 

Finally, at the very edge of this cloud, the moisture particles are continually freezing into balls of various sizes. These cannot expand because of the intense cold, but they come together with swift movement at the point where the sphere of the drop is formed. Therefore, hail is composed of [ . . . . ] many rounded shapes joined together.

The elements are transformed into one another. When air is changed into water by contact with the cold region, it furiously attracts all the surrounding air. This air moves violently to fill the vacuum <note>original: "place vacated"</note> left by the air that has escaped. In this way, one mass of air moves in succession behind another, until they have in part...

equalized the space from which the air has been divided, and this is the wind.

But if water is changed into air, then the air which first occupied the space into which the aforementioned increase flows must necessarily yield its place in speed and momentum to the air which has been produced, and this is the wind.

The mist that is in the wind is produced by heat, and it is struck and banished by the cold; this cold drives it forward, and where it has been driven away, the warmth is left cold. And because the mist which is driven cannot turn upward because of the cold that presses it down, and cannot turn downward because of the heat that raises it up, it therefore becomes necessary for it to move horizontally. For my part, I consider that it has no movement of its own, for as the said forces are equal, they confine the middle substance equally; and should it happen to escape, the fugitive is dispersed and scattered in every direction, just like a sponge filled with water which is squeezed so that the water escapes from the center of the sponge in every direction. In this way, therefore, the north wind becomes the producer of all the winds at one and the same time.

### [Of winds]

The north wind comes to us from high and frozen places and therefore it cannot give off moisture; consequently, it is pure and clean because it is cold and dry. For this reason, it is very light in itself, but its speed makes it powerful wherever it strikes.

The south wind does not have the same purity; since it is warm and dry, it dissolves the density of the watery vapors which the Mediterranean Sea exhales. These then follow in the wake of this wind and become dissolved in it; for this reason, as this wind strikes Europe, it becomes warm, damp, and heavy in its nature. Although its movement is sluggish, its impact is no less powerful than that of the north wind.

Every wind is by nature cold and dry, but it takes on as many different attributes as there are places through which it passes, leaving behind dampness and cold in dry and hot places, and taking from these same hot, dry places their dryness and heat. Thus, in its movement through each region, it takes on different attributes.

--- Page 386 ---
and in becoming warm and dry it weakens its power, and in resuming the things it had left behind it resumes the aforementioned forces along with them; for when the speed of movement is the same, the object of greater weight will produce a greater impact, and conversely, the lighter object will produce a lesser impact.

When the sun returns to the regions of Africa in summer, the humidity that had increased there during the winter dissolves and its volume expands, furiously seeking space to contain this increase. This is the south wind, which in autumn drives the maritime vapors of the Mediterranean before it and condenses them over our regions, until they fall back down because they lack the power to sustain themselves.

When many winds struggle together, the waves of the sea do not have a free course, but instead clash together and rise up, at times causing ships to sink; in such a contest, the stronger wind will be the victor because it is lighter and less intertwined or mingled with the other winds.

All objects have all their images and likenesses projected and mingled together throughout the entire extent of the surrounding atmosphere. The image of every point of their physical surfaces exists in every point of this atmosphere, and all the images of the objects are in every point of this atmosphere. Both the whole and a part of the likeness of the atmosphere exist in every point of the surface of the objects facing it. Therefore, the part and the whole of the images of the objects appear in all and in each part of the atmosphere opposite to them; and the substance of the atmosphere is seen reflected in the whole and in each part of the surface of these objects. Therefore, we may clearly say that the likeness of each object, either in whole or in part, is interchangeably in each part and in the whole of the objects opposite to it, as is seen with mirrors when placed opposite one another.

Those winds which, in descending, scour the parts of the mountains that lean toward the sea, penetrate to its bed and create waves with sides that resemble the shores from which they descend; consequently, these waves often have deep, narrow spaces between them, as I stated in the book on the movement of water. And this tempest lasts only a

<header>ATMOSPHERE</header>

For a short time after the wind strikes, it leaps back into the air until it finds another wind; striking against this, it compresses the air and leaps downward again, in the same manner as rivers do when they strike against their shores.

The wind is of great density on the summits of the mountains and in the mouths of valleys, especially when the mountains that enclose these valleys are of great height. The entry of opposite winds, one beneath the other with contrary movements, may occur for two reasons: either through the <term>reflex movement</term> <note>rebound or reflected motion</note> of the wind which turns back after having struck the mountains, or by clashing together when the weaker parts of opposing winds strike against the stronger parts. 

The revolutions or eddies of the winds are born as the winds spread out within the embrace of the mountains or a building; afterward, they join together and strike with great force. Their rebounding movements are not made in a straight line, for the wind is checked within its own sphere, being moved by a substance like itself <note>air</note> which has the power to check and bend its direct momentum. Therefore, since this wind is unable to extend further, it proceeds to exhaust its impulse by a [curving] movement; it moves upwards in order to dissipate its momentum. This is necessary for three reasons:
1. Because it cannot immediately turn back along the exact lines of its descent.
2. Because the winds strike at angles less than right angles.
3. Because they cannot leap back on lines equal to those of their <term>incidence</term> <note>the angle at which the wind hits the surface</note>.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 180 v. a</margin>
### [*Cloud, wind and thunderbolt*]

Just as water flows in different directions out of a squeezed sponge, or air from a pair of bellows, so it is with the thin, transparent clouds that have been driven up to a height through the upward reflection caused by heat. The first part of the cloud that reaches the top is the first to arrive at the cold region of the sky; here, it remains because of the cold and dryness and awaits its companion parts. That lower part of the cloud, as it ascends toward the stationary part above, treats the air trapped in the center as though it were a syringe. This air then escapes sideways and downwards; it does not go upwards because it finds the cloud above so thick that it cannot penetrate it.

For this reason, all the winds that wage war upon the earth's surface come down from above, and as they strike upon the resisting earth...

they produce a rebounding movement, and as this movement seeks to rise back up to a height, it encounters the other wind, which descends and suppresses its ascent. Because of this, the upward movement is forced to break its natural order, and taking a sideways path, it follows a violent course that constantly grazes the surface of the earth.

And when the aforementioned winds strike the salt waters, their form is clearly visible in the angle created by the line of impact and the line of the rebound, from which arise the proud, menacing, and engulfing waves, where one is for the most part the cause of the other.

At this point, someone might perhaps think to criticize me by arguing against my claim regarding the winds, saying that they cannot be produced by the clouds because it would then be necessary for one cloud to remain stationary while setting another in motion; and this does not appear to be the case, because when the north wind blows, the clouds all gather together and fly before it. The reply to this is that when the air is still and a full mass of clouds has risen to a height, and there above—as has been said—they press themselves together, they squeeze out so much air from within themselves that the force exerted creates such movement in the air that, as you can see, it communicates its motion to the other smaller clouds. And as they also drive the air forward in the same way, they even provide themselves with a reason for faster flight; for when a cloud is either in the midst of others or apart from them, if it produces the wind behind itself, the air between it and the following neighbor increases, and by increasing, it acts in the same way as gunpowder does in a mortar, for this expels the less heavy body and the lighter weight from the position near it. And this being the case, it follows that the cloud, in driving the wind toward the others that offer resistance, is the cause of putting those clouds themselves to flight. And by sending this vanguard of winds before itself, it also adds volume to the rest. And if it should send them sideways, it would form a kind of rotating circle around some cloud and then return in unison with the others.

Just as the natural warmth spread through the human limbs is driven back by the surrounding cold, which is its opposite and enemy, and flowing back to the lake of the heart and the liver fortifies itself there, making of these its fortress and defense, so the clouds, being made up

... of warmth and moisture, and in summer of certain dry vapors; finding themselves in the cold, dry region, they act like certain flowers and leaves which, when attacked by the cold hoar-frost, press themselves close together to offer greater resistance.

So these vapors, in their first contact with the cold air, begin to resist and do not wish to pass further forward. As others from below continue to rise constantly, the upper part—being stationary—begins to thicken. The warmth and dryness recede to the center, and the part above, abandoned by the warmth, begins to freeze—or to express it more exactly, to dissolve <note>In this context, Leonardo likely refers to condensation or the transition of vapor into precipitation.</note>. As the clouds below continue to rise, their warmth is brought nearer to the cold; thus, being forced to reduce itself to its primary element <note>In the Aristotelian physics of the time, "fire" was considered a primary element that naturally rose above the air.</note>, it is suddenly transformed into fire. This fire twines itself among the dry vapors and, in the center of the cloud, creates a great expansion. As it kindles itself within the cloud which has become cool, it makes a noise resembling water falling on boiling pitch or oil, or molten copper when plunged into cold water. In this same way, driven forth by its opposite <note>The "opposite" being the cold, wet cloud surrounding the hot, dry fire.</note>, it shatters the cloud that would withstand it, and hurtling through the air, it breaks and destroys everything that opposes it; and this is the thunderbolt. <margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 212 verso, column a</margin>

The air is compressible to infinity, and this is shown by the extremely swift movement of the radiance <note>original: "splendore"; here referring to the flash of lightning</note> which produces the mighty thunder of the heavens, which bends and twists itself in different directions as much as the air and cloud before it are compressed and...

### *Example of thunder*

The process of evaporation of water thrown upon burning coals is the same as that of the fire kindled among the clouds, which evaporate with such fury as to restrict the course of the brightness that has been created. That is to say, just as water is changed into vapor and becomes steam as it increases, so the cloud evaporates and is changed into air. By its increase, this air hems in and restricts the flame that is produced within it. <margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 213 recto, column a</margin>

Flame has its beginning and end in smoke. The smoke out of which the flame is produced is of much greater heat than the smoke in which this flame ends, because in the first...

The blue smoke represents the movement of the material fuel—that is, the grease within the candle. The white smoke surrounding the remains of the flame is the "spiritual" <note>In Leonardo’s time, "spiritual" often referred to refined, invisible, or gaseous substances, as opposed to "material" solids or liquids.</note> movement of the candle’s flame. Write about why the bell tower <term>campanile</term> shakes at the sound of its bells.

Southern winds are more powerful in northern regions than in southern ones, and stronger in summer than in winter. This happens because the sun evaporates <note>original: "dissolves"</note> all the moisture rising from the Mediterranean Sea. This moisture cannot evaporate during the cold of winter, when very few vapors rise, and those that do are turned into rain. However, when the sun passes the equinox <note>The time of year when day and night are of equal length, marking the transition between seasons.</note>—bringing winter here and summer to the other hemisphere—the sun evaporates all the vapors as they rise. These vapors then travel in "aerial waves" as far as the major mountains of Europe. There, meeting the autumn cold, they turn into rain; in winter, they are frozen <note>original: "knit together"</note> into snow and fall during snowstorms, which gradually stifle the strength <note>original: "breath"</note> of these winds.

The bottom part of the flame is the very beginning of the fire, through which all its fuel of fat passes; and this part is as much lower in heat than the rest of the flame as it is lower in brightness. It is blue in color and is the area where its fuel is purified and processed.

That part has the brighter flame, and this is the first to come into existence when the flame is created. It begins in a spherical shape, and after a brief moment, it produces above itself a very small flame, radiant in color and shaped like a heart with its point turned toward the sky. This proceeds to multiply continuously toward infinity by acquiring the substance that feeds it.

The blue flame is formed in a spherical shape because its heat is not great enough to exceed the lightness of the air; for this reason, it does not naturally form a pyramid shape, but remains spherical until it has sufficiently warmed the surrounding air. Because the primary warming of the air occurs above the main heat of this blue flame—this heat being produced in the area where the flame’s natural impulse is to move, which is toward the sphere of fire by the shortest path—the fire therefore comes into existence in the upper part of the blue spherical flame in a small round shape. The roundness of this shape immediately undergoes some extension and assumes the shape of a heart, the point of which is turned toward the sky. This shape immediately and with swift expansion overcomes the power that feeds it and penetrates the air that serves as its covering. But this blue color remains at the base of the flame, as can be seen in the light of a candle; this happens because the flame is always less warm in this position than elsewhere, since it is the first point of contact between the fuel and the flame. It is there that the first heat is produced, and it is feebler and causes less warmth because it is only the beginning of the heat. . . .

A wind will have a shorter movement if it has a more violent beginning; fire has taught us this as it bursts forth from mortars, for it shows us the form and speed of the movement in the smoke as it penetrates the air in front of it in a brief and spreading revolution.

--- Page 392 ---
But the force of the wind is fitful, as is shown by the dust that it raises in the air in its various twists and turns. One also perceives in the chains of the Alps how the clashing together of the winds is caused by the momentum of various forces. One sees also how the flags of ships flutter in different ways; how on the sea one part of the water is struck and not another; and the same thing happening in the squares and on the sandbanks of the rivers, where the dust is swept together furiously in one part and not in another. And since these effects give us experience of the nature of their causes, we can say with certainty that the wind which has the more violent origin will have the shorter movement, based on the experience referred to above regarding the brief movement of smoke from the mouth of a mortar. And this arises from the resistance that the air makes upon being compressed by the impact of this smoke, which also itself, as has been clearly seen, shows compression when it offers resistance to the wind. But if the wind is of slow movement, it will extend a long way in a straight course, because the air penetrated by it will not become condensed in front of it and thus thwart its movement, but will readily expand, spreading its course over a very great space.

## OF EDDYING WINDS

When a wind has been divided by mountains or other structures, if upon coming together again it should assume the shape of a rectangle, the movement which it makes after this reunion will be of a rotatory nature in the shape of a twisted column; and if the winds which are thus reunited should be equal, then this column will not change its position; but if the winds are unequal, the column will move in the direction of the weaker wind.

Fire or other heat lightens moisture and makes it lighter than the air; for which cause this moisture rises to the middle region of the air, and finding there the maximum cold of the air, the fire or heat infused through this cloud flies towards the center, and there becoming strong, separates the moist vapor from the dry; and it is for this reason that the fire becomes kindled there and turns into steam a great part of the moisture which is round about this fire. Whether the wind is caused within the air, it cannot make any movement unless it is supported in the place where it resists by the opposite side of the movement, as is seen to be the case with the rays driven by fire; for through the percussion that the fire makes against the air which offers some resistance to it, these fly more slowly than this fire; and if this were not the case, such a ray would be without movement.

Further we may say: the wind moves in a straight line and not in a circular line as Aristotle would have it; and we learn this from the movement of a storm at sea when there is no wind, for it is a sign that such wind follows its straight line, leaving the curve of the sea below it.

Why the clouds are formed with various round shapes which are separated at different distances from one another:

The movements of the air spring from the dispersal and collection of moisture.

Heat separates and disperses, and cold assembles and freezes or condenses.

## OF THE DROPS THAT FORM IN THE AIR

Drops are formed in the air through mists or clouds by various movements, such as when they encounter each other and become condensed, or unite during the movement of the same cloud in the same direction when one part of the cloud is swifter or slower than the other; for as the swifter part is behind the slower, it overcomes it in its course and overtakes it, condensing it and making one large drop out of many small ones, and this acquires weight and falls. But unless the drops are formed so as to be of considerable size, they are consumed by the friction they make with the air as they traverse it.

The moist wind which is found in caverns that have both an entrance and an exit can produce water, and this especially when these caverns have twisted and irregular sides; but this production of water is not permanent in its effect, for when the wind is lacking the supply ceases, and if a contrary wind should enter by the opposite mouth of

Concerning the four elements and two . . .

1. A stone thrown into water becomes the center of various circles, and these have as their center the spot that was struck.
2. In the same way, the air is filled with circles, the centers of which are the sounds and voices created within them.

How the various circles of water form around the spot that has been struck by the stone:

Where the stone strikes the surface of the water, it creates circles around itself that expand until they fade away. Similarly, the air—when struck by a voice or a noise—moves outward in a circular way and eventually dissipates, so that those nearby perceive it better, while those further away hear it less.

The quintessence is infused through the air just as the element of fire is, although each of these may have its purpose within itself or through itself; and since every particle is supplied with nutritive matter, it acquires growth and an increase of form; and if the nourishment is taken away from them, they suddenly abandon this body and return to their original nature.

The air is entirely present in the whole and entirely present in its image in the part positioned opposite it.

If there is no opaque body within the air, the whole of it has a capacity that extends over the whole and over the part, and the part has a capacity that extends over the part and over the whole.

Therefore, we may say that the air is entirely intertwined within itself, and is filled with the infinite rays of the images of the bodies situated within it; and this air is full of an infinite number of points, and every point is indivisible; and the parts of this indivisibility of all the images of the parts of bodies positioned opposite them have capacity, and in these points they are entirely united and entirely divided and separated without confusion from one another.

And the pyramids of the images are spread throughout the whole of this air without occupying each other's space, each existing for itself, and they are all divided through the whole and united through the whole.

And although the images approach the eye in the form of pyramids, the eye is not conscious of this unless it forms a pyramid opposite to the object seen.

Just as a stone thrown into the water becomes the center and cause of various circles, and a sound made in the air spreads itself out in circles, so every body placed within the luminous air spreads itself out in circles and fills the surrounding parts with an infinite number of images of itself, and appears entirely in the whole and entirely in each smallest part.

## OF COLD

I say that cold proceeds from two causes: the first is from the air being deprived of heat; the second is from the movement of the air. The air of itself is cold and dry and it is void of all matter or vapors, and it changes readily—or to put it more exactly, steeps itself in the nature and image of the things which touch it and which it has oppo-

Now, to return to this question of cold, I say that just as the many rays of a concave mirror converging at one point produce an extreme of heat, even so many bellows blowing on the same point produce an extreme cold.

### [*Concerning visibility*]

Naturally, if men wish to know whether the rain has started, they look into the air that is between the eye and some dark place; then the fine threads, which the minute drops of water cause to appear in the air as they are lit up, are easily visible against a dark background. But men judge the threads that are nearby and first as though they were the last and almost touched the dark place, not perceiving that this dark place is sometimes so remote that it would not even be possible to see a neighboring tower there.

The colors of the middle of the rainbow mingle with each other. The bow itself is neither in the rain nor in the eye that sees it, although it is produced by the rain, the sun, and the eye.

The rainbow is invariably seen by the eye which is situated between the rain and the body of the sun; consequently, when the sun is in the east and the rain is in the west, the rainbow is produced upon the western rain.

## OF THE POWER OF A VACUUM FORMED INSTANTANEOUSLY

I saw at Milan a thunderbolt strike the Torre della Credenza on its northern side. It traveled along it with a slow movement and then all at once parted from the tower, carrying with it and tearing away a part of the wall three <term>braccia</term> in breadth and length and two in depth. The wall was four <term>braccia</term> in width and was built of old bricks which were thin and small. It was torn away through the vacuum caused by the flame of the thunderbolt. ### OF THE WIND

The air moves like a river and carries the clouds with it, just as running water carries everything that floats upon it. This is proven because if the wind were to push through the air and drive the clouds, those clouds would be compressed <note>original: "condensed"</note> between the air and the moving force. They would take a lateral impression from the two opposing ends, just as wax does when pressed between the fingers.

### OF THE MOVEMENT OF AIR

Air moves when it is drawn away to fill a vacuum, or when it is driven by the expansion <note>original: "rarefaction"</note> of the moisture <note>original: "humidity"</note> in the clouds.

[*Reflex course of wind and water*]
The reflected <note>original: "reflex"</note> wind, as it turns back upon its course, weakens the oncoming wind until this reflected wind itself becomes feeble. It then regains its force when it joins with the downward movement. Such power arises from the compression <note>original: "condensation"</note> it acquires at the point of impact <note>original: "percussions"</note>. This compression always penetrates into the descending wind up to the point where it separates and its speed of movement decreases.
Water behaves the same way; however, this is not due to compression, but because it rises in the air and gains weight.

Why do the northern winds begin to blow at the winter solstice and continue until gloomy January?

At the winter solstice, which is in the middle of December, the northern winds are at their greatest strength.

### HOW THE WIND THAT STRIKES THE CLOUD ON ONE SIDE MAKES IT ROTATE

If the wind strikes the cloud on one side only, then even though its opposite side is in still air, this cloud will be driven forward and rotated; it will move in a circle like a mill wheel turned by water.

### WHAT CAUSES THE CLOUDS TO INCREASE IN HEIGHT?

When the movement of two opposing winds causes two clouds to collide, these clouds then merge into one another. Since they are unable to expand or descend because of the wind passing beneath them, these clouds extend in the direction where their path is least obstructed, which is upward.

### ON THE MEETING OF TWO CLOUDS MOVING DIFFERENTLY IN THE SAME PATH

When two clouds meet while driven by the same wind, the larger one—having a greater share of the more powerful wind—covers the smaller one. The two become condensed at their point of contact, and this causes rain.

If wind is created by an excess or lack of air, the southern regions that separate the humidity drawn to them begin to condense. Being unable to contain such an accumulation, they drive it back; it is then drawn by the vacuum created in the cold region where this humidity contracts to form clouds, or in the southern regions where other clouds are formed.

## ON THE SPEED OF CLOUDS

The movement of a cloud is inherently less swift than that of its shadow moving across the earth. This is proven as follows: Let *e* be the sun, *a* the cloud, and *c* its shadow. As the cloud moves from *a* to *b*, the shadow will move from *c* to *d*. Since the shadows cast from the earth to the cloud are formed by lines that converge at the center of the sun, we may say according to my fourth rule that this proposition is true. This fourth rule states: equidistant sections across the angle of two converging lines will be smaller the closer they are to the point of intersection. Therefore, as the clouds are closer to the sun than their shadows are, there can be no doubt that the shadow will travel a greater distance over the earth than the cloud travels through the air in the same amount of time.

The atmosphere is blue because of the darkness above it, for black and white together produce blue.

The part of the cloud nearest to the eye will seem faster than the part that is higher; for this reason, they often appear to be moving in opposite directions to one another.

### On the shapes that one element assumes as it penetrates another:

Air falling through fire will turn a mill just as fire issuing through air will; in the same way, air falling through water acts like water through air, or earth falling through water. You should describe the equality of these powers and resistances, and the shapes they assume as they pass through one another.

[Compressed air in rose-water at the barber's]

Whether air can be compressed within itself is demonstrated by the barber's vessel for dispensing rose-water, in which the air is doubled. Fire is quadrupled by the force of a space where it cannot expand.

### ON WATER AND AIR

Air that moves with force within other air is compressed within itself, as is shown in the expansion of solar rays; for if the wind moves their particles in various revolutions, you see these particles form themselves into marbled waves in the manner of watered silks or camlets (*gianbellotti*). What you see happening to these particles is done by the air which carries them enclosed within itself.

Water in such cases cannot be compressed, and since it has all these same movements within its body, it must displace other water from its position so that these movements appear on the surface.

When the sun strikes concave mirrors and reflects from them in a pyramidal path, that part of the pyramid will be proportionately warmer than its base as it is smaller in size; this occurs because its moisture becomes restricted. The hot steam mingled with it becomes more powerful as it is more concentrated, and as it is confined within a smaller space, it generates more heat. Consequently, it often catches fire and grows, forming into a thunderbolt out of the cloud; it then bursts the cloud with devastating lightning and thunder. When the cloud has been contracted by the cold, the small particles of water fasten themselves together and fall because of their weight. In this way, the clouds break up and return as rain to the lower regions.

The surfaces of transparent and polished bodies always reflect the objects that face their surfaces and are faced by them. Therefore, whatever is beneath the water is reflected in the surface of the air that borders that water, and whatever is in the air is reflected in the surface of the water that borders that air.

The course of the winds changes and follows the movement of some other wind because of the mouths of the valleys which it enters and exits; this happens more with low winds than with...

...the high winds, and this it does because it is flexible and able to be bent in any direction except that directly opposite to its course. Desiring to move and give place to the new wind, it must act as water does when it enters a pool in a straight line: it then turns into various channels, but flows more along the line that follows the path of the movement it makes at its entrance, and less along the path farthest away from this entrance.

Wind is compressed <note>original: "condensed"</note> above the places where it strikes, and more so on the summits of mountains than on the sea coasts it visits. This is because all the reflex winds—that is, the rebounding winds—gather there on the summits of the steep sides of the mountains where these winds strike. They do not extend entirely crosswise following the shape of the mountain's summit; instead, many proceed upward in a straight line, especially those that strike nearest the bases of the mountains. However, once they are above the mountain summit, they describe a curve, and after this process of curving, they straighten themselves into the course of the other wind which struck them and which first caused them to curve. <term>British Museum Manuscript, folio 276 recto</term>

### ON THE WIND

There are many times when the course of one wind is diverted into that of another. This arises from the percussion <note>original: "percussion"; the physical impact or collision of two bodies of air</note> which they make when their courses meet; since they are not able to penetrate into one another, necessity constrains them to leap back in opposite directions.

If, however, these winds are not of equal power with one another, their reflex movements will not follow the movement of the wind that struck them. Instead, the angle of percussion of the more powerful wind will be as much greater than that of the less powerful as the excess of the greater power is over the lesser.

Winds which blow in the same direction may be simple or mixed with other winds. That is, along one part of its side, the wind may be quite taut because the free wind strikes it and leaps back at equal angles—but never directly opposite to its source, because it would have to re-enter itself, and the movement of two bodies cannot penetrate within one another. Therefore, it follows that the part of the greater wind which is struck by the lesser wind would turn backward and follow the course of the lesser wind which has struck it, but it encounters it along the...

The same wind, therefore, produces different movements and different degrees of power within itself upon impact. This is because the portion of its width mentioned earlier, which drives forward the part that retreats, also creates a reflected movement against the wind it strikes. The same happens to the part that, when struck, puts the second part to flight, and the fourth part which strikes the third, in such a way that the wind becomes denser in these areas. However, the first density is greater than the last, similar to two streams of water striking one another, as I have demonstrated in the fourth chapter of the seventh book of the elements of mechanics; for an angle is formed at the point of the first impact which makes the water that strikes first leap up more than any other part of it.

### [*Movement of the winds*]

If the movement of the winds originates from Jupiter, the cause of the wind must occur within the twenty-four hours during which Jupiter moves from east to west and not from north to south; this is because an object moved by something else takes on the form and timing of its mover’s movement.

## QUESTIONS: THE MATERIALS WHICH PRODUCE WIND

If the wind is a vapor of the earth characterized by cold and dryness, and is carried by heat, it rises to the cold region of the air; once abandoned by heat, its conductor, it remains there. This is the reason why the vapor—being similar to the vapors in that location, that is to say, cold and dry—leaves that place and vapor, and flees from its own kind. Indeed, having ceased its upward movement and entering a place entirely similar to itself, it is free to remain motionless. And yet, if you grant it movement, it must still move through the cold region on its own. But we shall say that such a vapor, being cold and dry in its slow and late birth, becomes gradually mixed with the heat, and so, through a gradual expansion, it generates an almost imperceptible motion in proportion to this expansion. But the motion of the heat which car-

--- Page 405 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of atmospheric movements, completing the word "carries" from the previous page.</meta>

<page-num>395</page-num>
<header>ATMOSPHERE</header>

carries it upward is swift and guides it as far as the cold region of the air. There, having expelled the first part, the heat that conducted it departs and the vapor diminishes. Without the force <note>original: "wind"</note> provided by the heat previously mixed with it, the vapor—diminished in quantity—grows in weight relative to the air that sustains it. Consequently, it descends below the other vapor. Once it has descended, the heat that was separated from it is reunited with other heat and vapor; this provides an upward movement, raising all the vapor little by little until it chills the upper part that penetrates the cold. Gradually, it falls back due to the weight it has acquired, so that the entire mass becomes heavier than it was before. Thus, it descends in the form of clouds. As it approaches the heat refracted <note>Heat "refracted" or reflected off the earth's surface.</note> by the earth warmed by the sun, it dissolves and expands <note>original: "dilates"</note> with great force; and this is the wind.

The winds descend from above at various angles and, striking the water or the earth, create lateral movements along various lines, much like water penetrating other water.

You say that the movement of an effect follows the movement of its cause; and then you say that the twelve signs of the Zodiac are the cause of the motion of winds. You claim that the three fiery signs—the Ram, the Lion, and the Archer <note>Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius.</note>—belong to the east and move the eastern winds; and that the three cold and dry signs—the Bull, the Virgin, and the Goat <note>Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn.</note>—move the southern winds, and the other three signs move the western winds. This theory leaves the inventor of such causes in confusion, based on the very first proposition you agreed upon: that all bodies in motion follow the movement of their motive force. Now, these signs of the Zodiac move from east to west and circle the world in twenty-four hours. How then do you account for the fact that these signs, which move toward the west, would move the western winds? And yet, these winds should move toward the east, which would be contrary to the motion of their motive force? This contradicts your first assumption (which is true), proving your resulting theory is false.

You say that the vapor which generates the wind is carried upward by heat and pressed down again by cold. If that is so, it follows that this vapor, finding itself caught between two contrary motions, must escape to the sides; and this lateral movement is the wind.

which has a twisting movement because it cannot descend to the earth since the heat pushes it up, and it cannot move very high up because the cold presses it down; therefore, this necessity gives it a sideways and twisting movement. Now many drawbacks will follow from this theory of yours, the first of which is that the wind will never descend to the plain, and secondly that the cold, in being driven down by such a vapor, would be acting contrary to its inert nature.

Then again, it is possible that the vapor which collects in the cold region, by being abandoned by the heat that carries it there, becomes compressed and grows heavier; and the air which formerly supported it no longer resists it, and consequently gives way to it; and this vapor, being heavy, descends rapidly into the hot region near the earth. There it is entirely permeated with heat and consequently completely expanded and dissolved, and it moves in every direction around it and strikes the surface of the sea. And here one can see the cause of the origin of the kind of wind that moves the sea, for it is fleeing from the first place it struck. And in this case, the paths of the parts of this wind are not parallel because they move from the center to the circumference in straight lines.

The gathering of humidity scattered through the air, which comes together for the creation of clouds, creates wind in the air. And similarly, the breaking up of the clouds creates fine and penetrable humidity through the air; and this is the wind. The proof: one may see water boiling over a fire which creates a wind in the chimney above that fire; and again, boiling water which is shut into vessels escapes through little vents in such a vessel with great force in the manner of wind. And again, fires made in small rooms suck in the air through little cracks in the windows with great force and noise.
Windsor: Drawings 12671 v.

The force inherent in moving bodies has the result that movement is often contrary to the nature of the thing moved.

You say that the vapor of the wind is driven up by the heat which lifts it and is then pushed down again by the cold which joins with

--- Page 407 ---
it; and yet necessity gives it a lateral and a curved movement, since being enclosed between two contrary forces, it flies out sideways all over the earth.

But this theory denies that the vapor which has been mixed in the cold region of the air is pushed down by this cold, because it is necessary to say either that the vapor flees from the cold by its nature, or that the cold actually removes it by itself, which would be contrary to the nature of the vapor. And if such a vapor moves on its own, it does so after it has increased and not before, because at first, the power of the heat pressing it down makes itself greater than the power of the vapor which wishes to descend. Here it must be admitted that such a vapor, in increasing, acquires weight, and that with this weight it overcomes the force of the heat which sustains it; and here, cold does not press it down because, if it were natural for such cold to press it down, it would have been easier to expel the vapor when it was small in quantity and weak than when it had increased in quantity and in force. And so here we shall say that the vapor of the wind, having reached the cold region, stops there, because the heat which conducted it to this place is consumed by the cold; and the heat being consumed, the vapor remains without motive force, and so it stays there and awaits the parts which follow and join it. And these, not being at such an altitude, are not yet completely deprived of heat and, consequently, of movement; and so, not being stationary, they move until at last they arrive at the same altitude as the part which has been chilled, and they penetrate this and unite with it, and the heat being condensed there leaves the vapor. And so, subsequently rising one part after the other and penetrating the higher part, they are prevented from condensing, and from that weight of such a nature that the lower region cannot sustain it above itself. Hence, by necessity, it descends united with it until the heat makes it light and again lifts it upwards, and does the same as it did the first time; and so, once more joining with the cold part, it again acquires weight and again sinks down and again turns to vapor in the upper air. And so this would go on continually, and from this arises the motion of the wind spreading itself from high to low and not from here to there [vertically and not horizontally]. Well then, this theory given above is false, because experience shows itself to be in disagreement.

--- Page 408 ---
You say that the winds begin by being weak and continue to grow in strength because, in the beginning, there was only a small quantity of vapor generated by a small blast; but when such vapor has increased to a greater quantity, being struck by the cold, it descends with greater force, and from this arises the growth of the wind. To this we answer that any movement is born of a vacuum or a deficiency. If vapor is raised by heat, even though that heat penetrates it, the heat dissolves such vapor and creates a movement sideways or rather upwards, because that is the true direction of the movement of fire; and as this evaporation rises higher, the more it is compressed, and its exterior moves inward toward the center of the mass. This second movement is contrary to the first, because the first moved from the center to the extremities, and the second movement is from the extremities to the center; and between one and the other, the movement is more rapid in proportion to its distance from the center, because the extremities are more affected by heat and cold than are the parts near the middle. But to return to the matter at hand: the more the vapor rises, the more it is compressed because it draws nearer to the cold, which is the exact opposite of the heat that carries such vapor and compresses it.

This cannot create a wind that flows out from it, but it can create one if it runs contrary to it, because nature does not allow a vacuum; the place from which its parts are fleeing would remain a vacuum if the air did not fill them, and this air rushes to fill the vacuum with the same speed as the vapor when it is rushing away from the cold. And since the material, joined with the motive force that moves it, moves in the same amount of time as the movement made by this motive force, the vapor here will move for as long as the fire, its first motive force, accompanies it; and when the fire is separated from it, the vapor loses its movement. The cold does not give it movement unless it acts against half of its mass, or it may be that the part of the vapor which touches the cold first is the first to rush back toward the center; however, one cannot classify this as actual flight, but rather as the loss of its elevation.

You say that the wind does not blow continuously, but with various gusts separated from one another; and the cause of this is the vapor which rises to the cold, carried by heat in varying quantities. Here one

--- Page 409 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the mechanics of wind and vapor before transitioning into an observation on the blue color of the atmosphere, based on the author's ascent of Monte Rosa.</meta>

One might answer that the cold does not expel the vapor, but rather that the heat escaping from the cold brings back the vapor which it formerly carried into the cold regions. Furthermore, one could say that when heat first comes into contact with cold, it warms the cold in proportion to their contact; similarly, the cold chills the heat as it receives it. This interaction produces a storm, which results in the heat and cold losing some of their original force. In this case, the way is prepared for the transformation into vapor; this vapor, together with the heat, succeeds in penetrating more deeply into the cold and warming it to a greater altitude. 

The vapor penetrates so far that it passes through the cold region and reaches toward the element of fire <note>original: "element of fire" — In the Renaissance worldview, the "element of fire" was believed to be a sphere of heat located above the atmosphere.</note>. Being united with this heat, the vapor creates a massive outburst through all the surrounding regions. These outbursts are rapid movements in straight lines that result in a "flood" of air which strikes the sea above the horizon and provides the solution you seek.

## ON THE COLOR OF THE ATMOSPHERE

I maintain that the blue seen in the atmosphere is not its own intrinsic color. Instead, it is caused by heated moisture that has evaporated into the most minute, imperceptible particles; the solar rays strike these particles, making them appear luminous against the deep, intense darkness of the region of fire <note>original: "region of fire" — Leonardo is describing the phenomenon of Rayleigh scattering, where light hits particles in the air, making the sky look blue against the dark backdrop of space.</note> that forms a covering above them. 

This may be seen—as I myself saw it—by anyone who climbs Mon Boso (Monte Rosa), a peak in the Alpine chain that divides France from Italy. At the base of this mountain, four rivers spring forth and flow in four different directions to water all of Europe. There is no other mountain with a base at so great an elevation.

This mountain towers to such a height that it almost passes above all the clouds. Snow seldom falls there, only hail in the summer when the clouds are at their greatest height. This hail accumulates there, and if it were not for the rarity <gloss>1</gloss> of clouds rising and...

releasing their contents—which does not happen twice in a century—there would be an enormous mass of ice there, built up by various layers of hail. I found this ice to be very thick even in the middle of July. I also observed that the atmosphere was dark overhead, and the sun’s rays striking the mountain were much brighter than in the plains below. This is because there was less thickness of atmosphere between the mountain's summit and the sun.

To further illustrate the color of the atmosphere, consider the smoke produced by old, dry wood. As it exits a chimney, it appears to be a pronounced blue when viewed against a dark background. However, as it rises higher and moves between the eye and the bright atmosphere, it immediately turns into an ashen gray. This happens because it no longer has darkness behind it, but rather the luminous atmosphere. But if this smoke comes from fresh, green wood, it will not look blue. Because it is opaque and heavily saturated with moisture, it behaves like a dense cloud, showing distinct light and shadow as if it were a solid object.

The same principle applies to the atmosphere: excessive moisture makes it look white, while a small amount of moisture affected by heat makes it look dark and deep blue. This explains the atmosphere's color. However, one might also argue that if transparent blue were the atmosphere's natural color, then the sky should appear a deeper blue wherever there is a greater volume of air between the eye and the "element of fire" <note>original: "fiery element" — in the Renaissance worldview, the sphere of heat believed to exist above the atmosphere</note>. This is what happens with blue glass and sapphires, which look darker the thicker they are. 

Under these conditions, the atmosphere behaves in exactly the opposite way. Where there is a greater volume of air between the eye and the sphere of fire (as happens toward the horizon), the sky appears much whiter. Conversely, the less atmosphere there is between the eye and the sphere of fire, the deeper the blue appears, even when we are standing on the low plains. Therefore, I conclude that the atmosphere gains its blue color from particles of moisture that catch the luminous rays of the sun.

We may also observe the difference between the particles <note>original: "atoms"</note> of dust and those of smoke seen in the sun’s rays as they pass through cracks...

We may see also in the dark shadows of mountains far from the eye that the atmosphere which is between the eye and these shadows will appear very blue, and in the portion of these mountains which is in light, it will not vary much from its original color.

But whoever would see a final proof, should stain a board with various different colors, among which he should include a very strong black, and then over them all he should lay a thin transparent white; he will then perceive that the luster of the white will nowhere display a more beautiful blue than over the black—but it must be very thin and finely ground.

Smoke is swift at its beginning and becomes slower at every stage of its ascent, because it becomes colder and heavier, owing to the fact that a great part of it is condensed through the particles striking against each other and being pressed together and made to adhere to one another; and water does the same, for it is swift at the beginning of its movement.

Air, even if it changes its position, preserves the impression of its eddies more than water does, due to the fact of it being swifter and thinner.

An excess of smoke acts as a veil; a small quantity of it does not produce the perfection of this blue: it is by a moderate admixture of smoke, therefore, that the beautiful blue is created.

Experience is what shows how the air has darkness behind it and yet appears blue.

Make smoke of dry wood in a small quantity; let the rays of the sun fall upon this smoke, and behind it place a piece of black velvet, so that it shall be in shadow. You will then see that all the smoke which comes between the eye and the darkness of the velvet will show itself as a very beautiful blue color; and if instead of the velvet you put a white cloth, the smoke will become the color of ashes.

How water blown in the form of spray into a dark place, through which the solar rays pass, produces this blue ray—especially when this water has been distilled—and how the thin smoke becomes blue.

# XVII
## Flight

> "I have divided the *Treatise on Birds* <note>original: *Codice sul volo degli uccelli* (Codex on the Flight of Birds), written around 1505.</note> into four books. The first treats of their flight by beating their wings; the second of flight without beating their wings, aided by the wind; the third of flight in general, including birds, bats, fishes, animals, and insects; the last covers the mechanism of this movement."

<margin>On Flight, folio 4 verso</margin>

Those feathers which are farthest away from their points of attachment will be the most flexible.

Therefore, the tips of the wing feathers will always be higher than their roots. Because of this, we may reasonably say that the wing bones will always be lower than any other part of the wing when it is being lowered. Conversely, when the wing is raised, these bones will be higher than any other part. This is because the heavier part will always lead the movement.

I ask: at what point across the width of the wing's underside does it press against the air more than at any point along the wing's length?

Every rigid body—even if its individual parts vary in size and weight—will place equal weight upon all supports that are equidistant from its center of gravity <note>Leonardo was a pioneer in applying the concept of the center of gravity to aerodynamics.</note>, provided that center is in the middle of the body's width.

However, if the body is flexible and has varying thicknesses and weights, the support nearest the center of gravity (or the heaviest sections) will carry more weight than the supports under the lighter parts, even if the center of gravity is in the middle of its overall size.

A person in a flying machine must be free from the waist up so that they can balance themselves just as one does in a boat, so...

Sul Volo 6 [5] r.
When the bird desires to turn to the right or left side by flapping its wings, it will flap lower with the wing on the side toward which it wishes to turn; thus the bird will pivot its movement following the momentum of the wing that moves more, and performs the reflex movement under the wind from the opposite side.

When the bird desires to rise by flapping its wings, it raises its shoulders and flaps the tips of the wings toward itself, thereby condensing the air that is positioned between the wingtips and the bird's breast, and the pressure from this air lifts the bird up.

The kite and other birds that flap their wings only slightly go in search of the wind current; when the wind is blowing at a high altitude, they may be seen at a great elevation, but if it is blowing low down, then they remain low.

When there is no wind stirring in the air, the kite flaps its wings more rapidly in its flight, in such a way that it rises to a height and acquires momentum; with this momentum, then descending very gradually, it can travel for a great distance without moving its wings.

And when it has descended, it does the same thing again, and so continues many times in succession.

This method of descending without moving the wings serves as a means of resting in the air after the fatigue of the aforementioned flapping of the wings.

Sul Volo 6 [5] v.
All birds that fly in spurts rise to a height by flapping their wings; and during their descent, they proceed to rest themselves, for while descending they do not flap their wings.

### OF THE FOUR REFLEX AND FALLING MOVEMENTS MADE BY BIRDS UNDER DIFFERENT CONDITIONS OF THE WIND

The slanting descent of birds made against the wind will always be made beneath the wind, and their reflex movement will be made upon the wind.

But if this falling movement is made toward the east when the wind is blowing from the north, then the north wing will remain below the wind, and it will do the same during the reflex movement; therefore, at the end of this reflex movement, the bird will find itself facing north.

And if the bird descends toward the south while the wind is blowing from the north, it will make this descent upon the wind, and its reflex movement will be below the wind; but this is a complex question which shall be discussed in its proper place, for here it would seem that it could not make the reflex movement at all.

When the bird makes its reflex movement facing and upon the wind, it will rise much higher than its natural impetus requires, seeing that it is also helped by the wind which enters underneath it and acts like a wedge. But when it is at the end of its ascent, it will have used up its impetus and therefore will depend upon the help of the wind, which, as it strikes it on the breast, would flip it over if it were not for the fact that the bird lowers the right or left wing; for this will cause it to turn to the right or left, dropping down in a half-circle.

### [Of a flying machine]

The movement of the bird ought always to be above the clouds so that the wing does not get wet, and in order to survey more country and to escape the danger caused by the turbulence of the winds among the mountain defiles, which are always full of gusts and wind eddies. And if, moreover, the bird should be overturned, you will have plenty of time to turn it back again following the instructions I have given, before it falls back down to the ground.

If the tip of the wing is struck by the wind and the wind enters underneath the tip, the bird will then find itself liable to be overturned unless it employs one of two remedies; that is, it either suddenly tucks this tip under the wind or lowers the opposite wing from the middle forward.

The bird I have described ought to be able, with the help of the wind, to rise to a great height, and this will prove to be its safety; since even if all the previously mentioned rotations were to happen to it, it would still have time to regain a state of equilibrium; provided that its various parts have great structural resistance, so that they can safely withstand the fury and violence of the descent by using the defenses I have mentioned. Its joints should be made of strong tanned hide and sewn with cords of very strong raw silk. And let no one burden himself with iron bands, for these are very quickly broken at the joints or else they wear out, and consequently, it is best not to be burdened with them.

The cord *a*, intended for extending the wing, ought to be made of thick dressed hide, so that if the bird should be turned upside down, it may be able to resist the fury of the wind which strikes the wing and tries to close it, for this would cause the destruction of the bird. But to make it safer, you should install exactly the same system of cords on the outside as on the inside, and you will then avoid all fear of danger.

*a b c* are the terminating points of the cords from the three joints of the wing's fingers; *d* marks the position of the mechanism that moves the lever *a d*, which moves the wing.

When the edge of the wingtip meets the edge of the wind for a brief moment, this wing places itself either below or above this edge of the wind, and the same happens with the tip and sides of the tail, and likewise with the rudders at the shoulders of the wings.

The descent of the bird will always be led by that extremity which is nearest to its center of gravity.

4th. The heaviest part of the bird that descends headfirst will never remain above or level with the height of its lightest part.
