And if the bird is positioned with its length parallel to the wind, it is liable to be flipped upside down by the wind unless it instantly raises its tail. . . .

How the entire surface of the wing is not used in compressing the air; and for the truth of this, observe how the openings between the primary feathers are much wider spaces than the actual width of the feathers themselves.

You, therefore, who research winged creatures, do not include the entire surface area of the wing in your calculations, and take note of the different characteristics of the wings of all winged creatures.

When the wind strikes the bird during its flight from its center of gravity toward the wind, then the bird will turn with its spine toward the wind; and if the wind were more powerful below than above, the bird would be turned upside down if it were not instantly alert to pull in the lower wing and stretch out the upper wing; and by this means, it rights itself and returns to a position of equilibrium.

This is proven as follows: let *a c* be the wing folded up beneath the bird, and *a b* the extended wing; I say that the forces of the wind striking the two wings will have the same proportion as their extension—that is, *a b* compared to *a c*. It is true that *c* is wider than *b*, but it is so near the bird’s center of gravity that it offers little resistance in comparison with *b*.

But when the bird is struck by the wind beneath one of its wings, it would be possible for the wind to overturn it, were it not for the fact that as soon as it is turned with its breast to the wind, it extends the opposite wing toward the ground and pulls up the wing that was first struck by the wind (which remains uppermost), and thus it returns to a position of equilibrium. This is proven by the fourth [proposition] of the third [book], according to which an object is more easily overcome when it is opposed by a greater force; also by the fifth [proposition] of the third [book].

If a bird wishes to turn itself rapidly to one of its sides and follow a circular path, it will beat its wings twice on that side—moving the wing back like an oar—while keeping the other wing steady, or perhaps making only one beat with it for every two beats of the opposite wing.

Since wings are faster at compressing the air than the air is at escaping from beneath the wings, the air becomes condensed <note>original: "condensata"; Leonardo's way of describing air pressure/density</note> and resists the movement of the wings. The motive power of these wings, by overcoming the resistance of the air, raises itself in a movement contrary to the downward stroke of the wings.

A bird will descend with faster movement when its descent is at a shallower angle.

The descent of a bird will be at a shallower angle when the tips of the wings and the shoulders are brought closer together.

The paths of movement made by birds as they rise are of two kinds: one is always spiral, like a screw, and the other is straight and curved.

A bird will rise to a great height by using a circular, screw-shaped movement; it makes its reflex movement <term>reflex movement: an upward glide powered by the momentum of a previous descent or by the force of the wind</term> against the incoming wind and against the flight of that wind, turning always upon its right or left side.

Thus, if the north wind is blowing and you are rising in a reflex movement, you should glide against that wind until, in this straight process of rising, the wind reaches a state where it might overturn you. At that point, you are free to bank with the right or left wing. By holding the inner wing low, you will pursue a curving movement with the help of the tail, turning in the direction of the lower wing. You will continue descending and pivoting around the wing that is held low until you once again perform the reflex movement upward, heading back into the course of the wind; and when you are...

A bird, as it rises, always positions its wings above the wind without flapping them, and it always moves in a circular motion.

And if you wish to go to the west without flapping your wings when the north wind is blowing, make the downward movement straight and beneath the wind toward the west, and the upward reflex movement above the wind toward the north.

A bird makes the same use of its wings and tail in the air as a swimmer does of his arms and legs in the water.

If a man is swimming with his arms moving equally toward the east, and his body exactly faces the east, the swimmer’s movement will be toward the east. But if the northern arm is making a longer stroke than the southern arm, then the movement of his body will be toward the northeast. And if the right arm is making a longer movement than the left, the man’s movement will be toward the southeast.

The momentum of one of the wings extended edgewise toward the tail will cause the bird to make a sudden circling movement, following the momentum of the aforementioned wing.

When the bird raises itself in circles to a height above the wind without flapping its wings, driven by the force of the wind, it will be carried by this wind away from the area where it wishes to return, still without flapping its wings; then it turns so that it faces the oncoming wind, entering slantwise underneath this wind, and descends slightly until it finds itself above the spot where it wishes to return.

### TO ESCAPE THE DANGER OF DESTRUCTION

The destruction of these machines may happen in two ways: the first is if the machine breaks; the second is if it turns sideways or almost on its edge. The machine should always descend at a shallow angle and almost in a level line. Regarding the prevention of structural failure, one may guard against this by making the machine as strong as possible in whatever way...
->On Flight 10 [9] v.<-

<summary>Leonardo explains how birds balance opposing wind forces and why their center of gravity must be lower than their wings for stability. He also outlines the primary risks to a flying machine: structural failure and losing a level orientation during descent.</summary>
<keywords>aerodynamics, center of gravity, wing tips, propulsion, flight safety, structural integrity, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

it may turn in any direction—that is, falling edgewise with the head or tail in front, or with the tip of the right or left wing, or along lines that bisect or quarter these directions, as the sketch shows. One ought to guard against this from the start by preventing the machine from turning almost edgewise.

Regarding constructing the machine in such a way that, in descending, it finds a remedy prepared regardless of the direction it takes: you will achieve this by ensuring its **centre of gravity** is above that of the weight it carries, always in a vertical line, and with one always at a sufficient distance from the other. That is, if the machine is thirty **braccia** wide, the centers should be four **braccia** apart, with one beneath the other as previously stated. The heavier part is below because, as it descends, the heavier part always acts as the guide for the movement. In addition to this, if the bird attempts to fall head-downward with even a fraction of the slant that would cause it to flip over, this will not be able to happen; because the lighter part would be beneath the heavier part, and the light would be descending before the heavy, which is impossible in a descent of any length, as is proved in the fourth book of the **Elements of Mechanics**.

And if the bird should fall head-downward with the body slanting somewhat toward the ground, the undersides of the wings ought to turn flat against the earth, the tail should rise toward the back, and the head or the underside of the jaw should also be turned toward the ground. From this, there will immediately originate in this bird its **reflex movement**, which will cast it upward again toward the sky. For this reason, the bird would fall backward at the end of its reflex movement unless, while rising, it should lower one of its wings slightly, which would curve the movement and cause it to turn into a half-circle; then this bird will find itself at the end of this movement with its beak turned toward the spot where the reflex movement began. And if this is done against the direction of the wind, the end of the reflex movement will be much higher than the beginning of the falling movement. This is the way in which the bird rises to a height without beating its wings and by circling. The remainder of the circle I have mentioned is completed with the help of the wind, through a falling movement, with one wing and one side of the tail always kept low. And it subsequently makes a reflex

movement towards the direction of the wind and is left at the end with its bill turned in the direction of the wind, and then makes again the falling and reflex movements against the wind, always going in circles.

When the bird wishes suddenly to turn on one of its sides, it pushes out swiftly towards its tail the point of the wing on that side; and since *every movement tends to maintain itself, or rather every body that is moved continues to move so long as the impression of the force of its mover is retained in it*, therefore the violent movement of this wing in the direction of the tail—retaining at its end a portion of the said impression—not being able by itself to follow the movement which has already begun, will move the whole bird with it until the impetus of the moved air has been consumed.

When the tail is thrust forward with its surface exposed and the wind strikes upon it, it makes the bird move suddenly in an opposite direction.
Sul Volo 13 [12] r. and v.

<insert>[With drawing of bird with wings outstretched]</insert>

Here the primary feathers of the wings are those which keep the bird motionless in the air against the movement of the wind; that is, the wind moves, and the bird maintains itself upon it without beating its wings, and the bird does not change its position.

The reason is that the bird arranges its wings at such a slant that the wind which strikes it from below does not form a wedge of the kind that tends to raise it, raising it, however, just as much as its weight tends to lower it. That is to say, if the bird’s impulse to fall is expressed by two units of power, the wind’s impulse to rise will be expressed by two units also; and because things which are equal cannot overcome one another, the bird remains in its position without either rising or falling. It remains for us to speak of the motion which does not impel it either forward or backward; and that is, if the wind should tend to carry it along or drive it out of its position with a power expressed by four units, and the bird with the same power is slanting at the same angle against the wind. Here also, as the powers are equal, the bird will not move forward nor will it be driven back when the wind is equal. But inasmuch as the movements and powers

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s analysis of how birds maintain stability in variable winds and focuses on the anatomical function of the alula (the "big finger") and the tail as control surfaces for steering and compression.</meta>

# FLIGHT

...of the winds are variable, the angle of the wings ought not to change; because if the wind grows, the bird would have to alter the angle in order to avoid being driven upward by this wind.

In the instances mentioned above, the wind does not enter like a wedge underneath the slanted wings. Instead, it only meets the wing along the edge that is descending against the wind. There, it strikes the edge of the shoulder, which serves as a shield for the rest of the wing. There would be no protection here against the descent of the wing if it were not for the <term>big finger</term> <note>original: "big finger"; this refers to the **alula**, or "bastard wing," a small projection on the anterior edge of the wing of modern birds</note> labeled *a*, which then moves to the front and receives the full force of the wind, or less than the full force depending on the power of the wind.

->Sul Volo 14 [13] r.<- <note>original: *Sul Volo*; Leonardo da Vinci's "Codex on the Flight of Birds," written c. 1505</note>

<note>*[With drawing of wing]*</note>

The big finger *n* of the hand *m n* is the part which, when the hand is lowered, lowers itself even further than the hand. It does this in such a way as to close off and prevent the escape of the stream of air compressed by the lowering of the hand. Consequently, in this area, the air becomes condensed and offers resistance to the <term>oarage</term> <note>the rowing or paddling motion</note> of the wing. For this reason, nature has formed a bone of great strength in this big finger, to which very strong <term>sinews</term> <note>tendons</note> are attached. Its feathers are short and have greater strength than the other feathers on a bird's wings, because the bird leans upon it—and upon the already compressed air—with all the power and strength of the wing. It is through this mechanism that the bird moves forward.

This finger performs the same function for the wings that claws do for a cat when it climbs up trees.

However, when the wing regains fresh force during its return upward and forward, the big finger of the wing then aligns itself in a straight line with the other "fingers" (feathers). In this position, its sharp edge strikes the air and performs the duty of a <term>helm</term> or rudder, which continuously acts upon the air in upward or downward movements when the bird wishes to rise.

The second helm or rudder is located on the opposite side, beyond the bird’s center of gravity; this is its tail. If the wind strikes the tail from below, because it is located beyond the aforementioned center of gravity, it will cause the front part of the bird to lower.

But if the tail is struck from above, the bird's front part is raised. And if the tail is somewhat twisted, showing its front slanting under the right wing, the front part of the bird will be turned toward the right side. And if the slant of the lower side of the tail is turned toward the left wing, the bird will turn its front part toward the left side; and in both of these conditions, the bird will descend. But if the tail, in a slanting position, is struck by the wind on its upper part, the bird will turn by revolving slowly toward the side where the upper surface of the tail shows its slant.

The axis of the bird's shoulder is what is turned by the muscles of the breast and back; and it is here that the discretion of lowering or raising the tail originates, according to the will or necessity of the animal in motion.

I conclude that the rising of birds without beating their wings is produced by nothing other than their circular movement within the movement of the wind. When this movement ceases to have the support of the wind, the bird continues to descend until it reaches the point where the reflex movement begins. After this, having described a semicircle while revolving, it finds itself once again facing the wind and follows the reflex movement upward against the wind, continually revolving until, with the help of the wind, it reaches its highest ascent between its lowest descent and the arrival of the wind, remaining with its left wing to the wind. From this maximum elevation, circling again, it drops once more to the final falling movement, remaining with its right wing to the wind.

The equal power of resistance in a bird's wings is always due to the fact that their tips are equally distant from the bird's centre of gravity.

But when one of the wingtips is nearer to the bird's centre of gravity than the other, the bird will then descend on the side where the wingtip is closer to the centre of gravity.

The hand of the wing is the part that creates the impetus; and the elbow is then held edgewise so as not to hinder the movement that creates the impetus; and when this impetus is afterwards created, the

--- Page 426 ---
The elbow is lowered and positioned at an angle, and in slanting, it compresses the air upon which it rests almost into the shape of a wedge, upon which the wing proceeds to lift itself. If it did not do this, the movement of the bird during the time the wing returns forward would cause the bird to fall as its impetus is gradually consumed; however, it is unable to fall because as the impetus fails, the pressure exerted by the elbow resists the descent in equal proportion and raises the bird up again.

The creature's elbows are not lowered right at the beginning, because during the peak flight of the impetus, the bird will bound upward; instead, they are lowered by as much as may be necessary to check the descent, according to the bird's desire and discretion.

When the bird wishes to soar upward suddenly, it immediately lowers its elbows after it has produced the impetus.

But if it wishes to descend, it keeps its elbows rigid and raised up after the creation of the impetus.

Remember that your bird should have no other model than the bat, because its membranes serve as armor, or rather as a means of binding together the pieces of its armor—that is, the framework of the wings.

And if you take the wings of feathered birds as your pattern, these are more powerful in the structure of bone and sinew because they are penetrable; that is to say, the feathers are separated from one another and the air passes through them. But the bat is aided by its membrane, which binds the whole structure together and is not penetrated by the air.

<meta>This page continues Leonardo da Vinci’s investigations into the laws of nature and mechanics. While the previous page focused on the "machine" of a bird's flight and how it balances against the wind, this page applies similar geometric principles to the "machine" of the human body, specifically exploring the ideal proportions defined by the Roman architect Vitruvius.</meta>

<note>The following text is translated and modernized from Leonardo da Vinci's original mirror writing in Renaissance Italian.</note>

Vitruvius <note>original: Vitruvio</note>, the architect, states in his work on architecture that the measurements of the human body are distributed by Nature in this manner: that is, 4 fingers make a palm, 4 palms make a foot, 6 palms make a cubit <term>cubit: an ancient unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm, about 18 inches</term>, 4 cubits make a man, 4 cubits make a pace, and 24 palms make a man; he used these measurements in his buildings. 

If you open your legs so much that you lower your head by 1/14th of your height, and open and raise your arms until your middle fingers touch the line of the top of your head, know that the center of the outspread limbs will be the navel <note>original: 'l bellicho</note>, and the space formed between the legs will be an equilateral triangle.

---

<note>A scientific and artistic diagram follows, illustrating the proportions of the human body inscribed within a circle and a square.</note>

---

<note>The following section contains a linear scale below the drawing and further proportional notes.</note>

The span of a man's outstretched arms is equal to his height.

From the hairline to the bottom of the chin is one-tenth of a man's height; from below the chin to the top of the head is one-eighth of his height; from the top of the chest to the top of the head is one-sixth of his height. From the top of the chest to the hairline is the seventh part of the whole man. From the breasts to the top of the head is the fourth part of the man. The greatest width of the shoulders contains within itself the fourth part of the man. 

From the elbow to the tip of the hand is the fourth part of the man; from that same elbow to the end of the shoulder is the eighth part of the man. The whole hand is the tenth part of the man. The genitals <note>original: il membro virile</note> are located at the exact center of the man. The foot is the seventh part of the man. From the sole of the foot to below the knee is the fourth part of the man. From below the knee to the base of the genitals is the fourth part of the man. 

The spaces found between the chin and the nose, and between the hairline and the eyebrows—each individual space is equal to the size of the ear and is one-third of the face.

This is made in order to find the bird’s centre of gravity, and without this instrument this machine would have little value.

When the bird drops down, its centre of gravity is outside the centre of its resistance.

The bird can stay poised in the air without keeping its wings in a position of equality because, owing to its not having the centre of gravity in the middle of its axis as balances do, it is not necessarily obliged to keep its wings at an equal height like the said balances. ## AN ARGUMENT TO DISPOSE OF THE OBJECTIONS
## TO THE ATTEMPT

You will perhaps say that the sinews and muscles of a bird are incomparably more powerful than those of man, because all the girth of so many muscles and of the fleshy parts of the breast goes to aid and increase the movement of the wings, while the bone in the breast is all in one piece and consequently affords the bird very great power, the wings also being all covered with a network of thick sinews and other very strong ligaments of cartilage, and the skin being very thick with various muscles.

But the reply to this is that such great strength gives it a reserve of power beyond what it ordinarily uses to support itself on its wings,

--- Page 430 ---
<page-num>418</page-num>
<header>FLIGHT</header>

since it is necessary for it, whenever it may so desire, either to double or treble its rate of speed in order to escape from its pursuer or to follow its prey. Consequently, in such a case, it becomes necessary for it to put forth double or treble the amount of effort, and in addition to this, to carry through the air in its talons a weight corresponding to its own weight. So one sees a falcon carrying a duck and an eagle carrying a hare; which circumstance shows clearly enough where the excess of strength is spent; for they need but little force in order to sustain themselves, and to balance themselves on their wings, and flap them in the pathway of the wind and so direct the course of their journeyings; and a slight movement of the wings is sufficient for this, and the movement will be slower in proportion as the bird is greater in size.

<margin><term>Sul Volo</term> 17 [16] r.</margin>
Man is also possessed of a greater amount of strength in his legs than is required by his weight. And in order to show the truth of this, place a man to stand upon the sea-shore, and observe how far the marks of his feet sink in; and then set another man on his back, and you will see how much deeper the marks of his feet will be. Then take away the man from his back, and set him to jump straight up as high as he can; you will then find that the marks of his feet make a deeper impression where he has jumped than where he has had the other man on his back. This affords us a double proof that man is possessed of more than twice the amount of strength that is required to enable him to support himself. <insert>[With drawing]</insert> Leather bags with which a man falling from a height of six <term>braccia</term> will not do himself any harm, whether he falls into water or on land; and these leather bags, tied after the fashion of the beads of a rosary, are wrapped round by others.

If you should fall with the double chain of leather bags which you have tied underneath you, so manage that these are what first strike the ground.

When a bird has a great wingspan and a small tail and wishes to rise, it will raise its wings vigorously and, in turning, will catch the wind under its wings. Movements of the tail: sometimes it is flat and the bird keeps it level as it moves; sometimes it has the edges equally low, and it is then that the bird rises; sometimes it has the edges equally high, and this occurs when it descends. But when the tail is low and the left side is lower than the right, the bird will then rise with a circling movement toward the right side; this can be proved, but not here. And if, when the tail is low, the right edge is lower than the left, the bird will turn toward the left side. And if, when the tail is high, the left edge is higher than the right, the bird will then turn with its head toward the right side; but if, when the tail is high, the right edge is higher than the left, then the bird will circle toward the left side.

The bird that descends with or against the wind keeps its wings closed so as not to be held up or slowed by the air; it keeps them well above its body so that it may not be turned upside down by the momentum.

When the bird keeps the shoulders of its wings closed and their tips wide, it makes the air denser than the surrounding air through which it does not pass; and it does this in order to steady its movement and not deviate from its line of travel.

But when the bird opens the shoulders of its wings more than the tips, it intends to slow its movement more forcefully.

When the tips and the shoulders of the wings are equally distant from each other, the bird intends to descend without being hindered by the air.

When the bird uses its wings like oars, or beats the wings backward as they descend, it is a clear sign that it is increasing the speed of its descent.

Here, by observing the postures of the birds, one sees the results of their actions; both of these together reveal the intention of the bird.

A wing extended on one side and drawn in on the other shows the bird dropping in a circular motion around the wing that is drawn in.

Wings drawn in equally show that the bird intends to descend in a straight line.

When a bird is above the wind at the end of a <term>reflex movement</term> <note>original: "reflex movement"; Leonardo’s term for the upward momentum gained after a dive or when utilizing the wind's force to rise</note>, it will never keep its wings open equally, because it would be flipped upside down by the wind. Instead, it draws in the wing around which it wishes to pivot, and it descends and moves in a circle behind that wing when it wishes to rise or descend.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 66 recto a</margin>
The opponent <note>Leonardo often framed his scientific notes as a debate with a hypothetical critic</note> says that he has seen proof that a bird standing with its wings entirely open cannot descend perpendicularly in a way that would cause it injury or damage any part of its body. He admits the proofs that it cannot fall backward edgewise because he cannot deny the evidence provided, and also that it cannot fall with its head pointing down. However, he doubts whether—if the bird found itself with the breadth of its wings perpendicular to the ground—it would not descend edgewise along that line. The reply to this is that, in such a case, the heaviest part of the body would not be guiding the movement, and such a motion would contradict the fourth proposition of this treatise, which has been proven impossible.

The "rudders" of the wings <note>referring to the primary feathers or the trailing edge of the wing used for steering</note> are the parts that immediately position the bird above or below the oncoming wind. With a tiny movement, they cleave the air along whatever line the bird can then easily penetrate.

The bird will never descend backward because its center of gravity is closer to the head than to the tail.

The descent of the bird, in all or part of its movement, will always follow that line in which its center of gravity is closest to the extremities of the bird's width.

I have stated that the descent will be entirely toward that part which is nearest to the center of gravity when only one part is close to this center of gravity, and the extremities of the other opposite parts remain equidistant from this center; for example, when the bird presses its head close to its body and the wings remain equally distant from the center with the tail straight and wide, the bird will then descend headfirst, and the body along its central line will direct itself by this movement.

But when, during such movement, one of the wings narrows itself toward the said center, the line of the bird's descent will be between the retracted wing and the head of the bird.

And if, during the movement of the wings when they are opened equally, the tail should bend toward one of the wings, the movement will then continue between the head of the bird and the opposite wing.

And if only the head is bent down toward one of the wings while they are opened equally, the slanting descent will then proceed between the head and the wing that the head is near.

Swimming upon water teaches men how birds act upon the air.

## HOW THE BIRD STOPS ON THE WING ABOVE THE WIND AND DOES NOT MOVE FROM ITS POSITION

If the wind driving the bird forward is of the same power as the bird, which stays above the wind and desires to drop toward this wind, the bird will then be motionless; and the movement it was on the point of making will be made by the wind from the opposite side.

And if the wind is more powerful and the bird moves its wings backward like oars, the bird will be motionless.

And if the wind comes from above and in front, and the bird resists it from below and behind, then, according to the conditions of the places from which it might fall, the bird remains motionless.

But when the wind comes from the front and below, it will be more powerful than the weight of the bird; it will then be necessary for the wings

--- Page 436 ---
to contract and occupy less of the atmosphere, and consequently they will be struck by a smaller quantity of wind, and for the strokes it takes to have a somewhat backward direction, and then the bird will remain motionless.

The simple power of a man will never work a crow's wing with such speed as the crow did when it was attacked.

And the proof of this will be shown in the noise they make, for the man's effort will never produce as great a sound as the bird's wing made when it was attacked.

## WHY THE BIRD SUSTAINS ITSELF UPON THE AIR

The air which is struck with the greatest speed by a moving object is compressed to the highest degree within itself.

This is proved by the fact that a less dense flexible body will never support a denser one upon itself; for example, one sees an anvil floating upon melted bronze, and gold and silver when liquefied staying beneath a fusion of lead. For this reason, as the atmosphere is a body capable of being compressed, when it is struck by something moving at a greater rate of speed than the air's own displacement, it is compressed into itself and becomes like a cloud within the rest of the air—that is, it acquires the same density.

But when the bird finds itself within the wind, it can sustain itself above it without beating its wings, because the function which the wing performs against the air when the air is motionless is the same as that of the air moving against the wings when they are without motion.

## WHY THE BIRD FALLS IN A PARTICULAR LINE

On whichever side the weight of the bird is shifted as it drops from a level position, its descent will be toward that side.

And at whatever angle the bird positions itself, its descent will follow that same angle.

And if a part is bent forward and the wings are spread out at an equal slant, the movement of the bird will be in the center of the two inclined parts.

--- Page 437 ---
And this movement will slope more toward the part that bends more.

[Drawing]

That circle will be smaller in size when the bird positions itself on a less slanted line.

The slant of the wings always tends to be equal to the slant of the bird's body.

[Drawing a b]

<margin>C.A. 77 v. b</margin>
If the wings are held at a slant and the torso is in a level position, the bird will undoubtedly descend along the line of the wings' slant; however, this slant will vary to the right or left, as shown in the movement a b.

## IN HOW MANY WAYS DOES A BIRD TURN ITS STRAIGHT MOVEMENT INTO A CURVING MOVEMENT?

A bird that wishes to turn its straight course into a curved one without raising or lowering its altitude moves the wing on the outer side of its curve more frequently than it moves the wing on the inner side of the curve.

As the bird beats its wings, the shoulder is raised more in the front than in the back; it does this in order to gain momentum, because if the wings were to move up and down equally, the bird would not move from its original position.

The bird turns its straight course toward the side on which the wing is lowered most. It is as if this wing were struck by the wind more than the other.

## OF THE BIRD AS IT FLIES WITH BOUNDS (BALZI)

A bird that flies with a bound gains impetus during its descent because, by closing its wings during this phase, it gains weight and consequently speed; it follows, therefore, that the upward reflex movement is more powerful. When the bird adds a wingbeat to this, it creates double the power produced by a simple reflex movement alone. Because of this doubling, the upward movement becomes longer than it would have been without that addition

...produced by the beating of its wings. This is the actual reason why the upward movement <note>original: "reflex movement"; Leonardo uses this to describe the reaction or rebound after a downward stroke or descent</note> is equal to its descent, and why, at the end of the flight, the distance of its descent matches the distance of its ascent.

When a bird descends at a sharp angle without flapping its wings, all the tips of its wings and tail bend upward. This movement is slow because the bird is supported not only by the air beneath it but also by the air to its sides <note>lateral air</note>, against which the curved surface of the bent feathers spreads at equal angles.

When a bird rises from the ground to a certain height, it leaps and forcefully closes its open wings. This creates a wave of compressed air that strikes upward against its breast from below. As this momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note> continues, the movement drives the bird higher; it flaps its wings regularly during this process until it has reached a sufficient altitude.

A bird rising in a circular path maintains a tilted position with the span of its wings. The circle it traces will be larger in proportion to how steeply it is tilted; conversely, the circle will be smaller if the tilt is less pronounced.

A bird that moves one wing more than the other will fly in a circle. The movement will also be circular when one wing beats while the other is held still. The size of this circle will vary depending on whether the wing moves more slowly or more rapidly.

### Movement of a bird driven by the wind:

When a bird is driven by the wind and rises without flapping, it extends the turning process more during its descent than during its upward movement; it rises during the upward phase and lowers itself during the downward phase.

When descending against the wind, a bird lowers its feet as the wind hits them. It does this to prevent the tail from being pushed out of alignment with the rest of its body while it is trying to descend.

The bird can never move backward, because the tips of the wings when extended are never further forward than the center of gravity inherent in the bird's length, and this must necessarily be the case; whereas if it were to move backward, its feathers would flip forward and restrain the movement with their resistance; and the bird demonstrates this to us, for when it is resting, it always turns its beak toward the wind.

If the left tip of the tail is as far above the center line of movement, and above the center line of the weight the bird carries in its line of movement, as the right tip of this tail is below the said centers, the movement of the bird will necessarily be straight, because the left tip of the tail is as powerful in bending the straight movement of the bird to the right when it is above the bird as the right tip of this tail is in bending the bird to the left when it is below the bird.

The bird will always descend in the direction in which it is heaviest.

I have seen the sparrow and the lark fly upward in a straight line while they were in a level position. **Impetus** is a power of the mover applied to a movable object which causes the movable object to move after it is separated from its mover. [There will never be **impetus** unless the resistance of the movable object is completely subdued by its mover.] And especially when the dense friction of the bodies moved resists the movable object.

<meta>This page continues Leonardo da Vinci's observations on the physics of motion and bird flight, specifically discussing the relationship between a moving force (the mover) and the object being moved (the movable thing).</meta>

# FLIGHT 429

...moves as long as the oxen are in motion. When the cause of the motion has ceased, the effect fails as well—meaning that the movement of the beam ends at the same time the oxen stop moving.

When the friction between a moving object and the surface it moves over is very low, the power of the mover will remain joined with the moving object for a significant distance. This is because the object separates from the mover more easily when there is less friction to slow it down. For example, one sees a barge being towed through the water for a certain distance on its own momentum after it has been separated from the power of its mover. Similarly, a bird, after it has beaten its wings, moves upon the compressed air without any further wingbeats, carried for a long distance by its *impetus* <term>impetus: the momentum or force possessed by a moving body</term>.

Moving objects and their movers are of three kinds: 
1. The first moves across the same amount of space as the movement made by its mover; in this case, the object is only slightly influenced by the mover’s power. 
2. The second moves through much less space than that traversed by the mover; this object possesses greater resistance than the power of its mover (not accounting for the distance between them). 
3. The third moves in the same amount of time through a considerably greater space than its mover; this object has much less resistance than its mover.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 161 verso, section a</margin>
There are other relationships between movers and moving objects where the object follows the direction and path of its mover. Even after the mover stops, the object continues to exert the mover's force, traveling through a long stretch of space. This is seen in an arrow shot from a bowstring: it continues to move for a long time by itself after the bowstring has released it.

A bird may remain in the air without changing its position, even if the force of the wind is greater than the weight of the bird. It achieves this with quick, slight movements of the wings, using them like oars to push against the flow of the wind with a speed greater than the wind itself; in this way, it remains in a state of *equilibrium* <term>equilibrium: a state in which opposing forces or influences are balanced</term>.

The bird may also stay in the air without changing its wings or its position, even if the power of the movement of the air is more powerful than...

Sudden changes in the wings and tail of birds cause sudden changes in the paths of their movements. When the tail enters the line of the wind, it is struck from beneath by the movement of the air, the head is struck from above, and each of the wings is struck from beneath. ### HOW A BIRD LOWERS ITSELF WITHOUT USING THE WIND OR BEATING ITS WINGS

[Diagram]
When the bird's center of gravity is positioned in front of the wings' center of resistance, the bird will descend along a slanting line, consistently maintaining this specific angle of descent.

The bird’s descent will be faster when the slant is less steep. <note>Leonardo is observing that a shallower angle often results in higher forward velocity.</note>

A bird travels a longer distance when its descent is interrupted by many "reflex movements"—that is, moving in waves, as shown above. For example, suppose a bird is traveling from point *a* to point *b*. When it has traveled half a mile, it performs a reflex movement <term>reflex movement</term> <note>Leonardo's term for using the momentum gained from a descent to swoop upward without flapping.</note> at point *c d*, using the impetus gained from its descent to rise. It then returns its wings to their original slanted position and descends for another half-mile, before rising again and continuing this pattern until it reaches its destination.
[Diagram]
If a bird that is not flapping its wings does not wish to descend too quickly, it will perform a reflex movement after a certain amount of slanted descent. It will then begin to fly in a circle, rising upward in the same way cranes do. When cranes break their usual flight lines, they gather in a group and lift themselves through many spiraling turns, moving like a screw. Once they have reached a greater height, they return to their original path with a gentle descent until they gather again to circle and raise themselves once more.
[Diagram]
A bird that takes longer strokes with one wing than with the other will move in a circular path.
<meta>C.A. 220 v. c</meta>

With its wings expanded, the pelican measures five <term>braccia</term> <note>original: "braccia"; an Italian unit of measurement representing an "arm's length," roughly 23 inches or 58 cm.</note>, and it weighs twenty-five pounds. Its wingspan is therefore the square root of its weight. <note>5 is the square root of 25; Leonardo is attempting to find a mathematical ratio between weight and wing surface area.</note>

A man weighs four hundred pounds, and the square root of this figure is twenty. Therefore, a wingspan of twenty <term>braccia</term> is the necessary size for a man to fly.

The width of a pelican's wings is three-quarters of a <term>braccio</term> <note>original: "braccio"; an Italian unit of measurement roughly equal to 23 inches or an arm's length. The plural is "braccia."</note>. Therefore, if you divide the five <term>braccia</term> of its total wingspan into quarters, there are twenty quarters in its length and three quarters in its width. Thus, you could say the width is three-twentieths of the length.

Following this logic, if a man's wingspan were twenty <term>braccia</term>, the wings would also need to be three <term>braccia</term> wide—maintaining that ratio of three-twentieths of the twenty-<term>braccia</term> length at the widest point.

A bird’s backward movement against the wind's direction will always be greater than its forward movement. However, when the bird moves backward with the flow of the wind, its speed is increased by the wind, making it equal to its forward movement.

There are two ways birds rise without flapping their wings, using only the help of the wind and moving in circles: simple and complex. 

In a **simple movement**, the bird travels forward above the path of the wind. At the end of this stretch, it turns to face the wind, catching the wind's force from beneath its wings. This allows it to complete its backward movement against the wind. <note>Leonardo is describing "dynamic soaring," where birds gain energy by crossing between air masses of different velocities.</note>

The **complex movement** by which birds rise is also circular. it consists of a forward and backward movement against the wind's direction in a path shaped like a half-circle, combined with a forward and backward movement that follows the course of the wind.

The simple circular movement of rising without beating the wings always occurs when the winds are very strong. In this case, as the bird rises, it is also carried a considerable distance by the force of the wind. In contrast, the complex movement occurs when there are only light winds. Experience shows that in these complex movements, the bird rises through the air without... <note>The text ends mid-sentence in the original manuscript.</note>

My opponent says that he cannot deny that the bird cannot fall either backward or with its head underneath in a perpendicular line; but it seems to him that its descent may be sheer if it keeps its wings wide open and has one of the wings as well as the head below its center of gravity. To this argument, the answer is the same as to what preceded it; that is, that if this bird, being in such a position without having other means of aiding itself, were to drop perpendicularly, it would be contrary to the fourth part of the second book of the Elements, where it was proved that every body which falls freely through the air will fall in such a way that the heaviest part of it will become the guide of its movement; and here the heaviest part is found to be midway between the extremities of the open wings—that is, midway between the two lightest parts—and therefore, as has been proved, such a descent is impossible.

We have therefore proved that when a bird has its wings spread out and its head somewhat raised, it is impossible for it ever to fall or descend in a perpendicular line; on the contrary, it will always descend by a slanting line, and every tiny movement of the wings or tail changes the direction and slanting descent of this line to a reflex movement.

Nature has so provided that all large birds can stay at such a great elevation that the wind which increases their flight may be of a straight and powerful course. For if their flight were low, among mountains where the wind wanders and is perpetually full of eddies and whirlwinds, and where they cannot find any spot of shelter because of the fury of the icy blasts among the narrow mountain passes, nor can they so guide themselves with their great wings as to avoid being dashed upon the cliffs and high rocks and trees, would this not sometimes be the cause of their destruction? Thrushes and other small birds can make headway against the wind because they fly in spurts. [*Of the flight of the bat and of the eagle*]

I say that if the bat weighs two ounces and measures half a <term>braccio</term> with wings expanded, the eagle ought, according to this proportion, to measure with wings expanded not less than sixty <term>braccia</term>; yet we see by experience that its breadth is not more than three <term>braccia</term>. And it would seem to many who neither see nor have seen similar creatures that one of the two would not be able to fly, considering that if there exists the proper proportion between the bat's weight and the breadth of its wings, then in the case of the eagle they are not large enough; and if the eagle is properly equipped, the other has them too large, and they will be inconvenient and unsuitable for its use. We see, however, both the one and the other carried with the utmost dexterity by their wings, and especially the bat, which by its swift turns and feints overcomes the rapid twists and retreats of flies, gnats, and other similar creatures.

The reason why the eagle supports itself with its small wings as the bat does with its large ones is contained in the comparison. . .

When a single rush has the same proportion between its size and its length as a bundle of similar rushes has, it will in itself have the same strength and power of resistance as the said bundle. Therefore, if the bundle has nine heads and supports nine ounces, a single one of these similar rushes, of which there are nine heads, will by chance support one ounce.

Place on the top of a rush a <term>danaro</term> as a weight and you will see it bend down as far as the ground. Take a thousand of these rushes and tie them together stretched out, fix them at the base and make the heads level and load them; you will perceive that whereas by the first reasoning...

--- Page 451 ---
it ought to support about three and a half pounds, it will in fact support more than forty.

So for this reason it follows that the expanse of air that supports the bat—which weighs the two hundred and twentieth part of the weight of an eagle—would need to be sixty times larger if it had to be trodden down and pressed by the beating of the wings of the eagle.

When a bird, in beating its wings, raises them higher above its center of gravity than it lowers them beneath it, its head will be higher than its tail during its movement. This is proved by the fourteenth principle of this work: a moving object will bend its straight path more toward the side where its movement is less impeded than toward the side where it is more impeded; and by the eighth principle, which says: moving the air against a stationary object is the same as moving an object against stationary air. Therefore, when the wing moves farther downward than upward, it creates more impact against the air that borders it below than against the air that touches it above; and for this reason, its straight movement will slant upwards.

If the bird, while moving its wings an equal distance below and above its center of gravity, moves them more rapidly downwards than upwards, it will curve its level movement upwards. This is proved by the ninth principle mentioned previously, which said: of the equal movements made by the wings of birds, those which are the most rapid will have the most power to compress the air bordering them below; and by the seventeenth principle, which says: the impact of a moving object is deflected more when it has struck a spot that offers more resistance; therefore, it is concluded that if the wing, while making equal movements downward and upward, moves down more rapidly than up, it will curve its level movement upwards rather than downwards.

And by the converse of what has gone before, if the wings, while making equal movements below and above the bird’s center of gravity, should rise more swiftly than they fall, the bird’s movement will slant, inclining toward the ground.

The inclination of the wings of birds desiring to move at a constant height from the earth must necessarily always produce as much more fatigue when moving downwards than upwards as the bird weighs more downwards than it does during level movement. This

--- Page 452 ---
is proved by the thirteenth principle of this work, where it is said: the weight of every heavy object is directed along the line of its movement, and is increased or decreased in proportion to whether this movement is faster or slower.

### *Definition of impetus*

Impetus is a power created by movement and transmitted from the mover to the moved object; and this moved object possesses as much movement as the impetus has life.

The wings of birds experience as much more downward effort than upward effort when the bird wishes to rise, in proportion to how much more the bird weighs downward than upward.

A bird supporting itself upon the air against the movement of the winds possesses an internal power that seeks to descend, and there is another similar power in the wind striking it that seeks to raise it up.

And if these powers are equal to one another so that one cannot overcome the other, the bird will be unable to either raise or lower itself, and consequently will remain steady in its position in the air.

This is proved as follows: let *m* be a bird positioned in the air in the wind current *a b d c*. As this wind strikes it under the slant of the wing *n f*, it creates a wedge there which would carry it upward and backward in a slanting movement if it were not for the opposing power of its weight, which seeks to drop down and forward, as shown by its slant *g h*. And since powers that are equal to each other do not overcome but offer a complete resistance to one another, for this reason the bird will neither raise nor lower itself; therefore, it will remain steady in its position.

[Figures]

If the bird shown above lowers its wings, it makes itself more stable upon the air and supports itself with less difficulty, because it occupies more space by keeping its wings in a position of equilibrium than by either lowering or raising them. In keeping its wings high, however, it cannot bend them either to the right or the left with the same ease that it would if it kept them low. But it is more certain not to be overturned when keeping its wings high than when keeping them low.

--- Page 453 ---
low and bending them less to the right or the left, because as it lowers itself on the right side by using its tail as a rudder, there is an increase of resistance; this is because that wing catches more air than the other wing on the side where it descends abruptly while returning to a position of equilibrium. Consequently, it is a good strategy to descend with a straight and simple slant, which it would be unable to do if it held its wings lower than its body. For if it were to tilt toward one of its sides by using its tail as a rudder, it would immediately turn upside down, as the more extended wing catches more air and offers more resistance to the slanting descent than the other.

The tips of the wings bend much more when pressing against the air than when the air is passed through without the beating of the wings.

The flexible part of the wing is bent back during the swift, slanting descent of birds. This is proved by the third principle of this work, which says: among things that are flexible through the percussion of the air, that which is longest and least supported by the opposite side will bend the most.

Therefore, the longest feathers of the wings—not being covered by the other feathers that grow behind them and not touching each other from their center to their tip—will be flexible; and by the ninth principle of this work, which said: of things equally flexible, that which first opens the air will bend the most. And we shall prove this by the eleventh principle, which says: of equal and similar things bent by the wind, that which is struck by air of greater density will bend the most.

The helms placed on the shoulders of the wings are extremely necessary, for it is these parts that keep the bird poised and motionless in the air while facing the path of the winds.

[With drawing of wing]

This helm *a* is placed near the spot where the feathers of the wings bend, and because it is very strong, it bends very little or not at all. It is situated in a very strong position and equipped with powerful sinews, being itself made of hard bone and covered with very strong feathers, each of which serves as a support and protection for the other.

### *Simple slant*

If a bird’s slanting movement is made simply according to the direction of its length, this slant will be a straight line <note>original: "rectilinear"</note>.

### *Compound slant*

However, if the slant of the bird’s length is combined with the slant of the width <note>original: "breadth"</note> of its open wings, the bird’s movement will be curved. This curve will be concave on the side of the lower wing.

### *Irregular movement*

And if a bird is struck by the wind on the tip of its lower wing, its compound movement and slanting curve will be interrupted <note>original: "broken"</note> and will instead form a simple, straight slant.

The underside of a bird’s wing is always concave from the elbow to the shoulder, while the rest of it is convex.

In the concave part of the wing, the air swirls <note>original: "is whirled round"</note>, while in the convex part, it is pressed and condensed.

## WHY A BIRD TURNS BY BENDING ITS TAIL

All elongated bodies moving through the air will move in a straight line if their side <note>original: "lateral"</note> edges are at an equal distance from the center line of their mass <note>original: "bulk"</note>. This holds true regardless of whether the force <note>original: "impetus"</note> driving them is natural, forced <note>original: "violent"</note>, or a combination of both <note>In Renaissance physics, "natural" movement referred to gravity, while "violent" movement referred to an applied force like a catapult</note>.

However, if the sides of these elongated bodies are at unequal distances from the center line of their mass, the body's movement will form a curve in the air. This curve will be concave on the side where the edge of the body is further from the center line.

### Concerning complex slants in birds’ flight

A complex slant <note>Leonardo uses "complex" to describe a movement that happens in more than one dimension simultaneously</note> occurs when a bird moves through the air while keeping its tail higher than its head and one wing lower than the other.

When a bird flies in a complex slant, its movement in one direction will be faster than in the other to the degree that one path is less steep <note>original: "oblique"</note> than the other.

The movement of birds flying in a complex slant follows a curve.

The curve created by this complex movement will be more or less pronounced depending on whether the side slant <note>original: "lateral slant"</note> is less or greater.

Bird flight has very little power unless the tips of the wings are flexible. This is proven by the fifth principle of the *Elements* <note>Leonardo refers to his own projected treatise on mechanics or physics as the "Elements"</note>, which says: sideways force <note>original: "lateral power"</note> checks the descent of heavy objects. This can be seen in a person pressing their feet and back against two sides of a narrow space, as chimney sweepers do. In the same way, the bird uses the sideways twisting of its wingtips against the air, where they find support and bend.

When a bird is struck by wind under its wings during a direct descent, its path will become steeper <note>original: "slanting"</note> in proportion to the wind's power. This is proven by the ninth principle of this work, which states: among the direct descents of similar and equal heavy objects in the air, the one struck by wind with the greatest force <note>original: "impetus"</note> will slant the most.

If a bird flies with its wings at an equal height but lowers one side of its tail, its straight flight will become curved. This curve will bend toward the lowered side of the tail, and the wing on that side will move slower than the opposite wing in proportion to how sharp the curve is.

This is proven by the seventh principle of this work, which says: the part of a revolving wheel that moves the least is the part closest to the center of rotation. Therefore, as the tip of wing *a* touches the center *a* around which it turns, it moves less, while the tip of the opposite wing *d* moves through the distance *g b* <note>These letters refer to a specific diagram in Leonardo's original manuscript</note>.

The descent of birds is of two kinds: one is a certain descent toward a fixed position, while the other is uncertain, aimed at two positions or...

more. In the first case, its wings are open and the tips are raised above the back; with these held at an equal height, it drops in a straight, simple slant to its intended spot. The second bird, as it descends, holds the tips of its wings lower than its breast and bends its tail now to the right, now to the left, with a slant that is sometimes simple, sometimes complex, and occasionally irregular.
[Figure]
The bird that is struck on its side by the wind moves the wing facing the wind with a greater and swifter motion than it does the other wing, in proportion to the force of the wind's movement. This may be proved: let *a b c* be the bird moving along the line *a f* toward the wind *d*, which strikes it on the side at wing *a b*. The wind would carry the bird along the line of its own course if wing *a b* were not swifter in its movement than the wind. This is why, when the wind has struck the side of the bird and, through some eddying recoil, has folded itself back against the wing that has closed itself by flapping, this wing has thus gained a second support against the aforementioned bending of the bird's straight movement. It must therefore be concluded that the wide, swift movement—which the wing struck by the wind makes in excess of the opposite wing—combined with the wind that has struck the bird and been deflected back against that wing, is what prevents the straight course of birds from being diverted by the wind. Furthermore, unless the opposite wing were slow and moved very little, it would strike into the path of the wind and the wind would strike against it; thus, the wind would be most powerful in driving the bird off its course.

## WHY THE FLIGHT OF BIRDS DURING MIGRATION IS MADE AGAINST THE ONCOMING WIND

The flight of birds during migration is made against the movement of the wind, not so that their travel may be faster, but because it is more sustainable and less fatiguing. This occurs because, with a slight beating of their wings, they enter the wind with a slanting movement, this movement being positioned below the wind. After this forceful movement, they position themselves slantwise upon the course of the wind.

--- Page 457 ---
This wind, after entering under the bird's slant like a wedge, raises it up for as long as the acquired momentum takes to exhaust itself; after this, the bird descends again under the wind and once more acquires speed. It then repeats the aforementioned upward reflex movement against the wind until it has regained the altitude it lost, and so continues in succession.

## WHY BIRDS SELDOM FLY IN THE DIRECTION OF THE WIND CURRENT

It very seldom happens that the flight of birds is made in the direction of the wind current, and this is due to the fact that this current envelops them and separates the feathers from the back, and in addition to this, chills the bared flesh. But the greatest disadvantage is that after a slanted descent, its movement cannot enter into the wind and be thrown back by its help to the altitude it left unless it has already turned backward, which would not help it make progress on its journey.

The bird spreads out its wing feathers more and more as its flight becomes slower; and this is according to the seventh principle of the Elements, which says: that body will become lighter which acquires greater breadth.

A bird descending makes itself swifter the more it contracts its wings and tail. This is proved by the fourth principle of Gravity, which says: that heavy body makes a swifter descent which occupies a smaller quantity of air.

That bird is more rapid in its descent which descends by a less slanted line. This is proved by the second principle of Gravity, which says: that heavy body is swiftest which descends by the shortest path.

A bird in descending lessens its speed more and more as it is more extended. This is proved by the fifth principle of Weight, which says: that heavy body is most hindered in its descent which is most extended.

A bird making an upward reflex movement rises in proportion as it acquires greater breadth. This is proved by the fourteenth principle of Local Movement, which says: the heavy body that occupies less space of air in the line of its movement penetrates it more rapidly. Therefore, the widest expansion—

--- Page 458 ---
sion of the wings produces the greatest reduction in the bird's overall volume, and consequently, the impetus of its reflex movement is less obstructed; therefore, it rises higher at the end of this reflex movement.

When the bird descends toward the spot where it wishes to land, it raises its wings and spreads out half of its length, and so descends slowly upon the aforementioned low place.

There is as much force in moving the air against a stationary object as there is in moving an object against stationary air.

When the bird moves in a slow descent over a long distance without flapping its wings, and the incline leads it toward the ground more quickly than it intends, it then lowers its wings and moves them against the stationary air; this movement lifts the bird up just as if a wave of wind struck it from below. This is proved by the second-to-last principle.

### OF TWO CONTRARY SLANTS OF WHICH ONE IS DESCENDING AND THE OTHER IS A REFLEX MOVEMENT

The movement of a bird that descends by two contrary slants will be longer in proportion to how much the slant on which it rises resembles the slant by which it descends.

This may be proved: suppose that the slant with which the bird descends naturally produces a speed of one hundred miles an hour in order to descend to earth with a drop of one hundred braccia, and that the opposite slant along which it performs its reflex action at this time saves it half of this descent; I assert that the movement which was one hundred miles an hour will become fifty, as is proved in its proper place.

Birds always fly more slowly when they raise their wings than when they lower them. This is caused by the necessary period of rest required after the immediate fatigue of the tired limbs; moreover, speed is not necessary in raising these limbs as it is in lowering them, since the impetus that carries the bird is generated through a long duration of movement in the bird. It is sufficient for it merely to have raised its wings from where they first descended by the time the said impetus begins to decline, which reveals itself through the falling of the bird. But when the bird wishes to gain speed, it resumes the

--- Page 459 ---
impetus nearer to its inception and beats its wings more frequently and with the longest and most rapid movement possible.

### OF THE CIRCLING MOVEMENT MADE BY THE KITE IN RISING

The circling movement made by birds as they rise above the wind is produced by the bird entering the wind with one of its wings and balancing itself with the other in the direct line of the wind.

In addition to this, it lowers one of the corners of its tail toward the center of its circular movement, and because of this, the wind that strikes it on the inside checks the movement of the side that is lower and nearer to the center of this circle. And this is the cause of the circling movement, and the wing held above the wind causes the bird to rise to the maximum height of the wind.

The simple movement which the wings of birds make is easier when they rise than when they are lowered. And this ease of movement springs from two reasons, of which the first is that the weight in falling somewhat raises the wings up by themselves; the second is due to the fact that, because the wing is convex above and concave below, the air flows away more easily from the percussion of the wings as they rise than when they are lowered, for then the air being pent up within the concavity of the wing becomes compressed more easily than it escapes.

### OF THE EXPANSION OF THE TAIL IN THE REFLEX MOVEMENT OF BIRDS

Birds spread out their tails in their reflex movement because the air is compressed beneath them and resists the penetration of the bird in its maximum breadth, so that the impetus is consumed only by the edge or front of the wing. If this were not so, the impetus acquired in the falling movement would consume itself partly in the direction of the earth and partly in the reflex movement; and then this reflex movement would be as lacking in height as that which drops down by keeping the tail straight.

A bird acquires more lightness <note>In this context, "lightness" refers to aerodynamic lift or buoyancy rather than a loss of physical mass.</note> the more it spreads itself out and expands its wings and tail.

A heavy body appears lightest when it extends to its greatest breadth.

From this conclusion, one can infer that a man's weight can support itself in the air by means of a wide expanse of wings.

A body shows itself to be less heavy when it extends to a greater breadth.

### ON THE CAUSE OF THE CIRCULAR MOVEMENT OF BIRDS

The circular movement of birds is produced by the unequal movement of their wings. This is caused by the impact (<term>percussion</term> <note>original: "percussione" — the striking of one body against another, in this case, the air against the bird's surface</note>) created in the air by one of the corners of the tail that projects above or below the path made by the bird through the air it traverses.

Among things moved by external forces with a simple movement, the object being moved is as swift as the speed of its mover; therefore, a bird carried by the wind in the same direction as the wind will have a speed equal to it.

But if the objects carried by the wind slant more toward the ground than the direction of the wind's course, the object will be swifter than its mover. And if the slant of the objects carried by the wind turns toward the sky, this is a clear sign that the movement of the object is slower than that of the wind. The reason is that when the slant is turned toward the ground, it produces this movement by reason of its weight (<term>gravity</term> <note>original: "gravità" — Leonardo uses this to mean the natural heaviness or downward tendency of an object</note>) and not by the help of the wind. 

But when the slant of the movement is toward the sky, this slant is caused merely by the shape of the object. It bears itself like a leaf which, caught by the wind across its width, raises itself up merely by the help of the wind and moves as fast as its mover, as has been shown in its proper place.

When a bird is driven by the wind and follows a more slanting course than the course of the wind, it is much swifter than the said wind.

When a bird driven by the wind has its movement parallel to that of the wind, it also has a speed equal to that of the wind.

When birds are driven by the wind without beating their wings, the...
