A bird is swifter than the wind in proportion to how much more slanting its course is than that of the wind. This is proved as follows: suppose the wind, in a level position, moves one degree of space in one degree of time, and the bird driven by the same wind moves the same degree in the same time; these movements up to this point will be equal. But on account of the slant in the bird's movement, let us assume it acquires a second degree of movement in the same time that the wind is acquiring its first degree; it follows, therefore, that the bird in the same time can be twice as fast as the wind that drives it.

But this same slanting movement does not cover its distance within a level position, but between this level position and the center of the earth—as if the level position was the line *a c* along which the wind moves from *a* to *c*, and the bird moves by the help of the wind and by the help of its gravity from *a* to *d*. I say that in the same time in which the bird would be moved (without the help of its gravity) from *a* to *b*, it will be moved by the help of the wind and of its gravity from *a* to *d*, the one movement being in the proportion of one and a half compared with the other, from *a* to *d* upon the movement *a b*. But as regards the distance of the views, *a d* is the same as *a b*, as is shown to us by the perpendicular line *b d*.

### OF BIRDS WHICH FLY IN GROUPS

When birds that fly in groups come to make long journeys, and the wind happens to strike them on one side, they are greatly helped in their flight because the flight is made in loops without flapping their wings; because the falling movement is made downwind, with the wings somewhat close together, and in the direction in which they are traveling. But the rising movement is made against the wind; and with the wings held open, the bird rises up as the wind meets it. Consequently, the wind entering beneath the bird lifts it up toward the sky, in the manner of a wedge when it penetrates beneath a heavy body placed above it. By this means, after the birds have been lifted up to their proper height, which is the equivalent of that at the beginning of the falling movement, they return to their first

--- Page 462 ---
course, always restarting their falling movements in this course; and their reflex movements are always made against the wind.

## OF FLYING THINGS

Before birds start on long journeys, they wait for winds favorable to their movements, and these favorable winds are of a different kind for different sorts of birds. This is because those which fly in jerks or bounds are obliged to fly against the wind, while others receive the wind on one of their sides at different angles, and others receive it on both sides. But the birds that fly by jerks, such as fieldfares and other similar birds which fly in flocks, have the feathers of their wings weak and poorly protected by the smaller feathers that form a covering for the larger ones. And this is why it is necessary for their flight to be against the course of the wind, for the wind closes up and presses one feather upon another, thus making their surface smooth and slippery when the air tries to penetrate it. The opposite would happen if the wind were to strike these birds toward the tail, because then it would penetrate under each feather and turn them over toward the head; thus, their flight would have a confused movement, like that of a leaf blown about in the course of the winds, which goes perpetually whirling through the air and continually revolving. In addition to this, their flesh would be without protection against the buffeting of the cold winds. To avoid such accidents, they fly against the course of the wind with a curving movement, and their bounds acquire great impetus in their descent, which is made with wings closed under the wind. The reflex movement then proceeds with wings open above the wind, which brings the bird back to the same height in the air from which it first descended, and so it continues time after time until it arrives at the desired spot.

The reflex movement and the falling movement vary in birds in two ways: one is when the reflex movement is in the same direction as the falling movement; the second is when the reflex movement is in one direction and the falling movement is in another.

The bird closes its wings in the falling movement and opens them in the reflex movement: it does this because a bird becomes heavier in

--- Page 463 ---
proportionately as it folds its wings, and it becomes lighter as it opens its wings more.

The reflex movement is always made against the wind, and the falling movement is made in the direction in which the wind is moving.

If the bird's flight turns to the south without beating its wings when the wind is from the east, it will make the falling movement in a straight line with its wings somewhat contracted and positioned beneath the wind. But the reflex movement which follows this falling movement will be made with the wings and tail open, and it will have been directed toward the east.

At the end of this movement, it will turn its front back again to the south, and with its wings folded, it will create the next falling movement, which will be of the same nature as the first, as the bird desires to travel a long distance with the help of this wind; and the junction of the falling movement with the reflex movement will always be at a right angle, as will the junction of the reflex movement with the falling movement.

There are two ways in which the wind causes birds to become stationary in the air without beating their wings.

The first is when the wind strikes against the sides of steep mountains or other rocks by the sea; the bird then positions itself at such an angle that it places as much of its weight forward against the reflex wind as that wind in front has power in its resistance. And since equal forces cannot overcome each other, it follows that in such a position, a bird remains motionless through its imperceptible vibration. The second way is when the bird positions itself at such a slant above the course of the wind that it has as much power to descend as the wind has to resist its descent.

When, with the help of the wind, the bird rises without beating its wings and makes a circular movement, and when it spreads its tail at the uprising of the wind, it is being driven by two forces: one is the wind which strikes the wings in the hollow beneath them, and the other is the weight of the bird which is descending at a complex slant. And because it acquires such velocity, it happens that as it turns its breast to meet the onset of the wind—

--- Page 464 ---
This wind acts beneath the bird like a wedge that lifts a weight; thus, the bird makes its reflex movement much higher than the start of its falling movement. This is the true reason why birds rise some distance without beating their wings.

## DEFINITION OF THE MOVEMENTS

Straight movement is that which extends from one point to another by the shortest line.

Curved movement is that in which some part of a straight movement is found.

Spiral movement is formed from slanting and curved lines in which the lines drawn from the center to the circumference are all found to be of varying lengths. It is of four kinds: namely, convex spiral, level spiral, concave spiral, and the fourth is a spiral in cylindrical form. There is also circular movement, always made around a point at an equal distance, which is said to be revolving; for there are irregular movements which, although they are infinite, are made up of a blend of each of the aforementioned movements.

The start of the simple falling movement is always higher than the end of its simple reflex movement, provided the mobile generator of these movements is immobile in the air.

But the complex falling movement in conjunction with the complex reflex movement will have the opposite result to the simple one, provided that the falling movement is lower than the reflex movement. This arises from the fact that the bird, which creates this falling movement below the wind, presses down and lowers the course of this movement; but the reflex movement, which is produced above the wind with open wings, raises it considerably higher than the start of this falling movement.

## DEFINITION OF THE WAVES AND IMPETUS OF THE WIND AGAINST FLYING THINGS

The bird maintains itself in the air by imperceptible balancing when near mountains or lofty ocean crags; it does this by means of the curves of the winds which, as they strike against these projections,

--- Page 465 ---
being forced to preserve their initial momentum, they bend their straight course toward the sky with various revolutions. At the beginning of these, the birds come to a stop with their wings open, receiving beneath themselves the continual buffetings of the reflected currents of the winds; by the angle of their bodies, they acquire as much weight against the wind as the wind exerts force against that weight. And so, by such a state of equilibrium, the bird proceeds to employ the smallest beginnings of every variety of power that can be produced.

Concerning the movement and the eddies created by the current of air striking various projections of the mountains, and how birds steer themselves in the various tempests of the winds by the imperceptible balancing of their wings and tail:

The falling movement is always joined with the reflected movement, and the beginning of the reflected movement is joined with the end of the falling movement. If such movements form a continuous succession, always following one another, one will be the cause of the other, and the end of one will immediately produce the other, so that they will never both exist at the same time. The falling movement has a weak beginning and is continually increasing, while the reflected movement is the opposite.

### HOW THE TAIL OF THE BIRD IS USED AS A RUDDER

When the bird lowers its tail evenly, it descends by a straight, slanting movement. But if it is lowered more on the right side, then the straight line of the descent will become curved and will bend toward the right side, with a greater or lesser curve of movement in proportion to how much higher or lower the right point of the tail is; and if the left point of the tail is lowered, it will do the same on the left side.

But if the tail is raised evenly a little above the level of the bird's back, it will move along a straight line slanting upward. However, if it raises the right point of the tail more than the left, this movement will be curved toward the right side; and if it raises the left point of the tail, this straight movement will curve to the left side.

When two movements of momentum meet, the impact is more powerful than if they occurred without an encounter. Therefore, as the im-

--- Page 466 ---
momentum of the bird encounters the momentum of the wind, its simple momentum increases, and the reflex movement is greater and higher.

The bird moves against the wind without flapping its wings, and this is done beneath the wind as it descends; then it makes a reflex action above this wind until it has consumed the momentum already acquired. Here, it is necessary for the descent to be so much swifter than the wind that the loss of the acquired momentum at the end of the reflex movement is equal to the speed of the wind striking it from below.

## WHY SMALL BIRDS DO NOT FLY AT A GREAT HEIGHT AND LARGE ONES DO NOT LIKE TO FLY LOW

This arises from the fact that small birds, being without thick plumage, cannot endure the intense cold of the great heights of the air where eagles and other large birds fly, which have more power of movement and are covered with many rows of feathers. Also, small birds, having feeble and simple wings, support themselves in the lower air which is dense, and would not be able to support themselves in the rarefied air which offers less resistance.

The end of the reflex movement is much higher (for birds flying against the wind) than the beginning of their falling movement; and by this, Nature does not break her own laws, as is shown by what has been stated previously.

## HOW THE BIRD RISES BY MEANS OF THE WIND WITHOUT FLAPPING ITS WINGS

The bird rises to a great height without flapping its wings by means of the wind, which strikes it in a great mass underneath its wings and tail—positioned slantwise—and above its back, which is positioned at an opposite slant.

This may be proved: suppose the wind compressed beneath the bird has the same effect as what one sees happening when a wedge is driven beneath a weight; for the wedge, at each degree of its movement, causes the weight to gain a degree of height. But since the opposite slant of the body which the bird possesses is inclined to descend against the approach of the wind with the same power as that with

It is necessary to calculate the degrees of the slant here, for an object on the water or a bird in the air does not stop at any specific degree of slant; rather, their speed will be greater or less depending on whether their position is more or less slanted.

A bird effectively weighs less <note>In this context, Leonardo means it has more air resistance or "buoyancy" in the air</note> when it spreads itself out more, and conversely, it weighs more when it draws itself together more tightly. Butterflies demonstrate this in their descents.

### HOW A BIRD FALLING HEAD-DOWNWARDS GUIDES ITSELF

A bird that falls head-downwards guides itself by bending its tail toward its back. This is proved by the tenth proposition <note>This refers to one of the author's specific mathematical or physical rules of motion</note>, which says: the center of a heavy object that descends in the air will always remain below the center of its lightest part. 

Therefore, as *c d* (the central line of the bird's gravity) is at a distance from *a b* (the central line of the "levity" <term>the center of buoyancy or the point around which the lighter parts of a body are balanced</term> of the bird's tail), the two lines will necessarily align into the same vertical line over a short distance of the bird's descent. And since this is the case, one must admit that the direct vertical descent will necessarily become a slanted path. In becoming a slant, the descent will be as much slower as the movement is longer; or rather, the movement will be as much longer as the descent is slower—and the descent is longer and slower the more it becomes slanted.

### HOW A BIRD STEADIES ITSELF IF IT FALLS BACKWARDS

But if a bird is turned over in the air because of the wind, the tail should close up as tightly as it can and the wings should rise behind the head. In this position, the part in front of the center becomes heavy and the part behind it becomes light, because the center of gravity is not in the center of its total volume. 

This is explained by the ninth proposition, which says: the fact that the center of volume is not aligned <note>original: "concentric"</note> with the center of gravity is the reason why a body will never remain in a state of equilibrium along its greatest width. ...this: The center of gravity of bodies suspended in the air will always remain below the center of volume <note>original: "centre of the volume," referring to the geometric center of the bird's physical shape</note> of those same bodies.

**Why a bird makes use of the "helm" placed at the front of the wings, even though it has other ways of curving its straight path:**

A bird only uses one of the "helms" <term>the alula, or "bastard wing," a small group of feathers on the front edge of a bird's wing used for steering and maintaining airflow</term> located at the front of its wings when it wants to steer its straight movement into a level, horizontal curve.

However, when it happens that this turning process is complex—meaning it is a slanted curve—the bird will then pull in one of its wings slightly. This creates a curved movement that descends on the side where the wing is pulled in, resulting in a convex path.

But a maneuver like this carries the risk of the bird flipping over on its side and leaving its wingtip pointing toward the sky. To protect against this, it is necessary to extend the wing that was pulled in, always keeping the underside of the wing facing the ground; if the bird were to expose the top side <note>original: "right side"</note> of the wing to the air, it would flip upside down. Therefore, when you have extended the folded wing toward the ground in these conditions, you must simultaneously pull in the upper wing that was extended, continuing this until you return to a balanced, level position.

<margin>E 44 v.</margin>
Having demonstrated one of the dangers of deviating from straight flight—which occurs when a bird disrupts the equal air resistance created when its wings are evenly open and its center of gravity is positioned midway between the wingtips—we have also proved that it is safer to adjust one of the two "helms" than it is to pull in one of the wings.

### WHICH WING MOVEMENT IS THE FASTEST?

The movement of the wings is twofold: one part of the movement descends toward the earth, and the other part moves toward the direction from which the bird is flying <note>The author is describing the vector of the wing's stroke as it pushes against the air to move forward</note>. What it is in the bird that causes it to change its straight movement without either descending or raising itself:

The bird changes its straight movement, made in a position of equilibrium without raising or lowering itself, by means of the right or left helm placed in the front part of the wings. This is proved as follows: let *a p o g* be the bird which, moving in a position of equilibrium, changes the straight movement *m p a* to the curving movement *a b* by means of the helm *t* which is set in the front part of the left wing; and this occurs according to the ninth [rule] of this [work] which says: bodies with equal sides around the central line of their gravity will always maintain the straight line of their movement in the air—and if the volume of one of the sides is increased or diminished, the straight movement will describe a curve, showing the concave part of the curve on the side of the greater inequality of the object that is moved.

### OF THE UNDERSIDE OF THE WINGS

The resisting parts of the feathers beneath the wings of birds form coverings for one another, from *b* to *a*, behind the flow of the air or wind, so that this air or wind presses the part of the feathers that offer weak resistance against the opposite feathers which offer powerful resistance.

### WHY THE WEAK RESISTANCES ARE BENEATH THE POWERFUL ONES

The feathers that offer a weak resistance are placed beneath those which offer a powerful resistance, with their tips turned toward the tail of the bird, because the air underneath flying things is denser than it is above them, and denser in front than it is behind; and the necessity of flight ensures that these lateral extremities of the wings are not struck by the wind, because then they would immediately become spread out and separated from one another, and would be instantly penetrated by the wind. Consequently, these resistances are placed so that the parts which have a convex curve are turned towards

--- Page 470 ---
the sky, the more they are struck by the wind, the more they lower themselves and draw closer to the lower resistances with which they are in contact, and so prevent the wind from entering beneath the front of the lateral parts of these resistances.

### WHAT TEXTURE OF AIR SURROUNDS BIRDS AS THEY FLY

The air surrounding birds is as much lighter above than the ordinary lightness of other air as it is heavier below; and it is as much lighter behind than above as the bird’s movement is swifter in its transverse course than the movement of its wings toward the ground. Similarly, the heaviness of the air is greater in front of the bird's contact point than below it, in proportion to the two aforementioned degrees of air lightness.

The straight movement of birds in the air forms a curve toward the side on which the wing is drawn together. This arises entirely from the fact that every heavy body descends on the side where it meets less resistance; this movement, therefore, may be described as a complex curve formed from a lateral curve and the declining curve made by the bird on the side that is lower than itself.

### ON RAISING AND LOWERING THE WINGS

Birds raise their wings when open with greater ease than they lower them. This is proved by the third rule of this work, which says: parts of bodies that are convex are more suitable for penetrating the air than those that are concave.

It follows that since birds have wings that are convex on the upper side and concave on the underside, they will raise their wings with greater ease than they lower them.

### ON THE SPREADING OF THE FEATHERS AS THE WINGS ARE RAISED

The feathers spread out from one another in the wings of birds when these wings are raised. This happens because the wing rises and penetrates the thickness of the air with greater ease when it is perforated than when it is a solid surface.

--- Page 471 ---
## ON THE CLOSING OF THE FEATHERS AS THE WINGS ARE LOWERED

The spaces between the feathers in the wings of birds contract as the wings are lowered, so that by becoming a solid surface, these wings may prevent the air from penetrating between the feathers. Thus, with their percussion, they may have a more powerful stroke to press and condense the air that is struck by the wings.

## ON THE RESISTANCE OF THE FEATHERS IN THE WINGS OF BIRDS

The resistances of the feathers in the wings of birds, with their powerful curves, form shields for one another on the upper side against the penetration of the air or the onset of the wind. This ensures that the wind, as it enters, does not cause them to spread out, nor raise and open them, thereby separating the feathers from one another.

It is shown here below how the feathers under the wings, in order to support themselves, must rest and rub against the air that sustains them. Part of the resistance found in the feathers remains beneath the strong part of the adjacent feathers, for the feathers underneath the wings have their long, weak portions situated beneath the short, strong parts of the next row of feathers.

Why the sinews beneath the birds' wings are more powerful than those above. This is done for the sake of movement:

The shoulder where the helm of the wing is placed is hollow below like a spoon; being thus concave below, it is convex above. It is fashioned this way so that the process of rising may be easy and that of lowering itself difficult and met with resistance. It is especially useful for moving forward by drawing itself back in the manner of a file.

The extremities of the wings, when raised to their maximum height, are farther away from each other than when lowered as far as possible. And when these wings ascend again, their extremities continue the...

In the momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note> created in the air by birds, it is better and easier to bend a part of the wings than the whole. The part of the bird which bends in the air will cause the entire body to bend, just as one sees a ship turn through the movement of its rudder.

Based on what has been said above, the tips <note>original: "points"</note> of the wings produce a greater movement than their length alone would suggest, provided they are flexible. Of these two lines of movement, one is proven to be shorter than the other because one is only a part of the other.

However, because the wingtips move less than the feathers attached to them as they are raised and lowered, a specific mechanical reaction occurs. Before these wingtips begin to extend the feathers joined to them, they move in an opposite direction. It is therefore necessary for part of the ends of these feathers to turn back with the rest of the feather, while the tip moves forward. This is like a finger that raises itself by the same amount that the hand descends; one would describe such a finger as "immovable" because it does not change its position relative to the air. For this reason, we may say that the tip of a flexible wing has a movement resembling that of wings that are not flexible.

The air which is underneath the curves of the wingtips <note>original: "end parts of the wings"</note> as they descend is more compressed than any other portion of the air found underneath the bird. Therefore, in the case of the whole wing descending at the same time, that part has the most rapid movement which is most distant from the fixed part, and as a consequence, the air that is struck by the swiftest blow is the most compressed. It follows also that the bending of the tip of the wing is like a spring or a bow bent by force, and that this process of bending compresses the air with which it comes in contact.

If the movement of the wind had uniform power throughout its expanse, the bird would not be so often engaged in beating the wind and balancing itself with its wings.

The air in itself is capable of being compressed and rarefied to an infinite degree.

## WHETHER THE FOLDS IN THE EXTREMITIES OF THE WINGS ARE NECESSARY OR NOT

The curve created in the outer parts of the wings when these wings strike and press upon the air condensed beneath them has the effect of greatly increasing the bird's power of flight; for in addition to pressing on the air below them, they compress the adjacent lateral air, according to the fourth rule of the second book which says "every force seeks to undo itself along the very lines of the movement that produced it"; and by the seventh rule, "every straight object that is bent by force has the lines of its power converging toward the center of a complete circle formed by the curve started by this wing extremity." ## OF FLYING THINGS

If the sides of the bird shift from a position of equilibrium, the straight, slanted movement will change into a curved, slanted movement.

A bird that is thrown back into the air after its descent will never regain its previous height unless it beats its wings or is aided by the wind.

A bird that drops down with a straight slant before an oncoming wind will always have its upward reflex movement <note>Reflex movement: The secondary, rising motion that occurs after a bird dives or descends.</note> higher than its initial falling movement.

The curved slant observed when birds fly to meet an oncoming wind with a downward reflex movement is much steadier than the same movements performed in a straight slant.

## OF REFLEX WINDS

If birds are driven by the wind without flapping their wings, and the wind hits a wall directly opposite them, the bird will immediately encounter the reflected wind <note>original: "reflex wind"</note> while trying to avoid that wall.

If a bird is moving north on the wind, and the wind tries to push it toward the east, the bird—in order not to disrupt the equal wingspan that maintains its maximum lift <term>levity</term>—will lower the right tip of its tail. This allows it to catch the force of the wind more on the right than on the left, thereby maintaining its straight movement toward the north against the wind.

# OF THE THINGS THAT MOVE IN THE AIR AND THEIR DESCENT

A parallel board of uniform thickness and weight, placed flat in a level position within uniform resistance, will descend evenly in each of its parts. And if this board is placed in the air in a slanting position, the descent will slant uniformly, and this is proven in its proper place.

The shape of the front part or back part of the object that moves in the air or water is what bends its straight course.

An irregularity attached either in front of or behind the ends of a level object moving through the air is what diverts the straight movement of the aforementioned object to the right or left, up or down, or at some slant.

A bird which descends at a straight slant in one direction will not change the level position of its sides.

A bird in the air makes itself heavy or light whenever it pleases; and it does this by spreading out its wings and expanding its tail when it wishes to slow its swift descent, or by contracting its wings and tail when it wishes to quicken a descent that has been delayed.

The helms placed on the shoulders of the wings are formed of very strong feathers because they bear a greater strain than all the other feathers.

[Figure] a b the helms of the wings come into use when the bird is in swift descent. When it wishes to capture its prey and to turn from one direction to another without slowing its movement, it uses these helms; if these were not there, it would be necessary for it to employ the whole wing, and this, because of its size, would greatly hinder the intended movement.

# OF THE SLANTING MOVEMENT OF BIRDS

The bird which uses up its momentum against the oncoming wind with its wings open and without any movement—except for necessary balancing—will always rise if it finds itself above this wind.

But if the bird moves without beating its wings while under the wind, its momentum will be used up during its descent; however, this momentum will last longer the less steep the descent is.

If the bird moves with its wings open and without flapping—traveling at the same time and in the same direction as the wind—it will descend a certain amount for every unit of forward movement. ### OF EVERY KIND OF FLIGHT, DO THE OPPOSITE

When a bird is driven by the wind, it continually descends at a slanted angle. When it wishes to return to its previous height, it turns around and uses the momentum of the wind as a wedge. <note>This "wedge" concept is a frequent metaphor in Leonardo's studies, describing how the bird's wings split the air to create lift.</note>

#### *Scientific Principle*

The momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note> that the bird gains during its descent can be redirected in any direction—whether in a straight line or a gradual curve—until that momentum is exhausted.

#### *Rule*

When a bird is struck by the wind from below on its right side and wishes to descend to a specific spot, it lowers the wing on the side where it intends to land.

#### *Scientific Principle*

A bird that wishes to quickly exhaust the momentum it has gained fully extends its wings against the direction of travel toward the spot where it wants to stop—and it does this without the help of the wind.

# FLIGHT

When a bird desires to rise straight up without the wind by means of beating its wings, a turning movement is necessary.

But if the bird’s movement is to be in a straight line without the help of the wind, it is necessary that the movement should be made by frequent beatings of the wings, and for this reason the movement will be extremely slanted.

## THEORY OF FLYING THINGS

The movement made by a movable object which is long in shape and has uniform sides around its center-line will take a straight course through the air for as long as the impetus given to it by its mover remains within it.

The bird which flies in a curved line while in a level position moves one wing with a longer and more rapid movement than the other, but such movement does not raise or lower one wing more than the other.

But if the curved movement of birds is composed of both a curve and a slant, then in addition to the movement in one wing being swifter and longer than in the other, one wing will also go higher and lower than the other. And this is proved by the fourth rule which says, ‘wings of equal movement propel the bird in a straight line’, and by the converse, ‘wings of which the movement is unequal in length make a curved movement’. And if the movement of wings which are unequal is of equal height but of varying length, the movement of the bird will then be a curve in a level position. And if the movement of the wings, in addition to being unequal in length, is also unequal in height and depth—this being more in the case of one wing than the other—this movement is composed of both a curve and a slant.

## OF THE REVOLVING MOVEMENT

The pegtop or ‘chalmone’ which, by the rapidity of its revolving movement, overcomes the power that comes from the inequality of its weight around the center about which it revolves, because of the impetus that controls this object, is an object which will never have such a

--- Page 478 ---
tendency to fall as the inequality of its weight dictates, so long as the power of the impetus that moves this body does not become less than the power of this inequality.

But when the power of the inequality exceeds the power of the impetus, it makes itself the center of the revolving motion; and so this body, brought to a reclining position, completes the remainder of the aforementioned impetus upon this center.

And when the power of the inequality is equal to the power of the impetus, the top is bent obliquely, and the two powers contend in a concerted movement and move one another in a great circuit until the center of the second variety of revolving movement is established, and in this, the impetus exhausts its power.

The rows of feathers on the wings, placed one above the other, are set there for the purpose of strengthening the largest feathers.

First, perform the anatomy of the birds, then that of their wings stripped of feathers, and then with the feathers.

Parallel lines which, between their extremities, are equidistant from the same point are always curved, and one is shorter than the other if they are in contact with the two sides of the same triangle.

All the feathers of the wings that grow beneath the penultimate feathers of the same wings are in the process of bending during the bird's flight, and the most flexible are those which do not form a covering for one another—that is, those which are pierced during the flight.

In order that a bird flying against the wind may be able to settle on a high spot, it has to fly above the spot and then turn back and, without beating its wings, descend upon the aforementioned place. This is proven, for if the bird should wish to stop its flight in order to settle, the wind would throw it backward; this cannot happen when it acts in the aforementioned manner.

If the flight of the bird is determined by the length of the bird and the wind strikes it on the side, the movement of its flight must necessarily be between its length and the said side: as though the bird *a b* should wish to fly from *a* to *c* and the wind *f* should strike it on the flank or at the side, this bird will then direct its movement along the line *a g*, and the wind will continually bend the movement along the curve *m n c*; thus it will go where it wishes and will find itself at the spot marked *c*.

--- Page 479 ---
But should the wind deflect the bird’s course in a more pronounced curve than its will intends, the bird will then resume its flight against the wind as it did at first, and then with a second curving movement, the wind will lead it to the desired place.

Whether or not equal striking forces, made with equal lengths of movement at different times, will create equal lengths of movement in the objects moved: this is answered by the seventh rule of the ninth book, which says: among moving forces of equal power and of movements united with the objects they move, the one that separates its movable object from itself most swiftly will be the one that moves this object farthest from itself. At this point, the opponent says that moving forces of equal power will not vary their speed and therefore cannot, with a similar movement, drive one of two equal movable objects farther away than the other. The reply to this is that there are two kinds of moving forces, one of which is sensitive and the other is not: that which is sensitive has life, and the other is without life. But that which has life moves its objects by means of the expansion and contraction of the muscles that form parts of its limbs; this expansion and contraction can be performed with a greater or lesser amount of speed using the same power, as the swiftest cause is not necessarily the most powerful.

No other difference is found except that the greater or lesser speed compresses the air through which the arm of the moving force is exerted to a greater or lesser degree. But the insensitive moving force—such as catapults or mangonels or other similar engines which, by means of counterweights or by the force of cords or bent wood, drive objects forth from themselves. . . .

The bird which one sees, carried on by its momentum, flying higher than the spot on which it desires to land, spreads out its tail and lowers it; striking the air with it during its movement, the bird bends its straight course, causes it to curve, and makes it end upon the spot where it settles down.

The kite which descends to the east at a steep angle with the wind in the north will have its movement bent to the south-east by this wind, unless it lowers the right tip of its tail and bends its movement slightly to the north-east. This is proved as follows: let *a b c d* be the bird, moving to the east in the direction *n m*, and the north wind strikes it crosswise along the line *f n*, and would cause it to bend to the south-east.

When a bird with its wings extended wishes to make a circular movement to gain altitude with the help of the wind, it lowers one of its wings and one side of its tail toward the center of the circle in which it is revolving.

When a bird moves in a circle to raise itself higher without flapping its wings, it catches the wind under one of its wings during a quarter of that circle; in this way, the wind acts as a wedge and lifts the bird up. The wind would flip the bird upside down if the other wing did not provide support, sustaining it upon the air that swirls beneath it. This air is the same that was struck and compressed beneath the opposite wing.

### THINGS THAT FLY

The <term>helms</term> <note>original: "timoni." These are the small groups of feathers on the "thumb" of a bird's wing, known today as the alula.</note> formed on the shoulders of the wings are provided by resourceful nature as a convenient way to deflect the direct momentum that often occurs during a bird’s headlong flight. A bird finds it much more efficient to use direct force to bend one of the smallest parts of the wing than to move the entire wing. This is why these feathers are made very small and very strong, so that they may overlap one another, thereby strengthening and protecting each other with marvelous power. These feathers are anchored in small, thick bones and are moved by tendons <note>original: "sinews"</note> that flex them at their joints; these tendons are very large in these wings.

The movement and position of these bones on the shoulders of the wings are arranged and established in the same way as the thumb in the human hand. Being in the center of four tendons that surround its base at four equal intervals, it can produce an infinite number of movements, both curved and straight, by means of these tendons.

# FLIGHT

We may say the same of the rudder placed at the stern <note>original: "behind the movement"</note> of a ship, which is modeled after the tails of birds. Experience teaches us how much more easily this small rudder can be turned during the rapid movement of great ships than the entire hull of the ship itself.

### Why shipbuilders do not place rudders at the front, as is the case with the rudders located at the shoulders of bird wings:

This was not done with ships because waves are thrown up into the air to such a height when struck by the forceful impact of a moving ship. This would make moving a front-mounted rudder very difficult because of the weight <note>original: "gravity"</note> it would acquire from the water, and furthermore, it would often break. 

However, since air moving within air has no weight but instead possesses a density <note>original: "condensation"</note> that is very useful, the <term>helms</term> <note>These are the "thumb" feathers or alulae located at the front edge of a bird's wing, used for control at slow speeds.</note> on the shoulders of the wings function better in a thick substance than in a thin one, as the thicker air offers more resistance. The ship reacts similarly to the added weight of the water, as previously mentioned. For this reason, the rudder is placed at the rear of the ship where the water—furrowed and split open by the ship's course—falls back from the ridges created in the depth of the wake <note>original: "hollow created"</note>. In its descent, the water strikes the rudder with more or less power depending on the angle at which the falling water hits it. Additionally, the volume of water hemmed in at the center of this wake falls with great force against the stroke of the rudder, as has been stated.

But at the tail of the <term>kite</term> <note>The Red Kite (*Milvus milvus*), a bird Leonardo frequently studied for its soaring abilities.</note>, there is a rush of air that presses in furiously to fill the void <note>original: "closing up the void"</note> left by the bird’s movement. This occurs on each side of the vacuum created by the bird's passage.

The void that the bird leaves behind as it penetrates the air is struck on its sides by the parts of the bird that extend furthest from its central line.

If the impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> that the sides of the bird make against the air—specifically those parts furthest from the center line of its movement—occurs above the middle of its right side, then its straight movement will curve toward the right. If the impact is below the middle on the opposite side, the straight movement will then curve toward the left. It will behave the same way if struck above the middle of the left side as if struck below it on the right side, or from the side above or below; we will discuss the appearance of each of these movements in their proper place.

# FLIGHT

A bird's tail, when spread out, supports a portion of the bird's total weight. This proportion matches the size of the tail compared to the rest of the body—the torso <note>original: "bust"</note>, neck, head, and open wings. This effect is reduced the closer the whole bird's center of gravity is to the torso rather than the tail.

The air flows into the vacuum that the bird leaves behind as it pierces through the atmosphere, moving as fast as the bird flies forward while maintaining constant contact. Consequently, it is not the air closing up behind the bird that pushes it forward, but rather the bird's own momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note> that opens and drives the air. This movement creates a path <note>original: "sheath"</note> and draws the air along behind it.

A bird that rises with the help of the wind without moving its wings will descend half the distance it gained once it moves above the wind and turns its tail toward the breeze. This distance increases as the circle of flight becomes larger. <margin>Manuscript E, folio 52 verso and 53 recto.</margin>

When a bird flies in a curve while beating its wings, it flaps the wing on the outer <note>original: "convex"</note> side of the curve more frequently and with a wider motion than the wing on the inner <note>original: "concave"</note> side.

If a bird were to raise its wing above the wind on the side being struck, the bird would be flipped upside down. This is prevented by the fact that the opposite wing is lowered and angled beneath the impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> of the wind, extending past the center of gravity. This impact immediately restores the bird's balance through its wingtips.

A bird that stretches its body to be longer and thinner will be less affected by the impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> of the wind as it encounters it.

When a bird positions itself to catch the wind at an angle, the tip of the lower wing bends significantly and takes on the shape of a foot; in this way, it acts as a support for the bird's weight.

Birds with short tails have very wide wings. Because of their width, these wings take the place of the tail. These birds make frequent use of the <term>helms</term> <note>These are the "thumb" feathers or alulae located at the front edge of a bird's wing, used for control at slow speeds.</note> located on the front of the wings when they wish to turn toward any spot.

A bird that receives the wind directly from the front turns over as it rises and stretches its neck toward the sky; by lowering and open—

To provide the true science of the movement of birds in the air, it is necessary first to provide the science of the winds, which we shall demonstrate through the movement of water. This science can be understood through the senses; it will serve as a ladder to reach an understanding of things flying in the air and the wind.

## *Wind*

The wind, when passing over the summits of mountains, becomes fast and dense. As it flows beyond the mountains, it becomes thin and slow, like water that flows out from a narrow channel into the wide sea.

When a bird passes from a slow current of wind to a fast one, it allows itself to be carried by this wind until it has established a new way to support itself, as is demonstrated in this book.

When a bird moves with momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note> against the wind, it makes long, quick wing beats with a slanting motion; after flapping its wings in this way, it remains for a time with all its limbs <note>original: "members"</note> tucked in and low.

A bird will be overturned by the wind when, while in a less slanted position, it arranges itself so that it receives the impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> of a crosswind <note>original: "lateral wind"</note> underneath it.

<margin>Manuscript E, folio 54 recto.</margin>
If a bird struck by a crosswind is about to be overturned, it will fold its upper wing; this immediately returns it to a position where its body faces the ground. However, if it folds its lower wing, the wind will immediately flip it upside down.

### ON SWIMMING AND FLIGHT

When two forces strike against each other, it is always the swiftest which leaps backward. So it is with the hand of the swimmer when it strikes and presses upon the water and makes his body glide away with an opposing movement; so it is also with the wing of the bird in the air.

Before you write about creatures that can fly, write a book about inanimate objects that descend through the air without wind, and another on those which descend with the wind.

When the bird is moving to the east with the wind coming from the north and finds itself with its left wing above the said wind, it will be turned over, unless at the onset of this wind it puts its left wing under the wind and by some such movement throws itself toward the northeast and under the wind.

### AIR

Its onset is much more rapid than that of water, for there are many occasions when its wave flees from the place of its creation without the water changing its position; in the likeness of the waves which the course of the wind makes in the cornfields in May, when one sees the waves running over the fields without the ears of corn changing their place.

When a heavy substance descends through the air, and this air moves in an opposite direction in order to continuously fill the space left by

--- Page 485 ---
Regarding this heavy substance, the movement of this air follows a curve, because when the air seeks to rise by the shortest path, it is blocked by the heavy substance descending upon it; therefore, it is forced to bend and then return above this heavy substance to fill the vacuum it has left behind. If this were the case, the air would not be compressed beneath the speed of the heavy substance, and if that were so, birds would not be able to support themselves upon the air they strike. However, it is necessary to state here that the air is compressed beneath the object that strikes it, and it becomes thinned out above in order to fill the void left by what has struck it.

## BIRDS IN SLANTING MOVEMENT

The opponent argues that if the bird is struck from below by the wind, the bird will always rise, and this will certainly happen if the bird is flying against the wind. But if the bird and the wind move at the same speed along the same path, it must follow that for every degree of movement made by the wind, the bird loses a degree of height; we may therefore say that in the time it takes the wind to move one degree horizontally—a degree to which we may give a name . . .

A bird flying eastward without flapping its wings as it crosses the path of a south wind pulls in its right wing and extends its left. This inequality of the wings follows the ninth rule of the first book, which states: birds that support themselves without flapping their wings in the path of the wind, or that descend through still air, turn their straight movement toward the side where one of the wings is folded.

Therefore, the bird *p*, flying along the line *a f* with an equal extension of wings *n b*, will turn this movement from *c f* toward *d* by pulling in the right wing from *m* to *n*.

The opponent argues that if the bird's movement is slanted in the direction of the wind and maintained in a level position, the bird will be struck by the wind on its underside; and a bird struck from underneath continually rises upward.

### ON THE CONCLUSION OF A BIRD'S FLIGHT

The conclusion of flight in certain species of birds is performed with a straight, slanting movement, while in others it is done with a curved, slanting movement. But in the case of the straight slant, it is necessary that this movement should be very gradual—that is, the slant is almost horizontal, as shown in *m n* <note>referring to a diagram in the original manuscript</note>.

If the descent of these birds is very steep, then of necessity this movement must involve many changes in direction <note>original: "reflections"; here referring to the bird's maneuvers to shed speed</note>, especially toward the end, as will be shown in the appropriate section.

### ON THE CONCLUSION OF A FLIGHT THAT ASCENDS FROM BELOW

As the bird nears the end of its flight, it tilts its body only slightly along its length and spreads its wings and tail very wide. The wings reach this end with frequent, tiny flaps that use up the bird's momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note>. As the wings pull in, the bird hovers for a very brief moment above the spot where it finally settles with a very light impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> of its feet.

Bats, when they fly, must necessarily have their wings completely covered with a membrane, because the nocturnal creatures they feed upon seek to escape by means of erratic maneuvers, and this confusion is increased by their various twists and turns. As for the bats, it is sometimes necessary for them to follow their prey upside down, sometimes at a slant, and in various other ways; they could not do this without causing their own downfall if their wings were made of feathers that allowed air to pass through them.

### ON THE BEGINNING OF BIRDS’ FLIGHT

When birds wish to begin their flight, it is necessary for them to do so in one of two ways. One way begins by lowering their bodies toward the ground and then making a leap into the air by very rapidly extending their folded legs.

At the end of this leap, the wings have finished spreading, and the bird immediately lowers them swiftly toward the ground and ascends a second stage, which is slanted like the first; by continuing this in succession, it rises to whatever height it pleases. Some others first raise their wings at a forward slant and lower themselves as far as they can with their breasts toward the ground; in this position, they extend their legs very rapidly, leaping up and slanting forward, and then at the end of that effort, they drop their wings so that they slant downward and backward. Thus, they find themselves considerably higher than and in front of the place from which they started, and at the end of the effort, they are in a new position; and so their movement continues.

There are other birds which, after having lowered themselves to the ground and having their wings extended high and forward, lower their wings and extend their legs at the same time. Thus, the power produced by the first beat of the wings, combined with the power acquired by extending the legs, becomes very great; this united power is the greatest that can possibly be created for the start of these birds' flights.

The second method used by birds at the beginning of their flight is when they are descending from a height: they merely throw themselves forward and spread their wings at the same time.

--- Page 488 ---
high and forwards and then in the course of the leap lower their wings downwards and backwards, and so using them as oars continue their slanting descent.

Others have the habit of throwing themselves forward with wings closed and then opening the wings as they descend; having opened them, they are stopped by the resistance of the air, and then they close them and fall again.

### THE FLIGHT OF THE FOURTH SPECIES OF BUTTERFLIES
### THE DEVOURERS OF THE WINGED ANTS

The butterflies with four equal and separated wings (ant lions) always fly with the tail high, using it as a rudder for any sort of movement. That is to say, if one of these insects wishes to descend, it lowers its tail, and if it wishes to ascend, it raises its tail; if it wishes to turn to the right or left, it bends its tail to the right or left, and does the same with all sorts of angles of movement which lie between the four principal movements mentioned. And this is the largest butterfly of the aforementioned species, black and yellow in color.

It uses its four wings in short wheeling flights when it wishes to prey on the small winged ants, moving sometimes the right forward and the left backward, and sometimes the left forward and the right backward, because the rudder formed by the tail is not sufficient to regulate the speed of its movement.

### OF THE THREE CHIEF POSITIONS WHICH THE WINGS OF
### BIRDS ASSUME AS THEY DESCEND

Of the three chief positions which the wings of birds assume as they descend slantwise without beating their wings, the first is *a b c*, in which the wings have their tips at an equal height, as do the opposite angles of the tail; therefore, their movement will descend along the slant *a d*. The second arrangement will be *a e f*, in which the tips of the wings and the angles of the tail are at different heights, the left wing being higher, and its slanting movement being *a g*. The third arrangement of the slant of the same wings is the opposite of the second, for in it the left wing is lower than the right; its movement is at *a o*, and the position of the wings is *n m*.

# A SCREEN TO PREVENT THE WIND FROM TURNING THE BIRD UPSIDE DOWN

I have observed a bird being flipped upside down by the wind on its left side when it entered the wind with its left wing raised.

In the case of all birds that fly at high altitudes, their wings remain "perforated" <note>original: "perforated"; Leonardo is describing how feathers separate like the slats of a blind to let air pass through during the upstroke, reducing resistance</note> as they raise them, as is explained in the appropriate section. As the wings descend, the feathers stay tightly closed together. Because the compressed and dense air cannot move out of the way as quickly as the wing descends, the bird experiences a "reflex" <note>original: "reflex of such percussion"; Leonardo refers here to the aerodynamic reaction or lift generated by the wing striking the air</note> from this impact. This reaction lifts the bird and carries it upward through momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note> as long as that force lasts. During this time, the wings reopen and become perforated again by the spaces between the feathers; then, the bird beats its wings downward violently once more while closing the feathers, thus regaining the momentum it had lost. This is how all birds that rise in a straight path, such as the lark and similar species, operate. Those birds that do not have such a broad spread of feathers, such as birds of prey, must lift themselves by circling—that is, climbing in a spiral or "screw" shape, or otherwise moving in a circular path.

The butterfly and many similar insects all fly with four wings, with the rear wings being smaller than the front ones. The front wings partially cover the back wings. All insects of this class have the power to rise in a straight vertical movement; as they lift their wings, they become "perforated" because they keep the front wings much higher than those behind. This continues until the end of the momentum that pushes them upward; then, as they lower their wings, the larger wings join with the smaller ones to catch the air, and so they gain a fresh impulse as they descend.

There are also other kinds of flying insects which fly with four equal-sized wings, but these do not overlap one another during the downstroke any more than they do during the upstroke. Insects of this kind cannot rise in a straight vertical path.

### OF IMPACT—THE FLIGHT OF MAN

Of objects that fall through the air from the same height, the one that descends by the longer route will produce less impact; it follows that the one that descends by the shorter route will produce more impact.

This first movable object made of slightly curved paper begins its descent with the front *b* and moves from *a* to *c*; in this movement, *a* descends further than *b*. Consequently, at the end of the reflected movement, *a* finds itself at *c*, and *b* is raised to *d*. This is proved by the ninth rule of this work, which says: the object that strikes the air with a larger part of itself has less power to penetrate that air. And by the tenth: that object is swifter in penetrating the air which strikes it with less width. And by the eleventh: the heaviest part of a body moving through the air becomes the leader of that body’s movement.

This may be proved: let *a b* be the heavy substance which, although uniform in thickness and weight, being in a slanting position, has a front that carries more weight than any other part of its width equal to that front which serves as its face; for this reason, the front will become the leader of this descent. And by the twelfth: the air that is most compressed offers the most resistance to the object moving through it; therefore, that face weighs least in its parts which has compressed air beneath it. And by the thirteenth: the air that has the swiftest movement moves the most—it follows that a man can descend as is shown below.

This man will move toward the right side if he bends his right arm and extends his left arm; he will then move from right to left by changing the position of his arms.

### GRAVITY

Every slanting movement made by a heavy substance through the air divides the gravity of the moving object into two different aspects: one of which is directed toward the place where it is moving, and the other toward the cause that restrains it.

When the bird lowers one of its wings, necessity forces it to extend it immediately; if it did not do so, it would flip over completely. When a bird wishes to turn, it does not beat its wings with equal movement, but moves the wing on the outside of the circle more than the one on the inside. <sig>K 4 v.</sig> <note>original: "moves the one which makes the convex of the circle... more than that which makes the concave"</note>

If the rudder <term>the tail feathers used for steering</term> or tail of the bird is beneath the wind, the bird will be pulled down by the wind from its middle backward and turned with its front toward the wind. The bird often beats twice with one wing and once with the other; it does this when it has tilted too far over to one side. It also does the same when it wishes to turn toward one side: it takes two strokes with one wing backward, while keeping the opposite wing almost stationary, pointing toward the spot to which it intends to turn. <sig>K 5 v.</sig>

The helms of the wings <term>the primary feathers or wingtips used for maneuvering</term> are used when the bird is struck from behind by the wind and rests slantwise upon the air that supports it. The bird is then struck by the wind in the front of these "helms" and is thus driven upward, its counter-movement <note>original: "reflex movement"</note> being increased by the force of the wind. <sig>K 6 r.</sig>

On the bending of the wingtip even when the wing is not flapping.

The rudders located at the shoulders of the wings are necessary when a bird, gliding without flapping its wings, wishes to maintain its position in a section of air—whether it is sliding downward or rising—and when it wishes to turn upward, downward, to the right, or to the left. It uses these rudders in this manner: if the bird wishes to rise, it extends the rudder in the opposite direction to the way the wind hits it; if it wishes to descend, it extends the top part of the rudder at an angle to the wind's course. If it turns to the right, it extends the right rudder to the wind, and if it turns to the left, it extends the left rudder to the wind.

The bird uses the wing's rudder when, in flight, it supports itself on raised wings so that their vibration prevents it from descending; additionally, these rudders or "fingers" face the air through which the bird is gliding at an angle, and by striking the air with these rudders, the bird resists the glide.

The bird that has the shortest distance between its wingtips descends the most rapidly.

Birds that seek to fly into an oncoming wind are accustomed to fluttering to the right and left, like sailors tacking against the wind's direction. They do this to avoid a long descent; for if the bird did not prevent itself from descending too far, it would be driven back by the wind's current. By entering the wind at a lengthwise angle, it uses enough of its weight along that line to overcome the wind's resistance.

The "hands" of the bird appear in front, near the point where it descends at a straight angle, in order to exhaust the momentum it has gained.

By flapping its wings to stay aloft and moving forward by using the "hand" <note>In Leonardo's anatomical descriptions of wings, the "hand" refers to the outer section of the wing, similar to a human hand, which contains the primary flight feathers used for propulsion.</note> at the back, the bird maintains its height while the "hand" provides its forward progress.

<margin>k 9 v.</margin>
When a bird is carried along by the wind and wishes to turn toward it quickly, it will dive beneath the wind's current with the wing facing the wind. Then, by turning its tail feathers toward the wind, it catches the air; the force of the wind striking the tail allows the bird to turn much more rapidly.

The wing bends more significantly the faster the bird travels within a given period of time.

<margin>k 10 r.</margin>
Consider the difference between flexible and rigid wingtips. Is this bending motion necessary for flight? It appears to be so, because even a slight clipping of these tips almost entirely destroys the bird’s power of flight.

<margin>k 10 v.</margin>
When a bird rises by using the wind without flapping its wings, it spreads and raises its wings so that they form an arch with the curved <note>original: "concave"</note> side facing the sky. It catches the wind under its wings continuously as it moves to and fro. This movement would cause the bird to flip over entirely if the tip of its tail were not turned toward the wind as it enters the current. The tail’s resistance prevents the bird from overturning, because the tail restrains the wings so that their various forces are balanced. Consequently, the tail lowers slightly and the bird is lifted forward.

The wind that strikes the tail is always farther from the bird's center of gravity—and therefore more powerful—than the wind striking the wing.

The previous statement is proven here. I maintain that if the wing is positioned relative to the tail so that the amount of wind *a b* striking the wing *m o* is equal to the wind *b c* striking the top of the tail at *o n*, the bird will not turn. Instead, it will be carried along the straight course of the wind. However, if the wind striking the top of the tail is more powerful than the wind striking beneath the wing, the tail will be pushed aside by the force of the wind, and the wing will turn toward the wind, which will be more—

more powerful than it was before, because the movement that the wing makes against the wind increases in speed and power; thus, the wind entering beneath it forms a wedge there, raising and turning it.

When the bird wishes to ascend, it shifts its center of gravity behind the center of its wings, doing so in order to maintain a slanting position. It is the nature of a steady wind to straighten all the uneven parts of the bird, positioning it with its extremities equidistant from the center of its mass; this applies to birds that support themselves in the air with the help of the wind without flapping their wings. Consequently, it first makes a circling movement and then a straight movement.

When the bird wishes to avoid being overturned by the wind, it has two methods: one is to move the wing that was above the wind and suddenly place it below the wind (that is, the wing that was facing the wind); the other is to lower the opposite wing so that the wind striking it on the inside is more powerful than the wind striking the wing facing the wind.

In flight without the help of the wind, the bird drops half of the wing downward and thrusts the other half, toward the tip, backward; the part moved downward prevents the bird from descending, and the part moving backward drives the bird forward.

When the bird raises its wings, it brings their tips close together; while lowering them, it spreads them farther apart during the first part of the movement, but after this middle stage, as they continue to descend, it brings them together again.

The tip of the bird's wing serves to guide it through the air just as the blade of an oar does through the water, or the arm and hand of a swimmer beneath the water. But here a question arises: if, for instance, the bird is traveling along the line *f a* and the wing—or rather the tip—moves backward from *a* to *f*, does it make its path along *a b f*, driving the bird forward, and return toward *a* by the path above *f c a*? Or does it actually act like the hand of a swimmer under the water, which forces itself back along the line above *a c f* and returns along *f b a*?

--- Page 496 ---
When the bird is carried along by the help of the north wind and moves with it toward the south, it keeps one wing fixed to the northeast, slightly above the wind, and lowers the wing that is toward the southwest, making it serve as a cover to the wind by receiving the impact of the wind slantwise beneath it. It seldom beats this wing, but it is entirely by means of it that the bird maintains its equilibrium, whether the wind be stronger or weaker.

When the bird ascends by reflex movement against the wind, if it did not turn on its lower wing, it would be turned back by this reflex movement with its breast to the wind, and this wind would overthrow it.

And ascending by reflex movement with its spine to the wind, it would turn back with its spine below the wind.

The thrushes and other birds fly easily against the wind.

When the bird wishes to let itself fall on one of its sides, it throws its wing down rapidly on the side on which it wishes to descend, and the impetus of this movement causes the bird to drop on that side.

When the north wind blows and the bird is carried by the wind and wishes to return facing the wind, it drives the wing downward and turns and enters with its spine beneath the wind.

A bird beats its wings frequently as it settles after descending from a height, in order to break the impetus of the descent, to settle itself on the ground, and to diminish the force of the impact.

When birds ascend by wheeling around with the wind, they keep their wings very high so that the wedge of the wind and of the impetus may raise them.

When they move in a downward direction, they lower their wings for two reasons: the first is because less air sustains them; the other is because the wind serves as a wedge above them and drives them down, continually lowering them.

There are many times when the bird beats the corners of its tail in order to steer itself, and in this action the wings are used sometimes very little, and sometimes not at all.

The slanted movement made by the descent of birds begins with the wings straight and low. Gradually they stretch out their wings in order to dissipate the excess momentum which heavy bodies acquire at each stage of their descent. <insert>[Slanting flight of birds]</insert>
When the bird descends by any slant whatsoever, it brings the humerus of the wings near to its shoulders and draws the tips of the wings together toward the tail; this tail is also drawn in toward itself, and by doing so, it meets with a smaller volume of air to resist its descent.

But when this bird wishes to turn to the right or to the left, it will

--- Page 498 ---
extend its right or left wing—that is to say, the wing on the side toward which it wishes to turn. This extended wing encounters a greater volume of air and consequently meets with greater resistance, with the result that it slows its pace more than the opposite wing, which is more contracted. As one wing moves more than the other, the bird transforms its straight movement into a circular movement. However, if the wing that is more contracted toward the bird's body cannot expand with the ease the bird requires, it then spreads out its tail and twists it, open, toward the side where the wing is contracted. This bird will then fly in a straight line, and thus, as you see, it will abandon the circular movement.

There are two helms on the humerus of each bird's wings, and these, without making any change to the wings, have the power to cause the bird various movements between ascending and descending; it is only in transversal movements that the helm of the tail takes part.

### The flight of birds with the wind

The movement of flying things is much swifter than that of the wind. If it were not so, no bird could move against the wind. But its movement against the wind is as much less than its natural course in still air as the degrees of the wind's movement are less than those of the bird.

Let us say the bird moves in still air at a speed of six degrees and the wind itself moves at a speed of two degrees; then this wind, following its natural course, takes away two degrees of speed from the bird, and consequently, of the six degrees, four remain.

But if such a bird were to fly at six degrees of speed along with the course of the wind, which imparts its own two degrees to it, this bird would be flying at eight degrees of speed. Here, however, one should observe how the wing is supported in its percussion in motionless air, retreating air, or air that follows after it, and guide oneself according to these rules.

### Flight of birds—the lark

When the bird finds itself upside down, as is seen at *a*, the tips of the wings are driven toward the ground as is shown at *b*; and then

This flying machine will straighten itself into its initial position, but it bends its spread-out tail toward its spine.

And if it falls edgewise, it will raise its wings toward its spine and then straighten itself.

There are many varieties of birds that can only lift themselves spirally—that is, by revolving movements; the lark is an exception because, as it raises its wings, it proceeds to pierce them with air in such a way that they offer no resistance, being almost entirely permeated.

When the bird wishes to descend, it throws its wings backward so that their center of gravity moves away from the center of the wings' resistance, and thus it begins to fall forward.

The flight of many birds is swifter than the wind that carries them. This results from beating the wings within the wind that supports the bird. If this were not the case, birds that rest upon the wind would not be able to fly against it.

In raising its wings, the bird sends them partly forward and partly upward; the entire wing moves edgewise, as does each individual feather, and additionally, the wing remains permeated by air. As the wing moves downward, the bird thrusts it back against the air or the wind, and the gaps in the feathers and the entire wing become closed and solid.

When the kite, while descending, flips itself over and pierces the air headfirst, it is forced to bend its tail as far as possible in the opposite direction to the one it wishes to follow. Then, by swiftly bending the tail again toward the direction it wants to turn, the change in the bird's course corresponds to the movement of the tail—much like the rudder of a ship which, when turned, rotates the ship, but in the opposite direction.

When the wind is about to blow the bird backward, the bird pulls the shoulders of its wings together so that its weight is concentrated further forward than it was initially. Consequently, the heaviest part leads the descent, while the tail is simultaneously spread out and bent downward.

[*Tail and wings of birds*]

When one side of the tail of a flying body is lowered with a swift movement, the air it strikes becomes more compressed and, as a result, offers more resistance. Consequently, the bird necessarily tilts toward the opposite side, and thus the bird's movement curves in a circle around the lower part of the tail.

However, when first one side and then the other point of the tail forces it to lower itself—sometimes to the right and sometimes to the left—it does not move in a circle; instead, it is merely a way of striking the air as wings would do. When the bird feels itself dropping on one side, the tail beats the air on the opposite side, and in this way, it resists that tendency.

[*A goose swimming and flight*]

### OF MOVEMENT

Swimming illustrates the method of flying and shows that the largest mass finds the most resistance in the air. Observe a goose’s foot: if it were always open or always closed in the same way, the creature would be unable to move at all. It is true that the outward curve of the foot would encounter more water while moving forward than the foot would as it was drawn back; this shows that, given the same weight, the wider an object is, the slower its movement becomes.

--- Page 502 ---
Observe the goose moving through the water: notice how, as it moves its foot forward, it closes it so that it displaces very little water and consequently gains speed; then, as it draws the foot back, it spreads it out, making its movement slower, and at that point, the part in contact with the air becomes swifter.

When one wing bends at the same speed as the other but with a longer range of motion, it will cause a straight movement to curve.

### CONCERNING THINGS THAT CAN FLY

In the case of every heavy object descending freely, the heaviest part will lead its movement.

[Drawing—bird with wings extended]

This bird raises itself in circles by means of the wind. This creature is always struck from below by the wind at a slanted angle; when the wind strikes it from the front, it tilts its wings upward from the shoulders toward the sky; and when the wind catches it from the tail, it tilts its shoulders toward the ground. In this way, the bird always takes the wind at its center of gravity, whether from the front, the back, or the side.

The tail adds weight to or removes it from the bird's wings. Every heavy substance moves along the path where it meets the least resistance. A heavy substance finds the least resistance along the path where it carries the most weight.

A bird will raise itself in flight more easily if it gains momentum by dropping slightly at the beginning of its flight.

When a bird flies against the wind, it must progress against that wind in a line slanting toward the earth, entering beneath the wind. This is because its weight is more powerful than the force of the wind striking it at unequal angles, which would tend to press it down toward the ground if it were not for the fact that the air in front of its line of movement is far less in volume than the air beneath it. This movement alone is enough to overcome that resistance.

--- Page 503 ---
air which offers less resistance, and that air will offer less resistance which is less in quantity.
    Therefore, from what has been stated, we are certain that the bird will move itself against that part of the air which offers less resistance and which meets the leading edges of the wings, rather than against the air which meets it from below along the whole surface of these wings.

### *Rectilinear movement*

But when this bird wishes to rise to a height, it will enter above the wind, and it will retain enough of the momentum it has acquired in the descent we have spoken of, so that by means of the speed thus gained, it will lower its tail and likewise the elbows of its wings and will raise up their leading edges. It will then be above the wind, and as this momentum is forced neither to cease nor to be exhausted, its nature immediately compels it to follow along the line where the least amount of air impedes its movement. This will be along that line in which the wings show themselves edgewise to the air where they strike—that is, along the line where the air, as it is met, is always divided by the leading edges which form the thickness of the wings, and never along the line of their width.
    After having done this, the bird then rises up without beating its wings, for the wind which passes underneath it raises it up as a wedge raises a weight. For this reason, the wind would cause it to turn backwards if it were not for the fact that, in this act of rising, the bird is continually slowing down and exhausting the momentum already acquired. And after this impulse has been exhausted, the bird would be overturned by the wind which has carried it up to a height if it did not immediately lower the leading edges of the shoulders of the wings, enter underneath the wind, and lower its tail. Then the movement which has just ended commences anew, and as it drops, it acquires again the momentum which it had lost, with which it again rises up to a height with a reflex movement until it again loses the momentum that it has acquired.
    If, however, such movement were circular, then the bird would follow other rules which will subsequently be defined in due order.

## ON THE BIRD THAT MOVES WITHOUT WIND OR THE BEATING OF WINGS

The movement of a bird without beating its wings or having the help of the wind follows a line that slants steeply downward and then rises with a reflex movement. By this reflex movement, it raises itself seven-eighths of the height of its falling movement, and it continues doing this little by little until it reaches the ground.

### ON THE MOVEMENT AGAINST THE WIND WITHOUT BEATING WINGS WHICH RAISES THE BIRD

Here the falling movement is below the wind, and the reflex movement will be above the wind.
