I find in the wings of birds three sources of power, of which the first is *b*, which derives its strength from the muscle *a*; the second is *d c*; the third is *f e*. Now I ask: if the part *g* produces its force by means of *f e*, what force penetrates to *b a*, or to put it more exactly, what weight?

The reflex movement made by the bird against the course of the wind becomes considerably greater than its falling movement; and it is the same with the succeeding reflex movement because it is driven by the same course of the wind.

# XVIII

## Flying Machine

> *'I find that if this device, constructed with a screw, is well made—that is to say, made of linen whose pores are sealed with starch—and is turned rapidly, the said screw will create its spiral in the air and will rise high.'*

The man in the bird rests on an axis slightly higher than his center of gravity.

A bird is a mechanism operating according to mathematical law; it is within the capacity of man to reproduce this mechanism with all its movements, though not with an equivalent degree of strength, as it is deficient only in the power of maintaining balance. We may therefore say that such a device constructed by man lacks nothing except the life of the bird, and this life must necessarily be supplied by the life of the man.

The life that resides within the bird’s own limbs will undoubtedly adapt to their needs better than the life of a man which is separate from them, especially regarding the almost imperceptible movements that preserve balance. But since we see that the bird is equipped for many obvious varieties of movement, we can declare from this experience that the most fundamental of these movements can be understood by man’s intellect; and that he will, to a great extent, be able to prevent the destruction of that mechanism of which he himself has become the living soul and the propeller.

[Diagrams of mechanism of flying machine]

I conclude that the upright position is more useful than lying face down, because the machine cannot be overturned, and furthermore, long-standing habit requires this.

# FLYING MACHINE

Therefore, by presenting and explaining the reasons for these things, you will be able to understand that when a man has large wings attached to him, he can overcome and subdue the air by exerting his strength against its resistance, allowing him to lift himself up upon it.

[*Sketch—man with parachute*]

If a person has a tent made of linen with all its openings sealed, and it is twelve *braccia* <note>original: "braccia"; an Italian unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm. Twelve braccia is approximately 23 feet.</note> wide and twelve deep, they will be able to throw themselves down from any great height without suffering any injury.

[*With drawing of pair of balances in one of which the figure of a man is seen raising a wing*]

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 381 verso a</margin>
If you wish to determine what weight will support this wing, place yourself on one side of a pair of scales and place an equal weight on the other so that the two scales are balanced in the air. Then, if you fasten yourself to the lever where the wing is and cut the rope holding it up, you will see it fall suddenly. If the wing normally takes two units of time to fall on its own, you can make it fall in just one unit by pulling the lever with your hands. You should then add enough weight to the opposite side of the scale so that the two sides become balanced against that force. Whatever weight is in the other scale is the amount that will support the wing as it flies—and it will support even more as it beats against the air more vigorously.

[*With drawings*]

The mechanism *a b c* causes the section *m n* to lift quickly during the upward stroke, while *d e f* causes *m n* to descend rapidly during the downward stroke; in this way, the wing performs its function.

Make the mesh of this net one-eighth [of a braccio] wide.
*A* should be made of young fir wood, which is light and still has its bark.

->With a drawing of the flying machine<-

*a* twists the wing, *b* turns it with a lever, *c* lowers it, and *d* raises it up. The operator who controls the machine places his feet at *f* and *d*; foot *f* lowers the wings, and foot *d* raises them.
The pivot *M* should have its center of gravity offset from the vertical line so that as the wings descend, they also move forward toward the man's feet; it is this specific motion that causes a bird to move forward.
This machine should be tested over a lake, and you should wear a long wineskin as a belt so that if you fall, you will not drown.
It is also necessary that the downward stroke of the wings be powered by both feet at the same time. This allows you to regulate the movement and maintain your balance by lowering one wing more rapidly than the other as needed, just as you can see done by the kite <note>original: "kite"; a common bird of prey known for its graceful flight and use of its tail and wings for steering.</note> and other birds. Additionally, the downward movement of both feet produces twice as much power as using only one, though the movement is proportionately slower.
The wings are raised by the force of a spring, or if you prefer, by hand or by drawing your feet toward you. This last method is best, because it leaves your hands free.

# XIX

## Movement and Weight

> *‘Force along with physical movement, and weight*
> *along with impact, are the four incidental powers*
> *in which all the works of mortals have their*
> *existence and their end.’*

SPEAK first of movement, then of weight because it is produced by movement, then of force which proceeds from weight and movement, then of impact which springs from weight, movement, and often from force.

The action of a pole drawn through still water resembles that of running water against a stationary pole.

Nothing that can be moved is more powerful in its simple movement than the force that moves it.

### WHERE THE SCIENCE OF WEIGHTS IS LED INTO ERROR BY PRACTICE

The science of weights is led into error by its practice, and in many instances practice is not in harmony with this science, nor is it possible to bring it into harmony. This is caused by the pivots of the balances by means of which the science of such weights is formed; according to the ancient philosophers, these pivots were placed by nature as the poles of a mathematical line and in some cases as mathematical points. These points and lines are devoid of substance, whereas practice gives them substance, since necessity constrains them to be substantial in order to support the weight of these balances together with the weights that are measured upon them.

I have found that the ancients were in error in their calculation of weights, and that this error has arisen because in a considerable part of

--- Page 516 ---
their science they have made use of poles that had substance, and in large part mathematical poles—that is, those that exist only in the mind or are without substance; these errors I set down here below.

### OF MOVEMENT AND WEIGHT

In equal movements made in equal time, the mover will always have more power than the object being moved. And the mover will be more powerful than the moved object in proportion to how much the movement of that object exceeds the length of the movement of its mover; and the difference between the power of the mover and that of the moved object will be less in proportion to how much the length of the movement made by the moved object is less than the movement of its mover.

But observe, reader, that in this case you must take into account the air, which becomes more condensed in front of the moved object as that object moves at a greater speed; for this air is capable of being condensed to an infinite degree. This, however, could not happen with movements made by objects moved within water, for water is not capable of being condensed. This may be proved by placing it in a vessel with a narrow mouth; for, lacking some external driving force, you will not be able to place within it more than the natural capacity the vessel can contain. It is exactly the opposite with air; for if it is forced into vessels with very narrow mouths that contain a quantity of water, and the vessel is tilted at such an angle that the water trapped inside is between the mouth of the vessel and the air that has been condensed, the power of the condensed air drives the water from the vessel with such fury that it penetrates through the air for some distance, until the air remaining in the vessel can return to its original natural state.

But to return to our proposition, we may say that among movable objects of the same gravity, the one that will move more slowly is the one whose front, as it cleaves the air, occupies more space; and conversely, it moves faster as it occupies less air—provided it does not extend itself to such a degree of thinness that its weight fails, for where there is no weight, there is no local movement through the air.

--- Page 517 ---
<meta>The text continues the discussion on the physics of movement, air resistance, and the density of mediums. The previous page established that air can be condensed while water cannot, which significantly affects how objects move through these different environments.</meta>

<page-num>505</page-num>
<header>MOVEMENT AND WEIGHT</header>

There can be no <term>local movement</term> <note>original: "local movement"; movement from one place to another</note> through the air unless it results from a difference in density—whether greater or less—compared to the density of the air itself.

If an opponent should argue that the <term>condensed air</term> <note>original: "condensed air"; air that has been compressed or made more dense by the force of an object striking it</note> created in front of a moving object is the same as the air in front of the mover (the person or thing throwing it), and that the mover creates even more condensation because it strikes a larger quantity of air than the object it throws—as we see with a hand when it throws a stone—the answer is this: it is impossible for the movement of the mover, when added to the movement of the object, to be either faster or slower than the object's own movement. Furthermore, at no point during its <term>accidental movement</term> <note>original: "accidental movement"; in Renaissance physics, this refers to the motion of a projectile after it has left the hand or machine that launched it, as opposed to "natural" motion like falling</note> can the object's speed equal the speed of its mover. This is proven because the object loses speed at every stage of its flight, even though its <term>percussion</term> <note>original: "percussion"; the force of impact</note> might be greater at a certain distance from the mover than it is when it is close at hand.

We can see this principle with an arrow shot from a bow. If the tip of the arrow is resting directly against a piece of wood, even if the string drives it with the full force of the bow, it will only penetrate the wood a very short distance. However, it does the opposite if it has some distance to move first. Some claim that a moving arrow pushes a wave of air ahead of itself, and that this wave somehow prevents the arrow's flight from being hindered. This is incorrect, however, because everything being moved exhausts and hinders its own mover. Therefore, the air that moves in waves in front of the arrow does so only because of the arrow's movement. It provides little or no help to the arrow (which is being moved by the same force); instead, it actually blocks and shortens the movement of the object.

The <term>impetus</term> <note>original: "impetus"; the momentum or force of a moving body</note> generated in still water has a different effect than that generated in still air. This is proven by the fact that water is never compressed by any movement made below its surface, whereas air is compressed when struck by a moving object. We can easily see this from the bubbles that fill the water from the surface to its bed. These cluster around as the water fills the <term>vacuum</term> <note>original: "vacuum"; here meaning the low-pressure area or empty space</note> that a fish leaves behind as it swims through. The movement of this water then strikes and drives the fish forward, because water only has weight within water when it is in motion.

<summary>Leonardo argues that air resistance and condensation hinder the flight of projectiles, rejecting the theory that "waves" of air help propel an object forward. He also notes a key difference in fluid dynamics: unlike air, water does not compress, but instead flows into the space behind a moving object to help drive it forward.</summary>

<margin>C.A. 117 r. c</margin>
I find that force is infinite when combined with time; and that weight is finite, limited by the weight of the entire globe of the earth's mechanism <note>original: "terrestrial machine"</note>.

I find that the smallest unit <note>original: "stroke of indivisible time"</note> of time is movement, and that this movement has many varieties: namely natural, accidental <note>original: "accidental movement"; in Renaissance physics, motion caused by an external force, like a projectile, as opposed to "natural" motion like falling</note>, and participating. This participating movement reaches its greatest power when it shifts from accidental to natural—that is, in the middle of its path. Natural movement is more powerful at its end than at any other point, while accidental movement is strongest in its third part and weakest at its conclusion.

Weight, force, impact <note>original: "a blow"</note>, and impetus <note>original: "impetus"; the momentum or driving force of a moving body</note> are the children of movement because they are born from it.

Weight and force always seek their own end <note>original: "desire their death"</note>, and each is sustained only by external force <note>original: "violence"</note>.

<margin>C.A. 123 r. a</margin>
Impetus is frequently the reason why movement continues to fulfill the "desire" of the object in motion <note>Leonardo often described inanimate objects as having a "desire" to reach a state of rest or their natural place</note>.

<margin>C.A. 124 r. a</margin>
In water of uniform weight, depth, width, and slope <note>original: "declivity"</note>, the part that moves fastest is the part nearest the surface. This occurs because the water on top is in contact with the air, which offers very little resistance because it is lighter than the water. The water below is in contact with the ground, which offers great resistance because it is immovable and heavier than water. It follows that the part furthest from this base has less resistance than the water above it, which is in contact with the air, for the air is light and mobile.

<margin>C.A. 131 r. b</margin>
Gravity and lightness <note>original: "levity"</note> are external <note>original: "accidental"</note> powers produced when one element is drawn through or driven into another.

No element possesses gravity or lightness when it is surrounded by its own kind <note>original: "within its own element"</note>.

<margin>C.A. 153 r. a</margin>
If the entire seabed were covered with men lying down, these men would support the entire weight of the element of water. Consequently, each man would find that he had a column of water a mile high upon his back. For if the whole sea is supported by its bed, each part of the bed must support its specific portion of the water.

<summary>Leonardo explores the relationship between movement, force, and weight, defining "accidental" and "natural" motion while analyzing the fluid dynamics of water and the pressure exerted by the sea.</summary>
<keywords>physics, mechanics, impetus, fluid dynamics, gravity, levity, atmospheric pressure, Codice Atlantico</keywords>

--- Page 519 ---
Impetus decreases gradually at every stage of time, and the prolongation of its essence is caused by the air or the water, which closes up behind the moving object, filling the vacuum left by the moving object as it penetrates the medium. This air is more powerful in striking and compressing the moving object through direct impact than the air positioned to resist the object's penetration by becoming compressed; it is this compression of the air that diminishes the intensity of the aforementioned impetus in the moving object.

Impetus is the impression of local movement transferred from the mover to the moving object and maintained by the air or the water as they move to prevent a vacuum.

The impetus of an object moving within water is different from the impetus of an object moving within air, and these differences result from the variations in the aforementioned liquids, because air can be compressed infinitely and water cannot.

The impetus of water is divided into two parts because it possesses two natures, one of which is simple and the other complex. The simple is entirely beneath the surface of the water; the other is complex—that is, it exists between the air and the water, as is seen with boats.

Simple impetus does not compress the water in front of a moving fish, but moves the water behind the fish at the same speed as the mover; the wave of water facing it will never be swifter than its mover.

But the movement of a boat, called complex movement because it involves both water and air, is divided into three chief parts because this movement is carried out in three directions: namely, against the river's current, in the direction of its current, and crosswise, along the width of the river.

If the movement of an oar or a wing is swifter than the water or air driven by them, the amount of movement remaining in the water or air is completed by the oar or wing in an opposite movement.

But if the movement of this water or air is inherently swifter than that of the oar or wing, then the oar and wing will not move against this water or air.

# MOVEMENT AND WEIGHT

<margin>C.A. 175 v. b <note>Codex Atlanticus, folio 175 verso, b.</note></margin>
If the movement of the water or the air is inherently as fast as the movement of the oar or the wing that moves within it, then the oar and wing will simply follow the movement of the water and the air.

<margin>C.A. 176 v. a</margin>
The compression generated by a flame—which intensifies within the resisting walls of a mortar <note>A short-barreled cannon used to fire projectiles at high angles.</note>—is what produces the violent movement of its ball. This impetus cannot be created with a less dense flame or a slower rate of expansion. Such a rapid increase in pressure cannot take place within walls that offer less resistance than those of this mortar. It follows, therefore, that as the flame rushes out of the mortar into the open air, it expands and loses its density and directness of course. It loses as much density as it gains in its expansion, and it ceases to drive the flight of the ball as soon as it begins to disperse...

<margin>C.A. 184 v. a</margin>
The movement of water within water behaves exactly like the movement of air within air.

Anything that descends freely acquires fresh momentum at every stage of its movement.

<margin>C.A. 202 v. b</margin>
If a certain force can move a body through a specific space in a specific time, it does not necessarily follow that half of this force will move the whole body over half the space in the same amount of time, or over the full space in double the time.

Movements are of [various] kinds. The first is called <term>temporal movement</term>, because it is concerned solely with the passage of time, and this encompasses all the others. The second is concerned with the life of things. The third is termed <term>mental movement</term>, and this resides in living bodies. The fourth is the movement of the images of things which spread through the air in straight lines; this class does not appear to be subject to time, for it is made indivisible in time <note>Leonardo refers here to the "species," or visual images, which he believed traveled instantaneously to the eye.</note>, and that which cannot be divided in the mind is not found among us. The fifth is that of sounds which travel through the air—which will be discussed later, as will smells and tastes—and this we may call <term>movement of the senses</term>. The other is called <term>material movement</term>, which is the subject of this treatise.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the mechanics of propulsion in water and air, the ballistics of mortar fire, and provides a systematic classification of movement ranging from the passage of time to physical mechanics.</summary>
<keywords>fluid dynamics, ballistics, mortar, momentum, physics of falling bodies, temporal movement, mental movement, material movement, Codex Atlanticus</keywords>

--- Page 521 ---
But we shall define movements simply as being of two kinds, of which one is material and the other incorporeal, because it is not perceptible to the sense of sight; or we may say that one is visible and the other invisible, although among the invisible movements there are a considerable number of material movements, such as the movement of Saturn, or as there would be with a series of revolving wheels. Therefore, we may say that the two kinds of movement are such that one is united with bodies and the other with the spirit. But among these movements, that of the images of things through the air is the swiftest, because it covers a great space in a very brief time; and this loses [strength] through distance, because the air thickens; the second swiftest is that of the mind.

Of the movements of the senses, we will only mention that of hearing because it operates in visible bodies and works by means of time, as is shown in noises, peals of thunder, sounds, and voices. Of smell, taste, and touch we will not speak, because they do not form part of our subject.

Also, one might speak of the influences of the planets and of God.

### THE HEAVIEST PART OF A MOVABLE BODY BECOMES THE LEADER OF ITS MOVEMENT

If a power moves a weight a certain distance in a certain time, the same power will move half of this weight double the distance in the same time.

Or this total power will move the entire weight half the distance in half the time; or the total power in the same time will move double the weight half the distance; or the total power in half the time will move the entire weight half the distance.

### WHAT IS IMPETUS?

Impetus is a power transmitted from the mover to the movable object, and maintained by the wave of air within the air which this mover produces; and this arises from the vacuum which would be produced contrary to natural law if the air in front of it did not fill up the vacuum, thereby causing the air which is driven from its place by—

--- Page 522 ---
the aforesaid mover to flee away. And the air that precedes it would not fill the space from which it is separated if it were not that another body of air filled the space from which this air was separated; and so, of necessity, it follows in succession. And this movement would continue to infinity if the air were capable of being compressed to infinity.

### WHAT DIFFERENCE THERE IS BETWEEN FORCE AND WEIGHT

Force is a spiritual essence which, by accidental violence, is joined to heavy bodies, restraining them from following their natural inclination; in this state, although it is of brief duration, it nevertheless often reveals itself to be of marvelous power.

[*A hymn to force*]
Force is entirely present in the whole of itself and entirely present in every part of itself.
Force is a spiritual capacity, an invisible power which is implanted by accidental violence in all bodies that are kept from their natural inclination.
Force is nothing other than a spiritual capacity, an invisible power which is created and implanted by accidental violence by sentient bodies into insentient ones, giving to these a semblance of life; and this life is marvelous in its operations, constraining and transforming the position and shape of all created things, rushing with fury toward its own destruction, and producing different effects in its course as the situation requires.
Delay makes it great, and speed makes it weak.
It lives by violence and dies by liberty.
It transforms and constrains every body with changes of position and form.
Great power gives it a great desire for death.
It drives away with fury whatever opposes its destruction.
Transmuter of various forms.
It lives always in hostility toward whatever controls it.
It always sets itself against natural desires.
From small beginnings, it slowly becomes larger and makes itself a terrifying and marvelous power.

. . . force is entirely present in the whole, and entirely present in every part of the body where it is produced.
. . . Power <note>original: *potenza*</note> is only a desire for flight.
It always desires to grow weak and to spend itself.
When force is constrained, it constrains every body.
Without it, nothing moves.
Without it, no sound or voice is heard.
Its true seed is in sentient <note>In this context, "sentient" refers to living beings capable of movement.</note> bodies.
Weight is entirely present in its vertical obstacle and entirely present in every part of it.
If the slanted <note>original: "oblique"</note> obstacle opposed to the weight is loosened and free, it will offer no resistance to this weight but will fall down with it in ruin.
Weight naturally moves toward its desired position.
Every part of this force contains the whole, opposing weight.
And often, force and weight are victors over one another.
They are both subject to the same natural law, and the more powerful conquers the less.
Weight changes its position unwillingly, and force is always on the point of fleeing.
Weight is physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> and force is non-physical <note>original: "incorporeal"</note>.
Weight is material and force is spiritual <note>In Leonardo’s scientific writings, "spiritual" refers to an invisible, active energy or "power," rather than a religious concept.</note>.
If the one desires flight from itself and death, the other wishes for stability and permanence.
They are often producers of one another:
As weight brings forth force, and force brings forth weight.
As weight conquers force, and force conquers weight.
And if they are of a similar nature, they remain together for a long time.
If the one is eternal, the other is fleeting.

### Force

Force cannot exist in physical bodies without either force or weight combined with movement.

Force is caused by violent <note>In Renaissance physics, "violent" movement refers to motion caused by an external power, as opposed to the "natural" motion of an object falling toward the Earth.</note> movement through weight or another force.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 314 v. b</margin>
If an object in continuous motion is given fresh momentum by a greater movement, the object redoubles its velocity. For example, consider a revolving wheel, such as a potter’s lathe: by adding the movement of the foot, the wheel turns faster. Similarly, if a ball moving in a certain direction is struck by a player along the same line of its movement, that movement will be accelerated.

## THE MOVEMENT OF A HEAVY SUBSTANCE

The movement made by a heavy spherical object through the air.

There are two types of movement that a heavy spherical object can make in the air: one is called simple and the other compound. Simple movement is that in which the surface of the moving object moves at the same rate as its center. Compound movement is that in which the surface of the moving object moves faster than its center <note>Leonardo is describing the physics of a spinning object; in a rotating ball, the surface travels a greater distance than the center point in the same amount of time.</note>.

### *Simple movement*

Simple movement is that in which every part of the moving object moves equally.

In compound movement, no part moves at a speed equal to the whole, except for the diameter which serves as the axis for the revolving movement <note>Leonardo is referring to the stationary axis around which a body rotates.</note>.

<summary>Leonardo examines the mathematical relationship between force and distance in ballistics and defines the difference between linear motion (simple) and rotational motion (compound).</summary>

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 315 recto a</margin>
Compound movement <note>In Leonardo's physics, "compound movement" usually refers to an object that is both moving forward and rotating.</note> takes on as many different forms as there are different sides with which it strikes against the obstacles in its path.

Simple movement <note>Movement where the object does not rotate; all parts move at the same speed as the center.</note> is changed into compound movement if its motion is hindered on any of its sides.

Over a long distance, compound movement made in the air settles into simple movement. This fact makes it more certain that the cause of simple movement is also the cause of compound movement. This is demonstrated in every wheel to which a revolving momentum is given, for it lasts only a short time and is constantly decreasing.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 315 recto b</margin>
Every forceful movement <note>original: "impetuous movement"</note> bends toward the path of least resistance as it flees from the greater resistance.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 316 verso b</margin>
Force is generated by the movement of the lever against its counter-lever, and through this, it is infused into the bodies it moves.

Every heavy object that is not held back from its natural place <note>In the Aristotelian view held in the Renaissance, the "natural place" for heavy things was the center of the Earth.</note> tends to descend more in a straight line than in a curve <note>original: "by a direct line than by an arc"</note>. This is shown because every body, whatever it may be, that is away from its natural place (which preserves it), seeks to regain its original state in the shortest possible time. Since a straight line <note>original: "chord"</note> is shorter than a curve <note>original: "arc"</note> between the same two points, it follows that every body away from its natural place seeks to descend more quickly by a straight line than by a curve.

From this, three things follow:
1. The movement of gravity in a balance scale is not entirely natural. This is evident because the arms of this balance describe a curve as they descend, and consequently create curved lines.
2. The movement of weight in the descending arm of the balance is not entirely "violent" <note>In this context, "violent" means movement caused by an external force rather than gravity.</note>, since in this manner it acquires natural movement as it falls.
3. The movement of weight in the balance is halfway between the natural and the violent.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 335 verso f</margin>
This is evident, seeing that every natural movement is either violent or indeed is beyond nature.

Among bodies made of different substances but having a similar shape, the one with the most weight descends most rapidly. <note>Leonardo here follows the traditional view of physics before Galileo, which suggested heavier objects fall faster—an observation that often appears true in the air due to wind resistance.</note>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes how simple and compound motions are affected by resistance and describes the movement of a balance scale as a hybrid of "natural" gravity and "violent" mechanical force.</summary>

### *Proposition*

A spherical and heavy body moves most slowly when its point of contact with the surface it touches is closest to the perpendicular line drawn from its center.

### *Weight*

The center of every weight lies on a perpendicular line with the center of its support.

When a man, whether standing or sitting, takes a weight in his arms, the support on which he rests must be positioned in the middle between this weight and himself.

It is impossible for the force exerted by a man’s arm, along with the weight it supports, to extend beyond an upright position without the counter-action of the aforementioned opposite weight.

Suppose you were to say: "I wish to lean my entire back against a wall and sit on the ground with my legs extended so that my legs and back touch the entire corner; I will then take a weight in my hands, bring it near to me, and move it away using only the force of my arms. I will not move my back, my head, or any part of my body to create a counterweight to the weight moved by my arms, and yet this will be done effectively."

To this I reply that the effect the force exerts in this case will serve no other function than to keep the arms joined to the torso, as if they lacked flexible joints and were a single piece. This makes the body like an iron bar bent at two right angles, where the end of the upper part aligns perpendicularly with the middle of the base or the opposite lower part; if a heavy burden is placed upon this upper end, the weight will exert its force directly downward upon the perpendicular line of its base.

A man about to deliver a powerful blow with his arms positions himself so that all his power is on the side opposite to the place he intends to strike, for the object that moves the most exerts the most power upon the object that resists the movement.

Every impression is preserved for a time in the object that senses it; and that which possessed greater power will be preserved in its ob—

--- Page 527 ---
<header>MOVEMENT AND WEIGHT</header>
<page-num>515</page-num>

ject for a longer time, and for a shorter time with the less powerful.

In this connection, I apply the term <term>sensitive</term> to any object that is changed by an impression from what was originally an <term>insensitive</term> object—that is, one which, while changing from its original state, preserves within itself no impression of the thing that moved it. A sensible impression is like a blow received by a resonant substance, such as bells and similar things, or like a musical note in the ear. Indeed, unless the ear preserved the impression of the notes, it could never derive pleasure from hearing a voice alone; for when the voice passes immediately from the first to the fifth note, the effect is as though one heard these two notes at the same time, and thus perceived the true <term>harmony</term> that the first makes with the fifth. But if the impression of the first note did not remain in the ear for a noticeable amount of time, the fifth, which follows immediately after the first, would seem to stand alone; one note cannot create any harmony, and consequently, any song whatsoever occurring as a single note would seem to be devoid of charm.

So, too, the radiance of the sun or another luminous body remains in the eye for some time after it has been seen; and the motion of a single firebrand whirled rapidly in a circle causes this circle to appear as one continuous and uniform flame.

The drops of rainwater seem like continuous threads descending from the clouds; and so, in this, one may see how the eye preserves the impressions of the moving things it sees.

The insensitive objects that do not preserve the impressions of the things opposite to them are mirrors and any polished substance; as soon as the thing of which it bears the impression is removed from before it, the substance is at once entirely deprived of that impression. We may, therefore, conclude that it is the action of the mover pressing against the body it moves which drives this body in the direction in which it travels.

Among the cases of impressions being preserved in various bodies, we may also cite the wave, the eddies of water, the winds in the air, and a knife stuck into a table. When the knife is bent in one direction and then released, it retains a quivering movement for a long time; all its movements are reciprocal to one another, and all may be said to be approaching the <term>perpendicular</term> of the surface where the knife is fixed by its point.

The impact of liquid with solid bodies is of a different character from the above-mentioned cases of impact; and the impact of liquid with liquid also varies from the preceding examples.

An example of the impact of solid with liquid is seen on the shores of the ocean, which receive the waters full upon their rocks and hurl them against the steep crags; and it often happens that before the course of the wave is half completed, the stones carried by it return to the sea from which they came; and their power of destruction is increased by the force of the wave which falls back from the lofty cliffs.

<margin>C.A. 395 r. b</margin>

No element, when united, will have weight within its own element; therefore, the upper parts of the air do not weigh upon the lower parts.

No body of a different quality will come to rest within this air if it is at liberty, because as this body does not have the same quality as the air, it must necessarily be either heavier or lighter; and if it is heavier it will drop down, and if lighter it will penetrate upward.

The object that has the most similarity to the element surrounding it will move through it with the slowest motion.

And the object that is most unlike its surrounding element will separate itself from it with more forceful movement.

When a force generates movement swifter than the flight of the unresisting air, this air becomes compressed in the same way that feathers are pressed and crushed by the weight of a sleeper. And the object that drove the air, finding resistance in it, rebounds like a ball struck against a wall.

The line that is straightest offers the most resistance.

An object that, within a level line, finds itself at a greater distance from its support will be less sustained by it, as is shown below in *m n*.

An object that is at a greater distance from its support will be less sustained by it, and consequently will fulfill its natural inclination with greater freedom.

Violent movement grows weaker the more it is exerted; natural movement does the opposite.

An object that is at a greater distance from its support will be less sustained by it; being less sustained, it will possess more of its freedom, and since a weight that is free always descends, the object, being heavy, will therefore descend more swiftly.

The part of a pole which is farther from its support will be less sustained by that support. Being less sustained, it continues to follow its nature more freely; and since this part is heavy, and the nature of heavy things is to desire to descend, it will therefore descend more swiftly than any other part.

The air is capable of compression and water is not; and when the movements that drive the air are swifter than the flight of this air, the part that is most caught by its mover becomes denser and consequently offers more resistance. When the movement made in the air is more rapid than the escaping power of this air, its mover ends up taking a contrary movement. This is shown in the case of birds, which are not able to drive the tips of their wings downward with the same speed at which they themselves are moving, because their motive power moves them...

The bird raises itself up to the same degree that the tip of its wing fails to go down. This is similar to a man who keeps his hands and chest close to a wall and presses his hands against it; if the wall does not give way, the man must necessarily be pushed backward.

### ON THE BLOW

Every object hit against a resisting surface leaps back from that surface at an angle equal to the angle of impact.

The same is proved in the tenth proposition of the book concerning the nature of the blow, where it discusses a ball struck against a wall. ### AGAINST PERPETUAL MOTION

No inanimate object will move on its own; consequently, when it is in motion, it is moved by an unequal power—unequal in terms of time and velocity, or unequal in weight. When the impulse of the first motive power ceases, the second will cease abruptly.

--- Page 531 ---
Every spherical body with a thick and resisting surface, when moved by a specific force, will travel as far through the rebounds caused by its impact upon a solid ground as if it were thrown freely through the air.

How admirable is Your justice, O You First Mover! You have not willed that any power should lack the processes or qualities necessary for its results; for if a force has the capacity to drive an object it has mastered a distance of one hundred braccia, and this object, while obeying that force, meets with some obstacle, You have ordained that the force of the impact will cause a new movement which, through various rebounds, will complete the entire distance it was meant to traverse.

And if you were to measure the path made by these bounces, you will discover it to be of the same length as it would be if a similar object were propelled freely through the air by the same force.

You may conduct an experiment of this with a small glass ball as it strikes a surface of smooth, polished stone. Take a long staff and mark it with different colors from end to end, then give it to someone to hold, and position yourself at some distance away to watch the rebounds. Observe against the height of the staff which colors the ball reaches successively with each rebound, and make a note of them. If there are as many observers as there are rebounds, each person will remember the height more easily. However, either have the staff fixed at the top or with its base in a hole, for if someone held it with their hand, they would obstruct the judge's line of sight. Arrange it so that the first bounce occurs between two right angles so that the ball always falls in the same spot, because then the height of the rebounds against the staff can be more accurately perceived.

Then have this ball discharged by the same power in a free course and make a note of the spot where it hits; measure it, and you will find that the length of the second course is identical to the first.

If you were in a boat and exerted your utmost force there, the boat would never move from its position unless that force met a greater obstacle outside the boat than the one created within it.

Again, if you are all huddled up in a sack and make efforts within it...

## WHAT IS FORCE?

<margin>A 34 v.</margin>
Force I define as an incorporeal agency, an invisible power, which by means of unforeseen external pressure is caused by the movement stored up and diffused within bodies that are withheld and turned aside from their natural uses; imparting to these an active life of marvelous power, it compels all created things to change their form and position, and hastens furiously toward its desired death, changing as it goes according to circumstances. When it is slow its strength is increased, and speed weakens it. It is born in violence and dies in liberty; and the greater it is, the more quickly it is consumed. It drives away in fury whatever opposes its destruction. It desires to conquer and slay the cause of opposition, and in conquering, it destroys itself. It grows more powerful where it finds the greater obstacle. Everything instinctively flees from death. Everything, when under constraint, itself constrains other things. Without force, nothing moves.

The body in which it is born grows neither in weight nor in form. None of the movements that it makes are lasting.

It increases by effort and disappears when at rest. The body within which it is confined is deprived of liberty. Often also, by its movement, it generates new force.

Every weight desires to descend to the center by the shortest way; and where there is the greater weight, there is the greater desire. And that thing which weighs the most, if it is left free, falls the most.

--- Page 533 ---
<page-num>521</page-num>
<header>MOVEMENT AND WEIGHT</header>

rapidly. The less the slant of the opposing substance, the greater its resistance. But weight passes by nature into all that supports it, and thus penetrating from support to support, it grows heavier as it passes from body to body until it realizes its desire. Necessity draws it and abundance drives it away. It is entirely present in its vertical opposition and entirely present in each of its degrees. And that opposition which slants the most will not offer resistance to its descent, but, being free, will fall together with it. In its function of pressing and making things heavy, it is like force. Weight is subdued by force, just as force is by weight. One can see weight without force, but one cannot see force without weight. If weight has no neighbor, it seeks one with fury, and force drives it away with fury. If weight desires an unchangeable position, force readily flies from it. If weight desires stability and force is always desirous of flight, weight of itself is without fatigue, while force is never exempt from it.

<margin>A 35 r.</margin>
The more weight falls, the more it increases; and the more force falls, the more it diminishes. If one is eternal, the other is mortal. Weight is natural and force is accidental. Weight desires stability and permanence, and force desires flight and its own death. Weight, force, and a blow resemble each other in respect to pressure.

In the center of the direct path taken by heavy bodies which traverse the air with violent movement, there is greater power and greater striking force when an obstacle is met than in any other part of its line of travel.

The reason for this is that when the weight separates from the force of its mover, although this separation is in the initial stage of its power, it nevertheless finds the air without movement and finds it in the initial stage of its resistance; and although the sum total of the air's resistance is greater than the power of the weight pushed upon it, nevertheless, as it strikes only a small part, it succeeds in remaining the conqueror. Consequently, it drives the air from its place, and in so driving it, it somewhat impedes its own velocity. This air, therefore, after having been pushed, pushes and drives the other air, and generates revolving movements in its wake, of which the weight moved within it is always the center—after the fashion of circles formed in water, which have their center at the spot struck by the stone. And so, as one circle drives the other, all the air along the line in front

As its course changes, the air (which was "fleeting" or moving out of the way to prepare a path for its flight) no longer supports it. However, the more it drops, the more it encounters fresh resistance in the air and the more it slows down, until the point at which it resumes its natural movement <note>natural movement: the author refers to the downward acceleration caused by gravity as "natural," as opposed to the "violent" horizontal movement caused by a machine or thrower</note> and acquires fresh speed. In the same way, a barge slows down as it turns. 

Now, therefore, I conclude (according to what is demonstrated in the eighth proposition <note>eighth proposition: likely a reference to a specific theorem in the author's own organized notes on mechanics or physics</note>) that the part of the movement occurring between the first resistance of the air and the beginning of the object's drop is the most powerful. This is the center of the path made through the air in a straight, direct line.

### OF THE BLOW AND THE DISPLACEMENT CAUSED BY WEIGHT OR BY FORCE

I maintain that the displacement <note>displacement: in this context, the impact or the "dent" made in an object when it is struck</note> caused by a falling weight is equal to the displacement caused by force.

A body that receives a blow is not injured on the side opposite the impact as much as it is on the part that is actually struck. Proof of this is seen when a stone is struck while lying in a person's hands: the hand is not injured as much when holding the stone that is struck as it would be if the hand itself actually received the blow.

I affirm that the movement mentioned above is based upon several points of support.

Force is produced by the shortening and contraction of the muscles.

### OF THE NATURE OF MOVEMENT

If a wheel whose movement has become very rapid continues to make many revolutions after its motive power has abandoned it, then if this motive power continues to cause it to turn with the same speed of movement, it would seem that this continuation requires but little force.

And I conclude that in order to maintain this movement, only a slight effort by the motive power would be needed, and all the more so because by nature it tends to become stationary.

### CONCERNING WEIGHTS

I ask: if a weight of one pound falling two braccia buries itself in the earth to the depth of a hand, how deeply will it bury itself if it falls forty braccia, and how far will a weight of two pounds bury itself if it falls two braccia?

One may also ask: if the size of this weight is represented by a quantity *a* and then this quantity is doubled, while its weight remains the same and it falls from the same height, how much greater an impression will the smaller bulk make than the larger if the ground offers equal resistance?

### EXAMPLE OF THE BLOW AND OF THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN WEIGHT AND FORCE

The blow, since it is of very short and even of indivisible duration, suddenly produces its full and quick effect upon what opposes it, and this effect ends before it reaches the base of the object struck. For this reason, therefore, you will find more expansion at the top of the object struck than at its base. And if you wish to determine how much greater the power of the blow is upon the object struck at its top than at its base, calculate how many times the circumference of the base *m n* will go into that of the top *a c*; as many times as *m n*

## *The Blow*

<margin>c 7 r.</margin>
Since the blow is swifter than the movement, the object touched by the blow, even though it may be in motion, will obey the effect of this blow rather than that which accelerates the movement.

<margin>c 7 v.</margin>
If two people make the same journey in the same amount of time, the one who runs often, with frequent intervals for rest, will undergo as much fatigue as the one who travels gently and continuously.

## *Percussion*

<margin>c 15 r.</margin>
If two balls strike together at a right angle, one will deviate more from its original course than the other in proportion to how much smaller it is than the other.

The part of a log first severed from its end by the stroke of an axe flies off to a greater distance than any other part carried away by the same blow.

This is because the part of the log that first receives the blow receives it during the first stage of its power and consequently goes farther. The second part flies a shorter distance because the fury of the blow has already subsided, the third still less, and the fourth likewise.

The wood which is divided from the rest by the stroke of the axe will fly off with greater violence at one time than at another, just as the stroke is more powerful at one time than another, and the piece will fly off to a greater distance. This is because the blow is the most powerful and instantaneous thing that a man can do, as is shown in the fourth proposition which treats of the nature of the blow; when the axe—driven by man's strength and by the movement of the hands in falling—has entered within the surface of the close-grained wood due to the weight and blow of the hatchet, as soon as this fine edge has entered, the thick part of the hatchet immediately follows and proceeds with such

Water, air, and fire produce the same effect when they rebound from objects that oppose their course. A piece of wood separated from the rest by the blow of an axe will fly off from it at an angle equal to that of the blow.

<margin>C 22 v.</margin>
Every object with a solid surface that falls upon a resistant object will have a line of rebound at the same angle as its line of incidence <note>incidence: the angle at which an object hits a surface</note>.

->*Movement and percussion*<-

Among bodies of equal speed and size, the one with greater weight will deliver a more powerful blow <note>original: "percussion"</note> to the object that opposes its course. Since turbid <note>original: "turbid"; cloudy or muddy</note> water is heavier than clear water, the blow it delivers against an object opposing its course will be greater.

->*Movement of water*<-

An object with a thicker, harder surface will cause objects that strike it to bounce away with a more powerful and rapid rebound.

->*Water*<-

Water falling upon gravel mixed with sand and earth will hollow it out more deeply and rapidly—for the reason mentioned above—than if it fell upon plain soft mud. This is because when it falls upon gravel, it takes a swift, powerful leap and erodes <note>original: "gnaws away"</note> more of the material that first opposes its bounce, rising higher.

<margin>c 28 r.</margin>
The angle caused by the impact of equal spherical bodies is always equal to the angle of the rebound.

<margin>c 28 v.</margin>
Every weight tends to fall toward the center <note>the center of the Earth</note> by the shortest route.

<header>MOVEMENT AND WEIGHT</header>

## OF HUMAN MOVEMENT

<margin>E 15 r.</margin>
When you wish to represent a man in the act of moving a weight, consider that these movements are made in different directions. For instance, there is the simple movement from the ground upward, such as when a man stoops to lift a weight with the intention of raising it as he straightens his body. Other movements occur when he wishes to pull something backward, push it forward, or draw it down using a rope that passes over a pulley. In these cases, one should remember that a man’s weight pulls in proportion to how far his center of gravity is from his point of support. To this must be added the force exerted by his legs and bent spine as he straightens himself up.

<margin>E 20 v.</margin>
The mover <note>the source of force or the person/object initiating movement</note> is always more powerful than the thing being moved.

### Of the knowledge of weights proportioned to the forces of their movers:

<margin>E 28 v.</margin>
The force of the mover should always be proportional to the weight of the object it moves and the resistance of the medium (such as air or water) through which that weight travels. However, one cannot deduce the law of this action unless one first determines the amount of air compression <note>original: "condensation"</note> created when it is struck by any moving object. This compression will be more or less dense according to the speed of the moving object pressing against it. This is demonstrated in the flight of birds: the sound they make with their wings as they beat the air is deeper or more high-pitched <note>original: "shrill"</note> depending on whether the movement of the wings is slower or faster.

<margin>E 32 v.</margin>
The weight of every suspended heavy object is distributed throughout the entire length of the cord that supports it, and is present in every part of that cord.

## OF COMPOUND IMPETUS

**Compound impetus** <note>impetus: the force or momentum of a moving body</note> is the name given to movement that shares in the momentum of both the mover and the object moved. An example is the movement path *f b c*, which exists between two simple movements—one located near the beginning of the motion and the other near the end, marked *a g*.

is the first and *d e c* is at the end. But only the first obeys the mover, and the last is only the likeness of the thing moved.

## OF IRREGULAR IMPETUS

The irregular [composite] impetus accompanies the moved object with three kinds of momentum, two of which arise from the mover and the third from the object itself. The two that originate in the mover are the straight movement of the mover combined with the curved movement of the object; the third is the simple movement of the object, which tends merely to rotate at the center of its curve where it contacts the surface upon which it turns and settles.

## FRICTION

Friction is divided into three types: simple, compound, and irregular.

Simple friction is that created by the object upon the surface where it is dragged. Compound friction is that which the object creates between two immovable things. Irregular friction is that created by corners of different sides.

## OF THE WEIGHT DISTRIBUTED OVER THE LENGTH OF THE CORD WHICH SUPPORTS IT

A weight distributed over the entire length of the cord supporting it will place less strain on that cord than if it were suspended from its lowest point; this is proven by one of the *Elements*, which states: "Among cords of equal thickness, the longest is the weakest."

Consequently, the cord *a b*, which supports the weight distributed over the rest of the cord *b t*, is stronger than the opposite part of the cord *a c* in proportion to how much shorter it is.

One cord supports as many times the weight of another as the number of curves in the one exceeds the number in the other.

The division made by a cord with its pulley is never perfectly rectangular; this is proven by the fact that two simple cords hanging from the same pulley would eventually meet at the center of the earth.

### THE DIVISION OF WEIGHT

There are three conditions of weight <note>original: "gravity"</note>: the first is its simple natural weight, the second is its accidental weight <note>weight or force generated by motion, position, or leverage</note>, and the third is the friction produced by it. Natural weight is in itself unchangeable. Accidental weight, which is joined to it, can exert infinite force, and friction varies according to the places where it occurs—specifically, whether the surfaces are rough or smooth.

### DEFINITION OF COMPOUND BALANCES

We may define the nature of compound balances <note>mechanical systems like levers or pulleys</note> both in terms of circular balances—that is to say, pulleys and wheels—and also straight-line <note>original: "rectilinear"</note> balances. But first, I will perform an experiment before proceeding further, because it is my intention first to cite experience <note>here meaning "experimental observation"</note> and then to show through reasoning why this experience is forced to act in this manner. 

This is the rule that researchers <note>original: "speculators"</note> of natural effects must follow. Although nature begins with logic <note>original: "reason"</note> and ends in physical results <note>original: "experience"</note>, it is necessary for us to do the opposite: that is, to begin, as I said before, with experience and from there proceed to investigate the underlying reason.

I observe that in the compound straight-line balance, the second demonstration shows that for as much as one of the ends descends, the opposite end rises by the same amount; the cause of this is the equal length of their arms.

### ON WEIGHT AND ITS SUPPORTS

Weight <note>original: "gravity"</note> that is suspended or supported is felt entirely by its support and entirely by each part of that support.

A cord bent over a pulley supports more weight at its hanging ends than when it is stretched out in a continuous straight line. This may be proven as follows: suppose the cord bent over the pulley is marked *d c e f* and the ultimate limit of its resistance <note>breaking strength</note> is represented by 10. I claim that if the same cord is stretched straight, as shown at *a b*, it will not support more than five.

### WHAT PART OF THE CURVED CORD IS STRONGEST

<margin>E 55 v.</margin>
The maximum strength of the curved cord is in the middle of its bend. This is proven by the eighth [proposition] of this [treatise], which says: "That cord is strongest which is thickest." It follows that as the cord is compressed in its fold over the pulley where it is bent, it becomes widened and flattens <note>original: "lowers itself"</note> a little; for this reason, necessity constrains it to become thus compressed.

### OF MOVEMENT MADE BY A HEAVY OBJECT <note>original: "heavy substance"</note>

Every heavy object moves toward the side on which it weighs most.

And the movement of a heavy object is made toward the side where it encounters the least resistance.

The heaviest part of bodies that move through the air becomes the guide of their movements.

A heavy object descends more slowly through the air when it falls with its greatest width <note>meaning it presents its broadest surface to the air resistance</note>.

It follows that the heavy object will have the swiftest descent when it confines itself within the narrowest width.

The free descent of every heavy object is made along the line of its greatest diameter <note>meaning it naturally aligns its longest axis with the direction of the fall</note>.

The heavy object will be swiftest in movement when it reduces itself to the smallest volume <note>original: "bulk"</note>.

<margin>E 57 r.</margin>
The descent of a heavy object is slower in proportion to how much it extends in greater breadth.

### [Gravity and movement. Balances]

According to what is stated below, the balance does not exert all of its natural weight upon the center of its revolution; rather, it exerts as much less weight as the weight moving the upper arm has a more slanted movement, as is proven in this discourse.

The heavy substance in suspension exists entirely as a whole and entirely in every part of the center line of its support.

A staff placed at an angle has two kinds of gravity, one of which weighs diagonally between the center of the earth and the horizon. The other weighs vertically toward the center of the earth. One of these is accidental and the other is natural. This occurs where the mathematical center is not the center of the revolution of the balance. This is proven as follows: let *a b c d* be the balance and *s* its mathematical center; the center of the revolution will be *f*. I assert that when the balance is in such a position, the mathematical center *s* is in the same line that points toward the center of the earth—that is, *g h*—as the center of the revolution *f*, and this line *g h* divides the staff of the balance into two equal and similar parts, namely the part *a b e f* and the part *c d e f*. Whether one wishes to rest the balance upon point *s* or point *f* is immaterial, for both the one point and the other are in the central line *g h* which divides the weight equally.

There still remains the above-mentioned slanted weight which is above the center of the revolution *f*—that is, the weight which is above the line *n o*, which is *a b r f*—to which the counterweight *c d r f* offers no resistance in the above-mentioned slanted movement.

The power of the mover is always greater than the resistance of the thing moved.

### WEIGHT AND FORCE

The potential lever will never be exhausted by any power.

Whatever is divisible in reality is also divisible in potential; however, it is not the case that everything divisible in potential is divisible in reality. And if the divisions made potentially toward infinity change the substance of the divided matter, these divisions will return to the composition of their whole, the parts reuniting in the same stages in which they were divided. The force will be of greater effectiveness <note>original: "excellence"</note> as the potential lever is smaller in quantity.

### OF GRAVITY

It is impossible for the power of any motive force to be able, at the same time and with the same movement, to create a power greater than itself. This is proved by the third rule of this work, which says: "Powers that are equal to each other do not overcome each other."

If two cords of different lengths descend with their slants converging or diverging to the point of suspension at the ends of the beam, then if this beam is level, the slants of the two aforementioned cords will be equal to one another.

What is gravity, and whether it is natural or accidental—and one may ask the same concerning levity:

The answer is that both are accidental powers because each always awaits its own destruction, and one is never born or dies without the other. This is proved by the air that forms in the shape of a bubble or bladder at the bottom of the water; the very fact of its formation immediately creates its levity and creates the weight of the water above it. As soon as the bubble reaches the surface, its levity dies along with the gravity of the water that was above it.

### [Of a heavy body]

If the angle formed by the meeting of two cords that support a weight is divided by the <term>intercentric line</term> <note>intercentric line: a line connecting the centers of gravity of two bodies, or in this case, the line of force passing through the center of the weight</note> of this weight, then this angle is divided into two other angles. As these are divided again by the line of equilibrium <note>original: "line of the equality," referring to a horizontal level</note>, two triangles are produced. These triangles will have the same proportion between their bases as exists between their angles; they will also have the same proportion between their angles as exists between the triangles themselves. Furthermore, the proportion of one triangle to another is the same as the proportion of gravity to gravity—that is, the way the weight of the heavy substance is divided between the two cords by which it is suspended. However, this proportion is in an inverse ratio, because the greatest weight falls on the cord which forms the outer side of the smaller triangle.

How many centers does a heavy body have if it is not uniform?
There are three centers for a weight that is "uniformly irregular" <note>meaning a non-uniform object where the variation in density follows a consistent pattern</note>:
1. The first is the <term>center of natural gravity</term> <note>The inherent center of mass of the object itself</note>.
2. The second is the <term>center of accidental gravity</term> <note>Gravity caused by the object's position, motion, or external forces</note>.
3. The third is the <term>center of magnitude</term> <note>The geometric center of the object's physical volume or shape</note>.

However, the center of natural gravity does not align with the point of equilibrium if the heavy body is not uniform in weight and of a symmetrical shape, such as a sphere, a rectangular block <note>original: "parallel body"</note>, or other similar shapes.

The air becomes compressed <note>original: "condensed"</note> in front of bodies that penetrate it swiftly, acquiring more or less density depending on whether the speed is more or less violent.
