## [*Of the descent of heavy bodies in the air*]

### Conception

The air becomes as much more rarefied behind the movement of the movable thing as it becomes denser in front of the same movable thing.

Why the slanting descent does not keep its straightness.

The straight line of the oblique descent made by bodies of uniform thickness and weight in air of equal resistance will not be continued by a heavy substance that descends. And this is due to the fact that the air is pressed by the surface of the heavy substance that is penetrating it, and becomes condensed, resisting and stopping this surface; consequently, the opposite surface of this heavy substance, finding itself in rarefied air, immediately acquires gravity and falls with more speed than the side which is retarded by the thickness of the air condensed by it. And for this reason, the impetus to the right made by the movable thing is turned to the left, preserving its slant, up to the point at which the other air is condensed anew beneath it; this air again resists and again turns the left slanting descent to a right descent, then from right to left and from left to right until the point at which the movement ends.

The descent of the beam placed in any slanting position will always be made in a straight line. This is proved by the seventh rule of this work which says:—'Heavy substances of uniform shape and weight which descend through a uniform medium will have the same rate of speed'. If therefore a beam of uniform shape and weight be divided into equal and similar parts...

--- Page 549 ---
parts, their descent will be of equal and similar speed, and what the part does, the whole will do.

The opponent says that the whole beam united will not have a descent similar to the descent of its divided parts, because the whole gives the entirety of its weight slanting toward the lower surface, while the part gives the entirety of its weight to the surface of the part; and there is the same speed from surface to surface as there is from the whole to the part.

### OF BODIES NOT UNIFORM IN SHAPE

Of heavy substances not uniform in shape, the heavier part will always become the guide of their descent through the air.

With beams of uniform shape, at the end of the movement, the movable object will have always preserved the same slanting position that it had at the beginning of the movement.

This is proved by means of the beam suspended on the balance *n m*. The heavy substance weighs as much less in the air as its movement is more slanting.

And the straight descent of the beam weighs as much less in the air as this beam is less slanting.

### OF THINGS THAT DESCEND IN THE AIR

A heavy substance of uniform thickness and weight, placed in a position of equilibrium, will have a straight descent with equal height in each of its parts without ever deviating from the position of its first equilibrium, provided the air is motionless and of uniform resistance; and this movement will be very slow, as will be proved.

But if the heavy substance of uniform thickness is situated slantwise in air of uniform resistance, then its descent will be made slantwise, and it will be more rapid than the first one mentioned above.

### OF THE WEIGHING OF LIQUIDS

[Figure]

The balance *a e g* is formed of two tubes joined at an angle in the lower part, and the water that is enclosed within them is joined, having in one arm a quantity of oil and in the other plain water.

--- Page 550 ---
I say that the water level in one tube and the other will not remain at an equal height, nor will the surface of the oil be level with the surface of the water placed in the opposite tube. This is proven because oil is less heavy than water, and for this reason it remains above the water; its weight, combined in the same tube with the weight of the water beneath it, balances the weight of the water acting as a counterweight in the opposite tube. But since it is stated that oil is less heavy than water, it is necessary—if one wishes to create an equivalent to the weight of the water that is missing beneath it—that there should be a greater quantity of oil than of the water that is missing, and consequently it occupies more space in this tube than an equivalent weight of water would have occupied. Therefore, the surface of the oil in its tube is higher than the surface of the water in the opposite tube, and the surface of the water beneath the oil is lower than the surface of the water opposite.

## ON THE DESCENT OF HEAVY BODIES

Among heavy bodies that are not flexible and are of equal weight to one another, the proportion between the speed of their descent will be the same as the proportion of their uniform bulk.

*Whether the air that surrounds bodies moves together with these bodies.*

The air that surrounds bodies moves together with these bodies: experience shows us this when a horse runs along dusty roads.

*Whether the movement of the air is as swift as its mover.*

The air will never have a speed equal to that of its mover; this is shown to us by the movements of the dust I have already mentioned, which follows the path of the horse, for after having moved a very short distance it turns back with an eddying motion and thereby exhausts its impetus.

### [On movement]

First: If a power moves a body through a certain space in a certain time, the same power will move half the body twice the distance in the same time. Second: Or the same force will move half of this

--- Page 551 ---
body through this whole space in half this time. Third (as Second). Fourth: And half of this power will move half of this body through all this space in the same time. Fifth: And this power will move twice this movable body through the whole of this space in twice this time, and a thousand times this movable body through the whole of this space in a thousand such periods of time. Sixth: And half of this power will move this whole body through half of this space in this whole time, and a hundred times this body through the hundredth part of this space in the same time. Seventh: And if separate powers move two separate movable things through a given space in a given time, the same powers united will move the same bodies united through this same space in this same time, because in this case the initial proportions always remain the same.

## OF THE MOVEMENT OF THE AIR ENCLOSED BENEATH THE WATER

Whether the air escapes from beneath the water by its own nature or because it is pressed and driven by the water.

The reply is that since a heavy substance cannot be supported by a light one, this heavy substance will proceed to fall and seek what may support it, because every natural action seeks to be at rest; consequently, that water which surrounds this air above, on the sides, and below finds itself entirely pressed against the air enclosed by it. All that water which is above *d e n m* pushes this air downwards and would keep it below itself, were it not that the lateral sections *a b e f* and *a b c d*—which surround this air and rest upon its sides—constitute a greater weight than the water which is above it; consequently, this air escapes by the angles *n m* either on one side or on the other, and winds as it rises.

As much force is exerted when an object is moved against motionless air as when the air is moved against a motionless object.

I have seen movements of the air so violent as to carry away and scatter in their course immense forest trees and whole roofs of great palaces; and I have seen this same fury with its whirling movement bore a hole in and hollow out a bank of shingle and carry away in the air gravel, sand, and water for more than half a mile.

--- Page 552 ---
The same weight will be sustained in the air without falling if, while descending with a slanting movement, it is able afterward to raise itself very high with a reflected movement.

How much air is required to raise various heavy objects made of different materials?

How much water entering a boat will cause it to sink?

Which air supports more? That which is enclosed and rarefied, as is the case in cupping glasses? Or air in its natural state? Or when it is compressed, as it is in balls inflated by the force of a screw? There can be no doubt that the rarefied air supports most, then air in its natural state, and compressed air resists least.

Every part of the volume of water that falls from a river through the air follows the line in which the impetus began that led it to this fall.

## [*Movement of liquids*]

The natural movements of liquids in the air are swifter and more dispersed at the end than at the beginning.

The semi-natural movements made by water between the bed of a river and the air will be of equal speed if the bed of this river is straight and uniform in slant and width.

Accidental movements made within the air become slower at every stage of height.

The semi-accidental movements made between the bed of a canal and the air upon a bed of uniform slant and width always tend to become slower, but they last longer than simple accidental movements because they continue to support themselves and always lighten themselves of part of their weight.

First: If a power moves a body a certain distance in a certain time, the same power will move half of this body twice that distance in the same time.

Second: If any force moves any movable object through a certain distance in a certain time, the same force will move half of this movable object through the whole of this distance in half the time.

Third: If a force moves a body a certain distance in a certain time, the

--- Page 553 ---
same force will move half of this body across half of this space in the same time.

[Fourth?] If a force moves a body a certain distance in a certain time, it does not necessarily follow that this power can move twice this weight across twice the distance in twice the time, because it is possible that this force would not be sufficient to move such an object at all.

[Fifth?] If a force moves a body a certain distance in a particular time, it does not necessarily follow that half of this force can move this same body across half of the distance in the same time, for perhaps it would not be able to move it.

Sixth. If two separate forces move two separate objects, the same forces combined will move the two objects joined together across the same distance in the same time, because the same proportion still remains.

Fourth. If a power moves a body a certain distance in a particular time, half the force will move half of the object across half of this distance in the same time.

If every moving object continues its motion along the line of its beginning, what is it that causes the flight of an arrow or a thunderbolt to swerve and bend in so many directions while still in the air?

What has been said may arise from two causes, one of which is that the air, which is compressed before the fury of its onset, offers resistance to it; consequently, this movement becomes bent and takes on the nature of a reflected movement, though it does not proceed in straight lines. Its action is like that described in the third part of the fifth section concerning water, where it is shown how air issuing from the beds of swamps in the form of bubbles sometimes comes to the surface of the water with a winding, curving motion. The second cause of the winding movement of a lightning flash may arise from the fact that the substance of the thunderbolt discharges itself now to the right and now to the left, now upwards and now downwards, acting in the same way as a spark leaping from a glowing coal. For if the coal exhales gas from one of its sides, it becomes broken apart by the moisture expanding within it, and bursting into flame, it separates these pieces of coal and produces another spark, which at its birth strikes against the rest and drives it—

--- Page 554 ---
back; and this then does the same again in different directions, throwing out a succession of sparks into the air until it is itself consumed. But the first explanation pleases me more, because if the second were true, you would see that a single thunderbolt would produce many others, just as this spark does.

### CONCERNING THE LOCAL MOVEMENT OF FLEXIBLE DRY THINGS SUCH AS DUST AND THE LIKE

I say that when a table is struck in different places, the dust that is upon it is reduced to various shapes of mounds and tiny hillocks—and this arises from . . .

The dust which, when the table is struck, is divided into various hillocks, descends from the hypotenuse of these hillocks, enters beneath their base, and raises itself again around the axis of the peak of the hillock, and moves in such a way as to resemble a right-angled triangle; and this arises from . . .

When the dusty table is struck on one side, observe the manner in which the movement of the dust begins to create the aforementioned hillocks, and how this dust rises to the top of the hillock.

### MOVABLE THINGS IN THE AIR

The movement of the air is less in front of the movable thing that penetrates through it than it is behind this movable thing.

The air that fills the void which the movable thing leaves behind as it penetrates through this air has its whole mass moving at a speed equal to that possessed by this movable thing; but the parts of this air, because it is of the nature of a vortex—that is, with a circling movement in the form of eddies—are much swifter in themselves than the movement of the aforementioned movable thing.

Here it seems that because the movable thing has more swiftness of air behind it than in front, this air is the cause of the movement of this movable thing; and according to the seventh principle, this cannot be.

No movable thing is ever swifter than the swiftness of the power which moves it.

The wave that the air makes before the movable thing which pene-

## WHY THE MOVING OBJECT FOLLOWS THE MOTION STARTED BY ITS MOVER

No impulse can end immediately; instead, it continues to exhaust itself through stages of movement.

The air that was originally behind the hole made in the air by the moving object accompanies this moving object only a little way, according to the eighth principle.

**Eighth.** The air that successively surrounds the moving object as it travels through it creates various movements within itself. This is seen in the dust motes <note>original: "atoms"</note> found in the sunlight <note>original: "sphere of the sun"</note> when they penetrate through a window into a dark place. If one throws a stone along the length of the sunbeam, one can see the dust motes rearrange themselves around the path where the air filled the space left by the moving object, as is proved in the fifth principle.

**Fifth.** Nothing that lacks the power of sensation moves on its own; rather, its movement is caused by others. The movement produced acts very briefly in the time and space that necessity allows, *as is shown in the fourth.*<sup>1</sup>

**Fourth.** The air which moves to fill up the vacuum made in it by the moving object has within itself varying degrees of speed, density, and movement.

Every moving object that creates a reflected action <note>original: "reflex action"</note> ends its course along the line of its incidence <note>This refers to the law of reflection, where the angle of approach equals the angle of rebound.</note>.

This happens because the movement of its incidence is more powerful than the reflex movement, and that which is more powerful has a longer duration than that which is less powerful.

The movement of incidence of a moving object will be more powerful than its reflex movement, because the percussion of the incidence against a dense object partially diminishes the impetus joined to this moving object; this diminution ensures that the reflex movement is not as powerful as the movement of incidence was said to be. In every stage of movement, however, the impetus of the moving object diminishes on its own, quite apart from its percussion with a dense object; yet it does not follow that this percussion will not lessen it much more. Indeed, if you measure the movement that this moving object would have made without incidence against the movements produced by many bounds up and down, you will find that the continuous movement in the same spot will be longer than that which is frequently broken by incidences, even if the initial impetus in each case were of equal power.

The more deeply an object is submerged in water, the less it is moved by the wind that strikes the part of it above the water. This contradicts Battista Alberti, who gives a general rule for how far the wind drives a ship in an hour.

The very rapid friction of two thick bodies produces fire.

An object that has its sides positioned slantwise in the middle of a water current—even if the water strikes its smooth side—will move in greater bulk toward the side of the slant that is lower.

### OF THE AIR

And because, as is proved in the seventh, it is not contrary to the nature of air to become compressed and rarefied almost in a moment—and this is not found possible with water, which maintains its original form—it is therefore easier for the air at the side of and above the moving object to descend there to fill the vacuum left by this moving object above itself, than for the air beneath to bend and move.

--- Page 557 ---
in a long curving line in order to fill up this vacuum; and this is also impossible according to the eighth rule, which proves that every impetus moves the air along with it in the same direction in which the impetus is created, just as the wind moves as much air as its impetus drives, as is seen with the dust stirred by these winds or with the particles floating in the sun’s rays when they are blown about by it. Therefore, the air, being driven by the impetus of the heavy object descending through it, flies along the line of movement made by its mover; the air at the sides is transformed into lateral eddies, and the upper air descends from above, constantly filling the vacuum that the moving object leaves behind at each stage of its movement.

The air below the moving object which descends through it becomes dense, and above it, the air becomes rarefied.

The movement that air makes within air compresses both itself and the air that it strikes.

Air moved within a body that is thicker than itself compresses itself more than when it moves through other air.

Air moved within a body lighter than itself becomes rarefied.

Water moved within a body lighter than itself becomes rarefied, not in its quality, but in the extent of its dispersion and expansion.

Regarding the proportion of the movement of water poured out of the bottom of a very long trench, the exit of which is a hundred times narrower than the breadth and depth of the trench:

It may be asked how much slower the movement of the water in the upper part of the trench will be than the movement of the 'rozza' which is formed with the same breadth as the opening through which the water exits the trench.

I have learned from percussion that the falling movement exceeds the reflex movement.

## OF THE SCIENCE OF WEIGHTS

A heavy object that descends freely does not transfer its weight to any support. This may be proved: *a* is one and *b* is two; it follows that

## ON THE NATURE OF THE ROPES PLACED IN THE <term>TACKLES</term> <note>original: "tackles"; a system of ropes and pulleys used for lifting heavy weights</note>

The ropes of the pulley systems will break at the point where the rope of the <term>motive power</term> <note>the force or person pulling the rope</note> contacts the first pulley. This is proved by the ninth rule of this work, which states: "The ropes in the pulley systems that descend always undergo greater strain than those that rise." Furthermore, "Of the ropes that descend, the last feels less of the force of the motive power than the first." Finally, "The ropes of the pulley systems feel more weight in proportion to how quickly they move: among the ropes moving within the system, the last is swifter than any of the others."

## A QUESTION REGARDING DESCENDING WEIGHTS

<margin>G 17 v.</margin>
The question is whether weights descending through pulleys exert more or less of their weight upon the pivots of the pulleys while they are descending than when they are stationary.

## ON THE DIFFERENCES BETWEEN FORCE AND WEIGHT, AND FIRST REGARDING FORCE

Between a spring and a <term>counterpoise</term> <note>a hanging weight</note> of equal power, the spring is always more effective, seeing that its power is <term>pyramidal</term> <note>Leonardo uses "pyramidal" to describe a force that is greatest at its start and diminishes over time or distance</note>; its greatest power is at the very beginning of its movement. 

However, the counterpoise has a compound power, one part of which is <term>cylindrical</term> <note>Leonardo uses "cylindrical" to describe a constant, uniform force</note> and the other pyramidal. The cylindrical power is such that the weight is always equal in itself and pulls with a constant force at both the beginning and the end of the movement. But the pyramidal power begins in an instant and at a single point, and with every degree of movement and time, it acquires volume and speed, provided its movement is free and swift. Yet, in the slow movement made by a heavy substance, this pyramidal power (momentum) ceases to exist, and only the cylindrical power (the constant weight) remains.

Power, as previously stated, is worth as much at the beginning as it is at the middle, the end, or any other part of its movement.

## CONCERNING WEIGHTS

If the angle formed by the intersection of two slanted cords descending to the suspension point of a heavy body is divided by the center line of that body, the angle is split into two parts. These parts will have the same proportion to each other as the proportions into which the heavy body is divided between the two cords.

If the angle formed by the intersection of the two cords descending to the suspension point of a heavy body is divided by the intercentric line passing through this body, the angle is then divided into two other angles. Between these, there is the same proportion as that from base to base, from angle to angle, and likewise from the whole of one triangle to the whole of the other; these proportions correspond to the weight that the heavy body distributes to its supports.

The staff that is most uniform in thickness bends with the most perfect curve.

## ON THE MOVEMENT OF SHIPS [Drawings] *b a, d c, f e*

These three ships of uniform width, length, and depth, when propelled by equal power, will move at different speeds. The ship that presents its widest part at the front is faster, as it resembles the shape of birds and fishes such as the mullet. This ship displaces a great quantity of water with its sides and front, which then, through its turbulence, presses against the rear two-thirds of the vessel. The ship *d c* does the opposite, and *f e* has a speed midway between the two aforementioned.

## ON A MOVING OBJECT OF NON-UNIFORM WEIGHT MOVING IN AIR OR WATER

In moving objects that are uniform in substance but not uniform in weight, the heaviest part always acts as the leader.

A pyramidal weight of irregular size that is pushed by a bow with its point forward will immediately turn its base toward the direction in which the object is moving.

## ON THE MOVEMENT OF A MOVABLE OBJECT

An arrow shot from the prow of a ship in the direction the ship is moving will not appear to move from the spot where it was shot if the ship’s speed is equal to the speed of the arrow.

<margin>G 54 r.</margin>
But if the arrow is shot from such a ship in the opposite direction from which it is traveling at the aforementioned speed, this arrow will move away from the ship at twice its own speed.

*On the movement of a movable object that glides with continuous motion over a moving spot, or which, being movable, flows away.*

The movement of a liquid flowing through the bottom of a moving vessel will follow a slanted straight line; the slant will be at a greater or lesser angle depending on whether the movement of the vessel is faster or slower.

*On the movement made by the surface that receives the substance poured from a vessel.*

The same amount of force is required to receive a substance poured from a stationary vessel onto a moving surface as is required to move a vessel that pours a substance onto a stationary surface.

But if the movement of the pouring vessel equals the movement of the surface receiving the substance, the movement of the descending substance follows a slanted straight line, as shown above.

## ON THE MOVEMENT OF AN ARROW DRIVEN BY A BOW

An arrow shot from the center of the earth toward the highest part of the elements will ascend and descend along the same straight line, even though the elements may be in a state of revolution around their center.

The gravity that descends through the elements when they are in rotation <note>original: "circumvolution"</note> always has its movement corresponding to the direction of the line that extends from the starting point of the movement toward the center of the world. <margin>G 54 v. <note>Refers to Leonardo's Manuscript G, folio 54 verso.</note></margin>

## ON THE MOVEMENT OF THE MOVABLE OBJECT

Concerning a heavy substance descending through the air while the <term>elements</term> <note>The four classical elements: earth, water, air, and fire, which were thought to be arranged in concentric spheres around the Earth's center.</note> revolve, making their entire revolution in twenty-four hours:

The moving substance that descends from the uppermost part of the <term>sphere of fire</term> <note>In ancient and medieval cosmology, the region of the atmosphere highest above the earth, just below the moon's orbit.</note> will make a straight movement as far as the earth, even though the elements are in a perpetual revolving movement around the center of the world. This is proved: let *b* be the heavy substance that descends through the elements, which moves from *a* to descend to the center of the world *m*. I say that such a heavy substance, although it may make a curved descent in the form of a spiral line, will never deviate from its straight-line descent. By this descent, it advances continually between the place from which it separated and the center of the world. 

For if it started from point *a* and descended to *b*, during the time in which it has descended to *b*, it has been carried to *d*. The position of *a* has changed to *c*, and so the movable object finds itself in the <note>[line of]</note> direction that extends between *c* and the center of the world *m*. If the movable object descends from *d* to *f*, the beginning of the movement moves in the same time from *c* to *f*; and if *f* descends to *h*, it turns at *g*. Thus, in twenty-four hours, the movable object drops to the earth below the place from which it was first separated, and such a movement is composite <note>A movement made of two or more combined motions; in this case, a vertical fall combined with a horizontal rotation.</note>.

If the movable object descends from the highest to the lowest part of the elements in twenty-four hours, its movement is formed of both a straight line and a curve. I say straight because it will never deviate from the very short line which extends from the place from which it separated to the center of the elements; it will stop at the lowest extremity of that line of direction, which is always found according to the <term>zenith</term> <note>The point in the sky directly above an observer.</note> beneath the place from which this movable object separated. Yet, this movement is also curved in itself in all parts of the line, and as a consequence, the entire line is curved. And...

<summary>Leonardo explains that an object dropped from a height falls in a straight line relative to the Earth's surface (the zenith), even though its path is actually a "composite" spiral due to the Earth's 24-hour rotation.</summary>

From this, it follows that a stone thrown from a tower does not strike the side of the tower before reaching the ground.

### ON SIMPLE IMPETUS

Simple impetus is that which moves an arrow or a dart through the air.

Compound impetus is that which moves a stone when it is released from a sling; this impetus does not last long because the noise produced by the revolving motion of the object reveals to us that the object encounters resistance in the air it penetrates.

### ON IMPETUS

Impetus is the impression of movement transmitted by the mover to the object being moved.

Impetus is a power impressed by the mover onto the object. Every impression tends toward permanence or desires to remain. This is proven by the impression made by the sun in the eye of a spectator, and by the impression of the sound made by a clapper as it strikes a bell.

Every impression desires permanence, as is shown by the image of movement impressed upon the object.

### ON PERCUSSION

The air that is compressed beneath an object as it descends through it at an angle escapes more from the upper part than from the lower part of that object.

Continuous stretches of air are thinned out on one side as much as they are compressed on the other.

The thinned part of the air offers less resistance in proportion to the greater resistance offered by the compressed part. Therefore, the back part of the object, *b*, will descend with greater impetus than its front part; this is the reason why the front, *a*, which was initially below, is raised up at the end of the reflex movement.

## ON THE DESCENT OF HEAVY BODIES

<margin>G 75 r.</margin>
Every natural action follows the shortest path. This is why the free descent of a heavy body is directed toward the center of the world <note>original: "centre of the world"; at this time, the Earth was considered the center of the universe, and gravity was the tendency of objects to seek that center</note>, because it is the shortest distance between the moving object and the lowest point of the universe.

## ON WEIGHT

Every heavy substance, when it moves horizontally, exerts weight only along the line of its movement. This is demonstrated by the initial part of the movement made by a ball fired from a mortar <note>a type of early cannon used for high-angle fire</note>, as this movement begins in a horizontal direction.

However, a heavy substance carried by the wind in any direction will have more or less gravity <note>here meaning effective weight or downward pressure</note> at its front than at the beam of a balance, depending on whether the junction of the weight's pendulum with the arm of the balance is closer to a right angle.

<margin>G 77 r.</margin>
The more rapidly a weight revolves around the fixed point of its axis, the more "heaviness" <note>referring to momentum or centrifugal force</note> it will possess as a result of that rapid revolving movement.

## ON THE WEIGHT OF THE BALANCE BEAM

The weight of a balance beam is divided into two parts: one that pulls toward the center of the world, and another that is accidental <note>original: "accidental"; in Renaissance physics, "accidental" refers to motion or properties caused by external force rather than the object's innate nature</note>, because it moves by a transverse <note>sideways or lateral</note> movement. The first part, which directs its weight toward the center of the world, has equal lateral weights on either side; these weights—according to their centers of gravity and their distances—establish the mathematical center of the balance. 

The second mathematical center should rather be called the point of mathematical contact between the pivot <note>original: "pole"</note> of the balance and its support. This point is separated from the balance’s center of natural gravity by as much space as the upper part of this balance outweighs the lower part. For this reason, the transverse weight of this balance does not, by itself, add weight to either of the two centers mentioned above. This is proved in the sixth [proposition] of this [work], which states: "Every parallel body of uniform thickness and weight placed at an angle—" <note>The text ends mid-sentence.</note>

<summary>This page explores the principles of gravity and mechanics, specifically how heavy bodies seek the shortest path to the Earth's center and how motion affects the perceived weight and equilibrium of a balance beam.</summary>
<keywords>gravity, center of the world, mortar, ballistics, balance beam, center of gravity, centrifugal force, mechanics, accidental motion</keywords>

--- Page 564 ---
likewise possesses within it two separate gravities, of which one tends toward the center of the world and the other is transverse. But the first is natural and simple, while the other is accidental and compound.

But if such a body, situated in such a way, has a free descent through the air, the centers of the two gravities will transform into one another during some period of the movement; and in the end, there will remain one single center common to all the heavy substance that descends; and thus, with a straight movement, it will penetrate all the air that is below it.

### WHAT IS IMPETUS

Impetus is that which, under another name, is termed derived movement, which arises out of primary movement—that is to say, when the movable thing is joined to its mover.

In no part of the derived movement will one ever find a velocity equal to that of the primary movement. This is proven because, at every stage of movement—as with the string of a bow—there is a loss of the acquired power which has been communicated to it by its mover. And because every effect partakes of its cause, the derived movement of the arrow gradually diminishes its power, and thus participates in the power of the bow, which, as it was produced by degrees, is likewise destroyed by degrees.

The impetus impressed by the mover upon the movable thing is infused into all the united parts of this movable thing.

And this is shown because all the parts, both the internal ones and those on the surface, have equal movement, except regarding the movement of circumvolution; for in this, the more impetuous part always revolves around the less impetuous parts—that is, those which are nearer the center of the movable thing. And the part that was first moved always remains more distant from the beginning of its movement if it is not obstructed, and this is accepted because it is more potent in its capacity to revolve.

And if one were to say, with the opponent, that the impetus which moves the movable thing is in the air that surrounds it from the middle backward, one would deny this; because the air that follows the movable thing is drawn by the movable thing to fill the void left by it, and also because the air that is compressed in front of the movable thing escapes backward in the opposite direction.

--- Page 565 ---
And if the air turns back, it is clear proof that it strikes against what the movable object draws behind it; and when two things collide, the reflex movement of each begins, and these reflex movements are converted into whirling movements carried by the air that fills the vacuum left by the movable body. It is impossible for the movement of the mover to be increased by the movement of the movable body at the same time, because the mover is always more powerful than the movable thing.

## ON MOVEMENT AND THE MOVABLE THING

Which will move the same movable thing a greater distance: a great power with a small movement, or a lesser power with a greater movement?

The derived movement made by the same movable thing will be of greater length when it has a greater primary movement from the same mover.

This is proved because experience shows us that the same power always maintains such a proportion between its primary movement and the derived movement of its movable thing as . . .

It is proved by the fifth [rule] of this, which says: among the various lengths of the primary movement, one will find that the various lengths of the derived movement of the same movable thing are in the same proportions as their primary movements. This is because if the power of the same mover separates the movable thing from itself by the space of a finger in one interval of harmonic time, the same power in two intervals of harmonic time will separate the same movable thing twice that same finger’s space from itself. And this arises from the fact that the derived movement always maintains the same proportion as the primary movement.

The impetus is not always produced in the movable thing, because even the mover does not always have an impetuous movement.

This is shown by a light chariot drawn by oxen over a level tract; for as soon as the oxen end their movement, the movement of the chariot ends.

## ON THE FIVE DIRECTIONS OF MOVEMENT

There are five varieties of local movements: the first is upwards, the second downwards, the third is in a horizontal direction, the fourth is slanting upwards, and the fifth and last is slanting downwards.

*How the momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note> of movable objects joined by a cord passes from one movable object to the other.*

The momentum produced by movable objects joined by a cord—where each is reciprocally the mover of the other—will move the two objects a short distance from their first mover.

When two movable objects are joined by their two opposite ends to the same cord and one is smaller than the other, the total sum of their movement will be less than if these movements were equal to each other.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 86 verso</margin> When the larger of two weights joined to a cord is first to move, the movement of the two joined together will be greater than if the beginning of the movement had originated with the smaller movable object.

## WHAT IS PRIMARY MOVEMENT

Primary movement is that which is made by the movable object during the time when it is still joined to its mover <note>For example, the motion of a stone while it is still in the thrower's hand or a catapult's arm.</note>.

## ON DERIVED MOVEMENT

Derived movement is that which the movable object makes in the air after it is separated from its mover <note>This refers to what we now call projectile motion or inertia.</note>.

Derived movement has its origin in primary movement, and it never has a swiftness or power equal to the swiftness or power of the said primary movement.

The course of this movable object will be in conformity with the direction of the course of its mover when all the parts of this movable object have movement equal to the primary movement of their mover.

If all the parts of the movement made by the part of one whole are of equal movement, then this movable object will not rotate <note>original: "revolve"</note>; and this movement will receive the whole power of its mover, and it will ob—

### ON PULLEYS AND TACKLE

The ropes of the tackle share equally the weight that they support.

The power that moves the tackle is pyramidal, since it proceeds toward deceleration with a consistent rate of change down to the last rope.

And the movement of the ropes of this tackle is pyramidal because it proceeds toward deceleration with a consistent rate of change from the first cord to the last.

Therefore, the rope feels the power of the mover so much more when it is faster and so much less when it is slower.

The ropes feel the power of their mover so much more when they are nearer and so much less when they are farther away.
G 87 v.

### ON POWER

The same force is more powerful the more it is concentrated.

This is the case with heat, impact, weight, force, and many other things. And let us speak first of the heat of the sun, which impresses itself upon a concave mirror and is reflected by it in a pyramidal shape; this pyramid acquires proportionately more power as it becomes more narrow. That is to say, if the pyramid strikes the object at half its length, it contracts to half the thickness of its base; and if it strikes it at ninety-nine hundredths of its length, it contracts its base by ninety-nine hundredths and increases by ninety-nine hundredths the heat which this base receives from the aforementioned heat of the sun or of fire.

Furthermore, the impact of a pyramidal iron tool will penetrate the object struck by its point to a greater extent as the point becomes narrower.

A heavy substance is also of greater weight when concentrated into less space because a smaller quantity of air offers resistance to it. Of movement and force we shall speak elsewhere.

In a similar course made by water in its channel, the central part will be lower than the rest of the surface.

The impact is more powerful than the movement itself, and where the water strikes, every obstacle is removed; then, when the movement is subsequently created, it carries with it all the weight caused by the impact and discharges it in the impact made by the rebound, and so from rebound to rebound the force of the violent movement diminishes. Consequently, the heaviest stones are deposited, and since they cannot be carried along by the weak movements that follow, they remain there; and the final objects, which are at the furthest distance from their starting point, are the lightest things.

That part of an impact produced by a continuous cause will be more powerful the further it is from the cause of its movement.

### [*Weight and Water*]

A weight of water will be displaced from its position equal to the total weight that drives this water.

The weight supported on the water will be equal to the total weight of the water that makes way for these weights.

The center of every weight rests directly beneath the center of its support.

## OF MOVEMENT AND IMPACT

If someone descends from one step to another by jumping from one to the next, and you then add together all the forces of the impacts and the weights of these jumps, you will find that they are equal to the total impact and weight that such a man would produce if he fell in a straight vertical line from the top to the bottom of the height of this staircase.

Furthermore, if this man were to fall from a height, striking stage by stage upon objects that would bend like a spring, in such a way that the impact from one to the next was slight, you will find that at the final part of his descent this man’s impact will be diminished—compared to what it would have been in a free and vertical line—by the sum of all the combined impacts made at each stage of the descent upon the aforementioned springs.

Pagolo says that no instrument that moves another instrument in contact with it can avoid being moved by it. So, if the wheel moves its pinion, the pinion will also move this wheel. But such a thing is not universal; for though the cog *n* moves the wheel, the wheel will not move the cog *n* if it is turned against the ground.

The path of movement made by the course of two objects that strike, which does not bend upon meeting the first object, is the one that strikes the second object with more force in its reflex movement; and conversely, that which bends more in its impact with the first object will act with less force.

That body which, when moved, strikes the first object with a greater blow consumes more of its impetus in the impact, with the result that the blow made by the reflex movement will be weaker. And the path of movement that does not bend at all at its first impact strikes the second object with the most force.

A leap is always smaller than the descent made by the thing that leaps; and this leap is termed reflex movement, which is always weaker than the direct movement.

### [*The knife-grinder's wheel*]

The axle <note>original: "pole"</note> wears down most in the direction where the person moving it exerts the greatest force; this is shown by the knife-grinders who travel through the cities.

Every axle wears away on the side where the mover applies the most force. Observe a man sharpening knives by turning a wheel with his feet: as he drives his foot down, he generates the force that produces a full revolution. It is clear that as this movement moves further from its cause, it slows down and wears away its support less. Each time the movement is repeated, the pressure of the foot renews it with fresh momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note>; under this renewed force, the support is consumed again. Consequently, the axle is worn unevenly. I 45 r.

### [*Movement—falling and reflex*]

Why the short mortar makes a louder explosion when fired than the long one, as is heard when drawing the breeches of small cannons.

The movement made by the cord is much more rapid near the beginning than near the end. ## MOVEMENT INCREASED BY IMPETUS AND WEIGHT

This movement is at first increased by impetus, because the further the stone producing it falls, the more speed and gravity it acquires; secondly, the more the cord is unrolled from its circular path, the more distant it becomes from the center of movement; consequently, the more distant it becomes, the more it acquires weight and impetus.

There are some movements of moving objects which continue their direction while receiving percussion in the middle of this movement, and these are of great force.

I ask why field-lances or hunting-whips have a greater movement than the arm. I say that this happens because the hand describes a much wider circle as the arm moves than the elbow does; and consequently, moving at the same time, the hand covers twice as much space as the elbow, and therefore it may be said to have a speed double that of the movement of the elbow, and so it sends thrown objects a greater distance from itself.

### MOVEMENT AND WEIGHT. BALLS SHOT FROM MORTARS

Then diminish the movable object by half, as those agree to do who have written upon proportions, and you will see that it cannot be that the weight, being half as large, will be moved twice as quickly by the same power; that is to say, if it were twice as swift, it would go twice as far because the proportion of the movements is the same as that of the speeds. An <term>atom</term> <note>original: "atom"; here referring to the smallest possible particle or unit of matter</note> would be almost as fast as thought itself, or as the eye which roams in an instant to the height of the stars. Consequently, its journey would be infinite, because a thing that can be infinitely diminished would increase infinitely in speed and traverse an infinite distance, since every continuous quantity is divisible to infinity. This opinion, however, is disproven by logic and also by experience.

It would also follow that if a mortar throws its ball three miles with one hundred pounds of powder and one thousand pounds of balls in twenty divisions of <term>harmonic time</term> <note>original: "harmonic time"; time measured by musical beats or rhythms, a common method before precise mechanical stopwatches</note>, then by taking only one pound of balls, it would travel [much further] in the same time. Calculate by the <term>rule of three</term> <note>original: "rule of three"; a mathematical method for finding a fourth value from three known ratios (cross-multiplication)</note>, saying: if a thousand pounds of stone are thrown to me in two divisions of time—keeping the three thousand in your mind—and if a thousand pounds of balls are thrown to me at that distance in twenty divisions of time, in how many divisions of time will the same power throw me one pound of balls? If you reckon that a thousand gives you twenty, you will find what one gives you: it would be 20/1000 divisions of time, which is about 1/50th of a unit of time. 

Now, if one shoots with powder the weight of a single small grain, the experiment will show that the ball travels no farther than the mortar sends its smoke when one begins to fire. By the previous [theoretical] reasoning, however, the ball should have been sent a million miles in the same time it takes the thousand pounds of balls to go three miles. You researchers, therefore, should not trust those authors who, by employing only their imagination, have wished to make themselves interpreters between nature and man. Instead, trust only those who have exercised their intellects not just with the signs of nature, but with the actual results of their experiments.

### [Reflected movements]

The <term>reflex movement</term> will have greater strength when it is longer.
And that <term>reflex movement</term> will be longer which is produced between more diverse angles.

The <term>reflex movement</term> that is longer is less obstructed because it differs little from the <term>movement of percussion</term>, and this <term>percussion</term> has little strength; consequently, it loses little of the power of its first mover.

But if the <term>reflex movement</term> is shorter, it is a sign that it is more obstructed at the point of <term>percussion</term>, and it differs greatly from the <term>movement of incidence</term>; consequently, the power of the first movement is greatly diminished.

## OF PERCUSSION

The <term>reflex movement</term> will be weaker in proportion to how much shorter it is.
That <term>reflex movement</term> will be shorter which is caused by a greater <term>percussion</term>.

That <term>percussion</term> will have greater power which is made between more equal angles.

Of the <term>percussions</term> made between equal angles, the one that will have greater strength is that which is caused against a more compact object.

And in <term>percussions</term> made on objects of equal compactness, the one that will be more powerful is that which has an object of greater resistance.

The spherical body rotates more during the <term>reflex movement</term> the more the <term>percussion</term> is made between more unequal angles.

This proposition would be entirely confirmed by experience if it were not for the firm compression of the air driven by the force of the ball; for the air, not being naturally as fast as the movement caused by the force that drives it, becomes compressed, and it is compressed more as it is driven harder. ### RULE OF POWER

If a power moves a weight a certain distance in a certain time, half of that power will move that same body half of that distance in the same time, or the full distance in double the time.

Or, the full power will move a weight double the first weight half that distance in the same time.

Or, it will move the said weight half the distance in half the time.

Man and every animal undergoes more fatigue in going upwards than downwards, for as he ascends he carries his weight with him, and as he descends he simply lets it go.

The body that meets with the weakest resistance will show itself to be the heaviest, and a heavy body will meet with the weakest resistance when its center is farthest removed from the center-line of its support.

The center of every suspended weight stays below the center-line of the cord that supports it.

If two cords extend from the two equal arms of a balance, one being double the length of the other, then regarding the weight—and because these cords meet at the same spot to support a weight—one cord will feel as much more weight than the other as it is longer than the other.

Gravity suspended from a cord exists entirely in the whole length of the cord and entirely in each of its parts.

Why, when flat sand is made up of grains dissimilar in shape and size, the water flowing above it drives these grains with different strengths of movement:

Just as bodies differing in weight and shape make different movements in still air, so do air and water when they move between bodies at rest. And this is the reason why sand loses its flatness through the movement of the water passing over it; for the water moving over the sand performs the same function as the air moving over the water. And if one should prove that the bottom of the flat sand forms waves and becomes uneven through the uneven—

# MOVEMENT AND WEIGHT

<margin>M 43 v.</margin>
[*Of weights moving through the air*]

If two equal weights are placed vertically, one below the other, and allowed to fall at the same time, they will close the gap between them during a long descent and will eventually touch.

When the air is free of mist or clouds, you will find that at every degree of height, it becomes proportionally thinner. Similarly, at every degree lower down, it becomes denser. This is why, if two equal bodies are placed one below the other a <term>braccio's</term> <note>original: "braccio"; a Florentine unit of measurement approximately equal to 23 inches or 58 centimeters</note> space apart—that is, they are attached by a thread and let fall together in a long movement—they will touch. This happens because the lower body always finds itself in thicker air than the one above it; furthermore, the first body has the difficult work of "opening" the air and creating waves in it. Part of this air escapes upward and strikes the second body with its reflective movement, while the rest of the air above rushes in to fill the vacuum created behind the first body.

<margin>M 44 r.</margin>
Proof of the proportion of time and movement, together with the speed attained in the descent of heavy bodies in the shape of a pyramid. This is because the aforementioned powers are all "pyramidal," <note>Leonardo uses "pyramidal" to describe values that start at zero and increase at a constant rate, similar to how a triangle or pyramid widens from its point</note> seeing as they begin at nothing and increase by degrees of arithmetical proportion.

If you cut the pyramid at any stage of its height with a line parallel to its base, you will find that whatever the proportion is between the height of this section from its base and the total height of the pyramid, there will be the same proportion between the width of this section and the width of the entire base.

<margin>M 44 v.</margin>
This occurs in air of uniform thickness.

A falling heavy body acquires an additional degree of movement for every degree of time, compared to the previous degree of time. Similarly, it acquires a degree of speed greater than the degree of the preceding movement. Therefore, whenever the amount of time is doubled, the length of the descent is doubled, and the speed of the movement is also doubled. <note>Leonardo is exploring the concept of constant acceleration. While his logic here suggests a linear relationship between time and distance, it laid the groundwork for the later discovery that distance increases with the square of time ($d = 1/2 at^2$).</note>

It is shown here that whatever proportion one quantity of time has to another, the quantity of movement will have that same proportion, and likewise for the quantity of speed.

A heavy body that descends freely with every degree of time...

## [Waves of the air]

The wave of air produced by a body moving through it will be considerably swifter than the body that moves it.

What is set forth above happens because, since the body of the air is very volatile and moves very easily, when a body moves through it, it creates the first wave in its first movement; at the same time, that wave cannot be produced without causing another after it, and that another. And so this body moving through the air creates beneath it, in each stage of time, multiplications of waves, which in their flight prepare the path of movement for the motion of their mover.

The wave of the air, forming and reforming itself, prepares the way of movement for its mover.

The air which is compressed by force becomes heavier than that which is at liberty.

## [Weight moving through the air]

The heavy body which has a free descent acquires a degree of weight with every degree of movement.

This arises from the second principle of the first section, which says that "that body will be heavier which meets less resistance." In this case of the free descent of heavy bodies, one sees clearly by the previously cited example of the water wave that the air creates the same wave beneath the descending object, because the air finds itself pushed and drawn from the opposite side; that is, it creates a turning wave which helps to drive the body downward.

<margin>M 46 r.</margin>
Now, for these reasons, the air that flies in front of a weight—driven by that weight—shows clearly that it does not resist it, and consequently does not impede its movement. Therefore, the greater the descent of the wave (which travels more rapidly than the heavy body moving it), the longer the movement of this heavy body continues. As the leading wave moves further away, it prepares the air touching the weight for an even easier <note>original: "facile"</note> flight.

### [*Density of waves. Weight in the air*]

When waves are divided into tiny particles, that quantity which was united and powerful above begins to descend to the ground.

Falling objects may be "continuous quantities," such as staffs, beams, and similar things, or liquid bodies—though liquids cease to be continuous when their descent is long <note>Leonardo is observing how a stream of water eventually breaks into individual droplets during a long fall</note>.

Others are "discontinuous," such as stones and other bodies separated from one another. Others are intermediate <note>original: "neuter"</note>, such as grain from a mill hopper, sand, and similar collections of tiny bodies. You may test this at a great height: mark the difference between the unity of their exit from the hopper and their density when they arrive at the point of impact <note>original: "percussion"</note>.

If the air were of uniform thickness <note>density</note> at every part of its height, the bodies which descend would acquire equal degrees of speed at each stage of their movement.

### [*Weight. Movement. Waves of water*]

Now we have found that a discontinuous quantity <note>A collection of separate objects, like a handful of stones</note>, when moving, acquires a degree of speed at each stage of its movement. Thus, in each interval of harmonic time <note>Leonardo used musical intervals and ratios as a way to measure time and acceleration</note>, they gain a certain length of space from each other, and this acquisition follows an arithmetic proportion.

How, then, are we to account for the "continuous quantity" of liquid bodies in their descent? In each interval of harmonic time, the source pours out the same weight, yet at each stage of movement, the stream becomes longer and thinner, so that over a long course, it ends in a point like a pyramid. Consequently, one might think such a liquid body would not fall to earth, but rather that each great mass would remain suspended in the air, even if it were a massive river continually rolling away. Yet, experience shows the contrary: for as much as departs from the top strikes at the same time below. And if the same...

As the weight of this liquid body makes itself thinner, it meets with less resistance from the air and consequently acquires speed; and if by becoming thinner it has acquired speed, this same weight would also, for this second reason, begin to make itself longer and consequently even thinner, and so would descend more rapidly; and this would continue in succession infinitely. Therefore, either nature or necessity has brought it about that, in whatever manner the descent begins to take the form of a pyramid, it creates an intersection by switching its extremities from right to left and begins to divide itself; and the further it descends, the more it divides; and thus, through many ramifications, it manages to lighten itself and check its irregular movement.

### *Demonstration*

According to the fifth proposition of the first book, which states that a descending object acquires equal degrees of speed at every stage of its movement:
Therefore, for this reason, the movement at the end of a downward fall becomes much more rapid than the movement was at the beginning.
And according to the eighth proposition of the first book, which says that: the distance between the upper pair will have the same ratio to the distance of the lower pair as the speed of the lower pair has to the speed of the upper pair; conversely, the relationship of speed to distance is the same as the relationship of distance to speed.
To test the aforementioned conclusion regarding movement, the experiment should be conducted in this way: take two balls of similar weight and shape and drop them from a significant height, ensuring that they are touching each other at the start of their motion. The person conducting the experiment should station themselves on the ground to watch whether the balls remain in contact during their fall or not. This experiment should be repeated many times so that no accident occurs to hinder or invalidate the proof—for an experiment might be misleading regardless of whether the investigator realizes it.
<margin>Manuscript M, folio 57 recto and verso</margin>

## OF THE RESISTANCE OF THE AIR

Air becomes denser when it is compressed by a greater weight.
Although object *b* is as thick as object *a*, because it is twice as heavy, it makes the air that moves beneath it twice as dense; as the air becomes denser below the object, it becomes proportionately thinner above it.
<margin>Manuscript M, folio 58 recto</margin>

<insert>[*Weight, Percussion, Spring*]</insert>

A weight will appear to be lighter if it has a greater volume. <note>This refers to the principle of displacement or air resistance affecting the perceived weight of an object.</note>
A falling weight will produce a lesser impact <term>percussion: the force of a strike or collision</term> if it strikes with a part further away from its center of gravity, or if it strikes with a part that yields against the object as if it were pressing upon a spring. The impact is also lessened if the object strikes something that yields with a spring-like motion, or if it lands on its tiptoes.
<margin>Manuscript M, folio 59 recto</margin>

### THE CONVERSE

<margin>M 61 v. and 62 r.</margin>
Among weights of the same shape that are propelled by the same force, the one that has greater bulk <note>original: "bulk"; refers here to volume or physical size</note> will achieve less movement.

Aristotle says that if a force moves a body a certain distance in a certain time, the same force will move half of that body twice the distance in the same time. Therefore, the millionth part of this weight would be propelled by the same force a million times that distance in the same time; or, if this weight were an ounce and it was moved a mile in a period of time, the millionth part would be moved a million miles in the same period. <note>Leonardo is citing Aristotle’s *Physics*, which argued that speed is proportional to force and inversely proportional to mass—a theory Leonardo investigated through his own experiments.</note> And if you were to say that the air would create resistance, I maintain that in proportion as this body was less in weight than an ounce, the quantity of air that resisted its course would also be proportionately less.

## RULE OF THE PROPORTION OF REBOUNDS

If you twist the cord *n m* twenty times, it will uncoil and make thirty-nine revolutions in the opposite direction, and will then roll the other way and make thirty-eight; and so it will continue to diminish in succession in arithmetical proportion until its movement stops.

<margin>M 72 v.</margin>
The length of the first turn will have the same proportion to the second as the first right-hand twist has to the left-hand one.

## OF THE MOVEMENT OF THE ARROW

Although the force of the crossbow is greatest at the beginning and drops to nothing in the final stage, the movement of the cord becomes swifter toward the end than at the beginning because of the momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note> it has acquired. Therefore, we conclude that the arrow continues to accelerate until it reaches the end of the cord's movement.

### [Of the power of percussion]

Many small blows can drive a nail into wood, but if you combine these blows into one single strike, it will have much more power than the sum of its separate parts. Conversely, if a certain amount of impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> drives a nail entirely into a piece of wood, and that same power is then divided into many small parts, those small strikes could hit the nail for a long time without ever making it penetrate the wood to any significant degree.

If a ten-pound hammer drives a nail into a piece of wood with a single blow, a one-pound hammer will not drive the nail all the way into the wood with ten blows. Nor will a nail that is one-tenth the size of the first be driven deeper by that one-pound hammer in a single strike, even though the proportions seem equal. This is because the hardness of the wood does not decrease its resistance; it remains as hard as it was at the start.

If you wish to discuss the proportions of the movement of objects that have penetrated wood when driven by force...

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the physics of crossbows, noting how momentum causes the cord to accelerate as it slackens, and explains the mechanics of percussion, arguing that a single large impact is more effective than many smaller ones due to the constant resistance of the material.</summary>

### [Weight of pyramid]

<margin>M 85 v.</margin>
If you wish to divide a pyramid into two equal weights, divide its length into four equal parts. Then, join the quarter at the tip <note>original: "apex"</note> together with the quarter at the base. These two sections combined will be equal in weight and volume <note>original: "quantity"</note> to the two middle parts. This means that a single measurement will apply to them both exactly, as shown below.

### [Movement—crossbow]

Regarding movement occurring in such a way that the propelling force <note>original: "mover"</note> completes its path before the cord has finished returning to its resting state:

This movement will have the same power as that produced by the cord which stays taut when the arrow leaves the crossbow—provided that the propelling force ends its path with "pyramidal power." This means the power is greatest at the start and diminishes to nothing at the end. However, the movement of the arrow, which is also greatest at the beginning and ends in nothing, maintains the length of its moving power longer than the cord does. This is because the arrow's movement could potentially cover four hundred <term>braccia</term> <note>A "braccio" (plural: braccia) was an Italian unit of measurement roughly equal to the length of an arm, approximately 23 inches.</note>, whereas the movement of the cord that drove the arrow only covered one-third of a <term>braccio</term>.

### [Diagrams]

The pyramid representing the power and movement of the propelling force <note>original: "mover"</note>.
The pyramid representing the power and movement of the object being moved.

If the crossbow cord remains curved after it has launched the arrow, it is certain that its power has become increasingly slow and infinitely weak at every stage of its movement. Consequently, we can describe such power as "pyramidal" because it begins broad at the base and ends at a point.

<margin>M 90 r. and v.</margin>
The arrow driven by the crossbow cord is also pyramidal, because at every degree of movement it becomes slower and weaker. However, because this pyramid of force is longer than that of its propeller, the arrow detaches from the cord before the cord has even stopped moving—even when the propeller was at its maximum power.

## [Weight and counterweight. Crossbow]

### *Experiment*

One should experiment here with the same counterweight <note>original: "counterpoise"</note> and the same drop distance of that counterweight, but using different weights and shapes for the object being moved. First, determine which weight, when made into a spherical shape, will be driven further than any other by its propulsion source <note>original: "mover"</note>. 

Once you have found the ideal weight for a sphere, test how its movement changes when the object is reshaped to be longer and equipped with feathers, like an arrow. Furthermore, this arrow shape—while maintaining the same weight—can be made from different materials that are denser or lighter in themselves. 

Once you observe where such a shape stops in relation to the power of its propulsion source, you should then experiment to see if the speed of the source itself increases when the object’s travel distance becomes longer or shorter. However, this experiment should first be conducted while the object being moved is still spherical.

Remember to account for the intermediate components used between the power source and the object being moved, such as the weight of the instrument and other factors.
<meta>M 91 r. and v.</meta>

## [Movement—Water]

# OF THE PROPULSION SOURCE OF STABLE POWER

### *Water*

In this case, the object being moved can never travel slower than the movement of its propulsion source. In effect, if the object moved at the same speed as its source, the source could never strike it <note>original: "make percussion"</note>; it would only be able to move a weight equal to the volume of water that follows the movement of the wave driving it forward.
<meta>M 92 r.</meta>

### *[Counterweight and crossbow]*

## ON THE PROPULSION SOURCE OF INCREASING POWER <note>original: "mover of power capable of being increased"</note>

This type of movement is the opposite of that produced by a crossbow. The propulsion source <note>original: "mover"</note> in this case acquires degrees of momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note> at every stage of its motion. The crossbow does the opposite because its string begins at its maximum force and ends with none, whereas the counterweight <note>original: "counterpoise"</note>, as it falls, begins with nothing and ends with great power.

We can understand here that because of the rapid movement the crossbow string makes at the start of its release, the arrow—which is moved by this momentum—does not slow its motion at the same rate as the string. On the contrary, it maintains its initial speed and separates itself from the string before the string has finished its full movement.

<margin>Manuscript M, sheets 92 verso and 93 recto.</margin>

An object driven by a counterweight behaves in the opposite way. Since the weight begins slowly and ends with great momentum, the object being moved will never be able to separate itself from the source (as the arrow does from the crossbow) until the propulsion source has finished its own course.

### *[Crossbow]*

## ON THE PROPULSION SOURCE OF DECREASING POWER

If a weight of four hundred pounds pulls the string of the crossbow over the notch, the string possesses a force of four hundred pounds; however, as it is released, that force diminishes until it ends in nothingness.

This decrease in force occurs in stages, following the shape of a pyramid with equal sections. Consequently, we may say that the center of this pyramid is what may be called the "center of force." This is similar to how the weight of a simple staff acts: if you find its center, you find the weight of the entire object. We can find the center of the crossbow string's movement in the same way. 

By measuring the weight that pulls the string to this specific position, you will find that this weight is equal to the total weight of all the arrows that could be lined up along the length of the path the arrow travels from the notch to its release. This remains true whether the arrow is long and thin or short and thick...

<margin>British Museum MS, 54 recto</margin>
Excessive force applied against a similar resistance provides no benefit to the projectile. However, if the force of the mover is proportional to its projectile, the movement produced will be at its peak effectiveness <note>original: "in the first stage of its strength"</note>. It is as if I were to try to push a bladder filled with air <note>original: "wind"</note> against the atmosphere; if it were moved with excessive force, the air it strikes would offer such resistance—by becoming compressed—that the bladder striking it would bounce back just as if it had hit a wall. <margin>British Museum MS, 82 recto</margin>
There are two different types of impacts <note>original: "percussions"</note>: simple and complex. A "simple" impact is created by a moving object falling upon its target. A "complex" impact occurs when this first strike passes through the resistance of the object it hits first—as seen in the blow delivered to a sculptor’s chisel, which is then transferred to the marble being carved. 

This blow is also divided into two other types: the simple blow and the double blow. The simple blow has already been described; the double blow occurs when the hammer descends with force in its natural motion, then flies back, rebounding from the primary strike to create a secondary, weaker blow, thus making impacts in two places with the two opposite sides of the hammer. This impact diminishes in proportion to the number of obstacles placed between it and the final resistance, just as if someone were to strike the front page of a book; if all the pages are touching, the last page would feel the impact very slightly.

The other is composite. Simple movement is divided into two types: the first occurs when a body moves around its axis without changing its position, like a wheel, a millstone, or similar objects; the second is when an object moves from its position without any rotation. <note>Leonardo identifies this in the margin as "progressive movement."</note> Composite movement is that which, in addition to moving from its position, also rotates around its axis, such as the movement of the wheels of a wagon or other similar things.

Force is produced by scarcity or abundance <note>original: "dearth or profusion"</note>. This gravity is confined within the elements of water and earth, and this force is infinite; for by means of it, infinite worlds could be set in motion if it were possible to construct the instruments by which this force could be produced.

Force with material movement, and weight with impact <note>original: "percussion"</note>, are the four accidental powers <note>In Renaissance physics, "accidental" powers are external forces acting upon an object, rather than its "essential" or natural qualities.</note> in which all the works of mortals have their beginning and their end.

Force has its origin in spiritual movement, which courses through the limbs of sentient animals, thickening their muscles. By this process of thickening, the muscles contract and pull back the tendons connected to them; from this originates the force that exists in the limbs of men.

The quality and quantity of force in a man will have the power to give birth to other forces, and this will be proportionately greater according to how much longer the movement of the one is than that of the other.

Gravity and force, together with material movement and impact, are the four accidental powers by which the human race in its marvel—

[Marve]lous and varied works seem to reveal themselves as a second nature in this world; seeing that through the use of such powers, all the visible works of mortals have their existence and their end.

Movement can extend to infinite degrees of slowness.

No element possesses weight when it is within its own natural sphere; but when by chance an element passes into a lighter one, it instantly creates gravity.

Bend a piece of wood, such as is used in crossbows, so that it reaches from the hand to the chest. The reason for this is as follows: know that as the leap forward is swift, it lends one degree of force <note>original: "fury"; Leonardo uses this to mean intense impetus or kinetic energy</note> to the arrow; the extension of the arm, because it is swifter, lends a second; and the driving force of the cord, being swifter still, gives a third. ### CONCERNING WEIGHTS

<margin>Forster Codex I, 48 verso</margin>
Suppose there are two men holding the edges of a sheet, and in that sheet sits a man who weighs two hundred pounds. If each man pulls his end so hard that the weight does not touch the ground, know that each of those pulling is holding up a weight as great as the man in the middle weighs. This is because each man supports half the weight of the man in the center and also works against half the strength of the man pulling opposite him. Thus, it appears that while the weight in the center is two hundred pounds, since each of those pulling exerts two hundred pounds of force, the total force becomes four hundred pounds.

### OF WEIGHT

<margin>Forster Codex II, 45 recto</margin>
If you were to stand with your body in a state of perfectly equal balance with an opposite counterweight, and you then throw your arms upward forcefully while holding two weights in your hands, I am uncertain whether your weight would become lighter or heavier. ## CONCERNING MOVEMENT

The center of the world <note>Leonardo uses "world" to mean the Earth, following the common belief of his time that it sat at the center of the universe</note> is indivisible; therefore, since nothing else is indivisible, the center is equal to nothing. If one were to make a hole through the diameter of the world, passing through its center, and a weight were thrown into it, the further it moved, the greater its weight <note>momentum</note> would become.

<margin>Forster Codex II, 59 verso</margin>
Thus, having arrived at the center of the earth—which is a center in name only and is itself equal to nothing—the thrown weight would find no resistance at this center. Instead, it would pass through and then return <note>Leonardo is describing the oscillation of an object falling through a hole in the Earth, swinging back and forth across the center due to momentum</note>.

Every heavy object that descends freely directs its course toward the center of the world; and that which has the most weight descends most rapidly, and the further it descends, the faster it becomes.

<insert>[Sketch—ship in water]</insert>

<margin>Forster Codex II, 65 verso</margin>
The water that is moved from its place <note>displaced</note> by the ship weighs exactly as much as the actual weight of the ship itself.

<insert>[Diagram]</insert>

<margin>Forster Codex II, 67 verso</margin>
If two cords support the same weight but are not equal in their verticality or slant, they will not be burdened equally by this weight. Instead, one will receive more of the weight than the other in proportion to how much shorter it is, and according to the difference between the angles formed by the line of the cords and the beam above to which they are fixed.

Imagine I have ten measures of time, ten measures of force, ten measures of movement, and ten measures of weight, and I wish to raise this weight.

If I double the weight but do not increase the force used in the movement, it becomes necessary to double the time spent.

If I double the weight but do not increase the time or the force, it becomes necessary to halve the distance of the movement.

If I double the weight but do not change the movement or the time, it becomes necessary to double the force.

If I halve the weight and do not change the movement or the time, the required force is also halved.
