[Drawing]

If you wish to know the load on the cord that supports the final pulley, always multiply the weight attached to the end <note>original: "foot"; referring to the weight at the starting point of the pulley system</note> cubically by the number of pulleys. The result of this calculation will be the number of pounds of force that this last cord receives from the weight attached to its end.

Let us suppose, therefore, that this weight attached to the end is four pounds. You would then calculate: four pounds multiplied by four (the number of pulleys) makes sixteen; and then four times sixteen makes sixty-four. This is a cubic multiplication. Thus, this upper cord supports sixty-four pounds because of the four pounds attached at the end. 

If there were six such pulleys, you would say: four times six is twenty-four, and four times twenty-four is ninety-eight <note>original: "ninety-eight (*sic!*)"; Leonardo's calculation here is slightly incorrect, as 4 times 24 is 96</note>. Thus, this great weight is supported by the last cord by means of the four pounds attached to the end.

Here it is shown how the four pounds of force proceed to double continually; with the addition of each wheel, the previous weight is doubled. 

<margin>Forster Codex II, 82 verso</margin>

[Drawing]

A cord doubles its natural strength as many times as it is suspended from different points along its length.

<term>Gravity</term> <note>original: "gravity"; here Leonardo uses the term to mean a physical weight or a heavy body</note> acting upon a suspended cord creates specific degrees of weight at every degree of movement.

The force required to move a weight on a suspended cord will be just as great as the force required to move that same weight over rollers or balls placed beneath it.

But at this point, a doubt seems to arise based on the fifteenth proposition of the first book <note>This likely refers to a specific proposition in a classical or medieval text on mechanics, such as the *Liber de Ponderibus* (Book of Weights)</note>, where it says that the center of gravity of a suspended cord is beneath the center of this cord, and this center of gravity tends, as far as possible, to approach the center of the earth. If you pull this weight sideways, the fixed weight creates a revolving movement, raises itself up, and moves away from the center of the earth; in doing so, it increases the weight felt by its mover <note>original: "mover"; the force or person applying the movement</note>. However, a weight resting on balls <note>Leonardo is referring to ball bearings</note> on a smooth surface always keeps its center at an equal distance from the center of the world; consequently, it does not increase the resistance felt by its mover.

The resistance created by friction during the movement of weights is separate and distinct from the weight itself.

### Reason

This is demonstrated by the points made previously: it is clearly seen that movement made by weights along a horizontal line does not, in itself, offer any resistance to its mover other than the natural friction it creates with the smooth surface where it touches it. This movement becomes more difficult in proportion to how much the smooth surface becomes scoured or rough. To see the truth of this, move the weight upon balls on an absolutely smooth surface; you will then see that it moves without effort.

A weight whose movement is made difficult by the friction it creates with the smooth surface it moves upon will seem to increase in gravity as it lacks the ease provided by friction-free movement <note>Leonardo is observing that while the object's mass doesn't change, the force required to overcome friction feels like an increase in weight to the person moving it</note>.

For example, if there are two objects with different surfaces—where one is soft, polished, and well-greased or soaped, and it is moved upon a similar smooth surface—it will move much more easily than one that has been made rough by the use of lime or a rasping file <note>original: "rasping-file"; a coarse tool used for scraping or shaping</note>.

If you do not know this and do not wish to test it, set up an obstacle in your path that changes according to the slope of the road where the weight must be pulled. 

Different slopes create different degrees of resistance at their point of contact. The reason is that if the weight to be moved is placed on level ground and must be dragged, it will experience the maximum resistance because the entire weight rests upon the earth and none of it is supported by the cord that pulls it. However, if you wish to pull it up a very steep path, the weight supported by the pulling cord is subtracted from the friction at the point of contact. To provide a more obvious reason: you know that if you were to pull a weight straight up so that it barely grazes a wall, almost all the weight is supported by the cord, and only a tiny fraction rests against the wall where it rubs.

## ON FRICTION

<margin>Forster II 131 v.</margin>
The action of friction is divided into categories, one of which is "simple" and all others are "compound." Simple friction occurs when an object is dragged along a flat, smooth surface without anything placed in between them. This is the only form of friction that creates fire when it is powerful—that is, it produces heat—as is seen with water-wheels when the water between the sharpened iron and the wheel is removed <note>Leonardo identifies water here as a lubricant; without it, the friction between metal parts creates sparks or fire</note>.

The other types of friction are compound and are divided into two parts. The first is when any lubricant <note>original: "greasiness"</note> or thin substance is placed between the bodies which rub together. The second is when another type of friction is introduced, such as the friction at the axles <note>original: "poles"</note> of wheels. The first of these is also divided into two parts: the lubricants placed in the aforementioned second form of friction, and the use of ball bearings <note>original: "balls and things like these"</note>.

Anything and everything, no matter how thin it may be, which is placed between objects that rub together, reduces the difficulty of this friction.

Observe the friction of great weights during movement. As I have shown in the fourth section of the seventh book, the larger the wheel <note>referring to a roller or pulley</note> that is placed in between, the easier this movement becomes. Conversely, the movement becomes more difficult in proportion to how much thinner the intervening substance is, such as a thin layer of grease. Thus, using tiny grains such as millet makes the movement better and easier, and using ball bearings makes it even more so.

<summary>Leonardo classifies friction into "simple" (direct contact) and "compound" (using lubricants or bearings) while observing that impact is an instantaneous event rather than a divisible duration.</summary>
<keywords>percussion, simple friction, compound friction, lubrication, ball bearings, water-wheels, mechanics, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

Anything that is completely worn away <note>original: "consumed"</note> by the prolonged movement of its friction will have part of it worn away at the very beginning of that movement.

This demonstrates to us that it is impossible to produce or make anything with absolute precision. For if you wish to draw a perfect circle with the movement of one of the points of a pair of compasses, and you accept or confirm the principle set forth above—namely, that in the course of a long movement this point tends to wear away—it must be conceded that if the whole point is worn away over a certain total span of time, a proportional part of it will be worn away during a portion of that time. Furthermore, an infinitesimal <note>original: "indivisible"</note> moment of time may mark the beginning of such wear.

Consequently, the opposite point of these compasses—the one which rotates on its own axis at the center of this circle—is also constantly being worn down and wearing away the surface on which it rests. Therefore, we may say that the end of the circle does not truly join with its beginning; rather, the end of such a line is some imperceptible distance closer to the center of the circle.

The friction produced by the same weight will offer equal resistance at the start of its movement, even if the contact area is of different widths or lengths <note>Leonardo identifies a fundamental law of friction here: that it is independent of the surface area of the contact points</note>.

The larger the contact area made by solid bodies during friction, the more durability <note>original: "permanence"</note> it will have, as it has greater bulk; conversely, it will be much less enduring if it is of a smaller size.

<margin>Forster II 133 r. and 132 v.</margin>
This principle is demonstrated by the friction made by the head of a knife handle; over an equal amount of time, the wear there is more noticeable than the wear produced by the knife's point.

<margin>Forster II 141 v.</margin>
Impetus <term>momentum</term> carries a moving object beyond its natural position.

Every movement has a finite length, determined by the power that moves it, and from this one can establish a rule.

Every moving object that gains velocity during the act of movement is undergoing its "natural movement"; conversely, when it loses velocity, it moves with "accidental movement" <note>In the physics of Leonardo's time, "natural movement" referred to an object seeking its place in the world (like a heavy object falling), while "accidental" or "forced" movement was caused by an external power and eventually faded away</note>.

The variation in weight that this cord gains through its movement will be in the same proportion to the initial weight as its movement is to the rest of the pole.

The weights that shift between the two cords will be in the same proportion to each other as the spaces between the two cords and the center of the pole are to each other.

Furthermore, the weights remaining on these cords will have the same proportion to one another as the opposite spaces enclosed between the center of the pole and the two cords.

The weight that shifts between the cords is in the same proportion to the initial weights as the distance the cord has moved is to the rest of the pole.

<margin>Forster II 152 r.</margin>
A pole suspended by two cords at its ends <note>original: "extremities"</note> divides its weight equally between these cords. Even if these cords are moved toward the center of the pole at an equal rate, the weight they support does not change.

However, if one of the cords is moved toward the center of the pole while the other remains fixed at its end, every degree of movement causes the weight to vary. The weights remaining on the cords will then be in the same proportion to each other as the opposite spaces between the center of the pole and the two cords.

<margin>Forster II 152 v.</margin>
The proportion between the spaces located between the center of the suspended pole's length and the two cords supporting it will be the same as the proportion between the opposite weights the pole exerts on those supporting cords.

An object that moves by natural movement <note>natural movement: Leonardo’s term for motion toward the center of the Earth, such as a falling object</note> gains increments of speed with every degree of movement. These increments of speed will maintain the same proportion—the last to the second-to-last—as the second has to the first.

It is proven that the air does not push a moving object once it has been separated from the force of its original mover.

If a moving object, once separated from its mover, were propelled by the force of the air pushing from behind, then a bullet from a <term>carbine</term> <note>A short-barreled firearm, often used by cavalry.</note> penetrating a leather bottle full of water would stop moving the moment it entered. This would happen because the water would immediately close the entry hole and cut the bullet off from the air that was supposedly driving it. However, experience shows the opposite: this bullet continues to move for a long time after penetrating the water. 

And if you were to argue that the forceful movement of the air—or the water—rushing in to fill the vacuum created as the bullet moves is what forms a "wedge" against the back of the bullet to drive it forward; the reply is that the air is more powerful and more compressed in front of the bullet than it is on the opposite side. This is because the air behind the bullet is merely the air reflected by the bullet's impact. *The reflection of anything is always less powerful than its initial impact* <note>original Latin principle: "Reflexio cuiusque rei est semper minoris virtutis quam sua incidentia." Leonardo is applying the laws of optics and mechanics to air resistance.</note>. And if you should contradict me by arguing that this power cannot be in—

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s argument against the theory that air provides the driving force for a projectile (antiperistasis). He explores the idea of "impressed force" and uses the example of a wheel and water ripples to explain how motion is sustained.</meta>

<page-num>609</page-num>
<header>MOVEMENT AND WEIGHT</header>

...fused into the body that is moved, because "no moving object moves on its own unless its parts exert force against other bodies outside of it." For example, when a man in the middle of a boat pulls a rope attached to the stern to move the ship, his effort is futile unless the rope is tied to the bank toward which he wants to move, or unless he pushes oars in the water or a pole against the bottom. Therefore, since the power is not in the air that drives the bullet, it must be infused into the bullet itself. If it is infused in this way, the examples mentioned above illustrate the result. Furthermore, this infused power would be equally forceful on all sides, because it would be spread in equal amounts throughout the bullet. However, this is not the case, and you do not accept my other premise; let us therefore look for a third explanation that cannot be disputed.

"The power <note>original: "potency"</note> of the mover <note>original: "mover"; the source of the initial force, such as a hand or a bowstring</note> is entirely separated from the source and applied to the body it has moved. This power then gradually consumes itself over time as it penetrates the air, which is constantly compressed in front of the moving object." This happens because "every impression is maintained for a long time in the object upon which it was made." We see this in the ripples <note>original: "circles"</note> created by an impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> on the surface of water; these ripples move through the water for a long distance. We also see it in eddies and waves formed in one spot and carried by the momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note> of the water to another without being destroyed. Light <note>original: "radiance"</note> produces the same effect in the eye, and sound in the ear.

But if you were to say that the air preserves the power of the mover—accompanying and pushing the moving object—how can we explain the case of a wheel that continues to turn for a long time during a windstorm, even after the force that first moved it has been removed?

It is not the air that moves it. Because the wheel is perfectly balanced around its axle <note>original: "axis"</note> in both its shape and its weight, the wind (which surrounds it on only one side) may push the half of the wheel moving away from it, but it simultaneously opposes and resists the other half of the wheel moving toward it. Consequently, because the wind hinders the movement as much as it helps it, it provides no benefit or disadvantage to the wheel's rotation. Therefore, the power of the mover was left imprinted on the outside of the wheel and was not infused into the wheel's interior or into the surrounding air. If you wish to see the movement the air makes when it is penetrated by a moving object, look at an example in the water—specifically, underneath its surface—for

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s investigation into fluid dynamics and the physics of motion. He is specifically refuting the Aristotelian theory of "antiperistasis," which argued that projectiles are pushed forward by the air rushing in behind them to fill a vacuum.</meta>

<page-num>610</page-num>
<header>MOVEMENT AND WEIGHT</header>

You may mix into the water thin millet or other tiny seeds which float at every level of the water's depth. Afterward, place a floating object inside it and you will see the rotation <note>original: "revolution"</note> of the water. This experiment should be done in a square glass vessel shaped like a box. 

"Every natural act is transmitted from the source <note>original: "doer"</note> to the object in the shortest possible time." The air struck and compressed by the moving object does not necessarily have to be the same air that fills the vacuum left behind. As the moving object flies away, it creates a succession of vacuums. Instead, it is the air nearer the rear of the moving object—the area it is leaving—that continually thins out <note>original: "rarefies"</note> the air that was already compressed. Through this thinning <note>original: "rarefaction"</note>, the aforementioned vacuum is filled. 

"A greater power will never be overcome by a lesser power in the same amount of time." Therefore, the swift movement of the thinned air as it rushes to fill the vacuum left by the moving object is much weaker than the air that is being constantly compressed in front of that object. Thinner air can never be the cause of that compression. Therefore, we have concluded that a moving object does not move because of a "wave of air" created by the momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note> of the mover. 

If you wish to argue that the rushing air escaping in front of the object is what prepares its movement—moving with the air and then rushing after it to fill the thinning space—the reply is that this air is moved by the object, and not by its own power. "It is impossible for a mover to move an object and for that object to simultaneously move its mover." Therefore, your reasoning does not hold. If the aforementioned rushing air had to pull itself along after the cause of its own movement, it would be impossible, because "nothing can be the cause of its own creation; and those things which exist by themselves are eternal."

<margin>Codex Leicester, folio 29 verso.</margin>

Gravity <note>Leonardo often uses "gravity" to refer to the downward pressure or weight of an element</note> comes into being when an element is placed above another element less dense <note>original: "thinner"</note> than itself.

Gravity is caused by one element having been drawn within another.
<margin>On the Flight of Birds <note>original: "Sul Volo"</note>, folio 1 recto.</margin>

<summary>Leonardo argues against the idea that air pushes a projectile forward, asserting instead that the force of air compression in front of an object is much stronger than the air rushing into the vacuum behind it. He also provides a basic definition of gravity as the result of density imbalances between elements.</summary>

Gravity is caused by one element being placed <note>original: "situated"</note> within another; it moves along the shortest path toward its center, not by its own volition <note>original: "choice"</note>, nor because the center attracts it. # XX
## Mathematics

> 'There is no certainty in any area where one can apply neither the mathematical sciences nor any of those sciences based upon them.'

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 45 v. a</margin>
As I have shown here at the side <note>referring to a diagram in the original manuscript</note>, there are various ways of squaring the circle—that is, forming squares with an area equal to the area of a circle. Having provided the rules for continuing this process to infinity, I now begin the book called *The Geometric Game* <note>original: 'De Ludo Geometrico'</note>, and I also provide the method for continuing the process to infinity.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 91 v. a</margin>
A body is something whose boundaries form its surface. The surface is not part of the body itself, nor is it part of the air or water that surrounds it; rather, it is a common boundary... in which the body ends where it touches the air, and the air ends where it touches the [body].

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 131 r. b</margin>
What is that thing which does not define itself <note>original: "give itself"</note>, and which, if it were to define itself, would cease to exist? It is the infinite. If the infinite could be defined, it would be bounded and finite; this is because anything that can be defined has a boundary where it meets the thing surrounding its outer limits, and that which cannot be defined is that which has no boundaries.

Surface is the point of contact <note>original: 'contingenzia'</note> between the outer limits of bodies. That is, it is formed by the limits of the volume of air, together with the limits of the bodies enclosed by this air. It is the surface that, along with the air, completes and forms the boundary of the bodies surrounded by the air; likewise, it completes the air where it meets the bodies it covers. The surface does not belong specifically to the surrounding body nor to the surrounded body. It is, instead, the true common boundary of each, and it is that which divides the...

<summary>Leonardo argues that mathematics is the only foundation for certainty and defines the "surface" of an object not as a physical layer, but as the shared, dimensionless boundary where two substances meet. He also explores the paradox of the infinite, noting that to define or bound the infinite would be to destroy its very nature.</summary>

# ON SQUARING THE SURFACE OF A SPHERE THROUGH LINEAR MOTION

Knowledge of an <term>aliquot part</term> <note>a portion of a total that divides into the whole without a remainder (e.g., 1/8 is an aliquot part of 1)</note> provides knowledge of the whole. From this, it follows that <term>squaring</term> <note>original: "quadratura"; the process of finding a square with an area equal to a given shape, in this case, a curved surface</note> the eighth part of a sphere's surface reveals the square of the entire sphere. Let this eighth part of the sphere be represented by *a b c*.

**Second figure.** In the second figure, *c d e*, one divides the eighth part of the spherical surface into <term>parallels</term> <note>horizontal bands or concentric circles on the surface of the sphere</note> of equal width. One then straightens the curves of the two sides, *c d* and *d e*; this is achieved by moving the shape across a flat surface.

**Third figure.** In this third figure, the goal promised in the second is achieved: the straightened sides *f g* and *g h* represent all the parallels of the second figure. These have been widened and lengthened by their movement, because there are the same number of parallels created upon the extended lines *f g* and *g h* (which are equal to each other). As the whole has increased, the parts have also increased proportionally.

**Fourth figure.** In the fourth figure, one creates equal pyramidal divisions, as shown in *f g h*.

**Fifth figure.** In the fifth figure, the tips of the pyramids are opened and widened, the same number of pyramids are reproduced, and the square *n m o p* is formed. But first, by using motion, one straightens the line *i l*, which gives the area for one-quarter of the spherical surface.

The joining of the curves *c d e*, once straightened at *f g h*, forms a rectangle.

# DEFINITION OF A HELIX

A helix is a single curved line with a consistently irregular curvature that revolves around a point at a consistently irregular distance. <note>Leonardo is describing what we would often call a spiral, where the radius changes as it orbits a center point.</note>

# DEFINITION OF A HEMISPHERE

A hemisphere is a solid body consisting of half a sphere, contained by a flat circle and the curved surface of the half-sphere.

The motion of the hemisphere, beginning at the circumference of its largest circle and ending at the center of the hemisphere, describes a spiral curve.

### MENSURATION
<note>the art of measuring lengths, areas, and volumes</note>

When you wish to measure the breadth of a river, withdraw from its bank to a distance somewhat greater than the width of the stream and observe some fixed mark on the opposite bank. Let **a b** represent the width of the river, and **a c** the space to which you withdraw from the river—this being somewhat longer than the width of the river.

Next, draw at the end of this distance a perpendicular line of whatever length you please, and let this be the line **c d**.

And from this spot **d**, observe again the mark **b** which you noted on the opposite side of the river, and make a mark **f¹** upon the bank at the point which is in the same line as **d b**. After having done this, <term>bisect</term> <note>divide into two equal parts</note> the perpendicular line **c d** at the point **e**. From this point **e**, draw another perpendicular line at exact right angles, and make a mark where it intersects the line **d f¹**; from this, make the third perpendicular line **g f²**. 

You will thus have formed the <term>quadrilateral</term> <note>a four-sided figure</note> **c f² e g**, in which you know that the side **c f²** is equal to **f² b**. This is because just as the point **e** is in the center of the line **c d**, the point **f²** is in the center of the other line **c b**. Then, subtract the distance from the bank **a f²** from the total length **f² c** (this remaining segment being **f² h**), and you have left **h c**, a distance equal to the width of the said river.

## THE FIVE REGULAR BODIES
<note>The "Five Regular Bodies" are the Platonic solids: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note>

This section is written against certain commentators who criticize the ancient inventors—the very people from whom our grammar and sciences originate. These critics campaign against dead inventors because, through their own idleness, they have failed to become inventors themselves. Despite having access to so many books, they constantly try to refute their masters using false arguments:

They claim that the element of earth is <term>hexahedral</term> <note>original: "tetracedronica coe cubica" — a likely error in the original manuscript where Leonardo meant hexahedron</note>¹—meaning it is cubical, a body with six bases. They attempt to prove this by arguing that among the regular bodies, there is no shape less prone to movement or more stable than the cube. Furthermore, they attribute the <term>tetrahedron</term> (the pyramidal body) to the element of fire, because these philosophers believe it is more mobile than the earth. For this reason, they assign the pyramid to fire and the cube to earth.

However, if one were to consider the stability of the pyramidal body and compare it to that of the cube, the cube is actually far more capable of movement than the pyramid. This can be proven as follows:

The cube has six sides and the regular pyramid has four; these are illustrated in the margin at **a** and **b**, where **a** represents the cube and **b** the pyramid. To clarify this proof, I will take one side of the cube and one side of the pyramid, labeled **c** and **d**. I maintain that the cube (**c**) is more suited to a movement of <term>circumvolution</term> <note>rolling or revolving</note> than the pyramid (**d**). Let **e** and **f**, shown below, represent the beginning of these movements.

I state that, in fact, if the base of the cube and the base of the pyramid both rest on the same flat surface, the pyramid must rotate through one-third of its total bulk to fall onto its next side. In contrast, the cube only needs to rotate through one-fourth of its circuit to change sides and establish a new base. From these two demonstrations, it follows that a cube will complete a full rotation by moving across four of its sides on a flat plane, while the triangular pyramid will complete its rotation across only three of its sides. A pentagon <note>the face of a dodecahedron</note> rotates across all five of its sides. Thus, the more sides a figure has, the easier its movement becomes, because the figure ap— <note>The text likely intended to say "approaches the form of a circle or sphere."</note>

¹ The original manuscript has *tetracedronica coe cubica*—presumably a slip of the pen by the author.

# ON PROPORTION

If equal parts are taken away from two similar wholes, the proportion between the parts is the same as the proportion between the wholes.

It follows that if, of two circles, one is double the size of the other, then a quarter section of the larger circle is double the size of a quarter section of the smaller one.

Furthermore, there is the same proportion between one remainder and the other as there is between one whole and the other.

And there is the same proportion between part and part as there is between remainder and remainder.

When two circles touch the same square at four points <note>referring to a circle inscribed within a square and a circle circumscribed around it</note>, one circle is double the size of the other.

<margin>G 17 r.</margin>
Similarly, when two squares touch the same circle at four points, one square is double the size of the other.

# GEOMETRY

The circle that touches the three angles of an equilateral triangle <note>the circumscribed circle</note> is triple the size of the triangle that touches the three sides of the same triangle <note>the inscribed triangle</note>.

<margin>G 17 v.</margin>
The diameter of the largest circle that can be drawn inside a triangle <note>the inscribed circle</note> is equal to two-thirds the height <note>original: "axis"</note> of that same triangle.

The proportion between two circles is the same as the proportion between the two squares formed by multiplying their diameters by themselves <note>Leonardo is stating that the ratio of the areas of two circles is equal to the ratio of the squares of their diameters</note>. Now, create two squares in whatever proportion you please, and then create two circles: let one have the side of the larger square as its diameter, and let the other have the side of the smaller square as its diameter.

<margin>G 37 r.</margin>
Thus, by the converse of the first proposition, you will have two circles that will bear the same proportion to one another as that of the two squares.

# HOW TO FIND THE VOLUME OF A SPHERE

Once you have determined the area <note>original: "squared the surface"</note> of the circle, divide that area into as many small squares as you wish, provided they are equal to one another. Treat each square as the base of a pyramid whose height <note>original: "axis"</note> is the radius <note>original: "half diameter"</note> of the sphere whose volume <note>original: "cube"</note> you want to find; and let all these pyramids be equal. <note>Leonardo is describing a method of exhaustion to find the volume of a sphere, effectively treating the sphere as a sum of infinitely many tiny pyramids meeting at the center.</note>
<sig>G 39 v.</sig>

## [Circles and Squares]

Concentric circles <note>original: "circles made upon the same centre"</note> will have a ratio of two to one <note>the larger is double the smaller</note> if the square placed between them touches both of them <note>that is, if the square is inscribed in the larger circle and circumscribed around the smaller circle</note>. Similarly, squares sharing the same center will have a two-to-one ratio when the circle placed between them touches both squares.

This is proven because the larger square is composed of eight triangles, whereas the smaller square contains only four of them. <note>Leonardo likely refers to a geometric proof where the outer square is divided by its diagonals and midpoints into eight smaller right triangles, while the inner, rotated square occupies four of those triangles.</note>

The ratio between one circle and another is the same as the ratio between the squares formed by squaring their diameters.

Of all the segments of circles <note>original: "parts of circles"</note> that may be in contact inside a right angle, the largest is always equal to the sum of all the smaller ones. Furthermore, of all the parallel sections that contain these segments within themselves, the largest always contains and is the equivalent of all the smaller parallels formed in this right angle *a b c*.
<sig>G 40 r.</sig>

# DEFINITION OF FOUR TYPES OF PARALLELS

Parallel figures are of four kinds. The first is enclosed between two straight and equidistant lines. The second is between two equidistant lines of uniform curvature. The third is between two equidistant lines of varying curvature, such as the parallel lines drawn around the center of a circle. The fourth is formed by a single line curved around a point at an equal distance—that is, the line of the circumference around the center of its circle.

All these lines are of a uniform nature since, through movement, a straight line becomes curved and a curved line becomes straight, by...

## ON SQUARING THE CIRCLE AND WHO FIRST DISCOVERED IT

While Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio (c. 80–15 BC), a Roman architect and engineer.</note> was measuring the mile by counting the full revolutions of chariot wheels, he laid out many lines of the circumference of these wheels across the distance of his *stadia* <note>An ancient Greek and Roman unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note>. He observed this from the animals pulling the chariots, but he did not realize that this was the method for finding a square equal in area to a circle. This was first discovered by Archimedes of Syracuse, who found that multiplying half the diameter of a circle by half of its circumference produced a rectangle <note>original: "rectilinear quadrilateral"</note> equal in area to the circle. <margin>G 96 r.</margin>

There is no certainty in any field where one cannot apply the mathematical sciences, or any of those sciences built upon mathematical foundations. <margin>G 96 v.</margin>

Whether an object is lifted or pulled makes a great difference in the level of difficulty for the person moving it. If an object weighs a thousand pounds and one moves it by simply lifting it, it weighs the full thousand pounds. However, if it is pulled, the resistance is reduced by a third. If it is pulled on wheels, the effort required is reduced even further in proportion to the size of the wheels and how many wheels are used. With the same amount of time and power, one can complete the same journey; likewise, one can achieve the same movement in the same amount of time using different levels of power. The center of every hanging weight seeks to align itself <note>original: "desires to unite"</note> with the central line of its support.

## [*The Wonders of Mechanics*]

### Rule [*Diagram*]

Pivots designed to withstand the greatest force are used for movements that go back and forth, such as those of bells, saws, and similar mechanisms.

One pound of force applied at point *b* results in ten trillion <note>original: "ten thousand thousands of millions"</note> pounds of force at point *m*. The figure opposite behaves the same way, being of the same design and only differing in that the wheels are complete circles, as they must turn continuously in a single direction. Understand that when the top wheel completes one hundred trillion <note>original: "hundred thousand thousands of millions"</note> rotations, the bottom wheel completes only one full turn.

These are the wonders of the science of mechanics.

In this way, one could mount a bell on a pivot so that it could be rung by even a slight breeze, provided the bell has its counterweights equalized and placed at the same distance from its center.

[*Diagram*]

This arrangement will create a rotation of such long duration that it will seem incredible and almost against the laws of nature, because it continues to move long after the initial power source has stopped. It causes the weight *m* to fall from such a height that the wheel spins thirty times or more, and then it continues to spin freely like a spinning top. To prevent noise, this stone weight should fall onto straw.

It is only necessary to make each successive wheel larger than the one above it so that the rim of the lower wheel does not strike or obstruct the pivot of the wheel above it.

### PROPORTION IN ALL THINGS

<margin>Codex Forster II, 49 [48 and 15] recto <note>original: "r."; the front side of a page</note></margin>
Proportion is found not only in numbers and measurements but also in sounds, weights, durations of time, positions, and in every possible force <note>original: "power"</note> that may exist.

**How one of Xenophon’s propositions is incorrect:**
If unequal quantities are subtracted from unequal wholes, and the parts being removed are in the same proportion as the original wholes, then the remainders will maintain that same proportion. But if equal quantities are subtracted from unequal wholes, the remainders will still be unequal, but they will no longer be in the same proportion as before.

Consider these examples: first, let the parts taken away be in the same proportion as the wholes—for instance, let 2 and 4 represent the two wholes, so that one is double the other. If you take 1 away from 2, 1 remains; if you take 2 away from 4, 2 remains. These remainders (1 and 2) have the same proportion to each other as the original wholes and as the parts that were taken away. Therefore, if 1 is taken from 2 and 2 from 4, the same double proportion remains as at first. 

It follows that anyone who subtracts equal quantities would change the original proportion. That is to say, if you have two numbers where one is double the other, such as 2 and 4, and you were to subtract an equal amount—taking 1 from 2 and 1 from 4—you would be left with 1 and 3. In this case, one number is now three times the other, and therefore the difference is more than double.

<margin>Codex Forster II, 61 [12] recto and verso <note>original: "r. and v."; the front and back of the page</note></margin>
Therefore, you, Xenophon <note>Xenophon (c. 430–354 BC) was a Greek philosopher. Leonardo often engaged with classical authorities, testing their logic through mathematical proofs.</note>, who wished to subtract equal parts from unequal wholes believing that the remainders would stay in the same proportion as the originals, were deceiving yourself!

### DEFINITIONS OF A STRAIGHT LINE

**First.** A straight line is one in which every part is at an equal height <note>In Leonardo’s geometry, "height" often refers to the level or distance from a reference point or center of gravity.</note>.

**Second.** A curved line is one that has a uniformly changing height toward its ends, which are themselves at an equal height.

### MATHEMATICS

<margin>Manuscript K, 78 [30] verso and 79 [31] recto</margin>

The first and second definitions are incorrect because any object of equal height must have every part of its mass <note>original: "bulk"</note> at an equal distance from the center of the world <note>In Leonardo’s time, "height" was often defined relative to the Earth's center; therefore, a truly "level" line would follow the Earth's curvature.</note>. Therefore, the curve *f b o* would be considered straight because it remains at a uniform distance from this center, while the straight line *a b c* would be considered curved, because every part of its length varies uniformly in its distance from the center, even if its ends are at an equal distance.

And if you say that a straight line is one that contains three points of equal height along its length, you are still mistaken.

However, if you say that a straight line is the shortest distance between two given points, you will provide its true definition.

*[*With drawings*]*

<margin>Manuscript K, 79 [31] recto</margin>

A circle is equal in area to a rectangle <note>original: "rectangular parallelogram"</note> formed by one-quarter of its diameter and the whole of its circumference. You may also say it is equal to a rectangle formed by half of its diameter and half of its circumference <note>This is a correct geometric proof for the area of a circle: Area = Radius × (Circumference / 2).</note>.

Imagine the circle *e f* to be broken down into an almost infinite number of pyramids <note>Leonardo is envisioning the circle as a collection of many tiny triangles or "pyramids" meeting at the center.</note>. If these were then laid out along the straight line that touches their bases at *b d*, and half of their height were removed to form the parallel rectangle *a b c d*, this rectangle would be exactly equal in area to the given circle *e f*.

Regarding the circumference of the circle: it is useful to measure one quarter of it using a strip of cane bark <note>Leonardo often suggests using flexible materials like bark to measure curved surfaces by unrolling them into a straight line.</note>. By following its spiral curve and then stretching it out, you can establish a rule for where the center of the circle is located—the point from which the movement of the end of the measurement is directed—and similarly find the center of movement for its many parts. This allows you to create a general rule.

<margin>Manuscript K, 79 [31] verso and 80 [32] recto</margin>

The circle is a "parallel" figure because all the straight lines drawn from the center to the circumference (the radii) are equal. These lines meet the circumference at equal angles and spherical lines. The same principle applies to the transverse lines of a rectangle—namely, they meet their sides at right angles.

All straight-sided <note>original: "rectilinear"</note> pyramids, and those formed by curved lines on the same bases, are equal if they vary uniformly in width along their length between parallel lines of circumference.

For pyramids with equal bases, the proportion of the slopes of their sides will be the same as the proportion of their heights.

Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman architect and engineer whose work was rediscovered during the Renaissance.</note> claims that the performance of large-scale machines cannot be predicted by the results of small models. Regarding this, I intend to demonstrate below that his conclusion is false. I will do this by using the very same arguments from which he formed his opinion—specifically, the example of the auger <note>original: "auger"; a tool used for boring holes in wood.</note>. He points out that when a man's strength has bored a hole of a certain diameter, a hole of double that diameter cannot then be bored by doubling that man's strength, but requires much greater power. To this, one may easily reply by pointing out that a drill of double the size cannot be moved by double the power because the surface area of any object that is similar in shape but double the diameter is four times larger than the other, as is shown by the two figures *a* and *n*.

[Drawing] *a n.*

<margin>Manuscript L, 53 recto and 53 verso</margin>
In this case, each of these two drills removes an equal thickness of wood from each of the holes they make; but in order for the holes or drills to be double the size of the other, they must have four times the surface area and require four times the power <note>Leonardo is observing what modern engineers call the "square-cube law," noting that as the size of a tool increases, the surface area causing friction increases by the square (2² = 4).</note>.

<margin>Manuscript M, inside front cover, verso</margin>
The right angle is said to be the "first perfect angle" among all others because it sits exactly at the midpoint between an infinite variety of other angles. That is, it sits between an infinite number of obtuse angles and an infinite number of acute angles. Since all these infinite angles are balanced against each other, the right angle is equidistant to each of them, being in the middle.

<margin>Manuscript M, 1 recto</margin>
### THE THIRD LESSON OF THE FIRST PART

Triangles are of three kinds: the first has three acute angles, the second has one right angle and two acute angles, and the third has one obtuse angle and two acute angles.

The triangle with three acute angles may have three different shapes: the first has three equal sides <note>equilateral</note>, the second has two equal sides <note>isosceles</note>, and the third has three unequal sides <note>scalene</note>.

And the right-angled triangle may be of two kinds: one with two equal sides and one with three unequal sides.

<page-num>625</page-num>
<header>MATHEMATICS</header>

<margin>Manuscript M, 1 verso</margin>
A right-angled triangle with two equal sides <note>an isosceles right triangle</note> is derived from half of a square. A right-angled triangle with three unequal sides <note>a scalene right triangle</note> is formed by half of a long <term>rectangle</term> <note>original: "tetragon"</note>. An obtuse-angled triangle with two equal sides is formed by half of a <term>rhombus</term> cut along its greatest length <note>the long diagonal</note>.

A **square** is the name applied to a figure of four equal sides which form four right angles within them; that is to say, the lines that compose the angles are equal to each other.

### LONG RECTANGLE <note>original: "Long Tetragon"</note>

<margin>Manuscript M, 2 recto</margin>
The long <term>rectangle</term> <note>original: "tetragon"</note> is a surface figure contained by four sides and four right angles; and although its opposite sides are equal, it does not follow from this that the sides which form the right angle must be equal to each other.

The **rhombus** is of two kinds: the first is formed from a square and the second from a **parallelogram**. The first has its opposite angles equal and likewise all its sides equal; its only variation consists in the fact that no side ends in equal angles, but rather with one acute angle and one obtuse angle.

### RHOMBOID

<margin>Manuscript M, 2 verso</margin>
The **rhomboid** is the figure that is formed from the **rhombus**, but whereas the rhombus is formed from a square, the rhomboid is formed from a rectangle. It has opposite sides and angles equal to each other, but none of its angles are contained by equal sides.

**Parallel** or equidistant lines are those which, when extended continuously in a straight line, will never meet together at any point.

<margin>Manuscript M, 3 recto</margin>
Every whole is greater than its part.

If a thing is neither larger nor smaller, it is equal.

### OF FIVE POSTULATES <note>These are based on the foundational "Postulates" of Euclid's Elements.</note>

1. That a straight line may be drawn from one point to another.

2. That with a center point it is possible to make a circle of any size.

3. That all right angles are equal to each other.

Two straight lines cannot enclose a surface <note>two lines alone cannot form a closed shape like a triangle or square</note>.

### THE THIRD LESSON OF THE TENTH <note>A reference to Book 10 of Euclid's "Elements," which discusses irrational numbers and magnitudes</note>

<margin>Manuscript M, 6 verso</margin>
Concerning the comparison made between continuous quantity <note>measurable things like lines or time</note> and definite quantity <note>countable things like numbers</note>, and how a continuous quantity may have parts that communicate—that is to say, they are measured by a common measure. For example, a measure of one <term>braccio</term> <note>original: "braccio"; an Italian unit of length based on the arm's length, roughly 23 inches</note> is a measure that fits four times into a line of four *braccia*, and three times into a length of three *braccia*. It thus forms a unity which corresponds to the number four and also to the number three. There is the same proportion between four *braccia* and the number four as there is between one number and one *braccio*.

---

### OF FIVE [OR SIX?] POSTULATES

<margin>Manuscript M, 7 recto</margin>
The boundaries of a line are points; the boundaries of a surface are lines; and the boundaries of a solid body are surfaces.

A straight line may be drawn from any one point to another.

And this line may also be extended as far as one pleases beyond these points, but the boundaries of this line will always be two points.

Around the same point, one may draw many circles.

All right angles are equal to each other.

Parallel lines are those across which, if a <term>transversal</term> line is drawn, four angles are formed; when those on one side are taken together, they equal two right angles <note>180 degrees</note>.

<margin>Manuscript M, 9 recto</margin>
If two squared surfaces have the same proportion to each other as the squares of their side lengths, then their sides will be <term>commensurable</term> <note>having a common measure; their ratio can be expressed as a whole number</note> in length.

And if there are two squared surfaces whose sides are commensurable in length, it follows that the proportion between the surfaces will be the same as the proportion between the squares of their sides.

And if the squared surfaces do not have the same proportion to one another as the squares of their side lengths, then their sides will be <term>incommensurable</term> <note>having no common measure; an irrational ratio</note> in length.

<margin>Manuscript M, 13 verso and 14 recto</margin>
A straight line is one in which, if a point is placed in any position outside of it at such a distance that its length corresponds precisely to a given segment of that line, and if straight lines are drawn from that point to each of the line’s divisions, these lines can be divided in exactly the same way by each of those segments. <note>This is a complex way of describing the proportional relationship between a point and a partitioned line, effectively defining a straight line through the consistency of its segments.</note>

Suppose the line to be proven is *b f*, the given point is *a*, and the distance from the point to the end of the line is *a b*. The lengths (the segments *b, c, d, e, f*) are each equal to the distance *a b*. I state that the line *a c* is double the distance *a b*, the line *a d* is triple, *a e* is quadruple, and *a f* is quintuple.

## NINE PROPOSITIONS

<margin>Manuscript M, 16 recto</margin>
Things that are equal to the same thing are also equal to each other. And if equal things are added to equal things, the totals will still be equal.

If equal things are taken away from equal things, the remainders will still be equal. If equal things are taken away from unequal things, the remainders will remain unequal. If two things are equal to another thing, they will be equal to each other. If there are two things which are each half of the same thing, they will be equal to each other. If one thing is placed over another and fits it so that neither exceeds the other, these things will be equal to each other. <note>This refers to the principle of superposition—the idea that shapes are identical if they can be perfectly overlapped.</note> And every whole is greater than any of its parts.

<margin>Manuscript M, 18 recto</margin>
Geometry is infinite because every continuous quantity <note>a quantity that can be divided without end, like a line or time</note> is divisible to infinity in one direction or the other. However, a discontinuous quantity <note>countable things like whole numbers</note> begins at unity (one) and increases to infinity. As has been stated, a continuous quantity both increases to infinity and decreases to infinity. If you were to say that you could give me a line of twenty <term>braccia</term> <note>original: "braccia"; an Italian unit of length roughly equal to 23 inches</note>, I would show you how to make one of twenty-one.

<margin>Manuscript M, 31 verso</margin>
All the angles formed around a single point, when taken together, are equal to four right angles. <note>This equals 360 degrees.</note>

### [*A man’s leap*]

If a man, in taking a leap from a firm spot, jumps three *braccia* <note>original: *braccia* (plural of *braccio*); a Florentine unit of measurement approximately equal to 23 inches or 58 centimeters</note> and recoils by a third of a *braccio* as he takes his spring, how much would he fall short of his initial leap?

And in the same way, if the leap was increased by one-third of a *braccio*, how much would he have added to his leap?
<meta>Manuscript M, folio 55 recto</meta>

### [*Pyramids*]

Multiply the root of the number of the pyramid you choose by itself, and separate it toward one of the angles.

If I wanted to find the area of a cross-section at a point one-fourth of the height from the apex <note>Leonardo is discussing the relationship between the linear scale of a pyramid and its cross-sectional area. If the linear dimension is 1/4 of the total height, the area of that section is the square of that ratio (1/16)</note>—which corresponds to one-fourth of the length of the pyramid—I would say: four times four is sixteen. Therefore, the piece removed will be one-sixteenth of the whole pyramid's base. And if you take a section at half the height, which corresponds to half the length of this pyramid, you would say a half times a half is a quarter; therefore, the part taken away will be a quarter of the whole pyramid. If you multiply three-quarters of the base by three-quarters of the length of the pyramid, this will equal nine-sixteenths of the whole pyramid.

This curved pyramid will reach its point by completing its circles. But if such a pyramid were to extend for thousands of miles before meeting at a point, you would not be able to complete these circles; therefore, use the scale provided.
<meta>Manuscript M, folio 86 verso</meta>

### [*Curved lines and pyramids*]

If you make a cut above that is equidistant to the circle below, using its center *r*, and if you make a cut below that is equidistant to the circle above, using its center *a*, I want to know if these two lines are drawn with the same curve, at what distance they will meet; or, if they do not meet, where they will come closest to each other, how far apart they will remain, and how near they will ever get.

Regarding two given curved lines, I want to determine whether they are parallel or not. If they are not parallel, I want to see if they are positioned to form a pyramid <note>In this context, Leonardo uses "pyramid" to refer to any converging shape or a cone-like structure formed by lines meeting at an apex</note>, and if they are meant to form a pyramid, at what specific distance from the base their curved sides should meet.

To do this, you will proceed as follows: separate a portion between the base...

<insert>*[Geometrical paradox]*</insert>
If an angle is the point where two lines touch, and since lines end at a point, an infinite number of lines can start at that same point. Conversely, an infinite number of lines can end together at that point. Consequently, a single point can be the common beginning and end of countless lines.

It seems strange that a triangle ends in a single point at the angle opposite the base. Since one can divide the triangle into an infinite number of parts starting from the corners of the base, and because the point is the shared end of all these divisions, it suggests that the point itself—just like the triangle—is infinitely divisible.
<sig>Manuscript M, folio 87 verso</sig>

Lines that form circular parallels cannot have the same curvature; if they did, as they completed their circles, they would touch or intersect in two places.

Regarding the curved lines that make up parallel curves, it is necessary that every part and the whole of each line remain parallel <note>original: "equidistant"</note> to a single shared center.
<sig>Manuscript M, folio 89 recto</sig>

### SPHERICAL ANGLES EQUAL TO RIGHT ANGLES

Any four angles formed within the space of a circle are equal to four right angles <note>The sum of angles around a central point is 360 degrees, which is equivalent to four 90-degree right angles.</note>, whether the lines are curved and straight, all straight, or all curved.

Any number of lines that intersect at the same point will form as many angles around that point as there are lines radiating from it; all these angles joined together will be equal to four right angles.
<sig>Manuscript M, folio 89 verso</sig>

<page-num>630</page-num>

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library, folio 2 verso</margin>
*\[With diagram\]*
Pelacani¹ says that the longer arm of this balance will fall more rapidly than the shorter arm. He argues that during its descent, the longer arm describes its quarter-circle path more directly <note>meaning more vertically</note> than the shorter arm does. He claims that since the natural tendency of weights is to fall in a perpendicular <note>perfectly vertical</note> line, the more the circular path curves away from that line, the slower the movement will become.

The diagram *m n* contradicts this argument because the descent of the weights does not actually proceed in circles; nevertheless, the weight *m* on the longer arm does fall.

When an object is farther away from its base <note>its point of support</note>, it is less supported by it. Being less supported, it retains more of its liberty <note>freedom of movement</note>; and since a free weight always descends, the end of the balance rod that is most distant from the support point will—because it is heavy—descend on its own more rapidly than any other part.

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library, folio 3 recto</margin>
*\[Levers\]*
If a beam is of uniform thickness, the lower arm of the balance will be longer and heavier than the upper arm in the same proportion that the end of the upper part approaches the vertical line more closely than the end of the lower part.

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library, folio 3 verso</margin>
*\[Suspended bodies\]*
A suspended body that is perfectly round and smooth will fall in line with its center and will come to a stop directly under the center of the cord from which it is hanging.

The center of gravity of any suspended body will always stop in a perpendicular line directly beneath the center of its support.

<margin>British Museum, folio 37 verso</margin>
Gravity, force, and material movement, together with percussion <note>the shock of impact</note>, are the four accidental powers <term>accidental powers</term> <note>In Aristotelian physics, "accidental" refers to qualities that are not part of an object's essential nature but act upon it from the outside.</note> in which all the visible works of mortals have their beginning and their end.

Gravity is a certain "accidental" power created by movement and infused into one element which is either drawn or pushed by another. This gravity possesses life <note>active force</note> in proportion to how much that element strives to return to its former state.

The yolk <note>original: "redness"</note> of an egg remains in the center of the egg white <note>original: "albumen"</note> without sinking to either side. It must be either lighter, heavier, or the same weight as this white. If it were lighter, it would rise above all the white and stay in contact with the eggshell. If it were heavier, it would sink down. And if it were of the same weight, it would be able to stay at either end just as easily as in the center or at the bottom.

An object in motion will never move faster than the force that moves it.

## OF THE ELEMENTS

The bodies of the elements are unified, and within them, there is neither weight <note>original: "gravity"</note> nor lightness. Weight and lightness are only produced when these elements are mixed together. <note>In the science of the time, the four elements—earth, water, air, and fire—were thought to have "natural places." Weight was seen as the urge of an element to return to its proper level when mixed with others.</note>

A point is that which has no center. <note>Meaning it is indivisible and has no dimensions.</note>
A line is a length <note>extension</note> produced by the movement of a point, and its endpoints are points.
A surface is an area created by the sideways <note>transversal</note> movement of a line, and its boundaries are lines.
A body is a volume <note>quantity</note> formed by the lateral movement of a surface, and its boundaries are surfaces.
A point is that which has no center, and from this it follows that it has neither width, length, nor depth.
A point is that which has no center; therefore, it is indivisible from any angle, and nothing is smaller than it is.
A line is a length made by the movement of a point; therefore, it has neither width nor depth.
A body has length, width, and depth, formed by the sideways movement of its surface. 
<margin>British Museum, Arundel Manuscript, folio 160 recto</margin>

<insert>[Definitions]</insert>

A point has no parts; a line is the path <note>original: "transit"</note> of a point; points are the boundaries of a line.

<sig>B.M. 232 r.</sig>

...from the whole and from the parts of the objects <note>original: "bodies"</note>, so that from this extremity <note>meaning the apex or point of the pyramid</note> one may see the whole and its parts.

The air between objects is full of the intersections formed by the radiating images of these bodies.

The images of the shapes <note>original: "figures"</note> and colors of every object are transferred from one to another by means of a pyramid. <note>Leonardo uses the term "pyramid" to describe the cone-shaped path that light and images take as they travel from an object to the eye or another surface.</note>

Every object fills the surrounding air with these rays of its infinite images.

The image of every point exists within the whole and within every part of the line produced by that point.

Every point of one object is, by geometric correspondence, capable of serving as the entire base of another.

Every object becomes the base of innumerable and infinite pyramids.

A pyramid produced within more equal angles will provide a truer image of the object from which it originates.

The same base serves as the source for innumerable and infinite pyramids pointed in various directions and of various lengths.

The point <note>apex</note> of every pyramid contains within itself the entire image of its base.

The center line of a pyramid is filled with the infinite points of other pyramids.

One pyramid passes through another without causing confusion. <note>This is a fundamental observation in optics: light rays from different sources can cross the same space without distorting each other.</note>

The characteristics <note>original: "quality"</note> of the base are present in every part of the length of the pyramid.

The point of a pyramid that contains all the rays originating from the same angles will reveal less about the object it comes from than any other point contained within that pyramid.

A pyramid with a very sharp <note>original: "slender"</note> point will reveal less of the true form and quality of the object from which it starts.

A pyramid will be at its sharpest when the angles of its base are most different from one another.

The shortest pyramid will most greatly distort the similar and equal parts of its base.

Pyramids of infinite varieties of length can originate from the same arrangement of angles.

A pyramid with the widest point <note>meaning a more obtuse apex</note> will, more than any other, tint <note>original: "dye"</note> the spot it strikes with the color of the object from which it is derived.

### ON THE NATURE OF GRAVITY

Gravity is an accidental quality that bodies acquire when they are removed from their natural place. <note>Leonardo is referencing the Aristotelian view that elements have "natural places"—such as earth at the center and fire in the heavens—and that gravity is the force driving them back to those positions.</note>

### ON THE NATURE OF LEVITY

<margin>British Museum MS, 264 r.</margin>
Levity <note>original: "Levity"; the quality of being light or having upward buoyancy</note> is related to gravity in the same way that unequal weights are joined in a scale, or as light liquids are positioned beneath liquids or solids that are heavier than they are . . .

Take from one of the <term>five regular bodies</term> <note>These are the five Platonic solids: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note> a similar body, so that what remains retains the same shape.

I wish to subtract a given <term>pentagon</term> from another <term>pentagon</term> so that the remainder stays in the form of a <term>pentagon</term>, and these must be three-dimensional bodies rather than two-dimensional surfaces.

Convert the given <term>pentagon</term> into its equivalent <term>cube</term> <note>meaning a cube of the same volume</note>, and do the same with the larger <term>pentagon</term> from which you must extract the smaller one. Then, using the previously established rules, subtract the smaller <term>cube</term> from the larger <term>cube</term>. Finally, reconstruct the <term>pentagon</term> from the remainder of this larger <term>cube</term>, which has remained in a cubic form according to the mentioned rules.

<margin>Forster Codex I, 5 r.</margin>
What is said here about the <term>cube</term> applies to all bodies whose corners touch the surface of a <term>sphere</term> <note>these are inscribed solids</note>; for whatever can be done within a <term>sphere</term> can also be done within a <term>cube</term>.

All bodies possess three <term>dimensions</term>: width, thickness, and length.

There are six ways to change or manipulate bodies: shortening and lengthening, thickening and thinning, and enlarging and compressing.

A surface has width and length but is completely without thickness.

A board is a flat body that has width, length, and a uniform thickness.

<margin>Forster Codex I, 12 v.</margin>
Therefore, when a board has uniform thickness and its surface is of uniform quality, we can manipulate and divide it using the same methods and rules that we apply to the previously mentioned surfaces.

# METHODS OF MEASURING A HEIGHT

<margin>Forster I 48 v.</margin>
Let *c f* be the tower you wish to measure. Move as far away from it as you think appropriate and take its sighting <note>original: "take the range of it"; Leonardo is describing a surveying technique using a sighting tool to equate horizontal distance with vertical height.</note>, as shown in *c b a*. This tool may be the length of an arm and half as high. Adjust it so that the tower occupies the space *b a*; then, project the line *b a* along the level of the ground. It will occupy as much space on the ground as it occupied in height, and within that space of ground, you will find the true height <note>original: "altitude"</note> of the tower.

If two straight lines intersect to form four right angles and have their four ends equidistant from this intersection, it is necessary that these ends also be equidistant from one another.

## GRAVITY

Gravity is an accidental power <note>original: "accidental power"; Leonardo views these powers as 'accidental' because they are not inherent to a body at rest but are triggered by external circumstances or movement.</note> created by movement and infused into bodies that are held outside of their natural position.

## HEAVY AND LIGHT

Gravity and lightness are equal powers created when one element is transferred into another. In every function, they are so similar that for any single power named, they vary only in the bodies they inhabit and in the movement of their creation and removal.

A body is said to be heavy if, when it is free to move, it directs its motion toward the center of the world by the shortest path.

<margin>Forster II 116 v.</margin>
A body is said to be light if, when it is free to move, it flees from the center of the world; both heaviness and lightness are of equal power.

<margin>Forster II 117 r.</margin>
Gravity and force, along with percussion, can be called the mothers and children of one another, as well as sisters, because they are all produced by movement. They are also the producers and children of this movement; without these powers, movement cannot be created, nor can such powers be revealed without movement.

<margin>Forster II 125 v.</margin>
The accidental center of gravity <note>original: "accidental centre of gravity"; likely referring to the center of mass in a moving object as opposed to its static geometric center.</note> for a body descending freely will always align with the central line of its movement, even if the heavy object rotates as it falls.

# MATHEMATICS

To determine the force necessary to raise a specific weight, divide the weight (in pounds) by the number of wheels in the tackle <note>original: "tackle"; a system of ropes and pulleys used for lifting heavy weights.</note>. The result will be the "uncertain weight" <note>In this context, the "uncertain weight" refers to the variable force or input effort required to balance the fixed "certain" load.</note> which will resist the known weight with equal force. 
<margin>Forster III 82 v.</margin>

If you wish to understand clearly the function and force of the tackle, you must know either the weight of the thing that moves (the effort) or the weight of the thing being moved (the load). If you know the weight of the moving force, multiply it by the number of wheels in the tackle; the resulting total will be the maximum weight that can be moved by that force. 
<margin>Forster III 83 r.</margin>

The ratio between a weight suspended by a lever through a windlass <note>original: "windlass"; a winch mechanism consisting of a horizontal cylinder turned by a crank, used for hauling or lifting.</note> cord and the force exerted by the operator is the same as the ratio between the radius (half the diameter) of the windlass and the distance on the lever between the operator’s hand and the center of the windlass's thickness. 
<margin>Forster III 83 v.</margin>

<insert>*[Sketch]*</insert>
If you multiply your body weight (in pounds) by the number of wheels situated in the tackle, the resulting total will be the maximum number of pounds you are able to lift using your own weight. 
<margin>Forster III 84 r.</margin>

A body in which the parts between the surface and the center are uniform in substance, weight, and size will distribute its weight equally to its supports if it is suspended horizontally by its opposite ends.

A wheel where the center of the axis is also the center of its circle will remain perfectly balanced in all circumstances. Furthermore, equal weights suspended from opposite sides of such a circle will remain in perfect counterpoise <note>original: "counterpoise"; a weight that balances another; a state of equilibrium.</note> with one another.

## DEFINITION OF THE NATURE OF THE LINE

A line does not possess any matter or substance within itself; it might more accurately be called an incorporeal <note>non-physical or without a body</note> thing rather than a substance. Being of such a nature, it does not occupy space. Therefore, the intersections of an infinite number of lines may be imagined as occurring at a single point which has no dimensions. As for its thickness—if such a term can even be used—it is equal to the thickness of a single line.

## HOW WE CONCLUDE THAT THE SURFACE TERMINATES IN A POINT

<margin>Windsor MSS. R 47</margin>
The surface of an angle is reduced to a point when it reaches its vertex <note>original: "angle"; the point where the lines meet.</note>. If the sides of this angle are extended in a straight line, another surface is formed beyond this point, which may be smaller, equal to, or larger than the first.

Every point is the origin for an infinite number of lines. These lines spread out to form a base, and just as suddenly, lines from that base converge back to a single point to form a pyramid, revealing both its color and its shape.

<margin>Windsor MSS. R 62</margin>
As soon as a form is created or composed, it immediately produces an infinite number of angles and lines. These lines, spreading and intersecting through the air, give rise to an infinite number of angles opposite to one another. For each of these opposite angles, if a base is provided, a triangle will be formed that is identical in shape and proportion to the larger angle. If the base fits twice into each of the two lines of the pyramid, the same proportion will apply to the smaller triangle.

Archimedes provided a method for squaring a polygonal figure <note>original: "square of a polygonal figure"; the geometric challenge of constructing a square with the exact same area as another shape.</note>, but not for the circle. Therefore, Archimedes never found the square of any figure with curved sides; however, I have obtained the square of the circle, minus...

The smallest possible portion that the mind can imagine—that is, the smallest visible point.

<margin>Leic. 26 v.</margin>
If water is added to a vessel filled with wine at the same rate that the mixture of wine and water flows out of it, that vessel can never be completely emptied of wine. This follows from the fact that wine, being a continuous quantity <term>a substance that is not made of discrete parts but is solid and unbroken</term>, is divisible to infinity. Therefore, if a certain amount has poured away in a specific period of time, half of that amount will have poured away in another equal period, and in yet another, a fourth of that quantity. Because the remainder is constantly being replenished with water, and because during each successive interval of time half of what remains will be poured out, the wine will be divided over an infinite number of time intervals. Since infinity has no end in time, there will be no end to the number of times the wine is divided.

<margin>Sul Volo 3 r.</margin>
Mechanical science <note>original: "Instrumental or mechanical science"; Leonardo uses this to mean the study of how machines and bodies perform work.</note> is the noblest and most useful of all sciences, seeing as all living beings <note>original: "animated bodies"</note> that have the power of movement perform all their actions by means of it. The origin of these movements is at the center of gravity <term>the specific point where the weight of a body is balanced in all directions</term>. This center is positioned in the middle with unequal weights at its sides; it relies on the varying strength of muscles, as well as the action of a lever and counter-lever.

<term>divisible to infinity</term>: the mathematical concept that an object can be divided into smaller and smaller parts forever without ever reaching zero.
<term>continuous quantity</term>: a magnitude (like time, space, or a liquid) that is not composed of separate, individual units.
<term>mechanical science</term>: the study of motion and the forces that produce it.
<term>center of gravity</term>: the point at which the entire weight of a body may be considered as concentrated.
<term>lever and counter-lever</term>: a simple machine consisting of a beam pivoted at a fixed hinge, or fulcrum, used to multiply the physical force applied to an object.

# XXI

## The Nature of Water

> *“Just as veins branch out from a pool of blood to spread through the human body, in exactly the same way the ocean fills the body of the earth with an infinite number of veins of water.”* <note>Leonardo often used the "microcosm/macrocosm" theory, believing the laws governing the human body (the lesser world) mirrored those governing the earth (the greater world).</note>

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 20 r. a</margin>
If a drop of water falls into the sea when it is calm, the entire surface of the sea must inevitably rise by an imperceptible amount. This is because water, unlike air, cannot be compressed within itself.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 42 r. a</margin>
We may consider whether the surface of the air is bordered by the element of fire, just as the air borders the water and the water borders the earth. We might also ask whether the surface of the air forms waves and eddies <term>swirling currents or whirlpools</term> as the surface of the water does, and whether the revolutions of these eddies are more numerous in the air because air is thinner than water. 

Among the eddies of the water, some have centers filled with air, while others are filled with water. I do not know if the same is true for the eddies on the surface of the fire. All water eddies that begin at the surface are filled with air, and those that originate deep within the water are filled with water. These underwater eddies are more long-lasting because water submerged in water has no weight—unlike water that is suspended above the air. Therefore, the eddies of water that surround air have weight and quickly collapse.

### ON THE FLOODS OF THE GREATEST RIVERS

The floods <note>original: "deluges"</note> of rivers are created when the outlets of valleys cannot release the water they receive as quickly as the valleys are filled by it.

The flow of water is faster when it falls at a steeper angle.
