<header>THE NATURE OF WATER</header>

## ON WAVES

A wave is the recoil <note>original: "recoil of the stroke," referring to the reactionary movement following an initial impact</note> of an impact, and it will be greater or smaller in proportion to the force of the impact itself. A wave is never found in isolation, but is mixed with as many other waves as there are uneven places in the object where the wave is produced. 

At any given moment, there will be innumerable other waves traveling in different directions over the surface of the sea's largest wave. If you throw a stone into a sea with various shores, all the waves that strike against these shores are reflected back toward the spot where the stone hit; upon meeting other advancing waves, they never interrupt each other’s course. <note>Leonardo is describing the principle of wave superposition, where waves can pass through each other and maintain their form.</note> 

When waves of equal volume, speed <term>velocity</term>, and power encounter each other in opposing motion, they recoil at right angles from the force of the collision. A wave will reach a greater height if it is created by a stronger impact, and the same is true for the reverse. 

A wave produced in small bodies <term>tracts</term> of water will travel back and forth many times from the spot that was struck. The wave travels back and forth more frequently when the body of water that produces it is smaller, and less frequently when it is larger. Only on the high seas do the waves advance without ever turning back in recoil. In smaller bodies of water, the same impact gives birth to many alternating motions of advance and recoil. 

The largest wave is covered with countless other waves moving in different directions; these have a greater or lesser depth depending on whether they were caused by a greater or lesser force. The largest wave is covered with various smaller waves, which move in as many different directions as there were different places from which they originated. Within a small body of water, a wave will have a greater number of other waves proceeding over it, in proportion to the strength of its initial impact and its recoil from the opposite shores. 

The movement of the wave is faster than the movement of the water of which it is composed. <note>This is a significant scientific observation: Leonardo realized that while the wave pattern travels quickly across the surface, the actual molecules of water mostly move up and down in place.</note> Many waves turned in different directions can be created between the surface and the bottom of the same body of water at the same time. Swirling <term>eddying</term> movements can accompany the direct movements of each wave. 

All the impacts <term>impressions</term> caused by things striking the water can penetrate one another without being destroyed. One wave never physically merges with <note>original: "penetrates"</note> another; instead, they simply recoil from the spot where they strike.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, Sheet 84, verso a</margin>

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci details the mechanics of wave motion, observing how waves reflect off surfaces and overlap without destroying one another. He correctly identifies that a wave's motion travels faster than the physical water it is made of.</summary>

The movement of water within water behaves like the movement of air within air.

Among irreversible and destructive terrors, the floods caused by rivers in spate should certainly be ranked above every other dreadful and terrifying movement; nor is it, as some have thought, surpassed by destruction caused by fire. I find the opposite to be true, for fire consumes only what feeds it and is itself consumed along with its fuel <note>original: "food"</note>. The movement of water created by the slopes of the valleys does not end or fade until it has reached the lowest level of the valley. However, fire is sustained by what feeds it, while the movement of water is driven by its natural tendency <note>original: "wish"</note> to descend. The fuel for fire is disconnected, and the damage caused by it is localized and separate; the fire dies when it lacks fuel. The slope of the valley is continuous, and the damage done by the destructive path of the river will be continuous until—guided by its valleys—it ends in the sea, the universal base and only resting place for the wandering waters of the rivers.

But what words can I use to describe the abominable and awful evils against which no human resource is effective? These floods lay waste to high mountains with their surging and triumphant waves, knock down the strongest riverbanks, uproot deep-rooted trees, and—with ravenous waves laden with mud from crossing plowed fields—carry away the hard-earned labors of the miserable, weary farmers <note>original: "tillers of the soil"</note>, leaving the valleys bare and impoverished because of the destruction left behind.

### OF RIVERS AND THEIR COURSES

Among straight rivers that exist in land of the same character, with the same volume of water and with equal width, length, depth, and slope, the one that is more ancient will be the slower.

This can be proven with straight rivers. The oldest river will be the most winding, and a river that winds will become slower as it covers a greater distance <note>original: "acquires greater length"</note>.

Of waters that descend from the same height to the same depth, the one that travels by the longer path will be the slower.

Among rivers at their beginning <note>original: "commencement"</note>, the older one will be the slower. This happens because the river's course is constantly getting longer due to its increasing meanders; the reason for this is explained in the twelfth section.

The force that moves the bodily fluids <note>original: "humours"</note> in all living creatures against the natural law of gravity is the same force that moves the water trapped within the "veins" of the earth and distributes it through narrow passages. Just as blood from the lower body rises to flow through the cut veins of the forehead, or as water rises from the bottom of a grapevine to the spot where a branch has been pruned <note>original: "lopped"</note>, so too does water rise from the lowest depths of the sea to the peaks of the mountains. Finding the veins there burst open, the water falls through them and returns to the sea below. Thus, it moves both inside and outside the earth, constantly changing—now rising by chance movement and now descending in its natural freedom.

Joined together in this way, it ranges about in a cycle of continual revolution.

Rushing here and there, up and down, it never rests—neither in its movement nor in its own nature. It possesses nothing of its own but takes hold of everything, taking on as many different characteristics as there are different places through which it passes. It acts just like a mirror, which takes into itself as many images as there are objects passing before it. Thus, it is in a state of constant change.

<summary>Leonardo explains that older rivers flow more slowly because they develop more meanders over time, and he draws a famous parallel between the circulation of water through the earth and the circulation of blood through the human body.</summary>

### THE NATURE OF WATER

The entry of one river into another produces the first windings <note>original: "meanderings"</note> of the river.

The windings of rivers in plains are caused <note>original: "occasioned"</note> by the rivers discharging themselves there.

If a winding river is completely removed from its ancient bed and placed in a straight channel, the tributary rivers which flow into it from both sides must necessarily increase in length on one side as much as they lose on the other. The river that gains length will lose speed, while that speed is transferred to the one that becomes shorter.

Direct the smaller rivers to enter the larger rivers at sharp <note>original: "acute"</note> angles. The advantage of this is that the current of the larger river diverts the path of the smaller river and does not allow it to strike against the opposite bank.

However, if the smaller river is flooding at the time when the waters of the larger river are low, the impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> of the smaller river will break the opposite bank of the larger river.

The largest of the curves of a river in a valley will always have its outer <note>original: "convex"</note> side facing the lower part of the valley's width.

The windings of rivers are always greater the closer they are to the spot where the smaller river enters the larger one.

<margin>C.A. 185 r. b <note>Codex Atlanticus, folio 185 recto, section b</note></margin>
The ridges <note>original: "waves"</note> of earth formed by the banks <note>original: "embankment"</note> of the rivers are continually changing their positions; new ones are created where the previous ones have been washed away.

### OF THE FLOW AND EBB OF THE SEA AND ITS VARIATION

The flow and ebb <note>the tides</note> of the sea are caused by the course of the rivers, which return water to the sea more slowly than the movement of their own current; for this reason, the water is inevitably forced to rise to a height. This river then covers its own current again with a swift wave which, in its retreat <note>original: "recoil"</note>, meets the descending current of the river.

The river's wave flows back against its own current when the sea is at low tide <note>original: "ebb"</note>. After the wave returns to the shore, it gains new power from the approaching river water.

The flow and ebb of the sea are not caused by the moon or the sun <note>Leonardo here incorrectly disputes the celestial influence on tides, favoring a mechanical theory of resonance and river discharge</note>, but by the greatest wave as it advances and falls back. However, since the retreat is weaker than the advancing movement—being deprived of support—this oscillating <note>original: "hesitating"</note> movement would eventually stop if it were not renewed by the help of the rivers. For as these rivers are immediately swollen by the approaching wave of the aforementioned tide, the wave produced by the swollen river is added to this ebb. It strikes the opposite shores of the islands situated across from it and then leaps back, returning to its former course; and so it continues, as described above.

<margin>C.A. 281 r. a <note>Codex Atlanticus, folio 281 recto, section a</note></margin>
Experience has taught us this, for it is seen continually in every river, especially as the water strikes against the sides of its bays.

<header>THE NATURE OF WATER</header>

The spiral or revolving movement of any liquid is faster the closer it is to the center of its rotation.

This observation we are setting forth is worthy of note, because the movement in a circular wheel is actually slower the closer it is to the center of the revolving object. However, this same principle in water shows a similarity of movement in both speed and length during each complete revolution, whether in the circumference of its larger or its smaller circles. The curve of the smaller circle is as much smaller than the larger one as the larger circle is more curved than the smaller. Therefore, the movement of this water is uniform throughout all its revolutions; if it were not so, the hollow space <note>original: "concavity," referring here to the air-filled center of a whirlpool</note> would instantly be filled up again. But because the side-pressure <note>original: "lateral weight"</note> of this revolving circulation <note>original: *circulazion revertiginosa*</note> is doubled, that hollow space has no permanent movement. Of this doubling of weight, the first part is created by the revolving movement of the water, and the second is created in the sides of this hollow, where it supports itself before finally falling headlong down into the air that has filled the cavity.

<margin>C.A. 296 v. b <note>Codex Atlanticus, folio 296 verso, section b</note></margin>
The movements of air through the air are twofold: moving straight up in the form of a column, and moving with a revolving motion.
But water makes this movement downward, taking the shape of a pyramid <note>Leonardo often used "pyramid" to describe a conical vortex or the narrowing path of falling liquid</note>, and it moves more swiftly as the pyramid becomes more pointed.

## ON RIVERS

Water falls along the line forming the summit of its wave, and it moves more swiftly where this fall is less steep; it breaks more into foam where it meets with more resistance.

<margin>C.A. 354 r. b <note>Codex Atlanticus, folio 354 recto, section b</note></margin>
As previously stated, waves break against the river’s current and never in the same direction as the flow. This is because water falling onto flowing water cannot create a rebound against an object that is moving away and does not stay to receive the blow. However, when falling against the flow of the water, the wave does not strike water that is moving away from the impact, but rather water that is moving in the opposite direction. Consequently, if the falling wave has four degrees of velocity and the water it meets also has four degrees of velocity, the wave’s impetus <note>original: "impetus," referring here to the combined force or momentum of the collision</note> acquires eight degrees of velocity. Therefore, river waves break against their current. Similarly, sea waves break against the water flowing back from the shore they have struck, and not against the wind that drives them.

## ON THE FLOW AND EBB OF WATER

Every movement of water creates a flow and ebb <note>Leonardo is describing a surge or tidal-like oscillation caused by changes in current speed</note> in every part of a river where the speed of its course is obstructed.

<margin>C.A. 354 r. e <note>Codex Atlanticus, folio 354 recto, section e</note></margin>
This is proven by the fact that where the riverbed is steeper, the water flows faster; where it is more level, it flows slower. Therefore, a level area receives more water than it can discharge. For this reason, the water must rise to such a height that its weight eventually overcomes the force of the incoming water. Then, this accumulated water descends from its height around the base of this watery "hill." That portion which descends against the incoming current causes the current to swell and slow down, until the following water becomes so abundant that it overcomes this backflow <note>original: "ebb"</note> and creates a new forward flow.

The momentum <note>original: *impeto*</note> within a strong current maintains its path through still waves, just as a sunbeam maintains its course through the wind.

<summary>Leonardo explains why river waves break against the current using the logic of relative velocity and describes how changes in a riverbed's slope create "flow and ebb" surges as water piles up and then recedes.</summary>

Why does a blow upon the water create many waves?

A river that always maintains its depth at the center of its course will remain within its banks.

<margin>C.A. 361 r. b <note>Codex Atlanticus, folio 361 recto, section b</note></margin>
Where the channel is narrower, the water flows more powerfully than elsewhere. As it leaves the straight section, it spreads out violently, striking and wearing away the nearby banks that lie across its path, often shifting its course from one place to another.

The movement of the wind resembles that of the water.

What is the difference between water that is drawn and water that is driven?

Water is "drawn" when the Ocean, as it recedes, pulls the water of the Mediterranean Sea after it.

Water is "driven" by rivers which, as they enter the sea, push its water forward.

Among all the causes of the destruction of human property, it seems to me that rivers, because of their excessive and violent floods <note>original: "inundations"</note>, hold the primary place. If anyone were to argue that fire is more destructive than the fury of rushing rivers, such a person would seem to me to be lacking in judgment. Fire dies and goes out when fuel fails it, but against the irreparable flood caused by swollen and arrogant <note>original: "proud," a common personification of nature's power in this period</note> rivers, no human foresight can provide a remedy. In a succession of raging and boiling waves, gnawing and tearing away the high banks, turning murky <note>original: "turbid"</note> with the soil from plowed fields, destroying the houses within them and uprooting tall trees, the river carries these away as its prey down to the sea, which is its lair. It bears along men, trees, animals, houses, and lands, sweeping away every dike and every kind of barrier. It carries off light objects and devastates or destroys those of great weight, creating massive landslides <note>original: "landslips"</note> out of small cracks <note>original: "fissures"</note>, filling low valleys with its floods, and rushing headlong with an insistent and unstoppable <note>original: "inexorable"</note> mass of water.

What a desperate need there is to flee for anyone who is near! Oh, how many cities, how many lands, castles, villas, and houses has it consumed!

How many of the labors of miserable farmers <note>original: "husbandmen"</note> have been rendered idle and profitless! How many families has it brought to nothing <note>original: "naught"</note> and overwhelmed! What shall I say of the herds of cattle which have been drowned and lost!

<margin>C.A. 365 r. a <note>Codex Atlanticus, folio 365 recto, section a</note></margin>
Where the channel of the river slopes more steeply, the water has a faster <note>original: "swifter"</note> current; and where the water is faster, it wears away the bed of its river more, deepens it further, and causes the same volume of water to occupy less space.

The shorter the course of the rivers, the greater their speed will be. Conversely, the current will be slower in proportion to the length of the river’s course.

When an excess <note>original: "superabundance"</note> of water cannot be contained within the depth of its channel, necessity forces it to spill violently <note>original: "precipitately"</note> over its banks.

No part of an element has weight while inside its own element unless it is either moved within it by force <note>original: "impetus"</note>, or falls down within it after being drawn from another element.

<margin>A 23 v. <note>Manuscript A, folio 23 verso</note></margin>
The flow of a smaller body of water follows the path of the larger floods; it changes course to keep company with the greater volume and stops digging <note>original: "delving"</note> under the banks.

The proof of this is seen in the Po <note>The Po is the longest river in Italy, known for its frequent and historically devastating floods</note>. For when the river is low, its water often moves in cross-currents. Drawn toward low spots and directing its way toward them, it takes its course and strikes the foundations of the bank, hollowing them out and causing widespread destruction. But when the river flows in a full stream, the smaller volume of water—which previously struck and hollowed out the banks with its cross-currents—abandons that path. It is pulled along by the greater volume of water and, moving straight along the riverbed <note>original: "base"</note>, it stops damaging its banks.

Water that falls along a path nearest to the vertical is the water that descends most rapidly, striking the spot where it lands with the greatest impact and weight.

Water is, by its weight, the second element that surrounds the earth <note>In the classical Aristotelian view, the four elements were arranged in spheres: Earth at the center, then Water, Air, and Fire</note>, and any part of it that is outside its natural sphere will seek to return there rapidly. The higher it is raised above its natural position, the faster it will descend toward it. Its qualities are moisture and cold. It is its nature to always seek out low-lying places when it is not restricted. It easily rises as steam and mist, and once changed into clouds, falls back again as rain as the tiny particles of the cloud join together to form drops. At different altitudes, it takes different forms: namely water, snow, or hail. ### THE BEGINNING OF THE TREATISE ON WATER

Man has been called a "lesser world" <note>original: "microcosm"</note> by the ancients, and indeed the term is rightly applied. Since man is composed of earth, water, air, and fire, the body of the earth is composed of the same. As man has bones within himself as a support and framework for his flesh, the world has rocks which are the supports of the earth. As man has within him a pool of blood where the lungs expand and contract as he breathes, the body of the earth has its ocean, which also rises and falls every six hours with the "breathing" of the world <note>Leonardo is comparing the rhythm of the tides to human respiration</note>. Just as veins branch out from that pool of blood through the human body, the ocean fills the body of the earth with an infinite number of veins of water. However, the body of the earth lacks sinews <note>Leonardo uses "sinews" to mean muscles or tendons</note>; these are absent because sinews are created for the purpose of movement, and as the world is perpetually stable within itself, no such movement ever takes place there. In the absence of any movement, sinews are not necessary. But in all other things, man and the world show a great resemblance.

## ON THE SPRINGS OF WATER ON THE TOPS OF MOUNTAINS

It seems clear that the entire surface of the ocean, when not disturbed by storms, is at an equal distance from the center of the earth. Therefore, the peaks of mountains are farther from the center in proportion to how high they rise above sea level. Consequently, unless the earth functioned like a human body, it would be impossible for seawater—being so much lower than the mountains—to naturally rise to their summits. Therefore, we must believe that the same mechanism that keeps blood at the top of a man’s head also keeps water at the summits of mountains. <note>Leonardo is using the "microcosm" theory, common in the Renaissance, which suggests the Earth is a living organism where rivers are like veins and the tides are like breathing.</note>

## ON THE HEAT THAT IS IN THE WORLD

Where there is life, there is heat; and where there is vital heat, there is the movement of vapor. This is proven by observing how the "element of fire" <note>In the classical view of the four elements (Earth, Water, Air, Fire), fire was the lightest and always sought to rise upward</note> always draws toward itself damp vapors, thick mists, and dense clouds that are released by seas, lakes, rivers, and marshy valleys. As it draws these vapors bit by bit up to the "cold region" <note>the upper atmosphere</note>, they are forced to stop because warmth and moisture cannot coexist with cold and dryness. Once the first vapors have halted, they collect the others that follow, and as all these parts join together, they form thick, dark clouds.

These clouds are often swept and carried by the winds from one region to another, until eventually their density makes them so heavy that they fall as heavy rain. However, if the heat of the sun is added to the power of the "element of fire," the clouds are drawn up even higher into regions of more intense cold; there they freeze and produce hailstorms.

Thus, the same heat that supports the massive weight of water falling as rain also sucks water up from the "roots" <note>the underground base</note> of the mountains and draws it up to be trapped within the mountain peaks. There, the water finds crevices and, continuing its flow, it breaks out to create rivers.

Just as heat causes the movement of moisture, cold stops it. This has already been shown by the example of the cold atmospheric region, which stops...

...the clouds drawn by the element of fire <note>original: "the hot element"; referring to the classical element of Fire, which was believed to occupy the highest sphere of the world and naturally pull heat and vapor upward</note>. As for the proof that heat draws moisture, it is shown as follows: heat a jug and set it in a vase with the mouth downwards, and place some lighted charcoal there. You will see that the moisture, as it retreats from the heat, will rise and fill the jug with water, and the air that was enclosed in this jug will escape through its opening.

Also, if you take a wet cloth and hold it to the fire, you will see the dampness of the cloth leave its place. That part of the moisture which has the least substance will rise up, drawn by the proximity of the fire, which by its nature rises toward the region of its own element. In this way, the sun draws up moisture.

## EXPLANATION OF THE PRESENCE OF WATER AT THE SUMMITS OF THE MOUNTAINS

I say that it is just like the blood which the natural heat keeps in the veins at the top of a human being. When a person has died, this blood becomes cold and is brought back down into the lower parts of the body. As the sun warms a person's head, the amount of blood there increases, and it grows to such an excess there, along with the <term>humours</term> <note>original: "humours"; in Renaissance medicine, these were the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to determine a person's health and temperament</note>, as to overload the veins and frequently cause pains in the head. 

It is the same with the springs which branch through the body of the earth. Because of the natural heat spread through the entire body of the earth that contains them, the water stays in the springs and is raised to the high summits of the mountains. However, water that passes through a confined channel within the body of a mountain like a "dead thing" will not emerge from its initial low state, because it is not warmed by the vital heat of the primary spring. Moreover, the warmth of the element of fire, and the heat of the sun by day, have the power to stir up the dampness of low places and draw this to a height, in the same way as it draws the clouds and pulls their moisture from the expanses of the sea.

Regarding the opinion held by some that the water of some seas is higher than the highest summits of the mountains and that the water was driven up to these summits:

Water will not move from one spot to another unless it is seeking a lower level, and in the natural course of its current, it will never be able to—

That part of the sea which you mistakenly imagine to have been so high as to have flowed over the summits of the high mountains for so many centuries would have been entirely consumed and poured out through the water that has issued from these same mountains. You can easily imagine that during all the time that the Tigris and the Euphrates have flowed from the summits of the Armenian mountains, one might suppose the entire volume of water in the ocean to have passed many times over through their mouths.

<margin>A 56 recto and verso <note>These are specific page references in Leonardo's "Manuscript A."</note></margin>
Or do you not believe that the Nile has discharged more water into the sea than is currently contained in all the watery element <note>original: "watery element"; referring to the total volume of water on Earth, one of the four classical elements</note>? Surely this is the case. If, then, this water had simply fallen away from the body of the earth, the whole system would have run out of water long ago. Therefore, one may conclude that the water passes from the rivers to the sea, and from the sea back to the rivers, constantly making the same circuit, and that all the sea and the rivers have passed through the mouth of the Nile an infinite number of times.

## OF THE FOAM OF WATER

Water which falls from a height into other water traps a certain amount of air within itself, and through the force of the impact, this air is submerged along with it. Then, with a swift movement, it rises up again and returns to the surface it just left, encased in a thin, spherical film of moisture. It then moves in circles away from the spot where it first struck. 

In other cases, the water that falls down upon other water rushes away from the impact site in various different branches, splitting, mingling, and interlacing with one another. Some of these branches, being hollow <note>Leonardo is describing the structure of bubbles and turbulent water</note>, are dashed back upon the surface of the water. So great is the force of the weight and the shock caused by this falling water that, because of its extreme speed, the air is unable to escape into its own element <note>The element of Air</note>. Instead, it is forced underwater in the manner I described above.

## WHY RIVERS CHANGE THEIR POSITION AND OFTEN RAISE THEMSELVES AND MOUNT UPWARDS IN VARIOUS PLACES

The movement of water always tends to wear away its support. The softest parts offer the least resistance, and as the water clears these away, it leaves various hollows. In these gaps, the water whirls in diverse eddies <note>original: "divers"; meaning various or different</note>, wearing down and hollowing out these chasms until they grow larger. 

As the water strikes against newly exposed embankments <note>original: "dikes"</note>, it leaps back and hits the opposite banks, consuming, eating away, and destroying whatever stands in its path. It changes its course in the midst of the havoc it has made, dragging the lightest soil along with it and depositing it in calmer areas. As the river raises its own bed with this sediment, the quantity and force of the water are lessened, and its "fury" <note>Leonardo often personifies water as having "fury" or "desire" to describe its kinetic energy.</note> is transferred to the opposite side. When it reaches that bank, it eats it away and strips its foundations bare until it has uncovered new ground through great destruction. 

If the water encounters a plain, it floods it, hollowing out the land to form a new bed. If it comes upon buried stones, it uncovers them and lays them bare. However, it often happens that these stones, because of their size, offer resistance to the impetuous flood. After being driven against the rocks in the middle of its course, the water leaps back toward the opposite side, breaking and destroying the opposite bank.

-><sig>Manuscript A, folio 59 recto</sig><-

## WHY WATER DIGS OUT ROUND PITS WHEN IT FALLS WITH VIOLENCE

Water falling in the manner previously described does not enlarge the pit it creates. As the fact of it falling perpendicularly shows, there is very little force in the water driving it from behind; this is why it falls "broken" <note>meaning the stream has turned into droplets or spray rather than a solid column</note> and in a fine spray in an almost straight vertical line. 

The air trapped within this broken water—having an almost equal weight above it—cannot escape quickly enough to avoid being submerged by the weight and the impact. However, since air cannot be separated from its natural element <note>In the classical physics of the time, air "belonged" above water and would forcibly return to its "natural place" if submerged.</note> without external force, it yields to the fury of the blow and the weight, but then rises again quickly. It returns to the surface in round bubbles near the spot where it first struck. Because the air does not move any distance from this spot, it does not cause any damage to the banks of the pit. But when the...

A rushing river, swollen by recent rains, scours its banks. It falls with fury into the waters below, no longer descending peacefully in a spray mingled with air as it did previously. Instead, united and powerful, it strikes and tears open the depths it hits, reaching all the way down to the rocky bed. It uncovers and carries away buried stones, creating a new barrier for itself from the shingle <note>original: "shingle"; small, rounded pebbles or stones found on shores or riverbeds</note> carried from the pit it has made. The water then throws itself against this barrier, falls back defeated, and divides upon impact into two different streams. These separate and form semi-circles, devouring and consuming every obstacle and enlarging the riverbed into a circular shape.

To be more precise—when rivers are in flood, the waterfalls are less steep. Therefore, as the mass of water strikes the lower levels, the water following the impact does not move with the same violence as the falling water. Because of this, the lower water offers resistance; as it resists, the water level rises and the height of the fall decreases. Consequently, the water does not trap as much air, because the lower parts of the falling water are barely separated from the rest of the stream. Due to this, very little air can enter, and therefore the impact and weight of the water meet with no resistance <note>Leonardo is observing that aerated water (white water) has less density and force than a solid "green" column of water.</note>. The blow proceeds undiminished all the way to the bottom, displacing the gravel there, surrounding and washing over the stones, and increasing the depth of the pools.

### HOW PITS ARE FORMED IN THE COURSES OF RIVERS

The reason for this is that stones of various sizes are always found in riverbeds. As the water reaches the largest stones, it sinks down behind them and strikes the spot where it falls. This impact dislodges smaller stones from the point of contact, making the bed wider. As the fall increases in height, it becomes more powerful and hollows out the growing pit even further. This occurs because rivers constantly erode <note>original: "gnaw"</note> the mud of their beds, continually uncovering and exposing rocks of different shapes and sizes.

### WHY THE SURFACE OF FLOWING RIVERS ALWAYS SHOWS BUMPS AND HOLLOWS

The reason for this is that, just as a pair of stockings covering the legs reveals the shape of what is hidden beneath them, so the water on the surface reveals the nature of its bed <note>original: "base"</note>. This happens because the layer of water touching the bottom encounters various protrusions caused by stones; it strikes them and leaps upward, lifting all the other water flowing above it.

### WHY THE WATER BEYOND A SOLITARY ROCK IN A LEVEL STREAMBED FORMS MANY RIPPLES

The reason for this is that the water striking the rock subsequently descends and creates a kind of pit. In its course, the water flows into this hollow and then leaps back up to a height, falls back to the bottom, and repeats the same action. It continues this many times, much like a ball thrown on the ground that makes many bounces before it finishes its course, each bound being smaller than the one before it.

### WHAT CAUSES EDDIES IN WATER

All movements of the wind resemble those of water. Generally, all things seek to maintain themselves in their natural state. Therefore, moving water strives to maintain the course driven by the force <note>original: "power"</note> that sets it in motion. If it encounters an obstacle in its path, it completes the span of the course it has started by moving in a circular and revolving motion.

So, when water pours out of a narrow channel and descends with fury into the slow-moving currents of great seas—since a larger mass has greater power, and greater power offers more resistance than the lesser—the water descending upon the sea strikes its slow-moving mass. This mass cannot move out of the way fast enough because it is held back by the rest of the water. Consequently, the descending water, unwilling to slacken its pace, turns around after it has struck the surface and continues its initial movement in circling eddies, and so—

## THE EDDIES AT THE BOTTOM OF THE WATER MOVE IN AN OPPOSITE DIRECTION TO THOSE ABOVE

The reason for this is that if the circles, which are large at the surface, are reduced to a point as they are submerged and then continue their movement in the direction in which they began, the water at the bottom will move in a direction contrary to the water above as it moves away from its center.

Although sounds traveling through the air move out from their sources in circular waves, these circles—driven by different forces <note>original: "motive powers"</note>—nevertheless meet without any hindrance. They penetrate and pass through one another, always keeping their original sources as their centers.

Since water moves much like air, I will use it as an example of the aforementioned proposition. I say that if you throw two small stones into a large lake of still water at the same time, a certain distance apart, you will observe two distinct sets of circles forming around the two points where they struck. As these sets of circles grow larger, they meet and intersect with one another, yet each set keeps its own center at the spot where the stone struck the water. The reason for this is that although there is an appearance of movement, the water itself does not leave its place because the openings made by the stones are instantly closed. The movement caused by this sudden opening and closing of the water creates a vibration that one might define as a quivering rather than a movement <note>Leonardo is describing wave propagation, where energy moves through the medium without the medium itself being displaced.</note>. To make this more evident to you, consider those pieces of straw that float on the surface because of their lightness. They are not moved from their position by the wave that rolls beneath them as the circles widen. This disturbance of the water, there-

Therefore, being a vibration <note>original: "quivering"</note> rather than a physical movement, the circles cannot break one another as they meet. Since all parts of water are made of the same substance, it follows that these parts transmit the vibration from one to another without changing their location. As the water remains in its position, it can easily receive this vibration from the parts near it and pass it on to other neighboring parts, while its force steadily decreases until the end.

The winding courses of the water, caused by the rebounds from the impacts <note>original: "percussions"</note> against the banks, will cause the riverbed below them to be hollowed out more than any other part. At these points of impact, the water will reach a great depth. The water that whirls around near these deep places will serve to undermine and destroy the banks against which it strikes.

<margin>Folio 63 verso</margin>
One can clearly see and recognize that the waters striking the banks of rivers act in the same way as balls which, when struck against walls, rebound at angles similar to those at which they hit, and then proceed to strike the opposite side. So these waters, after having first struck one bank, leap back toward the opposite one and strike it with vigor, hollowing it out because there is a greater gathering <note>original: "confluence"</note> of water in that spot. 

The reason for this is that the water leaping back from one bank to another hollows out the part of the riverbed beneath it. The other water in the river, which cannot be contained in this deepened section, is repulsed and thrown back somewhat by the direct course of the river. Having no other way to escape, it returns to its natural course; because the riverbed is lower under the winding paths made by the aforementioned impacts of the water, this second body of water—having lost its temporary <note>original: "adventitious"</note> means of escape—resumes its natural course. It falls into the lower parts of the river and strikes the bank at the same spot as the first rebounds. As the bank is assailed by two entirely different sets of impacts, a larger hollow is created; while the first impacts strike the bank above, the others descend more steeply, devouring and exposing it at its base. This is the cause of the aforementioned destruction and collapse <note>original: "subsidence"</note> of riverbanks.

## ON WATER

No part of the element of water will raise itself or move farther from the common center <note>The "common center" refers to the center of gravity or the center of the Earth, according to the science of Leonardo's time.</note> except by force <note>original: "violence"</note>. No forced movement is permanent. <margin>Codex C, folio 15 recto</margin>

### THE LEAP OF WATER IS HIGHER IN A BUCKET THAN IN A LARGE LAKE

This happens because confined water, when struck by a blow, cannot allow its momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note> to spread from one circle to the next as it would in a large lake. Since the struck water is near the edges of the bucket—which are harder and more resistant than the surrounding water—it cannot expand outward. Consequently, all of its momentum is directed upward. Therefore, water struck by a stone throws its drops higher when its waves are confined than when they have a wide space to expand. <margin>Codex C, folio 22 recto</margin>

### *On the motion of water*

When water or any object falls into water, it causes the water receiving the impact to spread out beneath the blow and surround it. Once the water has passed over the cause of this impact, it continues to rise above it in a pyramid-like shape and then falls back to the general surface level.

The reason for this is that when a drop of water falls from a roof onto other water, the portion that receives the impact cannot find space or escape within the rest of the body of water as quickly as it is being hit. This is because it would need to displace too much weight to enter beneath such a large volume of water. Therefore, needing to follow its own course as well as the force driving it, and finding that the neighboring water (which did not receive the blow and is not ready to move) cannot be easily penetrated, it seeks the shortest path and flows through the substance that offers it less resistance: the air.

As the first circle surrounding the impact site closes in with force—having been raised above the common surface of the water—it squeezes the water that is escaping upward into the shape of a pyramid.

Every part of a body of water that is within other water and is without movement remains at rest relative to the parts situated at the same level.

Experience shows that if there were a very large lake, undisturbed by wind and with no water entering or leaving it, and if you were to cut away a very small section of the bank below the surface of the water, all the water above the level of that cut would pass through the opening. However, this movement will not disturb or pull with it any of the water that was already in the lake below that level before the outflow began.

In this instance, nature is bound by its own inherent laws: namely, that every part of a water's surface—when supported by banks without any opening or exit—is situated at an equal distance from the center of the earth <note>Leonardo is describing the principle of hydrostatic equilibrium: the surface of a liquid at rest will settle into a shape where every point is at the same gravitational potential.</note>.

# HOW IT IS POSSIBLE FOR LARGE STONES TO BE ROLLED OVER BY WATER

<margin>Codex C, folio 24 verso</margin>
Know that stones are rolled over by water because the water either surrounds them or flows over them. If it surrounds them, the currents meet again and intersect on the far side of the stone, hollowing out the soil or sand behind it. Once the stone has been laid bare in this way, it begins to roll of its own weight. 

If the water flows over the top of the stone, it falls back down in the same line of travel. By the force of its momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note>, it penetrates through the surface to the base of the surrounding water, where it gnaws at, tugs, and drags the stone away from the obstacles holding it. As a result, this stone also begins to roll, and it continues to move from place to place until it has traveled across the entire riverbed. If a smaller stone stands in its path, the water uncovers it using the same process. This is the method by which stones are rolled along the beds of flowing rivers.

This may be clearly demonstrated; for if you take a step in this water, you will find that it creates a wave that directs its course and moves in the same direction as the creature is traveling. This wave does not stop until it has achieved its goal and covered a small part of the shore.

A second step creates another wave with a similar result, and the same happens with the third and all subsequent steps. Each step by itself creates a wave that travels as far as the shore, so that the shore—which was previously dry—finds itself covered by water over a great distance. Then, when you have stepped out of this water, you will see it returning to its former position in a swift retreat.

Waves of rivers that flow against the direction of the winds will be taller than other waves.

Rivers that move against the direction of the wind will have a stronger current below the surface than above, because the surface is being driven by the wind and becomes slower than it was at first.

<margin>Codex C, folio 25 verso</margin>
The reason for this is that if the rivers—being of equal depth and width—have a uniform current at the bottom and on the surface, the resistance made by the wind against the surface current must necessarily cause the water to turn back. Since it is not enough for these waves to merely rise a little, they eventually fall and pass underneath the other waves, moving toward the bottom. Finding the other current at the bottom, this water joins it. Since the bank cannot contain this increase in volume, the current at the bottom must double its speed; if it were not so, one would see the water rising far above the banks of the rivers.

After this first impact <note>original: "percussion"</note>, many rebounds will follow; these will increase in size and decrease in power as they move further away from the first.

An embankment that allows the trunk of a tree it has nourished to project into the waves of a rapid river will cause the destruction of the opposite bank.

<margin>Codex C, folio 26 recto</margin>
The cause of this effect is that river water always "leaps" from one bank to the other. If nothing projects from a bank, many currents <note>original: "lines of water"</note> gather there, unite, and leap as a single mass toward the opposite bank. There, they intertwine with other currents they meet along the way; upon reaching the embankment, they gnaw at and destroy it. This creates new currents that leap back and damage the first bank. In this way, eddies of varying depths begin to form from place to place, which is why straight rivers eventually become winding and crooked.

# WHAT WATER IS

Of the four elements, water is the second least heavy and the second in terms of mobility. It is never at rest until it unites with its maritime element <note>In ancient and Renaissance science, the "maritime element" refers to the ocean as the natural home where the element of water seeks to rest.</note>. There, when not disturbed by winds, it settles and remains with its surface at an equal distance from the center of the world. It is the growth and lifeblood <note>original: "humour"</note> of all living bodies. Without it, nothing retains its original form. It unites and expands bodies through its growth.

Nothing lighter than water can penetrate it without force <note>original: "violence"</note>. Heat easily turns it into thin vapor that rises through the air. Cold causes it to freeze. Stagnation makes it foul. In other words: heat sets it in motion, cold freezes it, and immobility corrupts it.

It takes on every odor, color, and flavor, though by itself it has none. It filters <note>original: "percolates"</note> through all porous bodies. No human defense can withstand its fury for long. In its rapid course, it often supports objects heavier than itself. It can rise through movement or bounce back as high as it falls. In its headlong rush, it pulls down things lighter than itself. The flow of its course is sometimes on the surface, sometimes in the center, and sometimes at the bottom. One portion rises over the crossing <note>original: "transverse"</note> course of another; if it were not for this, the surfaces of running waters would be without ripples or undulations. Every small obstacle, whether on the bank or in the riverbed, will cause the bank or bed opposite it to erode <note>original: "falling away"</note>. When the water is low, it does more damage to the bank during its course than it does when it flows in a full stream. Its parts do not weigh upon the parts placed beneath them. No river will ever maintain a perfectly straight course between its banks. Its upper parts do not impart weight to the lower parts.

### WATER AND AIR

I want to show you how water can be supported by air while being divided and separated from it. Certainly, if you possess any reason, I believe you will not deny that if a leather bag were placed at the bottom of a well so that it touched all the sides—preventing water from passing beneath it—and if this leather bag were filled with air, it would exert no less force in rising to the surface to reach the atmosphere <note>original: "the other air"</note> than the water exerts in its "desire" <note>In the physics of this era, elements were thought to have a "natural desire" to return to their proper place: water toward the center of the earth and air toward the sky.</note> to touch the bottom of the well. And if this leather bag "desires" to rise up, it will push up the water placed above it. By raising this water, it removes the weight of the water from the bottom of the well. For this reason, it is almost as though the well were bottomless.

Where and why the movement of the water erodes the sand on the surface of the beds of flowing rivers—but first, let us speak of the impact <term>percussion</term> on the surface:

The faster the current of water along the slope of a smooth canal, the more powerful its impact <term>percussion</term> will be against whatever opposes it.

For all the elements, when removed from their natural position, "desire" to return to it—especially fire, water, and earth. The shorter the line along which this return is made, the straighter its course; and the straighter its course, the greater the impact <term>percussion</term> upon whatever opposes it.

# THE ORDER OF THE FIRST BOOK ON WATER

<margin>E 12 r.</margin>
Define first of all what height and depth are, and also how the elements are situated one within the other. Then define solid weight and liquid weight; but first of all, explain what weight and lightness consist of in themselves. Then describe why water moves and why its motion ceases; then why it becomes slower or more rapid, and in addition to this, how it continually descends when in contact with air that is lower than itself; and how the water rises into the air through the heat of the sun and then falls back as rain. 

Furthermore, explain why water springs from the summits of the mountains, and whether any spring of water higher than the ocean can pour forth water higher than the surface of that ocean; and how all the water that returns to the ocean is higher than the sphere of water <note>In the Aristotelian worldview used by Leonardo, elements were arranged in concentric spheres: Earth, then Water, then Air, then Fire.</note>. Also, explain how the water of the equatorial <note>original: "equinoctial"</note> seas is higher than the northern waters, and is higher beneath the body of the sun than in any other part of the equator's circle. For when an experiment is performed under the heat of a burning brand <note>A piece of burning wood used as a heat source.</note>, the water boils as a result of the heat, and the water around the center of where it boils descends in a circular wave. Finally, explain how the waters of the north are lower than the other seas, and become even lower as they grow colder, until they are changed into ice.

### [*Rivers*]

<margin>E 66 v.</margin>
That river which extends itself most through long, winding <note>original: "tortuous"</note> turns is the one that fills up most rapidly with sediment <note>original: "matter"</note>. This is proved by the twelfth rule, which says: the water that moves most slowly <note>original: "loiters"</note> deposits the matter it carries most rapidly. Therefore, the river which, by meandering more, makes its course longer through its twists and turns, makes its flow so much slower in proportion to its increased length.

## OF THE TROUGH FORMED BETWEEN WAVES

The valley <note>Often called a "trough" in modern terminology.</note> situated between waves is lower than the general surface of the water, as one observes when the water turns back to fill the gaps created by <term>water-spouts</term> <note>Likely referring to vortices or the columns of water displaced by a heavy impact.</note>.

## OF SURFACE EDDIES AND THOSE FORMED AT VARIOUS DEPTHS

Of those [eddies] that take up the entire depth of the water, and of those that move versus those that remain fixed. Of the long and the round. Of those that change their movement, those that divide, and those that merge into the eddies to which they unite. Which are the eddies that cause light objects to whirl around on the surface without submerging them? Which are those that submerge them, cause them to spin upon the bottom, and then deposit them there? Which are those that lift objects from the bottom and throw them back to the surface of the water? ### PLAN OF THE TREATISE ON WATER. SWIMMING

When you compile the science of the movements of water, remember to include the practical applications beneath each proposition, so that this science is not without use.

On the usefulness of the paths a swimmer should follow regarding the surface currents <note>original: "revolutions"; Leonardo uses this term to describe the circular motion or vortices of water.</note> of the waters and the eddies that pull swimmers under. Then, how one should navigate when submerged in order to save oneself, and so forth.

And at the end of each book, record the most remarkable things—for instance, how to break through the center <note>original: "thickness"</note> of eddies in any direction. Also, note what precautions one should take when swimming in a rough sea, and how to avoid being dashed against rocks or the rudders of ships.

Regarding objects carried by water: the smallest object will perform the greatest rotation.

This happens because large eddies are rare in river currents, while small eddies are almost countless. Large objects are only turned by large eddies and not by small ones, whereas small objects spin in both small and large eddies.

Among objects of equal length and width carried by a current, those that sit deepest in the water will make the fewest rotations.

This happens because these rotations vary greatly from the surface to the bottom of the water, where as many rotations are produced as the depth allows. Therefore, an object carried by the water that is deeply submerged is buffeted by many rotations at different depths. For this reason, it remains in a state of instability <note>original: "hesitance"</note>, often responding to none of them—or if it does respond, it follows the most powerful one.

Among objects of equal shape and size, the one submerged deepest will respond the least to the water's rotations.

The high and low tide <note>original: "flow and ebb"</note> occurs twice within the same body of water. This happens because the tide will cycle several times at the mouth of this body of water before there is any decrease in the main body itself. This occurs because the wave of the first flow runs strongly into the body of water; while this wave follows its own momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note>, the tide at the mouth is already receding. 

Before the wave that has penetrated into the channel <note>original: "neck"</note> feels the receding tide at the mouth *g a*, the next high tide begins again at that same entrance. During this time, the wave which had penetrated the channel pauses, losing its momentum just as the second wave begins a new penetration. In this way, so many of these waves enter the channel that the body of water is raised, and its waters return with force behind the receding tide. This receding tide does not penetrate far enough into the third or fourth wave to push the original water out of the entrance.

In small whirlpools, the water drills downward and carves out a hollow in the center of the vortex.

A river does not remain uniform. After the current passes, it deposits gravel <note>original: "shingle"</note>, and after this deposit, it creates a new current. The movement of this new current is directed either toward the bank, the center, or toward any number of different spots, depending on the various slopes of the mounds of gravel left at the bottom by the previous currents.

## WATER—QUESTIONS

Why the eddies of the water are hollowed out in the center by their rotation <note>original: "revolution"</note>.

Why the impressions <note>In this context, Leonardo likely refers to ripples, waves, or bubbles created by an impact or disturbance on the surface.</note> produced on the surface of the water will maintain themselves for some time while being carried by the course of the water.

Why the movements of the impressions on the water penetrate each other without changing their original shape.

Rules regarding the measurements of water: what breadth, depth, and rapidity of movement a given section of current should have in a specific amount of time.

Given the resistance of a wheel and given the slope and descent of the waterfall, one asks how great its volume must be to be equal to that resistance.

Given the volume of the waterfall and its length and slope, one asks whether the power of the wheel is equal to this power of the water.

Given the resistance of the wheel and the slope of the water and its volume, one asks for the length of the fall.

# ON THE MEASUREMENT OF WATER AND THE MANY WAYS IT CAN VARY

Water that flows out through a <term>mouth</term> <note>original: "mouth"; an opening or orifice, such as a sluice gate or nozzle, used to discharge water.</note> of the same size may vary in quantity to a greater or lesser degree in several ways. 

The first is that the surface of the water may be at a greater or lesser height above the opening through which it pours. The second is that the water may move with more or less speed past the bank where this opening is made. The third is that the slope below the thickness of the opening where the water passes may be more or less slanted. The fourth is the variation in the slant of the sides of this opening. The fifth is the thickness of the <term>lip</term> <note>the edge or rim of the opening.</note> of this opening. The sixth is the shape of the opening—that is, whether it is round, square, rectangular, or elongated. The seventh is whether this opening is positioned at a greater or lesser slant along the length of the bank. The eighth is whether this opening is placed at a greater or lesser slant relative to the height of the bank. The ninth is whether it is situated in the concave or convex parts of the bank. The tenth is whether it is placed toward the wider or narrower parts of the canal. The eleventh is whether the current at the top of the canal moves faster or slower at the top of the opening than it does elsewhere. The twelfth is whether the canal bed has rounded bumps or hollows opposite this opening, or higher or lower than it. The thirteenth is whether the water passing through this opening is affected by the wind or not. The fourteenth is whether the water falling from this opening falls through air that is enclosed on one side, or on all sides except the front. The fifteenth is whether the water falling into such an enclosure is deep or shallow. The sixteenth is whether the falling water makes a long drop or a short one. The seventeenth is whether the walls of the canal where this water descends are hollow, bulging, straight, or curved.

<sig>F 9 v.</sig>

**Concerning the eddies of water which frequently reverse their circular motion:**

Concerning falling and <term>reflex</term> <note>original: "reflex"; referring to the rebounding or backward flow of water after hitting a surface or another current.</note> eddies: An eddy sometimes gains power while its diameter decreases, and sometimes loses strength while its diameter increases.

The first movement occurs when the water drains from its base; the water forming the eddy becomes swifter as it gets lower, because it has a greater weight of water pressing down from above, and therefore it accelerates.

### OF THE ACCIDENTAL EDDY

When the hand is turned in a circular movement in a <term>vase</term> <note>original: "vase"; here meaning a jar, bowl, or similar vessel.</note> half-filled with water, it causes an <term>accidental eddy</term> <note>an "accidental" motion is one caused by an external, artificial force—like a hand—rather than the natural flow of gravity or a current.</note>. This will expose the bottom of the vase to the air. Even when its <term>motive power</term> <note>the source of the motion.</note> is at rest, this eddy will continue the same movement, but it will diminish continually until the end of the <term>impetus</term> <note>momentum or force.</note> imparted to it by its motive power.

### OF THE HOLLOW AND UTILITY OF EDDIES OF WATER

The eddy with the deeper hollow will be the one produced in water of swifter movement.

Furthermore, an eddy will have a smaller hollow if it is produced in deeper water that does not share the same movement but is slower.

With water of equal speed, the eddy will maintain a larger hollow where a greater depth of water turns with its movement.

This is said because eddies are often produced in a straight current within a large expanse of slowly moving water. Because this water is partly supported by the eddy—which revolves in a thin coil between the surrounding water and the air in the hollow—this <term>lateral water</term> <note>the water pressing in from the sides.</note>, being of great weight, pushes upon the sides of the eddy where it leans. Finding those sides weak, it compresses them.

You have the fourth [proposition] of the seventh [book] which proves that every heavy substance exerts weight only along the line of its movement and in no other direction. Here you see very deep eddies formed in the manner of...

## OF WATERFALLS

Write first about the simple hollows created by simple waterfalls onto a riverbed of a uniform material, and then onto a bed made of various materials. Then, consider obstacles placed in the path the water takes as it descends; then, obstacles placed where the water strikes the bed; then, in its <term>reflex movement</term> <note>original: "reflex movement"; refers to the rebounding or backward flow of water after it hits an obstacle or the bottom.</note>, starting at the beginning of its fall.

## OF THE EDDIES OF WATER

It is possible for the depth underneath a current to be shallower than the depth in front of it or at its sides.

Let *o c n* represent the current and *a* represent an eddy of double strength, according to the ninth rule concerning eddies <note>Leonardo da Vinci often organized his observations into numbered rules and "books" within his notebooks.</note>. Besides its circular motion, this eddy strikes against the bank and leaps up into the air; falling back upon the rest of the water, it pierces through it, striking and hollowing out the riverbed into a sudden chasm. This happens because, in addition to the force of the impact, there is the spiral "drilling" action caused by the aforementioned revolution. By this means, the material shaken by the blow is stirred up and carried away; this process becomes more powerful as the water becomes more turbid <note>original: "turbid"; thick or cloudy with suspended sediment.</note>.

And this is the most effective method that can be used to dislodge and carry away soil to create a large pit.

The riverbed will become raised beneath a current when the flow of that current dies out in stagnant water.

According to the sixth rule of the ninth book: where the flow of water fails, the sediment that the water brought with it remains behind.

<margin>Folio 17 verso</margin>

When a volume of water strikes an object, the lower part is the first to hit the bottom, and it is instantly reflected back toward the surface. The water in the middle does not reach the bottom; instead, it encounters the first part of the water being reflected upward. It strikes this reflected water and is knocked back, so that it also turns back in the same lines and circular motions <note>original: "revolutions".</note>.

When the lower body of water meets the higher, the two unite and revolve together at their point of contact.

Of the water that falls into other water, the part nearest the center of the fall is the most slanted, and the part nearest the edges is the straightest.

### ON WATERS THAT CROSS ONE ANOTHER AT DIFFERENT ANGLES

Regarding waters that intersect at various angles during their reflected movements <note>original: "reflex movements"; the secondary or backward flow of water after it hits an obstacle or another current.</note>, and those that intersect at the crests of the waves; those that cross a descending wave and those that meet in the troughs <note>original: "valley"; the low point between two wave crests.</note> of the waves.

Some currents cross at different angles: a large reflected flow meeting a small reflected flow, and similarly a large wave meeting a small one. Or, a downward-rushing flow meeting water in a trough or a reflected flow—the small interacting with the large.

Sometimes there is a reflected flow meeting a downward flow; sometimes a trough meeting a wave; sometimes a downward flow meeting a reflected flow, in varying sizes and at different angles.

Sometimes fast-moving waters meet slow ones; sometimes whirlpools <note>original: "eddies"</note> meet waves, troughs, or reflected flows; or the downward-rushing movements of water flowing along different paths may cross one another.

These courses may follow different paths, layered one above the other.

## OF THE ELEMENT OF WATER

Here follows the proof of what is said on the opposite page:

I say that no part of the surface of water moves of its own accord unless it descends. Therefore, as the "sphere of water" <note>Leonardo conceptualizes the Earth's water as a perfect geometric sphere centered on the Earth's center of gravity.</note> does not have the power to descend at any part of its surface, it follows from the first principle <note>original: "conception"; referring to a logical axiom or starting rule of his physics.</note> that it does not move of its own accord. 

And if you carefully consider each minute particle of this surface, you will find it surrounded by other similar particles which are at an equal distance from the center of the earth. That particle which is surrounded by them is also at the same distance from this center. Therefore, by the third principle, that particle of water will not move of itself because it is surrounded by edges of equal height. 

In this way, every circle formed of such particles creates a "vessel" for the particles enclosed within it. This vessel has edges formed by a circle of equal height. In this respect, this particle resembles all the other similar ones that make up the surface of the sphere of water. By necessity, it will be without movement on its own. Consequently, because each particle is at an equal height from the center of the world <note>In the Renaissance view, the center of the Earth was considered the center of the universe.</note>, necessity makes their surface spherical. However, it is not necessary that they should be spherical on their underside, as reason and experience show <note>While the surface follows the Earth's curve, the "bottom" of the water follows the uneven terrain of the seabed or riverbed.</note>.

That which is said of the surface of the water bordering the air is also understood to be said of the surface of the air bordering the fire <note>The "sphere of fire" was traditionally thought to be the highest elemental layer, above the air.</note>. This fire would often evaporate in the manner of clouds drawn by the heat of the sun, just as water is drawn through the air by that same heat in the form of clouds. In the same way, fire is drawn by a greater heat than its own—that is to say, by the sun. It is proved in the sixth book that the sun is warm by its own nature <note>original: "essence"</note> and not merely by its power <note>original: "virtue"; Leonardo is arguing against the idea that the sun is not inherently hot but only causes heat through its rays.</note>, as many would have it.

So, having proved by the evidence of these spheres that the flexible elements <note>Water, air, and fire, which take the shape of their containers or follow gravitational curves.</note> are spherical, it is my purpose to investigate nature both in its universal aspect and in the specific details of each of its elements: first <margin>Folio 26 verso</margin> of fire, then of air, and then of water.

## BOOK FORTY-TWO. OF RAIN

The water that falls from a cloud is sometimes broken down into such minute particles that, because of the friction it has with the air, it cannot cut through the air but seems to change itself into air itself. Sometimes, as it descends, it grows in volume because it encounters even smaller particles of water which were falling slowly due to their lightness. It incorporates them into itself, and at every stage of its descent, it acquires a new quantity of water <note>Leonardo is describing the process of coalescence, where falling droplets collide with smaller ones to grow larger.</note>. Sometimes the winds bend the rain and cause it to fall at an angle; for this reason, its descent becomes slow and drawn out. It frequently happens that rain is converted into such fine particles that it can no longer fall and so remains suspended in the air.

The wave that a moving force <term>motive power</term> <note>Leonardo’s term for the kinetic energy or force acting upon a medium.</note> creates ahead of itself in the air, or between the surface and the bed of a body of water, is shaped like a hemisphere <note>original: "half sphere"</note>.

Regarding water falling from river weirs <term>weirs</term> <note>A low dam or barrier built across a river to regulate flow or raise water levels.</note>: the section that has the most powerful fall will have its straight course obstructed.

This occurs because water falling with great force hollows out the soil at the spot where it strikes. It then deposits that soil in areas where the current is weaker than the rebounding <note>original: "reflex movement"; referring to the upward surge of water after it hits the riverbed.</note> movement of the water. As this water moves upward toward the surface, it grows weaker with every stage of its movement until it finally loses all its power.

As the power of this rebounding action fades, it drops all the heavy material it carried from the spot where it struck. After this surge <note>original: "inundation"</note>, the water level drops and finds itself trapped between the sediment it previously carried and the bank from which it descended.

Among the waters that descend in torrents from river weirs, only the part where the fall was weakest and slowest will maintain its straight course beyond the turbulent flow.

This happens because slow-moving water strikes with little force; therefore, it follows that it only rises slightly from the bed it strikes and, consequently, deposits very little sediment during its upward movement. This is why, after such a surge <note>original: "deluge"</note>, the bank here...

### Concerning objects carried by the water that are partially in the air and partially in the water:

If an object <term>movable thing</term> <note>Leonardo often uses the term "mobile" to refer to any body in motion.</note> is carried by the water, being half submerged and half exposed to the air, and the air moves at a speed equal to the speed of the water, then this object will move at its maximum potential speed.

<margin>F 43 v.</margin>
If the air moves more slowly than the water which is flowing in the same direction, the movement of the object will be slower than if the speeds of the air and water were equal. The object's speed will decrease in proportion to the difference between the speeds of the air and the water.

If the movement of the air is faster than that of the water <note>original: "aria" (Italian for air).</note> which moves in the same direction, then the movement of the object will become more rapid; it will move faster as the air's speed exceeds that of the water.

If the movement of the air against the current of the water is of equal speed to that of the water against the air, the object will follow the course of the water if it has more surface area in contact with the water than with the air. Conversely, it will follow the air if it has more contact with the air than with the water.

## THE ORDER OF THE BOOK

To describe the conditions of the waters that fall through the air, and their impacts <note>original: "percussions"; Leonardo uses this term to describe the physical force of one body striking another</note> made with different degrees of power, volume, length of movement, and variety of inclination <note>original: "slant"</note>, I will make a comparison between the four principal winds: north, south, east, and west. With these conditions, I will prepare myself to provide information regarding the aforementioned movements of water within the air; as a result, this description will be briefer and more efficient.

<margin>F 45 r.</margin>
These are the four ways in which waters, moving in the same manner, penetrate one another along lines that tilt <note>original: "slant"</note> toward the center of the earth.

These four demonstrations are sufficient to prove the four principal effects that water produces when streams strike one another within the air. The first of these is when the more steeply tilted stream penetrates the less tilted one, piercing it in part and carrying away the portion that was struck.

In the second demonstration, the less tilted stream penetrates the more steeply tilted one in part, carrying away the portion that was struck. In the third demonstration, the more tilted water carries away the less tilted water entirely. The fourth does the opposite, in that the less tilted water carries away the more tilted water entirely.

<margin>F 45 v.</margin>
If the earth were [not] spherical, no part of it would be left uncovered by the sphere of water.

You will never find a flat section of the earth where the water sitting in the middle of that level surface does not take on a convex <term>curved outward</term> shape. And this water will never move toward the edges of this plain. Therefore, upon a surface that is absolutely flat, there may be water of varying degrees of depth.

It is impossible to find any truly flat part in the surface of any very great expanse of water.

The deep trenches in the ocean bed are permanent, while the summits of the mountains are the opposite <note>meaning they are subject to change and erosion</note>. It follows that the earth is spherical and entirely covered with water, and that it will be inhabitable <note>original: "inhabitable"; Leonardo is likely exploring the theoretical state of the elements where water naturally encircles the earth, or referencing the "habitable world" as known in classical geography</note>.

Concerning an object carried by a water current: if it is caught in a current of lesser power and tilts downward, it will move toward the bottom, following the direction of its slant.

Of objects carried between two currents of water, only the one positioned exactly between two currents of equal speed will proceed without flipping over.

When the upper and lower parts of an object’s straight side are struck by equal currents, the object will rotate sideways.

After water strikes against an object, it divides into four primary movements: right and left, upward and downward. The downward movement causes damage to the riverbed <note>original: "injury to its bed"</note>.

Of the four primary movements water makes when it divides in its rebound <note>original: "reflex action"</note>, the fastest will be the one reflected at the sharpest <note>original: "more acute"</note> angle.

### EDDIES

Eddies are always the result of two streams of water intermingling—specifically, the falling stream and the rebounding <note>original: "reflex"</note> stream.

All the water that lingers behind objects within river currents has no other way to exit than by coming into contact with those same currents.

The eddies that turn backward are always formed by the fastest water.

And the eddies that turn in the same direction the stream is flowing are those formed by the water that lingers in the stream's path.

Here, the law of water regarding eddies holds true: because the water that slows down turns back and creates eddies in the opposite direction of its movement, just as the eddies of the fastest water do. For this reason, these eddies—whether of slow or rapid water—mingle together and redouble their power. However, they do not do so entirely, because the slow eddy, in mingling with the swift one, becomes faster than...
