## <insert>[Movement of water in the air and in the water]</insert>

The movement that water makes in the air follows, for some distance, the shape of the small holes through which it descends. This is not the case with a solid object [discontinuous quantity] <note>original: "discontinuous quantity"; Leonardo uses this term to distinguish a discrete solid, like a stone, from a continuous fluid like water</note> such as a stone thrown by the circular movement of a man’s arm. The stone follows a straight path [tangent to the arc]; the water does not do this because it spreads out into a sheet, and over a long distance, this movement pulls all the parts of the water together.

The patterns [impressions] made by water moving within other water are more permanent than the patterns water makes within the air. This occurs because water within water has no relative weight <note>Leonardo is observing the effects of buoyancy; an object has no "weight" when submerged in a medium of the same density</note>, as is proved in the fifth book; only the momentum [impetus] carries weight, and this force moves the weightless water until the energy is spent [consumed].

The patterns of water movement are more permanent when the water driven by momentum enters a large body of water [pelago] <note>original: "pelago"; a poetic or scientific term for a sea or deep pool of water</note> that is moving more slowly, and vice versa.

The patterns made by water within the air are destroyed at the very start of their movement toward the earth, because the momentum is spent by the natural downward movement [gravity] produced in the water. <note>Folio 71 recto</note>

# OF THE MOVEMENTS OF WATER

Falling streams of water that intersect in the air become filled with air during their rebounding [reflex] movement.

Of two falling streams of equal thickness that strike each other in the air, the one descending from a higher part of its reservoir will merge with the path of the lower stream and complete its course along with it.

Falling water that then runs over stone ledges [terraces] causes a great deal of erosion to its bed at the edges of these ledges.

### [On the rising of water in nature and by artifice]

If the water that gushes from high mountain peaks comes from the sea (pushed up by the sea's weight so that it reaches higher than the mountains), why is this specific portion of water able to raise itself to such a great height and penetrate the earth through such difficult and time-consuming paths? Why hasn't the rest of the element of water been granted the power to do the same, even though the rest of the ocean borders the air, which would not be able to resist it or prevent the whole body of water from rising to that same height?

You who have come up with such a theory <note>original: "invention"</note> must return to the study of natural things; otherwise, you will be found lacking in the necessary scientific knowledge. You have relied too much on the resources and properties of the friar which you have come to possess. <note>Leonardo is likely addressing a contemporary theorist whose work he found flawed, possibly someone who inherited papers from a monk.</note>¹

## SEA-MUD AND FOSSILS

If the mountains had not remained largely uncovered by the waters, the river courses would not have been able to carry the massive amounts of mud into the sea that now exist at great elevations, mixed with the remains of animals <note>Leonardo is correctly identifying fossils of marine creatures found high in the mountains</note> that were encased within it.

The rotations of the rebounding <note>original: "reflex"</note> water as it returns to the main river current penetrate it more deeply in its lower parts than on its surface. This occurs because the current—according to the seventh proposition <note>referring to Leonardo's internal numbering of hydraulic rules</note>—is faster at the top than at the bottom. Consequently, the current is more powerful at the top and is therefore less affected by the impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> of this rebounding water at the surface than it is below.

<margin>F 78 v.</margin>
The eddies formed by the impact of the rebounding water within the path of falling water are of two kinds. One is created toward the bottom and rotates vertically along the length of the stream; the other occurs on the surface and rotates right and left across the width of the stream. The lower eddy is produced by the churning <note>original: "seething"</note> mass falling back down toward the bottom, while the surface eddy is caused by the rotating movement striking the surface current.

<margin>F 81 r.</margin>
Water rotates in front of falling water like a mill wheel.

Concerning the movements of objects that have fallen with the water moving through the air, and also what they do within this body of water.

Concerning the objects that float upon the middle water <note>the central area of a pool receiving a fall</note>, and how they become submerged when they are located between the center of the middle water and the waterfall. They are pulled down along with the fall that enters the body of water, striking the bottom and breaking into pieces.

Therefore, write down all the effects of objects that become submerged at any edge <note>original: "extremity"</note> of this middle water. These edges always cause submersion because the middle water is at the center of all the rebounding movements directed toward the bottom of the body of water.

**Concerning the earth.** Every heavy substance tends to descend, and high things will not maintain their height forever; over time, they will all sink. Thus, in time, the earth will become a perfect sphere. As a consequence, it will be completely covered with water, and the underground channels will become stagnant <note>original: "without movement"</note>.

**Concerning the convex wave.** Whether the wave created by water falling into a canal of uniform width and depth will travel a long distance or not.

**Concerning the concave wave.** Whether the concave wave created by water falling abruptly from an open canal under a sluice <note>A sliding gate used to control the flow of water</note> will travel a long distance in a canal of uniform width and depth.

<margin>F 86 v.</margin>
Water that runs through a canal of uniform capacity <note>original: "emptiness"</note> and fills the first smooth section will also fill all the other straight and slanting sections, moving with equal speed throughout.

The movements of heavy elements toward the center of the earth do not happen because they specifically seek the center, but because the medium in which they exist (such as air) cannot support them. When they encounter resistance in their own element (such as water within water), the body no longer has relative weight and does not seek to penetrate further toward the center.

Water in the air has weight and descends by the shortest path. It divides and opens the air directly beneath its center of gravity equally on all sides. It does not divide the air at its sides because it is not situated above it. Because of this, it creates a narrow passage <note>original: "hollow"</note> in the air until it reaches something that resists it. Since this resistance is that of other water, the water falling through the air no longer seeks the center because it can no longer displace the water below it as it did the air. Therefore, a heavy substance moves downward only where it meets no resistance, not because of a desire to reach the center.

First, write about water in each of its movements. Then, describe all its beds <note>The channels or floors over which water flows</note> and the materials within them, always providing the rules <note>original: "propositions"</note> regarding the aforementioned waters. Ensure the order is logical, for otherwise, the work will be in confusion.

Describe all the shapes that water assumes, from its largest to its smallest wave, and explain their causes.

## CURRENTS OF RIVERS

If the course of a river is narrowed <note>original: "contracted"</note> on one of its sides, it produces a swift, half-cylindrical wave. The eddies produced between the narrowed bank and this cylindrical wave cause the bank to be stripped bare and eroded away.

If the banks narrow equally and opposite to each other, the cylindrical waves will intersect. After this intersection, they will descend and strike the banks, causing them to collapse.

However, if the narrowing of one bank is lower than that of the other, the upper cylindrical wave can pass underneath the lower one.

At this point in the commentary, it is necessary to define the distances and the widths of these narrow sections of the banks.

<margin>F 91 r.</margin>
<insert>[Of canals, rivers, and eddies]</insert>

A bank that is curved inward to make a canal wider causes the sudden formation of an eddy. This eddy bores downward, digging a deep hole at the base of the bank and causing it to collapse.

This is proven by the first proposition of the third book <note>Leonardo frequently cited his own numbered scientific axioms</note>, which shows that when a river suddenly gains more space, it also gains a greater volume of water. As the water spreads out, its depth decreases. This creates a sudden current that hurls itself against the bank where it has widened. Upon striking the bank, the water divides into two eddies. The more powerful of these (labeled *c b a* in the diagram) throws itself vigorously toward the bottom to remain contained. This is further supported by the ninth proposition, which says that an eddy is most easily penetrated when its edges <note>original: "lips of its mouth"</note> are the least slanted—meaning they are quite vertical.

Water causes the collapse of any bank where the canal suddenly becomes wider.

If the canal suddenly widens on both sides, it produces eddies on

### [Cylindrical waves]

The further a half-cylindrical wave travels, the more it descends; as it spreads itself out, its speed increases.

When there are two unequal cylindrical waves and the larger one is created before the smaller one, the smaller wave will intersect the larger one and pass over it. This happens because the larger wave, having been created first, is already spread out and lowered by the time it is opposite the smaller one. The smaller wave, being higher when it strikes, hits the low point of the larger wave. Finding no obstacle as high as itself, it runs over the larger wave, falls down the opposite side, and continues with its original momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note>.

<margin>F 92 r.</margin>
However, if the smaller of these unequal cylindrical waves begins further upstream <note>original: "higher in the river"</note> than the larger one, the larger wave follows its natural course, and the smaller one follows the course of the larger.

If cylindrical waves clash but do not intersect at their centers, the middle section that collides will leap backward and pass over the part that did not collide.

When two cylindrical waves of equal size and power clash directly, they both turn back completely without either one penetrating the other.

But if the cylindrical waves are of unequal size, neither the larger nor the smaller will follow their usual physical laws; the larger wave does not bend, and the smaller wave merges with the larger one.

<margin>F 92 v.</margin>
If the waves are equal but one rises before the other, their impacts <note>original: "blows"</note> will not be delivered with equal power. Consequently, the path of the second wave will bend before that of the first.

Water moving between a bank and a straight, smooth bed will not produce a wave of any kind.

This occurs because a wave is only created by a rebounding movement <note>original: "reflex movement"</note>, and this rebound arises from the impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> of a falling movement as it hits a specific object.

<summary>Leonardo examines the physics of "cylindrical waves" in rivers, detailing how waves of different sizes and timings interact, overlap, or repel one another upon impact. He concludes that waves are the result of water rebounding after striking an obstacle.</summary>

<keywords>cylindrical waves, fluid dynamics, wave intersection, momentum, hydraulic physics, reflex movement</keywords>

### [Currents and falls of water]

In water of ordinary speed, the water in the middle will have tiny ripples. The water located between the surface level and the bed is not of the same nature as the surface; for this surface level receives the impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> of both the falling and the reflected <note>original: "reflex"</note> water. For both to remain within the boundary, one falls upon the other water, striking the air like a heavy object, and as a heavy object, it penetrates the water it has struck.

The water falls at first, then rises up again, lifting itself with its semi-cylindrical wave above the opposing semi-cylindrical wave that made its fall more slanted.

### [The current of rivers]

Water that descends in a straight river always moves in a slanted course, from the center to the opposite banks and from these opposite banks back to the center of the river. This is proved by the ninth proposition of this work, where it is stated: "The flow of straight rivers is always higher in the center of their width and at the sides than it is in the area between the center and those sides." And this was proved by the seventh proposition, in which it was stated: "The water of straight rivers never flows in a straight line because it moves faster as its obstruction is [lesser]..." <note>The text here breaks off, but the principle describes how friction at the banks and the bed creates different speeds and pressures within the current.</note>

### HOW THE OCEAN DOES NOT PENETRATE WITHIN THE EARTH

The Ocean does not penetrate deep into the earth, and we learn this from the many and varied springs of fresh water which, in various places of this Ocean, penetrate from the bottom up to its surface. The same thing is also shown to us by wells, dug at a distance of more than a mile from the Ocean, which are filled with fresh water; this takes place because fresh water is lighter than salt water and, as a consequence, more penetrating.

Which weighs more: water that is frozen or water that is not frozen?

Fresh water penetrates more into salt water than salt water does into fresh water.

That fresh water penetrates farther into salt water than salt water does into fresh water is shown to us by a thin, dry, and old cloth that hangs with its opposite ends at an equal depth in two different bodies of water, where the surfaces are equally low. You will then see how the fresh water will raise itself so much higher up on this piece of cloth than the salt water, because it is lighter.
<sig>Manuscript G, folio 38 recto</sig>

## ON THE MOVEMENT OF A RIVER THAT SUDDENLY RUSHES ONTO ITS DRY BED

The path that water takes when it flows from a lake into a dry riverbed is slower or faster depending on whether the river is wide or narrow, or whether the ground is more level in one place than in another.

<margin>Manuscript G, folio 48 recto</margin>
Based on these principles, the ebb and flow of the sea—moving from the Ocean into the Mediterranean—along with the rivers that meet it, causes the water to rise more or less depending on how narrow the sea is at that point.

### WHY THE SEA IS SALTY

Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (AD 23–79), a Roman author and naturalist whose "Natural History" was a standard reference in Leonardo's time</note> says in the 103rd chapter of his second book that sea water is salty because the sun's heat scorches and dries up the moisture. He claims the sun draws up the fresh water, which greatly increases the salty flavor of the sea.

However, this cannot be accepted. If saltiness were caused by the sun's heat, then lakes, pools, and marshes would undoubtedly be even saltier, since their waters move less and are shallower. On the contrary, experience shows us that the waters of these marshes are entirely free of salt. Pliny also states in the same chapter that this saltiness might arise because the heat easily draws away every sweet and thin <note>original: "tenuous"</note> part of the water, leaving behind the more bitter and coarse portions. Consequently, he suggests the water on the surface is sweeter than the water at the bottom. But this is contradicted by the reasons given above; if it were true, the same thing would happen to marshes and other bodies of water that are dried up by heat. It has also been claimed that the saltiness of the sea is the "sweat of the earth." To this we may reply that if it were so, all the springs of water that pass through the earth would also be salty.

Therefore, the conclusion is that the saltiness of the sea is caused by numerous springs of water. As they penetrate the earth, they find salt mines; they dissolve parts of these mines and carry them away to the Ocean and other seas. From there, the salt is never lifted back up by the clouds that produce the rivers. Thus, the sea would be saltier in our times than it has ever been at any time before; and if it

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the speed of water entering dry riverbeds and presents a geological argument for the sea's salinity, refuting Pliny the Elder's theories about solar evaporation.</summary>
<keywords>hydrology, salinity, Pliny the Elder, Mediterranean, salt mines, evaporation, riverbeds, Manuscript G</keywords>

--- Page 714 ---
<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s investigation into the salinity of the sea. Having previously refuted Pliny’s theory that the sun’s heat "scorches" the water into salt, Leonardo now proposes his own theory based on the recycling of matter and the constant movement of water through the earth and living bodies.</meta>

<page-num>700</page-num>
<header>THE NATURE OF WATER</header>

If an opponent were to argue that over an infinite span of time the sea would either dry up entirely or solidify into salt, I reply that salt is restored to the earth. This happens through the uplifting of the land, which carries with it the salt it has acquired, and the rivers then return this salt to the soil over which they flow.

But—to explain this better—if we grant that the world is eternal, it must follow that its population is also eternal. Therefore, the human race has perpetually been, and will always be, consumers of salt. If the entire mass of the earth were composed of salt, it would not be enough to provide food for all of humanity forever. For this reason, we are forced to conclude either that the substance of salt is eternal, just as the world is, or that it "dies" and is renewed along with the men who consume it. 

However, experience teaches us that salt does not disappear. We know this because fire does not consume it; because water becomes saltier as more salt is dissolved in it; and because when water evaporates, the original quantity of salt remains. Therefore, an amount of salt equal to what is brought into cities every year must pass through human bodies as urine, perspiration, or other bodily excretions. We may say, then, that the rains which penetrate the earth are what carry this salt—originally taken from the sea—back through the passages of the earth beneath the foundations of cities and their people. Furthermore, the shifting of the sea, which once covered all the mountains, has left salt behind in the mines that are now found within those mountains.

As a third and final reason, we can say that salt exists in all created things. We can learn this by passing water through ashes and the refuse of burnt objects, as well as from animal urine, the waste that proceeds from their bodies, and the earth into which all things are changed through decay <note>original: "corruption"</note>.

<sig>Manuscript G, folios 48 verso and 49 recto</sig>

### ON THE CHANGES OF THE EARTH <note>original: "della vibratio della terra" — likely referring to the movement or shifting of the earth's crust</note>

The subterranean courses of water, like those that flow between the air and the earth, are what unceasingly wear away and deepen the beds of their channels.

<summary>Leonardo explains that salt is not destroyed but cycled through the environment and the human body, eventually returning to the sea or being deposited in mountains. He also observes that underground rivers erode the earth just like surface rivers.</summary>

# THE NATURE OF WATER

The soil carried away by rivers is deposited in the final stages of their flow; or rather, the soil carried away by the upper reaches of the rivers is deposited in the lowest points of their descent.

Where fresh water rises to the surface of the sea, it is a clear sign of the creation of an island. This island will be uncovered more slowly or more rapidly depending on whether the quantity of rising water is small or large. This island is produced by the accumulation of earth or the deposit of stones moved by the underground <note>original: subterranean</note> course of the water through the places where it flows.
<sig>G 49 v.</sig>

## HOW WATER ERODES AS IT FALLS

The waterfalls that occur at riverbanks always wear away the bases of those banks, causing them to collapse upon their own foundations. This is proven: if the height of the bank *a c* from which the water *a n* falls—striking and eroding the point of impact *m n c*—is the center of the <term>percussion</term> <note>the point where the falling water strikes the surface with force</note> upon which the <term>reflex movements</term> <note>the rebounding or swirling secondary currents caused by the initial impact</note> *n m o* and *n c b* are divided, these movements consume the bank in each direction as it is worn away by their swirling motion. Consequently, as the banks are eroded in this way, their supports collapse on the side where their prop fails.

The water falling from *a b* to *n m* will continue to deepen the entire bed from where it falls down to the lowest level of that place, from *a b* to *c d*.
<sig>G 50 v.</sig>

## WHETHER WATER CAN RISE FROM THE SEA TO THE TOPS OF MOUNTAINS

The water of the sea cannot penetrate from the base to the summits of the mountains that border it; it only raises itself as far as the dryness <note>original: aridity</note> of the mountain <gloss>1</gloss> draws it up <note>Leonardo is describing capillary action, where porous material pulls liquid upward</note>. On the other hand, if the rain—which penetrates from the summit of the mountain to its base near the sea—descends and moistens the opposite slope of that same mountain, it draws the water continually, much like a siphon <note>original: syphon</note> that pours through its longest side. This must be the mechanism that draws the sea water up to a height; thus if *s n* were the surface of the sea and...

If rain descends from the mountain peak from *a* to *n* on one side and from *a* to *m* on the other, this would undoubtedly be the same process as the filtering of a <term>distillation</term> <note>original: distillation of a filter; Leonardo refers to the way water moves through a porous medium or a wick</note> or the movement of water through a tube called a <term>syphon</term>. The water that has saturated the mountain through heavy rain falling on both sides would constantly draw rain from the longer side *a n*, as well as water from the sea, if the side of the mountain *a m* were longer than the side *a n*. However, this is impossible because no part of the earth that is not submerged by the ocean can be lower than the ocean itself. <sig>G 70 r.</sig>

<note>[With drawings]</note>

These <term>convolutions</term> <note>swirling patterns or vortices</note> should be created using colored water poured blindly into clear water. <sig>G 90 v.</sig>

Flowing water contains an infinite number of motions within itself that are either faster or slower than its main current.

This is proven by observing objects floating within two equal streams of water, provided the objects weigh the same as the water. If the water is clear, it reveals the true movement of the currents carrying these objects. Sometimes the downward rush of a wave carries them to the bottom, where they strike the ground. They would then be bounced back to the surface with the current if the floating object were spherical. However, it often happens that the wave does not carry them back up because the objects are wider or narrower in one direction than the other. Because they are irregularly shaped, their largest side is struck by another <term>reflex wave</term> <note>a rebounding or secondary current</note>. This causes the object to roll over and over as it is carried along. Its movement is sometimes fast and sometimes slow; it turns right and then left; one moment it moves upward and the next downward. It flips and turns back on itself, shifting direction constantly. It obeys all the forces that act upon it, and in the struggle between these competing forces, it always moves as the victim of whichever force is strongest. <sig>G 93 r.</sig>

There can be no <term>flow and ebb</term> <note>the rising and falling of tides</note> unless several rivers empty themselves into the same large body of water. <sig>G 95 r.</sig>

Over the course of a year, the amount of water that rises into the air will be equal to the amount that descends back down through rain and rivers. <sig>H 29 v.</sig>

## OF THE COURSES OF MILLS

<margin>H 30 v.</margin>
The water that encounters less resistance <note>original: "gives less weight to its course"</note> in its path moves more swiftly.

Faster-moving water drives its wheel at a higher speed.

The path that is straighter offers the least resistance to the water's flow.

Mill water should strike the blades of the wheels at right angles <note>90 degrees</note>.

Water that flows at a shallower slant will strike the wheel further from the vertical line of its fall.

Water that strikes further from the vertical line of its fall delivers a weaker blow.

<margin>H 31 r.</margin>
The wave created by the impact of water against a riverbed will produce a motion from below that is opposite to the motion above.

A wave moves most slowly at the peak of its height.

The parts of a wave that move most quickly are those near the end of its descent.

Sand remains piled higher under the peak of a wave than under its lower parts.

When a stone is thrown into still water, it creates ripples that expand uniformly if the water is of a consistent depth.

If two stones are thrown near one another within the distance of a <term>braccio</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement roughly equal to 23 inches (58 cm), or the length of an arm.</note>, the circles in the water will expand equally into one another without one destroying the other.

However, if the bottom is not level, the circles will not expand with uniform movement except on the surface.

When a long-shaped object is thrown into the water, it creates an oval-shaped wave pattern.

<margin>H 53 [5] v.</margin>

### [The circulation of water]

<margin>H 101 [42 r.] v.</margin>
The water that enters from the lowest depths of the sea is driven by the force of its mover <note>original: "mover"; in Renaissance physics, this refers to the source of motion, often theorized by Leonardo as the Earth's internal heat.</note> to the high summits of the mountains. There, finding the open channels <note>original: "severed veins"</note>, it pours itself down and returns by the shortest route to the depths of the sea. 

It raises itself again through the network <note>original: "ramification"</note> of its channels and falls back once more. Thus, coming and going—sometimes high and sometimes low, inwards and outwards—it rotates with natural or forced <note>original: "accidental"</note> movement like a screw. Meanwhile, the water that is poured away through its broken branches and falls back upon itself rises again through its courses and returns to the same points of descent.

If the bottom of a riverbed where the water plunges is hollow in the center, the water moving from the sides toward this center will rise up before it falls.

<margin>I 62 [14] r.</margin>
If a flowing river strikes against a rock, it will leap upward; the place it hits as it falls back down will take on the nature of a well <note>This refers to the formation of a plunge pool, a deep depression carved into the riverbed by the force of falling water.</note>.

<margin>I 67 [19] v.</margin>
If a rock in a river projects above the surface and divides the water's course, and the water reunites after passing this rock, the space found between the rock and the point of reunion is the place where sand will be deposited.

But if the rock dividing the water's flow is submerged only at its base <note>original: "lower parts"</note>, the water flowing over the top will fall behind it, carving out a hollow at the rock's base and causing the current to swirl. The water falling headlong into this chasm turns in a vortex, moving both upward and downward; this happens because the merging of the two streams—which had been divided by the rock—does not allow the water to immediately continue its forward journey.

<margin>I 68 [20] r.</margin>
Every natural and continuous motion tends to maintain its course along the path of its beginning; that is, regardless of how the terrain varies, it proceeds according to its initial direction <note>Leonardo is describing an early concept of inertia, where an object in motion stays in motion along a straight line unless acted upon by another force.</note>.

This aforementioned movement occurs in the course of rivers, which always attack and erode whatever obstructs their direct path.

However, if these rivers were perfectly straight, with uniform width, depth, and slope <note>original: "slant"</note>, you would find that with every degree of movement, they would gain a degree of speed.

Consequently, if there is a change or difference in their slope, there is a change in their flow. Where the width is more uniform <note>original: "less inequality in breadth"</note>, the water becomes deeper; and given an equal slope, the water slows down where the channel is wider. Therefore, the water—which "seeks" a straight course and aims to become faster at each stage of its movement—slows down when it finds the places through which it passes to be wider and deeper, subsequently eroding the riverbed or the bank.

<header>THE NATURE OF WATER</header>
<page-num>713</page-num>

Air is capable of being compressed, and the more it is compressed, the more weight it carries within the surrounding air. The greater its weight, the greater its impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> against an object. This is seen with winds that are forced from a wide area to pass through a narrow mountain pass: if there were no opening above them, they would not be able to fill the spaces in front of them. However, they can expand upward very easily because there are large spaces between the hills, and the wind flies easily toward the heights. Recall how Augustus made a vow in Gaul to the wind Circius <note>original: "Cirrius." The Circius was a famously violent wind in the Roman province of Gallia Narbonensis, modern-day Provence</note> because he nearly lost his army to its force; he even built a temple there in its honor. <margin>I 68 [20] v., 69 [21] r. and v.</margin>

Water will splash up much higher than the height from which it fell. This is caused by the violent movement of air trapped inside water bubbles, which then rise and float like bells upon the surface. When the water returns to the place where it strikes, it is submerged again by the blow. Consequently, the air is hemmed in between the water driving it down and the water it encounters. Being pressed upon with such fury and violence, the air suddenly bursts through the water covering it. Like a thunderbolt emerging from the clouds, this air escapes the water, carrying with it a portion of the water <note>The original manuscript uses the word "aria" (air), but contextually Leonardo likely meant "water" as the medium being carried</note> that previously formed its covering. <margin>I 69 [21] v.</margin>

### *[Water in canals]*

When water moving through a narrow canal reaches a wider section, it immediately becomes shallower and faster because it encounters a slope where it moves with more vigor. It continues along its path until it reaches and strikes the base of its dike <note>term: dike; here referring to an embankment or the side wall of an artificial waterway</note>.

After this impact, the water turns upward and proceeds in a swirling motion, hollowing out the foundation of the bank until it returns to the surface. This process of erosion carves a shape like the hull of a ship: narrow at the beginning and the end, but deep and wide in the center. <margin>I 70 [22] r.</margin>

## BEGINNING OF THE BOOK OF WATER

The name *wide sea* or *large lake* <note>original: "pelago"</note> is applied to a large and deep area where the waters lie with little movement. A *whirlpool* or *abyss* <note>original: "gorgo"</note> is of the same nature as a *pelago*, except for one specific difference: the waters that enter a *pelago* do so without heavy impacts <note>original: "percussions"</note>, while those of a whirlpool are made of great falls, bubbling, and surges caused by the continuous revolution of the waters. A *river* <note>original: "fiume"</note> is that which occupies the lowest part of a valley and flows continuously. A torrent is that which flows only with rains; it also makes its way through the low parts of valleys and joins with the rivers.

A canal is the term applied to waters regulated within banks by human effort. *Sources* <note>original: "fonti"</note> is the name given to the birthplaces of rivers. An *embankment* <note>original: "argine"</note> is a steep barrier that withstands the widening of rivers, canals, and torrents. The *high bank* <note>original: "ripa"</note> is higher than the embankment. The *shore* <note>original: "riva"</note> is lower than the embankment. The *beach* <note>original: "spiaggia"</note> is among the lowest of the parts that form boundaries with the water. A *lake* <note>original: "lago"</note> is a place where river waters expand to a great width. *Marshes* <note>original: "paludi"</note> are stagnant waters. *Grottos* <note>original: "grotte"</note> are hollows formed in the banks of rivers by the current; their length follows the line of the water's course, and they have some depth, even finding their way under the foundations of the bank and losing their shape as they near the end of their course. Caverns are shaped like ovens that extend far beneath the bank; the waters within them are in a state of wild turmoil and are constantly increasing.

*River-pits* <note>original: "pozzi" (literally "wells," here referring to deep depressions in a riverbed)</note> are the sudden depths of rivers. *Stagnant pools* <note>original: "stagni"</note> are the...

...places of refuge for the waters of floods or storms, their beds being firm and thick so that the soil can neither absorb <note>original: "drink in"</note> nor dry up these waters. **Chasms** <note>original: "Baratri"</note> are also places where the water suddenly becomes deep. **Storms** <note>original: "Procelle"</note> are tempests of water. **Bubblings and wellings up** <note>original: "Polulamenti e surgimenti"</note> are the points where waters begin; however, "bubblings" rise from below upward, while "wellings" move horizontally, falling from a grotto. **Submersion** <note>original: "Sommergere"</note> refers to objects that sink beneath the water. When the general course of a river is constricted—as when it leaves a valley and enters a narrow mountain pass—the water will pile up in the wider section. It will then descend rapidly and move with great force through the narrow passage. After passing the midpoint of this constriction, the water will carve out a deep hollow. Once it returns to a wider area, the river will lose its depth in proportion to the increase in width, until the flow becomes steady and equalized once more.

This lack of depth occurs after the "leap" of the water because the area becomes filled with gravel <note>original: "shingle"</note> deposited beneath the highest point of the water's surge.

If a waterfall is the same width as the river, the water that strikes the bottom will surge upward. It then falls back along every path radiating from the center of this surging mass; the farther these paths descend from the surge, the more they spread out. Part of this water is moved by the main current of the stream. Consequently, the water must make three distinct movements, each of which significantly erodes <note>original: "consumes"</note> the base <note>original: "foot"</note> of the riverbank.

The water falling from the peak of the surge strikes toward the bottom. Because this descent is slanted, it moves toward the base of the bank. Since this descent also follows the general flow of the river, the surging mass falls with a threefold downward movement: one going straight down, one toward the bank, and one following the course of the river. All three erode the base of the bank, by reason of the...

<insert>[Of the movement of water—bubbles]</insert>

<margin>I 76 [28] verso</margin>
When one sees mounds <note>original: "mountains"</note> rising in running waters in the form of bubbles, it serves as a sign of the great depth from which these bubbles spring after the impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> made by the water upon the bottom. By the speed of its rebound, it bores through and penetrates the surrounding water and then turns toward the surface of the running water and passes through it, rising up in this way. Thereafter, as it acquires weight, it loses its initial force and falls down again along every line around its center, returning once more toward its bed.

## CURRENTS

Regarding the difference water makes in its course if its sides strike a shore, a bank, or other water—that is, when passing through a section of stagnant water or through running water crosswise.

One should also observe what differences occur in rivers if they fall upon beds of different materials, namely upon stone, earth, tufa <note>A porous rock typically formed from volcanic ash or calcium carbonate deposits</note>, clay, sand, or mud; or if they meet stagnant or running water. This applies whether the contact is crosswise, slanted, from the opposite direction, or along the same line as the water itself—that is, following the path of the same current but moving slower or faster than the water it strikes, or at a more level or slanted angle.

## OF EDDIES

One asks why the impact of water within water creates circular movements and eddies, rather than a straight "leap" like the water that beats upon its shores and banks.

Why bubbles are not continuous, even when the waterfalls themselves are:

## THE NATURE OF WATER

The reason is that the water which flows on the surface after falling is swifter than the water flowing underneath. When the water below plunges into a chasm, it surges back toward the surface with almost the same force <note>original: "impetus"</note>; sometimes it overpowers the water flowing above, and sometimes it is overpowered by it.

Being thus in a state of balance <note>original: "equilibrium"</note> regarding its force of movement, sometimes one prevails and sometimes the other.

<sig>I 77 [29] recto and verso</sig>

Objects lighter than water do not follow the path of the water's rebound and intersection. Instead, they pass along the center of the current or near the areas where they first entered the flow. They are not hindered unless they face equal pressure; this is because if a right-hand rebounding wave meets a left-hand one, and they are of equal power, the point of their collision <note>original: "percussion"</note> must be pushed back equally on both sides.

Consequently, objects in this location moving upon the water—not being driven more by one impact than the other—remain in the same line of the current. But if the force of one wave is greater than the other (due to the swiftness of its current), the object will move. I do not mean a force arising from a larger volume of water, for if one body of water were much thinner than the other, it would not matter. 

For example, let us suppose one body of water has less than double the volume of another but acquires double the speed. Since these bodies of water are of equal size at their point of contact—as I have proved in the third [proposition] of the fifth [book]—the larger being a square <term>braccio</term> <note>An Italian unit of length, roughly 23 inches (about 58 cm)</note> and the smaller being half a <term>braccio</term>, the smaller only strikes half of the larger. In the same way, the larger strikes the smaller with only half of its surface. Thus, the areas of contact made by the impacts <note>original: "percussions"</note> are equal in size but unequal in power, because the speed of one is double that of the other.

### OF THE EDDIES

Sometimes there are many eddies which contain a strong current of water in their center, and they grow larger as they approach the end of the current. These are created on the surface by water that turns back after the impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> it makes within the swiftest current; the front portions of these waters, being themselves...

<page-num>718</page-num>
<header>THE NATURE OF WATER</header>

<margin>I 78 [30] recto and verso, 79 [31] recto</margin>
Slow waters, when struck by a swift movement, are suddenly accelerated to that same speed. As a result, the water touching them from behind is pulled and drawn by force, torn away from the rest of the body of water. This causes the water to turn in succession, one wave following the next with equal speed. If the current cannot absorb this movement without rising above the surface—and since it cannot do that—it must turn back on itself and dissipate these swift movements. From that point, these <term>eddies</term> <note>original: "vortici" (vortices or whirlpools)</note> use various revolving motions to dissipate the <term>impetus</term> <note>momentum or driving force</note> that was initiated. These eddies do not stay in one place; once formed, they are carried along by the momentum of the water while maintaining their shape. In this way, they perform two movements: one is the internal revolution of the eddy itself, and the other is the movement as it follows the course of the water that carries it, even as it gradually dissipates.

### *[Air and Water]*

<margin>I 80 [32] verso</margin>
Water that, through a gentle movement, traps air just beneath its surface, rises back out with a slight force. It carries a thin covering of water that, being balanced by the weight of the trapped air, remains above the surface in the shape of a hemisphere <note>original: "half-spherical figure"</note>.

However, if air is driven underwater with great force, it returns to the surface with a fury proportional to the depth it reached. Driven by the surrounding weight, it leaps out of the water, breaking the surface with its momentum. It then flows in a straight path, like air escaping from a bellows in a steady stream. Therefore, unlike the gentle bubbles mentioned before, it does not remain trapped under a film of water on the surface.

How all the air that rebounds with the water does not stay on the surface, but is pulled back down by its own momentum into the swirling revolutions of the water:

How the movement of water within other bodies of water is not forced to follow a straight line rather than a curved one; and how, after rebounding, these waters are not required to come to rest, but instead return to a lower level with a revolving motion—

## BEND OF CURRENT

If the entry of the water into the pool (*<term>pelago</term>* <note>original: "pelago"; an expanse of water, basin, or pool</note>) is circular in shape, the hollow at its base will be shaped like a crescent, gathering the <term>shingle</term> <note>original: "ghiaia"; small, rounded pebbles or gravel found in riverbeds</note> within its curve or between the two horns of this figure.

I ask whether, if the current should make a bend, it will become hollowed out at the bottom, in the middle, or at the surface. I also ask about the "leaps" <note>cascades or rapids</note> which follow afterward against the riverbank—assuming the bed is made of a uniform substance—and also about the bank where it is raised or where it slopes, and the methods for repairing it.

I ask about the shape that water assumes at different angles of its descent in each of its falls, and what shape the hollow will take when the water strikes a bed of uniform substance. ## HOW TO STRAIGHTEN RIVERS WHEN THEY HAVE A SLOW COURSE

Because the straighter a river is, the swifter its course will be, and the more aggressively it will erode and consume the bank and its bed. It is therefore necessary either to enlarge these rivers considerably, send them through many twists and turns, or divide them into a number of branches.

And if a river becomes slow and marshy because of many twists and turns, you should then straighten it in such a way that the water acquires enough movement and does not cause destruction to the banks or dikes. If there should be a deep spot near a dike, you should fill up the area with <term>gabions</term> <note>original: "gabbioni"; cages or baskets filled with rocks or earth used in hydraulic engineering</note> together...

### [*On the earth carried by water*]

When floodwaters begin to find a place where they can flow, they start with a weak inundation, stripping and carrying away the lightest materials. They deposit these where the current slows down. Then, as the flood grows, it carries away heavier materials such as sand, depositing them on top of the earlier sediment. Even if the water level does not increase, the mere fact of its continued flow gradually carries away materials from the streambed. However, because of their weight, it cannot carry them as far forward as the initial lighter materials; if it carries away heavier items, it deposits them proportionately close to the spot from which it took them.

## How to restore soil to places stripped bare by water on hills, mountains, or in sandy areas.

<margin>I 83 [35] recto</margin>
To manage rainfall or provide an outlet for other waters, one should construct canals or river mouths. In places where the current is so strong that the water becomes <term>turbid</term> <note>original: "turbid"; cloudy, thick, or opaque with suspended sediment</note> because of the earth it carries and causes the landscape to change, these canals should be divided into many small channels, much like furrows. This reduces their force, allowing them to become clear again as the soil settles.

### [*On flowing water*]

Where the river is narrowed, its bed will be stripped of earth, leaving the stones or <term>tufa</term> <note>original: "tufa"; a type of porous rock formed by the precipitation of calcium carbonate from water</note> exposed.

Where the river widens, small stones and sand will be deposited.

Where the river widens significantly, mud or <term>ooze</term> <note>original: "ooze"; soft, watery mud or slime typically found at the bottom of a body of water</note>, bits of timber, and other light materials will be discharged.

Where several currents flow together, a hollow will immediately be formed that will be deep enough for navigation.

Sometimes minor floods carry branches covered with leaves from the plains and deposit them where there is little movement. Then, as the flood grows stronger, it heaps sand upon the edges of these branches. As the water continues to increase, it carries shingle and large, tall stones to that same spot.

They will travel together with their center away from the spot where the circle was first made, following the course of the stream. . .

## OF WATER

Rivers, when they are straight, flow with a much greater force in the center of their width than they do at their sides.

When water strikes the sides of a river with equal impact, if it finds a narrower part of the channel, it will leap toward the middle of the river. These waves will then create a new impact where they meet; as a consequence, they will bounce back toward the banks equally. That water, forming a conical shape enclosed between the first impact against the bank and the second impact in the center of the stream, will slow down at its base and move swiftly near its crest. Upon striking the bottom, the water will afterward rise equally to the height of the intersection; however, the water in the center will always be swifter than the water that leaps backward.

Water moving through a channel of consistent width and over an even bed will have as many different thicknesses (depths) as there are different slopes in the bed where it runs. To the degree that the water is swifter in one place than another, it will be proportionately more shallow.  
I 105 [57] v., 106 [58] r.

## OF MOVEMENT

Water falling from a height of one <term>fathom</term> <note>original: "fathom"; a unit of length equal to six feet</note> will never return to that same height, except in the form of small drops. These drops will leap much higher because the motion of the upward bounce is much more rapid than that of the descent. In fact, when the water falls, it carries a great quantity of air down with it; after the rest of the water has been struck, it leaps back toward the surface with a force that creates a movement almost as rapid as the descent was—though not quite as rapid, for the reason...

This is discussed in the second [part] of the seventh [book], where it is stated that the movement of a rebound will never be as swift as the descent of the substance that rebounds; or rather: a subsequent rebound will never be equal to the one that preceded it. Consequently, the rebound made by water proceeds from the base where it was created with nearly the same speed as the descent that produced it. In addition to this, a second <term>momentum</term> <note>original: "momentum"; the force or quantity of motion of a moving body</note> is added which increases this motion: namely, the momentum of the air that is submerged by the falling water. This air, surrounded by water, bounds up furiously and leaps back into its own element like wind driven by a bellows. It carries with it the surface water and, through this added force, causes it to leap up much farther than its own nature would have required.

The farther a circular wave is removed from its cause, the slower it will become. <margin>I 114 [66] r.</margin>

### [*The meeting of water-courses*]

If the courses of two lines of water—which cross each other in the middle or in part of their riverbeds—pass either into one another or one over the other, do they then leap back after the <term>percussion</term> <note>original: "percussion"; the impact or collision between two bodies</note>? They certainly leap, because it is impossible for two physical bodies to pass through one another.

But after the two bodies have clashed together, they will widen at their point of contact. After striking, they will recoil to an equal distance from the center of the impact. The body that moves upward follows its natural inclination, while the other body—below the center of the impact—which would naturally go downward but cannot, instead increases the force of the water moving upward. <margin>I 114 [66] v.</margin>

### [*Movements of water*]

If water were a **discrete** quantity <gloss>separate parts</gloss> <note>original: "disscreta"; in classical physics, a "discrete quantity" is composed of individual, separate units, whereas a "continuous quantity" is a single, unbroken substance</note> rather than a continuous one, the movement it makes between the highest peaks and lowest depths of its waves would be unequal.

In effect, the part that rises becomes increasingly slower with every degree of movement, so that at its greatest height, it reaches its point of extreme slowness.

Afterward, as it descends, it gains degrees of speed with every degree of movement, so that at its lowest depth it achieves its greatest movement. Therefore, the resistance that ends its descent is what receives the impact <note>original: "hurt"; meaning the force or damage caused by the collision</note>, while the point that ends the height of its rise receives no such impact.

But if the quantity is continuous: a continuous substance has equal movements when its river is of equal size and depth. Because the water is all united together, it is necessary that in every part of its movement each part pulls and is pulled, pushes and is pushed—or drives and is driven. It is necessary that this occurs with equal movement and power. If it were not so, the water would accumulate more where it was slowest and would fail where it had the most movement.

<margin>I 116 [68]</margin>
Where the water divides, it rises; and afterward, as it falls down again, it strengthens its course due to the increased descent that follows.

Where the waters join, they rise; and then the nearby movement that follows becomes slow.

When there are two currents of water in the course of a river, starting far from one another and meeting in a place where they clash together, they will rise up after this percussion <note>original: "percussion"; the physical impact or collision of the two bodies of water</note>. Their bed will be eroded very little because the water moves away from it; afterward, they will fall back again as they separate and fall asunder, and falling back...

## [The height and depth of the waves]

### OF THE SUMMIT OF THE WAVES

The highest <term>elevation</term> <note>the peak or crest</note> of a wave will not wear away the riverbed directly beneath itself. In effect, it barely touches the bed, according to the rule (the fifth [proposition] of the sixth [book]) <note>original: "per il quinto del sesto"; Leonardo frequently references mathematical or physical propositions from classical texts like Euclid’s Elements</note> which says that everything exerts weight along the line of its movement. From this, we may say that this wave moves toward the air as it rebounds from its impact and exerts its weight toward the air. If, however, the amount of <term>friction</term> is slight, it will have very little force and will erode the bed only slightly.

### HOW WAVES ATTAIN THEIR GREATEST DEPTH

Whatever obstacle acts as the primary cause in breaking the straight course of the water will be the part most worn away and displaced by it.

<margin>I 117 [69] v.</margin>
Therefore, we may say that if the air were the reason why the straightness of the wave's rise is broken, the air itself would be worn away by this impact of water. But air is not the cause of the breaking of such a course; the only cause is the force which the water acquires as it rises out of its natural element. The water would slow its pace in such a position if it were a "sensible" quantity <note>original: "quantità sensibile"; likely referring to a discrete quantity composed of individual, perceptible parts</note>, but since it is a <term>continuous quantity</term> <note>a substance that is single and unbroken</note>, it is necessary that one body of water pushes and the other pulls, because they are united.

*Whether the water moves more swiftly while the wave is falling than while it is rising, and at what point this water lingers the most.*

<margin>I 118 [70] r.</margin>
The water that moves in the formation of waves will move at the same speed during its <term>ascent</term> <note>rising</note> as during its <term>descent</term> <note>falling</note>. It will have as much speed in the middle of its lowest depth as at its greatest height. If its movement were not equal, its depth and breadth would not be equal. Furthermore, if it were of equal length and depth but not of equal movement, the water would pile up and form a great height in the place where it slowed down the most.

<summary>Leonardo explains that waves erode the riverbed through impact (percussion) and that water, as a continuous substance, maintains a consistent speed during both its rise and fall to prevent piling up.</summary>

Water flows more powerfully at the sides of a submerged rock than above it or after it has passed it. For this reason, the water twists the waves created by its rebounds, producing crescent-shaped patterns on the surface.
<meta>I 123 [75] r.</meta>

### *[Different Types of Water Rebounds]*

Water rebounds are of two kinds, arising from two different causes. One cause is the unevenness of the riverbed over which the water passes. The other occurs when parts of the water strike against the irregular parts of the bank and leap back toward the opposite bank. Upon striking, these masses of water spring back toward the opposite side, pressing and driving themselves against the first wave they encounter; as they swell, they leap toward the sky. Each wave flies back from the place where it struck, only to be driven back by another wave, and then pushed forward by yet another.

In this succession, they fill the surface of the river with a trellis-like pattern, always rising at the points where these impacts occur.
<meta>I 127 [79] v.</meta>

### *[Rule for Rebounds: An Experiment]*

I ask this concerning the rebound: if the first rebound covers ten <term>braccia</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement based on the length of an arm, roughly 23–27 inches or 58–68 cm.</note>, tell me how far the second will be. Dye a ball so that it leaves a mark where it strikes marble or another hard substance; study the position of each successive rebound, and from this, deduce the mathematical rule.
<meta>I 128 [80] r.</meta>

If you throw sawdust into a running stream, you will be able to observe where the water—turning upside down after striking the banks—throws this sawdust back toward the center of the stream. You can also see the rotations of the water and where other currents join or separate from it, along with many other phenomena.
<meta>K 1 r.</meta>

### RIVERS

<margin>K 60 [11] v.</margin>
**Simple movement:** There are many rivers that increase their volume at every stage of their flow without any loss of water.

**Simple movement:** There are many that lose water without ever gaining any.

**Composite movement:** There is also a significant number which gain more water than they lose.

**Composite movement:** And a significant number lose more water than they gain.

<margin>K 65 [18] r.</margin>
I have recorded the various ways in which water hollows out the riverbed and the various ways it deposits earth upon it. The same applies to the banks: where the water builds them up and where it forms them, the many ways it erodes the soil of the banks, and the lands where it spreads beyond its banks during floods.

<margin>K 93 [13] v.</margin>
Water eddies are always produced in the <term>middle water</term> <note>Leonardo uses this term to describe the transitional zone or the core of a current where different forces or directions of flow interact.</note>.

The middle water is located above the mouth of the water that is bent across near the point where it runs into a canal.

The middle water is that which exists between falling water and water that is being thrown back.

<margin>K 94 [14] r.</margin>
If two streams of water should encounter each other and then curve together in the same path, the "middle water" will be found beyond this path on the side of the current that has less power.

When the surface of the water curves away from its straight course toward a side outlet, it will always be higher in the center than at the sides.

<margin>K 94 [14] v.</margin>
Regarding the water that is poured through a hole of uniform size situated at the bottom of its reservoir: the part that is nearest to the wall of this hole will have a greater height and faster movement than the parts at the sides.

<margin>K 94 [15] r.</margin>
When water is poured in different streams from one reservoir into another, the water poured through a narrower hole will rise higher above that opening. The proportion of the height will be the same as the proportion of the width of the holes.

## RIVERS AND BANKS

All the embankments of rivers against which the waters strike ought to be slanted more steeply in proportion to the force of the water's impact <note>original: "percussion"</note>.

Water rises higher upon the bank it strikes when that bank is more slanted; consequently, it descends with greater force <note>original: "impetus"</note> to strike against the opposite bank. <margin>k 102 [22] v.</margin>

What difference there is between the impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> of the same quantity of water when it falls through the air or falls enclosed in a pipe <note>original: "conduit"</note>: 

The water that falls in a straight vertical line becomes high-pitched <note>original: "shrill"</note> at some stage of its descent. When it falls through a pipe, the pipe is left partially empty, and here the air "fights" with the water, as will be explained in its proper place. You should not forget, however, to mention that this descent of the water is slowed by the compression <note>original: "condensation"</note> of the air in the pipe where the water is located. <margin>k 103 [23] v.</margin>

If the water entering a reservoir or flowing out of it has exit holes equal in size to the entry holes, and the drop <note>original: "fall"</note> of the entry is longer than that of the exit, the volume entering will be greater than the volume exiting until the water in the basin rises, at which point they will become equal. <margin>k 104 [24] r.</margin>

And if the drop of the entry is further beneath the surface than the drop of the exit—even if they are of the same size—the entry will be greater than the exit until their forces equalize.

What shape should a specific quantity of water moving along a set incline have in order to move as swiftly as possible?

It should have the shape that makes the least contact with the bottom—that is, a semicircle <note>original: "half-circle"</note>.

*[*The relationship between waves and wind*] [*Diagram*]*

The wave grows because the wind increases.

In the diagram, *D b e f* represents the wind; it strikes *e f*, the water, and causes it to swell. *d a e c*, the second part of the same wind, finds *c e* already prepared to swell (having been moved by the first part of the wind, *e f*) and follows behind it with its force. This doubles the power *t v e f* and thus makes the wave twice as large.

One must consider whether the impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> made by water against an object is equal in force to the entire mass of the water that strikes it while falling through the air, or not.

Which is easier: to raise the sluice gate of a mill while the water is flowing—whether upward, downward, or across—or when the water is still?

Vessels of equal capacity, filled with water in a two-to-one ratio <note>original: "double proportion"</note> and which empty themselves through holes made at their lowest depth, will change the ratio of their discharge volumes <note>original: "copiousness of their discharges"</note> at every interval of time.

I maintain that if at the start of the discharge one vessel has twice the quantity of water, the rate of discharge is immediately twice as much in that case as in the other, though this changes instantly. For example, if the water levels are divided into six stages in the smaller vessel and twelve in the larger, once both have dropped by five stages, the smaller vessel is left with one stage of water height and the larger with seven—meaning the larger now contains seven times as much.

### [Fall of water]

Water that falls in the shape of a cone <note>original: "pyramid"</note> along a vertical line onto a flat surface will bounce back up to a certain height. Its tip will point back toward the base of this cone; it will then cross through itself, pass beyond, and fall back down. <margin>Codex L, folio 1 recto</margin>

### [Air replacing water]

Why the air that fills the vacuum <note>original: "void"</note> in a vessel <note>original: "globe"</note> as water flows out enters with the same force <note>original: "impetus"</note> as the water leaving. Anything floating on this water moves in the opposite direction to the water's flow. <margin>Codex L, folio 17 verso</margin>

### [Rivers]

A long object of uniform thickness expands just as much on two opposite sides as it narrows on the other two opposite sides.

In this case, water confined within a river of uniform width <note>original: "parallel river"</note> gains as much in height as it loses in width. Consequently, as it falls, it erodes <note>original: "hollows out"</note> the spot where it hits.

Uniform rivers may be constricted along their length in two ways: either between the surface and the riverbed, or between their opposite banks. <margin>Codex L, folio 30 recto</margin>

### [Falls of water]

When two streams meet at a very acute angle, the more powerful current erodes its side of the channel the most, creating a sudden depth.

This is the correct method for creating a waterfall while protecting the riverbank from the descending water. <margin>Codex L, folio 31 verso</margin>

### [The course of rivers]

Naturally exposed riverbeds do not accurately reflect the type or amount of materials carried by the water. This is because, in deep water, many areas are filled with sand. Later, as the river's side-currents shift, these sand deposits are carried over the pebbles <note>original: "shingle"</note> they once rested on, or the pebbles are exposed beneath them. This causes the raised sandbanks to continuously erode <note>original: "subsidence"</note>; because sand is light, it travels with the current and settles where the water becomes calmer <note>original: "tranquil"</note>.

### Falls and the Flow of Water

Water that has fallen with great force <note>original: "impetus"</note> from a dam mimics the winding patterns of rivers based on the angle and direction of its fall. However, when the water levels drop, even if a specific channel *a–b* stays in place during a future flood, that channel *a–b* will eventually fill with sand, and the volume of water will return to its natural path.

### Water Impact <note>original: "percussion"</note>

When water strikes a surface, it rises upward and gains weight in proportion to how high it leaps above its normal level. As this water falls back down, more incoming water strikes it and pushes it down to the riverbed. This process constantly erodes the bed, creating a hollow along the sides of the object that was struck.

<margin>L 33 r.</margin>
To prevent this erosion, a flat surface can be built around any column <note>such as a bridge pier</note> that has a firm foundation. This base should be wide enough so that the falling water is forced to land on it rather than hitting the riverbed directly.

<margin>L 36 v.</margin>
The straighter <note>original: "less curved"</note> a riverbank is where the current strikes it, the farther the water will bounce <note>original: "leap"</note> before it hits the bank a second time.

The eddies <note>swirling currents</note> of rivers come in several varieties. Some are hollow in the center, shaped like an inverted cone <note>original: "concave pyramid"</note>; others are raised in the center like a mound <note>original: "raised cone"</note>. Some eddies dredge up sediment from the bottom, while others pull floating objects down from the surface. One type carves out a hollow beneath the riverbank, while the other fills it with sediment.

<margin>B.M. 30 v.</margin>
Through their rotations and delays, these eddies serve to slow down and balance the excessive speed of rivers. Because side eddies are often restricted by the narrowness of the channel, other types of eddies naturally form to turn the water over from the surface to the bottom at various angles. Some of these meet at the riverbed and churn up the soil that surface eddies had previously deposited. Other eddies perform this same action against the riverbanks.

### [*Of water*]

Water wears away the high peaks of the mountains. It strips bare and carries off great rocks. It pushes the sea away from its ancient shores, for it raises the seafloor <note>original: "raises its base"</note> with the sediment it carries there. It shatters and destroys high riverbanks; no stability can ever be found in these banks that the nature of water does not suddenly bring to nothing. It flows through every sloping valley, using its rivers to either carry away or deposit fresh soil. Therefore, it could be said that many rivers have carried all the water of the element at different times; the sea has retreated from the land many times, and no part of the earth is so high that the sea has not once been at its foundations, nor is any part of the ocean so deep that the highest mountains do not have their bases there.

And so, water is sometimes sharp and sometimes strong, sometimes acidic and sometimes bitter, sometimes sweet and sometimes thick or thin. Sometimes it is seen bringing harm or pestilence, and at other times it is health-giving or even poisonous. One might say that it changes into as many natures as there are different places through which it passes. Just as a mirror changes its appearance based on the color of the object it reflects, water changes based on the nature of the place it flows through: health-giving, harmful <note>original: "noisome"</note>, laxative, astringent, sulphurous, salty, blood-red <note>original: "incarnadined"</note>, mournful, raging, angry, red, yellow, green, black, blue, greasy, fatty, or thin.

Sometimes it starts a fire, and sometimes it puts one out. It is both warm and cold. It carries things away or sets them down; it hollows out land or raises it up; it tears down structures or establishes them; it fills or empties; it rises up or burrows down. It moves at great speed or stays still. It is the cause, at different times, of life or death, of growth or loss. It sometimes provides nourishment and at other times does the opposite. At times it has a tang of salt, and at times it has no flavor at all. Sometimes it submerges wide valleys with great floods. With time, everything changes. <margin>British Museum, 57 r.</margin>

At times it twists toward the northern regions, eroding the base of its bank; at times it collapses the opposite bank to the south; at times it bores toward the center of the earth, consuming the foundation that supports it; at times it leaps up, seething and boiling toward the— <note>the sentence ends abruptly in the original manuscript</note>

## [*Why the beds of straight rivers are deeper in the center than at the sides*]

The current of a straight river is higher in the center than at the sides. It rises toward the sky with larger waves and carves out a greater depth toward the center of the earth.

This occurs because the current is the collision or intersection of the reflected <note>original: "reflex"</note> movement of the waves. These waves leap back after striking against the bank. As they run back toward the opposite bank, they clash with opposing movements. Because they resist each other and neither can pass through the other, they leap high out of the water. Then, falling back—having gained momentum <note>original: "acquired weight while in the air"</note>—they plunge beneath the water at the point where they strike it.

---

## How rivers widen their valleys and wear away the bases <note>original: "roots"</note> of the mountains at their sides:

As their valleys grow deeper, the bases of the hills are sloped back <note>original: "bent back"</note> toward the course of the river, as if they wished to demand back from the speeding river the soil of which it has stripped them <note>original: "despoiled them"</note>.

This follows from the nineteenth principle of this treatise, which says: the current of the river eats away the base of the mountain on the side where it strikes and deposits it on the opposite side to which the water is deflected.

In large valleys, the river changes its course <note>original: "bed"</note>.

Rivers in large valleys change their beds more significantly the further they are from the base <note>original: "roots"</note> of the mountains. Because of their great size, they are continually eroding the waves that flow from their banks, drawing them back into the main current of the river.

## ON CHANGES IN THE MOUTHS OF RIVERS

The mouths of rivers are continually shifting and moving downstream relative to the course of their main stream. This happens because of the previously mentioned rule: water erodes the bank where it strikes and deposits sediment on the opposite bank where it is deflected.

Valleys are continually growing deeper.

<margin>British Museum MS 161 r.</margin>
Valleys grow wider and deeper over time, and rivers constantly change their position.

## THE IMPACT <note>original: "percussion"</note> OF WATER FALLING UPON VARIOUS OBJECTS

<margin>British Museum MS 167 v.</margin>
Water that falls in a perfectly vertical line through a round pipe onto a flat surface will create a circular wave around the point of impact. In this way, water rises from the lowest depths of the sea to the summits of the mountains and falls down through broken veins <note>Leonardo frequently used the term "veins" to describe the underground channels he believed carried water up into mountains</note>. At the same time, other water is rising; thus, the entire element circulates, passing many times through the rivers that flow into the sea.

At one moment, it is transformed into the highest clouds, and later it is trapped within the deep caverns of the earth.

It has no inherent qualities of its own, but it moves and carries everything with it, as is clearly seen when it is distilled <note>original: "distilled" — the process of purifying a liquid by heating and cooling, which Leonardo used to show that water itself is neutral but carries minerals and debris</note>.

Thus, it travels here and there, up and down, never resting in stillness, always flowing to help wherever the <term>vital humour</term> <note>Life-sustaining fluids; in this context, the water that feeds the "living" Earth</note> is lacking.

Sometimes it carries away the soil, sometimes it adds to it; here it deposits logs, and there stones; in one place it leaves sand and in another mud, with no stability in its bed or its banks.

Now it rushes on with a headlong course, and now it descends peacefully. At times it shows a fierce appearance, and at others it appears bright and calm. Sometimes it mingles with the air as a fine spray, and sometimes it falls in tempestuous rain; it changes into snow or hailstorms, or bathes the air with a fine mist. It also turns to ice and becomes hot, never maintaining any stability. Sometimes it rises high as a thin cloud, compressing the air where it is trapped, so that it moves through the atmosphere like a sponge being squeezed under water: when the sponge is squeezed, whatever is trapped inside is driven out through the surrounding water.

It flows from the vast depths of the mighty ocean into the deep, wide caverns that lie hidden within the bowels of the earth. From there, through spreading <term>veins</term> <note>Leonardo believed that underground water channels were analogous to the veins and arteries of a living organism</note>, it rises upward against its natural course in a continual ascent to the high summits of the mountains, eventually returning through broken veins back to the deep.

Water serves as the <term>vital humour</term> <note>Life-sustaining fluids; in this context, the water that feeds the "living" Earth</note> of the dry earth. The force that moves it through these veins is exactly the same as that which moves the fluids in every species of living body.

<margin>British Museum Manuscript 234 v.</margin>
Water, which serves as the vital humour of the dry earth and moves through the spreading veins for this same purpose, is poured into the earth and works within it just as blood does in human bodies.

The same cause moves the water through its spreading veins as moves the blood in the human species. Just as blood flows out from the lower parts through broken veins in the top of a man, so too is water poured out through the broken veins in the summits of the mountains.

Once water has emerged from the veins of the earth, it is abandoned by the moving force that led it there.

In falling from the high summits, water follows the "desire" <note>original: "desire" — Leonardo uses this to describe the natural tendency or gravitational pull of heavy objects to return to their place of rest</note> of all other heavy things.

To the great wonder of those who observe it, water raises itself from the lowest depths of the sea to the highest summits of the mountains; then, pouring through broken veins, it returns to the shallow parts of the sea, only to rise again swiftly and return in a similar descent. Thus, in the course of time, the entire element circulates.

So it proceeds from high to low, passing in and out, moving sometimes by natural laws and sometimes by chance <note>original: "fortuitous movement"</note>, yet always together and unified. It travels in a continual cycle, much like the water within a grapevine. As the sap pours through its pruned branches and falls back upon its roots, it rises again through the passages and returns in a similar revolution.

The water that "sees" the air through the broken veins of the high mountain summits is suddenly abandoned by the power which—
