## [A pedometer] [Figure]

To determine how far one travels in an hour, use a potter’s wheel constructed as shown. Place the center of the instrument upon a circular line that has a circumference of exactly five *braccia*, the diameter being one and 19/22 *braccia*. Then, close the instrument tightly and use "harmonic time" <note>original: "tempo armonico"; likely referring to a steady rhythm or a musical beat used as a primitive metronome</note>. Coat the entire inside of the instrument with turpentine <note>A sticky resin used here to catch and hold dust particles during rotation.</note>. 

Turn the wheel uniformly and observe where the top layer of dust has stuck to the turpentine; then see how many revolutions the wheel has made and in how many beats of harmonic time. If the wheel has made two revolutions in one beat of time—which equals ten *braccia*, or the three-hundredth part of a mile—you will be able to say that this instrument has moved one mile in three hundred beats of time. Since an hour consists of one thousand and eighty beats of time, this would equate to a speed of three miles and 180 three-hundredths of a mile per hour <note>approximately 3.6 miles per hour</note>.
<sig>F 48 v.</sig>

## [A decoration]

If you make small pipes in the shape of goose quills that are opaque white—coated with black on the inside and then made transparent—and with sardonyx <note>A translucent variety of onyx with reddish-brown and white bands.</note> on the outside and then transparent again; let the entire thickness of these pipes be composed of these mixtures. Moisten them, press them, and leave them to dry in a press. If you press them flat, they will produce one visual effect; if you press them into a rectangle, they will produce another; and similarly if you press them into a triangle. You will also achieve good results if you press them from the front or fold them in various ways.

If you use a small stylus to apply a mixture of different colors to the transparent part exposed to the sun—especially opaque black and white, and yellow made from burnt orpiment <note>A deep yellow pigment made from arsenic trisulfide.</note>—you can create very beautiful patterns and various small markings with lines similar to those found in agate.
<sig>F 55 v.</sig>

## LAMP

[Drawing]

A lamp in which the wick rises as the oil becomes low.

This works because the wheel that raises the wick rests upon the oil. As the oil level drops, the wheel descends; as it descends, it rotates by means of a thread wrapped around its axle. The cogs of this wheel then push the notched <note>original: "toothed"</note> pipe that holds the wick.

The same result can be achieved if the axle of the wheel *a* does not descend, and the only part that drops is the float *b* which sits upon the oil. This float descends along with the surface of the oil and causes the wheel to turn; the wheel’s cogs then push up the aforementioned notched pipe with a slow, steady movement.

<sig>G 41 r.</sig>

## THE MINT OF ROME

[With drawings]

This device can also be constructed without a spring, but the screw above must always be connected to the part of the movable sheath.

No coins can be considered of high quality unless they have a perfect rim; and in order to ensure the rim is perfect, it is first necessary for the coins to be absolutely round.

To achieve this, the coin must first be made perfect in weight, width, and thickness. Therefore, you must first have many metal plates produced at a uniform width and thickness by being drawn through the same press. These should remain in the form of strips. From these strips, you should stamp out the round coins in the same manner that holes are punched in sieves for chestnuts. These coins are then stamped using the method described above.

The cavity of the mold should be slightly and imperceptibly higher at the top than at the bottom.

This method cuts coins with perfect roundness, thickness, and weight. It eliminates the need for workers who manually cut and weigh the metal, and also eliminates the need for the worker who rounds the coins by hand.

Therefore, the coins pass only through the hands of the plate-maker and the stamper, resulting in very fine coinage.

<sig>G 43 r.</sig>

## ON PERCUSSION

Among the accidental forces of nature, percussion <note>The physics of impact or collision.</note> greatly exceeds all others created by the motive forces of heavy bodies moving with equal time, movement, weight, and force. This percussion is divided into "simple" and "compound." 

**Simple percussion** occurs when the motive force (the striker) is directly joined with the moving object at the point where it hits the target. 

**Compound percussion** is that in which the moving object does not end its movement at the point of impact. An example is a hammer striking a die <note>A specialized tool used to engrave or stamp designs onto metal.</note> that stamps coins. This compound percussion is much weaker than simple percussion. 

If the flat face <note>original: *bocha*, meaning mouth or opening; here referring to the striking face of the hammer.</note> of the hammer's head were attached directly to the coin it had to stamp, and if the hammer struck the mold where the impression was located—such that the relief of the coin was engraved in reverse on the hammer's face—the resulting impression would be more distinct and clear on the side struck with simple movement than on the side where the percussion is compound. This is seen with coins that remain struck in the die where the hammer hit them during its descent; the percussion is reflected and thrown back against the face of the hammer.

## SIPHON CLOCK and SLOW TIME-FUSE

*[Regarding the siphon]*

A preparation of mercury drawn through a very fine copper tube shaped like a siphon—the walls of which are of imperceptible thickness—will function as a timepiece in the manner of an hourglass. This allows for the slowest and most precisely graduated descent that can be made; it is so slow that it may happen that not even a single grain of mercury passes from one vessel to the other in an hour.

The surface level of its container is easy to observe because mercury is opaque. The "skin" <note>The surface tension or upper level.</note> of this mercury lowers imperceptibly as the siphon discharges. By this means, you will be able to create a fire which, by means of per— <note>The text likely cuts off the word "percussion." Leonardo is describing a mechanical trigger for an incendiary device or "time-fuse."</note>

### TO KNOW HOW FAR A SHIP TRAVELS IN AN HOUR

The ancients used various methods to discover what distance a ship travels every hour. Among them is Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio (c. 80–15 BC), a Roman architect and engineer whose "De Architectura" was a major influence on Renaissance thinkers.</note>, who explains one in his work on architecture, but his method is as flawed as the others. It consists of a mill-wheel touching the ocean waves at its edges; through its complete revolutions, it describes a straight line representing the circumference of the wheel laid out flat <note>Vitruvius proposed an odometer for ships using a paddle wheel that dropped a pebble into a container every time it completed a rotation.</note>. However, this device is only useful on the smooth, still surface of lakes. If the water moves in the same direction and at the same speed as the ship, the wheel remains motionless. If the movement of the water is either faster or slower than the ship, the wheel will not move at the same speed as the ship; therefore, such an invention is of little value.

Another method can be tested by experiment over a known distance between two islands; this involves using a light board that is struck by the wind. The board slants to a greater or lesser degree depending on whether the wind striking it is faster or slower; this method is found in the work of Battista Alberti <note>Leon Battista Alberti (1404–1472), a famous Renaissance polymath and architect.</note>.

<margin>G 54 r.</margin>
Regarding Battista Alberti’s method—which is based on an experiment over a known distance from one island to another—such an invention will only work successfully with a ship similar to the one used in the experiment. It is also necessary that it be carried out with the same cargo weight, the same amount of sail, the sail in the same position, and waves of the same size. However, my method works with every kind of ship, whether it is powered by oars or sails. Whether the vessel is small or large, narrow or long, high or low, it always works.

<summary>Leonardo concludes a discussion on a long-term timed device before critiquing the ship-speed measurement methods of Vitruvius and Alberti, arguing that they fail to account for currents and varying ship designs.</summary>

Furthermore, you might set yourself to prove that by equipping such a wheel with many balances <note>In this context, weights or counter-levers intended to provide momentum.</note>, every part—however small—that turned over as a result of the impact <note>original: *percussion*</note> would suddenly cause another balance to fall, and by this, the wheel would remain in perpetual motion. 

But in this, you would be deceiving yourself. Since there are twelve pieces and only one moves upon impact, and since this impact may cause the wheel to move by only one-twentieth part of its circle, then if you give it twenty-four balances, the weight would be doubled. Consequently, the force of the impact of the descending weight would be reduced by half, and the resulting movement would be lessened by half. Therefore, if the first movement was one-twentieth of the circle, this second would be one-fortieth; it would always decrease in proportion, continuing to infinity.
->Forster II 89 v.<-

### PAPER ON WHICH IT IS POSSIBLE TO DRAW IN BLACK WITH SALIVA

### XXVI

## Warfare

> ‘When besieged by ambitious tyrants, I find a means of attack and defense in order to preserve the greatest gift of nature, which is liberty.’
>
> ‘I can noiselessly construct subterranean passages to any required location, whether straight or winding, passing if necessary underneath trenches or a river.’

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 176 r. c</margin>
[*How to make a pontoon*] <note>A pontoon is a floating bridge supported by barges or hollow cylinders.</note>
Since every river current is swifter in the center of its width than at its sides, and flows faster on its surface than at its bed when the course is uniform, and a movable bridge made upon barges is naturally weaker in the middle of its length than at its ends; therefore, I conclude that as the greater weakness of the bridge is met by the greater impact of the water, this bridge will break in the center.

Construct it so that when the bridge is in motion, the length of the barges will always be aligned with the current. In this way, movement will be much easier as the barges receive less impact from the force of the water.

[*Fortification*]
The tower must be massive as far as the top of the <term>scarp</term> <note>original: *scarp*; the sloping bank or wall forming the inner side of a defensive ditch.</note>. Then, to ensure that incendiary powder cannot be thrown there, you must place the windows high up.

### A WAY TO MAKE A CUIRASS <note>A piece of armor consisting of a breastplate and backplate joined together.</note>

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 358 v. a</margin>
If you place scales of iron <note>original: *ferro*</note> between two thicknesses of cloth and use this to make a <term>doublet</term> <note>a man’s snug-fitting padded jacket.</note>, you may be certain that no pointed weapon will ever be able to penetrate it.

<page-num>807</page-num>

# WARFARE

Furthermore, a <term>bombard</term> <note>A large, early muzzle-loading cannon used primarily in sieges for throwing heavy stone balls.</note> capable of firing a projectile weighing a hundred pounds is significantly more useful in the field than a small cannon. This is because the bombard's stone projectiles inflict considerable damage on the enemy, whereas a small cannon's lead ball—due to its density and weight—does not bounce after the first impact, making it less effective.

If you place an arrow in perfect balance on top of a stone that is on the verge of tipping over, you will see that a large bombard fired even ten miles away will cause the ground to tremble so much that it will make the arrow or the stone fall.

Additionally, if you fire a small bombard in a courtyard enclosed by walls, any nearby vessels or windows covered with cloth or linen will be instantly shattered. Even roofs will be lifted and shaken from their supports; the walls and ground will shake as if during a massive earthquake. Spiderwebs will fall, small animals will die, and every body nearby that contains air <note>This likely refers to lungs or air-filled organs, suggesting the lethal nature of a blast's pressure wave.</note> will suffer immediate damage and some degree of loss.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 363 v. d</margin>
However, this small bombard should be fired without its projectile, or if you prefer, in the style of a <term>curtall</term> <note>original: *cortaldo*; a type of short-barreled cannon used in the 16th and 17th centuries.</note>. The resulting shockwave will cause women and any animals carrying young to miscarry, and chicks will perish inside their shells.

When you need to build earthen mounds on opposite banks of a river, this is the fastest way to do it, provided you have men equipped with hand-barrows:

Allocate six shovelfuls to each hand-barrow, and throw the earth a great distance:

The diggers marked *d* dig from underneath a shovelful, always stepping back, while the diggers marked *b* make a second cut below—that is, deeper down—always moving forward. If there were two more lines of diggers, they would work on the third and fourth levels, and so they would be able to continue the work successively from hand to hand.

--- Page 824 ---
<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s technical observations on military engineering and logistics, moving from the destructive power of artillery mentioned on the previous page to the practical management of labor, cannon construction, and defensive tactics against night attacks.</meta>

<page-num>808</page-num>
<header>WARFARE</header>

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 370 r. b</margin>
In this task, many men become tired merely by carrying loads over such a great distance. Therefore, we must consider whether it is more efficient for the men to remain in one spot and pass the soil from one person to another, or if everyone should be employed in both digging and throwing the earth. Alternatively, we must decide if some should serve solely as carriers of this soil while others act as throwers. Regarding the final place where this earth is deposited, it requires the same amount of effort for a shovelful to reach its destination whether it is moved by the first method or the second; therefore, nothing needs to be considered here except the convenience and physical endurance of the workers.

<insert>*[Accompanied by a sketch of a cannon]*</insert>

<margin>Trivulzianus Manuscript 61 a</margin>
The mouth of the cannon should be one-eighth of its diameter in thickness, and at the point where it joins the breech <note>original: "tail"; the rear part of the cannon barrel.</note>, it should be one-quarter of its diameter thick.

If you are attacked by night in your quarters—or if you fear you might be—take care to have <term>mangonels</term> <note>A type of siege engine or catapult used for throwing heavy projectiles.</note> ready that can throw iron <term>caltrops</term> <note>An anti-personnel weapon made of four sharp spikes so arranged that one always points upward.</note>. If you are attacked, hurl them among the enemy; this will give you time to organize your men against the assailants. The outwitted enemies, slowed by the pain of the wounds in their feet, will be able to achieve very little. You should organize your counter-attack in this way: divide your men into two units <note>original: "squadrons"</note> to encircle the enemy. However, ensure that you have thick soles on your shoes and that your horses are shod with iron, as I have stated before, since the <term>caltrops</term> will not distinguish between your own men and those of the enemy. Ensure that each <term>mangonel</term> throws a full cartload of these caltrops.

### HOW TO PROTECT ONESELF FROM CALTROPS

If you wear an inner sole made of cloth woven from cotton cords the thickness of a finger between your foot and the sole of your shoe, you will be safe from <term>caltrops</term>, as they will not be able to pierce through to your feet.

<margin>Trivulzianus Manuscript 88 a</margin>
If you wish to be safe from light, shifting sand upon the <term>galleys</term> <note>Low-built warships propelled mainly by oars.</note>, scatter heavy river sand upon the gangway and wherever you must step; pitch will help fix this sand in place. Keep sacks of it always ready for when they may be needed.

You should manufacture <term>caltrops</term> using plaster molds made in three parts, with an iron frame <note>original: "arch"</note>, and then the points should be filed sharp.

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s tactical advice on the use of caltrops, moving from their general defensive utility to specific methods for protecting one's own troops and horses from them, as well as applying these tactics to naval combat.</meta>

<page-num>809</page-num>
<header>WARFARE</header>

[<note>sketches of three caltrops with four points and of one with eight, each of the four being duplicated close together—below this is written ‘double caltrop’.</note>]

These <term>caltrops</term> <note>original: "triboli"; anti-personnel weapons made of four or more sharp spikes arranged so that one always points upward.</note> should be kept in a leather bag at each soldier's side. If an expected victory should turn into a defeat because of the enemy's strength, scattering these behind you will halt the speed of the pursuing horses and bring about an unexpected victory.

However, to prevent these same caltrops from causing a similar disaster for your own troops during a retreat, you should first prepare horseshoes in the form shown below. You must nail a steel plate—as thick and wide as the horseshoe itself—between the iron shoe and the horse’s hoof.

In the case of infantry, they should have iron plates fastened to the soles of their shoes. These should not be tied tightly, so that the soldiers can easily raise their heels, take steps, and run when necessary without any hindrance. The loose binding should be fastened as it is represented here below.

Furthermore, if every naval combatant has a small bag of these caltrops and throws them by hand onto the enemy’s galleys or ships, they will be sowing the seeds of an approaching victory. However, you must have your shoes reinforced with iron, as described above, and the soles should be covered with tiny spikes. This is so that if the enemy throws <term>soft soap</term> <note>Used as a chemical weapon to make the wooden decks of ships dangerously slippery during boarding actions.</note> upon your ship, you will be able to keep your footing—even if the enemy throws powdered chalk in such a dense cloud that it chokes the air you breathe.

You should set up four stations at four positions along the length of the ship. At each of these four stations, place a small barrel with a quantity of water and large <term>syringes</term> <note>Hand-operated pumps or sprayers used to discharge liquids.</note> that serve to force the water out through many small holes. This changes the water into a fine spray that will catch the chalk dust and pull it downward to the deck.

syringe; iron sole for shoes; horseshoe for caltrops.

As this ball is thrown, its flame is suppressed, but once it reaches the ground, the reeds—which are bound at the top with linen cloth and set on fire—are driven into the ball. This ignites the gunpowder surrounding a piece of <term>tow</term> <note>original: "tow"; the coarse, broken fibers of flax or hemp used for stuffing or as tinder.</note> that has been soaked in turpentine. The rest of the device is wrapped in hemp, which has also been soaked in turpentine, linseed oil, and pitch. These wrappings must be thin so that the flames can receive air; otherwise, the device will not work.

## RHOMPHEA

<margin>B 7 r.</margin>
This *rhomphea* <note>An ancient Greek polearm or sword; here, Leonardo describes a specialized defensive barrier.</note> can be drawn by army horses, just as the ancients pulled other war machines.

This instrument [indicated by a small drawing] is attached to the center of a plank, a piece of chain, or a stout cord. This is then fastened to a stone that is heavier than the plank itself, so it can be dragged behind. The front edge of this plank is filled with <term>spontoons</term> <note>original: "spontoons"; a type of half-pike or spear used as an infantry weapon.</note> the length of a <term>cubit</term> <note>An ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches (45 centimeters).</note>. The plank itself should be twelve <term>braccia</term> <note>A traditional Italian unit of length; twelve braccia is approximately 23 feet (7 meters).</note> long, and its surface is studded with nails.

## SCORPIONS

A scorpion is a machine designed to hurl stones, darts, and arrows. If it is built on a large scale, it is effective for destroying the enemy's own war machines.

<margin>B 7 v.</margin>
Other authors believe that a "scorpion" is a poisoned arrow that causes instant death even if it only slightly touches the blood. It is said that this weapon was invented by the Scythians <note>Ancient nomadic people of Central Asia and Eastern Europe.</note>, while others say it originated with the inhabitants of <term>Candia</term> <note>The historical name for the island of Crete.</note>. The poison was made from a mixture of human blood and serpent’s venom. This weapon should never be used except against traitors, for it is a weapon fit only for them.

### RHOMPHEA

The *rhomphea* <note>An ancient weapon; while previously described as a barrier, Leonardo here defines it as an incendiary launcher.</note> is an instrument which throws out long firebrands of burning wood. According to the author Aulus Gellius, it was used among the Thracians, and by men of other nations it was called a *flammea* <note>original: *flammea*; Latin for "flaming" or "fiery."</note>.

### THE BOW

The bow is said to have been invented by the inhabitants of Arcadia, though some say it was by Apollo. Those of Candia <note>original: "Candia"; the Venetian name for the island of Crete.</note> call it "Scythian," as it originally came from Scythia. It is widely used among Eastern peoples. They make arrows of canes for these bows, and in their battles there are sometimes so many of them in the air that the day becomes so darkened as to seem like night. For this reason, they have a hatred of clouds, rain, and winds, because these elements divert the course of their arrows; these conditions often lead them to seek treaties and peace.

The spikes (*murici*) or <term>caltrops</term> <note>original: *triboli*; small weapons with four projecting spikes, designed so that one always points upward to wound the feet of horses or soldiers.</note> are for use on the field of battle. They are scattered on the side where an assault from the enemy is expected, and are also thrown among the enemy when they are pursuing a victory.

The *scalpro* <note>original: *scalpro*; a Latin term for a chisel or scraper.</note> was a sharpened iron tool used to prick and control elephants. Livy, in the seventh book of his history of the Carthaginian War, says that many more elephants were killed by their own drivers than by the enemy. When these beasts became enraged and turned on their own side, the driver, with a mighty blow, would thrust the sharp *scalpro* between the ears where the neck joins the spinal column. This was the most rapid death that could be given to such a huge beast.

The *veruina* <note>A light javelin or spit-shaped spear.</note>, according to what I find in a comedy by Plautus ^1, is a long spear with a sharp iron point used for hurling.

---

^1 The reference is to Plautus's *Bacchides*, Act 4, Scene 8, line 46: "If you have a sword, we also have a spear at home" <note>original Latin: *Si tibi est machaera, et nobis veruina est domi.*</note>.

<page-num>812</page-num>
<header>WARFARE</header>

The *soliferreo* <note>original: *soliferreum*; a Roman heavy javelin made entirely of iron.</note> is a type of weapon made completely of iron which soldiers used to throw during their first assault. Livy mentions it in the fourth book of the Macedonian War.

The *fonda* <note>original: *funda*; a sling.</note> is made of a double cord and is somewhat wide where it is bent. Being weighted with a stone and then swung twice in rapid succession by the arm, it releases one of the cords, and the stone flies through the air with a noise as if it had been shot from a catapult. Flavius ¹ says that it is found among the inhabitants of the Balearic Isles, who possess supreme skill in its use; their mothers do not allow their children any food other than what they have hit as a target with a stone shot from a sling. Pliny, on the other hand, says that this sling was invented by the Syrophoenician peoples.

<margin>B 9 r.</margin>
*Glande* <note>original: *glandes*; literally "acorns," referring to leaden bullets.</note> are leaden balls shot from catapults and slings.

*Auctori* according to Celidonius are sickle-shaped weapons with a cutting edge on only one side and a length of about a <term>braccio</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement roughly equal to 23 inches or the length of an arm.</note>. They have a forked handle shaped like the tail of a swallow. They are not carried in a sheath but bare, attached to the belt.

Danish [axes] are a rather long type of hatchet; they are said to have been much in use among the Danish people. However, what must be considered regarding iron instruments of warfare is that those steeped in oil will have a fine edge, while those immersed in water will be rough and brittle. Those soaked in the blood of a goat will be the hardest. Oil, white lead, and pitch preserve iron from all rust.

The *falce* <note>original: *falx*; a scythe or sickle-shaped blade.</note> is made of iron, is crescent-shaped, and has a staff fastened to one of its "horns" or ends. This weapon was widely used among the Thracians and in naval combat no less than on land. It was later adapted for the use of farmers and peasants.

These were used by the Romans upon their ships; they were of an unprecedented size and skillfully manipulated by ropes. They severed the rigging of the lateen yards <note>The diagonal spars that hold the triangular sails typical of Mediterranean ships.</note> as easily as razors, causing the sails and the yards to fall at the same time. In this way, what should have helped the enemy became a great hindrance to them.

### CHARIOT WITH SCYTHES

<note>[Drawing of a horse-drawn chariot with rotating blades]</note>

These chariots armed with scythes were of various kinds and often did no less injury to friends than they did to enemies. The commanders of the armies, thinking to throw the ranks of the enemy into confusion by their use, instead created fear and loss among their own men. Against these chariots, one should employ archers, slingers, and spear-throwers, and hurl all manner of darts, spears, stones, and bombs, accompanied by the beating of drums and shouting. Those who are acting in this way should be dispersed so that the scythes do not harm them. By this means, you will spread panic among the horses and they will charge at their own side in a frenzy, despite the efforts of their drivers, and so cause great obstruction and loss to their own troops. As a protection against these, the Romans were accustomed to scatter iron <term>caltrops</term> <note>A weapon with four metal points arranged so that one always points upward, used to disable the feet of horses</note>, which brought the horses to a standstill and caused them to fall to the ground in pain, leaving the chariots without any power of movement. <sig>B 10 r.</sig>

### FOR CROSSING A RIVER

When you wish to cross a river with an army, you ought to make use of wine-skins attached to the saddle. Since the horses are not able to swim very well on account of the waves leaping up, you should carry an oar fastened behind the neck so that the rider can work it when necessary. <sig>B 10 v.</sig>

<sig>B 30 v.</sig>

Ethiopian wool, after being soaked in this mixture, is twisted into the shape of a ball, filled with sharp spikes, and thrown onto ships with a cord using a sling.

This substance is called <term>Greek fire</term> <note>A legendary incendiary weapon used by the Byzantine Empire that could burn even on water</note>. It is a marvelous thing and sets fire to everything, even under the water. Callimachus the architect was the first to share its secret with the Romans, who later used it extensively. It was notably employed by the Emperor Leo when Eastern peoples attacked Constantinople with a vast number of ships, all of which were set ablaze by this substance.

*Pilocrotho*, *arzilla*, *crusida*, *flammea*, and *lampade* <note>Archaic names for various types of incendiary devices or fire-pots</note>, although they differ in name, are made of nearly the same substance. Their fire is similar to the Greek fire mentioned above—specifically the *flammea* variety—except for the addition of **liquid varnish**, **petroleum oil**, **turpentine**, and **strong vinegar** to the mixture. These ingredients are first squeezed together and left to dry in the sun, then wrapped around a hemp rope and formed into a round shape. Afterward, the ball is thrown with a cord. Some builders drive a dart into the center, securing it by wetting the shaft, while others embed very sharp nails within the mass. A hole is left in the ball for the purpose of lighting it, and the rest of the exterior is smeared with **resin** and **sulfur**. Our ancestors used this compound, pressed tightly and bound to the end of a spear, to ward off and resist the violent attacks of enemy ships.

Lucan <note>Marcus Annaeus Lucanus (39–65 AD), a Roman poet who wrote the epic 'Pharsalia'</note> says that Julius Caesar used this type of fire, throwing it by means of lamps upon the ships of the Cerusci, a Germanic tribe. He burned not only their ships, but even the buildings constructed along the seashore were consumed by the same fire.

The *folgorea* <note>original: *folgorea*; likely meaning "the thunderer," referring to an early type of explosive mortar</note> is a **mortar** <note>A short-barreled cannon used for firing projectiles at high angles</note> with a circular opening at its base. In the center of this opening is a thin *chanicula* <gloss>small iron tube or ignition chamber</gloss> that is finely perforated and filled with **fine gunpowder**. It is designed this way for two reasons: first, so that when the fire reaches the center of the ball, it passes through the chamber and instantly ignites all the powder packed inside; and second, so that the vent of the mortar does not become worn down. This round opening will not withstand the force of the powder unless it is made of **fine copper**, though the rest of the device may be made with four...

The <term>clotonbrot</term> <note>A Germanic-derived term for a "clot-bread" or cluster-shot; an early form of a fragmentation or incendiary bomb</note> is a ball thrown by a <term>trabiculo</term> <note>original: "trabiculo"; a small trebuchet or catapult</note>, which is a smaller version of a <term>mangonel</term> <note>A medieval stone-throwing engine</note>. But if you throw six or eight of these balls among the enemy, you will certainly be the victor; therefore, it is good to throw it into the midst of them and light the internal fuse, which will eventually set fire to the centers of all the sticks.

->This is for ships.<-

When ships are engaged in combat, use fuses to keep the enemy back. At that moment, throw balls filled with lighted fuses among the enemy—that is to say, onto their ships. While the enemy is occupied with protecting themselves from the fire, they will abandon their defenses.

<margin>B 32 r.</margin>
<note>*With drawing of two cannon placed vertically with a stand between them*</note>

Whoever wishes to test which cannon is the better must stand them upright on their ends, with two judges positioned in the center. After first firing one, note how much time passes from the moment of the explosion to the return of the ball to the ground. Then, do the same with the other cannon. The one that takes longer <note>indicating a higher vertical launch and thus more power</note> will have the honor of being the best.

But you must ensure that the tubes are of equal length, that the touch-holes work freely, that the balls are of the same weight, and that the powder comes from the same keg.

Fill the body of the boat with gravel. When you are at the place you wish to cross, open the gravel storage from the bottom so that it falls to the riverbed. <margin>B 32 v.</margin>
[*With drawing*]
To make an airgun <note>A pneumatic weapon using compressed air or mechanical tension to propel a projectile</note> which shoots with marvelous force, you should proceed as follows: stretch a steel wire the width of a finger on a wire-drawing machine by means of a windlass; then temper it <note>Heat the metal to improve its hardness and elasticity</note>, and beat two plates of fine copper around it, which you then stretch on the wire-drawing machine. Then, solder them together evenly with silver, wind thick copper wire around it, and then smooth it with a hammer, but solder it first. Repeat this process three or four times in the same way. Make the airgun two <term>braccia</term> <note>An Italian unit of length, roughly 23 inches</note> long and design it so that it can shoot a steel dart one-third of a <term>braccio</term> in length.

<margin>B 33 r.</margin>
The <term>architronito</term> <note>A name coined by Leonardo, meaning "powerful thunderer"; it is a steam-powered cannon he attributed to the ancient Greek inventor Archimedes</note> is a machine made of fine copper—an invention of Archimedes—and it throws iron balls with great noise and fury. It is used in this manner: the third part of the instrument stands within a large quantity of burning coals. When it has been thoroughly heated by these, tighten the screw **d** which is above the water cistern **a b c**. As the screw above is tightened, it will cause the one below to loosen. Consequently, the water will fall out and descend into the heated part of the machine. There, it will instantly be changed into so much steam that it will seem marvelous, especially when one sees its fury and hears its roar. This machine has driven a ball weighing one <term>talent</term> <note>An ancient unit of weight, roughly 60 to 100 pounds depending on the region</note> a distance of six <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance; six stadia is roughly 1,100 meters or two-thirds of a mile</note>.

[*Fire-ball*] [*With drawing*]
This ball should be made of melted pitch, sulfur, and hemp <term>tow</term> <note>Coarse, broken fibers of flax or hemp used for stuffing or as tinder</note> rubbed together, so that when it burns, the enemy may not be able to steal the design of the invention.

This ball should be two and a half <term>braccia</term> in height and filled with tubes that can throw a pound of smaller balls; these should be coated with pitch inside the tubes so that they do not fall out.

The tubes should be one <term>braccio</term> in length and made of pasteboard <note>An early form of thick paper or cardboard</note> in the shape of wheel-spokes. The space between them should be filled with plaster and wadding, and the ball should be thrown onto the <term>bastions</term> <note>Projecting parts of a fortification</note> by means of a <term>mangonel</term> <note>A type of catapult or siege engine used for throwing stones or incendiaries</note>.

<insert>[With drawings]</insert>

**Cortalds** <note>Short-barreled, large-caliber cannons</note> are effective against large ships.

The **serpentine** <note>Also known as a *passavolante*; a long, thin, light piece of artillery</note> is useful for light galleys, allowing them to attack the enemy from a distance. It can fire a four-pound lead ball and its barrel should be as long as forty cannonballs laid end-to-end.

This **spontoon** <note>A type of boarding pike or harpoon</note> will fasten the device into the enemy ship if the impact is strong enough.

This **zepata** <note>A fire-ship or floating incendiary device</note> is useful for setting fire to ships that are maintaining a blockade after besieging a harbor or other ships within the harbor. It should be constructed as follows: first, place wood one <term>braccio</term> <note>Approximately 23 inches</note> above the water, then tow <note>Coarse flax or hemp fibers used for tinder</note>, then the kind of powder used for a large cannon <note>original: "bombard"</note>, then small bundles of sticks <note>original: "faggots"</note>, and then gradually larger ones. Place iron wires and burning rags on top. When the wind is in your favor, steer it with the rudder. As the fire spreads through the ship, the bent wires will ignite the powder and complete the task.

It is also useful for setting fire to bridges at night, but you should make its sail black for concealment. <sig>B 39 v.</sig>

## NAMES OF WEAPONS

***Acinace***. *Acinace* <note>A short Persian sword or dagger</note> is the name of this knife. It was called this among the Scythians and Medes, according to the writings of Helenius Acro <note>A 2nd-century commentator on Horace</note>.

***Daga***. This weapon was called a *daga* <note>A dagger</note> among the Ligurian people.

***Ensis. Gladius.*** <note>Latin: "Sword. Sword."</note> *Ensis* and *gladius* are types of weapons, and according to Quintilian in the tenth book of his *Institutions*, they refer to the same thing.

According to Pliny in the sixth book of *Natural History*, the *gladius* <note>The standard short sword of the Roman infantry</note> was invented by the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>.

According to Varro, when the *gaesum* <note>A heavy iron javelin used by the Gauls</note> became obsolete, the *gladius* was used in its place. It has been called *aclis* <note>A small throwing-dart or javelin</note> because it was used for the destruction and death of the enemy.

*Spada* <note>Italian: sword</note>, *ensis*, and *gladius* are names of arms that are known everywhere, and were especially well-known among the ancient peoples.

# WARFARE

<margin>B 41 r.</margin>

The **Arpa** <note>original: "Arpa"; likely referring to the *harpe*, a sickle-sword</note>, according to Lucan in his ninth book, is said to be a sword shaped like a sickle, which Perseus used to slay the Gorgon.

The bows were called **manubaleste** <note>Hand-ballistae or powerful hand-held crossbows</note>.

The **Lingula** <note>literally "little tongue"</note>, according to what Naevius says in one of his tragedies called *Ceisonia*, was the name of a small knife shaped like a bird's tongue.

The **Machaera** <note>A Greek-style single-edged sword or large knife</note> is a type of long weapon with one edge sharpened. Caesar mentions it in the second book of his *Commentaries*.

The **Stragula** <note>A javelin or throwing spear</note> is a kind of lance used for throwing or for hand-to-hand combat. Caesar also mentions this in the second book of his *Commentaries*.

**Doloni** <note>Daggers or "stingers" often concealed in walking sticks</note> are a type of weapon mentioned by Plutarch in his *Life of Gracchus*. Others are of the opinion that *doloni* are whips with daggers concealed in their handles.

<margin>B 41 v.</margin>

The **Sica** <note>A curved dagger</note> is a small knife used by assassins in ancient times. These men were called *sicarii* after the name of the knife, according to Quintilian in the ninth book of his *Institutes*.¹

The **Pugio** <note>A Roman dagger</note>, according to Pompeius Festus, is a short, double-pointed knife. Varro, however, says that *pugio* is the name given to a long, iron-tipped lance.

The **Clunade** <note>original: *clunaculum*; a sacrificial knife worn at the haunch</note> is a sacrificial knife.

The **Secespita** <note>A long ritual knife</note> is a long knife with a round handle made of ivory and ornamented with gold and silver. It is used by the high priests and the **flamens** <note>Ancient Roman priests dedicated to specific gods</note> for sacrifices. Some say it is an axe <note>original: "scura"</note>, and some say its edge resembles that of the **manara** <note>A sacrificial cleaver</note>.

**Mucro** <note>The sharp point or edge of a blade</note> is identical with *ensis* <note>A formal word for sword</note> and *gladius* <note>The standard Roman short sword</note>, according to Priscian in the second book of the *Art of Grammar*.

<margin>B 42 r.</margin>

**Aclides** <note>A type of spiked club or javelin tied to a thong</note>, according to the opinion of Servius, are a kind of weapon so ancient that they have been entirely overlooked in war. Nevertheless, we read that they were pieces of wood—some half a cubit <note>About 9 inches</note> in length and some circular—studded with sharp, projecting iron points. They were hurled at the enemy using a cord or leather thongs, and he who received the blow soon knew who had given it.

# WARFARE

<margin>B 42 v.</margin>
<margin>B 43 r.</margin>

**Telo** <note>original: *telum*</note> was the word generally applied by the ancients to all those things which, in war, were suitable to be thrown by hand, such as darts, clubs, arrows, spears, lances, stakes, and stones.

**Veruto**. The **veruto** <note>original: *verutum*, a short javelin</note>, according to Nonius Marcellus, is a small and very straight weapon.

**Fusti**. **Fusti** <note>original: *fustis*, a club or staff</note> were the first weapons that the human race used. Today, they are called stakes by country folk; their points were often hardened by being slightly charred in a fire.

**Baculo**. The **baculo** <note>original: *baculum*</note> is a stick without a hook that was used to beat wretched slaves.

**Haste**. The **haste** <note>original: *hasta*, a spear</note> is said to have been invented by the Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans</note>. They are excellent and superior <note>original: *plestante*, likely meaning sturdy or outstanding</note> when made of ash or hazel, but they are better still when made from the service tree, because that wood is more supple and flexible.

**Astili** <note>original: *hastile*, the shaft of a spear or a light spear</note> are the smaller lances which are thrown skillfully by hand.

**Cuncti** <note>original: *contus*, a long pike or pole</note> are very long and stout pikes without iron heads, having only their wooden points sharpened. The poet Lucan makes mention of them.

**Lancea**. Pliny says that the lance was invented by the Aetolians. Varro says that *lancia* is a Spanish word.

**Pilo**. The **pilo** <note>original: *pilum*</note> was a spear used by the Romans, resembling the *gaesum* of the Gauls and the *sarissa* of the Macedonians. These spears were divided along their length into two equal parts, with the heads placed at each end. They were joined together with fish glue and bound with gut at every half-cubit <note>approximately every 9 inches</note>. Writers say that these spears were so perfectly balanced that if they were suspended by a cord like a scale, they would not bend. If a soldier first draws it back and then drives it forward with fury, there is no armor strong enough to resist it. They were widely used among the Britons.

**Giese**. The **giese** <note>original: *gaesum*</note> is a weapon used by the people of Gaul; they are no less useful for throwing than for use in any other form of combat.

**Ruma, pilum, rumex**, and **telum** <note>various types of javelins or darts</note> resemble each other, and they also resemble the **sparus** <note>a small hunting spear</note> used by the Gauls.

**Jaculo**. The **jaculo** <note>original: *iaculum*, a javelin</note> is said to have been invented by Aetolus, the son of Mars. To this, Hermes, Varro, and Pompeius Festus bear witness, affirming that javelins are simple weapons fashioned by rustics of low social standing, yet they are effective for scattering in all directions.

# WARFARE

**Sarissa.** The **sarissa**, according to Pompeius <note>original: Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note>, is a Macedonian spear.

**Gabina.** **Gabina** is the name given by the Illyrians to a certain kind of weapon shaped like a hunting spear <note>original: *venabulum*</note> or a pike.

**Securis** <note>original: *securis*, a battle-axe</note> is also called a *semicuris* or *semiquiris*.

**Tragula.** The **tragula** is a spear with a very sharp point, shaped like a javelin or dart, which can be thrown by hand according to Varro, Pompeius, and Caesar in the fifth book of his *Commentaries* <note>Caesar’s *Gallic War*</note>.

**Clava.** The **clava** <note>club</note> is a kind of weapon that was used by Hercules. It was called this because it was a large, strong stick studded with sharp nails; in those primitive <note>original: "rude"</note> times, it would have been considered a very magnificent weapon.

**Cathegia.** <note>Possibly a boomerang or returning spear</note> Some believe this *clava* to have been the **cathegia**, which Horace calls a **caia** <note>a stick or cudgel</note>. The *cathegia* was a kind of dart used among the Gauls that returns to the thrower's hand. According to Virgil, it was widely used among the Germans; their knights made great use of it against infantry.

**Dolabra**, <note>a pick-axe or mattock</note> that is, "double-cutting."

It is named after "two lips" <note>original: *labbri*</note> according to what Livy states in the eleventh book¹ of the Punic War. There, he relates that Hannibal sent five hundred Africans armed with these in order to level the foundations of a town’s walls.

**Bipenna.** This weapon is named so because it has a sharp edge on both sides <note>a double-headed axe</note>. This term is usually applied to it by Quintilian in the first book of the *Institutes* <note>original: *Institutio Oratoria*</note>.

The **cross** <note>likely a throwing weapon or caltrop-like device</note> was invented among the Germans. This weapon is said to be in the front rank of deadly weapons because, whether it is thrown with a cord or without one into the enemy's ranks, it never falls in vain. This is because it flies edgewise through the air; if it does not strike the enemy with one of its points, it catches him with two. If it does not find an enemy, it is driven into the ground, where it inflicts no less damage upon the enemy than if it... <note>The text ends mid-sentence.</note>

***Telico.*** These were used by early humans. They were made from cane; a piece of cane with two joints <note>original: "knots"</note> was taken, and one joint was split down the middle to serve as the fletching <note>original: "feather"</note> of the arrow. If any of the ship’s defenders try to approach, the pirates wound them and drive them back. They then return to the ship's edge where they were before and dig the hooks deep into the hull so the vessel cannot escape.

***Sirile*** is a very long spear; it was found among the Numidians <note>an ancient North African people</note>. They often used it to knock down their enemies. These warriors rode on horseback without saddles or stirrups, wearing only a cotton-padded jacket <note>original: "doublet"</note>. The hooks of the long *sirile* were fastened over this garment, and unsuspecting enemies were easily pulled down.

***Cariffe*** is a broad-headed spear with which one can attack from a distance. **Miricide** <note>A specialized type of polearm or extending spear</note> is a spear three braccia <note>a Florentine unit of length, approximately 23 inches or 58 cm</note> in length, and five and a half braccia when extended. **Syrian bow**, made from the horns of buffalo.

The **bow dart**, by which the arrow remains attached to the cord, is an awl a quarter of a braccio in length, made entirely of finely tempered iron. The feathers of the tail section detach from the arrow as it flies on its way. There are some types that make a puncture resembling that of a needle filled with poison.

<page-num>823</page-num>
<header>WARFARE</header>
<sig>B 46 v.</sig>

These <term>carabineers</term> <note>mounted soldiers armed with carbines, a shorter type of firearm</note> should be provided with pouches full of rolls of plain paper filled with powder <note>an early form of a paper cartridge</note>, so that by frequently inserting them, they can overwhelm the large numbers of the enemy. These carabineers should stand in squadrons just as cross-bowmen do, so that when one group fires, the other loads. However, first ensure that you have accustomed the horses to such noises, or else stop up their ears.

**Order of mounted cross-bowmen on the open field:**
*m n* are cross-bowmen who, as they turn left, draw back to load; *r t* are those who go forward with loaded cross-bows, and these four files constitute one maneuver. *a b* are four files of cross-bowmen who turn with unloaded bows in order to reload them; *c d* are those who charge the enemy with their bows loaded. This arrangement of eight lines is employed in the open field.

Arrange it so that those who have unloaded their weapons return through the center. In this way, if they are occasionally routed by the enemy, the cross-bowmen who are still loaded—holding their positions on the flanks—may strike greater fear into those same enemies.

**Order of mounted carabineers:**

Ensure that they are well supplied with guns and thin, single-folded paper cartridges filled with powder and the ball within, so that they only have to insert them and set them alight. Being thus prepared, they will have no need to turn away to load as the cross-bowmen must do.

If anyone designed to capture a tower situated by the sea, he would cause one of his followers to take service with the commander. Then, when the guard was withdrawn, this follower would affix a rope-ladder (provided by the enemy) to the battlements and fill the walls with soldiers. In order to prevent this, you should divide the tower into eight sets of spiral staircases and divide the <term>ramparts</term> <note>defensive walls</note> and the soldiers’ living quarters below into eight separate sections. Then, if one of the mercenaries intends to be a traitor, the others cannot communicate with him; furthermore, the section of the rampart will be so small that no more than four men could occupy it at once. The commander, whose quarters are above everyone else's, can drive them out by attacking them through the <term>machicolations</term> <note>floor openings in the battlements through which stones or projectiles can be dropped</note>, or trap them by means of the <term>portcullis</term> <note>a heavy, vertically-closing gate</note> and then use smoke at the entrance to force them out.

### NAMES OF ENGINEERS

Callias of Rhodes.¹ Epimachus the Athenian.² Diogenes, philosopher, of Rhodes.³ Calcedonius of Thrace. Febar of Tyre.⁴ Callimachus, architect and master of fire.⁵

**Preparation of a fireball:**
Take tow <note>original: "tow"; coarse, broken fibers of flax or hemp used for stuffing or fuel</note> smeared with pitch, turpentine, and linseed oil, and twist it around to form a ball. Over this, place hemp soaked in double-distilled turpentine. Once you have formed the ball, make four or six holes in it, each as thick as your arm. Fill these holes with fine hemp soaked in double-distilled turpentine and gunpowder for a <term>bombard</term> <note>an early type of large-caliber cannon used to throw heavy stone balls</note>; then place the ball into the <term>bombard</term>.

# HOW TO SCALE A FORTRESS BY NIGHT

[*With drawings*]

If you do not have any information from an accomplice inside the fortress as to who will pull up the rope ladders, you must ascend first by placing these iron pegs into the crevices of the wall, spaced one <term>braccio</term> <note>original: "braccio"; an Italian unit of measurement meaning "arm," roughly 23 to 27 inches</note> apart, in the manner shown above.

When you reach the top, fix the rope ladder where you see the iron marked *m*. Then, if it seems necessary to pull up additional ladders, do so; if not, have the attackers ascend quickly. The hook, which is attached to a pair of ropes, has a ring above it to which a rope is fixed; this is drawn up by a <term>jack</term> <note>original: "jack"; a mechanical device used for lifting or pulling with significant force</note> to the iron peg above, and to this you attach the hook of the aforementioned ropes a second time.

These ladders are designed to carry two men at once. They are also useful for a tower where you fear the enemy might detach a standard rope ladder; the pegs should be driven so far into the wall that three-eighths of a <term>braccio</term> is buried and one-eighth remains free. These pyramidal irons should be half a <term>braccio</term> in length and spaced half a <term>braccio</term> apart.

# SACKS FOR USE IN CROSSING OVER WATER

One must also consider how to cross rivers at one’s convenience. First, place a man upon two bags tied together. Then, if you find the riverbed is suitable but the river is dangerous because of its rapid current, use the method represented below.

If the river is dangerous due to its current, you should position two lines of horses across the river at a distance of six <term>braccia</term> from one another. The horses in these lines should be so close that they almost touch each other, and the line or company of horses should have their heads turned toward the current of the water. This is done solely to check and break the fury and momentum of the water. Between the first company and the second, the soldiers should pass—both those with and those

Construct shelters by interlocking shields to withstand the force of heavy volleys of arrows. 

This is the method used by the Germans: when in close formation, they link and interweave their long lances against the enemy, crouching down and bracing one end of the lance against the ground while holding the other part in their hands.

[*With drawings*]

If the water is so high that infantry and cavalry cannot pass, the river's depth should be reduced by diverting it into many smaller streams. Cyrus, King of the Persians, did this during the capture of Babylon on the river <note>original: "Ganges"; Leonardo likely meant the Euphrates, as Babylon is located on the Euphrates and not the Ganges</note>, which at its widest point is ten thousand <term>braccia</term> <note>original: "braccia"; an Italian unit of measurement roughly 23 to 27 inches</note> wide. Alexander did the same on that river, as did Caesar on the river Sicoris.

If a river is so deep that it cannot be crossed by fording, the commander should create a sufficient number of channels to carry away the water, later returning it to the riverbed further downstream. In this way, the river level will be lowered and can be crossed with ease. Alexander employed this method in India against King Porus at the crossing of the Hydaspes River, and Caesar did the same in Gaul (and also in Spain) on the river Loire. Having arranged his cavalry into two groups, Caesar had the soldiers pass through the middle of them. Hannibal used a similar tactic on the River Po using elephants.

They carry these instead of <term>saddle-bows</term> <note>original: "saddle-bows"; the arched, structural pieces at the front and back of a saddle</note> above and at the sides, ensuring they are well-covered.

<insert>[How infantry cross rivers]</insert>
If infantry must cross a river that is dangerous due to a powerful current, here is a reliable method. The soldiers should link arms with one another to form a line, similar to a wooden stockade. These files should advance in the direction of the water’s flow rather than directly across the current. This is a secure method because the man positioned furthest upstream bears the initial force of the water. If he were alone, the current would knock him down, but the others positioned below him provide support and use him as a shield. In this way, they can all cross safely, one after another.

The same principle applies to everyone in the line. If the river flows from right to left, each man in the file—as he moves from the first bank to the second—breaks the flow of the stream with his right shoulder. On his left, he is supported by the right shoulder of his companion as the water flows past.
<sig>B 62 r.</sig>

### Small Boat <note>original: "NAVICULA"</note>

<insert>[With drawings]</insert>
The small boats used by the Assyrians were made from thin willow branches woven over willow rods and shaped into a small craft. These were then plastered with a mixture of fine dust soaked in oil or turpentine, creating a mud-like paste. This coating was waterproof and did not split apart from impacts because it always remained flexible.

According to the account of the poet Lucan, Caesar covered this type of small boat with oxhide when he crossed the Sicoris, a river in Spain.¹

### How to release a torrent of water against an army's rear or against the bridges and walls of a town.

If you wish to flood a battlefield or break through walls without using cannons, and you have access to a river, proceed as shown in the drawing above. Set piles as high as the riverbank and place them half a <term>braccio</term> <note>braccio: an Italian unit of length, approximately 23 inches or 58 cm</note> apart, or further if you have wider planks. Then, place these planks between each of the piles to fill the gaps. When these are filled, raise the connecting rod *M*; the upper part of the plank *a* will move forward and the lower part *b* will move back. In this way, the planks will turn edgewise, and the water will be free to escape. 

Ensure all the sluice gates open at the shot of a <term>carbine</term> <note>carbine: a short-barreled firearm, used here as a signal</note> or another signal so they may all open at the same time. This ensures the flow of water against the opposing object is driven by a greater impact and a more impetuous force. If the river has a steep descent, build one of these every half mile, and let each of the panels be opened by a rope to ensure they work together and to keep the person who unlocks them in safety.

### How to storm a bastion that has been built to block a passage

Construct portable sections of bastions for a sudden, aggressive assault. These should be filled with hay and have pointed fronts so that the impact of artillery fire is deflected without causing damage. When joined together, these sections should form a fortification large enough to face all the enemy’s cannons and the fire from the bridges. In this way, the attackers will be able to engage the enemy with a significant advantage.

### *How to attack a fortress using underground tunnels (with drawings)*

A rod filled with rockets designed to confront the enemy at the exit of a subterranean gallery <note>original: "subterranean gallery" — an underground tunnel or passage used in siege warfare</note> that opens from below upwards; this will clear the ground of any defenders stationed at the entrance.

A rod with rockets to be placed in a tunnel that leads into a fortress cellar, even if that cellar is well-guarded.

*m a b.* The path of a winding tunnel designed to deceive a besieged enemy.

It is clear that those under siege will employ every possible method to discover the secret stratagems of the attacker. Therefore, if you seek to accomplish your goals through underground passages, reflect carefully on how alert your enemy will be. If you dig a tunnel on one side, they will dig a trench to intercept it, guarding it day and night because they will naturally assume your secret way will exit into that trench.

Therefore, you should use your digging operations to show that you intend to emerge in one particular spot; then, by tunneling around the perimeter of the fortress, you can emerge on the opposite side. This is illustrated above in the diagram *m b a*: point *b* is where you are almost at the exit in cellar *a*. You must have a large reserve of men ready so that when the wall between you and the cellar is broken...

<term>Stlocladle</term> <note>original: *Stlocladle* — likely a phonetic transcription or specific name for an incendiary ball</note>. Place powder made of dried fungi in the center.

These balls filled with rockets are to be thrown inside the enemy's bastions <note>bastions: projecting parts of a fortification that allow defensive fire in several directions</note>.

The <term>stlocladle</term> is a ball a foot wide made of hemp and fish-glue. It is covered with the tails of rockets, and these tails do not exceed the length of a finger. Each tail is made of fine, veined copper or of stiffened pasteboard. All of these tails have their ends pierced by a tiny hole, and they are all attached to a copper ball. This ball is full of many paths arranged like a labyrinth and filled with gunpowder; these paths are full of intersecting holes that connect with the holes in the rockets.

Then, one sets fire to it using a bellows, and the fire hurls itself through eight holes so that no one can control it or . . . [<unclear>ariegi?</unclear>]. When the fire has penetrated to the center, the rockets suddenly begin, one after another, to spit out their deadly missiles with a dreadful noise. If you wish to use it on a galley <note>galley: a type of ship propelled primarily by rowing</note>, make the rockets out of pasteboard and fill the space between them with pitch mixed with powdered sulfur. This will serve three purposes: first, it will cause harm with the rockets; second, it will start a fire that cannot be put out and will burn the wooden ship; and third, no one will be able to get near it because of the terrible stench.

<term>Buffonico</term> <note>original: *buffonico* — a primitive fire-lance or pole-mounted firearm</note>. The <term>buffonico</term> is an instrument set at the end of a lance. It is two *braccia* <note>about 4 feet or 1.2 meters; a *braccio* was a Renaissance unit of length based on the arm</note> long and an eighth of a *braccio* <note>about 3 inches or 7.5 centimeters</note> thick. It is tipped with iron and has a thin tube with a sight placed on the end through which the fire passes.

First of all, fill the cannon with the powder—well-crammed, pressed, and beaten—through the mouth *a b*. Then, make a small hole an eighth of a *braccio* long and insert a small tube with a very fine hole. The powder should be fine and mixed with lead dust made with a file or by fire; this will cause great terror and loss to the horses and the enemy. <sig>B 80 v.</sig>

## THE SIEGE ENGINE THAT MAKES THE LOUDER NOISE HAS THE LESSER FORCE

This is proved by the ninth principle, "Concerning Impact" <note>original: "Percussion"</note>, which says: 
> Among moving objects—relative to the power of the mover and the resistance of the air <note>original: "medium"</note>—that which strikes with a larger surface area will make a louder noise and a less violent impact; on the other hand, that which strikes with a smaller surface area will make less noise and penetrate farther into the target.

An example has been given of a sword striking first with the flat side and then with the edge: in the first case, the stroke makes a great noise but penetrates very little, and in the second, it penetrates deeply but makes very little noise. Therefore, as the flame is proportional to the projectiles driven by the <term>ordnance</term> <note>artillery or cannons</note>, the flame that spreads the least after emerging from the cannon will be the one that drives the ball out with the most force <note>original: "impetus"</note>; conversely, the flame that spreads out rapidly will have the opposite effect.

## CONCERNING CANNONS THAT FIRE MANY BALLS AT ONCE

<margin>E 27 v.</margin>
A piece of artillery which throws a single ball a distance proportionate to its power will, in the same amount of time, throw six of the same balls only a sixth of that distance.

## CONCERNING ARTILLERY AND THE WEIGHT OF PROJECTILES PROPORTIONATE TO THEIR POWER

Among the powder chambers <note>original: "receptacles for powder"</note> of artillery pieces, one finds three different shapes; of which one is wide at the bottom and...

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s notes on the mechanics of warfare, shifting from the construction of siege engines and armored vehicles to the physics of gunpowder ignition, ancient military organization, and ballistics calculations.</meta>

<page-num>834</page-num>
<header>WARFARE</header>

One type of cannon is narrow at the mouth; another is narrow at the bottom and wide at the mouth; a third is of uniform width throughout.

There are five <note>original: "four [?five]"</note> points where one can ignite the powder in pieces of artillery. The first is at the very top of the rear chamber; the second is in the middle of the base of this chamber; the third is at a distance from the base equal to half the diameter of the chamber's bottom; the fourth receives the fire in the same position as the third, but in the center of the powder's thickness; in the fifth, the chamber is spherical and the fire is set in the very center of the chamber. 

These instruments, and others designed to ignite the powder almost instantly, must be made of high-quality metal and be well-compressed. Such compression rarely occurs when the casting is very thick; because the metal is thicker, it stays liquid longer, and the parts furthest from the center of that thickness are the ones that solidify and compress first.
<margin>E 28 r.</margin>

## [*Of the trajectory of a bombard*]

<note>A "bombard" was an early, large-caliber cannon used for throwing heavy stone balls.</note>

If a bombard hits a target in a straight line at ten <term>braccia</term> <note>original: *braccia* — an Italian unit of measurement, literally "arms," approximately 23 inches or 58 cm</note>, how far will it fire at its maximum range?

And conversely, if it fires three miles at its maximum range, how far will it carry in a straight, "point-blank" line?

If a bombard fires at different distances with different curved paths of movement, I ask: at what point in its flight will the curve reach its highest altitude?
<margin>I 128 [80] v.</margin>

## [*Bombards*]

If a bombard, using its maximum power, throws a ball weighing one hundred pounds a distance of three miles, how far will it throw a ball of two hundred or three hundred pounds, or any other weight more or less than a hundred?

If a bombard using four pounds of powder throws a four-pound ball two miles at maximum power, by how much must I increase the powder to make it carry four miles?

### [Gunpowder for a bomb-ketch]
<note>A bomb-ketch was a specialized wooden sailing vessel designed to carry heavy mortars for coastal bombardment.</note>

One pound of charcoal
eleven ounces of sulphur
five pounds of saltpetre.

Mix these well and moisten the mixture with good brandy, then dry it in the sun or by a fire. Next, grind the mixture until no speck of sulphur or saltpetre is visible; it should be entirely black, uniform, and fine. Moisten it again with the brandy and store it in that state. To use it, dry it in the sun until it forms grains, and crush only as much as is needed to prime the touch-hole; this will be sufficient.

### [For digging trenches]
### [With plan]
<note>Leonardo is describing an efficient labor cycle for excavating earth, likely using a diagram of a circular or elliptical path for workers.</note>

At the start of the trench excavations, you must station men according to the marks shown in the plan. First, begin the digging as far as possible from the spot where the earth is being piled. For example, the earth is dug at point *a g*, carried along the path *r c*, and unloaded at the line *c f*. The worker then turns back along the path *f d* and reloads at the line *r d*, ensuring the operation is in constant motion.

There is no other method of movement as useful for this task as one that removes the soil from the area marked by the path *r c*.

### [Fortifications]

The wall should be fifteen feet thick at the base and thirteen feet thick at the top.

The trench is to be forty-two <term>arm-lengths</term> <note>original: "braccia" — an Italian unit of measurement roughly 23 inches (58 cm) long</note> wide at the bottom and fifty at its mouth; it should be twenty <term>arm-lengths</term> deep, containing water four <term>arm-lengths</term> deep.

It is fifteen steps and a span from the battlements down to the water—measured from the base of the battlements. These steps are defined by the distance from one tip of the hand to the other when the palms are stretched as far as possible against a straight measure. There are eight and one-sixth <term>arm-lengths</term> from the base of the battlements to the top of the turret.

### [On digging a trench]

Determine the width and depth of the trench. Also, calculate the diameter of the wheel, the thickness of the beam and the rope, the position of the men who turn the wheel, and the total number of men required to operate it. Note how many men are in position, what weight they can lift at one time, and the time required to fill the containers and move the earth.

If the <term>bombard</term> <note>A large-caliber medieval cannon used for throwing heavy stone balls.</note> has a recoil of a quarter of a <term>braccio</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement (plural: braccia) roughly equal to 23 inches.</note>, how much will it lose from its true and intended range?

### [*Breeches of bombards*]

That part of the <term>bronze</term> is most compressed within its <term>mould</term> which is most liquid.

And that is most liquid which is hottest, and that is hottest which comes first out of the <term>furnace</term>. One ought, therefore, to always cast that part of the <term>cannon</term> which has to receive the powder <note>The breech.</note> first, before the part that contains the <term>muzzle</term>.

<margin>M 54 v.</margin>
A long <term>breech</term> is an embarrassment; it fills up space uselessly and unserviceably, and causes a loss of speed.

### [*Mines*]

If you wish to find out where a <term>mine</term> <note>A tunnel dug under a fortification to collapse it or plant explosives.</note> is being dug, set a <term>drum</term> over all the places where you suspect the <term>mine</term> is being made. On this <term>drum</term>, place a pair of <term>dice</term>. When you are near the place where the <term>mining</term> is occurring, the <term>dice</term> will jump up slightly on the <term>drum</term> because of the vibrations caused underground by digging out the earth.

The shields of infantrymen should be made of cotton spun into thread and formed into cords; these should be woven tightly in a circle in the style of a buckler <note>A small, round shield held by a handle or worn on the forearm.</note>.

And if you wish, the threads should be thoroughly moistened before you make cords out of them, and then smeared with the powdered slag of iron <note>original: "dross of iron"</note>.

Then plait it into cords a second time—first with two strands, then with four, then with eight—and soak them every time in water with borax, linseed, or the seeds of quinces <note>These substances acted as traditional binders or hardening agents for fabric armor.</note>. If you make a doublet <note>A close-fitting padded jacket, here designed to serve as light body armor.</note>, let it be supple, light, and impenetrable.

If a town is besieged and the mines made by the enemy have not yet penetrated within the walls, you should place men with the greatest possible care at intervals of ten <term>braccia</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement (singular: braccio) roughly equal to 23 inches; ten braccia is about 19 feet.</note> in the area where your suspicions are focused. Have them place their ears to the ground, and as soon as the vibration of the sound reaches them, have them dig a very deep cross-trench which will be ready to intercept the mine when it reaches it. Then, have ready an iron or copper vessel with holes in the bottom; place the nozzle of a blacksmith’s bellows into the hole, cover the mouth with a perforated iron plate, and fill it with fine feathers. Turn the mouth toward the mine once it is discovered and blow with the bellows, after first mixing the feathers with sulfur and lighting them; the smoke that issues forth will drive away the enemy.

If, however, you do not wish to dig the aforementioned trench inside the circuit of the walls—so as not to interfere with the patrols of the soldiers defending the walls—you should use a drill as was shown previously. With this, at intervals of two <term>braccia</term>, you can drill a hole six <term>braccia</term> deep, making these in a circular line within the walls.

### OF THE SPEED OF BOMBARDS WITH EQUAL TIME, POWDER, AND WEIGHT OF BALL

<margin>Forster II 71 r.</margin>
Among many <term>bombards</term> that are equal in terms of powder and projectile weight, the one in which a greater quantity of fire is ignited in the same amount of time will hurl its ball more swiftly and to a greater distance.

Of balls of equal weight, the one that is swifter will act as if it were heavier and will produce a greater <term>percussion</term> <note>impact</note>.

If the <term>bombard</term> uses a stone flattened like a wheel of cheese, and the bore <note>original: "hollow"</note> of the <term>bombard</term> has a matching shape, and the center—the center of the breech—is not aligned with the center of the stone so that it spins through the air, it will undoubtedly travel with extreme speed.

For if you take a ball of six ounces and a wheel of the same weight with smooth edges, you will see how much greater a distance the wheel will be sent by its launcher than the ball; and this is also due in part to the rotation of its additional mass. This happens because while the projectiles are equal in weight, the round ball strikes more air and finds more resistance, whereas the flattened projectile enters...

### [*War Machines: with drawing*]

## XXVII
## Naval Warfare

> *“Design it so that the wine-skin which serves as a boat, along with the equipment and the man within it, shall be positioned midway between the surface and the bottom of the sea.”*

[Notes relating to a submarine attack]
Do not share your knowledge, and you will be the only one to excel. 
Choose an uneducated youth and have the suit stitched at home. 
Halt the <term>galleys</term> <note>original: "galleys"; large, low-built ships propelled by oars and sails, common in the Mediterranean.</note> of the captains, then sink the others and fire upon the fort with the cannon.

[With drawings of parts of the apparatus]
Everything remains underwater—that is, all the fastenings. 
Here the man stands. <term>Doublet</term> <note>A man's snug-fitting buttoned jacket, common in the Renaissance.</note>. <term>Hose</term> <note>Leg coverings similar to tight-fitting breeches or stockings.</note>. Level frame.

When the watch has completed its patrol, bring a small <term>skiff</term> <note>A small, light boat used for rowing or sailing.</note> under the <term>poop</term> <note>The stern or rear-most deck of a ship.</note> and suddenly set the entire vessel on fire.

[With drawing of boat and chain]
To secure a galley to the seafloor at point *m*, on the side opposite the anchor.

[With drawing of figure in diving dress (half length)]
Provide a breastplate of armor along with a hood, doublet, and hose, and a small <term>wine-skin</term> <note>A bag made from animal hide, traditionally for wine but here repurposed for technical use.</note> for passing water. When you inflate it, you will return to the surface of the water.

Provide a mask with protruding glass eyes, but ensure its weight is such that you can lift it as you swim. 

Carry a sharp knife so that you do not get caught in a net.

# Naval Warfare

Carry two or three small, deflated wine-skins with you that can be inflated like balls if necessary. 

Take whatever provisions you need, wrap them carefully, and hide them on the riverbank. But first, establish a clear agreement regarding the ransom: ensure that half of it will be yours without any deductions. The storage room of the prisons is located near Manetti, and the payment for the said ransom may be made directly into Manetti's hands.

Carry a horn to signal whether or not the mission has been successful.

You need to take an <term>impression</term>¹ <note>original: "improntare"; to make a mold or stamp.</note> of one of the three iron screws from the workshop of Santa Liberata, including the plaster figure and the wax cast.

<insert>[*With a drawing of a man in a diving suit. His right arm is extended, holding a staff that touches a square of cork. Two bags are suspended from his shoulders.*]</insert>

It can be detached from the suit if it becomes necessary to break it.

The cork is to be fixed midway between the surface and the bottom.

Bags of sand.

Carry forty <term>braccia</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement; one "braccio" is roughly 23 to 27 inches (the length of an arm).</note> of rope fastened to a bag of sand.² <term>C.A. 333 v. a</term> <note>original: "Codice Atlantico"; this refers to the specific page in Leonardo's largest collection of manuscripts.</note>

I will destroy the harbor.

Unless you surrender within four hours, you will go to the bottom.

<insert>[*Notes with drawings of three heads showing diving apparatus fitted over the nostrils.*]</insert>

Keep the mentioned bag for your mouth ready for use when you are in the sea—for was this not your secret?

---

¹ The original manuscript uses the word *protare*, which the scholar Piumati transcribed as *portare* (to carry). I have instead followed Müller-Walde’s reading of *prontare* for *improntare* (to make an impression or mold).

² Alvise Manetti was sent by the Venetian Senate on a diplomatic mission to the Turks from October 1499 to March 1500. By February 1500, reports from Manetti suggested the mission would likely fail. It was likely at this time that Leonardo, who was in Venice, began designing methods to rescue the prisoners via Manetti's influence, while also planning to destroy the enemy's fleet by piercing their hulls below the water-line.
