## GREEK FIRE

Take willow charcoal, saltpeter, <term>aqua vitæ</term> <note>Latin: "water of life"; a term for concentrated alcohol or distilled spirits.</note>, sulphur, pitch, along with incense, camphor, and Ethiopian wool, and boil them all together. This fire is so highly combustible <note>original: "eager to burn"</note> that it will spread along wood even when it is under water. You should add liquid varnish, petroleum <note>original: "olio petrolio"</note>, turpentine, and strong vinegar to the mixture. Mix everything together and dry it in the sun, or in an oven after the bread has been taken out. Then, stick it around hemp or other fibers <note>original: "tow"</note>, molding it into a round shape and driving very sharp nails into every side of it. Leave, however, an opening in this ball to serve as a fuse, and then cover it with resin and sulphur.

Furthermore, when this fire is fixed to the top of a long lance—which has one <term>braccio</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement; one "braccio" is roughly 23 inches, or the length of an arm.</note> of its point covered with iron so that it may not be burnt by the flames—it is useful for fending off and warding off hostile ships so as not to be overwhelmed by their attack.

Also, throw glass vessels filled with pitch onto the enemy ships while their crews are engaged in battle. By then throwing similar lighted balls after these, you will have it in your power to set every ship on fire.
<margin>Manuscript Trivulzianus, 43 a</margin>

Ships made of beams.
Ships made of <term>osier</term> <note>Flexible willow twigs commonly used in basketry and weaving.</note> twigs, woven and bound with leather, for the use of privateers.

In order to fight against walls that face the sea or towers, withdraw the galleys. Before they come to the encounter, raise the oars within so that the edges touch together, and move the ship with the—

### To throw poison in the form of powder upon galleys.
Chalk, fine <term>sulfide of arsenic</term> <note>A highly toxic mineral compound used here as a chemical weapon.</note>, and powdered <term>verdigris</term> <note>A green pigment or crust that forms on copper or brass; it was known to be poisonous if inhaled or ingested.</note> may be thrown among the enemy ships using small <term>mangonels</term> <note>Medieval engines or catapults used for throwing projectiles.</note>. Anyone who inhales this powder as they breathe will be asphyxiated.

But take care to have the wind at your back so that it does not blow the powder back onto you, or keep your nose and mouth covered with a fine cloth dipped in water so that the powder cannot enter. It would also be effective to throw baskets covered with paper and filled with this powder from the crow’s nest or the deck of the ship. <note>original: "B 69 v"; refers to Manuscript B, page 69 verso.</note>

[*With drawings*]
A ship equipped with <term>scorpions</term> <note>In this context, "scorpions" are specialized scythe-like machines designed to sabotage enemy rigging.</note> suitable for cutting the ropes of large ships. From one tip of the sickles to the other should be four <term>braccia</term> [roughly 7.5 feet]. The sickle should be shaped like a crescent, one foot at its widest point and as thick as a finger. <note>original: "B 76 r"; refers to Manuscript B, page 76 recto.</note>

[*With drawings*]
*Circunfulgore* <note>original: "Circunfulgore"; likely from the Latin "circum" (around) and "fulgur" (lightning), implying an "all-around flash."</note>. The *circunfulgore* is a naval machine invented by the inhabitants of Majorca. It consists of a circle of <term>bombards</term> <note>Early large-caliber cannons designed to throw heavy stone balls.</note>. You may use as many as you like, provided the number is even. In order for the strike to be powerful and yet prevent the vessel from recoiling <note>original: "spring back"</note>, it is necessary that one bombard serves as a support and counter-weight to another. To achieve this, it is necessary to fire two bombards placed opposite to each other at the exact same instant, so that if one tries to push the ship to one side, the other opposes it. <note>original: "B 82 v"; refers to Manuscript B, page 82 verso.</note>

### HOW TO SMASH THE BOWS OF A SHIP

[*With drawing*]
It is necessary first that the ships be engaged—that is, fastened together—in such a way that you can unlock yourself whenever you wish. This ensures that when the enemy ship goes to the bottom, it does not drag yours down with it. This should be done as follows: draw a weight up to a height and then release it; as it falls, it will strike a blow similar to a <term>pile-driver</term> <note>A heavy machine used to drive poles into the ground by dropping a weight onto them.</note>. As it falls, it will pull back the top of a beam that is balanced upright; as the top of this beam moves back, the bottom end moves forward and smashes into the bow of the enemy ship. 

But see to it that the beam has a sharp, cutting edge so that the water does not offer resistance as it rushes to deliver the stroke. Above all, ensure that the chains holding the ships together can be severed from your side at your discretion, so that the enemy’s ship does not drag you down as it sinks.

[*Drawing*]
If, in a battle between ships and <term>galleys</term> <note>original: "galleys"; low-built ships propelled by oars, often disadvantaged by the height of taller sailing ships.</note>, the ships are winning because of the height of their mast-heads, you should draw the <term>lateen yard</term> <note>A long, diagonal spar used to hold a triangular sail.</note> almost up to the top of the mast. Attach a small cage to the end of this yard—specifically the end that projects toward the enemy. This cage should be wrapped at the bottom and all around with a large mattress stuffed with cotton to prevent it from being damaged by <term>bombs</term> <note>Early incendiary or explosive projectiles.</note>.

Then, pull down the other end of the <term>lateen yard</term> using the <term>capstan</term> <note>A rotating machine used to wind in heavy ropes or cables.</note>. This will cause the cage at the opposite end to rise to such a height that it will be far above the mast-head of the enemy ship, allowing you to easily drive out the men who are inside it. 

However, it is necessary that the men in the galley should go to the oppo—

If you wish to build a fleet for combat, you should use these ships specifically to ram the enemy’s vessels. You should build ships one hundred feet long and eight feet wide. Arrange them so that the rowers of the left oars sit on the right side of the ship, and the rowers of the right oars sit on the left side, as shown at M (*in the figure*). This is done so that the leverage of the oars may be longer. This ship should be one and a half feet thick—that is, constructed of beams fastened inside and outside by planks set crosswise.

The vessel must have a spike fastened to it one foot below the waterline. This spike should be shod with iron and have the weight and size of an anvil. By the power of the oars, this vessel will be able to pull back after it has struck the first blow, and then hurl itself forward again with fury to deal a second and then a third blow, and as many more as are needed to destroy the enemy ship.

[*Drawing of a narrow ramming galley*]

<margin>National Library, Manuscript 2037, page 4 verso</margin>
This is the shape of the <term>bomb-ketch</term> <note>original: "vessel [?bomb-ketch]"; a sturdy ship designed to carry mortars for bombardment.</note> which carries the <term>mortars</term> <note>Short-barreled cannons that fire projectiles at high angles.</note> described above. I would specifically remind you to aim the cannonballs attached to scythes toward the mast-head, where many ropes meet and where the scythes will be most effective.

The scythes should be four <term>braccia</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement. One Florentine *braccio* was approximately 23 inches or 58 centimeters; four braccia is about 7.5 feet.</note> long and four braccia from one point to the other. They should be shot into the rigging of the large ships to make the sails fall down. Ensure that the ketch carrying them has an ample supply. It should be built of stout beams so that the enemy's cannons cannot break them into pieces, and the cannonballs should weigh two hundred pounds.

These are the means of defense in case the enemy should throw soft soap <note>Used to make the decks of a ship dangerously slippery for the crew.</note>, or <term>caltrops</term> <note>Four-pronged iron spikes designed so that one point always faces upward to pierce the feet of sailors.</note>, or small boards studded with nails, or similar hazards upon the ships.

You should follow this advice: when you go into combat, wear iron soles underneath your shoes. These should be divided in the middle, as shown in the drawing above, to allow the feet to bend. ## A SCORPION

<insert>[Figures]</insert>

This machine is designed so that its scythe springs upward when it is triggered. Ships carrying these scythes should be designed without masts or sails and powered by a great many oars to ensure they are fast. They lack sails because the masts, sails, and rigging would interfere with the movement of the large scythe. This machine is called a "scorpion" because its shape resembles one and because of the damage it deals with its "tail." <term>Mantelets</term> <note>Protective screens or shutters used to shield sailors from enemy fire.</note> are fixed over the rowers so that combatants positioned at the mast-heads of enemy ships cannot harm them. These shields should be covered with wet hides to protect against fire thrown by the enemy.

A way of protecting against this machine is for ships to be equipped with rope chains reaching a height of six <term>braccia</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches; six braccia is about 11.5 feet.</note>.

<margin>National Library, Manuscript 2037, page 8 recto</margin>

<insert>[Figure]</insert> This ship is designed to serve as a defense against cannon fire, while attacking other vessels with its own cannons. It is covered with sheet metal <note>original: *coperto di tole*</note> as a protection against fire and is covered in sharp nail points so the enemy cannot board it without being injured.

<insert>[Drawing]</insert>

Some sailors in the Tyrrhenian Sea <note>The part of the Mediterranean Sea off the western coast of Italy.</note> use this method: they fasten an anchor to one end of the <term>lateen yard</term> <note>A long spar used to support a triangular sail.</note> and a rope to the other end. This rope is attached to a second anchor at its bottom. In battle, they hook the first anchor onto the oars of the enemy’s ship and use the force of the <term>capstan</term> <note>A rotating machine used on ships to pull in heavy ropes or cables.</note> to pull the enemy vessel alongside.

### SUBMARINE WARFARE

How, by using a specific appliance, many people are able to remain underwater for some time. I do not describe my method for remaining underwater for as long as I can go without food; I do not publish or divulge this because of the evil nature of men. They would use it to commit assassinations at the bottom of the sea by breaking the hulls of ships in their lowest parts and sinking them along with the crews inside. Although I will provide details of other devices, they are only those that are not dangerous, because the air supply remains above the surface of the water.

## XXVIII

# Comparison of the Arts

> "If you know how to describe and write down the appearance of shapes, the painter can create them so that they appear alive, using light and shadow to produce the very expression of the faces. In this, you cannot achieve with a pen what he achieves with a brush."

How painting surpasses all human works because of the subtle possibilities it contains:

The eye, which is called the window of the soul, is the primary means by which the intellect <note>original: "understanding"</note> can most fully and richly appreciate the infinite works of nature. The ear is second, gaining its importance because it hears about the things the eye has already seen. If you historians, poets, or mathematicians had never seen things with your eyes, you would be poorly equipped to describe them in your writings. 

And if you, O poet, represent a story by describing it with your pen, the painter with his brush will render it in a way that is more easily satisfying and less tedious to understand. If you call painting "mute poetry," <note>original: "dumb poetry," a reference to the Latin phrase *muta poesis* attributed to Simonides of Ceos.</note> then the painter may say the poet’s art is "blind painting." Consider, then, which is the more serious affliction: to be blind or to be mute! 

Although the poet has as wide a choice of subjects as the painter, his creations fail to provide as much satisfaction to humanity as paintings do. While poetry attempts to represent forms, actions, and scenes with words, the painter employs the actual images of these forms in order to reproduce them. Consider, then, what is more fundamental to a person: their name or their image? A name changes from country to country, but the human form is unchanged except by death.

And if the poet serves the intellect by way of the ear, the painter does so by the eye, which is the nobler sense.

<vocab>painting, poetry, window of the soul, nature, mute poetry, blind painting, Paragone <note>Italian: "comparison." This refers to the Renaissance debate over the relative merits of the different arts.</note></vocab>

<summary>Leonardo argues for the superiority of painting over poetry, asserting that the eye is the most noble sense and that visual art communicates universal truths more effectively than words.</summary>
<keywords>Paragone, painting vs. poetry, window of the soul, visual perception, Renaissance art theory, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

--- Page 869 ---
<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s defense of painting, moving from the superiority of visual images over written descriptions to a debate on whether painting should be considered a "mechanical art" or a "liberal art."</meta>

<page-num>853</page-num>

<header>COMPARISON OF THE ARTS</header>

I will give just one example of this: if a skilled painter depicts the fury of a battle and a poet also describes one, and both descriptions are shown together to the public, you will quickly see which one attracts the most spectators. You will see where there is the most discussion, which receives the most praise, and which gives the most satisfaction. There is no doubt that the painting—which is by far more useful and beautiful—will provide the greater pleasure. If you write the name of God in any place and set His image opposite to it, you will see which will be held in greater reverence!

Since painting encompasses within itself all the forms of nature, you <note>referring to the poet</note> have omitted nothing except the names, and names are not universal like forms are. If you possess the results of nature's processes, we possess the processes that produce those results.

Consider the case of a poet describing the beauty of a lady to her lover and a painter making a portrait of her; you will see which way nature leads the enamored judge to lean. Surely the proof of the matter ought to rest upon the verdict of experience!

You have categorized painting among the mechanical arts! <term>mechanical arts</term> <note>In the Renaissance, "mechanical arts" were manual trades or crafts, considered inferior to the "liberal arts" (like poetry, logic, and music) which were seen as purely intellectual. Leonardo argues that painting is an intellectual science.</note> Truly, if painters were as well-equipped as you are to praise their own works in writing, I doubt painting would endure the insult of such a lowly name. If you call it "mechanical" because the hands must represent through manual work what the imagination creates, your writers are also setting down with a pen, through manual work, what originates in the mind. If you call it "mechanical" because it is done for money, who falls into this "error"—if indeed it can be called an error—more than you yourselves? If you lecture for the schools, do you not go to whoever pays you the most? Do you do any work without some reward?

And yet I do not say this in order to criticize such opinions, for every laborer looks for their reward. And if the poet should say, "I will create a fiction which shall express great things," the painter can do the same, just as Apelles created *The Calumny*. <note>Apelles was a celebrated painter of ancient Greece. *The Calumny* was a famous allegorical painting described in ancient texts and reconstructed by Renaissance artists like Botticelli.</note> If you say that poetry is more enduring, I would reply that the works of a coppersmith are more enduring still, since time preserves them longer than either your works or ours; nevertheless, they show very little imagination. Furthermore, painting can be made far more enduring if it is done in enamel colors upon copper.

In Art, we may be said to be the grandchildren of God. <note>Leonardo’s philosophy holds that Nature is the daughter of God, and since Art imitates Nature, Art is the grandchild of God.</note> If poetry treats—

<summary>Leonardo argues that painting is superior to poetry because it is universal and evokes more immediate emotion. He also defends painting against the "mechanical art" label, noting that both writing and painting require manual labor and intellectual imagination.</summary>

<header>COMPARISON OF THE ARTS</header>

...of moral philosophy, painting has to do with natural philosophy <note>In the Renaissance, "moral philosophy" referred to the study of human behavior and ethics, while "natural philosophy" was the study of the physical world and its laws (what we now call science).</note>. If the one describes the workings of the mind, the other considers what the mind achieves through the movements of the body. If the one dismays people with hellish fictions, the other does the same by showing those very things in action. 

Suppose the poet sets himself to represent an image of beauty or terror, something vile and foul, or some monstrous thing, in a contest with the painter. Even if the poet, in his own way, changes forms as he pleases, will the painter not still be more satisfying? Have we not seen pictures that bear so close a resemblance to the actual thing that they have deceived both men and beasts?

If you know how to describe and write down the appearance of forms, the painter can make them so they appear enlivened with light and shadow, creating the very expression of the faces. In this, you cannot achieve with the pen what he achieves with the brush.

### How he who despises painting has no love for the philosophy in nature:

<margin>MS. 2038 National Library of France, 20 r.</margin>
If you despise painting, which is the sole imitator of all the visible works of nature, it is certain that you are despising a subtle invention. With philosophical and ingenious speculation, painting takes as its theme all the various kinds of forms: atmospheres and scenes, plants, animals, grasses, and flowers, all of which are surrounded by light and shade. 

And this truly is a science and the true-born daughter of nature, since painting is the offspring of nature. But to speak more correctly, we may call it the grandchild of nature; for all visible things derive their existence from nature, and from these same things painting is born. Therefore, we may justly speak of it as the grandchild of nature and as related to God himself <note>Leonardo’s logic: God created Nature, Nature created physical objects, and the Painter creates the image of those objects—making the artist part of a divine lineage of creation.</note>.

As I practice the art of sculpture no less than that of painting, and perform both to the same degree, it seems to me that I may venture an opinion without suspicion of unfairness as to which of the two is more intellectual, and which possesses greater difficulty and perfection.

In the first place, sculpture is dependent on certain lights, namely...

The sculptor cannot represent the different qualities of the various colors of objects, while painting does not fail to do so in any detail. The lines of perspective used by sculptors do not seem at all true, whereas those of painters can appear to extend a hundred miles beyond the work itself. 

The effects of aerial perspective <note>The technique of creating an illusion of depth by depicting distant objects as paler, greener, or bluer and less distinct.</note> are outside the scope of a sculptor’s work. They can neither represent transparent bodies, nor luminous bodies, nor angles of reflection, nor shining objects like mirrors and similar glittering surfaces. They cannot depict mists, nor gloomy weather, nor an infinite number of other things which I will refrain from mentioning so as not to become tedious.

The single advantage that sculpture has is that it offers greater resistance to time; yet, painting offers a similar resistance if it is done on thick copper covered with white enamel, painted with enamel colors, and then placed in a fire and fused. In terms of permanence, it then surpasses even sculpture.

It may be argued that if a mistake is made in sculpture, it is not easy to fix; however, it is a poor argument to try to prove that because a mistake is irremediable, the work is somehow more noble. I would say, indeed, that it is more difficult to correct the mind of the master who makes such mistakes than to fix the work he has spoiled.

We know very well that a skilled and experienced painter will not make such mistakes; on the contrary, by following sound rules, he will proceed by removing so little at a time that his work will progress well. Similarly, if the sculptor is working in clay or wax, he can either take away from it or add to it. When the model is completed, it is easy to cast it in bronze; this is the final process and the most enduring form of sculpture, since a work made only of marble is liable to be destroyed, but not one made of bronze.

But painting done on copper—which can be either subtracted from or altered using standard painting methods—is like the bronze process. Just as you first make the wax model for a bronze which can still be reduced or changed, the painting on copper allows for similar adjustments. While sculpture in bronze is imperish—

### [Of poetry and painting]

<margin>Notebooks III, 7 r.</margin>
When a poet stops using words to represent what exists in nature, he ceases to be the painter's equal. For if the poet moves away from such representation and instead describes the polished and persuasive words of a character he wants to depict speaking, he becomes an orator and is no longer a poet or a painter. If he describes the heavens, he makes himself an astronomer <note>original: "astrologer"; in the Renaissance, astronomy and astrology were often viewed as parts of the same discipline</note>; if he speaks of the things of nature or of God, he becomes a philosopher or a theologian. But if he returns to representing specific things, he would only be the painter's equal if he could satisfy the eye with words as the painter does with brush and color. With these, the painter creates a harmony for the eye, just as *music* creates harmony in an instant for the ear.

## XXIX
### Precepts of the Painter

->*'Painting is concerned with all ten attributes*<-
->*of sight: namely darkness, brightness, substance*<-
->*and color, form and place, distance*<-
->*and closeness, movement and rest; and it is with*<-
->*these attributes that this, my small book, will be*<-
->*interwoven.'*<-

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France, 1 r.</margin>
Which is more difficult: light and shade, or good design?
I maintain that a thing which is confined by a boundary is more difficult than one which is free. Shadows have their boundaries at certain stages, and when a painter is ignorant of this, his works will lack that relief <note>relief: the illusion of three-dimensional depth on a flat surface</note> which is the importance and the very soul of painting. Design is free, in so much as if you see an infinite number of faces, they will all be different—one with a long nose and one with a short one. The painter, therefore, must also adopt this liberty; and where there is liberty, there is no fixed rule.

### PAINTING

The mind of the painter should be like a mirror, which always takes the color of the thing that it reflects, and which is filled by as many images as there are things placed before it. Knowing, therefore, that you cannot be a good master unless you have a universal power of representing through your art all the varieties of the forms which nature produces—which indeed you will not know how to do unless you see them and retain them in your mind—see to it, O Painter, that when you go into the fields, you pay attention to various objects. Look carefully in turn, first at one thing and then at another, making a collection of different things selected and chosen from among those of lesser value <note>The author suggests that even common or "lesser" objects are worthy of study to build a complete mental library of forms.</note>. And do not act like some painters who, when tired by imaginative work, lay aside their task and take exercise...

## ON THE NATURE OF FOLDS IN DRAPERY

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France, 4 r.</margin>
The part of a fold that is farthest from the ends where it is held will return most closely to its original form. Everything naturally desires to remain in its own state. Since drapery has a uniform density and thickness on both the front and back, it naturally tends to lie flat. Consequently, whenever any folds or pleats force it to depart from this flat condition, it obeys the law of that force at the point where it is most constricted; however, you will find that the part farthest away from such constraint returns most nearly to its original state—that is to say, lying extended and full.

The air is filled with an infinite number of pyramids <note>pyramids: Leonardo’s geometric model for how light and images travel through space to the eye.</note> composed of radiating straight lines. These are created by the boundaries of the surfaces of objects in shadow. The farther these lines are from the object that produces them, the more acute their angle becomes. And although these lines intersect and interlace as they pass through the air, they do not become confused with one another; instead, they proceed on divergent courses, spreading out and diffusing through all the surrounding air.

These lines are of equal power among themselves—all equal to each, and each equal to all. By means of them, the images of objects are transmitted; these images are transmitted as a whole in every part, and as a whole in...

### PRECEPTS OF PAINTING

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France, 8 v.</margin>
Let the sketches for <term>historical subjects</term> <note>historical subjects: From the Italian *istoria*, referring to complex narrative paintings depicting scenes from the Bible, mythology, or history.</note> be rapid, and do not finish the limbs with too much detail. <margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France, 9 v.</margin>
Among <term>shadows</term> of equal strength, the one that is nearest to the eye will seem to be of less density.

All <term>colors</term> in distant <term>shadows</term> are indistinguishable and cannot be discerned.

In the distance, all <term>colors</term> are indistinguishable within <term>shadows</term> because an object not touched by the principal light has no power to transmit its image through the more luminous atmosphere to the eye; the lesser light is conquered by the greater.

For example, we see in a house that all the <term>colors</term> on the surface of the walls are visible instantly and clearly when the windows of the house are open. However, if we go outside the house and look through the windows from a short distance to see the paintings on the walls, we shall see uniform darkness instead.

The <term>painter</term> ought first to exercise his hand by copying drawings by good masters. Having acquired facility in this under the advice of his instructor, he ought to set himself to copy good <term>reliefs</term> <note>reliefs: Three-dimensional sculptures where the figures or forms stand out from a flat background.</note>, following the rules given below.

### OF DRAWING FROM RELIEF

He who draws from <term>relief</term> ought to position himself so that the eye of the figure he is drawing is on a level with his own. This should be done whenever a head is drawn from nature, because generally the people you meet in the streets all have their eyes at the same level as yours; if you make them higher or lower, you will find that your portrait will not resemble them.

### OF THE WAY TO DRAW FIGURES FOR NARRATIVE SCENES

A painter must always consider the height of the position where he intends to place his figures on a wall. When he makes studies from nature for this purpose, he should keep his eye as far below the subject he is drawing as that subject will appear above the spectator's eye in the final painting. Otherwise, the work will be worthy of criticism.

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France, 10 r.</margin>

### WHY A PAINTING CAN NEVER APPEAR TO STAND OUT IN RELIEF AS NATURAL THINGS DO

Painters often despair of their ability to imitate nature when they notice how their pictures lack the power of <term>relief</term> <note>relief: The illusion of three-dimensional depth and volume on a flat surface.</note> and vividness that objects possess when seen in a mirror. They claim they have colors that, in clarity and depth, far surpass the quality of the lights and shadows of the object seen in the mirror. In saying this, they blame reason rather than their own ignorance, for they fail to recognize that it is impossible for a painted object to appear in such relief as to be comparable to objects in a mirror—even though both are on a flat surface—unless they are viewed with a single eye.

The reason for this is that when two eyes see one thing after another (as in the case of eyes *a* and *b* seeing objects *n* and *m*), *m* cannot entirely cover *n* because the base of the visual lines is so broad that it allows one to see the second object beyond the first. If, however, you close one eye (as at point *s*), the object *f* will cover up *r*. This is because the visual line starts from a single point and forms its base at the first object, with the result that the second object, being of equal size, is never seen.

As far as the function of the eye is concerned, every bodily form is divided into three parts: <term>substance</term>, shape, and color. <note>substance: Here, Leonardo refers to the perceived mass or physical presence of an object, distinct from its outer silhouette or surface tint.</note> The image of its substance projects itself further from its source than its color or its shape; the color also projects itself further than the shape, though this law does not apply to luminous <note>original: "luminous bodies"</note> objects.

The above proposition is clearly shown and confirmed by experience; for if you see a man nearby, you will be able to recognize the character of his substance, his shape, and even his color. However, [if he moves further away...]

<summary>Leonardo explains that painters must adjust their perspective based on a viewer's eye level and describes the optical limitations of painting, noting that binocular vision prevents a flat image from appearing as "real" as a three-dimensional object.</summary>
<keywords>perspective, binocular vision, relief, optics, substance, shape, color, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s "Precepts of the Painter," shifting from the geometry of vision to the optical effects of distance on the human form, the physics of how images travel through air, and the subtle rendering of shadows and reflections.</meta>

<page-num>861</page-num>
<header>PRECEPTS OF THE PAINTER</header>

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France, 12 v.</margin>
If a person moves some distance away from you, you will no longer be able to recognize who they are because their shape will lack distinctive character. If they move even farther away, you will not be able to distinguish their color; instead, they will merely seem like a dark object. Farther away still, they will appear as a very small, round, dark body. They will appear round because distance diminishes the various parts so much that nothing remains visible except the overall mass. 

The reason for this is as follows: we know very well that all the images of objects penetrate to the *<term>imprensiva</term>*¹ <note>imprensiva: Leonardo’s term for the "perceptive faculty" or the part of the brain that receives and processes sensory impressions from the eyes.</note> through a small aperture <note>aperture: The pupil of the eye.</note> in the eye. Therefore, if the entire horizon *a d* enters through such a small opening, and the object *b c* is a very small part of this horizon, what tiny fraction of space must it occupy in the minute representation of such a vast hemisphere? 

Furthermore, because luminous bodies have more power in darkness than any others, and because the opening of the eye is naturally in shadow (as is the case with all holes), it is inevitable that the images of distant objects blend within the great light of the sky. Or, if they do remain visible, they appear dark and black, as every small body must when seen against the clarity of the air.

### [Images in the air]

All bodies together, and each one individually, fill the surrounding air with an infinite number of their images. These images exist throughout all the air and in every part of it, carrying with them the nature, the color, and the form of the object that produced them.

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France, 13 r.</margin>
Perspective is the bridle and rudder of painting.

Shadows that you see with difficulty, and whose boundaries you cannot clearly define—which you only perceive and reproduce in your work with some hesitation of judgment—should not be represented as finished or sharply defined. If you do, the result will be that your work appears "wooden" <note>wooden: In art, this refers to a stiff, lifeless, or unnatural quality lacking the soft transitions found in nature.</note>.

## OF REFLECTION

Reflections are caused by objects of a bright nature with a smooth and semi-opaque surface. When struck by light, these surfaces drive it back again toward the first object, much like the rebound of a ball.

¹ Imprensiva: See Volume I, Optics, pages 237–238.

## WHERE THERE CAN BE NO LUMINOUS REFLECTION

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France, 14 v.</margin>
The surfaces of all solid bodies are covered by various degrees of light and shadow. Light is of two kinds: one is called "original" and the other "derived." I call "original" that light which proceeds from the flame of a fire, from the sun, or from the atmosphere. "Derived" light is reflected light. 

However, returning to the definition I promised, I state that there is no <term>luminous reflection</term> <note>luminous reflection: Light that bounces off one object and onto another, illuminating the second object's shadowed side.</note> on the side of a body that faces objects in shadow—such as shaded scenes, meadows with grass of varying heights, or green or bare woods. This is because, although the part of every branch turned toward the original light is infused with the qualities of that light, there are nevertheless so many shadows cast by each individual branch, and so many shadows cast by one branch onto another, that the entire mass becomes so deeply shadowed that the light is negligible. Therefore, objects like these cannot cast any reflected light onto bodies facing them.

## WHY PAINTING GROUPS OF FIGURES ONE ABOVE ANOTHER SHOULD BE AVOIDED

This practice, which is universally adopted by painters for the walls of chapels, is rightly to be strongly criticized. These painters represent one composition at one level with its own landscape and buildings, and then they climb to the level above it to create another, changing the <term>point of sight</term> <note>point of sight: Also known as the "vanishing point" or the horizon line in perspective; it is the point directly opposite the viewer's eye.</note> from that of the first painting. They then make a third and a fourth, so that the work on a single wall displays four different points of sight. This is extreme foolishness on the part of such masters.

We know that the point of sight is directly opposite the eye of the person viewing the composition. If you were to ask me how I would represent the life of a saint when it is divided into several scenes on the same wall, I would reply that you should place the foreground with its point of sight at the eye level of the spectators. On this same plane, you should depict the main episode on a large scale. Then, by gradually diminishing the size of the figures and buildings across various hills and plains, you should represent all the other incidents of the story. And on the rest of the wall up to the top, you... <note>The sentence in the original manuscript ends abruptly here.</note>

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France, 16 r.</margin>
Figures in relief <note>original: "Figures in relief" refers to paintings that appear three-dimensional, as if they are standing out from the surface like a sculpture.</note> captured in the act of movement will, in their standing position, seem naturally to be falling forward.

A young student ought first to learn <term>perspective</term> <note>perspective: The mathematical system for representing three-dimensional space and distance on a flat surface.</note>, then the <term>proportions</term> of all things. Next, he should learn from the hand of a skilled master in order to accustom himself to drawing beautiful limbs. Then he should study from nature to confirm for himself the reasons for what he has learned. After that, he should spend time studying the works of various masters; finally, he should make it a habit to practice and work at his art.

**The Origin of Painting**
The first picture was nothing more than a line drawn around the shadow of a man cast by the sun onto a wall.

**On Composition**
<term>Historical pictures</term> <note>historical pictures: Narrative paintings that tell a story, usually from the Bible, mythology, or history.</note> should not be crowded or confused by too many figures.

**On Depicting the Elderly**
Old men should be shown with slow, weary movements. When standing, their legs should be bent at the knees, their feet parallel and spaced apart, the spine curved low, the head leaning forward, and the arms held not too far from the body.

**On Depicting Women**
Women should be represented in modest poses, with their legs close together, arms folded, and their heads held low and tilted to the side.

**On Depicting Old Women**
Old women should be represented as bold, with swift, passionate movements like the infernal <term>furies</term> <note>furies: In classical mythology, these were monstrous female spirits of vengeance; Leonardo suggests using their wild, aggressive energy as a model for portraying elderly women.</note>. These movements should appear faster in the arms and heads than in the legs.

**On Depicting Children**
When sitting, little children should be shown twisting and turning with quick movements, and in shy, timid poses when standing up.

**On the Treatment of Fabric**
One should not give <term>drapery</term> <note>drapery: The artistic arrangement of clothing or fabric.</note> a confusing mess of many folds. Instead, create folds only where the fabric is held by the hands or arms; let the rest fall naturally according to its weight. Do not allow the outline of the figure to be broken by too many lines or interrupted folds.

## THE THREE KINDS OF PERSPECTIVE

Perspective is of three kinds. The first deals with the causes of diminution—or what is called "diminishing perspective"—of objects as they recede from the eye. The second deals with the manner in which colors are changed as they recede from the eye. The third and last consists of defining how objects should be less carefully finished as they move farther away. Their names are as follows:

->Linear Perspective<-
->Perspective of Color<-
->Vanishing Perspective<- <note>vanishing perspective: Also known as atmospheric perspective, this refers to how distance causes objects to lose their sharp outlines and detail.</note>

## ON MINIMIZING FOLDS IN DRAPERY

When figures are dressed in a cloak, they should not show the shape of the body to such an extent that the cloak appears to be touching the skin. Surely you would not want the cloak to be next to the skin, since you must realize that between the cloak and the skin there are other garments. These layers prevent the shape of the limbs from being visible or appearing through the cloak. 

For those limbs that you do make visible, make them look thick enough so that there appears to be other clothing underneath the cloak. You should only allow the nearly identical thickness of the limbs to be visible in a <term>nymph</term> <note>nymph: In art, these mythological spirits were often depicted in thin, clinging, or fluttering robes to emphasize movement.</note> or an angel, for these are represented wearing light draperies that are driven and pressed against the limbs by the blowing wind.

<summary>Leonardo explains how to accurately depict different fabric textures and defines the three types of perspective: linear, color, and the loss of detail over distance. He also cautions artists against showing too much body detail through heavy outer clothing, except when depicting ethereal figures like nymphs.</summary>

# ON THE METHOD OF DEPICTING DISTANT OBJECTS IN PAINTING

It is evident that the part of the atmosphere which lies nearest the level ground is denser than the rest, and that the higher it rises, the thinner and more transparent it becomes.

In the case of large and lofty objects which are some distance away from you, their lower parts will not be clearly visible, because the line of sight through which you see them passes through the thickest and densest portion of the atmosphere. But the summits of these heights are seen along a line which—although it is projected through the denser atmosphere where it starts at your eye—ends at the highest point of the object and thus finishes its course in an atmosphere far more <term>rarefied</term> <note>rarefied: Thinned out or less dense; in this context, the clearer air found at higher altitudes.</note> than that at its base. Consequently, the farther away from you this line extends from point to point, the greater the change is in the fine quality of the atmosphere.

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France, 18 r.</margin>Therefore, painter, when you represent mountains, see to it that from hill to hill the bases are always paler than the summits. The farther away you place them from one another, the paler the bases should be in proportion; and the loftier the mountains are, the more they should reveal their true shape and color.

### How the atmosphere should be represented as paler the lower it is shown:

Since the atmosphere is dense near the ground and becomes thinner the higher it rises, when the sun is in the east and you look toward the west—taking in a view to the north and to the south—you will see that this dense air receives more light from the sun than the thinner air does, because the sun’s rays encounter more resistance there. 

If your view of the horizon is bounded by a low plain, that farthest region of the sky will be seen through that thicker, whiter atmosphere, and this will obscure the true color seen through such a medium. The sky will seem whiter there than it does overhead, where the line of vision traverses a smaller space of atmosphere filled with thick <term>vapors</term> <note>vapors: Mist, fog, or moisture in the air that affects visibility and light scattering.</note>. But if you look toward the east, the atmosphere will appear darker the lower it is, for in this lower atmosphere the luminous rays pass less freely.

<summary>Leonardo explains the principles of atmospheric perspective, noting that air is densest near the ground, which makes the bases of distant mountains appear paler and less distinct than their summits.</summary>
<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, atmospheric perspective, aerial perspective, mountain painting, air density, light scattering, horizon, artistic technique</keywords>

### How shadows are distributed in different positions, and concerning the objects situated in them:

If the sun is in the east and you look towards the west, you will see that all objects that are illuminated are entirely without shadow, because what you are looking at is exactly what the sun sees.

And if you look to the south or the north, you will see that all bodies are surrounded by light and shade, because you are looking at both the part that does not see the sun and the part that does. And if you look towards the pathway of the sun, all the objects will present their shaded side to you, because this side cannot be seen by the sun.

## ON THE METHOD OF REPRESENTING A NIGHT SCENE

Whatever is entirely deprived of light is complete darkness. When night is in such a condition, if you wish to represent a scene within it, you must arrange to introduce a great fire there. Then, the things which are nearest to the fire will be more deeply tinted with its color, for whatever is nearest to an object partakes most fully of its nature. Making the fire a reddish color, you should represent all the things illuminated by it as also having a <term>ruddy</term> <note>ruddy: A healthy reddish color, here specifically referring to the warm glow produced by firelight.</note> hue, while those which are farther away from the fire should be dyed more deeply with the black color of the night. 

The figures which are between you and the fire will appear dark against the brightness of the flame, for that part of the object which you perceive is colored by the darkness of the night, and not by the brightness of the fire. Those which are at the sides should be half in shadow and half in reddish light; and those visible beyond the edge of the flames will all be lit up with reddish light against a dark background. As for their actions, show those who are near the fire shielding themselves with their hands and cloaks as a protection against the unbearable heat, with faces turned away as though on the point of flight; while for those farther away, you should show a great number pressing their hands upon their eyes, pained by the intolerable glare.

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France, 18 v.</margin>

I will, nevertheless, attempt to prove it, if not completely then at least in part. Linear perspective <note>original: diminishing perspective; the mathematical system used to create the illusion of depth on a flat surface</note> demonstrates through reason that objects diminish in size in proportion to their distance from the eye, and this theory is entirely confirmed by experience. Now, the lines of sight between an object and the eye are all intercepted at a uniform boundary when they reach the surface of the painting; whereas the lines that pass from the eye to a piece of sculpture have different boundaries and are of varying lengths. 

The line that is the longest extends to a limb that is farther away than the rest, and consequently, this limb appears smaller. There are many lines longer than others because there are many small parts, one farther away than another; being farther away, these must necessarily appear smaller, and by appearing smaller, they cause a corresponding decrease in the object’s overall mass. But this does not happen in a painting, because as the lines of sight all end at the same distance (the canvas), it follows that they do not undergo this physical diminution. Since the parts themselves are not physically receding, they do not lessen the whole mass of the object; consequently, this specific type of diminution is not perceptible in a painting as it is in sculpture.

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library <note>original: Bibliothèque Nationale</note>, folio 19 recto.</margin>

### HOW WHITE BODIES OUGHT TO BE REPRESENTED

When you are representing a white body surrounded by ample space, since white has no color of its own, it is tinted and partially transformed by the color of whatever is positioned across from it. If you are looking at a woman dressed in white in the middle of a landscape, the side of her that is exposed to the sun will be so dazzling in color that parts of it, like the sun itself, will cause pain to the eyes. As for the side exposed to the atmosphere—which is luminous because the rays of the sun are interwoven with it and penetrate it—since this atmosphere is itself blue, the side of the woman exposed to it will appear steeped in blue. 

If the surface of the ground near her consists of meadows, and the woman is placed between a sunlit meadow and the sun itself, you will find that all the parts of the folds of her dress turned toward the meadow will be dyed by the reflected rays with the color of the grass. Thus, she becomes changed into the colors of the objects nearby, both those that are luminous and those that are not.

### HOW TO REPRESENT THE LIMBS

Represent limbs that must endure fatigue as muscular; those that are not used for such labor should be depicted without defined muscles and soft.

### OF THE ACTION OF FIGURES

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library <note>original: Bibliothèque Nationale</note>, folio 20 recto.</margin>
Depict figures with movements that clearly show what is in the figure's mind; otherwise, your art will not be worthy of praise.

### OF THE CHOICE OF THE LIGHT WHICH GIVES A GRACE TO FACES

If you have a courtyard that you can cover with a linen awning whenever you wish, the light there will be excellent. Or, when you wish to paint a portrait, do so in overcast weather or at twilight <note>original: at the fall of the evening</note>, placing the sitter with their back against one of the courtyard walls. Observe the faces of men and women in the streets at twilight during overcast weather—notice what grace and softness they display! 

Therefore, painter, you should prepare a courtyard with walls painted black and a roof that projects slightly beyond the wall. Its width should be ten <term>braccia</term> <note>an Italian unit of measurement; one "braccio" is approximately 23 inches or 58 centimeters</note>, its length twenty <term>braccia</term>, and its height ten <term>braccia</term>. You should cover it with an awning when the sun is shining; otherwise, you should paint your portrait during the twilight hour or when it is cloudy or misty, for the light is perfect then.

### WHY FACES AT A DISTANCE APPEAR DARK

It is clear that the images of all visible things, whether large or small, enter our senses through the tiny pupil of the eye. If, then, the images of the immense sky and earth pass through such a small opening, the face of a man—being almost nothing compared to such vast images and further diminished by the distance—occupies so little of the pupil that it becomes indistinguishable. Furthermore, having to pass from the outer surface to...

### ON SHADOWS IN THE FAR DISTANCE

Shadows are lost in the far distance because the vast expanse of luminous atmosphere lying between the eye and the object fills <note>original: "suffuses"</note> the shadows of the object with its own color.

### WHY A MAN SEEN AT A CERTAIN DISTANCE CANNOT BE RECOGNIZED

Linear perspective <note>original: "diminishing perspective"</note> shows us that the farther away an object is, the smaller it becomes. If you look at a man who is the distance of a bowshot <note>the distance an arrow travels, roughly 200–300 yards</note> away from you and place the eye of a small needle close to your own eye, you will be able to see the images of many men transmitted to your eye through it; these will all be contained at once within the eye of that needle. If, then, the image of a man who is a bowshot's distance away is transmitted to your eye so that it occupies only a tiny part of a needle's eye, how could you possibly distinguish or discern the nose, mouth, or any detail of the body in such a small figure?

And without seeing these, you cannot recognize the man, since he does not show you the features that cause individuals to differ in appearance.

### ON PHYSICAL POSES <note>original: "attitudes"</note>

The pit of the throat <note>the indentation at the base of the neck, between the collarbones</note> is positioned directly above the weight-bearing foot. If an arm is thrown forward, the pit of the throat moves from its position above the foot; if the leg is thrown backward, the pit of the throat moves forward. Thus, it shifts with every change in pose.

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library <note>original: Bibliothèque Nationale</note>, folio 20 verso.</margin>

### HOW TO REPRESENT A TEMPEST

If you wish to represent a tempest <note>a violent, windy storm</note> properly, consider and record exactly what happens when the wind, blowing over the face of the sea and the land, lifts and carries with it everything that is not firmly fixed to the ground. In order to properly depict this storm, you must first of all show the clouds, split and torn apart <note>original: "riven"</note>, swept along in the path of the wind, together with storms of sand blown up from the seashores. Show branches and leaves caught up by the irresistible fury of the gale and scattered through the air, along with many other lightweight objects. 

The trees and shrubs should be bent to the ground as if showing their desire to follow the direction of the wind, with their branches twisted out of their natural growth and their leaves tossed and turned inside out. Of the people who are there, some should have fallen and be lying wrapped in their own clothes, almost invisible because of the dust. Those who are still standing should be shown behind a tree, with their arms thrown around it to prevent the wind from dragging them away. Others should be shown crouching on the ground, their hands over their eyes because of the dust, their garments and hair streaming in the wind. Let the sea be wild and stormy; between the crests of its waves, it should be covered with swirling foam, and the wind should carry the fine spray through the stormy air like a thick and all-enveloping mist.

As for the ships that are there, you should show some with torn sails, the shreds of them flapping in the air along with broken ropes <note>original: "halyards"; the lines used to hoist sails</note>. Some masts should be broken and fallen overboard <note>original: "gone by the board"</note>, and the vessel itself should lie disabled and broken by the fury of the waves, with some of the crew shrieking and clinging to the fragments of the wreck. You should show the clouds, driven by the violent <note>original: "impetuous"</note> winds, hurled against the high mountain peaks, swirling and circling there like waves beating against rocks. The very air should strike terror through the murky darkness caused by the dust, mist, and thick clouds.

## HOW TO REPRESENT SOMEONE SPEAKING TO A GROUP

When you wish to represent someone speaking among a group of people, you should first consider the subject they are discussing and how to arrange their movements so that they match the topic. For instance, if the subject is meant to be persuasive, the gestures should serve that goal. If the topic is one that needs to be explained point-by-point, the speaker should grasp a finger of his left hand between two fingers of his right, keeping the two smaller fingers closed <note>original: "serate"; this describes a common rhetorical gesture for counting off arguments or points</note>, and let his face be expressive and turned toward the people. His mouth should be slightly open to give the impression that he is speaking. 

If he is seated, let him appear to be in the act of straightening himself, leaning his head forward. If you represent him standing, show him leaning slightly forward with his head and shoulders toward the crowd. You should depict the audience as silent and attentive, all watching the face of the speaker with expressions of wonder. Show the mouths of some of the old men with the corners pulled down in amazement at what they hear, drawing the cheeks into many deep lines, with their eyebrows raised where they meet to create wrinkles on their foreheads. Show some listeners sitting with their fingers interlaced, clutching their tired knees, and others—fragile old men—with their legs crossed, one hand resting on a knee to cradle the opposite elbow, while that hand supports a bearded chin.

## How to increase the three-dimensional effect <note>original: "relief"</note> in a painting using artificial light and shadow:

To make a figure stand out more in a painting, you should make it a habit to place a line of bright light between the figure and any nearby object that is in its shadow; this serves to separate the figure from the shaded background. On that same background object, you should create two bright areas; between these, place the shadow that the figure casts against the wall. You should apply this technique often to the limbs that you want to appear as if they are standing out somewhat from

### ON SURROUNDING BODIES WITH VARIOUS SHAPES OF SHADOW

Take care that the shadows cast upon the surfaces of bodies by different objects are always undulating, with varying curves produced by the different shapes of the limbs casting the shadows and the shape of the object receiving the shadow.

### ON THE ESSENTIAL NATURE OF SHADOW

Shadow shares the nature of universal things, which are all most powerful at their beginning and grow weaker toward their end. I am referring to the beginning of all forms and qualities, whether visible or invisible, and not to things that grow from small beginnings to a mighty size over time—like a great oak tree that has its humble start in a tiny acorn. Even so, I would argue the oak is most powerful at the point where it is born in the ground, for that is the site of its greatest growth. 

Darkness, therefore, is the first stage of shadow, and light is the last. Therefore, painter, see to it that you make your shadow darkest near its source, and let the end of it blend into light so that the shadow appears to have no sharp edge.

**How shadows cast by specific light sources should be avoided because their edges are as harsh as their centers:**

### WHAT SHADOW AND LIGHT ARE

Shadow is the absence of light; it is simply the obstruction caused by opaque bodies <note>opaque bodies: solid objects that do not allow light to pass through them</note> placed in the path of luminous rays. Shadow is of the nature of darkness, while light is of the nature of brightness. The one hides and the other reveals. They are always found together, attached to physical bodies. Shadow is more powerful than light, for it can obstruct and completely deprive objects of brightness, whereas brightness can never altogether drive shadow away from bodies—that is, from opaque bodies.

#### The difference between a shadow inseparable from a body and a cast shadow:

An inseparable shadow <note>often called an "attached shadow" in modern art theory</note> is one which is never parted from the illuminated object, as is the case with a ball; when it is in the light, it always has one of its sides covered by shadow, and this shadow never separates from it regardless of any change in the position of the ball. A cast shadow, by contrast, may or may not be produced by the body itself upon another surface. Let us suppose a ball is at a distance of a <term>braccio</term> <note>original: "braccio"; a Renaissance Italian unit of measurement, approximately 23 inches or the length of an arm</note> from a wall and the light is coming from the opposite side: this light will throw just as broad a shadow upon the wall as is found upon the side of the ball that faces the wall. Part of a cast shadow will not be visible when the light is below the ball, for its shadow will then pass upward toward the sky; finding no obstruction in its course, it will become lost.

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library [Paris], folio 22 recto</margin>

## OF THE TEN ATTRIBUTES OF SIGHT WHICH ALL FIND EXPRESSION IN PAINTING

Painting is concerned with all the ten attributes of sight: darkness and brightness, substance and color, form and location, distance and closeness, and movement and rest. This small book of mine will be woven from these attributes, reminding the painter of the rules and methods by which he should use his art to imitate all things created by nature and the beauty of the world.

## HOW THE PAINTER SHOULD PRACTICE THE PERSPECTIVE OF COLORS

As a means of practicing this perspective—specifically the variation, loss, or fading of the true quality of colors over distance—pick objects in a landscape, such as trees, houses, men, and locations, spaced one hundred <term>braccia</term> <note>original: "braccia"; an Italian Renaissance unit of measurement, approximately 23 inches or the length of an arm</note> apart. In front of the first tree, fix a pane of glass so that it is perfectly steady. Keep your eye still and trace the outline of the tree onto the glass directly over the real tree. Afterward, move the glass to one side until the actual tree appears right next to the one you have drawn.

Then, color your drawing in such a way that the two are identical in color and form, so that if you close one eye, both the real tree and the drawing seem to be painted on the glass and at the same distance away. Proceed in the same way with a second and a third tree at distances of one hundred <term>braccia</term> from each other. These will always serve as your standards and teachers when you are working on pictures where these principles apply; they will ensure that your work is successful in depicting depth.

### ON UNDULATING MOVEMENTS AND COUNTERPOISE IN HUMAN AND ANIMAL FIGURES

Whenever you create a figure of a person or a graceful animal, remember to avoid making it appear "wooden." It should move with counterpoise and balance so that it does not look like a stiff block of wood.

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library, folio 22 verso</margin>
Those whom you wish to represent as strong should be shown as such primarily through the way they turn their heads upon their shoulders. <note>Leonardo suggests that physical power is expressed through the tension and rotation of the neck and torso, rather than just static muscle size.</note>

### ON LINEAR PERSPECTIVE

Linear perspective deals with the function of the lines of sight. It proves through measurement how much smaller a second object is than the first, and a third smaller than the second, and so on until the very limit of what the eye can see.

I have found through experience that if a second object is as far away from the first as the first is from your eye—even if the objects are actually the same size—the second will appear half as large as the first. If a third object is equal in size to the second and is as far beyond the second as the second is from the first <note>The original manuscript incorrectly says "third" here.</note>, it will appear half the size of the second. Thus, by successive degrees at equal distances, objects will be continually reduced by half—the second being half the first—provided that the intervening space is less than twenty <term>braccia</term>.

At a distance of twenty <term>braccia</term>, a figure similar to yours will lose four-fifths of its apparent size; at a distance of forty <term>braccia</term>, it will lose nine-tenths; and at sixty <term>braccia</term>, it will lose nineteen-twentieths. It will continue to diminish by these degrees as long as the surface of the picture is twice your own height away from you. If the distance from your eye to the picture is only equal to your height, there is a much greater difference in size between the first set of <term>braccia</term> and the second.

### ON PLACING A FIGURE IN THE FOREGROUND OF AN HISTORICAL COMPOSITION <note>original: "historical composition"; in Renaissance art theory, this refers to a "storia," a complex narrative painting depicting a scene from history, scripture, or mythology.</note>

You should make the figure in the foreground of an historical composition proportionately smaller than life-size, according to the number of <term>braccia</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement roughly equal to the length of an arm, about 23 inches.</note> that you place it behind the front line; then, make the other figures in proportion to the first one using the rule mentioned above.

I establish the degrees of objects seen by the eye just as a musician does for the sounds heard by the ear:

Even though objects seen by the eye appear to touch as they recede, I will nonetheless base my rule on intervals of twenty <term>braccia</term>, just as the musician has done with sounds. For although sounds are united and connected together, he has nevertheless fixed the degrees from sound to sound—calling them the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth—and so, from degree to degree, he has given names to the variations of the human voice as it becomes higher or lower.

### A method for making the shadows on figures match their light and their shape:

When you are painting a figure and wish to see whether the shadow corresponds to the light—and that it is neither redder nor yellower than the true nature of the color you wish to show in shadow—you should do the following: use your finger to cast a shadow upon the illuminated part of your painting. If the accidental shadow <note>A shadow cast by a physical object (like the finger) onto the surface of the painting.</note> made by your finger looks like the natural shadow <note>The shadow that is actually painted onto the figure in the composition.</note> you have painted, then it is correct. By moving your finger closer or farther away, you can make the test shadows darker or lighter, constantly comparing them with your own work.

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library, folio 23 recto</margin>

### WHY AN OBJECT PLACED CLOSE TO THE EYE WILL HAVE INDISTINCT EDGES

Any object placed directly opposite the eye that is too close to it will have edges that are difficult to discern. This is similar to what happens when objects are placed near a light source and cast a large, blurry shadow. In all cases of <term>linear perspective</term> <note>The mathematical system of representing three-dimensional objects on a two-dimensional surface.</note>, the way the eye functions is similar to the behavior of light. The reason for this is that the eye has...

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s technical instructions for artists, moving from the mathematical rules of distance to the physical mechanics of the eye and practical exercises for mastering drawing from memory and perspective.</meta>

<page-num>877</page-num>
<header>PRECEPTS OF THE PAINTER</header>

There is one principal line of vision that expands as it gains distance and encompasses large things far away with the same precision as it does small things close at hand. The eye, however, sends out a multitude of other lines on either side of this central line; these have less power to see clearly the further they are from the center of this radiation. Consequently, when an object is placed very close to the eye, this principal line of vision is not capable of distinguishing the edges of the object. Therefore, these edges inevitably fall among the lines that have poor visual clarity. Their role in the function of the eye is like that of hunting dogs <note>original: "setters at the chase"</note> who flush out the prey but cannot catch it. While these outer lines cannot perceive the edges clearly themselves, they are the reason why the principal line of sight is directed toward the objects touched by these lines.

<margin>Manuscript 2038, sheet 23 verso.</margin>
It follows, therefore, that objects whose edges are judged by these secondary lines appear indistinct.

## HOW TO MEMORIZE YOUR SUBJECTS EFFECTIVELY

When you wish to memorize something you have studied, follow this method: when you have drawn the same thing so many times that you feel you know it by heart, try to draw it without the model. However, have a tracing made of the model upon a thin piece of smooth glass, and lay this tracing over the drawing you made from memory. Note carefully where the tracing and your drawing do not match, and where you find you have made an error, keep it in mind so as not to make the mistake again. Even return to the model to copy the part where you were wrong as many times as necessary to fix it in your mind. If you cannot obtain smooth glass to make a tracing of the object, take a piece of very fine parchment that has been well-oiled and then dried; once you have used it for one drawing, you can wipe it clean with a sponge and use it for another.

## A WAY OF LEARNING HOW TO POSITION A FIGURE WELL

If you wish to thoroughly accustom yourself to correct and good positions for your figures, fasten a frame or "loom" divided into squares by threads between your eye and the nude figure which you are representing. Then, draw the same squares very faintly upon the paper where you wish to draw the figure. You should then place a pellet of wax on a part of the network to serve as a mark; as you look at your model, this mark should always cover the pit of the throat, or if the model has turned their back, make it cover one of the vertebrae of the neck. 

These threads will instruct you as to all the parts of the body which, in each attitude, are found below the pit of the throat, below the angles of the shoulders, below the breasts, the hips, and the other parts of the body. The transverse lines of the network will show you how much higher the figure is above the leg on which it is posed than above the other, and the same with the hips, the knees, and the feet. But always fix the net by a perpendicular line, and then ensure that all the divisions the nude figure occupies in the network are the same divisions the nude you draw occupies in the network of your sketch. 

The squares you draw on paper may be as much smaller than those of the frame as you wish, in proportion to how much less than life-size you want your figure to be. Then, keep in mind for the figures you create the rule of the corresponding proportions of the limbs as the network has revealed them to you. This frame should be three and a half *braccia* in height and three wide, positioned at a distance of seven *braccia* from you and one from the nude figure.

# HOW THE MIRROR IS THE MASTER OF PAINTERS

When you want to see if the overall effect of your painting matches the object you are copying from nature, take a mirror and set it so that it reflects the actual thing. Then compare the reflection with your painting, and consider carefully whether the subject in both images matches, studying the mirror especially. The mirror should be used as a guide—specifically the flat mirror—because on its surface, objects have many similarities to a painting. For instance, you see a painting made on a single flat plane showing things that appear in <term>relief</term> <note>The illusion of three-dimensional depth and volume on a two-dimensional surface.</note>, and the mirror does the same on its flat surface. The painting is a single surface, and the mirror is the same.

The painting is intangible, in that things which appear rounded and separate cannot be grasped in your hands; the mirror is the same. Both the mirror and the painting present images of things surrounded by shadow and light, and both seem to project significantly from the flat surface they are on. Since you know that the mirror shows you separate objects by using outlines, shadows, and highlights—and since you have even more powerful shadows and lights among your colors than those in the mirror—it is certain that if you know how to compose your painting well, it will look like a real thing seen in a large mirror.

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France, sheet 24 verso <note>original: "24 v."; the back side of the 24th leaf of the manuscript.</note></margin>

## *Regarding the poor excuses made by those who falsely and unworthily call themselves painters:*

There is a certain class of painters who, although they have paid very little attention to study, claim the right to live amidst the beauty of gold and <term>azure</term> <note>original: "azure"; specifically ultramarine blue, an extremely expensive pigment made from lapis lazuli. The artist is criticizing those who want the prestige and expensive materials of a master without putting in the work.</note>. Because of their own foolishness, they claim that they cannot work to their highest standard because they are paid so poorly, but they insist they have the knowledge and could do as well as anyone else if they were paid well.

But look at these foolish people! They don't have the common sense to keep some samples of their good work on hand so they can say, "This one has a high price, that one has a moderate price, and this one is quite cheap," thereby showing that they have work available at all price points.

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France, sheet 25 recto <note>original: "25 r."; the front side of the 25th leaf of the manuscript.</note></margin>

## ON AERIAL PERSPECTIVE

There is another kind of perspective which I call <term>aerial</term> <note>Also known as atmospheric perspective; the method of creating the illusion of depth by modulating color and clarity to simulate changes caused by the atmosphere.</note>, because through variations in the atmosphere one is able to distinguish the different distances of various buildings when their bases appear to end on a single line. This is the appearance presented by a group of buildings on the far side of a wall, all of which—when seen above the top of the wall—look to be the same size. If in painting you wish to make one seem farther away than another, you must make the atmosphere appear somewhat thick. 

You know that in an atmosphere of uniform density, the most distant things seen through it (such as mountains) will appear blue, almost the same color as the sky when the sun is in the east. This happens because of the great volume of atmosphere between your eye and the mountains. Therefore, you should paint the building that is nearest above the wall in its natural color; make the one that is more distant less defined and bluer. A building that you want to seem twice as far away should be painted with double the depth of blue, and one you want to seem five times as far away should be five times as blue. By following this rule, buildings that appear to be the same size above a given line will be clearly distinguished, showing which are more distant and which are larger than others.

## WHY A PAINTER IS NOT WORTHY OF PRAISE UNLESS HE IS UNIVERSAL

We must frankly admit that some people deceive themselves when they give the title of "good master" to a painter who can only paint a head or a figure well. Surely it is no great achievement if, by studying only one thing during his entire lifetime, he attains some degree of excellence in it! 

But since we know that painting encompasses and contains within itself everything that nature produces, everything that results from the <term>fortuitous</term> <note>original: "fortuitous"; occurring by chance or accident.</note> actions of men, and, in short, whatever can be perceived by the eyes, it seems to me that a painter who only depicts a single figure well is but a poor master. For do you not see how many and how varied are the actions performed by men alone? Do you not see how many different...

### ON STUDYING AS SOON AS YOU AWAKE, OR BEFORE YOU GO TO SLEEP IN BED IN THE DARK

I have found in my own experience that it is of no small benefit, when lying in bed in the dark, to go over again in the imagination the main outlines of the forms previously studied, or of other noteworthy things conceived through creative <note>original: "ingenious"</note> speculation. This exercise is entirely to be commended, as it is useful for fixing things in the memory.

### *How the painter should be eager to hear everyone's opinion on the progress of his work:*

Certainly, when a person is painting a picture, they should not refuse to hear anyone's opinion. We know very well that even if a person is not a painter, they may have a true understanding <note>original: "conception"</note> of the human form, and can judge correctly whether a figure is hump-backed, has one shoulder higher than the other, or has an oversized mouth or nose, or other defects.

Since we recognize that people are able to form a true judgment regarding the works of nature, how much more must we admit <note>original: "it behove us to admit"</note> that they are able to judge the faults in our work? For you know how much a person can be deceived by their own work; if you do not recognize this in your own case, observe it in others, and then you will profit by their mistakes. Therefore, you should be eager to listen patiently to the opinions of others. Consider and reflect carefully whether or not the person who criticizes <note>original: "censures"</note> you has a valid reason for their criticism; and if they do, correct your work...
