### Why a man should not trust his memory so much that he refuses to draw from nature when creating important works:

Any master who suggests that he can recall all the forms and effects of nature from memory alone seems very ignorant to me. This is because the effects of nature are infinite, and our memory does not have enough capacity to hold them all.

Therefore, O painter, take care that the greed for money does not prove to be a stronger motivation than achieving fame in your art; for achieving this fame is a far greater thing than the renown of riches.

For these and other reasons, you should apply yourself first of all to drawing. This allows you to present to the eye in a visible form the purpose and invention originally created in your imagination. Then, proceed to take away from it or add to it until you are satisfied with yourself. After that, have men arranged as models—clothed <note>original: "draped"</note> or nude—in the same positions you have designed for your work. Make the proportions and size in accordance with perspective, so that no part of the work remains that is not guided by reason and by the actual effects found in nature.

And this will be the way to make yourself famous in your art.

An object represented in white and black will appear in more pronounced relief <term>relief</term> <note>relief: the illusion of three-dimensional depth on a flat surface</note> than any other. Therefore, I would remind you, O painter, that you should clothe your figures in colors as bright as you can. If you make them dark in color, they will have only a slight sense of depth and will be very difficult to see from a distance. This is because the shadows of all objects are dark; if you make a garment dark, there will be only a slight difference between its highlights and its shadows, whereas with bright colors, there are many distinct levels of difference.

<margin>Manuscript 2038 National Library, 26 r.</margin>

...heads, eyes, noses, mouths, chins, throats, and also necks and shoulders. Take noses as an example: they are of ten types—straight, bulbous, hollow, prominent either above or below the center, aquiline <note>original: "aquiline"; hooked like an eagle's beak</note>, regular, simian <note>original: "simian"; resembling a monkey</note>, round, and pointed. Similarly, you will find variety in the other features; you should make studies of these things from nature to fix them in your mind. Alternatively, when you have to draw a face from memory, carry a small notebook with you in which you have noted such features. Then, once you have glanced at the face of the person you wish to draw, you can look privately at your notes to see which nose or mouth resembles it, and make a tiny mark against it so you can recognize it again at home. I say nothing here of abnormal faces, for they are remembered without difficulty.

## ON THE GAMES IN WHICH ARTISTS SHOULD INDULGE

When you, artists <note>original: "draughtsmen"</note>, wish to find some profitable recreation in games, you should always practice things that may be of use in your profession—that is, by giving your eye accuracy of judgment so that it may know how to estimate the truth regarding the length and width of objects. 

To accustom the mind to such things, let one of you draw a straight line anywhere on a wall. Then, let each of you take a light reed or straw in your hand, and let each cut his own to the length that the line on the wall appears to him when he is at a distance of ten <term>braccia</term> <note>braccio: an Italian unit of measurement based on the length of an arm, roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters</note>. Then, let each person go up to the original line to measure it against the length he judged it to be. The one whose measure comes nearest to the length of the original has done best and is the winner; he should receive from everyone the prize that was previously agreed upon. Furthermore, you should take foreshortened measurements—that is, you should take a spear or some other stick and look ahead to a certain point at a distance, and then let each person estimate how many times that measure is contained...

### WHETHER IT IS BETTER TO DRAW WITH OTHERS OR ALONE

I say, and am prepared to prove, that it is much better to be in the company of others when you draw rather than alone, for many reasons. The first is that you will be ashamed of being seen in the ranks of the artists <note>original: "draughtsmen"</note> if you are outclassed by them, and this feeling of shame will cause you to make progress in your studies. Secondly, a commendable sense of envy will stimulate you to join the number of those who are praised more than you are, for the praise given to others will serve as a spur to you. Yet another reason is that you will acquire something of the technique <note>original: "manner"</note> of anyone whose work is better than yours; meanwhile, if you are better than the others, you will profit by seeing how to avoid their errors, and the praise of others will tend to increase your own powers.

### ON THE PROPER TIME FOR STUDYING THE SELECTION OF SUBJECTS

Youthful students should spend winter evenings studying the things prepared during the summer. That is, all the drawings of the nude which you made in the summer should be gathered together, and you should make a choice from among them of the best limbs and bodies to practice and learn by heart.

### ON POSES <note>original: "attitudes"</note>

Have him perform various graceful and elegant movements. If he fails to show his muscles very clearly within the outlines...

### HOW IT IS NECESSARY FOR THE PAINTER TO KNOW THE INNER STRUCTURE OF MAN

The painter who has acquired a knowledge of the nature of the sinews <note>In historical anatomy, "sinews" often referred collectively to tendons, ligaments, and nerves</note>, muscles, and tendons will know exactly which sinews are the cause of any movement in a limb, and which muscle, by its swelling, causes that sinew to contract. He will also know which sinews, having been transformed into very delicate cartilage, surround and contain that muscle. 

In this way, he will be able to indicate the various muscles universally in the different poses of his figures. He will not be like many painters who, in every different action, always make the same structures appear in the arm, the back, the chest, and the legs; such errors as these should not be considered minor faults.

### OF THE CHOICE OF BEAUTIFUL FACES

<margin>Manuscript 2038 National Library <note>original: "Bib. Nat." referring to the Bibliothèque Nationale de France</note> 27 r.</margin>

It seems to me no small gift in a painter to be able to give a pleasing air to his figures, and whoever is not naturally possessed of this talent may acquire it by study, as opportunity offers, in the following manner. Be on the watch to take the best parts of many beautiful faces, whose beauty is established by general reputation rather than by your own judgment alone. For you may easily deceive yourself by selecting faces that resemble your own, as it often seems that such similarities please us. If you were unattractive, you would not select beautiful faces, but would be creating ugly faces like many painters whose figures often resemble their master. Therefore, choose beautiful ones as I have said, and fix them in your mind.

If you are alone, you belong entirely to yourself; if you are accompanied even by a single companion, you belong only half to yourself—or even less, in proportion to the thoughtlessness of his conduct. If you have more than one companion, you will fall even more deeply into the same plight.

If you should say, "I will take my own course; I will retire apart so that I may be better able to investigate the forms of natural objects," then I say this is bound to turn out badly. You will not be able to prevent yourself from often lending an ear to their chatter; and since you cannot serve two masters, you will perform the duty of companionship poorly, and perform even worse the task of trying to realize your conceptions in art.

But suppose you say, "I will withdraw so far away that their words shall not reach me nor in any way disturb me." I reply that, in this case, you will be looked upon as mad—and bear in mind that in doing so, you will then be solitary anyway.

If you must have companionship, choose it from your studio; it may then help you to obtain the advantages which result from different methods of study. All other companionship may prove extremely harmful. <note>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France <note>original: "Bib. ### On the method of learning correctly how to compose groups of figures in historical paintings:

When you have thoroughly learned <term>perspective</term> <note>The mathematical system used to create the illusion of three-dimensional space on a flat surface</note>, and have fixed in your memory all the various parts and forms of things, you should often amuse yourself when you take a walk for recreation. Watch and take note of the attitudes and actions of men as they talk and dispute, or laugh or come to blows with one another—noting both their actions and those of the bystanders who either intervene or stand looking on. Note these down with rapid strokes in this way¹ in a little pocket-book, which you ought always to carry with you. ## HOW ONE OUGHT FIRST TO LEARN DILIGENCE RATHER THAN SPEED

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France <note>original: "Bib. Nat." referring to the Bibliothèque Nationale</note>, sheet 27 verso</margin>
If, as a <term>draughtsman</term> <note>a person who practices the art of drawing</note>, you wish to study well and profitably, accustom yourself when you are drawing to work slowly. Determine which among the various lights possess the highest degree and measure of brightness, and similarly for the shadows, determine which are darker than the rest and in what manner they blend together. Compare their dimensions one with another. Likewise, observe the direction of the contours, and for the lines, note which part of each is curved in one way or another, and where they are more or less prominent—and consequently thick or fine. Finally, ensure that your shadows and lights blend without visible strokes or lines, in the manner of <term>smoke</term> <note>original: "fumo," referring to "sfumato," Leonardo's technique of softening the transition between colors and tones to mimic a hazy atmosphere</note>. When you have trained your hand and judgment with this level of care, it will soon come to pass that you will no longer need to give it conscious thought.

---

## ON JUDGING YOUR OWN PICTURE

We know well that mistakes are more easily detected in the works of others than in one’s own, and that often, while criticizing the small faults of others, you will overlook your own great faults. In order to avoid such ignorance, make yourself first of all a master of <term>perspective</term> <note>the mathematical system for representing three-dimensional space on a flat surface</note>. Then, gain a complete knowledge of the <term>proportions</term> <note>the relationship in size between different parts of a body or object</note> of man and other animals. Also, make yourself a good architect—at least regarding the form of buildings and other things upon the earth, which are infinite in shape. The more knowledge you have of these, the more your work will be worthy of praise. For those things in which you have no practice, do not disdain to draw from <term>nature</term> <note>drawing from life or the physical world rather than from imagination or other artworks</note>. But to return to what was promised above, I say that when you are painting you should take a flat mirror

...and often look at your work within [a mirror], and it will then be seen in reverse. It will appear to be by the hand of some other master, and you will be better able to judge its faults than in any other way.

It is also a good plan to go away and have a little relaxation every now and then; for then, when you return to the work, your judgment will be surer. To remain constantly at work will cause you to lose your power of judgment.

It is also advisable to go some distance away, because then the work appears smaller and more of it can be taken in at a glance. In this way, a lack of harmony or proportion in the various parts and in the colors of the objects is more easily seen.

### THIS RULE OUGHT TO BE GIVEN TO STUDENTS <note>original: "Children who Paint"</note>

We know clearly that sight is one of the fastest actions that can exist, for in the same instant it surveys an infinite number of forms; nevertheless, it can only focus on one thing at a time. To take an instance: you, O Reader, might look at the whole of this written page at a glance, and you would instantly decide that it is full of various letters; but you will not recognize in this amount of time either what letters they are or what they intend to say. Therefore, it is necessary for you, if you wish to gain a knowledge of these letters, to take them word by word and line by line.

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library of France <note>original: "Bib. Nat. 28 r." referring to folio 28 recto of the Bibliothèque Nationale</note></margin>
Again, if you wish to reach the summit of a building, it will be necessary for you to ascend step by step; otherwise, it will be impossible to reach the top. So I say to you, whom nature draws toward this art, that if you would have a true knowledge of the forms of different objects, you should begin with their details. Do not pass on to the second detail until the first is well-fixed in your memory and you have practiced it. If you do otherwise, you will be throwing away time, and you will certainly prolong the period of your study. And remember to acquire **diligence** rather than <term>facility</term> <note>original: "facility," meaning the ease or speed of execution</note>.

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s technical instructions for artists, moving from the general principles of observation and study to the specific anatomical differences between humans at different stages of life, focusing on how age affects the appearance of muscles, joints, and body proportions.</meta>

<page-num>889</page-num>
<header>PRECEPTS OF THE PAINTER</header>

The appearance of the body changes not only with the size of the body but also with its age. So the limbs of youths should have few muscles and veins, and have a soft surface that is rounded and pleasing in color; in men, they should be sinewy and full of muscles; in old men, the surface should be wrinkled, rough, covered with veins, and with the sinews greatly protruding.

### How little children have joints that are the reverse of men’s in their thickness:

Little children have all their joints slender while the parts between the joints are thick. This is because the joints are only covered by skin and there is no flesh over them at all; this skin acts as a sinew to gird and bind the bones together. A flabby layer of flesh is found between one joint and the next, tucked between the skin and the bone. 

But because the bones are thicker at the joints than between them, as a man grows up he loses that excess <note>original: "superfluity"</note> of flesh that existed between the skin and the bone. Consequently, the skin is drawn nearer to the bone and causes the limbs to seem more slender. However, since there is nothing above the joints except cartilaginous and sinewy skin, this cannot dry up, and because it does not dry up, it does not shrink. For these reasons, the limbs of children are slender at the joints and thick between them—as seen in the joints of the fingers, arms, and shoulders, which are slender and have deep dimples. A man, on the contrary, has thick joints in his fingers, arms, and legs; where children have hollows, men have protruding joints.

## OF THE DIFFERENCE OF THE MEASUREMENTS IN BOYS AND MEN

I find a great difference between men and small boys in the length from one joint to another. In a man, the distance from the shoulder joint to the elbow, from the elbow to the tip of the thumb, and the width from one shoulder <term>humerus</term> to the other, is equal to the length of two heads. In a child, these distances are only equal to one head, because nature fashions the size of the seat of the intellect <note>original: "sede dell'intelletto"; referring to the head, which Leonardo observed reaches its proportional maturity much earlier than the rest of the limbs.</note> for us before that of its active members.

## HOW TO REPRESENT LIGHT AND SHADOW

First, apply a general shadow over the entire area that is not reached by light. Then, add the mid-tones <note>original: "half shadows"</note> and the deep shadows, contrasting them with one another.

<margin>National Library of France, Manuscript 2038, folio 28 verso</margin>
Similarly, apply a mid-tone to the larger areas of light, later adding the soft highlights and the brightest highlights, contrasting these in the same way.

### How to draw a head so its features are correctly positioned:

To draw a head so that its features align correctly when the head turns or bends, use this method: you know that the eyes, eyebrows, nostrils, corners of the mouth, sides of the chin, jaw, cheeks, ears, and all parts of a face are set in fixed positions on the head. Therefore, once you have sketched the face, draw lines that pass from one corner of the eye to the other; do the same for the position of every other feature. After extending these lines beyond the sides of the face, check if the spaces on the right and left sides within the same parallel lines are equal. However, I would specifically remind you that these lines must converge toward your vanishing point <note>original: "point of your vision"; Leonardo is applying the rules of linear perspective to the human face</note>.

### How to represent the eighteen actions of man:
[These are] rest, movement, and speed; standing, leaning, sitting, bending, kneeling, lying down, and hanging; carrying and being carried, pushing and dragging, striking and being struck, and pushing down and lifting up.

You should first discuss the light cast through windows, which you will call "restricted light." Then, discuss the light of a landscape, which you will call "free light" <note>This refers to ambient or outdoor light</note>. Finally, discuss the light emitted by luminous bodies <note>such as the sun, fire, or candles</note>.

*A figure is not worthy of praise unless it displays the action necessary to express the passions of the soul:*
The figure most worthy of praise is the one that, through its physical actions, best expresses the internal emotion <note>original: "passion"; in this context, it refers to any intense state of mind or "suffering" of the soul</note> that motivates it.

## HOW TO REPRESENT AN ANGRY FIGURE

An angry figure should be shown seizing someone by the hair and forcing their head down to the ground, with one knee pressed into the victim's ribs and the right arm and fist raised high. Let his hair be disheveled, his eyebrows low and knit together, and his teeth clenched. The two corners of his mouth should be arched downward, and his neck—swollen and strained as he bends over his foe—should be full of deep wrinkles <note>original: "furrows"</note>.

## HOW TO REPRESENT A MAN IN DESPAIR

You should depict a man in despair turning a knife against himself and tearing at his clothes with his hands; one hand should be shown in the act of ripping open his own wound. Show him with his feet apart, his legs slightly bent, and his entire body stooped toward the ground, with his hair torn and disheveled.

To create a figure <note>The text continues from a discussion on how to depict specific types of people.</note> which shall possess a charm of its own, you should make its limbs graceful and extended, without showing too many of the muscles. The few muscles that your purpose requires you to show should be indicated briefly—that is, without giving them prominence—and with the shadows not sharply defined. The limbs, and especially the arms, should be <term>easy</term> <note>original: "easy"; meaning natural, relaxed, or fluid in motion</note>, so that no limb is in a perfectly straight line with the part that adjoins it. If the hips, which form the <term>poles of the man</term> <note>Leonardo views the hips as the central axis or pivot points of the human frame</note>, are positioned so that the right hip is higher than the left, you should position the top shoulder-joint so that a line drawn perpendicularly from it falls on the most prominent part of the hip; and let this right shoulder be lower than the left.

And let the pit of the throat always be positioned exactly over the middle of the ankle joint of the foot which is resting on the ground. The leg which does not support the weight should have its knee lower than the other and near to the supporting leg.

The possible positions of the head and arms are infinite, and therefore I will not attempt to give any specific rule; it will suffice that they should be natural and pleasing, bending and turning in various ways with the joints moving freely so that they do not look like rigid pieces of wood.

## HOW A CAST SHADOW IS NEVER EQUAL IN SIZE TO THE OBJECT THAT CAUSES IT

<margin>National Library of France <note>original: "Bib. Nat." (Bibliothèque Nationale de France)</note>, Manuscript 2038, folio 29 verso</margin>

As experience shows, if luminous rays come from a single point and travel in the form of a sphere radiating and spreading out from this point through the air, the farther they go, the more they disperse. Therefore, an object placed between the light and the wall is always reproduced larger in its shadow, because the rays that strike the object have spread out even further by the time they reach the wall.

## ON THE ARRANGEMENT OF THE LIMBS

As regards the arrangement of the limbs, you should bear in mind that when you wish to represent someone who happens to be turning either backward or to one side, you must not make him move his feet and all his limbs in the same direction that he turns his head. Instead, you should show the movement distributed across the joints...

You should show the movement <note>original: "process"; here referring to the physical adjustment of the body as it shifts its weight</note> spreading itself and taking effect over the four sets of joints, namely those of the foot, the knee, the hip, and the neck. If you let the figure's weight rest on the right leg, you should make the left knee bend inwards. Its foot should be slightly raised on the outside, and the left shoulder should be somewhat lower than the right. The nape of the neck should be positioned exactly above the outer curve of the ankle of the left foot, and the left shoulder should be directly above the toe of the right foot in a perpendicular line. 

Always arrange your figures so that the direction in which the head is turned is not the same as the direction the chest faces. Nature has, for our convenience, formed the neck so that it can easily serve the various needs of the eye when it desires to look in different directions, and the other joints are partly responsive to this same movement. Furthermore, if you ever show a man sitting with his hands working on something by his side, make the chest turn upon the hip joints.

## CONCERNING THE SHADOW CAST BY A BODY PLACED BETWEEN TWO EQUAL LIGHTS

A body that is placed between two equal lights will cast two shadows, which will follow the paths of the two lights equally. If you move the body farther away or bring it nearer to one of the lights, the shadow that points toward the nearer light will be less intense <note>original: "deep"</note> than the one pointing toward the more distant light.

## THE BODY NEARER TO THE LIGHT WILL CAST THE LARGER SHADOW, AND WHY

If an object placed in front of a specific light is very close to it, you will see it cast a very large shadow on the opposite wall. The farther you move the object from the light, the smaller the shadow will become.

## WHY A SHADOW WHICH IS LARGER THAN THE OBJECT CAUSING IT WILL BE DISPROPORTIONATE

### WHY A SHADOW WHICH IS BIGGER THAN THE BODY THAT CAUSES IT HAS BLURRY EDGES

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library, 30 r.</margin>
The atmosphere surrounding a light almost takes on the nature of that light in its brightness and warmth; the further away it recedes, the more it loses this resemblance. An object that casts a large shadow is positioned near the light and is therefore lit up by both the light itself and the glowing <note>original: "luminous"</note> atmosphere. Consequently, this atmosphere makes the edges <note>original: "contours"</note> of the shadow look indistinct.

### THE WAY TO REPRESENT A BATTLE

First, show the smoke of the cannons <note>original: "artillery"</note> mingled in the air with the dust stirred up by the movement of the horses and the fighters <note>original: "combatants"</note>. You should depict this process as follows: Since dust is made of earth, it has weight. Although its fineness allows it to easily rise and mix with the air, it will nevertheless readily fall back down. The greatest height will be reached by the finest dust; consequently, that part will be the least visible and will appear almost the color of the air itself.

The smoke that is mixed with the dust-laden air will look more and more like a dark cloud as it rises to a certain height. At the peak of this cloud, the smoke will be more clearly visible than the dust. The smoke will take on a bluish tint, while the dust will keep its natural color. From the side where the light comes, this mixture of air, smoke, and dust will appear far brighter than on the opposite side.

As for the fighters, the more they are in the middle of this chaos <note>original: "turmoil"</note>, the less visible they will be, and the less contrast there will be between their highlights and shadows.

You should give a reddish <note>original: "ruddy"</note> glow to the faces, the figures, and the air around them—especially to the gunners and those near them. This glow should grow fainter as it moves further away from its source. The figures positioned between you and the light, if they are far away, will appear

## HOW SMALL FIGURES SHOULD CONSEQUENTLY BE LEFT UNFINISHED

I state that when objects appear very small in size, it is because those objects are at a great distance from the eye. When this is the case, there must necessarily be a considerable amount of atmosphere between the eye and the object. This atmosphere interferes with the clarity of the objects' shapes; consequently, the tiny details of these bodies will become impossible to distinguish or recognize.

Therefore, painter, you should make your smaller figures only suggested, and not highly finished. If you do otherwise, you will produce effects that contradict those of nature, who is your mistress <note>In this context, Leonardo refers to nature as the artist's ultimate teacher and authority.</note>.

An object appears small because of the great distance between it and the eye. This large space contains a great quantity of atmosphere, and this atmosphere forms a dense body that interposes itself and hides the minute details of objects from the eye.

## WHAT BACKGROUND A PAINTER SHOULD CHOOSE FOR HIS WORKS

Since experience shows that all bodies are surrounded by shadow and light, it is practical, painter, for you to arrange the illuminated part so that it is outlined against a dark object, and in the same way, the shadowed part of the body should be outlined against a bright object. This rule will be a great help to you in giving relief <term>relief</term> <note>The illusion of three-dimensional depth, solidity, and "pop" on a flat surface.</note> to your figures.

## ON DRAWING

When you draw from nature, stand three times as far away as the size of the object you are drawing.

Kind nature provides so well that you will find something worth imitating everywhere in the world.

## ON SHADOW

Where a shadow meets the light, observe carefully where it is lighter or darker, and where it becomes more or less blurred as it moves toward the light. Above all, I remind you that when painting youthful figures, you should not make the shadows end abruptly like the edges of a stone. Flesh has a slight transparency, which you can see for yourself by holding your hand between your eyes and the sun; the hand will appear to glow red with a luminous transparency.

The area with the most vivid color should be placed between the highlights and the shadows. If you want to determine the proper depth of shadow needed for flesh, cast a shadow over your work with your finger. By holding your finger closer to or farther away from the picture to make the shadow darker or lighter, you can then copy that exact tone.

## HOW TO DEPICT A WILD LANDSCAPE

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library, 31 verso <note>original: "MS. 2038 Bib. Nat. 31 v." "Verso" refers to the back side of a page in a manuscript.</note></margin>
Trees and shrubs that are divided into many thin branches should have less dense shadows. Conversely, trees and shrubs with larger leaves cast a deeper, more solid shadow.

## HOW TO ARRANGE THE LIGHTING ON FIGURES

The arrangement of light should harmonize with the natural conditions in which you are representing your figure. For instance, if you are depicting a scene in sunlight, make the shadows dark with large areas of bright light, and include the shadows cast by all surrounding objects upon the ground. 

If you represent a figure in dull or overcast weather, create only a slight difference between the lights and shadows, and do not place a distinct shadow at the feet. If you represent a figure indoors, create a strong contrast between the lights and shadows and show the shadow cast on the ground. However, if you are depicting a room where the light comes through a window covered by a curtain and the wall is white, there should be very little difference between the lights and the shadows. 

If the scene is lit by a fire, you should make the light reddish and powerful and the shadows dark; these shadows should be sharply defined where they strike the walls or the floor, and the

...the further they extend away from the body, the broader and larger they should become. If a figure is lit partly by fire and partly by the atmosphere <note>meaning natural daylight</note>, make the part lit by the atmosphere the stronger, and let the part lit by the fire be almost as red as the fire itself. Above all, ensure that the figures you paint have sufficient light coming from above—specifically for all living people you depict. This is because people you see in the streets are always lit from above; I want you to know that even with your most intimate acquaintance, you would find it difficult to recognize them if the light fell on them from below.

## THE ORDER OF LEARNING TO DRAW

First, copy drawings by a skilled master that were created through his art from nature, rather than mere exercises. Next, draw from a relief <note>a sculpture or carving where the forms stand out from a flat background</note>, while keeping a drawing done from that same relief by your side for comparison. Finally, draw from a good model; you should make a regular practice of this.

## AT WHAT HEIGHT THE LIGHT SHOULD BE IN ORDER TO DRAW FROM NATURE

When you are drawing from nature, the light should come from the north so that it does not vary. If the light comes from the south, keep the window covered with a curtain so that even if the sun shines on it all day, the light will undergo no change. The height of the light source should be positioned so that every object casts a shadow on the ground that is exactly as long as the object is tall <note>this creates a 45-degree angle of light, which Leonardo considered ideal for defining form</note>.

## WHY BEAUTIFUL COLORS SHOULD BE IN THE LIGHTS

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library, 33 recto <note>original: "ms. 2038 Bib. Nat. 33 r." "Recto" refers to the front side of a page in a manuscript.</note></margin>
Since we can see that the quality of colors is revealed by light, it follows that the true quality of a color will be most visible where the light is strongest. Conversely, where there is the most shadow, the color will be most affected by the color of that shadow. Therefore, painter, be careful to show the true quality of colors in the parts of your work that are in the light.

### OF LIGHT AND SHADE

Every part of an object’s surface is partially influenced by the color of whatever is opposite to it.

->*Example*<-

If you place a spherical object <note>Leonardo often used spheres as the primary model for studying how light and shadow wrap around curved forms</note> among different items—for example, with sunlight on one side and a sunlit wall on the other (which might be green or another color), resting on a red surface with dark sides—you will see the natural color of that object take on the hues of the colors facing it. The strongest hue will be the one coming from the direct light; the second strongest will come from the illuminated wall; and the third will be that of the shadow. However, there will still be a portion of the object that takes its tint from the color of the edges.

The greatest misfortune is when theory outstrips performance <note>original: "when theory outstrips performance"—Leonardo is warning that an artist's intellectual understanding of art should not exceed their technical ability to execute it</note>.

When choosing figures, aim for softness and delicacy rather than making them appear stiff and wooden.

### HOW THE CONDITION OF THE ATMOSPHERE AFFECTS THE LIGHTS AND SHADOWS

An object will show the strongest contrast between its highlights and shadows when viewed under the strongest light, such as direct sunlight or, at night, the light of a fire. However, this should rarely be used in painting because the work will appear harsh and lacking in grace.

An object in moderate light will have very little difference between its highlights and shadows. This occurs at dusk or when the sky is cloudy. Works painted in such light are soft in feeling, and every kind of face gains a certain charm.

Thus, in every way, extremes are harmful. An excess of light makes things appear harsh,¹ and too much darkness prevents us from seeing them. The middle ground is excellent.

---

¹ The manuscript reads *il tropo lume fa crudo* <note>original Italian: "excessive light makes things harsh"</note>. Dr. Richter agrees with this. The text by M. Ravaisson-Mollien uses the word *facendo* <note>meaning "making"</note> instead of *fa crudo*.

<summary>Leonardo explains how surfaces reflect the colors of their surroundings and argues that moderate, soft lighting—like that of dusk—is superior to harsh sunlight for creating graceful paintings.</summary>

### OF SMALL LIGHTS

<margin>Manuscript 2038, National Library, folio 33 v. <note>original: "Bib. Nat." refers to the Bibliothèque Nationale in Paris</note></margin>
Light shining from small windows creates a harsh contrast between light and shadow, especially if the room being lit is large; this effect is not ideal for use in painting.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 76 r. a <note>The Codex Atlanticus (C.A.) is the largest collection of Leonardo’s drawings and writings</note></margin>
The painter who draws by habit and the judgment of the eye alone, without using reason, is like a mirror: it reflects every object placed before it without having any knowledge of them.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 111 v. b</margin>
A face in a painting that looks directly at the artist who creates it will always appear to be looking at every spectator. Furthermore, a figure painted as if seen from above will always appear that way, even if the viewer’s eye is positioned lower than the painting itself.

### OF THE PARTS OF THE FACE

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 119 v. a</margin>
If nature used only one fixed standard for facial proportions, then all human faces would resemble each other so closely that it would be impossible to tell them apart. Instead, she has varied the five parts of the face <note>Leonardo likely refers to the forehead, eyes, nose, mouth, and chin</note> in such a way that while there is an almost universal standard for their size, she has varied them enough across different individuals so that everyone remains clearly distinguishable.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 122 v. a</margin>
Just as a body moving slowly through a long, opposing arc covers more space and delivers a stronger impact—whereas quick, short movements have little power—so too does studying the same subject at long intervals of time make one's judgment more perfect and better able to recognize its own mistakes. The same principle applies when a painter steps back to look at their work from a distance.

A painting or any representation of figures should be executed in such a way that the viewers can easily recognize from—

Similarly, if you have to represent a violent man, show him with aggressive movements, flinging his arms toward his listener; his head and chest should lean forward beyond his feet, appearing to follow the speaker's hands.

In this way, a deaf-mute who sees two people talking—though unable to hear—is still able to understand the subject of their discussion through the movements and gestures of the speakers.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 139 r. d</margin>
I once saw a man in Florence who had become deaf. He could not understand you if you spoke to him loudly, but if you spoke softly without letting your voice make any sound, he understood you merely from the movement of your lips. Perhaps, however, you will say to me: "But does a man who speaks loudly not move his lips just like one who speaks softly? And since one moves his lips like the other, will he not be understood the same way?" As to this, I leave the decision to the test of experience. Have someone speak softly and then more loudly, and watch their lips closely.

### How Painting Declines Over Time When Painters Rely Only on Existing Works

A painter will produce work of little value if he takes the works of others as his standard; but if he applies himself to learn from the objects of nature, he will produce excellent results. We see that this was the case with the painters who lived after the time of the Romans; they continually imitated each other, and from age to age, their art steadily declined.

After these came Giotto the Florentine. Raised in the solitude of the mountains inhabited only by goats and similar beasts, he turned directly from nature to his art. He began to draw the movements of the goats he was herding upon the rocks, and he began to draw the figures of all the animals found in the countryside. After much study, he not only surpassed the masters of his own day but all those of many preceding centuries. After him, art declined once more, because everyone imitated the pictures that had already been painted.

<summary>Leonardo emphasizes that physical gestures must reveal a character's internal state and argues that the history of art shows a cycle of decline whenever painters prioritize imitating previous masters over studying nature itself.</summary>

I would say the same about these mathematical subjects: those who study only the authorities <note>By "authorities," Leonardo means the established scholars or ancient texts rather than original research.</note> and not the works of nature are, in art, the grandsons and not the sons of nature, which is the supreme guide of the good authorities themselves.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 141 recto b</margin>
Notice the supreme folly of those who criticize people for learning from nature, yet leave uncriticized the "authorities" who were themselves the disciples of that very same nature!

## ON COMPOSING HISTORICAL SCENES <note>original: "historical subjects," referring to large-scale narrative paintings of history, mythology, or scripture.</note>

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 160 recto a</margin>
On not neglecting the limbs of the figures in historical scenes, as many do who, in the process of making whole figures, ruin their arrangement. When you place figures one behind another, make sure you draw them in their entirety. This ensures that the limbs which are seen appearing beyond the surface of the first figure retain their natural length and position.

When a running man wishes to exhaust the momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note> that is carrying him forward, he prepares an opposing force by leaning backward. This can be proven: if the momentum carries the moving body forward with a force of four, and the impulse of the moving body to turn and lean back also has a force of four, one force will neutralize the other opposing one, and so the momentum is used up.

## THE LIFE OF THE PAINTER IN THE COUNTRY

A painter requires such knowledge of mathematics as is relevant to painting, and separation from companions who do not share an interest in his studies. His mind should have the power of adapting itself to the nature of the objects that appear before it, and he should be free from all other worries. 

If, while considering and examining one subject, a second should interrupt—as happens when a new idea occupies the mind—he ought to decide which of these subjects is more difficult to investigate and follow that one until it becomes entirely clear, and only afterward pursue the investigation of the other. Above all, he should keep his mind as clear as the surface of a mirror, which changes to as many different colors as the objects reflected within it. His companions should resemble him in their love for these studies; if he fails to find any such people, he should get used to being alone in his research, for in the end, he will find no more profitable companionship than his own.
<sig>Codex Atlanticus, folio 184 verso c</sig>

## OF THE ORDER TO BE OBSERVED IN STUDY

I say that one ought first to learn about the limbs and how they function <note>original: "how they are worked," referring to the mechanical and anatomical movement of muscles and joints.</note>. After completing this knowledge, one should study their actions in the different situations in which people are placed. Thirdly, one should design figure compositions <note>original: "histories," meaning narrative paintings of historical or biblical scenes.</note>; the studies for these should be taken from natural actions observed as opportunities arise. One should be constantly observant in the streets, squares, and fields...

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 199 verso a</margin>
My opponent argues that in order to gain experience and learn how to work quickly, it is better for the first period of study to be spent copying various compositions made by different masters, either on paper or on walls, because one acquires speed in execution and a good technique from these. But to this it may be replied that such a method would only be good if it were based on works that were excellent in composition and made by diligent masters. Since such masters are so rare that few can be found, it is safer to go directly to the works of nature than to those which have been imitated from her originals with great deterioration—and thereby acquire a bad technique. For he who has access to the fountain does not go to the water jar <note>original: "water-pot"</note>.

These rules are to be used solely for testing figures; for every man makes certain mistakes in his first compositions, and if he does not become aware of them, he cannot correct them. Therefore, to discover mistakes, you should test your work, and where you find those errors, correct them—and remember never to fall into them again. However, if you were to attempt to apply all these rules while actually composing, you would never even get started and would only cause confusion in your work.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 221 verso d</margin>
These rules are intended to help you develop a free and sound judgment; for good judgment proceeds from good understanding, and good understanding comes from reason trained by good rules, and good rules are the children of sound experience, which is the common mother of all the sciences and arts. If, therefore, you keep the precepts of my rules well in mind, you will be able, simply through the accuracy of your judgment, to criticize and identify every error in proportion in any work, whether it is in the perspective, the figures, or other elements.

The limbs of every kind of animal should correspond to its age. That is, young animals should not show their veins or tendons <note>original: "nerves"; in the 15th century, "nerves" often referred to tendons or ligaments as well as actual nerves</note> as most <gloss>painters</gloss> do in order to show off their skill <note>original: "dexterity"</note> in art, ruining the whole work with mistakes in the limbs.

Every part of an animal should correspond with the whole; for instance, when a man is short and thickset, you must ensure that each of his limbs is also short and thickset.

The movements of men should be depicted in a way that is appropriate to their social standing—whether they possess dignity or are of low status <note>original: "meanness"</note>.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 349 recto b</margin>
Ensure your work aligns with your purpose and design. When you create a figure, you should carefully consider who the person is and what you intend for them to be doing.

To depict a similar action in a painting of an old man and a young man, you must make the young man's movement appear more vigorous, reflecting how much more powerful he is than the elderly man. You should apply this same logic when comparing a young man to an infant.

If you have to depict a man moving, lifting, pulling, or carrying a weight equal to his own, how should you position the legs beneath his body?

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 354 recto d</margin>
Painters often deceive themselves when representing water by showing only what a person sees. However, the water "sees" the object from one angle, while the person sees it from another. It frequently happens that the painter sees a thing from above, while the water reflects it from below. Thus, the same body is seen from the front and back, or above and below, because the water reflects the image of the object in one way while the eye perceives it in another.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 375 recto c</margin>
We consider someone with a very large head and short legs to be a monstrosity; likewise, we see it as a monstrosity when someone in great poverty wears rich garments. Therefore, we should consider a person well-proportioned only when their parts are in harmony with the whole.

When you draw nudes, be careful to always sketch the whole figure first. Then, finish whichever limb seems the best, while simultaneously studying its relationship to the other limbs. Otherwise, you may develop the habit of never properly connecting the limbs together.

### OF SHADOWS AND LIGHTS

You who reproduce the works of nature: observe the dimensions, the degrees of intensity, and the shapes of the lights and shadows of every muscle. Note along the length of the figures which muscle they are directed toward by the axis of their central lines. <margin>Manuscript E, folio 3 recto</margin>

### OF THE BACKGROUND OF THE FIGURES IN PAINTING

The background that surrounds the figures in any composition should be darker than the illuminated parts of those figures, and lighter than the parts that are in shadow. <margin>Manuscript E, folio 4 recto</margin>

Every part of a whole should be in proportion to the whole body. For instance, if a man has a short, thickset figure, he should be the same in every one of his limbs—that is, with short, thick arms, large hands, and thick, short fingers with joints of the same character. The same principle applies to the rest of the body.

### HOW TO PAINT WIND

In representing wind, besides showing the bending of the branches and the flipping over of their leaves as the wind approaches, you should also represent the clouds of fine dust mingled with the turbulent air.

### THE ESSENTIALS OF PAINTING

The first essential of painting is that the bodies it represents should appear in <term>relief</term> <note>original: "relief"; a technique where objects appear three-dimensional, standing out from the flat background</note>. The scenes surrounding them, which create the effect of distance, should appear to recede into the surface where the picture is produced. This is achieved through the three parts of perspective: the reduction in the sharpness of an object's form, the reduction in its size, and the fading of its color. Of these three divisions of perspective, the first originates in the eye itself, while the other two result from the atmosphere positioned between the eye and the objects being viewed.

The second essential of painting is that the actions should be appropriate and the figures should be varied, so that the men do not all look as if they were brothers.

### ON VARIETY IN FIGURES

A painter should strive to be <term>universal</term> <note>original: "universal"; meaning a painter should be capable of depicting all subjects of nature, not just a single specialty like the human form</note>. There is a great lack of dignity in doing one thing well and another poorly, as is the case with many who study only the measurements and proportions of the nude figure and do not seek variety. After all, a man may be correctly proportioned and yet still be fat and short, tall and thin, or medium-sized. Anyone who does not take these variations into account will always create figures from a single mold, making them all look like sisters; this practice deserves severe criticism.

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci outlines the three types of perspective—form, size, and color—and emphasizes that a "universal" painter must master variety in human figures to avoid repetitive, identical characters.</summary>

## ON THE METHOD FOR ACHIEVING THIS UNIVERSALITY

It is an easy matter for anyone who knows how to depict the human form to later achieve this <term>universality</term> <note>original: "universality"; meaning the ability to paint all aspects of nature, rather than specializing in only one subject</note>. This is because all land animals resemble each other in their limbs—specifically in their muscles, tendons, and bones—and they do not vary at all except in length or thickness, as will be demonstrated in the section on <term>anatomy</term> <note>referring to Leonardo’s extensive anatomical studies and drawings</note>. There are also aquatic animals, of which there are many different kinds; however, I do not advise the painter to establish a fixed standard for these, as they possess an almost infinite variety. The same is also true of the insect world.

## DEPICTING A GREAT FLOOD

The air was dark from the heavy rain falling at an angle, driven by conflicting winds. It formed waves in the air much like the drifts seen in blowing dust, with the only difference being that these air-drifts were streaked by the lines of falling raindrops. The scene was tinted by the color of fire produced by the lightning strikes that tore the clouds asunder. These flashes struck and split open the vast waters of the flooded valleys, revealing in their depths¹ the bowed tops of submerged trees.

<term>Neptune</term> <note>The Roman god of the sea</note> might be seen with his trident in the midst of the waters, and <term>Aeolus</term> <note>The Greek god of the winds</note> with his winds should be depicted entangling the floating trees, which had been uprooted and mixed into the massive waves.

The horizon and the entire sky were overcast and glowed with the flashes of continuous lightning.

Men and birds could be seen huddling together on the tall trees that rose above the swollen waters, which formed hills surrounding the great depths.

## ON THE ERROR COMMITTED BY THOSE WHO PRACTICE WITHOUT SCIENCE¹

Those who are in love with practice without science are like a pilot who boards a ship without a rudder or a compass, and who therefore can never be certain where he is going.

<margin>G 8 r.</margin>
Practice should always be built upon a sound knowledge of theory, for which <term>perspective</term> <note>The mathematical science of representing three-dimensional objects on a two-dimensional surface to create the illusion of depth</note> is the guide and the gateway; without it, nothing can be executed well in any kind of painting.

### Concerning the light on the lower limbs of bodies packed closely together, such as men in battle:

When depicting men and horses struggling in battle, their various parts should be darker the closer they are to the ground. This is proven by the sides of wells, which grow darker as they get deeper; this happens because the lowest part of a well "sees" (and is reached by) less of the luminous atmosphere than any other part of it. Furthermore, when the pavement is the same color as the legs of the men and horses, the ground will always appear to be in brighter light—when viewed at equal angles—than the legs themselves.
<margin>G 15 r.</margin>

## HOW TO JUDGE A PAINTER’S WORK

First, you should consider whether the figures possess the <term>relief</term> <note>original: "relief"; the illusion of three-dimensional depth that makes a figure appear to stand out from the flat surface</note> required by their position and the light illuminating them. The shadows should not be the same at the edges of the composition as they are in the center, because it is one thing for a figure to be surrounded by shadows and another for it to have shadows on only one side. 

Figures positioned toward the center of the composition are surrounded by shadows because they are shaded by the dark figures standing between them and the light source. On the other hand, those figures positioned between the light and the main group are shaded on only one side; where they do not face the light, they face the group and reflect the darkness cast by that group, and where they do not face the group, they face the brightness of the light and reflect its radiance.

Secondly, you should consider whether the distribution or arrangement of the figures is designed in a way that matches the circumstances of the action you wish to represent.

Thirdly, observe whether the figures are actively and convincingly engaged in their intended purpose.

<margin>G 23 v.</margin>
### ON PAINTING

A very important part of painting involves the backgrounds of the subjects depicted. Against these backgrounds, the <term>contour lines</term> <note>The outer edges or outlines that define the shape of an object</note> of physical bodies with <term>convex</term> <note>Outward-curving</note> curves will always reveal the shapes of those bodies, even if the colors of the bodies are the same hue as the background.

This occurs because the outward-curving boundaries of objects are not illuminated in the same way as the background, even when they are hit by the same light source. Consequently, these outlines are frequently either lighter or darker than the background itself.

However, if these outlines were to be the exact same color and brightness as the background, that part of the picture would undoubtedly make it difficult to perceive the figure formed by those contour lines. A skilled painter must use their judgment to avoid such a predicament, since the painter’s goal is to make their figures appear to stand out from the background. In the instance mentioned above, the opposite happens—not only in the painting but also in physical objects in <term>relief</term> <note>Three-dimensional carvings or sculptures</note>.

<margin>G 25 r.</margin>
### SIGNS THAT A YOUTH HAS AN APTITUDE FOR PAINTING

There are many people who have a desire and love for drawing but no natural talent for it. This can be identified in children if they are not diligent and never finish their practice sketches with proper shading.

A painter does not deserve praise if they only do one thing well—such as the nude figure, a head, drapery, animals, landscapes, or any other specific subject. There is no one so dull of understanding that they would fail to do one thing well after devoting themselves to that single subject and practicing it constantly.

### *[The representation of things in movement]*

On the imitation of things that move in one place but do not reveal their true form while in motion.

<margin>G 35 r.</margin>
Drops of falling rain, a spindle, a spinning wheel, stones caught in rushing water, and firebrands <note>Burning sticks or torches</note> whirled in a circle all appear to move continuously, even though they are among things that are not in a state of constant, uniform motion.

## THE BOUNDARIES OF BODIES ARE THE SMALLEST OF ALL THINGS

The truth of this proposition is proved by the fact that the boundary of a physical substance is a surface. This surface is neither a part of the body it encloses, nor a part of the atmosphere surrounding that body; rather, it is the medium positioned between the atmosphere and the body, as has been proven in its proper place.

<margin>G 37 r.</margin>
However, the lateral boundaries <note>The side edges or outlines</note> of these bodies are merely the boundary line of the surface, and a line has no thickness. Therefore, O painter, do not surround your bodies with outlines—especially when painting objects smaller than their natural size. For in such cases, not only are the lateral boundaries impossible to see, but their individual parts will also be invisible due to the distance.

## ON PAINTING

<margin>H 90 [42] v.</margin>
The highlights or the <term>lustre</term> <note>The shine or reflection on a glossy surface</note> of any particular object will not remain fixed in the center of the illuminated part; instead, the highlights will shift their position as often as the eye of the person beholding them moves.

<margin>I 48 v.</margin>
Painters have an excellent opportunity to observe human actions by watching players, especially during games of ball, tennis, or those played with a mallet <note>Likely referring to pall-mall, a precursor to croquet</note> when they are competing. These offer better observations than almost any other place or exercise.

<margin>I 92 [44] v.</margin>
It is the <term>extremities</term> <note>The outer edges, hands, or feet</note> of all things that give them either grace or a lack of grace.

<margin>K 110 [30] v.</margin>
Men and words are real, and you, painter, if you do not know how to compose your figures, will be like an orator <note>A public speaker or rhetorician</note> who does not know how to use his words.

<meta>This page continues Leonardo da Vinci’s technical instructions for painters, focusing on the anatomical knowledge required to paint the human form accurately and the complex behavior of light and drapery.</meta>

<page-num>913</page-num>
<header>PRECEPTS OF THE PAINTER</header>

<margin>L 79 r.</margin>
It is necessary for a painter to understand the anatomy of the sinews, bones, muscles, and tendons in order to correctly depict limbs in the various positions and actions they perform when nude. By knowing this, the artist learns which sinew or muscle causes each specific movement and impulse, allowing them to emphasize and thicken only those specific parts. They should not make every muscle bulge across the entire limb, as many artists do. In an effort to appear like great draftsmen <note>original: "draughtsmen"</note>, these painters make their nudes look stiff and ungraceful; as a result, their figures look more like a sack of nuts than a human form, or like a bundle of radishes rather than the natural muscles of a nude figure.

<margin>M 80 r.</margin>
In everything that is seen, one must consider three factors: the position of the eye that sees, the position of the object being seen, and the position of the light that illuminates that body.

<margin>B.M. 44 r.</margin>
<insert>[With sketch]</insert>

In the outer folds of any joint, everything that was raised <note>original: "in relief"</note> becomes a hollow when the limb moves. Similarly, every hollow in those folds turns into a protrusion <note>original: "protuberance"</note> when the end of the limb is straightened.

An artist who does not understand this often makes major errors by relying too much on their own skill rather than turning to the imitation of nature. Such variations are found more on the sides of the body than in the front, and more in the back than on the sides.

<margin>Forster III 44 v.</margin>
The painter competes with and rivals nature.

<insert>[On draperies]</insert>

There should be variety in the subjects. Draperies should be thin, thick, new, or old, with folds that are broken or pleated. Use clear and soft lights <note>original: *cride dolci*</note>, as well as dark shadows and lighter shadows, with or without reflections, making them distinct or blurry depending on the distance and various colors. 

Clothing should also reflect the social rank of those wearing them—long or short, fluttering or stiff, in accordance with their movement. The garments should wrap around the figures so that they bend or flutter, with the ends streaming upward or downward according to the folds. They should cling close to the feet or flow away from them, depending on whether the legs are shown at rest, bending, twisting, or striking together. The cloth should either fit tightly or pull away from the joints.

## ON A FLOOD AND ITS REPRESENTATION IN PAINTING

Let the dark, gloomy air be seen buffeted by the rush of opposing winds, wreathed in perpetual rain mixed with hail, and carrying here and there a vast network of torn tree branches mixed together with an infinite number of leaves. All around, let ancient trees be seen uprooted and torn to pieces by the fury of the winds. You should show how fragments of mountains, which have already been stripped bare by rushing torrents, fall headlong into these very torrents and choke up the valleys, until the dammed-up rivers rise in flood and overflow.

Ah me, how many lamentations! How many, in their terror, flung themselves down from the rocks! How many boats were capsized and lying—some whole, others broken in pieces—on top of men struggling to escape with actions and gestures of despair that foretold an awful...

## DESCRIPTION OF THE DELUGE

First of all, let there be represented the summit of a rugged mountain with some of the valleys that surround its base. On its sides, let the surface of the soil be seen slipping down along with the tiny roots of small shrubs, leaving bare a large portion of the surrounding rocks. Sweeping down in devastation from these precipices, let the soil pursue its headlong course, striking and exposing the twisted and gnarled roots of the great trees and overturning them in ruin. 

The mountains, as they become bare, should reveal the deep fissures <note>original: "fissures," meaning deep cracks or crevices</note> made in them by ancient earthquakes. Let the bases of the mountains be largely covered and buried under the debris of the shrubs which have fallen headlong from the sides of the high peaks of those mountains; let these be mixed together with mud, roots, and branches of trees...

...with various kinds of leaves pressed in among the mud, earth, and stones. Let the fragments of some of the mountains have fallen into the depths of one of the valleys, forming a barrier to the swollen waters of its river. These waters, having already burst the barrier, rush onward with immense waves, the greatest of which are striking and laying to ruin the walls of the cities and farms in the valley. From the ruins of the tall buildings of these cities, let a great quantity of dust rise up, mounting into the air with the appearance of smoke or of swirling clouds that battle against the falling rain.

The swollen waters should be swirling around the pool that contains them, striking against various obstacles with whirling eddies and leaping up into the air in muddy <note>original: "turbid," meaning thick or opaque with suspended matter</note> foam. Then, as it falls back, the water causes the surface where it strikes to be dashed up into the air. The circling waves that recede from the point of contact are driven by their momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note> right across the course of other circling waves moving in the opposite direction. After striking against these, they leap up into the air without becoming detached from their base.

And where the water flows out from this pool, the dying waves are seen spreading toward the outlet. After this, as it falls or descends through the air, the water gains weight and momentum. Then, piercing the water where it strikes, it tears the surface apart and plunges violently to reach the bottom. Rebounding, it springs back again toward the surface of the lake, accompanied by the air that was submerged with it. This air remains in the sticky <note>original: "visscichosa," a variation of the Italian word "vischiosa," meaning viscous or slimy</note> foam, mingled with driftwood and other things lighter than the water. Around these objects, the beginnings of new waves are formed, which increase in circumference as they move further away. This movement makes the waves lower as they acquire a wider base, and therefore they become almost invisible as they die away. But if the waves rebound against various obstacles, then they leap back and oppose the approach of the other waves, following the same laws of physics in their curves as they showed in their original movement. The rain, as it falls from the clouds, is the same color as those clouds—at least on its shaded side—unless, however, the rays of the sun...

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s "Description of the Deluge," focusing on the physics of water impact, the formation of mist and clouds from spray, and the movement of survivors toward higher ground.</meta>

<page-num>919</page-num>
<header>PRECEPTS OF THE PAINTER</header>

...should penetrate there; for if this were so, the rain would appear less dark than the cloud. If the great masses of debris from huge mountains or large buildings strike mighty lakes as they fall, then a vast quantity of water will rebound into the air. Its course will be in the opposite direction to that of the object which struck the water—that is to say, the angle of reflection will be equal to the angle of incidence <note>The law of reflection: the angle at which an object hits a surface (incidence) is the same as the angle at which it bounces off (reflection).</note>.

Of the objects carried along by the current, those that are heavier or larger will be at a greater distance from the two opposite banks. The water's eddies revolve most swiftly in the parts closest to their center. The crests of the sea waves fall forward toward their base, beating and rubbing against the smooth particles that form their face. By this friction, the falling water is ground into tiny particles ¹ <note>original: "minute particles"</note> and turns into a thick mist. This mist mingles with the wind currents like swirling smoke or winding clouds, eventually rising into the air and becoming clouds. 

But the rain falling through the air, being beaten and driven by the wind currents, becomes thin or dense according to the thinness or density <note>original: "rarity or density"</note> of these winds. In this way, a flood of transparent clouds is produced throughout the air, formed by the aforementioned rain. These clouds become visible within it because of the lines made by the falling rain near the spectator's eye.² The waves of the sea, beating against the sloping <note>original: "shelving"</note> base of the mountains that confine it, rush ³ foaming and fast up to the ridges of those same hills. Turning back, they meet the onset of the next wave and, after a loud roaring, return in a mighty flood to the sea from which they came. Many inhabitants—both humans and various animals—may be seen driven by the rising deluge toward the summits of the hills bordering these waters.

# XXX
## Colour

> ‘Adjust the perspective of colors so that it does not conflict with the size of an object; that is, ensure that colors lose part of their natural character in the same proportion that objects at various distances lose their perceived size <note>original: "natural quantity"</note>.’

### OF COLOURS

Among objects of equal whiteness, the one on the darkest background will seem the most dazzling, and black will seem most intense when it is placed against a background of greater whiteness.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 184 verso, c</margin>
Red will also appear most vivid when set against a yellow background; the same principle applies to all colors when they are placed against those that provide the sharpest contrasts.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 262 recto, c</margin>
The whiter an object is, the more it will be tinted <note>original: "tinged"</note> with the color of the illuminated or luminous object reflecting upon it.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 305 recto, a</margin>
However, in the far distance, the object that is naturally darkest in color will appear to be the most blue. <note>This refers to Leonardo's discovery of "aerial perspective," where the atmosphere makes distant dark objects, like mountains, appear blue.</note>

Every object that has no color of its own is tinted either entirely or in part by the color of the object placed opposite to it. This can be seen through experience, for every object that serves as a mirror is tinted with the color of the thing reflected in it. If a white object is partially tinted, the portion of it illuminated by red will appear red, and the same applies to every other color, whether it be light or dark.

<margin>Manuscript A, folio 19 verso</margin>
Every opaque object that lacks its own color takes on the color of whatever is opposite to it, as happens with a white wall.

[*A discussion on the colors of shadows*]

## PAINTING

Colors seen in shadow will reveal more or less of their natural beauty in proportion to whether they are in faint or deep shadow.

But if the colors happen to be in a luminous space, they will show themselves to be of greater beauty in proportion to how intense the light is.

->The Opponent<-

> The varieties in the colors of shadows are as numerous as the varieties in the colors of the objects which are in those shadows.

->The Response<-

Colors seen in shadow will show less variety one with another as the shadows in which they lie become deeper. There is evidence of this from those who look from a brightly lit space into the doorways of shadowy temples; there, the pictures, though painted in various <note>original: "divers"</note> colors, all seem to be shrouded in darkness.

# PAINTING

Since white is not a color but is capable of receiving every color, when a white object is seen in the open air, all its shadows appear blue. This occurs in accordance with the fourth proposition, which states that the surface of every opaque body takes on the color of its surrounding objects. Therefore, as this white object is deprived of direct sunlight by some object standing between it and the sun, all the parts exposed to both the sun and the atmosphere continue to take on the color of the sun and the atmosphere. However, the part that is not exposed to the sun remains in shadow and takes on only the color of the atmosphere <note>The "color of the atmosphere" refers to the blue light of the sky, which Leonardo observed fills the shadows of white objects outdoors.</note>.

And if this white object did not reflect the green of the fields stretching out to the horizon, nor face the brightness of the horizon itself, it would undoubtedly appear to be the same simple color as the atmosphere.
<sig>F 75 r.</sig>

## OF THE ACCIDENTAL COLOURS OF TREES

There are four "accidental" colors <term>accidental colors</term> <note>original: "colori accidentali"; in Renaissance art theory, these are colors caused by external conditions like light, shadow, and environment, rather than the object's "true" or inherent color.</note> of tree leaves: namely shadow, light, luster <note>original: "lustro"; the bright reflection or "glint" on a smooth surface</note>, and transparency.

## OF THE VISIBILITY OF THESE ACCIDENTAL COLOURS

At a great distance, the accidental parts of plant leaves will blend into a mixture in which the accidental color of the largest part predominates.
<sig>G 24 r.</sig>

## OF PAINTING

The color of an illuminated object takes on the color of the light source that illuminates it.

[*The apparent colors of smoke on the horizon*]

The thickest part of smoke appears white from the horizon downward, but from the horizon upward, it appears dark. Although this smoke is actually all the same color, this uniformity appears different because of the different backgrounds <note>original: "space"</note> against which it is seen.

## PAINTING

The surface of every opaque body <term>opaque body</term> <note>An object that does not allow light to pass through it.</note> takes on <note>original: "participates in"</note> the color of the objects facing it. 

The surface of an opaque body is more completely saturated <note>original: "steeped"</note> with the color of the object it faces to the degree that the rays of the images from those objects strike the surface at more direct <note>original: "equal"</note> angles. 

Furthermore, the surface of an opaque body is more saturated with the color of its object when that surface is whiter, and the color of the object being reflected is brighter or more illuminated. Quaderni VI 22 r.

## WHETHER THE COLORS OF THE RAINBOW ARE CREATED BY THE SUN

The colors of the rainbow are not created by the sun, because these colors can be produced in many ways without the sun. This happens, for example, when you hold a glass of water close to your eye; for in the glass, there are tiny bubbles which are usually seen in glass that is not perfectly refined. Even when these bubbles are not in direct sunlight, they will produce all the colors of the rainbow on one side. You will see this if you place the glass between the air <note>original: "atmosphere"</note> and your eye so that it is in contact with your eye. Have one side of the glass exposed to the light of the sky, and on the other, have the shadow of the wall on either the right or left side of the window (it does not matter which side). By turning this glass around, you will see the aforementioned colors surrounding those bubbles in the glass. We will speak of other methods in their proper place.

## OF THE COLORS FOUND IN THE FEATHERS OF CERTAIN BIRDS

In various regions of the world, there are many birds whose feathers display most radiant colors as they move. We see this happen among our own local birds, such as in the feathers of peacocks or on the necks of ducks and pigeons.

Furthermore, on the surface of ancient glass found buried in the earth, and on the roots of radishes which have been kept for a long time at the bottom of wells or other stagnant water, we see that each of these objects is surrounded by a sequence of colors like those of the rainbow. This is also seen when an oily substance spreads across the surface of water, as well as in the solar rays reflected from the surface of a diamond or beryl <term>beryl</term> <note>A transparent gemstone; varieties include emerald and aquamarine.</note>. Additionally, through the facet of a beryl, every dark object viewed against the sky <note>original: "atmosphere"</note> or another clear background is surrounded by this sequence of colors positioned between the sky and the dark object. There are many other examples of this which I will omit, as these are sufficient for the present topic.

## XXXI

# Landscape

->*"Describe landscapes with wind and water, and at the setting and rising of the sun."*<-

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 38 r. b</margin>
In the spaces between the falling rain, one can see the redness of the sun—specifically, the color of the clouds situated between the sun and the rain.

The waves located between the rain and the observer never show the darkness of the rain to the eye. This is because the side of the wave that is visible does not face the rain, nor is the rain reflected in it.

And the clouds appear as a dark purple.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 76 r. b</margin>
When objects are viewed through mist, the parts nearest to their outer edges <note>original: "extremities"</note> will be less visible; they become even harder to see the further away they are.

Consider a mountain rising above a city that kicks up dust like clouds. The color of this dust is altered by the color of the clouds above it. Where the rain falls most heavily, the color of the dust is least visible; conversely, where the dust is thickest, the rain is least visible. Where rain, wind, and dust are all mixed together, the clouds formed by the rain are more transparent than those formed by the dust.

When the flames of a fire mingle with clouds of smoke and steam, it creates very dark and dense clouds.

The rest of this discussion will be explained clearly in the *Book of Painting* <note>Leonardo often referred to his projected "Trattato della Pittura" (Treatise on Painting), a collection of his notes on art theory.</note>.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 79 r. c</margin>
<insert>[With drawing]</insert>

Trees, struck by the path of the winds, bend toward the direction the wind is blowing. After the wind has passed, they swing back in the opposite direction; this is known as the reflex <term>reflex movement</term> <note>The natural recoil or counter-movement of a flexible object returning to its original position.</note>.

The mighty fury of the wind is driven by avalanches falling from the mountains into gaping <note>original: "yawning"</note> caverns; this is caused by the avalanches of the mountains which had previously served as a roof or covering to these caverns <note>Leonardo is describing the massive displacement of air—a "blast"—caused by a structural collapse or landslide into an enclosed space.</note>.
