Why towers and bell towers <term>original: campaniles</term> at a great distance appear like inverted pyramids, even though they are of uniform thickness.

This happens because the lower layers of air, being thick and misty, obscure them more completely. The more an object is obscured, the less its edges <note>original: "extremities"</note> can be seen; as a result, the viewer's perception of the object tends to concentrate around its center line.

### WHERE SHADOW IS LESS THAN LIGHT

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 160 r. a</margin>
In a city, one can observe that the divisions between houses are clear when there is mist below. If the eye is above the level of the houses, the lines of vision—as they descend into the space between buildings—plunge into mist that is more dense. This mist, being less transparent, appears whiter. If one house is taller than another, its true form is easier to see because it sits in thinner air. Therefore, buildings appear more indistinct the lower they are <note>The original manuscript uses the word "più" (more), indicating that the lower buildings are more obscured by the density of the mist near the ground.</note>.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 165 v. b</margin>
This occurred because of the clouds positioned between the earth and the sun. For this reason, as the sun set in the west, it grew red; with its reddish glow, it lit everything visible to it as if through a haze. This effect was more or less intense depending on whether the objects were near or far away.

At the first hour of the day, the atmosphere in the south near the horizon has a faint haze of rose-colored clouds. Toward the west, the sky grows darker, while toward the east, the damp vapor of the horizon...

## ON PAINTING IN THE COUNTRY

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 184 v. c</margin>
If the slope of a hill that drops toward the eye stands between the eye and the horizon, and the eye is positioned at about the middle of the height of the slope, then the hill will become darker at every stage of its length. This is proved by the seventh proposition of this work <note>Leonardo frequently refers to his own numbered "propositions" or rules regarding optics and perspective throughout his notebooks.</note>, which says: that plant will appear darker which is seen from further below. Therefore, the statement is confirmed, because the hill shows all its plants from the center downward in parts that are illuminated by the brightness of the sky, just as the part in shadow is shaded by the darkness of the earth. For this reason, it is necessary that these plants should be of a moderate darkness; from this point on toward the bases of the hills, the plants continually become brighter through the opposite of the seventh proposition. By this seventh proposition, the nearer such plants are to the summit of the hill, the darker they must necessarily become. And it follows that this darkness is not proportional to the distance, according to the eighth proposition, which says: an object will appear darker when it is in clearer <note>original: "finer"</note> air; and by the tenth: that which borders on a brighter background will appear darker.

### Why higher objects at a distance are darker than lower ones, even when the mist is of uniform thickness:

Regarding objects situated in mist or any other dense atmosphere—whether this arises from vapor, smoke, or distance—the highest part will be the most visible. Among objects of equal height, the one seen against a background of the deepest mist will appear the darkest. 

For example, consider the eye at point *h* looking at *a*, *b*, and *c*, which are towers of equal height. The eye sees *c*, the top of the first tower, at point *r*, which is situated two degrees deep in the mist. However, it sees the top of the center tower, *b*, through only one degree of mist. Therefore, the top of tower *c* will appear darker than the top of tower *b*.

## PAINTING

Landscapes depicted in winter scenes should not show the mountains as blue as they appear in summer. This is proven by the fourth part of this chapter, which states that among mountains seen at a great distance, those that are naturally darker will appear to be a deeper blue. 

When trees are stripped of their leaves, they appear grey in color; when they have their leaves, they are green. Because green is a darker color than grey, the green trees will appear to be a more intense blue than the grey ones. Furthermore, according to the fifth part of this chapter, the shadows of trees covered with leaves are darker than the shadows of bare trees, just as leafy trees are denser than those without leaves. Thus, we have established our proposition.

The scientific definition of the atmosphere's blue color explains why landscapes have a deeper shade of blue in summer than in winter. <note>Leonardo believed that the "blue" of the sky was not the air's own color, but a result of light reflecting off moisture/density against the darkness of outer space; therefore, denser or darker backgrounds (like summer trees) enhance this blue effect.</note>

The fourth rule states that opaque <note>solid objects that do not let light pass through</note> bodies placed between the light source and the eye will appear entirely in shadow. According to the fifth rule: the eye that is positioned between the opaque body and the light source sees the opaque body fully illuminated. By the sixth rule: when the eye and the opaque body are both positioned between the darkness and the light, the body will be seen half in shadow and half in light.

## ON THE ATMOSPHERE LOCATED BETWEEN THE EYE AND THE VISIBLE OBJECT

An object will appear more or less distinct at the same distance depending on whether the atmosphere located between the eye and that object is more or less clear.

Since you are aware that the greater or lesser amount of atmosphere between the eye and the object causes the outlines of those objects to seem more or less blurred, you should represent the stages of loss of definition in these bodies in the same proportion to each other as their distances from the eye of the beholder.

When smoke from dry wood comes between the eye of the observer and a dark space, it appears blue.

Similarly, the atmosphere appears blue because of the darkness <note>Leonardo refers here to the darkness of outer space</note> which lies beyond it. If you look toward the horizon of the sky, you will see that the atmosphere is not blue, and this is due to its density. Therefore, at every stage as you raise your eyes from the horizon to the sky directly above you, you will find that the atmosphere seems darker; this is because a smaller quantity of air exists between your eye and the darkness of space.

If you are on the top of a high mountain, the atmosphere will seem darker above you, in proportion to how much thinner <note>original: "rarer"</note> the air becomes between you and the said darkness. This effect will be intensified at every successive stage of its height, until at last it remains blue.

Smoke will appear the most blue when it comes from the driest wood and is nearest to its point of origin, provided it is seen against the darkest background with the light of the sun shining upon it.

<header>LANDSCAPE</header>

<margin>Folio 88 recto</margin>
When smoke from a large fire fed by damp wood passes through thick air, it does not mix with it. Instead, it appears denser at the top than in the center, especially when the air is chilly. The faint light that passes through the air is always warm and grows progressively weaker. Of the dust particles passing through the air, the finest ones rise the highest.

Although smooth leaves usually have the same color on their upper side <note>original: "right side"</note> as on their underside <note>original: "reverse"</note>, the side exposed to the atmosphere reflects the color of the sky. It appears to take on the sky's color more clearly when the eye is closer to it or sees the leaf more <term>foreshortened</term> <note>an artistic technique used to create the illusion of an object receding strongly into the distance or background</note>. Furthermore, shadows will always appear darker on the upper side than on the underside because of the contrast created by bright highlights appearing next to the shadow.

The underside of the leaf, even if its actual color is the same as the upper side, appears more beautiful. This color is a green tending toward yellow; this occurs when the leaf is placed between the eye and the light source that illuminates it from the opposite side. Its shadows are also located in the same positions as those on the opposite side.

<margin>G 3 recto and 2 verso</margin>
Therefore, painter, when you paint trees nearby, remember that when your eye is somewhat below the level of the tree, you will see some leaves from the upper side and some from the underside. The upper sides will appear a deeper blue the more they are <term>foreshortened</term>. Sometimes the same leaf will show part of its upper side and part of its underside; consequently, you must paint it using two different colors.

When there is one layer <note>original: "belt"</note> of green foliage behind another, the highlights on the leaves and the light shining through them <note>translucency</note> show more strongly than those seen against the brightness of the open sky.

If the sun illuminates the leaves without the leaves being between the sun and the eye, and without the eye looking directly into the sun, then the highlights and the light passing through the leaves are extremely vivid.

It is very useful to paint some of the lower branches as dark shapes. These should serve as a background for the illuminated layers of green that are a short distance behind them.

<sig>G 4 r., G 4 v., G 9 v.</sig>

When viewing dark greens from below, the part closest to the eye is the darkest; that is to say, the part furthest from the bright sky <note>original: "luminous atmosphere"</note>.

Never paint leaves as if they are transparent in the sun, because they always appear indistinct. This happens because the shadow of one leaf is cast onto the translucent surface of another leaf above or below it. This shadow has sharp outlines and a consistent density. Sometimes half or a third of the leaf is in shadow, and consequently, the structure of such a leaf is blurred; therefore, imitating this effect should be avoided <note>Leonardo advises against this because the overlapping shadows on translucent surfaces create visual "noise" that ruins the clarity of a painting</note>.

The upper branches of a tree's spreading limbs stay closer to the main bough than the lower branches do.

A leaf is less transparent when it catches the light at a sharper <note>original: "more acute"</note> angle.

## THE PLANTS OF THE FIELDS

Regarding plants that are shaded by trees growing among them: those positioned in front of the shadow have their stems <note>original: "stalks"</note> lit up against a dark background of shadow. Conversely, those plants that are actually in the shadow have dark stems seen against a light background—that is, the bright area that lies beyond the shadow.

## TREES POSITIONED BETWEEN THE EYE AND THE LIGHT

When trees are located between the eye and the light source, the side facing the viewer will be bright. This brightness will be varied by the branching <note>original: "ramification"</note> of the translucent leaves—as seen from the underside—mixed with the glossy leaves seen from the top <note>original: "right side"</note>. In the background, lower down and further back, the foliage <note>original: "verdure"</note> will be dark because it is shaded by the front part of the tree. This occurs in trees that are taller than the viewer's eye level.

### OF TREES AND THEIR LIGHT

<margin>G 11 v.</margin>
The best practical method for depicting countryside scenes—or rather, landscapes and their trees—is to choose a time when the sun is hidden in the sky. This allows the fields to receive a diffused light rather than the direct light of the sun, which creates shadows that are too sharply defined and starkly different from the illuminated areas.

### OF THE SHADOWS OF VERDURE

The shadows of <term>verdure</term> <note>original: "verdure" — Lush green vegetation or foliage</note> always tend toward a blue color; the same is true for the shadows of all other objects. They shift toward this color more completely as they become more distant from the eye, and less so as they are closer.

The leaves that reflect the blue of the atmosphere always present themselves edgewise to the viewer.

### OF THE ILLUMINATED PARTS OF VERDURE AND OF MOUNTAINS

<margin>G 15 r.</margin>
The illuminated part of an object will show more of its natural color at a great distance when it is struck by the most powerful light.

### OF SHADOWS AND LIGHTS ON CITIES

When the sun is in the east and the viewer is looking down upon a city from above, the viewer will see the southern part of the city with its roofs half in shadow and half in light; the same applies to the northern part. However, the eastern part will be entirely in shadow, and the western part will be entirely in light.

### OF TREES IN THE SOUTH

When the sun is in the east, the trees in the south and north are lit almost equally between light and shadow. However, the total amount of light is greater the further west they are located, and the total amount of shadow is greater the further east they are located.

### OF MEADOWS

When the sun is in the east, the grasses in the meadows and other small plants are of the most brilliant green because they are transparent to the sun's rays. This does not happen with meadows in the west; in those to the south and north, the grasses show only a moderate brilliance in their green color.

### THE ASPECTS OF LANDSCAPES

When the sun is in the east, all parts of the trees illuminated by it are of a most brilliant green. This is due to the fact that the leaves illuminated by the sun within the eastern half of our <term>hemisphere</term> <note>original: "hemisphere" — here referring to the visible arc of the sky</note> are transparent. Meanwhile, within the western semicircle, the <term>verdure</term> <note>original: "verdure" — green vegetation or foliage</note> has a dark hue and the air is damp and heavy, the color of dark ashes. Therefore, it is not transparent like the air in the east, which is radiant—and all the more so when it is full of moisture.

The shadows of the trees in the east cover a large portion of the tree, and they are darker in proportion to how thick the trees are with leaves.

During the year, the trees in the south and north will be half in shadow and half in light. They will appear more or less in shadow or light depending on whether they are positioned further to the east or to the west.

Whether the viewer's eye is high or low causes a variation in the shadows and lights of trees. When the eye is positioned above, it sees the trees with very little shadow; when it is below, it sees a great deal of shadow.

The different shades of green in plants are as varied as their individual species.

### OF THE SHADOWS OF TREES

When the sun is in the east, the trees toward the west will appear to the eye with very little <term>relief</term> <note>original: "relief" — the quality of appearing three-dimensional or standing out from the background</note> and with an almost imperceptible <term>gradation</term> <note>original: "gradation" — the subtle transition between light and dark tones</note>. This is due to the atmosphere, which is very thick between the eye and these trees, according to the seventh part of this treatise. These trees are deprived of distinct shadow; for although a shadow exists in every part of the <term>ramification</term> <note>original: "ramification" — the arrangement and structure of the branches</note>, the images of shadow and light that reach the eye are confused and blended together. They cannot be discerned because of their small size. The highest lights are in the center of the trees and the shadows are toward their edges. Their separation is marked by the shadows in the spaces between these trees when the forests are dense; in those forests that are more scattered, the <term>contours</term> <note>original: "contours" — the outlines or shapes of the trees</note> are barely seen.

### OF TREES IN THE EAST

When the sun is in the east, the trees in that direction are dark toward the center, while their edges are caught in the light.

### OF THE SMOKE OF CITIES

Smoke is seen better and more distinctly in the eastern quarter than in the western quarter when the sun is in the east. This is due to two causes: first, the sun shines its rays through the particles of the smoke, lighting them up and making them visible. Second, the roofs of the houses seen in the east at this hour are in shadow because their slope prevents them from being lit by the sun. The same happens with dust; both smoke and dust...

## OF SMOKE AND DUST

When the sun is in the east, the smoke of cities will not be visible in the west. This is because it is neither seen with the sun's rays shining through it nor viewed against a dark background. Since the roofs of the houses turn the same side to the eye as they do to the sun, the smoke is positioned against a bright background and will be scarcely visible. However, dust seen under these same conditions will appear darker than smoke, because its substance is denser than that of smoke, which is made up of <term>vapor</term> <note>original: "vapour" — Leonardo distinguishes between the light, translucent nature of water vapor and the solid, opaque nature of dust particles</note>.

<margin>G 23 r.</margin>
[*Of trees permeated by the air*]

## OF THE OPEN SPACES WITHIN THE TREES THEMSELVES

The <term>intervening region</term> <note>original: "intervening region" — the pockets of air caught within the structure of the tree</note> of the air within the bodies of trees, and the spaces between trees seen from a great distance, do not reveal themselves clearly to the eye. Where it requires an effort just to discern the whole tree, it is naturally difficult to distinguish its small parts. Instead, it forms a confused mixture, which takes its character mostly from whatever occupies the largest mass. Since the open spaces of the tree are made up of particles of illuminated air and are much smaller than the tree itself, the eye loses sight of them much sooner than it does of the tree; but it does not therefore follow that they are not there. Consequently, there is a necessary blending of the air and the darkness of the shaded tree, which flow together to meet the eye of the beholder.

## OF TREES THAT HIDE THESE OPEN SPACES IN ONE ANOTHER

That part of a tree will show fewer open spaces when it has the greater mass of another tree behind it, positioned between the first tree and the open sky. For example, in tree *a* the open spaces are not covered, nor are they in *b*, because there are no trees behind them. But in *c*, only half the open space is visible; that is to say, *c* is covered by tree *d*, and part of tree *d* is <note>The text ends mid-sentence, continuing Leonardo's geometric explanation of overlapping foliage.</note>

## OF TREES

What outlines do trees show at a distance against the atmosphere that serves as their background? The outlines of a tree's structure against the luminous atmosphere approach a spherical shape more closely as they become more remote; conversely, the closer they are, the more they show a greater divergence from that spherical form.

Therefore, the first tree, *a* <note>The original manuscript contains a sketch of a row of trees seen in perspective to illustrate this point.</note>, being near to the eye, displays the true form of its <term>ramification</term> <note>original: "ramification" — the arrangement and pattern of a tree's branches</note>. However, this is somewhat less visible in tree *b* and disappears altogether in tree *c*. In the case of tree *c*, not only are none of the branches visible, but the entire tree can only be recognized with great difficulty.

Every object in shadow—regardless of its shape—will appear spherical at a great distance. This occurs because if an object is rectangular, its angles become invisible at even a short distance. A little further away, it loses more of its shorter sides than it retains. Thus, before the whole object disappears, its individual parts vanish first, since they are smaller than the whole.

<margin>G 26 v.</margin>
This is also true for a man in such a situation: you lose sight of the legs, arms, and head before the trunk. Then, the extremities of his height are lost before those of his width. When these dimensions appear equal, the shape would be a square if the angles remained visible; but as the angles are lost, the shape appears as a sphere.

<margin>G 27 v.</margin>
When representing trees in leaf, be careful not to repeat the same color too often against another tree of the same color in the background. Instead, vary it by making the foliage lighter or darker, or a more vivid green.

### OF THE LIGHTS ON LEAVES OF YELLOWISH GREEN

But yellowish-green leaves, when they reflect the atmosphere, do not create a reflection that borders on blue; for every object, when seen in a reflection, takes on part of the color of that reflecting surface. Therefore, the blue of the atmosphere reflected in the yellow of the leaf appears green, because blue and yellow mixed together form a most brilliant green. Consequently, the <term>lustre</term> <note>original: "lustre" — the shiny highlight or reflection on a surface</note> on light-colored leaves that are yellowish in hue will appear as a greenish-yellow.

### OF TREES WHICH ARE ILLUMINATED BY THE SUN OR BY THE ATMOSPHERE

Trees that are illuminated by both the sun and the atmosphere, and which have dark-colored leaves, will be illuminated on one side by the atmosphere alone. As a result of being lit this way, they will take on its blue tint. On the opposite side, they will be illuminated by both the atmosphere and the sun, and the part that the eye sees illuminated by the sun will be brilliant.

The tips of the branches of trees, if not weighed down by the gravity of their fruit, turn toward the sky as much as possible.

The upper sides of their leaves are turned toward the sky in order to receive nourishment from the dew that falls at night.

The sun gives spirit and life to plants, and the earth nourishes them with moisture. In this connection, I once conducted an experiment: I left only one small root on a gourd and kept this single root nourished with water. The gourd successfully brought to maturity all the fruits it could produce, which were about sixty gourds of the long species. I applied myself diligently to consider the source of its life, and I perceived that it was the dew of the night which soaked it abundantly with its moisture... <note>Leonardo often combined his artistic observations with scientific experiments; here he correctly identifies that plants can absorb moisture through their surfaces, though his theory on the "dew of the night" as a primary life source was an early botanical hypothesis.</note>

The rule regarding the leaves produced on the final branches of the year is that on twin branches they grow in opposite directions. That is, as the leaves first grow, they turn themselves around toward the branch in such a way that the sixth leaf above grows directly over the sixth leaf below. The way they turn is such that if one turns toward its pair on the right, the other turns to the left.

The leaf acts like a breast to nourish the branch or fruit that grows in the following year. <gloss>G 32 v.</gloss>

## ON LANDSCAPES

The dark colors of shadows on mountains at a great distance take on a more beautiful and purer blue than those parts which are in the light. From this, it follows that when the mountain rock is reddish, the parts in the light are fawn-colored; the more brightly it is illuminated, the more closely it will keep its natural color. <gloss>I 48 r.</gloss>

## ON SMOKE

Smoke enters the air in the form of a wave, similar to the wave water makes when its force causes it to burst through other water. <gloss>I 106 [58] r.</gloss>

Reeds in direct light are barely visible, but they stand out clearly when positioned between the light and the shade.

To paint landscapes, choose a time when the sun is at its highest point (the <term>meridian</term> <note>original: "meridian" — the highest point reached by the sun in the sky at noon</note>) and turn to the west or the east to begin your work.

If you turn toward the north, every object on that side will be without shadow—especially those closest to the shadow cast by your own head. If you turn toward the south, every object on 그쪽 side will be completely in shadow.

All trees positioned toward the sun that have the sky as their background will appear dark. Other trees that have this darkness as their background will be black in the center and lighter toward the edges. <gloss>L 87 r.</gloss>

## CLASSIFICATION OF TREES

<margin>L 87 v.</margin>
Trees may be classified as: low, tall, thin, or thick—that is, dense with leaves; dark, light, yellow, or red; those with branches pointing upwards, those with branches facing the viewer, and those with branches pointing downwards; those with white trunks; those that appear transparent against the air and those that do not; those massed together and those spread out.

<margin>M 36 v.</margin>
The line of level <term>equality</term> <note>original: "equalità" — referring here to the horizontal plane or eye level</note> and the horizon line are one and the same.

Landscapes possess a more beautiful blue <note>original: "azzurro" — azure or blue</note> when the weather is fine and the sun is at its <term>noon</term> <note>original: "mezzo dì" — midday or noon</note> than at any other hour of the day, because the atmosphere is free from moisture. Viewing them under such conditions, you can see the trees looking beautiful at their edges, while the shadows are dark toward the center. In the far distance, the air that lies between you and the trees appears more beautiful when there is a darker object behind it; consequently, the blue is at its most vibrant.

Objects seen from the side where the sun is shining will not reveal their shadows to you. However, if you are positioned lower than the sun, you will see parts that the sun does not reach, and those will be entirely in shadow.

The leaves of trees positioned between you and the sun exhibit five primary shades of color: a most beautiful green; a shining surface that acts as a mirror for the atmosphere (which lights up parts the sun cannot see); the parts in shadow that face only the earth; and those darkest parts which are surrounded by something other than darkness.

Trees in open country situated between you and the sun appear much more beautiful than those where you are standing between the sun and the trees. This is because the trees positioned toward the sun show their leaves as transparent at the edges; the parts that are not transparent—the very tips—are shining. It is true that the shadows are dark, because they are not covered by anything.

When you place yourself between the trees and the sun, the trees will only show you their clear and natural color, which is not very prominent on its own. In addition to this, they will show certain reflected lights...

### IN THE WIND

But if you are on the side from which the wind is blowing, you will see the trees looking much lighter than if you viewed them from the other sides. This is due to the fact that the wind turns up the undersides of the leaves, which are in all cases much paler than their top sides. They will appear especially light if the wind blows from the direction where the sun happens to be, and if you have your back turned toward it.

<margin>B.M. 113 v.</margin>
<note>original: "B.M. 113 v." — refers to the British Museum MS 263, also known as the Codex Arundel, folio 113 verso.</note>
All trees seen against the sun appear dark toward their center; this darkness will take the shape of the tree when it stands apart from others.

The shadows cast by trees in direct sunlight are as dark as the center of the tree itself.

The shadow cast by a tree is never smaller in mass than the tree itself; however, it grows larger in proportion to how much the ground where it falls slopes toward the center of the earth <note>Leonardo is describing how shadows lengthen on sloping terrain or as the angle of light changes</note>.

A shadow will be densest toward the center of a tree when it has fewer branches.

Every branch falls within the central shadow of every other branch and, consequently, within the shadow of the entire tree.

The shape of every shadow cast by a branch or tree is bordered by a bright area on the side from which the light comes; this brightness will follow the same shape as the shadow and may appear to extend for a mile <note>Leonardo frequently uses "a mile" as a rhetorical device to indicate a great distance in perspective</note> from the side where the sun is.

If a cloud should cast a shadow on some part of the hills, the trees there will undergo less visible change than those in the far distance or on the plains. This is because the trees on the hills have thicker branches, as their yearly growth is less than that of trees in the plains. Therefore, since they are among those objects that are naturally dark and full of shade, the shadows of the clouds cannot make them much darker. Furthermore, the level spaces that come between the trees, which have not lost any shadow...

<margin>B.M. 114 r.</margin> <note>original: "B.M. 114 r." — refers to the British Museum MS 263, also known as the Codex Arundel, folio 114 recto.</note>
Landscape colors vary greatly in tone, especially those areas that are not green—such as cultivated fields, the jagged destruction found in mountain ranges, or their barren and rugged surfaces.

When trees are positioned against the skyline, they appear to be the same color unless they are packed very closely together with dense foliage, such as pines and similar trees.

When you view trees from the side illuminated by the sun, they will appear almost uniformly bright. The internal shadows of the tree will be hidden by the lit leaves positioned between your eye and those shadows.

When trees are situated between the sun and the viewer, you will see a green translucency <note>original: "transparence"</note> in the leaves positioned outside the central shadow. However, this translucency will be interrupted in many spots by the shadowed leaves and branches that come between you and the light. In the upper sections of the tree, this effect will be accompanied by many reflections bouncing off the leaf surfaces.

<margin>B.M. 114 v.</margin> <note>original: "B.M. 114 v." — refers to the Codex Arundel, folio 114 verso.</note>
When the sun is covered by clouds, objects become less distinct because there is very little contrast between the highlights and shadows of trees and buildings. This happens because they are illuminated by the vastness of the atmosphere, which surrounds objects so completely that shadows are rare; those few that remain grow increasingly faint until their edges are lost in the haze.

Trees in a landscape display various shades of green. In some—such as firs, pines, cypresses, laurels, boxwoods, and the like—the color borders on black. In others, such as walnut and pear trees, grapevines, and young foliage, the color leans toward yellow. Others, such as chestnuts and oaks, show darker shades of yellow. Some turn red as autumn approaches, such as sorb trees <note>The sorb, or service tree, produces small, edible fruit similar to a pear or plum.</note>, pomegranates, vines, and cherry trees. Finally, others like willows, olives, and bamboos tend to appear almost white.

## XXXII
# Light and Shade

> ‘*No substance can be understood without light and shade; light and shade are caused by light.*’

The area that is most shaded is where the greatest number of shadow rays converge <note>Leonardo uses "converge" to describe how multiple shadows overlapping create deeper darkness.</note>.

The spot hit by shadow rays at the sharpest angle is the darkest.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 31 verso b</margin>
The area will be the brightest from which the greatest number of light rays are reflected.

Light is what drives away darkness. Shadow is the withholding of light. Primary light is the source that causes the illumination of shaded objects.

Derived lights are those parts of objects that are illuminated by the primary light.

Primary shadow is the side of an object where the light does not fall.

Derived shadow is simply the impact of shadow rays hitting a surface <note>This refers to what we now call a "cast shadow."</note>.

Every object that creates a gathering <note>original: "concourse"</note> of rays fills the surrounding air with an infinite number of its images.

A shaded or luminous gathering is the mass of rays emanating from a dark or bright object that travels through the air without hitting anything.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 116 recto b</margin>
Shaded or luminous impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> occurs when something blocks or cuts across the path of the gathering rays of light or shadow.

The shadow in transparent <note>original: "diaphanous"</note> and spherical objects is darker at the top than in the hollow center, and darker within the darkness of the derived shadow cast by the body of the sphere.

Every visible object is surrounded by secondary objects, and from this it—

This is observable in images passed through a hole or at the edge of any dark obstacle.

This happens because the images tint the spot where they fall with their own color. When different images approach the same spot, they create a blend of their colors; this blend takes on more of one color than another based on which color is present in a greater quantity.

## THE ACTION OF LIGHT FROM ITS CENTER

If the whole light source were what caused the shadows behind the bodies placed against it, it would be necessary that a body, which is much smaller than the light, should have a pyramidal shadow <note>original: "pyramidal shadow," a cone-shaped shadow that tapers to a point.</note> behind itself; and as experience does not confirm this, it must be that it is the center of the light which performs this function.

---

## WHY NO SPHERICAL BODY CAN REVOLVE CONTINUOUSLY AS IT MOVES

The cannonball from the mortar, if it be of uniform material, and its surface be equidistant from its center, and the fire strikes it in the middle, as reason would suggest, must necessarily take its course without any rotation <note>original: "revolution"</note>. Seeing that the fire that expels it is of uniform nature, it drives equally the air which resists its course, and as this resistance also is equal, it offers equal resistance on all sides.

Thus for example, one sees the moon, which is also a spherical body and meets with equal resistance, to be much swifter as compared with

### A PROOF OF HOW IMAGES ENTER THE EYE

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 204 recto a</margin>
If you look at the sun or another luminous object and then shut your eyes, you will see its form lingering within your eye for a long time. This is a sign that images actually enter inside the eye.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 241 recto c</margin>
When the intersection of two columns of shadow produces "derived shadows" <note>original: "derived shadows," the secondary shadows cast by an object into the surrounding space</note> by means of two light sources, it follows that four derived shadows are produced. These shadows are "composite" <note>original: "composite shadow," referring to the penumbra or areas where shadows overlap and vary in intensity</note>, and they intersect at four places. Of these intersections, two form "simple shadow" <note>original: "simple shadow," the umbra or the darkest part of a shadow where all light is blocked</note> and two form composite shadow. These two simple shadows are produced where neither of the two lights can be seen, and the composite shadows are produced where only one of the two lights is blocked from shining.

Furthermore, the intersections of the composite shadows are always produced by a single luminous body, while the simple ones are produced by two luminous bodies. The right-hand intersection of the composite shadow is produced by the light on the left, and the left-hand intersection is produced by the light on the right. However, the two intersections of the simple shadows—both the upper and the lower—are produced by both luminous bodies together: that is, the light on the right and the light on the left.

Many tiny reflections <note>original: "lustres," referring to glints of light or highlights on a surface</note> remain visible even from a great distance and make themselves noticed.

### THE NATURE OF LIGHT PASSING THROUGH APERTURES

Regarding the light that penetrates vent holes <note>original: "vent holes," small openings or apertures, similar to a pinhole camera effect</note>, it is worth questioning whether the spreading <note>original: "dilatation"</note> of its rays allows the light to recreate an image beyond the hole that is as wide as the original object that produced the rays.

--- Page 968 ---
<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s geometric investigations into optics, specifically focusing on how light rays expand after passing through an aperture and how the intensity of light and shadow changes with distance.</meta>

<page-num>952</page-num>
<header>LIGHT AND SHADE</header>

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 241 recto d</margin>
In addition to this, we must consider whether this expansion <note>original: "dilatation," the spreading out of light rays after passing through a point</note> has a power equal to that of the light source <note>original: "luminous body"</note>. Regarding the first doubt, the reply is that the expansion made by the rays after they intersect recreates as much width beyond the aperture <note>original: "vent hole," a small opening or pinhole used in optical experiments</note> as it had in front of the aperture, provided there is as much space from the light source to the aperture as there is from the aperture to the projection <note>original: "impress"</note> of its rays. This is proved by the straightness of the light rays, from which it follows that the proportion between their width is the same as the proportion between the distances at which they intersect.

However, power <note>referring to intensity of light or heat</note> does not diminish in that same proportion. This is proved by the statement: the same proportion exists between the heat and the radiance in the various light rays as exists between their distances from their source. It is proved, therefore, that the light ray loses heat and radiance in proportion to its distance from the light source. It is true, however, that the overlapping shadows <note>original: "composite shadows," the penumbra where shadows from multiple sources or an extended source overlap</note>—which are "derived shadows" <note>shadows cast into space</note> starting from the edges of these apertures—break this rule because of their intersections. This is treated fully in the second book concerning shadow.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 241 verso c</margin>
The rays of the shaded and luminous images intersect after they have penetrated the apertures, flipping every part of their thickness in opposite directions <note>Leonardo is describing the "camera obscura" effect where an image appears upside down and inverted after passing through a pinhole</note>.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 241 verso d</margin>
A shadow will never appear to have a uniform density where it falls <note>original: "place of its incidence"</note> unless that surface is at an equal distance from the light source at all points. This is proved by the seventh rule, which says: a shadow will appear lighter or darker depending on whether it is against a darker or lighter background. It is also proved by the eighth rule: a background will have parts that are darker or lighter depending on how far or near they are to the light source. Among the surfaces at an equal distance from the light source, the one that receives the rays at more direct angles <note>original: "equal angles," meaning perpendicular or nearly so</note> will appear more illuminated. No matter how unevenly a shadow is positioned, its boundaries will always appear equal to the object casting the shadow <note>original: "shaded body"</note> if the eye is positioned at the center of the light source.

The shadow that is further away from the object casting it will appear darker.

### PREFACE
<note>original: "PROEM"</note>

Since I have, I believe, sufficiently discussed the nature and different characteristics of primary and derived shadows and the manner in which they fall, I think it is now time to explain the various results produced on the different surfaces that are touched by these shadows.

### SHADOW IS THE WITHHOLDING OF LIGHT

It seems to me that shadows are of the highest importance in perspective, seeing as without them opaque and solid bodies would be indistinct—both regarding what lies within their boundaries and the boundaries themselves—unless they are seen against a background of a different color than the object itself. Consequently, in the first proposition, I deal with shadows and state that every opaque body is surrounded by and has its surface covered with shadows and lights; I devote the first book to this. 

Furthermore, these shadows vary in their degree of darkness because they have been deprived of varying amounts of light rays. I call these <term>primary shadows</term> <note>The "shady side" of an object, where the light cannot reach its surface directly</note> because they are the first shadows and form a covering over the bodies to which they attach themselves; I shall devote the second book to this. From these primary shadows come certain dark rays which spread through the air and vary in intensity according to the types of primary shadows from which they originate. Consequently, I call these <term>derived shadows</term> <note>Shadows cast into space or onto other objects, originating from the primary shadow</note> because they have their origin in other shadows; I will make this the third book. 

Moreover, these derived shadows create as many different effects as there are different places where they strike; I will make this the fourth book. And since the place where the derived shadow strikes is always surrounded by the...

<margin>C.A. 250 r. a <note>Codex Atlanticus, folio 250 recto, section a</note></margin>
...When light rays strike a surface, they leap back in a reflected stream toward their source. This reflected light meets the <term>primary shadow</term> <note>original: "ombra originale"; the shadow on the unlit side of an object</note>, mingles with it, and changes it, slightly altering the shadow's nature. I will devote the fifth book to this subject. In addition, I will dedicate the sixth book to investigating the many different ways reflected rays bounce back. These reflections modify the primary shadow with as many different colors as there are points from which these luminous reflected rays originate. Furthermore, I will make the seventh division treat the various distances that may exist between the impact point of each reflected ray and its point of origin, as well as the different shades of color the ray acquires when it strikes against opaque bodies.

<margin>C.A. 250 v. a <note>Codex Atlanticus, folio 250 verso, section a</note></margin>
The closer a light source is to a shadowed object, the more light it casts—provided the light source is larger than the object.

The further a light source is from a shadowed object, the more light it provides if the light source is smaller than the object.

Similarly, if the light source is smaller than the shadowed object, it will provide more light as it is moved further away from that object.

And if a light source that is larger than the shadowed object is moved further away, the total area illuminated will continue to shrink until only approximately half the object is lit.

### THE ACTION OF COMPOUND SHADOW
<note>A compound shadow is created when light from multiple sources or a broad source overlaps, creating various gradients of shade.</note>

The behavior of <term>compound shadows</term> always involves opposing movements. This means that if an opaque body interrupts a gathering of light rays before they reach their point of intersection, all the shadows of that body that break into the upper ray will appear beyond the intersection point where the lower ray strikes. Because the upper ray becomes the lower ray after they cross, any movements the shadowed body makes within the upper ray will appear as the opposite movement after this intersection. This effect will be revealed when the <term>percussion</term> <note>The point or surface where light or shadow hits</note> of the compound shadow falls upon a floor or a wall that is struck by the sun or another light source.

<summary>Leonardo outlines his plans for the fifth, sixth, and seventh books of his treatise, focusing on reflected light and its effect on shadow color, and explains the geometry of "compound shadows" where light rays intersect.</summary>
<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, Codex Atlanticus, optics, light and shade, reflected rays, primary shadow, compound shadow, intersection of rays, geometry of light</keywords>

--- Page 971 ---
<meta>This page continues Leonardo da Vinci’s technical notes on the physics of light and shadow, moving from the movement of shadows to the fundamental rules for painters regarding how light interacts with transparent and opaque bodies.</meta>

<page-num>955</page-num>
<header>LIGHT AND SHADE</header>

But if a light ray is blocked by an opaque object at some distance from the point where the rays intersect, the impact <note>original: "percussion"</note> of the resulting shadow will move in a manner similar to the movement of the object itself.

And if these rays are blocked at the exact point of their intersection, then the shadows of the opaque object will be doubled, and they will move in opposite directions to one another before they reach the point where they join together.

<margin>C.A. 277 v. a <note>Codex Atlanticus, folio 277 verso, section a</note></margin>
The <term>secondary compound shadow</term> <note>original: "derived compound shadow"; a shadow cast onto a surface, influenced by multiple light sources or reflections</note> is the reason why the impact of a sunbeam, when passing through any kind of corner or angle, does not leave its exact mark on that angle. The spot that is most luminous will change based on the different positions of the eye and the light source. The shadow, however, will always remain fixed in its place; for whatever change in position occurs, the eye still perceives it there.

No solid object can be visible unless its surface is covered by both light and shadow.

The air and every transparent substance becomes a pathway for images to travel from objects to the eye, whether those objects are located within or beyond those substances.

Secondary light <note>original: "derived light"; light reflected from one surface onto another</note> should be surrounded by <term>primary shadow</term> <note>original: "primitive shadow"; the shadow on the unlit side of the object itself</note>.

Secondary shadow will be surrounded by secondary light.

Secondary light should be surrounded, either entirely or partially, by primary or secondary shadows.

<margin>C.A. 349 v. d <note>Codex Atlanticus, folio 349 verso, section d</note></margin>
Every solid object projects its image as a whole, and into every part of the transparent medium that surrounds it.

### [Movement of shadows]

<margin>c 3 v.</margin>

## SHADOW AND LIGHT

<margin>c 7 v.</margin>
Shadows take three forms: for if the object casting the shadow is equal in size to the light source, the shadow is like a column that has no end. If the object is larger than the light source, its shadow is like a pyramid that grows wider as it moves away and has no end. But if the object is smaller than the light source, the shadow resembles a pyramid and comes to a point, as is seen in lunar eclipses.

## OF LIGHT

<margin>c 8 r.</margin>
The shape of a <term>luminous body</term> <note>original: "luminous body"; any source of light, such as a flame, a lamp, or a star</note>, even if it is elongated, will appear round when viewed from a great distance.

This is demonstrated by a candle flame; although it is long, it appears round at a great distance. The same thing may happen with the stars; even if they were crescent-shaped <note>original: "horned like the moon"</note>, they would still appear round because of their immense distance from us.

<margin>c 8 v.</margin>
Among objects that are equal in size and length, and also equal in their form and the depth of their shade, the one that is surrounded by a brighter <note>original: "more luminous"</note> background will appear smaller. <note>This describes the optical illusion known as irradiation, where light areas appear to bleed into and shrink adjacent dark areas.</note>

A shaded object placed between equal lights will cast as many shadows as there are light sources. One of these shadows will be darker than the others if the light situated on the opposite side is closer to the object than the other lights are.

A shaded object placed at an equal distance between two lights will cast two shadows; one will be darker than the other in proportion to how much more powerful one light source is than the other.

<margin>c 9 r.</margin>
The areas occupied by shadows cast by a small light source are, in terms of size, similar and corresponding to the areas from which the <term>visual rays</term> <note>original: "visual rays"; Leonardo refers to the straight lines of light traveling from the source or to the eye</note> are blocked.

When a light ray passes through a small hole and strikes an opposing object nearby, the shape of the <term>impact</term> <note>original: "percussion"; the point where light hits a surface</note> resembles the hole through which it passed more than the light source from which it originated.

<margin>c 10 r.</margin>
The greater the brilliance of a light source, the deeper the shadows will be on the objects it illuminates.

All shaded objects larger than the pupil of the eye that are placed between the eye and the light source will appear dark.

If the eye is positioned between the light source and the illuminated objects, it will see those objects without any visible shadow.

When a light ray passes through a hole of an unusual shape and travels a long distance, the image it casts where it strikes will resemble the light source from which it originates. <note>Leonardo is describing the principle of the camera obscura: at a distance, the shape of the aperture matters less than the shape of the light source (like the sun) itself.</note>

### [*On Broken Shadows*]

A <term>derived shadow</term> produced by a round object and a round light source—which is "broken" because it strikes various surfaces at different distances—will still appear round to an observer standing near the center of the original shadow's path.

<margin>c 12 v.</margin>
A round, spherical object will cast a circular shadow with soft edges <note>original: "blended [of light and shade]"</note> when another object of the same material is placed between it and the sun.

Among shadows of the same intensity, the one closest to the eye will appear the least dark. <note>This relates to "aerial perspective," where distance affects the perceived clarity and darkness of objects.</note>

A shadow will be darker when it is produced by a greater number of different objects and light sources.

<margin>c 13 v.</margin>
It is impossible for <term>simple derived shadows</term>, which come from different objects and are caused by a single light source, to ever merge or touch each other.

### [*Why Nearby Objects May Appear Separated*]

<margin>c 14 r.</margin>
If many objects are placed so close together that they are almost touching, but are viewed against a bright background from a great distance, they will appear to be separated by a wide space.

### [*When separated bodies will appear adjacent*]

If many light sources are viewed in a distant landscape, they will appear united and joined together, even if they are actually separated from one another.

### [*Definitions*]

Darkness is the total absence of light.
Shadow is the reduction of light.
<term>Primitive shadow</term> <note>original: "primitive shadow"; also known as "attached shadow," this is the shadow found on the object itself</note> is that which is attached to the shaded body.
<term>Derived shadow</term> <note>original: "derived shadow"; a "cast shadow" that moves through the air away from the object</note> is that which separates itself from the shaded body and travels through the air.
<term>Reflected shadow</term> <note>original: "repercussed shadow"; a shadow that is struck or influenced by light bouncing off another surface</note> is that which is surrounded by an illuminated surface.
The <term>simple shadow</term> is that which does not "see" any part of the light source that creates it.
<margin>Codex C, 14 v.</margin> The simple shadow begins at the line that separates it from the edges of the light sources.

Light rays that are doubled by intersecting in areas of light or shadow also result in double the brightness or double the darkness.

Primitive light and reflected light, when they surround thick and spherical bodies, cause the boundaries of the <term>primitive shadows</term> on these bodies to be much more distinct. These boundaries are more defined in the areas near the light sources when the reflected light is clearer than the original light.

That is said to be "primitive light" which first illuminates a shaded body; "derived light" is that which bounces back from other bodies onto the parts of the object that are distant from the primary light.

That part of the primitive shadow will be more luminous which can see the centers of the reflected light sources more directly.

This occurs because the more the shadow separates from its center, the more it is reached by a greater quantity of light rays; and every person knows that where there is more light, there is less shadow.

## *Definition*

<margin>Codex C, folio 17 verso</margin>
The sun creates as many <term>pyramids</term> <note>original: "pyramids"; here referring to the cone-like path of light rays converging at a single point, such as the eye</note> as there are holes and crevices through which its rays can penetrate, and as many as there are eyes of living creatures that look upon it. Therefore, since the sun is always the base of each pyramid, the sun's reflection in the water appears to the eye to be as far below the surface as the actual sun is above it; this reflected sun forms the base of the pyramid which converges at the eye. And this reflected sun will appear to be the same size as the section of the pyramid where it is cut by the surface of the water at point *n* [referring to a figure].

<margin>Codex C, folio 18 recto</margin>
Even if the <term>luminous body</term> <note>original: "luminous body"; the light source</note> and the <term>shaded body</term> <note>original: "shaded body"; the object blocking the light</note> are both perfectly spherical and of equal size, the <term>derived shadow</term> <note>original: "derived shadow"; the shadow cast through the air or onto a surface</note> will not match the roundness of the object it comes from. Instead, it will take an elongated shape if it falls upon a surface at unequal angles.

<insert>[Of the shapes of shadows]</insert>

The shapes of shadows often resemble the object that creates them, and often resemble the light source that causes them.

If the shape and size of the light source match those of the object, the <term>primitive shadow</term> <note>original: "primitive shadow"; the shadow that stays on the object itself</note> and the derived shadow will have the same shape and size as those bodies, provided they fall at equal angles.

At a certain distance, the cast shadow will never resemble the shape of the object it comes from, unless the shape of the light source itself resembles the shape of the illuminated object.

A light source that is elongated in shape will cause the shadow of a round body to appear wide and low, even if the light strikes the surface (<term>percussion</term> <note>original: "percussion"; the point or surface where light or shadow hits</note>) at equal angles.

<margin>Codex C, folio 18 verso</margin>
It is impossible for the shape of a cast shadow to resemble the object that created it, unless the light source is identical in shape and size to that object.

The difference in darkness between two partially shaded rays will be equal to the difference between the shadow formed by their blending and its original state.

<margin>Codex C, folio 20 recto</margin>
Generally, all the points that form the tips of the <term>pyramidal images</term> <note>original: "pyramidal images"; Leonardo used the term "pyramid" to describe the cone-shaped path of light rays that converge from an object to a single point, such as the eye.</note> of things are constantly present throughout the air, united and joined together without any interruption.

Necessity dictates that nature ordains—or has ordained—that at every point in the air, the images of all things opposite to them converge. This happens through the meeting of the pyramidal rays that have emanated from these things. If this were not so, the eye would not be able to discern the shape and quality of the object facing it from every point in the air that exists between the eye and the thing being seen.

A pyramid that extends from its base with more unequal angles will be narrower, and it will give a less accurate impression of the true width of its base.

Among the many pyramids that are founded upon a single base, the one that is largest will be more powerful; and the largest will be the one whose base angles are most equal to one another.

<margin>Codex C, folio 20 verso</margin>
The dimmer the <term>derived light</term> <note>original: "derived light"; light that has been reflected or transmitted from a primary source</note> is compared to the original light, the less its pyramids will illuminate the spot they strike.

The pyramids will illuminate the spot they strike less as their angles become finer.

The farther the <term>derived shadow</term> <note>original: "derived shadow"; the shadow cast away from an object into space or onto a surface</note> extends from the <term>primitive shadow</term> <note>original: "primitive shadow"; the shadow found on the surface of the object itself</note>, the brighter it becomes.

The same proportion that exists between the diameter of the derived shadow and that of the primitive shadow will also be found between the darkness of the primitive shadow and that of the derived.

If the size of the <term>illuminating body</term> <note>original: "illuminating body"; the light source</note> is larger than the body being illuminated, it will form an intersection of shadow. Beyond this point, the divided shadows will branch off in two different directions, as if they originated from two different lights.

Every visible object is defined by light and shade.

In this way, the shadow will appear so that its furthest edge seems to be as far "below" the surface on which it is cast as the top of the object is "above" that surface, as can be seen on a wall.

## CONCERNING THE THREE KINDS OF LIGHT THAT ILLUMINATE OPAQUE OBJECTS

<margin>Manuscript E, folio 3 verso</margin>

The second is **universal** light, which is seen in cloudy weather, in mist, or in similar conditions. The third is **composite** light; this occurs when the sun is entirely below the horizon in the evening or the morning.

<margin>Manuscript E, folio 15 recto</margin>

## PAINTING

When drawing, you will notice how some shadows are indistinguishable in their <term>gradation</term> <note>The soft transition from light to dark.</note> and form. This is proven by the fifth principle, which says: spherical surfaces have as many different degrees of light and shadow as there are variations of brightness and darkness reflected from the objects surrounding them.

The part of an opaque object that will be more in shadow—or more in light—is the part nearest to the dark body that shades it, or to the luminous body that provides its light.

The surface of every opaque object takes on the color of the object it faces, but the impression is stronger or weaker in proportion to whether that object is near or remote, and whether its power <note>referring to the intensity of its color or light</note> is greater or lesser.

<margin>Manuscript E, folio 17 recto</margin>
Objects seen between light and shadow will appear in greater **relief** <note>original: "relief"; the illusion of being three-dimensional or "standing out" from the flat surface of a painting.</note> than those which are situated entirely in the light or entirely in the shadow.

From the position of an eye that sees the illuminated parts of plants facing the light, no two plants will ever appear illuminated in exactly the same way. ### QUALITY OF SHADOWS

Regarding the even spread of light, there will be the same ratio between the levels of darkness <note>original: "obscurity"</note> in the shadows produced as there is between the levels of darkness in the colors to which those shadows are attached.

### OF THE MOVEMENT OF SHADOW

If the <term>luminous body</term> <note>A "luminous body" is any object that emits light, such as the sun, a lamp, or a candle.</note> is stationary, the movement of a shadow is always faster than the movement of the object casting it. This can be proved as follows: let *a* be the light source, *b* the object casting the shadow, and *d* the shadow itself. I maintain that the object *b* moves to point *c* in the same amount of time that the shadow *d* moves to point *e*. The ratio of their speeds over that time is the same as the ratio of the distance each one travels. Therefore, the ratio of the distance moved by the object *b* (to point *c*) compared to the distance moved by the shadow *d* (to point *e*) is the same as the ratio between their respective speeds.

However, if the light source moves at the same speed as the object, then the shadow and the object will move at the same speed as each other. And if the light source moves faster than the...

### OF THE PYRAMIDAL SHADOW

The <term>pyramidal shadow</term> <note>A cone-shaped shadow that tapers to a point.</note> produced by a parallel-sided body will be narrower than the body casting the shadow, in proportion to how far the <term>simple derived shadow</term> <note>In Leonardo's terminology, a "derived shadow" is the shadow cast into the air or onto a surface, as opposed to the "primary shadow" located on the dark side of the object itself.</note> is intercepted from that body.

### OF SIMPLE DERIVED SHADOWS

Simple derived shadows are of two kinds: one is finite in length, and two are infinite. The finite shadow is pyramidal. Of the two infinite shadows, one is <term>columnar</term> <note>A shadow shaped like a cylinder, maintaining a constant width.</note> and the other is expanding. 

All three types have straight sides. However, the convergent (that is, the pyramidal shadow) originates from a shaded body that is smaller than the light source. The columnar shadow originates from a shaded body that is equal in size to the light source. The expanding shadow originates from a shaded body that is larger than the light source.

### OF COMPOUND DERIVED SHADOWS

<term>Compound derived shadows</term> <note>Shadows created by multiple light sources or complex lighting, often resulting in overlapping areas of varying darkness (like the umbra and penumbra).</note> are of two types: columnar and expanding.

### OF LIGHT AND LUSTRE

This is the difference between general light and <term>lustre</term> <note>original: "lustre"; Leonardo uses this term to describe "specular reflection"—the bright glint or highlight seen on polished surfaces that appears to move as the viewer moves.</note> as they appear on the smooth surface of opaque <note>Objects that do not allow light to pass through them.</note> bodies: 

The light produced on the smooth surfaces of stationary opaque bodies will remain stationary, even if the eye that sees them moves. However, lustres (highlights) will appear on those same bodies at as many different points on the surface as there are positions where the eye rests.

**Which bodies are those that have light without lustre?**

Opaque bodies that have a thick, rough surface will never produce lustre on any part of their illuminated surface.

Which bodies are those that have <term>lustre</term> <note>original: "lustre"; here referring to specular highlights or the glossy reflection seen on polished surfaces.</note> but no visible illuminated part?

Thick, opaque bodies with smooth surfaces are those which show highlights in every place on their illuminated side where the <term>angle of incidence</term> <note>The angle at which light hits a surface, which determines where the reflection or highlight will appear to the viewer.</note> of the light matches the position of the eye. The cause of this contradiction is the elongated shape of the light source.

### OF SHADOW

Cast shadows are of three types: one that expands, one shaped like a column, and a third that tapers to a point where its sides intersect, then continues beyond that point infinitely in a straight line. If you were to argue that this third shadow ends at the angle where its sides meet and does not go any further, this is disproven by a principle from the first book on shadows: a thing is only completely finished when no part of it extends beyond its boundary lines. In the case of this shadow, we see the opposite; where this cast shadow originates, two shaded pyramids are clearly created, meeting at their points <note>Leonardo is describing the "X" shape formed when light passes an object smaller than the light source; the shadow tapers to a point (the umbra) and then appears to expand again beyond that point.</note>. 

If, however—as an opponent might say—the first shaded pyramid ends the cast shadow at its point, then where does the second shaded pyramid come from? The opponent claims it is caused by the point itself and not by the object casting the shadow. This is refuted by the second principle of this study, which states: a shadow is a phenomenon created by an object placed between the shadow's location and the light source.

Thus, it has become clear that the shadow is not produced by the point where the cast shadow converges, but only by the object itself.

If a spherical object is lit by an elongated light source, the shadow produced by the longest part of this light...

This is proved by the seventh point of this study, which shows that the edges of any object placed between the eye and the light will never appear sharp. Instead, they appear blurred because the air becomes darker near these edges; this darkness intensifies as it gets closer to these contours.

Two separate lights will, at a certain distance, appear joined and united.
In this case, many who have studied <term>perspective</term><note>The art and science of representing three-dimensional objects on a two-dimensional surface to show their depth and position relative to each other.</note> have argued that the air surrounding these lights is so illuminated at a great distance that it takes on the quality of the light itself. Therefore, they believe the light and the surrounding air appear as a single body.
What they say is incorrect. If the air surrounding these lights were truly illuminated so that it appeared uniformly bright, this would be more easily seen up close—where the exact shape of the light is clear—than from a distance. If the perception of the light's exact shape is lost at a distance because its radiance decreases slightly, how much greater would be the loss of radiance in the air, which is already much less **effulgent** <note>original: "effulgent"; shining brightly or radiant.</note> than the light itself?

We will demonstrate, therefore, that this perceived increase in size is caused by two images within the eye.

<margin>F 35 v.</margin>
The excessive brilliance of light when close to the eye weakens the <term>visual faculty</term><note>The physical ability or power of sight.</note>. This happens because the pupil, being irritated by the glare, contracts and becomes smaller. However, as the light moves further away, the irritation to the eye ceases because the light is less intense. Consequently, the pupil dilates <note>original: "increases"</note> and perceives a greater amount of light.

If two glowing bodies are positioned somewhat near to each other but viewed from a great distance, they will appear to be joined.

This can happen for two reasons. The first is that when you are close to these lights, you can immediately perceive the distance or space that separates them; the images they imprint on our eyes are very distinct, and their rays do not overlap. On the other hand, at a long distance, these images appear so close that not only their rays but the glowing bodies themselves seem to touch.

Furthermore, at this great distance, the pupil—which was initially contracted when near the light—becomes enlarged. This is because the brightness of the light is not as powerful as when it was close to the eye. Because the eye increases the size of its pupil, the object appears to be enlarged.

<margin>F 36 r.</margin>
If all images were to converge at an angle, they would meet at a <term>mathematical point</term><note>In geometry, a point that indicates a precise location but has no actual size or dimensions.</note>. Since this point is indivisible, all the different types of light would appear to you as if they were united. Being joined together, the senses would be unable to distinguish any difference between them.

<margin>F 36 v.</margin>
If a glowing body is viewed through a tiny hole made in a piece of paper, bring your eye as close to the light as possible. Even though the object may still be seen in its entirety, it will appear much smaller than before, proportional to the small size of the hole.

<margin>F 62 v.</margin>
If the shape of waves were semicircular—like the bubbles on the water's surface—the converging lines of the sun's images reflected from these waves to the eye would form a very wide angle, provided the eye was positioned at the edge of the sea between the observer and the sun.

Why does every glowing object with an elongated shape appear round from a great distance?

### OF LIGHTS

The lights which illuminate opaque bodies are of four kinds: 
1. **Universal light**, such as the atmosphere within our horizon.
2. **Particular light**, like that of the sun, a window, a door, or another defined space.
3. **Reflected light**.
4. **Filtered light**, which passes through substances with a degree of transparency like linen, paper, or similar things. 

This fourth type is different from light passing through fully transparent substances like glass, crystal, or other <term>diaphanous</term><note>Allowing light to pass through clearly; translucent or transparent.</note> bodies, where the effect is the same as if nothing were placed between the body in shadow and the light that illuminates it. We shall treat each of these separately in our discourse.

<insert>[Transparency of leaves]</insert>
The shadows on transparent leaves seen from the underside are the same shadows as those on the top <note>original: "right side"</note> of the leaf. The shadow is seen through the material on the reverse at the same time as the illuminated part; however, the <term>lustre</term><note>The shiny, reflective highlight on a surface.</note> can never be seen through transparency.

When trees are seen from below and against the light, positioned one behind the other at a short distance, the topmost part of the first will be largely transparent and clear. It will stand out against the dark part of the second tree; this will be the case with all trees in succession that are situated under the same conditions.

The shadows of plants are never truly black, for wherever the atmosphere penetrates, there cannot be utter darkness.

<insert>[Foliage in light]</insert>
If the light comes from *m* and the eye is at *n*, the eye will see the color of the leaves *a* and *b* all affected by the color of *m* (that is, the atmosphere). Meanwhile, the leaves *b* and *c* will be seen on the underside in transparency, with a very beautiful green color that borders on yellow.

<margin>G 9 r.</margin>
Willow trees and others like them that are <term>pollarded</term><note>A method of pruning where the upper branches of a tree are removed, promoting a dense head of foliage and branches.</note> every three or four years grow very straight branches. Their shadow is concentrated toward the center where these branches sprout, while near their tips they cast very little shade because their leaves are small and their branches are few and slender.

Consequently, the branches reaching toward the sky will have minimal shadow and little <term>relief</term><note>The appearance of three-dimensionality or standing out from the background.</note>. However, the branches pointing downward toward the horizon emerge from the dark part of the shadow. These become progressively brighter toward their tips and appear in strong relief, as their varying stages of brightness are set against a dark background of shadow.

The plant with the fewest branches and leaves will cast the least shadow.

<margin>G 10 v.</margin>
A leaf with a concave surface viewed from below will sometimes appear half in shadow and half transparent. For example, let *o p* be the leaf, *m* the light source, and *n* the eye. The eye will see *o* in shadow because the light does not strike it at equal angles on either the top side or the reverse; however, *p* is illuminated on the top side, and its light is visible through the transparency of its reverse side.

### OF SHADOWS ON BODIES

<margin>G 11 v.</margin>
When depicting deep shadows on shaded objects, always represent the cause of that darkness, and you should do the same for reflections. This is because dark shadows originate from dark objects, and reflections originate from objects with little brightness—that is, from diminished light sources. The relationship between the part of an object directly illuminated and the part lit by reflection is proportional to the relationship between the primary light source and the source of the reflection.

He also establishes a rule for artists to depict shadows and reflections based on the brightness of their sources.</summary>

## ON HOW GENERAL LIGHT ILLUMINATES TREES

The parts of a tree farthest from the ground will have the lightest shadows <note>original: "shadows of least obscurity"</note>.

This can be proven: let *a p* represent the tree, and *n b c* represent the sky <note>original: "illuminated hemisphere"</note>. The lower part of the tree faces the earth *p c* (on the side marked *o*), and it only faces a small portion of the sky at *c d*. However, the highest part of the curve *a* is exposed to the largest portion of the sky, *b c*. For this reason—and because it does not face the darkness of the earth—it remains more brightly illuminated. 

But if the tree is dense with foliage, such as <term>laurel</term>, <term>arbutus</term><note>Also known as the strawberry tree.</note>, <term>box</term>, or <term>ilex</term><note>The evergreen or holm oak.</note>, then the effect is different. Although the top *a* does not face the earth, it sees the darkness of the internal leaves, which are divided by many shadows. This darkness is reflected upward onto the undersides of the leaves above them. In these types of trees, the shadows are darker the closer they are to the center of the tree.

## ON LIGHTS SURROUNDED BY SHADOWS

When drawing any object, remember that when you compare the intensity <note>original: "potency"</note> of light on its illuminated parts, the eye is often deceived into thinking one area is brighter than it actually is. This happens because we compare those areas with the parts that border them. 

For instance, if you have two areas of unequal brightness, and the dimmer area borders a dark part while the brighter area is set against a light background (such as the sky or a similar bright surface), then the dimmer area will appear more radiant, and the brighter area will seem darker.

## ON THE LIGHTS OF SHADED OBJECTS

Painters often deceive themselves when representing the primary highlights <note>original: "principal lights"</note>.

Regarding the representation of a group of objects illuminated by a specific light source, such as the sun or another light-giving body <note>original: "luminous body"</note>.
