## SHADOWS AND LIGHTS OF CITIES

When the sun is in the east and the viewer’s eye is positioned above the center of a city, the eye will see the southern part of the city with its roofs half in shadow and half in light, and the same will be true toward the north. However, those buildings in the east will be entirely in shadow, and those in the west will be entirely in light. <note>This describes the effect of "backlighting" and "front-lighting" on a large scale; from an aerial view, buildings between the viewer and the sun appear as dark silhouettes.</note>

## ON PAINTING

The outlines and forms of every part of a body in shadow are poorly defined within their own shadows and highlights; however, in those areas located between the light and the shadow, the parts of these bodies are at their highest degree of distinctness.

## ON SITUATION <note>In this context, "situation" refers to the specific environment or lighting conditions in which a subject is placed.</note>

Take careful note of the situation of your figures, for the light and shade will appear different if the object is in a dark place with a specific light source, or if it is in a bright place with the direct light of the sun. It will also differ if the object is in a dark place with the soft, diffused light of evening or in dull weather, or if it is in the diffused light of the atmosphere illuminated by the sun.

That part of the <term>primary shadow</term> <note>original: "ombra originale"; the shadow that is on the object itself, also called "attached shadow."</note> will be the least dark when it is at the farthest distance from its edges.

The <term>derived shadow</term> <note>original: "ombra derivativa"; the shadow cast by an object onto another surface, also called a "cast shadow."</note> which borders on the <term>primary shadow</term> will be darker than the <term>primary shadow</term> itself.

An area will be most luminous when it is farthest away from mountains.

The <term>derived shadow</term> is never the same shape as the body from which it originates, unless the light source is of the same shape and size as the object in shadow.

The <term>derived shadow</term> cannot match the <term>primitive shadow</term> <note>Another term for the primary or attached shadow.</note> in shape unless it strikes a surface at equal angles.

### ON LIGHT RAYS AND THE STRENGTH OF THEIR REACH <note>original: "extremities"; referring to the limits or endpoints of the rays' reach.</note>

<margin>I 33 r.</margin>
[Diagram]
Because a light ray has a <term>pyramidal power</term> <note>Leonardo conceptualized light spreading out from a point source as a pyramid or cone. The "power" or intensity changes relative to the distance from the apex.</note>, especially when the air is consistent, it follows that when two rays coming from equal light sources meet in a straight line, the light will be doubled everywhere and have a uniform strength. This is because where one ray has the tip of its pyramid, the other has its base, as shown by *n m*.

<margin>I 37 v.</margin>
The shape of a shadow cast by any object of uniform thickness will never exactly match the body it comes from.

Even if a shaded object is pyramidal and every part of it is at an equal distance from the light source, the part of that pyramid which is smaller than the light illuminating it will not cast its shadow any distance away from its source. <note>Leonardo is observing that if a light source is larger than the object, the resulting shadow (the umbra) eventually tapers to a point and disappears.</note>

### ON PAINTING

<margin>K 105 [25] v.</margin>
Shadows and highlights are observed by the eye from three different positions. The first is when the eye and the light source are both on the same side of the object being viewed. The second is when the eye is in front of the object and the light is behind it. The third is when the eye is in front of the object and the light is at the side, so that the line extending from the object to the eye and the line extending from the object to the light form a right angle where they meet.

<margin>K 106 [26] r.</margin>
There is another category: the nature of the <term>reflected object</term> <note>This refers to how an object appears when it is catching reflected light rather than direct light.</note> when it is placed between the eye and the light in various positions.

### PAINTING

[Derived shadow]
The <term>derived shadow</term> <note>original: "ombra derivativa"; the shadow cast by an object onto another surface, as opposed to the "primary shadow" on the object itself.</note> is stronger the closer it is to its source.

## [*Luminous rays*]

<margin>M 77 v.</margin>
The part of an object that will be most illuminated is the part struck by light rays <term>luminous rays</term> at more direct or equal angles. <note>In other words, surfaces perpendicular to the light source appear brightest.</note>

The reflection of the sun will appear brighter in small waves than in large ones. This happens because the reflections of the sun occur more frequently in small waves than in large ones, and a greater number of bright points produce a stronger light than a smaller number.

<margin>B.M. 25 r.</margin>
Waves that overlap like the scales of a fir-cone reflect the sun with the greatest brilliance. This occurs because there are as many individual images of the sun as there are ridges of waves visible to it. The shadows that exist between these waves are small and not very dark; the radiance of so many reflections blends together as it reaches the eye, making the intervening shadows imperceptible.

<margin>B.M. 170 v.</margin>
There are two different kinds of light: one is called <term>free</term> and the other <term>restricted</term>. Free light is that which illuminates objects from the open air; restricted light is that which illuminates objects through an opening, such as a hole or a window.

Lights are also categorized by two different natures: one is separated from bodies, and the other is joined to them.

"Separated" light is the source that illuminates the body; "united" light is the specific part of the body that is illuminated. The first is called <term>primary light</term>, and the second is called <term>derived light</term>.

<margin>B.M. 171 r.</margin>
In the same way, there are two kinds of shadows: primary and derived. A <term>primary shadow</term> is one attached to the object itself. A <term>derived shadow</term> is one that is separated from the object, carrying the likeness of the object that caused it onto the surface of walls or other planes.

A <term>simple shadow</term> is one that is not reached by any light source.

<margin>B.M. 248 v.</margin>
A <term>compound shadow</term> is one that is partially illuminated by one or more secondary light sources.

### [*Of shadow*]

Shadow is the reduction of light and of darkness, and it is positioned between darkness and light.

Shadow is capable of infinite darkness <term>obscurity</term>, and this darkness may be infinitely reduced.

The beginnings and the ends of a shadow lie between light and darkness, and they can be infinitely reduced or increased.

Shadow is the means by which the form and shape of bodies are expressed.

The shapes of objects will provide no understanding of their character <term>quality</term> without shadow.

A shadow always shares the color of the object it falls upon.

Regarding the boundaries of shadows: some are soft like smoke <note>original: "like smoke"; a reference to Leonardo’s famous *sfumato* technique, where boundaries are blurred to create a sense of depth and realism.</note>, with edges that cannot be perceived; in others, the edges are sharp and distinct.

Keep the drawings for the end of the [book on] shadows. They may—

## PAINTING

Among objects of equal size and distance, the one that is most luminous colors its opposite object most strongly with its own essence <note>original: "tinges most with its essence"; referring to how light carries the color or quality of its source to other surfaces.</note>.

Among objects of equal luminosity, the one with the largest surface area <note>original: "largest in outline"</note> colors the greatest portion of its target object, provided the distance is the same for all.

<margin>Notebooks II 16 r. <note>original: "Quaderni"; Leonardo’s anatomical and scientific notebooks.</note></margin>
Among objects that are equal in luminosity and size, the one that is nearest colors its target object the most.

The reason we know that light possesses a single center within itself is as follows: we can clearly see that a large light source often dwarfs <note>original: "outspans"</note> a small object. Even though the light rays surround the object more than twice over, the object still casts a visible shadow on the nearest surface.

Let *c f* represent the large light source and *n* the object in front of it that produces the shadow on the wall, and *a b* the wall. It is clear that the shadow of *n* is not cast by the entire large light source itself; rather, because light has a central point, I can prove through experiment that the shadow is cast upon the wall as shown at points *m*, *o*, *t*, and *r*. [*Diagram*]

Why, when three objects are presented before two eyes, do they appear as only two?

Why, when surveying a direction using two sight-points, does the first one appear inaccurate?

I maintain that the eye projects an infinite number of lines, and these connect or mingle with the rays coming toward the eye from the objects being viewed. Only the central line of this visual faculty <term>perceptive faculty</term> is capable of accurately identifying and judging shapes and colors; all the other lines are unreliable <note>original: "false and deceitful"; Leonardo is distinguishing between focused central vision and less distinct peripheral vision.</note>.

If you place two objects a cubit <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> apart, with the first one very close to the eye, the surface of the closer object will appear much more blurred <note>original: "confused"</note> than the second. This is because the closer object is crossed by a greater number of "false" peripheral lines of vision than the second, and is therefore less distinct.

The central ray carries the truth when testing shadows. When an object placed in front of it is overcome too quickly by faint rays, it will cast a broad shadow that is disproportionately large and poorly defined. However, when the object producing the shadow intersects the light rays and is near the point of impact <note>original: "percussion"; the surface where the light or shadow falls</note>, then the shadow becomes distinct. This is especially true when the light source is distant, because over a long distance, the central ray is less interfered with by secondary rays <note>original: "false rays"</note>, since the lines of vision <note>original: "lines of the eye"</note> and the solar or other light rays traveling through the air are forced to follow a straight path. 

Otherwise, if they were hindered by the atmosphere being denser or thinner <note>original: "more rarefied"</note>, they would bend at some point; but if the air is free from density or moisture, they will maintain their straight nature, always carrying the image of the blocking <note>original: "intercepting"</note> object back to their point of origin. If the point of origin is the eye, the blocking object will be perceived by its color as well as by its shape and size. However, if the surface of that blocking object has a small hole that leads into a room that is dark—not because of its color, but due to the absence of light—you will see the rays entering through this small hole. They will transmit to the wall beyond all the features of their original source, both in color and form, except that everything will be inverted <note>Leonardo is describing the phenomenon of the *camera obscura*, where light passing through a pinhole projects an upside-down image of the outside world onto a surface.</note>.

The way in which the images of objects intersect at the edges of the small holes through which they pass:

### CONCERNING THE MOVEMENT OF THE RIGHT, LEFT, UPPER, OR LOWER EDGE

If you move the right side of the opening, the image projected on the left will move, since it belongs to the object on the right that entered through this opening. The same will happen with all the other sides of this opening. This is proven by the second section of this treatise, which states: all the rays that carry the images of objects <note>original: "bodies"</note> through the air travel in straight lines. Therefore, because the images of even the largest objects must pass through the smallest openings and then expand to their full size beyond that opening, it is necessary for these paths to cross over one another <note>original: "this intersection be uninterrupted"</note>. <margin>Windsor: Drawings 19149 r.</margin>

The images of objects are spread throughout the air that "sees" them, and they exist entirely within every part of it. 
This is proven: let *a*, *c*, and *e* be objects whose images penetrate into a dark place through the small holes *n* and *p*, and imprint themselves on the wall *f* and *i* opposite these holes. As many images will be created in as many different places on this wall as there are small holes.

### A demonstration and argument as to why some parts of an illuminated object are more brightly lit than others.

[Diagram]

Since it has been proven that every light source with fixed boundaries emanates—or appears to emanate—from a single point, the part illuminated by it will be brightest where the line of radiance <note>original: "line of radiance"; the path the light takes from the source to the object.</note> falls between two equal angles, as is shown above in the lines *a-g*, *a-h*, and *a-l*. In this way, you will also be able to identify the parts deprived of light, as seen at *m* and *k*.

When the angles made by the lines of incidence are more equal, the area will have more light, and where they are more unequal, it will be darker.

### XXXIII

## Perspective

> ‘*Perspective is a logical proof <note>original: "rational demonstration"</note> whereby experience confirms that all things transmit their images to the eye by pyramidal lines.*’ <note>Leonardo refers to the "visual pyramid," the idea that lines of sight form a pyramid shape with the object as the base and the eye as the point.</note>

Sandro! You do not explain why these second objects seem lower than the third.¹

[*Diagram*]

<margin>Codex Atlanticus <note>original: "C.A."</note> 120 r. d</margin>
The eye, when positioned between two parallel lines, will never see them at such a great distance that they actually meet at a single point. <note>Leonardo is discussing the "vanishing point" in linear perspective.</note>

All cases of perspective are expressed by means of the five mathematical terms, namely: point, line, angle, surface, and body. 

Of these, the **point** is unique in its kind; this point has neither height nor width, nor length nor depth, wherefore we conclude that it is indivisible and does not occupy space. 

A **line** is of three kinds, namely straight, curved, and bent. It has neither width, height, nor depth; consequently, it is indivisible except in its length. Its ends are two points.

An **angle** is the meeting of two lines at a point. They are of three kinds, namely: right angles, acute angles, and obtuse angles.

**Surface** is the name given to that which is the boundary of bodies. It is without depth; it is as indivisible in its depth as a line or a point, being divided only in respect to its length or width. There are as many different kinds of surfaces as there are bodies that create them.

**Body** is that which has height, width, length, and depth, and in all these attributes it is divisible. These bodies are of infinite and varied forms. Visible bodies are of two kinds only, of which the first is—

References to Sandro are also found in other manuscripts including the *Codex Atlanticus* and the *Treatise on Painting*.</note>

<summary>Leonardo defines the geometric foundations of perspective—point, line, angle, surface, and body—and notes a disagreement with Sandro Botticelli regarding the height of receding objects.</summary>

<header>PERSPECTIVE</header>

...without shape or any distinct or definite edges <note>original: "extremities"</note>, and although these are present, they are imperceptible; consequently, their color is difficult to determine. The second kind of visible bodies is that in which the surface defines and distinguishes the shape.

The first kind, which lacks a surface, consists of bodies that are fluid or liquid, which easily melt into and mingle with other fluid bodies—such as mud with water, mist or smoke with air, or the element of air with fire, and other similar things. Because their edges blend with the bodies surrounding them, their boundaries become confused and imperceptible. For this reason, they are considered to be without a surface, as they permeate one another's bodies; consequently, such bodies are said to be without a surface.

The second kind is divided into two further categories: transparent and opaque. A transparent body is one that reveals its entire self from every side, with nothing hidden behind it—as is the case with glass, crystal, water, and the like. The second division of bodies, where the surface reveals and defines the shape, is called opaque.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus <note>original: "C.A."</note> 132 r. b</margin>
It is necessary for us to discuss this at some length, seeing as an infinite number of cases are derived from it.

## *Perspective*

The air is filled with an infinite number of images of the objects distributed through it, and all of these are represented in all places, all in one, and all in each. Consequently, it happens that if two mirrors are placed so they exactly face each other, the first will be reflected in the second and the second in the first. Now, the first mirror being reflected in the second carries its own image to it, along with all the images already represented within it—among these being the image of the second mirror itself. This continues from image to image unto infinity, in such a way that each mirror contains an infinite number of mirrors within it, each smaller than the last, and nested one inside another.

By this example, it is clearly proved that every object transmits its own image to all those places where the object itself is visible; conversely, an object is able to receive into itself all the images of the things positioned in front of it.

<summary>Leonardo classifies visible bodies into those with and without distinct surfaces, while explaining the "infinite" nature of perspective through the metaphor of facing mirrors.</summary>
<keywords>perspective, fluid bodies, transparent vs opaque, optics, mirror reflection, infinite images, visual theory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s exploration of the physics of light and vision, focusing on the way images (or "species") propagate through the air and interact with mirrors and the human eye.</meta>

<page-num>988</page-num>
<header>PERSPECTIVE</header>

<margin>Codex Atlanticus <note>original: "C.A."</note> 138 r. b</margin>
Consequently, the eye transmits its own image through the air to all the objects in front of it and receives their images back into itself—specifically onto its surface. From there, the intellect <note>original: "understanding"</note> takes these images and considers them; those it finds pleasing, it commits to memory.

Therefore, I hold that the invisible power of the images within the eye may project outward toward the object, just as the images of the object project toward the eye.

An example of how the images of all things are spread through the air can be seen when several mirrors are placed in a circle. They will reflect each other an infinite number of times; for as the image of one reaches another, it bounces back to its source, and then, becoming smaller, bounces back again toward the object, and then returns. This process continues for an infinite number of times.

If at night you place a light between two flat mirrors that are a cubit's <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> distance apart, you will see an infinite number of lights in each of these mirrors, one smaller than the next in succession.

If at night you place a light within the walls of a room, every part of these walls will be colored by the images of this light. All those parts exposed to the light will likewise be directly illuminated by it, provided there is no obstacle between them to interrupt the transmission of the images.

This same principle is even more apparent in the transmission of solar rays. These rays pass through all objects and, consequently, into every minute part of every object; each individual ray carries the image of its source to the object it strikes.

These instances clearly show that every single body fills the surrounding air with its own images. Simultaneously, this same air is able to receive the images of countless other bodies within it. Each body is seen in its entirety throughout the whole of the atmosphere, and each is present in every minute part of it; all are present throughout the whole of it, and all are in every minute part. Each is in all, and all are in every part.

A body formed through perspective by Leonardo da Vinci, a disciple of experience.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 191 recto, a <note>The Codex Atlanticus is the largest collection of Leonardo's drawings and writings.</note></margin>
This body may be created without using any other object as a model, but rather by using simple lines alone.

Among the various studies of natural processes, the study of light gives the most pleasure to those who contemplate it. Among the noteworthy characteristics of mathematical science, the certainty of its demonstrations is what acts most powerfully to elevate the minds of those who investigate it.

Perspective, therefore, is to be preferred above all the formulas and systems of the traditional scholars <note>original: "schoolmen" — academic philosophers and theologians of the medieval period</note>. Within the field of perspective, the complex beam of light is shown through the stages of its development. Here, one finds the glory of not only mathematical science but also physical science, as perspective is adorned with the finest qualities of both. 

While its principles have often been expanded upon with much wordiness <note>original: "circumlocution"</note>, I will summarize them with conclusive brevity. I will introduce illustrations drawn either from nature or from mathematical science, depending on the subject. Sometimes I will deduce the results from the causes, and at other times, the causes from the results. I will also add some of my own conclusions that are not contained in existing works but which can nonetheless be inferred from them. I will do this as the Lord, who is the Light of all things, sees fit to reveal them to me as I seek to interpret this light. Consequently, I will divide the present work into three parts.

When light strikes objects that are turned toward it, it retains part of their images. This conclusion is proven by experience; when the vision looks directly at a bright light, it feels a sense of distress <note>original: "fear"</note>. Likewise, after looking at something bright, the images of these vivid objects remain in the eye. They make a place with less light appear to be in shadow until the eye has lost the impression left by the stronger light.

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s exploration of the physics of optics, specifically demonstrating how the behavior of light rays is identical to the behavior of visual rays in the eye, reinforcing his argument that perspective is a mathematical science.</meta>

<page-num>990</page-num>
<header>PERSPECTIVE</header>

Place an object in the corner <note>Leonardo is describing a setup to test how light and sight interact in a three-dimensional space.</note> and draw its outline with charcoal. Your eye must be positioned exactly at the hole where the light passed through. Just as the light from the window follows a specific path to do its work, the line of sight follows that same path. Consequently, the walls joined together in the corner will not appear any darker than one another because of the shadow.

## THE BEHAVIOR OF LIGHT UNDER THE LAW OF PERSPECTIVE IS IDENTICAL TO THAT OF THE EYE

Light does not differ from the eye in how it loses sight of objects hidden behind a foreground object. The reason for this is that the ray of vision and the ray of light resemble each other in both their speed of movement and in the convergence <note>original: "concourse" — the meeting or intersection of lines</note> of their straight lines. 

As an example: suppose you hold a coin near to your eye. The space between the coin and the background <note>original: "boundary of the position"</note> will be more capable of expansion in proportion to how much of that background is hidden from the eye. The nearer the coin is brought to the eye, the more the background will be blocked from view.

## CONCERNING LIGHT

**Concerning the eye.** The same process may be seen with light. As you bring the coin nearer to or remove it farther from this light, you will see the shadow on the opposite wall growing larger or shrinking. If you wish to see an example, try this: place many different objects <note>original: "bodies"</note> in a large room. Then, take a long pole with a piece of charcoal at the tip and, from a fixed point, mark on the ground and along the walls all the outlines of the objects <note>original: *cose* (things). The manuscript reads *delle pariete* (of the walls).</note> as they appear against the surfaces of the wall.

**Concerning the light.** Then, place a light at that same distance and height where your eye was. You will see the shadows of those objects covering exactly the same amount of the wall as the area enclosed within the charcoal marks you made with the tip of the pole.

<summary>Leonardo demonstrates that light rays and visual rays follow the same geometric rules of perspective, proving this through an experiment where shadows perfectly align with traced visual outlines.</summary>

### *Experiment*

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 204 v. b</margin>
If you wish to see a similar experiment, place a light upon a table and then move a certain distance away. You will see that all the shadows of the objects placed between the wall and the light are cast <note>original: "stamped"</note> with the shape of those objects. Furthermore, all the lines of their length converge toward the point where the light source is located.

Afterward, bring your eye closer to this light, using the blade of a knife as a screen so that the brightness does not hurt your eyes. You will see all the objects opposite you without their shadows; the shadows that were previously visible on the wall surfaces <note>original: "partitions of the walls"</note> will now be hidden from your view by the objects placed in front of them.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 221 v. c</margin>
Of things of equal size situated at an equal distance from the eye, the one that is whiter in color will appear larger.

Equal things at an equal distance from the eye will be judged by the eye to be of equal size.

Equal things, by being at different distances from the eye, will appear to be of unequal size.

Unequal things, by reason of their different distances from the eye, may appear equal.

---

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 249 r. c</margin>
Many things of large size <note>original: "great bulk"</note> become invisible at a great distance because of their color, while many small things at a great distance remain visible because of their color.

An object with a color similar to that of the air remains visible at a moderate distance. An object that is lighter <note>original: "paler"</note> than the air remains visible at a great distance, while an object that is darker than the air ceases to be visible at a short distance.

However, of these three kinds of objects, the one that will be visible at the greatest distance is the one whose color presents the strongest contrast to its surroundings.

Every ray of light that passes through air of uniform density travels in a straight line from its source to its object, or the place where it strikes.

## ON THE DIMINUTION OF OBJECTS AT VARIOUS DISTANCES

A second object placed as far away from the first as the first is from the eye will appear to be half the size of the first, even if they are actually the same size.

A small object close by and a large one in the distance will appear to be the same size if they are viewed within equal angles.

I ask how far away the eye can see a <term>non-luminous: an object that does not produce its own light, such as a rock or tree, but is only visible by reflected light</term> body, such as a mountain. It will be seen most clearly if the sun is behind it, and it will appear to be at a greater or lesser distance depending on the sun's position in the sky.

Perspective is a logical demonstration in which experience confirms how all things transmit their images to the eye through pyramidal lines. By "pyramidal lines," I mean those lines which start from the edges of the surface of an object and, by gradually converging from a distance, arrive at the same point. This point, as I shall show, is in this specific case located in the eye, which acts as the universal judge of all objects. I define a "point" as something that cannot be divided into any parts; and since this point within the eye is indivisible, no object can be seen by the eye unless it is larger than this point. Because of this, it is necessary that the lines extending from the object to the point must be pyramidal. 

If anyone tries to argue that the power of sight does not belong to this single point, but rather to that black spot seen in the center of the pupil <note>Leonardo is distinguishing between a mathematical point of focus and the physical anatomy of the eye</note>, one could reply to him that if this were true, a small object—such as a grain of millet or <term>panic-seed: a type of tiny grain or grass seed</term>—could never appear to shrink regardless of distance. Furthermore, any object larger than that point could never be seen in its entirety.

No object is so large that it will not appear smaller to the eye at a great distance than a smaller object that is closer.

A wall surface <note>original: "pariete." This refers to the "picture plane," the imaginary flat surface or window through which an artist views a scene to draw it in perspective</note> is a perpendicular plane represented in front of the common point where the <term>concourse: the meeting or coming together of lines</term> of the pyramids converges. And

This wall surface performs the same function for the aforementioned point <note>the eye's focal point</note> as a flat piece of glass upon which you drew the various objects that you saw through it. The things drawn would be smaller than the originals in the same proportion as the distance between the glass and the eye was less than the distance between the glass and the object.

The convergence <note>original: "concourse"</note> of the visual pyramids created by these objects will show upon the wall surface the variety of the size and distance of the objects that cause them.

All these planes <note>referring to horizontal surfaces, like floors or ceilings</note> which have their edges joined by perpendicular lines forming right angles must necessarily, if they are of equal size, appear less visible <note>meaning more foreshortened or thinner</note> the closer they rise to the level of the eye; the farther they pass beyond the eye level (either above or below), the more their true size will be seen.

The farther a spherical body is from the eye, the more of its surface is visible. <note>Leonardo is observing that as a sphere recedes, the lines of sight become more parallel, allowing the eye to perceive more of the sphere's hemisphere.</note>

As soon as the air is illuminated, it is filled with an infinite number of images caused by the various substances and colors collected together within it; the eye acts as both the target and the magnet for these images.

## PRINCIPLE OF PERSPECTIVE

<margin>A 36 v.</margin>
All things transmit their image to the eye by means of pyramids; the closer to the eye these pyramids are intersected <note>cut across by the painting surface or "picture plane"</note>, the smaller the image of their cause <note>the object</note> will appear.

If you should ask how you can demonstrate these points to me through experience, I would tell you—regarding the vanishing point which moves with you—to notice as you walk along lands ploughed in straight furrows, the ends of which start from the path where you are walking. You will see that each pair of furrows continually seems to approach the other and to join at their far ends.

<margin>A 37 r. and v.</margin>
As for the point that enters the eye, it may be understood with greater ease; for if you look into the eye of another person, you will see your own image there. Consequently, if you imagine two lines starting from your ears and proceeding to the ears of the image you see of yourself in the other person's eye, you will clearly recognize that these lines narrow so much that when they have continued only a little way beyond your image as mirrored in that eye, they will meet at a single point.

# PERSPECTIVE

<margin>A 38 r.</margin>
An object that is closer to the eye always appears larger than another object of the same size that is further away.

<margin>A 38 v.</margin>
Perspective is of such a nature that it makes flat surfaces appear to have three-dimensional relief, and three-dimensional objects appear flat.

The perspective used to represent an object will be better understood when it is viewed from the same vantage point <note>original: "view-point"</note> from which it was originally drawn.

If you wish to represent a nearby object so that it produces the effect of a natural thing, it is impossible for your perspective not to appear distorted—due to all the visual illusions and proportional errors that occur in even average work—unless the person looking at this perspective stands at the exact distance, height, and angle where you were positioned when you created it. Therefore, it would be necessary to create a frame the size of your face, or even a small hole, through which you would look at the work. If you do this, your work will undoubtedly produce the effect of nature (provided the light and shadow are correctly rendered), and you will find it difficult to believe that these things are merely painted. Otherwise, do not bother trying to represent anything unless you set your vantage point at a distance at least twenty times the maximum width and height of the object you are depicting; this distance will satisfy any observer who stands in front of the work at any angle whatsoever.

<margin>A 40 v.</margin>
If you wish to see a quick proof of this, take a wooden rod shaped like a small column that is eight times higher than its width, without a base <note>original: "plinth"</note> or a decorative top <note>original: "capital"</note>. Then, mark forty equal spaces on a flat wall that correspond to these dimensions; these will represent forty columns similar to your small rod. Next, place a thin iron strip in front of the center of these spaces, at a distance of four <term>braccia</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement roughly equal to 23 inches, or the length of an arm.</note> from the wall. In the center of this strip, there should be a small round hole the size of a large pearl. Place a light right next to this hole, then go and place your column over each mark on the wall and trace the outline of its shadow. Finally, shade the drawings and observe them through the hole in the iron strip.

<vocab>perspective, three-dimensional relief, vantage point, light and shade, arm-lengths (braccia), shadow</vocab>

<summary>Leonardo explains that for a perspective drawing to look truly realistic, the viewer must stand at the same vantage point as the artist, otherwise the proportions will appear distorted. He suggests that for public viewing, an artist should use a distant vantage point to minimize these optical errors.</summary>

### PERSPECTIVE

<margin>C 23 r.</margin>
No visible body can be understood or properly judged by human eyes except by the contrast of the background where the outer edges <note>original: "extremities"</note> of this body end and are bounded. As far as its outlines are concerned, no object will seem to be separated from its background unless there is a difference in color or light. For example, although the moon is far distant from the body of the sun, when it passes between our eyes and the sun during an eclipse, it will appear to human eyes to be joined and attached to the sun because the sun serves as its background.

<margin>C 27 v.</margin>
Perspective comes to our aid where our natural judgment fails to understand objects as they diminish in the distance.

### [Of perspective in nature and in art]

It is possible to arrange things so that the eye does not see distant objects as being as small as they appear in natural perspective. In nature, objects diminish because of the curvature <note>original: "convexity"</note> of the eye, which is forced to intersect the pyramids of vision <note>original: "pyramids of every kind of image"; Leonardo conceptualized light rays as forming a pyramid with the object as the base and the eye as the point</note> as they reach the surface of the eye at right angles.

However, the method I am illustrating here in the margin cuts these pyramids at right angles near the surface of the pupil. While the curved pupil of the eye can take in our entire hemisphere, this method will show only a single star. But where many small stars transmit their images to the surface of the pupil, they appear very small; here, only one will be visible, but it will appear large. In this way, the moon will seem larger in size and its spots will be more distinct. To achieve this, you should place close to the eye a glass filled with the water mentioned in chapter four of Book II, ‘Concerning Natural Things’—water which causes things enclosed <note>original: "congealed"</note> in balls of crystal glass to appear as though they were not inside glass at all.

Regarding the eye: of objects smaller than the pupil of the eye, the one that is closest to it will be the least visible to the pupil. From this experiment, it follows that the power of sight is not concentrated into a single point.

Instead, the images of objects that meet in the pupil are spread over its surface in the same way they are spread throughout the air. The proof of this is shown to us when we look at the...

...starry heavens without fixing our gaze more upon one star than upon another; for then the sky shows itself to us strewn with stars, and they appear to the eye in the same proportions as they are in the sky, and the spaces between them also appear the same.

Natural perspective acts in the opposite way, for the greater the distance, the smaller the object appears, and the shorter the distance, the larger it appears. But this invention <note>referring to a specific method of artificial perspective</note> forces the viewer to look through a small hole, and only through this small hole will the image be seen correctly. However, since many eyes often come together to see the same work of art at the same time, only one of them will have a proper view of how this perspective functions, and all the others will only see it confusedly. It is better, therefore, to avoid this compound perspective <note>a complex method of perspective that requires a single fixed viewpoint</note> and to keep to simple perspective, which does not attempt to view planes as foreshortened <term>foreshortening: a technique used to make an object appear to recede in space by compressing its dimensions</term> but as far as possible in their exact form.

An example of this simple perspective—in which the flat surface intersects the pyramid of light <note>original: "pyramid"; Leonardo conceptualized light rays as forming a pyramid with the object as the base and the eye as the point</note> that carries images to the eye at an equal distance from the eyesight <note>original: "visual faculty"</note>—is provided for us by the curve of the pupil of the eye. On this curve, these pyramids intersect at an equal distance from the eyesight.

### FOR OBJECTS OF EQUAL SIZE, THE MORE DISTANT APPEARS SMALLER

The practice of perspective is divided into [two] parts. The first deals with everything seen by the eye at any distance, and this by itself shows all these things shrinking <note>original: "diminished"</note> as the eye beholds them, without requiring the viewer to stand in one place rather than another—as long as the wall <note>the surface upon which the perspective is drawn</note> does not distort <term>foreshorten</term> it a second time.

But the second practice is a combination of perspective created partly by art and partly by nature. Work produced according to its rules has no part that is not influenced by both natural and accidental perspective. By "natural perspective," I understand the relationship to the flat surface on which this perspective is represented. Although this surface is parallel in its length and height, it is forced to make the distant parts appear smaller than the near ones. This is proven by the principles stated above, and this shrinking <note>original: "diminution"</note> is natural.

Accidental perspective—that is, the perspective created by art—acts in...

## THE PERSPECTIVE OF THE DISAPPEARANCE OF THE OUTLINES OF SOLID OBJECTS <note>original: "opaque bodies"</note>

<margin>E 80 r.</margin>
If the true outlines of solid objects <note>original: "opaque bodies"</note> become indistinguishable at a short distance, they will be even more invisible at great distances. Since it is through these outlines that we recognize the true shape of any solid object, whenever distance prevents us from perceiving the whole, we will lose our perception of its individual parts and edges even more.

### ON PAINTING AND PERSPECTIVE

There are three divisions of perspective as used in painting. The first relates to the reduction <note>original: "diminution"</note> in the size <note>original: "volume"</note> of solid objects. The second deals with the reduction and eventual disappearance of the outlines of these solid objects. The third is the reduction and loss of their color when viewed from a great distance.

### ON THE PERSPECTIVE OF THE REDUCTION OF SOLID OBJECTS

Among solid objects of equal size, the apparent reduction in their scale will vary based on their distance from the eye that sees them. However, this occurs in inverse proportion: at a greater distance, the solid object appears smaller, and at a closer distance, the same object appears larger. This principle is the foundation of linear perspective. 

Secondly, demonstrate how every object at a great distance first loses sight of its thinnest parts. For example, a horse would appear to lose its legs sooner than its head because the legs are thinner than the head; similarly, it would lose the neck before the torso <note>original: "trunk"</note> for the same reason. It follows, therefore, that the last part of the horse the eye will be able to distinguish is the torso, which maintains its oval form but begins to resemble a cylinder, eventually losing even its perceived thickness...

...is called double because if the first object is one *braccio* <term>braccio: an Italian unit of measurement meaning "arm," approximately 23 inches</term> away from the eye and the second is at a distance of two *braccia*, the second space is double the first. For this reason, the first object will appear to be twice as large as the second. If you move the first to a distance of one hundred *braccia* and the second to one hundred and one *braccia*, you will find that the first is larger than the second only by the small ratio that one hundred is less than one hundred and one—and the same applies in reverse.

The same principle is also proven by the fourth proposition of this work, which states: in the case of equal objects, the ratio of their size is the same as the ratio of their distance from the eye that sees them. <sig>G 29 v.</sig>

## DISCOURSE ON PAINTING

Perspective, as it concerns painting, is divided into three chief parts. The first treats of the reduction <note>original: "diminution"</note> in the size of bodies at different distances. The second treats of the fading <note>original: "diminution"</note> of the color of these bodies. The third concerns the gradual loss of clarity <note>original: "distinctness"</note> of the forms and outlines of these bodies at various distances.

In measuring distances, perspective employs two opposite pyramids. One of these has its point <note>original: "apex"</note> in the eye and its base as far away as the horizon. The other has its base at the eye and its point on the horizon. The first pyramid is concerned with the universe, embracing the entire mass of objects that pass before the eye, as though a vast landscape were seen through a small hole. The number of objects seen through such a hole becomes greater as the objects become more remote from the eye; thus, the base is formed on the horizon and the point is in the eye, as I have said above.

The second pyramid has to do with a specific quality of the landscape: it appears so much smaller as it recedes farther from the eye. This second instance of perspective springs from the first.

### *[Perspective of disappearance]*

In every figure placed at a great distance, you first lose the ability to recognize its most minute parts. You preserve to the last the sight of the larger parts, losing, however, the perception of all their edges; they become oval or spherical in shape, and their boundaries are blurry <note>original: "indistinct"</note>. <sig>G 53 v.</sig>

## OF ORDINARY PERSPECTIVE

An object of uniform thickness and color seen against a background of various colors will appear as if it is not of uniform thickness.

And if an object of uniform thickness but of various colors is seen against a background of uniform color, the object will seem to be of varying thickness.

<margin>I 17 v.</margin>
In proportion to how much variety there is in the colors of the background—or of the object seen against that background—the more their thickness will seem to vary, even though the objects seen against the background are actually of equal thickness.

A dark object seen against a light background will seem smaller than it actually is.

<margin>I 18 r.</margin>
A light object will appear larger in size when it is seen against a background that is darker in color.

If the eye is positioned in the middle of a track with two horses running toward their goal along parallel paths, it will seem to the observer that they are running to meet one another.

<margin>K 120 [40] v.</margin>
This phenomenon occurs because the images of the horses which impress themselves upon the eye are moving toward the center of the surface of the eye's pupil.

## PAINTING

<margin>L 21 r.</margin>
Foreshorten the outlines of land holdings and their divisions on the summits and sides of hills; as for the objects turned directly toward you, depict them in their true shape.

<margin>B.M. 134 v.</margin>
Among objects moving at the same speed, the one further from the eye will appear to move more slowly. Conversely, the one closer to the eye will appear faster.

<insert>*[Aerial perspective]*</insert>
In the morning, the mist is thicker at higher altitudes than in the lower parts because the sun draws it upward. Therefore, with tall buildings, the summit may be invisible even though it is the same distance away as the base. This is also why the sky appears darker at the top and toward the horizon; it does not look blue, but instead takes on the color of smoke and dust.

When the atmosphere is filled with mist, it loses all its blue color and simply appears the color of the clouds—which turn white in fair weather. The further west you look, the darker the sky will appear, while it becomes brighter and clearer toward the east. The greenery <note>original: "verdure"</note> of the countryside will take on a bluish tint in light mist, but will turn black when the mist is thicker.

Buildings facing west show only their illuminated side; the mist hides the rest.

As the sun rises and clears the mists, the hills begin to look distinct on the side where the mist is lifting. They take on a blue color and appear to emit smoke toward the retreating mist. Buildings reveal their light and shadow; where the mist is thinner, only their highlights are visible, and where it is thicker, nothing can be seen. At this time, the movement of the mist causes it to drift horizontally, making its edges barely visible against the blue sky, while against the ground it looks almost like rising dust.

As the atmosphere becomes denser, buildings in a city and trees in a landscape will appear less frequent, as only the most prominent and largest will be visible.

The mountains will also seem fewer in number, for only those will be...

### OF PERSPECTIVE

When the eye turns away from a white object illuminated by the sun and moves to a place with less light, everything there will seem dark. This happens because the eye, while resting upon that white, illuminated object, contracts its pupil to such an extent that it loses more than three-quarters of its original visible surface; thus, reduced in size, the pupil is also reduced in power.

You might argue: "A small bird, then, would see very little by comparison; because of its tiny pupils, white objects would appear black to it." To this, I would reply that we are here considering the proportion of the mass of the brain dedicated to the sense of sight, and nothing else. Or—to return to the point—our pupil expands and contracts according to the brightness or darkness of the object it views, and since it requires a certain interval of time...

### FOR STAMPING MEDALS

A diamond is crushed by being wrapped in lead and beaten with a hammer. The lead should be spread out and folded up again several times, and it must be kept wrapped in paper so that the powder is not scattered. Then melt the lead; the powder rises to the surface of the lead once it has melted. It is afterwards rubbed between two plates of steel so that it becomes a very fine powder. Finally, wash it with nitric acid <note>original: "aqua fortis"</note>, and the black coating from the iron will be dissolved, leaving the powder clean.

Lumps of emery can be broken up by placing them in a cloth folded many times and hitting the bundle on the side with a hammer. ## Commissions

> ->*"Works of renown, through which I might show to those"*<-
> ->*"who are to come that I once existed."*<-

[Memorandum of the order of events in the Battle of Anghiari <note>Fought on June 29, 1440, between the forces of Milan and a coalition led by the Republic of Florence. Leonardo was commissioned to paint this scene in the Great Council Hall, but the mural was never finished and is now lost.</note>, drawn up apparently for Leonardo to consult while composing his painting on the wall of the Council Chamber of the Palazzo della Signoria in Florence.]

**Leaders of the Florentines:**

Neri di Gino Capponi.
Bernardetto de’ Medici.
Niccolò da Pisa.
Count Francesco <note>Francesco Sforza, who later became the Duke of Milan.</note>.
Micheletto <note>Micheletto Attendolo.</note>.
Pietro Gian Paolo.
Guelfo Orsino.
Messer Rinaldo degli Albizi.

You should commence with the speech of Niccolò Piccinino <note>The commander of the Milanese forces.</note> to his soldiers and the banished Florentines, among whom was Messer Rinaldo degli Albizi. Then you should show him first mounting his horse in full armor, with the entire army following him: forty squadrons of cavalry and two thousand infantry <note>original: "foot soldiers"</note> went with him.

And the Patriarch <note>Ludovico Trevisan, the Patriarch of Aquileia, who commanded the Papal troops allied with Florence.</note> at an early hour of the morning ascended a hill in order to scout the terrain—that is, the hills, fields, and a valley watered by a river. He saw Niccolò Piccinino approaching from Borgo San Sepolcro <note>A town in Tuscany, now known as Sansepolcro.</note> with his men in a great cloud of dust; and having spotted him, he turned to the captains of his own men and spoke with them.

And having spoken, he clasped his hands and prayed to God; and presently he saw a cloud, and from the cloud St. Peter emerged and—

<summary>Leonardo outlines the narrative sequence for his "Battle of Anghiari" mural, detailing the key military leaders and the opening scenes of the battle, including speeches, troop movements, and a divine vision.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the detailed military narrative of the Battle of Anghiari, describing the tactical maneuvers around the bridge and the eventual rout of the Milanese forces by the Florentine coalition.</meta>

<page-num>1009</page-num>

# COMMISSIONS

The message was spoken to the Patriarch. Five hundred cavalry were dispatched by the Patriarch to hinder or check the enemy's attack.

In the leading troop was Francesco, the son of Niccolò Piccinino; he arrived first to attack the bridge, which was defended by the Patriarch <note>original: "PP." (the manuscript abbreviation for the Patriarch, Ludovico Trevisan)</note> and the Florentines.

Behind the bridge, on the left, he sent the infantry to engage our men, who beat off the attack. Their leader was Micheletto <note>Micheletto Attendolo</note>, who was the officer of the watch at the court. Here at this bridge, a great fight broke out: the enemy would conquer, and then the enemy would be repulsed.

Then Guido and his brother Astorre, the Lord of Faenza, reformed and renewed the combat with many of their men. They hurled themselves upon the Florentines with such vigor that they regained possession of the bridge and pushed their advance as far as the tents.

Opposite them came Simonetto with six hundred cavalry to harass the enemy; he drove them back from the spot and reoccupied the bridge.

Behind him followed another company with two thousand cavalry, and for a long time, the battle swayed back and forth.

Then, to throw the enemy's ranks into disorder, the Patriarch sent forward Niccolò da Pisa and Napoleone Orsini—a beardless youth <note>Napoleone Orsini was a young commander at the time of the battle in 1440.</note>—along with a great multitude of men; there, another great feat of arms was performed.

At this time, Niccolò Piccinino pushed forward another unit of his followers, which caused our men to advance yet again. Had the Patriarch not thrown himself into the midst of the struggle, sustaining his commanders with both words and deeds, the enemy would have driven them into flight.

The Patriarch ordered certain pieces of artillery to be set up on the hill, which he used to spread confusion among the enemy's infantry. This disorder became so great that Niccolò began to call back his son and all his followers, and they started to flee toward the Borgo <note>Borgo San Sepolcro.</note>. At this location, a great slaughter of men occurred; none escaped except those who were the first to flee or those who hid themselves.

The combat continued until the setting of the sun.

# COMMISSIONS

## [For heraldic designs—with drawings]

### MASTER ANTONIO GRI, A VENETIAN AND COMPANION TO ANTONIO MARIA

On the left side, place a wheel; let its center cover the center of the horse’s rear thigh-armor. In this center, Prudence should be shown dressed in red, representing Charity, sitting in a fiery chariot. She should hold a sprig of laurel in her hand to symbolize the hope that arises from good service.

On the opposite side, place Fortitude in a similar way, holding her necklace in her hand. She is clothed in white, which signifies <unclear>...</unclear> <note>The original manuscript is incomplete here.</note>. Both figures are crowned, and Prudence is depicted with three eyes <note>A traditional Renaissance representation of Prudence, symbolizing her ability to see the past, present, and future.</note>.

The horse’s housing <note>original: "housing"; the decorative cloth covering for a horse's back and sides.</note> should be woven of plain gold and decorated with many peacock "eyes." This pattern applies to all the horse's coverings and the man's coat.

The crest of the man’s helmet and his hauberk <note>original: "hauberk"; usually a coat of mail, but here referring to a decorative tunic worn over armor.</note> are to be made of peacock feathers on a gold background.

Above the helmet, place a half-globe to represent our hemisphere in the form of a world. Upon it, place a peacock with its tail spread out to extend beyond the group. It should be richly decorated. Every ornament belonging to the horse should be made of peacock feathers on a gold ground to represent the beauty that comes from the grace given to one who serves well.

<margin>British Museum MS, folio 250 recto</margin>
In the shield, place a large mirror to signify that anyone who truly desires favor should see their own virtues reflected.

->How well the learned art answers to nature:<-

# XXXVI
## Sculpture

->*“As I practice the art of sculpture no less*<-
->*than that of painting, and perform both*<-
->*to the same degree of excellence.”*<-

[Notes made in preparation for a statue]
In the statue at Pavia,¹ the movement is more deserving of praise than anything else.
It is better to copy antique works than modern ones.
You cannot combine utility with beauty, as is evident in fortresses and in the forms of men. <note>Leonardo argues that functional requirements often detract from pure aesthetic beauty.</note>
The trot is almost like the natural movement of a horse in the wild.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 147 r. b</margin>
Where natural liveliness is lacking, it is necessary to create it through artifice <note>original: "fortuitously"</note>.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 215 v. d</margin>
The sculptor cannot represent transparent or luminous things.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 216 v. a</margin>
All the heads of the large iron pins.²

How the eye cannot discern the shapes of bodies within their boundaries except by means of shadows and lights; and there are many sciences which would be nothing without the science of these shadows and lights: such as painting, sculpture, astronomy, a great part of perspective, and the like.

As may be shown, the sculptor cannot work without the help of—

---

<header>SCULPTURE</header>

...shadows and lights, since without these the material carved would remain all of one color; and by the ninth section of this book it is shown that a level surface lit by uniform light does not vary in any part the brightness or darkness of its natural color. This uniformity of color goes to prove the uniform smoothness of its surface. It would follow, therefore, that if the material carved were not shaped by shadows and lights—which are made necessary by the prominences of certain muscles and the hollows placed between them—the sculptor would not be able to see the continuous progress of his own work. Yet the work he is carving requires this visibility; without it, what he fashioned during the day would be almost as though it had been made in the darkness of the night.

## OF STATUES

If you wish to make a marble figure, first make one of clay. After you have finished it and let it dry, set it in a case <note>a "pointing box" used to transfer measurements from a model to a block of stone</note>. This case should be large enough that—after the clay figure has been removed—it can hold the block of marble in which you intend to reveal a figure resembling the one in clay. 

Then, after you have placed the clay figure inside this case, make pegs so that they fit exactly into holes in the case. Drive them into each hole until each white peg touches the figure at a different spot. Stain the parts of the pegs that project out of the case black, and make a distinguishing mark for each peg and its corresponding hole so that you may fit them together easily. 

Next, take the clay model out of the case and place the block of marble in it. Carve away enough from the marble so that all the pegs are hidden in the holes up to their marks. In order to be able to do this better, make the case...

## ON THE FORCE OF THE SCULPTOR’S BLOW

Because the moment of a blow is instantaneous, just like the contact caused by that blow, its action is so swift that time does not allow the impact to transfer itself to the base of the object being struck. The force is already spent in the upper parts before it can travel downward. This is similar to how a mason can break a stone held in his hand with a hammer without causing violence or damage to the hand itself.

And this is why, after a chisel <note>original: "iron *a b*"</note> has been struck by a hammer on its upper part (*a*), this part reacts to the nature of the blow rather than transferring the energy to its base (*b*). As a result, the top edge is flattened and enlarged <note>This refers to the "mushrooming" effect on the head of a metal tool after repeated striking.</note> more than the base.

From this, it follows that sculptors work more effectively upon their marble when they "rough-hew" <term>Rough-hew: to carve a material into a coarse, approximate shape before fine detailing.</term> with a pointed hammer rather than with a chisel struck by a hammer.

<margin>Manuscript C, folio 6 v.</margin>
A sharp sword will also cut a roll <note>likely a roll of fabric or paper</note> in mid-air.

<margin>Notebooks <note>original: "Quaderni"</note> VI, folio 10 r.</margin>
Some have made the mistake of teaching sculptors to wrap wires around the limbs of their figures, as if they believed these limbs were perfectly cylindrical at every point where the wires touched them.

# XXXVII

## Casting

> *‘Of the horse I will say nothing because I know the times.’* <note>Leonardo is likely referring to his ill-fated "Sforza Horse" monument in Milan. The "times" refers to the French invasion and political instability that ultimately prevented the massive bronze statue from being cast.</note>

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, 352 r. c</margin>
...the cooling material will reach a sufficient thickness where it touches the plaster; then, you pour out the remainder and fill the center with plaster. Next, break the outer mold and insert iron pins across it, boring through the wax and the plaster core. Then, you can clean the wax at your own pace. 

Afterward, place it in a protective casing and apply a plaster mold over it, leaving air vents and a "mouth" <term>Mouth: the opening through which molten metal is poured into a mold.</term> for the casting. Turn the mold upside down through this mouth; once it has been heated, you will be able to drain out the wax contained within it. You can then fill the resulting vacuum with your liquefied metal, and the cast object will be hollow. However, to prevent the plaster from breaking while it is being fired again, you must place within it the materials you are already familiar with <note>Leonardo is likely referring to binders such as animal hair, cloth scraps, or organic fibers used to reinforce the plaster against thermal shock.</note>.

<margin>Trivulzian Manuscript, 29 a</margin>
*\[With a drawing of the apparatus]*
This is the way in which the molds are dried rapidly, being continually turned like meat on a roasting spit.

### HOW CASTS OUGHT TO BE POLISHED

You should make a bundle of iron wire as thick as fine string and scrub the casts with it and water. Keep a tub beneath the work so that the runoff does not create a mess of mud on the floor.

### HOW TO REMOVE THE ROUGH EDGES OF THE BRONZE

You should make an iron rod shaped like a large chisel and rub it along the seams <note>original: "edges... caused by the joins in the mould"</note> that remain on the casts of cannons. Ensure that the rod has significant weight and that your strokes are long and sweeping.

<page-num>1021</page-num>

# CASTING

### TO FACILITATE THE MELTING

First, melt a portion of the alloy in the crucible and then place it into the furnace. This metal, once it is in a molten state, will act as a "starter" to begin the melting process of the copper.

### TO GUARD AGAINST THE COPPER COOLING IN THE FURNACE

If you notice the copper beginning to cool in the furnace, act immediately. As soon as you see this happening, use a stirring pole to slice into the metal while it is still a thick paste. If it has already become entirely cold and solid, cut it into pieces with large, broad chisels, just as you would cut through lead.

### FOR THE MAKING OF A LARGE CAST

If you have to create a cast weighing one hundred thousand pounds, prepare it using five furnaces, allocating two thousand pounds to each—or three thousand pounds at the very most. <note>Trivulzian Manuscript, 47 a. Note: The math here (5 furnaces x 2,000 lbs = 10,000 lbs) does not total the 100,000 lbs mentioned; Leonardo may have intended to specify fifty furnaces or a smaller total weight.</note>

### HOW THE BOARD SHOULD BE PLACED WHICH SUPPORTS THE MORTAR

The template board that serves as a guide for the shape of the mortar <note>original: "mortar"; a short-barreled cannon used for lobbing projectiles at high angles</note> should be reinforced from the center backwards by the width of a thick plank. This is done to ensure it does not warp or twist. The side of this board that carries the impression of the cannon’s frame and form is the "face," not the edge. When you apply the tallow <term>Tallow: rendered animal fat used as a lubricant or to create a smooth surface on a mold.</term>, burnish this face with a pig’s tooth so that the surface becomes solid and smooth. Ensure the tallow is finely strained so that as the mold turns, it does not leave any uneven marks.

### WHAT TO DO IN ORDER TO BREAK UP A LARGE MASS OF BRONZE

If you wish to break apart a large mass of bronze, first suspend it in the air. Then, build a four-sided wall around it in the shape of a brick-layer's hod and build a large fire inside. When the bronze is glowing red-hot, strike it with a heavy weight dropped from a height, using great force.

### ON CASTING MANY SMALL CANNON SIMULTANEOUSLY

Construct the channels <note>original: "courses"; the runners or conduits through which molten metal flows into the molds</note> for the bronze as shown in the diagram. Keep the plugs *d*, *b*, and *c* closed, but leave the channel *a* completely open. Once that mold is full, unplug *b*; when that is full, unplug *c*, and finally *d*. The doors or "gates" of these channels should be made of brick about three fingers thick <term>Three fingers: an informal unit of measurement, approximately 2.25 inches or 5.7 centimeters.</term> and well-coated with ashes. These are then opened using pincers. The branches of these channels, when they are also being cast, should be separated by small iron plates covered in earth before they are secured.

->Tr. 48 a<- <note>original: "Tr. 48 a"; refers to the Trivulzian Manuscript, folio 48, recto.</note>

### HOW TO BLEND LEAD WITH OTHER METALS

If you wish to use lead in the alloy for the sake of economy and to reduce the amount of tin required, first alloy the lead with the tin and then add that mixture to the molten copper.

### ON THE NECESSARY STRUCTURE FOR A MELTING FURNACE

The furnace should be situated between four pillars supported by strong foundations.

### ON THE THICKNESS OF THE MOLD COATING

The coating should not exceed a thickness of two fingers. It should be applied in four layers over the fine clay and prepared carefully. It should be annealed <note>original: "annealed"; a process of heating and slow cooling to toughen the material and prevent cracking</note> only on the inside and then finished with a fine dressing of ashes and cattle dung <note>Cattle dung was a common historical additive in mold-making; the organic fibers helped the clay withstand the heat of the molten metal without shattering.</note>.

### ON THE THICKNESS OF THE MORTAR

A mortar <note>original: "mortar"; a short-barreled cannon used to fire projectiles at high angles</note> should be capable of firing a ball weighing six hundred pounds or more. To determine the correct dimensions, take the measurement of the ball's diameter and divide it into six parts. One of these parts will define the thickness of the metal at the muzzle <term>Muzzle: the front end of the cannon where the ball exits.</term>. The thickness at the breech <term>Breech: the rear part of the cannon where the explosion occurs.</term> will always be half of that measurement <note>Leonardo's notes here suggest a specific ratio for the metal's thickness relative to the projectile's size, though historically the breech was made thicker than the muzzle to withstand the pressure of the gunpowder.</note>. If the ball is to weigh seven hundred pounds, the thickness at the muzzle should be one-seventh of the ball's diameter; if the ball is to be eight... <note>The text ends mid-sentence as the rule of proportions continues.</note>

[If it weighs eight] hundred pounds, the thickness will be one-eighth of its diameter at the muzzle; if it weighs nine hundred, one-eighth and a half; and if it weighs one thousand, one-ninth.

## OF THE LENGTH OF THE TUBE OF THE MORTAR

If you wish it to throw a stone ball, make the length of the tube six or up to seven times the diameter of the ball. If the ball is to be made of iron, make this tube up to twelve times the diameter of the ball; and if the ball is to be made of lead, make it up to eighteen times. I mean this to apply when the mortar <term>Mortar: a short-barreled piece of artillery designed to fire projectiles at high trajectories.</term> is sized to receive a stone ball weighing six hundred pounds or more.

## OF THE THICKNESS OF SMALL CANNON

The thickness of small cannon at the muzzle ought not to exceed one-third to one-half of the diameter of the ball, nor should the length exceed thirty to thirty-six times its diameter. <insert>Tr. 49 a</insert> <note>original: "Tr. 49 a"; refers to the Trivulzian Manuscript, folio 49, recto.</note>

## OF LUTING THE FURNACE ON THE INSIDE

Before you put the metal in, the furnace ought to be luted <term>Luting: the act of sealing or coating a surface with a clay-like material to protect it from heat or make it airtight.</term> with earth from Valenza <note>Earth from Valenza: a specific type of fine, silty clay from the Valenza region of Italy, highly valued by Renaissance craftsmen for its heat-resistant properties.</note>, and covered with a layer of ashes.

## OF RESTORING THE METAL WHEN IT SEEMS ON THE POINT OF COOLING

When you see that the bronze is on the point of becoming solidified <note>original: "congealed"</note>, take willow wood cut into small chips and build up the fire with it.

## THE CAUSE OF ITS CONGEALING

I say the cause of this solidification is often caused by there being too much fire, and also from the wood being only half-dried.

## TO KNOW THE CONDITION OF THE FIRE

You will know when the fire is good and suitable by the clear flames; if you see the tips of these flames are murky and ending in much [smoke]...

<header>CASTING</header>

If there is smoke, do not trust it, especially when the molten metal is almost in a completely fluid state.

### WHAT KINDS OF WOOD ARE SUITABLE

Wood is suitable for the furnace if it is young willow; if willow cannot be obtained, get alder, and ensure that each branch is young and well-dried.

### ON ALLOYING THE METAL

The metal used for bombards <term>Bombard: a large-caliber medieval cannon, typically used for siege warfare to throw heavy stone balls.</term> must invariably be made with six or even eight parts of tin to one hundred parts of copper. Note, however, that the less tin you add, the stronger the bombard will be.

### WHEN THE TIN SHOULD BE ADDED TO THE COPPER

The tin should be added to the copper only when the copper has been fully transformed into a fluid state.

### HOW THE PROCESS OF MELTING MAY BE SPEEDED UP

You can speed up the process of melting once the copper is two-thirds changed into a fluid state. By using a chestnut rod, you will be able to stir the remaining solid copper into the melted portion. <insert>Tr. 50 a</insert> <note>original: "Tr. 50 a"; refers to the Trivulzian Manuscript, folio 50, recto.</note>

### THE FINE EARTH FOR THE BOMBARDS

<note>The "fine earth" refers to the refractory clay mixture used to create the molds for casting the bronze cannons.</note>

Take the dust of wool clippings and fix it on a wall in thin plaster so that it dries well. Then pound it and sift it into a fine powder. To fifty parts of this powder, add ten parts of brick that is not over-baked, well-pounded, and sifted. Add also a small quantity of fine wool clippings or fustian cloth <term>Fustian: a sturdy, heavy fabric made of cotton and linen, used here to reinforce the molding clay.</term>. Then, to this compound, add six parts of ashes which you have sifted and moistened with well-salted water. Apply this mixture while it is liquid and thin, two or three times, using a plasterer's brush; leave it to dry naturally each time without using a fire. It would also be advisable to first add to this mixture the ashes of burnt ox-dung moistened with salt water.

## ON THE PREPARATION OF TALLOW
The tallow <term>Tallow: rendered animal fat, used here as a lubricant and sealant for the casting molds.</term> should be mixed with soot from a blacksmith and ground as fine as possible. If you prefer, you may also use the ashes of ox-dung.

## ON THE CONSTRUCTION OF THE FRAMES
The frames <note>These are the cores or mandrels around which the mold for the cannon is built.</note> should be wound almost to the limit of the cord, similar to the way one winds a string around a peg-top. Once this is done, the frames should be finished with fine earth and polished using the mixture of tallow and soot mentioned above. The decorative ornaments should be crafted from wax.

## THE REAR FRAME
The frame for the "tail" <note>The breech or rear section of the cannon.</note> of the bombard should have a final covering made of a square section containing brickdust and ashes mixed with salt water. Alternatively, it is even better to apply ox-dung ashes mixed with salt water over this frame.

## ON ADJUSTING AND HARDENING THE FRAME
First, place the frame in the trench using grappling hooks, as you have seen previously. Then, anneal <term>Anneal: a process of heating and slow cooling to toughen the material and remove moisture.</term> it gradually until it takes on a color similar to brick. Next, work it with a small piece of wood <note>original: "di poi lau [?] con uno negnietto"; likely *lavora con uno legnetto*.</note>, striking it softly bit by bit. Wherever the frame produces a hollow ringing sound, bind it tightly with iron wire. To ensure accuracy and prevent the frame from warping, place it so that it can be rotated freely in all directions.

## EARTH SUITABLE FOR GENERAL USE
The earth used for general casting should be the same type used to make bricks, mixed with either ox-dung or clippings of woolen cloth. <insert>Trivulzian Manuscript, folio 51, recto</insert> <note>original: "Tr. 51 a"</note>

The bottom of the furnace should consist of three rows of unbaked bricks made of ordinary clay, topped with an inch and a half of ashes. The vaulted ceiling should have one layer of unbaked bricks made of Valenza clay <note>Valenza: a town in Piedmont, Italy, known for its high-quality refractory clay.</note> and another layer of baked bricks.

Loose earth <unclear>i calossi</unclear> <note>The original manuscript uses "i calossi." The editor suggests this refers to *terra loscia*, meaning loose or crumbly earth.</note> should be mixed with the ashes.

The wooden core of the frame for the bombards should be protected by a layer of cinders one inch deep.

## NOTES ON THE USE OF THE 'SAGOMA' <note>original: 'Sagoma'—A template, mould, or instrument used for shaping and polishing a surface to a specific profile.</note>

Extend the plumb-line in two opposite directions from the center of the poles *a* and *c*. Form the flat surface bit by bit using plaster (labeled *gesso* <note>In the original manuscript, Leonardo wrote this as "osseg," his typical mirror-writing for *gesso*.</note> in the manuscript) as you move the template tool.

<margin>Manuscript G, folio 14 r.</margin>
Once the floor is entirely finished, the whole surface should be refined again in minute detail with the template tool. When using this tool on the prepared plastered surface (labeled *gessato* <note>original: "otasseg," mirror-writing for *gessato* (plastered).</note> in the manuscript), it should be handled with the greatest possible care.

### [*On the friction of the template tool*]

When rubbing the polishing instrument against the surface, you should not use the edge of the tool, except during the initial preparation of that surface. However, when it is time to refine the surface, the tool should be at least half as wide as the surface itself. 

This can be proven: imagine *f e d c* is the polishing tool and *f e n m* is the surface being smoothed. I maintain that if this polishing tool had only one cutting edge (as seen at *d c* compared to *a b*), it would exert much greater weight when the vertical line was over the *d c* part of the surface than when it was at the *f e* position. For this reason, it would wear away the rubbed parts much more if it were held straight rather than at a slant. Furthermore, the curve of the surface would become unequal—a flaw that cannot occur when there is significant contact between the polishing tool and the surface it is refining.

It would be even better if the tool and the surface were equal in size. If the tool is too small, when one of its sides reaches the middle of the surface, its outer edge would bear the full, accidental weight of the entire instrument, leading to an uneven finish.

<summary>Leonardo describes the construction of furnace flues using heat-resistant Valenza clay and provides technical instructions for using a 'sagoma' (template tool) to create perfectly smooth, level surfaces for casting.</summary>
