The gear teeth (cogs) that drive the movement of the <term>sagoma</term> <note>original: 'sagoma'—a template or shaping tool used to ensure a surface matches a specific profile.</note> are set into their grooves.

The <term>sagoma</term> should be designed like the one used on the road to Fiesole—operating with water. <note>Leonardo likely refers to water-powered stone-cutting or grinding tools used in the quarries or roads near Fiesole, a town overlooking Florence.</note>

<margin>G 43 v.</margin>
Because it is necessary for the instrument to wear itself down in proportion to how much it is lowered, and because it becomes very rigid after being lowered, it is essential to make the pulleys with nuts so that screws can turn within them. This allows the tool to open and close between points *a* and *c* (as shown by *b*). These rings, which act as nuts for the screws, should be pulled using the cords *d, e, f,* and *g*.

### VARNISH FOR THE FIRED SURFACE <gloss>Varnish of the fire <note>original: 'Vernicie della igna'—likely a reference to a glaze or metallic finish applied to a surface that has been fired in a furnace.</note></gloss>

<margin>G 46 v.</margin>
Mercury with Jupiter and Venus: <gloss>Quicksilver with tin and copper <note>original: Leonardo uses alchemical symbols for these metals. In this context, Mercury is quicksilver, Jupiter is tin, and Venus is copper.</note></gloss>. After the paste has been made, it should be worked upon the <term>sagoma</term> continually until the Mercury is entirely separated from the Jupiter and Venus.

### USE OF THE SAGOMA

Before it is varnished, the concave surface should be pressed with the instrument several times, moving it backwards and forwards. Then, the varnish should be applied to the moist surface and spread using a sieve. Use the mould two or three times, then place it in the furnace. As soon as the surface acquires a luster (becomes shiny), immediately apply the mould while it is still hot.

The center of rotation for the mould upon the structure must be fixed. It should be adjustable so that it can be raised, lowered, and moved forward or backward, ensuring its [axis] aligns perfectly with the center of the mould.

The base of the oven should be the same shape as the object placed inside it; it is best if this base is made from a single piece.

## HOW TO CREATE A CURVE THAT LEAVES THE PLATE PERFECTLY PARALLEL

Construct a frame made of strong walnut wood. Upon this, build a square frame with a raised center. On this center, fix both ends of the drawn plate <note>A metal plate formed by being pulled through a die to achieve a specific thickness.</note>. This plate is separated at its ends from the sides of the wall, and it supports all the other plates that are nailed above it. This frame should always be used with the dark plates mentioned previously.

<margin>G 75 v.</margin>

### STUCCO

Cover the boss <note>A protruding decorative or functional element.</note> of the fire-resistant <note>original: *ingnea* (igneous), written backwards as *aengni* in the manuscript</note> plaster with stucco. This stucco should be made of marble and lime <note>original: *erenev* (Venus) and *oirucrem* (Mercury), written backwards. In Leonardo's alchemical shorthand, Venus often represents copper or marble, and Mercury represents quicksilver or lime</note>. Smear this boss thoroughly with a uniform layer the thickness of a knife blade, using a template <term>sagoma</term> <note>A tool used to ensure a surface follows a specific profile or curve.</note> to guide you. Cover this with the body of a bell so that any moisture may drip off, allowing you to recover the liquid used to form the paste. Dry the remaining material well and then fire it. Afterward, beat or burnish it with a high-quality burnisher, making it thicker toward the sides.

Powder the glass into a paste using borax and water to create a type of stucco; then drain it so it can dry. Afterward, glaze it using fire so that it achieves a high shine.

<margin>Forster II 46 v.</margin>

If you wish to make a large, thin metal plate of lead, create a smooth, level surface and fill it with glowing coals. Melt the lead within it, then use a smooth rake to remove the coals. Allow the metal to cool, and the plate is finished.

<margin>Forster II 64 v.</margin>

When you wish to cast in wax, burn off the dross <note>original: "scum"; the impurities that rise to the surface of molten material</note> with a candle, and the cast will emerge without any holes or bubbles.

Grind verdigris <note>A green pigment or crust caused by the oxidation of copper.</note> with rue <note>A bitter herb often used in historical chemical recipes.</note> several times, mixing it with lemon juice. Keep this mixture away from Naples yellow <note>A poisonous yellow pigment made of lead antimonate.</note>.

The steel is first beaten well to extend its length, then broken into squares. These squares are stacked one above another and thoroughly covered with earth of Valenza <note>A fine clay used for molds and insulation</note> and powdered talc. This is dried over a slow fire and gradually heated until the heat has completely penetrated both the inside and the outside.

Burnt and powdered tartar <note>original: *tartaro*; a byproduct of winemaking (potassium bitartrate), used here to help the plaster consistency</note> mixed with plaster for casting causes the plaster to hold together when it is annealed <term>anneal</term> <note>A process of heating and slow cooling to toughen the material and remove internal stresses.</note>. ### MOULD OF THE HORSE

Construct the horse's framework upon iron legs, making it strong and firm on a solid foundation. Then, rub it with tallow <note>Animal fat used as a lubricant or release agent.</note> and apply a thick coating, allowing it to dry thoroughly layer by layer. By doing this, you will increase its thickness by the width of three fingers. Then, secure and bind it with iron supports as needed. Additionally, hollow out the mold, refine it to the required thickness, and then fill the mold again gradually until it is completely filled. Finally, bind it round with its iron straps and secure it, then anneal the inner surface where it will come into contact with the molten bronze.

### ON MAKING THE MOLD IN PIECES

Once the horse is finished, mark upon it all the pieces of the mold with which you wish to cover it. After the clay has been laid on, cut it to correspond with every piece, so that when the mold is finished, you can take it off and then replace it in its original position using alignment marks <note>original: "countersigns"; marks used to ensure pieces of a mold fit back together perfectly</note>.

The square block *a b* will be placed between the outer cover and the core <note>In casting, the "core" is the inner mold that creates the hollow center, while the "cover" or "cope" is the outer mold</note>—that is, in the hollow space where the liquefied bronze is to flow. These square blocks of bronze will keep the spaces between the mold and the cover at an equal distance; for this reason, these blocks are of great importance.

The clay must be mixed with sand.

Take wax to replace and pay for what has been used <note>This likely refers to calculating the volume of metal needed based on the weight of the wax used in the "lost-wax" process</note>.

Dry the mold one layer after another. Make the outer mold out of plaster in order to save time in drying and the cost of wood. Use this plaster to fasten the iron bands on both the outside and inside to a thickness of two fingers; create the terra cotta <note>original: *terra cotta*; Italian for "baked earth," referring here to the fired clay mold</note>.

This mold will take you a day to make; half a boat-load of plaster will be sufficient for your needs.

Good.

Seal it up again with paste and clay, or with egg whites, crushed brick, and rubble. <margin>Windsor: Drawings 12347 r.</margin>

Three irons which bind the mold¹

If you wish to make casts rapidly and simply, make them with a box of river sand moistened with vinegar.

After having made the mold upon the horse, you will create the thickness of the metal using clay.

In the alloying process, note how many hours are needed for each hundredweight <note>A unit of weight; in England, traditionally 112 pounds</note>. While casting each piece, keep the furnace and its fire closed up. Let the entire inside of the mold be saturated with linseed oil or turpentine. Then take a handful of powdered borax and hard rosin with <term>distilled spirits</term> <note>original: *aqua vitae*; literally "water of life," a high-proof alcohol used as a solvent</note> and put a coat of pitch over the mold so that while it is buried underground, the dampness may not damage it.

In order to manage the large mold, first make a model of a small mold; create a small room in proportion to it.

If the usual width of the river is equal to a single arch, construct this bridge with three arches; do this in order to allow for the increased flow during floods.

[Ground-plan of a castle with a lake and boats on it]
[The palace of the prince ought to have a piazza <note>an open public square or marketplace</note> in front] <insert>This sentence was crossed out in the original manuscript.</insert>

The rooms which you intend to use for dancing, or for performing different kinds of jumps or various movements with a crowd of people, should be located on the ground floor; for I have seen floors collapse and cause the death of many. Above all, ensure that every wall, however thin it may be, has its foundations directly on the ground or on well-set arches.

Let the mezzanines <note>intermediate floors between the main stories of a building</note> of the dwellings be divided by walls made of narrow bricks, and built without wooden beams because of the risk of fire.

All the latrines <note>original: "privies"</note> should have ventilation openings built through the thickness of the walls, and designed in such a way that air may come in through the roofs.

Let the mezzanines be vaulted; these will be significantly stronger if they are fewer in number.

Let the oak support bands be enclosed within the walls to prevent them from being damaged by fire.

Let the latrines be numerous and connected to one another so that the smell may not spread through the rooms, and their doors should all close automatically.

<page-num>1035</page-num>

# ARCHITECTURE

Subordinates <note>original: "mates"; likely meaning dependents or subjects</note> are allied with and bound to their lords in two ways: either by blood relations or by the ties of property. Blood relations work when their sons are held like hostages, acting as a guarantee and a pledge against any suspicion regarding their loyalty. The tie of property works when you allow each of them to build one or two houses within your city, from which they may earn some income. Furthermore, he will draw resources from ten cities of five thousand houses containing thirty thousand dwellings. In this way, you will disperse the massive crowds of people who—huddling together like goats, piled one on top of another and filling every corner with their stench—sow the seeds of plague <note>original: "pestilence"</note> and death.

The city will be as beautiful as its reputation suggests, proving useful to you through its tax revenues and the lasting fame of its expansion.

The city of Lodi will bear the costs and keep the revenue that it once paid annually to the Duke.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 65 verso b</margin>
A foreigner who owns a house in Milan will often choose to live in his own home to enjoy a more prestigious location. Anyone in a position to build must have some wealth; thus, the poor will be separated from these settlers. Consequently, tax assessments and the city's reputation for greatness will increase. Even if he does not wish to live in Milan full-time, he will remain loyal so as not to lose both the profit from his house and his invested capital.

<insert>[*Architectural drawings: ground plans*]</insert>

### Pantry. Kitchen. Household.

The person working in the pantry <note>original: "buttery"; a room for storing liquor and provisions</note> should have the kitchen entrance directly behind him to work efficiently. The kitchen window should face the pantry so he can easily bring in the firewood.

The drawing I have made shows a larger rear facade than the front, though it ought to be the other way around.

The large room for the household <note>original: "family"; in this context, Leonardo refers to the servants or staff of the estate</note> should be located away from the kitchen so the master of the house does not hear their noise. The kitchen should be conveniently placed for washing the pewter dishes, ensuring they are not seen being carried through the house.

Large room for the master. Room. Kitchen. Larder. Guard room. Large room for the family.

The larder, woodpile, kitchen, hen-coop (<term>pollaro</term> <note>original: "pollaro"; a coop for poultry</note>), and hall should be—and indeed must be—connected for the sake of convenience. [*A plan for laying out a water-garden*]

The staircase is one and three-quarters <term>braccia</term> wide <note>original: "braccio" (singular) and "braccia" (plural); an Italian unit of measurement based on the length of an arm, roughly 23–27 inches</note> and is bent like a knee. <margin>Tr. 13 a</margin>
An inverted arch <note>An arch that curves downward, often used in foundations to distribute pressure across the ground.</note> is better for creating a support than an ordinary one, because the inverted arch finds a wall below it which resists its weakness, while the ordinary arch finds nothing but air where it is weakest.

## WHAT IS AN ARCH?

An arch is nothing other than a strength caused by two weaknesses. For an arch in a building is made up of two segments of a circle, and each of these segments, being very weak on its own, tends to fall. But as one withstands the downfall of the other, the two weaknesses are converted into a single strength.

## ON THE NATURE OF WEIGHT IN ARCHES

<margin>A 50 r.</margin>
Once the arch has been set up, it remains in a state of equilibrium, for one side pushes the other as much as the other pushes it. However, if one of the segments of the circle weighs more than the other, the stability is ended and destroyed, because the greater weight will overcome the lesser.

# ARCHITECTURE

The road should have a slope of half a <term>braccio</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement based on the length of an arm, roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note> from the edges to the center. In this center, every <term>braccio</term>, there should be an opening one <term>braccio</term> long and as wide as a finger, through which rainwater may drain into channels made at the level of the lower roads marked *p* and *s*. On each side, at the edge of this road's width, there should be an arcade six <term>braccia</term> wide resting on columns. Note that if anyone wishes to travel through the entire city using the high-level roads, they will be able to do so; likewise, anyone who wishes to travel by the low-level roads may do the same.

The high-level roads are not to be used by wagons or similar vehicles, as they are intended solely for the convenience of the nobility. All carts and heavy loads used for the service and convenience of the common people should be restricted to the low-level roads.

One house must be built with its back to another, leaving the low-level road between them. The doors marked *n* serve for bringing in provisions such as wood, wine, and similar goods. The privies, stables, and other such unpleasant places are emptied through underground passages located three hundred <term>braccia</term> apart from one arch to the next. Each passage receives light through openings in the streets above. At every arch, there should be a spiral staircase; it should be circular because people are prone to "committing nuisances" <note>A polite euphemism for public urination or defecation, which Leonardo sought to prevent by eliminating dark corners.</note> in the corners of square ones. At the first turn of the stairs, there should be an entrance to the privies and public urinals, and this staircase should allow a person to descend from the high-level road to the low-level road.

<margin>Manuscript B, folio 16 recto and 15 verso.</margin>

The high-level roads begin outside the city gates, and by the time they reach the city, they have attained a height of six <term>braccia</term>. The site for the city should be chosen near the sea or a large river, so that the impurities of the city, moved by water, may be carried far away.

### *[Castle of Milan]*

*[With drawing]*

The moats of the castle of Milan, located within the "Garland" <note>original: *Ghirlanda*; the name for the outer defensive wall of the Sforza Castle.</note>, are thirty <term>braccia</term> wide <note>A <term>braccio</term> is approximately 23 inches.</note>. The ramparts are sixteen <term>braccia</term> high and forty wide; this section constitutes the Garland.

The outer walls are eight <term>braccia</term> thick and forty high, while the inner walls of the castle are sixty <term>braccia</term> high. I would be entirely satisfied with this design, except that I want to ensure that the <term>bombardiers</term> <note>Soldiers who operate cannons or mortars.</note> stationed within the walls of the Garland do not exit into the secret inner passage (marked *S*). Instead, they should descend one at a time, as shown at *m f*.

Since skilled <term>bombardiers</term> always aim for the <term>embrasures</term> <note>The openings in a wall through which a cannon is fired.</note> of a fortress, they might succeed in breaking a single <term>embrasure</term> in the Garland. If they do, they could enter through the breach like cats and seize control of all the towers, walls, and secret passages of the Garland. 

Therefore, if the <term>embrasures</term> are positioned at *m f* and a mortar shell happens to destroy one, allowing the enemy to enter, they will be unable to go any further. They can then be beaten back and driven away by a soldier stationed in the <term>machicolations</term> <note>Floor openings in a projecting gallery used to drop stones or liquids on attackers.</note> above. The passage *f* should continue through all the walls from the three-quarters mark downwards, having no exit above in the walls or towers except for the main entrance located within the fortress. This secret passage *f* must not have any air-holes on the outside; instead, it should receive light from the fortress side through frequent <term>loopholes</term> <note>Narrow vertical slits in a wall for observation or firing.</note>.

*[*With architectural drawing*]*

A <term>campanile</term> <note>original: "campanile"; a freestanding bell tower, common in Italian architecture.</note> neither can nor should be built here. Instead, it must stand separately, as it does at the cathedral <note>Santa Maria del Fiore</note> and at San Giovanni <note>The Baptistery</note> in Florence. The same is true of the cathedral at Pisa, for there the bell tower can be seen by itself—round in shape and standing apart—just as the cathedral does. In this way, each building can fully reveal its own perfection.

<margin>MS. 2037 National Library of France, 5 v.</margin>
If, however, anyone should desire to make the tower part of the church, they should make the <term>lantern-tower</term> <note>A structure on top of a dome or roof with windows to admit light, often also used to house bells.</note> serve as a bell tower, as is done in the church of <term>Chiaravalle</term> <note>Chiaravalle Abbey near Milan, famous for its tall, multi-tiered central tower.</note>.

<margin>British Museum, 63 v.</margin>
Mills should not be built near stagnant water, nor by the seashore, because storms choke every man-made canal along the coast with sand.

*[*Foundations*]*

The first and most essential requirement for any building is stability.

Regarding the foundations of the various parts of temples and other public buildings: their depths should be proportional to the weight they are intended to support.

At any given location, the depth of the earth is arranged in layers. Each of these layers has a heavier and a lighter part, with the heavier material settled at the bottom.

This occurs because these layers are formed by the <term>sediment</term> <note>Matter such as sand or mud that settles to the bottom of a liquid.</note> from water discharged into the sea by the currents of the rivers flowing into it. The heaviest part of this sediment was deposited first, and this process continued over time. This is how water behaves: it carries material while it is moving and lets it drop when it becomes still.

These layers of soil are visible in the banks of rivers which, in their continuous course, have cut through and separated hills into deep gorges. In these places, the water level has receded from the <term>shingle</term> <note>Small, rounded pebbles or gravel found on shores or riverbeds.</note> of the banks; this caused the material to dry out and turn into hard stone—especially the mud that had the finest texture. This leads us to conclude that every part of the earth’s surface was once the center of the earth, and vice versa <note>Leonardo is observing that geological layers shift over vast periods of time, suggesting that land that is now on the surface was once deeply buried or submerged.</note>.

<summary>Leonardo discusses the aesthetic and practical reasons for detached bell towers and explains how river sedimentation creates the geological layers necessary for stable architectural foundations.</summary>

<header>ARCHITECTURE</header>

# ON CRACKS IN WALLS THAT ARE WIDE AT THE BASE AND NARROW AT THE TOP, AND THEIR CAUSE

A wall will always crack if it does not dry uniformly throughout.

A wall of uniform thickness does not dry all at once unless it is in contact with the same environment everywhere. For example, if a wall is built so that part of it touches a damp mound while the rest is exposed to the air, the exposed part will shrink slightly as it dries, while the damp portion will keep its original size.

This happens because the part dried by the air pulls itself together and shrinks, whereas the part in contact with the damp does not dry. Consequently, the dry part easily breaks away from the damp part, because the damp section lacks the <term>coherence</term> <note>original: "coherence"; here meaning the physical integrity or bonding strength.</note> needed to follow the movement of the section that is currently drying.

## ON ARCH-SHAPED CRACKS THAT ARE WIDE AT THE TOP AND NARROW AT THE BOTTOM

<margin>British Museum Manuscript 138 r.</margin>
Those arched cracks—wide at the top and narrow at the bottom—originate in walled-up doorways. These doorways contract more in height than in width because their height is greater than their breadth, and because there are more mortar joints in the vertical height than in the horizontal width.

<margin>British Museum Manuscript 141 v.</margin>
When either a full dome or a half-dome is <term>vanquished</term> <note>original: "vanquished"; overwhelmed or crushed by weight.</note> by an unbearable weight from above, the <term>vault</term> <note>An arched masonry structure forming a ceiling or roof.</note> will burst apart. The resulting crack will be small at the top and wide at the bottom, and narrow on the inside while wide on the outside. This is similar to the skin of a pomegranate or an orange, which splits lengthwise into many pieces; the more it is squeezed from opposite ends, the wider the joints will open at the points furthest from the source of the pressure. 

For this reason, the arches of the vaults of any <term>apse</term> <note>A semicircular or polygonal recess in a building, usually at the end of a church, covered with a vault or semi-dome.</note> should never be loaded more heavily than the arches of the main building it belongs to. This is especially important because the heaviest parts press most strongly on the sections below, driving them down into their foundations. This does not happen with lighter structures like the aforementioned apses.

<vocab>cracks, walls, arches, dome, vault, apse, foundations, mortar, contraction, pressure</vocab>

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci explains the mechanics of structural failure, attributing cracks in walls and domes to uneven drying and the distribution of excessive weight.</summary>
<keywords>architecture, structural engineering, cracks, masonry, domes, vaults, Leonardo da Vinci, building materials</keywords>

<page-num>1048</page-num>
<header>ARCHITECTURE</header>

<meta>British Museum Manuscript 157 r.</meta>

First, create a treatise on the causes that lead to the collapse of walls, and then, separately, a treatise on the remedies.

Parallel cracks frequently appear in buildings constructed in mountainous areas where the rock is <term>stratified</term> <note>arranged in layers</note> and those layers run at an angle. In these slanted seams, water and other moisture often penetrate, carrying a quantity of greasy and slimy earth. Since these layers do not continue all the way down to the bottom of the valleys, the rocks slide down the slope. They do not stop moving until they have reached the bottom of the valley, carrying with them—in the manner of a boat—whatever part of the building they have broken away from the rest of the structure.

The remedy for this is to build numerous piers under the wall that is sliding away, with arches connecting one to another. These should be well-buttressed <note>original: "abarbanati," likely meaning anchored or firmly rooted</note>, and the pillars must have their bases firmly set into the solid stratified rock so that they do not break away.

In order to find the immovable part of the aforementioned rock layer, it is necessary to sink a shaft through it to a great depth beneath the foot of the wall. In this shaft, polish a smooth surface the width of a hand from the top to the bottom of the side where the hill slopes down. After some time, this smooth portion made on the side of the shaft will show very clearly which part of the mountain is moving.

### OF STONES WHICH BECOME SEPARATED FROM THEIR MORTAR

Stones that are built up in equal numbers from bottom to top and laid with a consistent quantity of mortar will settle down equally as the moisture that softens the mortar evaporates.

Cracks in walls will never be parallel unless the part of the wall that is separated from the rest does not sink downward.

### THE LAW WHICH IMPARTS STABILITY TO BUILDINGS

The stability of buildings results from a law that is the converse of the two previous points: namely, that the walls should be built up entirely equally in equal [proportions]...

<page-num>1049</page-num>
<header>ARCHITECTURE</header>

...stages, which should embrace the whole circuit of the building and the total thickness of the walls, no matter of what kind. Although a thin wall dries more rapidly than a thick one, it will not necessarily crack under the weight it gains from day to day; for if a wall half as thick dries in one day, a wall of double the thickness would dry in roughly two days. Thus, a slight difference in weight is balanced by a slight difference in drying time.

## OF THE POSITION OF FOUNDATIONS AND IN WHAT PLACES THEY ARE A CAUSE OF DESTRUCTION

<margin>British Museum Manuscript 157 v.</margin>
When a crack in a wall is wider at the top than at the bottom, it is a clear sign that the source of the wall's collapse lies outside the perpendicular line of the crack. <note>Leonardo is observing that structural failure often originates at a point diagonal to the visible damage.</note>

## OF THE CAUSE OF THE COLLAPSE OF PUBLIC AND PRIVATE BUILDINGS

<margin>British Museum Manuscript 158 r.</margin>
Walls collapse as a result of cracks which are either vertical or slanting. Vertical cracks are caused by new walls being built in conjunction with old walls, either by building them straight up against each other or by using <term>toothings</term> <note>interlocking stones or bricks left protruding from a wall so that another wall can be bonded into it</note> fitted into the old walls. Because these toothings cannot offer enough resistance to the massive weight of the new wall joined to them, they must inevitably break and allow the new wall to settle down. In this process, the wall will sink about one <term>braccio</term> <note>original: "braccio," an Italian unit of measurement roughly equal to 23 inches or 58 centimeters</note> for every ten <term>braccia</term> of height. The amount of sinking may be more or less depending on whether a large or small quantity of mortar was used for the stones, and whether that mortar was very liquid or not.

Remember to always build the main walls first and then add the facing stones <note>the decorative or protective outer layer of a wall</note> later. If this is not done, the <term>subsidence</term> <note>the gradual sinking or settling of a structure</note> of the main wall as it settles will be greater than that of the outer shell. This will cause the toothings set in the sides of the wall to break, because the stones used for facing the walls are larger than those used in the internal construction and therefore require less mortar in their joints, leading to less settling. This failure cannot happen if the facing is added only after the main wall has had sufficient time to dry.

<summary>Leonardo explains that buildings should be constructed in uniform stages to allow for even drying and warns that new walls will always settle more than old ones, causing cracks if not properly joined. He advises building the core of a wall first and letting it settle before applying the outer facing stones to prevent structural failure.</summary>

<margin>Windsor Royal Library: Drawings 12585 verso</margin>

<insert>*Water-stair in the Sforzesca*</insert> <note>The Sforzesca was a model farm and villa estate built by Ludovico Sforza near Vigevano.</note>

When the descent from the floodgates has been excavated so that the end of its drop is below the bed of the river, the waters descending from them will never create a cavity at the foot of the bank. They will not carry away soil when they rebound, and thus they will not form new obstacles; instead, they will follow a transverse course along the length of the base of the floodgate from the underside.

Moreover, if the lowest part of the bank, which lies diagonally across the course of the water, is constructed with deep, broad steps in the style of a staircase, the waters will be managed more effectively. Usually, as water descends, it falls perpendicularly from the start of this lowest stage and digs out the foundations of the bank. With this design, the water will no longer be able to descend with such an irresistible impact.

I offer as an example of this the staircase down which the water falls from the meadows of the Sforzesca at Vigevano; the running water there falls from a height of fifty <term>braccia</term> <note>original: "braccia," an Italian unit of measurement; fifty braccia is approximately 95 feet or 29 meters</note>.
<margin>Codex Leicester, 21 recto</margin>

<insert>*With drawing*</insert>

These are the stairs of Vigevano, below the Sforzesca, consisting of one hundred and thirty steps. Each step is a quarter of a <term>braccio</term> <note>about 6 inches or 15 cm</note> high and half a <term>braccio</term> <note>about 12 inches or 30 cm</note> wide. The water falls down these steps without wearing anything away by the time it finishes its descent. Through these stairs, so much soil has been carried down that it has filled in and dried up a swamp; it has successfully transformed deep swamps into productive meadows.
<margin>Codex Leicester, 32 recto</margin>

# XXXIX
## Music

->*"Music which is consumed in the very act of its birth."* (Treatise on Painting <note>original: "TRATTATO"; Leonardo often compared music to painting, noting that music dies as it is performed while painting endures.</note> I 29)<-

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 382 verso a</margin>
Music has two misfortunes: one is fatal and the other is diminishing. The fatal misfortune is that music is always tied to the very moment following its performance <note>Meaning it vanishes instantly once the sound is made</note>. The diminishing misfortune lies in its repetition, which makes it seem tiresome and common.

<margin>Manuscript B 50 verso</margin>
[With drawing]
This is the mechanism for the movement of a viol player’s bow. If you make the notches of the wheel in two different sizes <note>original: "tempi," likely referring to the spacing or timing of the teeth</note>, so that one set of teeth is smaller than the other and they do not meet together (as seen at points *a* and *b*), the bow will have a steady movement. Otherwise, it will move in jerks. But if you make it the way I describe, the small gear <term>pinion</term> *f* will always move at a constant speed.

<margin>British Museum Manuscript 137 verso</margin>
[Drawing]
Here you should create a wheel with pipes that serve as mechanical players for a musical round called a <term>Canon</term> <note>A musical form where a melody is played and then repeated by other voices entering at different times</note>, which is sung in four parts, with each singer performing the whole round. Therefore, I have designed a wheel here with four gears so that each gear represents one singer.

<margin>Forster Codex II 35 verso</margin>
I have several strings <note>original: "cords"</note> tuned in octaves, one above the other, and I want each to be stretched one finger's width more than the one before. I ask: what weight would be required to stretch it—whether the string is of equal size or double the size—and what sound would be produced?

<margin>Leicester Codex 27 recto</margin>
Regarding the music created by water falling into its container.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 271 verso a</margin>
With the help of a watermill, I will create continuous sounds from all sorts of instruments, which will play for as long as the mill continues to turn.

# XL
## Tales

->'I will create a fiction which shall express great things.'<-

A certain man stopped associating with one of his friends because the friend had a habit of speaking maliciously about everyone he knew. This former friend eventually reproached him, and after many complaints, begged him to explain why he had abandoned such a great friendship. The man replied: "I am no longer willing to be seen in your company because I actually like you. I do not want you to talk maliciously about me to others while I am still your friend, because then they would form a bad impression of *you*—just as I have by listening to you talk about others. Therefore, since we no longer have anything to do with each other, it will appear that we have become enemies. Then, when you speak ill of me as you usually do, it will not be as shameful for your reputation as it would be if we were still close companions." <note>original: "c.a. 306 v. b" refers to Codex Atlanticus, folio 306 verso, section b.</note>
->Codex Atlanticus 306 verso b<-

Dear Benedetto <note>Benedetto Dei (1418–1492) was a Florentine merchant and traveler who was a friend of Leonardo; Leonardo often wrote him letters—some real, some purely fictional—describing fantastic adventures.</note>,—To give you news of events here in the East: you should know that in the month of June, a giant appeared who came from the Libyan desert. This giant was born on Mount Atlas and was black. He fought against Artaxerxes <note>A name used for several ancient Persian kings; here it adds a sense of epic, ancient history to the story.</note> alongside the Egyptians, Arabs, Medes, and Persians. He lived in the sea, surviving on whales, great <term>leviathans</term> <note>Biblical or mythical sea monsters</note>, and even ships. When this savage giant fell—because the ground was covered in blood and mire—it seemed as if a mountain had collapsed. The entire country shook as if there were an earthquake, terrifying Pluto <note>The Roman god of the Underworld</note> in Hell; even Mars <note>The god of war</note>, fearing for his life, fled for refuge under the protection of Jove <note>Jupiter, king of the gods</note>.¹

But for us wretched mortals, flight is of no use, since this monster—even when moving slowly—far exceeds the speed of the fastest warhorse <note>original: "courser"</note>.

<margin>Forster III 34 v.</margin>
A workman was in the habit of frequently going to wait upon a certain lord, even though he had no petition <note>A formal request or appeal to a person in power.</note> to make to him. The lord asked him what his purpose was in coming so often. 

The workman replied that he went there to enjoy a pleasure that the lord himself could not have. He explained that it gave him pleasure to look at people who were grander than himself, as is the way with common people. By contrast, the lord could only look at people who were of less importance than himself, and consequently, lords were cut off from this particular pleasure.

## Jests

> "*You should frequently amuse yourself when you go for a walk for recreation by watching and taking note of the attitudes and actions of people as they talk and argue, or laugh or fight with one another—observing both their own actions and those of the bystanders who either intervene or stand by watching.*"

### A JEST

A priest was making his rounds through the parish on the Saturday before Easter to sprinkle the houses with holy water, as was his custom. Arriving at a painter's studio, he began to sprinkle the water onto some of the paintings. The painter, turning around in annoyance, asked him why he was sprinkling his pictures in this manner. 

The priest replied that it was the custom and his duty to do so; he claimed he was performing a good deed and that anyone who does a good deed should expect a reward <note>original: recompense</note> just as great or even greater. For God has promised that for every good deed we do on Earth, we shall be rewarded a hundredfold <note>A hundred times over.</note> from on high. 

The painter waited until the priest had left, then went to a window above and dumped a large bucket of water down onto the priest's back, shouting to him: "Look! There is the reward that comes to you a hundredfold from on high, just as you said it would, because of the 'good deed' you did me with your holy water—which has nearly ruined my paintings!"
<margin>Codex Atlanticus <note>Leonardo’s largest collection of drawings and writings.</note>, folio 119 r. a</margin>

Now, a pair of these friars traveling under these conditions happened to arrive at an inn at the same time as...

<meta>This page continues the collection of "Jests" from Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks. ...a certain merchant sat down at the same table, and because the inn was poor, nothing was served except one roasted rooster <note>original: cockerel</note>. At this, the merchant—seeing it would be meager fare for himself—turned to the friars and said: "On days like these, if I remember correctly, you are not permitted in your monasteries to eat any kind of meat." The friars, hearing these words, were forced by their religious rule to admit without argument that this was indeed the case. So the merchant got his wish and devoured the chicken, while the friars fared as best they could.

Now, after dining in this way, all three companions set out on their journey together. After traveling a certain distance, they came to a river of considerable width and depth. Since all three were on foot—the friars because of their poverty and the merchant because of his stinginess <note>original: niggardliness</note>—custom required that one of the friars, who were barefoot <note>original: had no shoes and stockings</note>, should carry the merchant on his shoulders. Consequently, the friar gave the merchant his wooden clogs to hold and took the man on his back. 

But as it happened, when the friar reached the middle of the stream, he remembered another of his rules. Coming to a stop like Saint Christopher <note>The patron saint of travelers, often depicted carrying the Christ Child across a river.</note>, he raised his head toward the man who was weighing heavily on him and said: "Tell me, do you have any money on you?" "Why, you know very well that I do," replied the merchant. "How do you think a man like me could travel otherwise?" "Alas!" said the friar, "Our rule forbids us to carry any money on our backs!" And he immediately threw the merchant into the water.

Because the merchant realized this was done as a joke and as revenge for the injury he had done to them, he smiled pleasantly and peacefully. Blushing deeply with shame, he endured their revenge.

# JESTS

## A WORD SAID BY A YOUNG MAN TO AN OLD ONE

<margin>Tr. 71 a</margin>
When an old man was openly insulting a young man and boldly proclaiming that he had no fear of him, the young man replied that the man's advanced age protected him better than either his tongue or his physical strength ever could.

## JEST

<margin>H 62 [14] v.</margin>
### Why the Hungarians keep the double cross.

A man wished to prove, using the authority of Pythagoras <note>original: Pythagoras; the Greek philosopher who famously taught the doctrine of metempsychosis, or the transmigration of souls into new bodies after death.</note>, that he had lived in the world on a former occasion. When another man would not allow him to finish his argument, the first man said to the second: "And this is proof that I was here before: I remember that you were a miller." The other man, feeling provoked by these words, agreed that it was true—for he also remembered that the speaker had been the donkey <note>original: ass</note> who had carried the flour for him.

<margin>M 58 v.</margin>
A painter was asked why he had made his children so ugly, when the figures in his paintings—which were merely inanimate things—were so beautiful. His reply was that he made his paintings by day, but he made his children at night.

<margin>Forster II 30 v.</margin>
A sick man who was at the point of death heard someone knocking at the door. When he asked one of his servants who was knocking, the servant replied that it was someone who called herself Madame Bona <note>In Italian, *Bona* means "Good." The joke relies on the man's cynical view that a truly "good woman" is a miracle worth seeing.</note>.

At this, the sick man raised his arms to heaven and praised God with a loud voice. He then told the servants to let her in immediately so that he might see a "good woman" before he died, because in all his life he had never seen one.

<margin>Forster II 31 r.</margin>
Someone told a man that he should get out of bed because the sun had already risen. To this he replied: "If I had to travel as far and do as much as the sun does, I would have already risen too; but as I have such a short way to go, I do not wish to get up just yet."

The privet tree, feeling its tender branches—which were laden with new fruit—being pricked by the sharp claws and beak of a troublesome blackbird, complained to the bird with pitiful reproaches. It begged the bird that even if she plucked off its delicious fruit, she would at least not deprive it of the leaves that protected it from the scorching rays of the sun, nor tear away and strip bare its tender bark with her sharp claws.

But to this, the blackbird replied with an insolent rebuke: “Silence, you coarse bramble! Do you not know that Nature created you to produce these fruits for my nourishment? Can you not see that you came into the world only to supply me with this very food? Do you not know, vile thing that you are, that next winter you will serve only as fuel and food for the fire?” The tree listened to these words patiently and not without tears.

But a short time afterward, the blackbird was caught in a net, and some boughs were cut to make a cage to imprison her. Among the rest, some were cut from that same tender privet to serve as the rods for the cage. When these branches realized that they would be the cause of the blackbird being deprived of her liberty, they rejoiced and said: “We are here, O blackbird, not yet consumed by the fire as you predicted; we shall see you in prison before you see us burnt.”

The laurel and the myrtle, seeing a pear tree being cut down, cried out with a loud voice: “O pear tree, where are you going? Where is the pride you had when you were laden with ripe fruit? Now you will no longer provide shade for us with your thick foliage.” Then the pear tree replied: “I am going with the <term>husbandman</term> <note>original: husbandman; a farmer or someone who cultivates the land.</note> who is cutting me down, and who will take me to the workshop of a good...

The chestnut tree, seeing a man in the fig tree bending its branches toward himself, picking its ripe fruit and putting it in his mouth—tearing and crushing it with his hard teeth—shook its boughs and said in a mournful whisper: ‘O fig tree, how much less favored by Nature you are than I! But I am touched carefully by his hands, and not with sticks and stones like you.’

The idle, fluttering moth—not content with its power to fly wherever it pleased through the air—was enthralled by the seductive flame of a candle and resolved to fly into it. Some flames had already been burning for a month in a glassmaking furnace <note>original: "glass-furnace"</note> when they saw a candle approaching in a beautiful and glittering candlestick. They felt a great longing to reach it; one of their number left its natural path and wound itself into a piece of unburnt wood <note>original: "unburnt brand"</note> upon which it fed. It then passed out the other end through a small crack toward the candle which was nearby. It flung itself upon the candle and, devouring it with the utmost greed, consumed it almost entirely. Then, desiring to prolong its own life, the flame tried in vain to return to the furnace it had left, but it was forced to wither and die along with the candle. So, at last, in lamentation and regret, it was changed to foul smoke, leaving all its sister flames behind in a glowing and lasting life of beauty.

Wine, the divine liquor of the grape, found itself in a golden, intricately engraved <note>original: "richly chased"</note> cup upon Muhammad’s <note>original: "Mahomet’s" — an archaic spelling of the Prophet Muhammad</note> table. After being overwhelmed with pride at such an honor, it was suddenly struck by an opposite feeling and said to itself: "What am I doing? What is it that I am celebrating? Can I not see that I am near my death, in that I am about to leave my golden home in this cup and enter the foul and stinking caverns of the human body? There, I will be transformed from a sweet, fragrant nectar into a disgusting fluid. And as if such an evil were not enough, I must then lie for a long time in filthy containers with other nasty and rotting matter excreted from the human intestines." It cried to heaven, demanding vengeance for such an injury and praying that an end might be put to such an insult. It asked that since that part of the country produced the most beautiful and finest grapes in the whole world, these at least should not be turned into wine. Then Jove <note>original: "Jove" — the Roman king of the gods, often used in Renaissance literature as a general term for the divine</note> caused the wine which Muhammad drank to rise as a spirit up to his brain, and to infect it to such a degree that it made him mad. He committed so many foolish acts that when he regained his senses, he issued a decree that no one in Asia <note>original: "Asiatic"</note> should drink wine; and thus the vine and its fruits were left in peace.

A rat was being besieged in its tiny house by a weasel that was waiting with unceasing vigilance for the rat's destruction. Through a tiny crack, the rat considered the great danger it was in. Meanwhile, a cat arrived, suddenly seized the weasel, and immediately devoured it. At this, the rat—profoundly grateful to its deity—offered some of its hazelnuts as a sacrifice to Jove <note>The Roman king of the gods, also known as Jupiter.</note>. It then emerged from its hole to reclaim the liberty it had lost, only to be instantly deprived of both its freedom and its life by the cruel claws and teeth of the cat.

Fable of the tongue bitten by the teeth.

The cedar tree, arrogant because of its beauty, despised the plants surrounding it and had them all removed from its presence. But afterward, the wind, no longer meeting any obstacles, tore the tree up by its roots and threw it to the ground.

An ant found a grain of millet. Feeling itself seized, the grain cried out: "If you will do me the great favor of allowing me to fulfill my desire to germinate <note>original: "germinate" — to begin to grow or sprout</note>, I will give you a hundred times more of myself." And so it happened.

A spider found a bunch of grapes which, because of its sweetness, was frequently visited by bees and various types of flies. The spider imagined it had found a spot perfectly suited for its traps. After lowering itself down by a fine thread and entering its new home, it settled into the tiny holes and spaces between the grapes. There, day after day, like a robber, it assaulted the wretched insects that were not on their guard. But after some days had passed, the keeper of the vineyard cut this bunch off and placed it with the others, and it was pressed with them. The grapes, therefore, served as a trap and a snare for the deceitful spider, just as they had for the flies he had tricked.

# FABLES

The traveller’s joy <note>original: "traveller’s joy" — a climbing plant (Clematis vitalba) often found in hedgerows.</note>, not being content to stay within its own hedge, began to stretch its branches across the main road to attach itself to the opposite hedge. As a result, it was broken and torn by the people passing by.

A donkey fell asleep on the ice of a deep lake. The heat of its body caused the ice to melt, and the donkey, finding itself underwater, woke up in great distress and quickly drowned.

A certain patch of snow found itself clinging to the top of a rock perched on the very summit of a high mountain. Left to its own thoughts, it began to reflect, saying to itself: "Will I not be considered arrogant and proud for placing myself in such an exalted spot, when I am really just a tiny morsel of snow? How can I allow such a vast quantity of snow as I see around me to take a lower place than mine? Truly, my small size does not deserve this height. As proof of my insignificance, I can look at the fate that befell my companions yesterday; they were destroyed by the sun in just a few hours because they placed themselves higher than they should have. I will flee from the sun's anger, humble myself, and find a place that suits my modest size."

Throwing itself down, it began to descend, rolling from the high crags onto other snow. The more it sought a lowly place, the more its bulk increased, until finally ending its journey on a hill, it found itself almost the same size as the hill it rested upon. Because of its great mass, it was the last of the snow to be melted by the sun that summer.

This is said for those who are exalted by humbling themselves.

A hawk was unable to patiently endure the way a duck hid from him by diving under the water. He decided to pursue her beneath the surface; however, his wings became soaked and heavy, and he remained trapped in the water. The duck then rose into the air and mocked the hawk as he drowned.

A spider, hoping to catch a fly in its hidden web, was cruelly killed on top of it by a hornet.

An eagle, wanting to mock an owl, got its wings smeared with bird-lime <term>A sticky substance, often made from holly bark or mistletoe, smeared on branches to trap birds.</term> and was captured and killed by a man.

## THE CEDAR

The cedar, having conceived a desire to bear a large and beautiful fruit at its summit, set itself to carry out this plan with all the power of its sap. However, after this fruit had grown, its weight caused the tall and slender top of the tree to bend down.

## THE PEACH-TREE

The peach-tree, being envious of the great quantity of fruit it saw on its neighbor, the nut-tree <note>likely a walnut tree</note>, decided to do the same. It loaded itself with so much fruit that the weight threw the tree down, uprooting and breaking it against the ground.

## THE NUT-TREE

The nut-tree displayed the richness of its fruit to those passing by on the road, and because of this, every man threw stones at it.

When the fig-tree stood without fruit, no one looked at it. Wishing to be praised by men by producing fruit, it was instead bent and broken by them.

The fig-tree, standing near an elm, perceived that the elm's boughs bore no fruit themselves, yet the elm had the boldness to block the sun from the fig-tree's own unripe figs. The fig-tree rebuked her, saying: "O Elm, are you not ashamed to stand in front of me? Only wait until my children are fully grown and you will see where you find yourself." But when her offspring were ripe, a regiment of soldiers came to that place; they tore off the branches of the fig-tree in order to take her figs, leaving her entirely stripped and broken.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 76 recto a</margin>
And as she stood there, maimed in all her limbs, the elm questioned her, saying: "O Fig-tree, how much better was it to be without children than to be brought to such a wretched state by them?"

The fire, rejoicing in the dried wood it had found in the fireplace and having taken hold of it, perceived that it had grown enormously above the wood and had made itself of considerable— <note>The text ends mid-sentence as the fable continues on the following page.</note>

This enterprise, however, after much sweat, it found to be impossible because the hairs were so thick they almost touched each other, leaving no space where the flea could reach <note>original: "taste"</note> the skin. Consequently, after long labor and fatigue, it began to wish to go back to its dog—which, however, had already departed. So, after long repentance and bitter tears, it was forced to die of hunger.

Once upon a time, a razor emerged from the handle which served as its sheath and, placing itself in the sun, saw the sun reflected on its surface. It took great pride in this and, turning the thought over in its mind, began to say to itself: "Am I to go back any more to that shop from which I have just come? Surely not! It cannot be the will <note>original: "pleasure"</note> of the gods that such radiant beauty should stoop to such vile uses! What madness would lead me to scrape the lathered chins of rustic peasants and perform such menial service? Is this body made for actions such as these? Certainly not! I will go and hide myself in some secluded spot and there pass my life in tranquil ease."

And so, having hidden itself away for several months, it returned one day to the light. Coming out of its sheath, it perceived that it had acquired the appearance of a rusty saw, and that its surface no longer reflected the sun’s radiance. In vain, with useless repentance, it bemoaned its irreparable damage <note>original: "hurt"</note>, saying to itself: "Ah, how much better would it have been to have let the barber use that lost edge of mine that had such rare sharpness! Where now is the glittering surface? In truth, the foul and insidious rust has consumed it away!"

The same thing happens with minds that, instead of exercising, give themselves up to laziness <note>original: "sloth"</note>; for these, like the razor, lose their keen edge, and the rust of ignorance destroys them <note>original: "destroys their form"</note>.

So it happens to those who, leaving a life of solitude and contemplation, choose to come and live in cities among people full of limitless wickedness.

As the colorful <note>original: "painted"</note> butterfly was idly wandering and flitting about through the dark air, a light came into view. It immediately flew toward it, circling it in various patterns and marveling greatly at such radiant beauty. Not satisfied merely to look, it began to treat the light as it usually treated fragrant flowers; directing its flight, it approached with bold resolve close to the light. The flame then burnt the tips of its wings, its legs, and its other extremities. Dropping down to the base of it, the butterfly began to consider with astonishment how this accident had occurred; for it could not even imagine that any evil or harm could possibly come from something so beautiful. 

Then, having partially regained the strength it had lost, it took another flight and passed right through the body of the flame. In an instant, it fell down, burned, into the oil that fed the flame, keeping only enough life to reflect on the cause of its destruction, saying: “O accursed light! I thought that in you I had found my happiness! In vain do I mourn my mad desire, and through my ruin I have come to know your greedy <note>original: "rapacious"</note> and destructive nature.”

To which the light replied: “This is how I treat whoever does not know how to use me correctly.”

When the flint was struck by the steel, it marveled greatly and said in a stern voice: "What arrogance drives you to annoy me? Do not trouble me, for you have chosen me by mistake; I have never done harm to anyone." To which the steel replied: "If you are patient, you will see what a marvelous result will come from you."

At these words, the flint was calmed and patiently endured its suffering <note>original: "martyrdom"</note>, and it saw itself give birth to the marvelous element of fire which, through its power, became a factor in countless things.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 257 recto b</margin>
This is said for those who are discouraged at the beginning of their studies, but then set out to gain mastery over themselves and patiently apply themselves continuously to their work, from which one eventually sees results that are marvelous to describe.

# FABLES

<margin>British Museum, Arundel Manuscript 263, folio 42 verso</margin>

The vine that has grown old upon an old tree falls when that tree is destroyed. Because of its bad company, the vine failed along with it.

The mountain stream <note>original: "torrent"</note> carried so much earth and stone into its own bed that it was forced to change its course.

The net that was used to catch fish was instead destroyed and swept away by the fury of the fish.

The snowball grew larger and larger the more it rolled as it descended from the snowy mountains.

The willow grew long shoots to surpass every other plant and became the companion of the vine. But because the vine is pruned every year, the willow was also constantly cut back.

---

<margin>Forster Codex III, folio 2 recto</margin>

When the water found itself in the proud sea—its natural home—it was seized with a desire to rise above the air. With the help of the element of fire, it rose up as a thin vapor and seemed almost as light as the air itself. After it had risen to a great height, it reached a place where the air was thinner and colder. There, it was abandoned by the fire. The small particles of vapor were pressed together, united, and became heavy. As they fell, the water's pride was defeated; it tumbled from the sky and was swallowed up by the parched earth, where it lay imprisoned for a long time to do penance for its sin.

<margin>Forster Codex III, folio 21 recto</margin>

The flame above the candle is like fire on a chain; by consuming the candle, it consumes itself.

The wine consumed by a drunkard takes its revenge upon the drinker.

<margin>Forster Codex III, folio 27 recto</margin>

The ink is accused of being black by the white paper, which sees itself stained by it.

The paper, seeing itself all spotted by the murky blackness of the ink, grieves over its condition. But the ink shows the paper that the words composed upon it are the very reason for the paper's preservation <note>Leonardo suggests that a blank sheet of paper is easily discarded, while one with writing is kept for its information</note>.

# XLIII
# A Bestiary

->*‘Nature has given such power of understanding to animals that, in addition to perceiving what is to their own advantage, they also know what is to the disadvantage of their enemies.’*<-

## LOVE OF VIRTUE

The lark is a bird about which it is told that if it is brought into the presence of someone who is ill, the bird can predict the outcome: if the sick person is going to die, the bird turns its head away and refuses to look at them. But if the sick person is going to recover, the bird never takes its eyes off them, and it is the cause of all their sickness leaving them.

Similarly, the love of virtue never looks upon anything base <note>original: "mean"</note> or wicked, but instead always dwells among honest and virtuous things. It makes its home <note>original: "repatriates itself"</note> in noble hearts, just as birds do in green forests upon flowering branches. This love reveals itself more in times of adversity than in prosperity, acting like a light which shines brightest where it finds the darkest spot.

## ENVY

One reads that when the kite <note>A type of bird of prey in the hawk family.</note> sees that its chicks in the nest are too fat, it pecks their sides out of envy and keeps them without food.

## CHEERFULNESS

Cheerfulness is characteristic of the cock <note>A rooster.</note>, for it rejoices over every little thing and sings with varied and joyous movements.

Il ‘Fiore di Virtu’ e L’Acerba di Cecco d’Ascoli"</note>. *Lombard Historical Archive* <note>original: "Archivio Storico Lombardo"</note>, Year 25, Issue 19, 1898.

<header>A BESTIARY</header>

### SADNESS

Sadness may be compared to the raven. Upon seeing that its newborn chicks are white, the raven departs in great grief and abandons them with sad cries <note>original: "lamentations"</note>. It does not give them any food until it sees a few black feathers begin to grow. <sig>H 5 v.</sig>

### PEACE

One reads of the beaver that when it is pursued, it knows it is being hunted for the medicinal properties <note>original: "virtue"</note> of its testicles. When it can no longer flee, it stops; in order to be at peace with its pursuers, it bites off its own testicles with its sharp teeth and leaves them for its enemies.

### ANGER

It is said of the bear that when he goes to beehives to take honey, the bees begin to sting him. He leaves the honey and rushes to avenge himself. Because he tries to take vengeance on every bee biting him, he fails to take vengeance on any. Consequently, his anger turns into a frenzy. In his frustration <note>original: "exasperation"</note>, he throws himself on the ground, vainly trying to defend himself with his paws <note>original: "hands and feet"</note>. <sig>H 6 r.</sig>

### GRATITUDE

The virtue of gratitude is said to be found especially in the birds called hoopoes. Being mindful of the care <note>original: "benefits"</note> and nourishment they received from their parents, they return the favor when they see them growing old. They build a nest for them, cherishing and feeding them. They pluck out the parents' old and shabby feathers with their beaks and restore their sight using certain herbs, so that the parents return to a state of health and well-being <note>original: "prosperity"</note>.

### AVARICE

The toad feeds on earth but always remains thin <note>original: "lean"</note> because it never eats its fill <note>original: "satisfies itself"</note>. Its fear is so great that the supply of earth might run out. <sig>H 6 v.</sig>

<header>A BESTIARY</header>

## INGRATITUDE

The pigeons serve as a symbol of ingratitude. When they reach an age where they no longer need to be fed, they begin to fight with their father. This combat does not end until the young pigeon has driven his father out and taken his father's mate <note>original: "wife"</note> for his own.

## CRUELTY

<margin>H 7 r.</margin>
The basilisk <note>a mythical serpent or dragon-like creature said to kill with its breath or its glance</note> is so exceedingly cruel that when it cannot kill animals with the venom of its gaze, it turns toward the herbs and plants. By looking fixedly upon them, it makes them wither away.

## MAGNANIMITY

Of the eagle, it is said that it never has such a great hunger that it does not leave some of its prey for the birds that are nearby. Since these other birds are not able to forage for themselves, they must pay court to <note>original: "pay court to," meaning to seek the favor of or attend to</note> the eagle, because it is through this means that they are fed.

## CORRECTION

<margin>H 7 v.</margin>
If a wolf, while prowling warily around a cattle pen <note>original: "cattle-stall"</note>, should happen to step in a trap so that he makes a noise, he bites his own foot off in order to punish himself for his mistake.

## BLANDISHMENTS

The siren <note>a mythical creature, often depicted as half-woman and half-bird or fish, whose song lured sailors to their destruction</note> sings so sweetly that she lulls the sailors to sleep. Then, she climbs onto the ships and kills the sleeping mariners.

## PRUDENCE

Through its natural sagacity <note>original: "sagacity," meaning wisdom or keen judgment</note>, the ant provides in the summer for the winter. After gathering seeds, it kills them so that they may not germinate <note>original: "grow"</note>, and then, in due time, it eats them.

<header>A BESTIARY</header>

## MADNESS

<margin>H 8 r.</margin>
Just as the wild bull hates the color red, hunters drape the trunk of a tree in red fabric. The bull charges it furiously and gets his horns stuck in the wood, allowing the huntsmen to kill him.

## JUSTICE

We may compare the virtue of justice to the king of the bees <note>original: "king of the bees." In the Renaissance, it was commonly believed that a male king ruled the hive; modern biology identifies this leader as the queen.</note>, who organizes and arranges everything according to a system. Some bees are ordered to go among the flowers, others are ordered to work, others to fight off wasps, others to remove waste, and others to accompany and attend to the king. When the king becomes old and loses his wings, they carry him; if any one of them fails in their duty, they are punished without any mercy.

## TRUTH

<margin>H 8 v.</margin>
Although partridges steal each other’s eggs, the chicks <note>original: "children"</note> hatched from these eggs always return to their true mother.

## FIDELITY OR LOYALTY

Cranes are so faithful and loyal to their king that at night while he is asleep, some pace up and down the meadow to keep guard over him from a distance. Others stand near at hand, and each holds a stone in its foot <note>This refers to a common medieval myth that cranes held stones so that if they fell asleep, the dropping stone would wake them.</note>; if sleep should overcome them, the stone would fall and make such a noise that they would be awakened. There are others who sleep together around the king, taking turns every night so that their king never finds them failing in their duty.

## DECEIT

<margin>H 9 r.</margin>
When the fox sees a flock of magpies, jackdaws, or birds of this kind, he instantly throws himself on the ground with his mouth open to appear dead. When the birds move in to peck at his tongue, he snaps his jaws and bites off their heads.

<vocab>Bestiary, Madness, Justice, Truth, Fidelity, Loyalty, Deceit, bull, bees, partridges, cranes, fox, magpies, jackdaws, virtue, Manuscript H</vocab>

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci uses animal folklore—such as the organized society of bees and the vigilant nature of cranes—to illustrate the human virtues of Justice and Loyalty, while using the fox and bull to warn against Deceit and Madness.</summary>

### A LIE

The mole has very small eyes and always remains underground; it lives as long as it stays concealed, but as soon as it comes into the light, it instantly dies because it becomes known. So it is with a lie.

### FORTITUDE

The lion never feels fear; on the contrary, it fights with a courageous <note>original: "stout"</note> heart in fierce combat against a crowd of hunters, always seeking to injure the first one who has injured him.

### FEAR OR COWARDICE

The hare is always timid; the leaves that fall from the trees in autumn keep it in constant fear and often cause it to flee.

### MAGNANIMITY

The falcon preys only on large birds, and it would let itself die of hunger before it would feed on the young or eat rotting <note>original: "putrid"</note> flesh.

<sig>H 10 r.</sig>

### VAINGLORY

Regarding this vice, we read that the peacock is more subject to it than any other creature. This is because it is always contemplating the beauty of its tail, spreading it out in the shape of a wheel and attracting the attention of the surrounding animals with its cries.

And this is the last vice that can be conquered.

### CONSTANCY

The phoenix serves as a symbol <note>original: "type"</note> of constancy; because it understands by its very nature its own renewal, it is steadfast in enduring the burning flames which consume it, and then it is born anew.

### INCONSTANCY

The swift represents <note>original: "is put for"</note> inconstancy, for it is always in motion, since it cannot endure the slightest discomfort.

<summary>In this selection from his bestiary, Leonardo da Vinci uses the behaviors of various animals—such as the mole's preference for darkness and the phoenix's endurance of fire—as allegories for human virtues and vices. These entries illustrate moral lessons on the nature of lies, courage, pride, and the difficulty of overcoming vanity.</summary>
<keywords>Bestiary, Leonardo da Vinci, Allegory, Animal Symbolism, Virtues and Vices, Phoenix, Peacock, Fortitude, Vainglory</keywords>

<page-num>1079</page-num>
<header>A BESTIARY</header>

## TEMPERANCE

<margin>H 10 v.</margin>
The camel is the most lustful animal that there is, and it will follow the female for a thousand miles. However, if it lived continually with its mother or sister, it would never touch them, so well does it know how to control itself.

## INTEMPERANCE

The unicorn, through its lack of temperance and because it does not know how to control itself for the delight that it has for young maidens, forgets its ferocity and wildness. Laying aside all fear, it goes up to a seated maiden and goes to sleep in her lap; in this way, the hunters capture it.

## HUMILITY

<margin>H 11 r.</margin>
Of humility, one sees the supreme instance in the lamb, which submits itself to every animal. When lambs are given as food to lions in captivity, they submit themselves to them as if to their own mothers, so that it has often been seen that the lions are unwilling to kill them.

## PRIDE

The falcon, from its haughtiness and pride, thinks to overcome and lord it over all the other birds of prey because it wishes to reign alone. Many times the falcon has been seen to attack the eagle, the queen of birds.

## ABSTINENCE

The wild ass, if it should find the water muddy when going to the spring to drink, never has so great a thirst that it cannot abstain from drinking and wait until the water grows clear.

## GLUTTONY

<margin>H 11 v.</margin>
The vulture is so given up to gluttony that it would travel a thousand miles in order to feed on carrion, and this is why it follows armies.

<summary>This page uses animal allegories to illustrate moral virtues and vices, such as the camel's self-restraint and the unicorn's downfall through its lack of temperance. These entries reflect the medieval and Renaissance tradition of the bestiary, where natural history serves as a tool for ethical instruction.</summary>

<header>A BESTIARY</header>

## CHASTITY

The turtle-dove is never unfaithful to its mate; if one dies, the other maintains perpetual chastity. It never again rests upon a green branch or drinks from clear water <note>Legend held that the mourning turtle-dove only drank from muddy water and sat on dead branches to reflect its grief.</note>.

## LEWDNESS

Because of its unbridled lewdness, the bat does not follow any natural law in mating. Instead, males pair with males and females with females, just as they happen to find themselves together.

## MODERATION

<margin>Folio 12 recto</margin>
Because of its moderation, the ermine eats only once a day. It would rather allow itself to be captured by hunters than take refuge in a muddy lair, choosing death over staining its own purity <note>The ermine was a symbol of purity; its white fur was highly prized and it was believed the animal would die to keep it clean.</note>.

## THE EAGLE

When the eagle grows old, it flies so high that it scorches its feathers; nature then allows it to renew its youth by plunging into shallow water <note>This refers to the ancient myth of the eagle's rebirth, similar to the phoenix.</note>.

If its young cannot bear to gaze directly at the sun, the eagle refuses to feed them. No bird that wishes to live should approach its nest. While other animals live in great fear of it, the eagle does not harm them; it always leaves them a portion of its prey.

## THE *LUMERPA* <note>A mythical bird, likely derived from Leonardo's reading of medieval bestiaries.</note>. FAME.

<margin>Folio 12 verso</margin>
This bird is born in Greater Asia <note>original: "Asia Magna"</note> and shines so brightly that it makes its own shadows disappear. Even in death, it does not lose this light, and its feathers never fall out. However, a feather that is pulled out ceases to shine.

## THE PELICAN

The pelican has a great love for its young. If it finds them killed in the nest by a serpent, it stabs itself in the heart in their presence. By bathing them in a shower of its own blood, it restores them to life <note>In Christian art and bestiaries, the pelican "in her piety" is a common symbol for the sacrifice of Christ.</note>.

## THE SALAMANDER

The salamander refines its rough skin in the fire.—A symbol for virtue.
It has no digestive organs and seeks no nourishment other than fire; it frequently uses the flame to renew its rough skin <note>In medieval lore, the salamander was believed to be fireproof and even capable of extinguishing flames with its cold body.</note>.

## THE CHAMELEON

This creature lives on air, and there it is at the mercy of all birds. In order to be safer, it flies above the clouds; there it finds air so thin and rarefied that it cannot support any bird that would try to follow it <note>Leonardo here reflects a common myth that chameleons lived on air alone, though his description of them flying above clouds is a unique poetic or symbolic addition, perhaps conflating them with birds of paradise.</note>.

<margin>Folio 13 recto</margin>
At this height, nothing flies except those to whom the heavens have granted the ability: it is there that the chameleon flies.

## *ALEPO*. FISH <note>original: "Alepo". Likely referring to a specific species mentioned in Leonardo’s sources, though the name is obscure.</note>

The *alepo* cannot live out of water.

## OSTRICH

A symbol for armies and the food of commanders.
It extracts nourishment from iron <note>It was a long-held myth that ostriches could digest metal, particularly iron horseshoes or nails.</note>; it hatches its eggs simply by its gaze.

## SWAN

The swan is perfectly white without any spots. It sings sweetly as it dies, and this song marks the end of its life <note>This is the origin of the phrase "swan song."</note>.

## STORK

<margin>Folio 13 verso</margin>
The stork cures itself of sickness by drinking salt water. If it finds its mate has been unfaithful, it abandons her. When a stork grows old, its young ones brood over it and nourish it until it dies <note>This behavior, known as "filial piety," made the stork a symbol of parental care and gratitude in the Renaissance.</note>.

## GRASSHOPPER <note>Likely the cicada, known for its song during the heat of summer.</note>

With its song, this insect puts the cuckoo to silence. It dies in oil but is revived in vinegar. It continues to sing even through the most burning heat.

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci describes the legendary characteristics of several animals, including the fire-dwelling salamander, the air-breathing chameleon, and the dutiful stork, using them as allegories for virtue and nature's wonders.</summary>

### BAT

A symbol for vice, which cannot exist where virtue is present.
The bat loses its sight more as the light becomes more radiant, and it becomes increasingly blinded the more it looks toward the sun <note>Leonardo uses the bat's nocturnal nature as an allegory for how those who embrace "vice" are blinded by the "light" of truth or virtue.</note>.

---

### PARTRIDGE

This bird changes from female to male and forgets its former sex <note>This was a common medieval belief about partridges, likely stemming from observations of their complex mating displays.</note>. Out of envy, it steals the eggs of others and hatches them, but the young ones eventually follow their true mother.

---

<margin>Manuscript H, folio 14 recto</margin>
### SWALLOW

This bird uses the juices of the celandine plant to open the eyes of its little ones when they are blind <note>original: "celandine". Also known as "swallow-wort" (Chelidonium majus), this plant was long believed in herbal medicine to cure eye ailments because of this legend.</note>.

---

### OYSTER—FOR TREASON

The oyster opens completely when the moon is full. When the crab sees this, it throws a piece of stone or a twig into the shell to prevent it from closing up again, so that the oyster may serve as the crab's meal.
In the same way, when a mouth opens to tell its secret, it puts itself at the mercy of an indiscreet listener.

---

### BASILISK—CRUELTY

The <term>basilisk</term> <note>A mythical king of serpents said to kill with a single glance.</note> is shunned by all other serpents. The weasel fights it using <term>rue</term> and slays it. Rue stands for virtue <note>Rue (Ruta graveolens) is a bitter herb that was traditionally thought to protect against poison and witchcraft; here it represents the power of virtue to overcome the "venom" of cruelty.</note>.

---

<margin>Manuscript H, folio 14 verso</margin>
### ASP

This serpent carries sudden death in its fangs. In order to avoid hearing the charms of an enchanter, it stops up its ears with its own tail <note>This reflects a common medieval interpretation of Psalm 58:4, describing the "deaf adder" that stops its ears to the charmer's voice.</note>.

---

### DRAGON

The dragon twines itself around the legs of the elephant, causing the elephant to fall upon it so that both die. Even in death, the dragon achieves its revenge <note>The eternal struggle between the dragon and the elephant was a staple of medieval bestiaries, often symbolizing the conflict between different elemental forces.</note>.
