## VIPER

During mating, she buries her mouth and, at the end, clenches her teeth and kills her husband. Afterward, the offspring, having grown large within her body, tear open her belly and slay their mother <note>The legend of the viper's "matricide" and "patricide" was a common medieval allegory for the destructive nature of lust and the cycle of sin.</note>.

## SCORPION

<margin>Manuscript H, folio 15 recto</margin>
The saliva spat upon a scorpion by someone who is fasting kills it. This is similar to abstinence from gluttony, which removes and ends the illnesses that result from overindulgence and opens the path toward the virtues.

## CROCODILE—HYPOCRISY

This animal seizes a man and instantly kills him. After he is dead, it mourns for him with a piteous voice and many tears; but once its lament has ended, it cruelly devours him. It is the same with the hypocrite, whose face is bathed in tears over every small thing, even though his heart is as fierce as a tiger's. He rejoices in his heart over the misfortunes of others while his face is bedewed with tears <note>This is the origin of the phrase "crocodile tears," referring to insincere grief.</note>.

## TOAD

<margin>Manuscript H, folio 17 recto</margin>
The toad shuns the light of the sun. If, however, it is kept in the sunlight by force, it puffs itself up so much that it hides its head below and deprives itself of the sun's rays. This is how the enemy of clear and radiant virtue acts; such a person cannot remain in virtue's presence except by force, emboldened only by a puffed-up spirit.

## THE CATERPILLAR—FOR VIRTUE IN GENERAL

The caterpillar, through the care it takes in weaving its new home with admirable design and ingenious workmanship, afterward emerges with beautiful, colorful wings, rising upon them toward heaven.

## THE SPIDER

The spider produces from within herself a delicate and intricate web, which rewards her efforts by catching the prey she seeks.

<sig>H 18 r.</sig>

## THE LION

This animal, with its resounding roar, awakens its cubs on the third day after their birth <note>In medieval bestiaries, it was believed lion cubs were born dead and only "awakened" to life three days later by the father’s breath or roar—a common allegory for the Resurrection of Christ.</note> and teaches them how to use all their dormant senses; at this sound, all the wild creatures in the forest flee.

One may liken these cubs to the children of virtue, who are awakened by the sound of praise. Their studies grow in distinction, elevating them more and more, and at the sound of their reputation, all that is evil flees away, shunning those who are virtuous.

The lion also covers its tracks so as to leave nothing to indicate its path to its enemies. Similarly, it is wise for military captains to conceal the secrets of their minds, so that the enemy has no idea of their plans.

## TARANTULA

The bite of the tarantula fixes a man in his current purpose; that is, he remains stuck in whatever he was thinking about at the moment he was bitten.

<sig>H 18 v.</sig>

## LONG-EARED OWL AND LITTLE OWL

These birds punish those who engage in a skirmish with them by killing them; nature has ordained this so that the owls may be fed.

## THE ELEPHANT

The great elephant possesses natural qualities that rarely occur among men: namely integrity <note>original: probity</note>, prudence, a sense of justice, and religious devotion. Consequently, when there is a new moon, they go to the rivers; there, having solemnly purified themselves, they bathe. After thus saluting the planet <note>In the Renaissance, the Moon was classified as one of the seven "planets" orbiting the Earth.</note>, they return to the woods. When they are ill, they throw themselves upon their backs and...

...they toss up plants toward heaven as though they wished to offer a sacrifice. They bury their tusks when they fall out due to old age. Of these two tusks, they use one to dig up roots for food and keep the point of the other sharp for fighting.

When they are hunted and overcome by exhaustion, the elephants clash their tusks together; having thus broken them off, they use the ivory as a ransom <note>A common medieval belief held that elephants understood the value of their ivory and would offer it to hunters to spare their lives.</note> for their lives.

They are mild-mannered and aware of dangers. If one of them should happen upon a lone man who has lost his way, the elephant peacefully guides him back to the path from which he wandered. If the elephant sees a man’s footprints before seeing the man himself, he fears a trap <note>original: snare</note>; he stops and blows through his trunk to alert the other elephants. They then form themselves into a group and advance cautiously.

These animals always travel in groups. The oldest leads the way, and the second-oldest brings up the rear, thereby protecting the herd.

Out of a sense of shame, they only mate at night and in secret; they do not rejoin the herd after mating until they have first bathed themselves in the river.

They do not fight over females as other creatures do.

The elephant is so peaceful that its nature does not allow it to willingly injure creatures smaller than itself. If it happens to meet a drove or flock of sheep, it gently moves them aside with its trunk to avoid trampling them; it never harms others unless it is provoked. When an elephant has fallen into a pit, the others fill the pit with branches, earth, and stones to raise the floor so that the fallen animal may easily escape. 

They have a great dread of the grunting of pigs and retreat hastily from it, causing as much damage to one another with their feet as they do to their enemies. They delight in rivers and are always wandering near them; however, because of their great weight, they are unable to swim. They eat stones, and the trunks of trees are their favorite food. They hate rats. Flies are greatly attracted to their scent, and as they settle on the elephant's back, the animal wrinkles its skin, deepening its tight folds to trap and kill them.

### THE DRAGON

These creatures band together in groups and entwine themselves like roots. They cross swamps with their heads raised and swim toward areas where they find better pasture; if they did not combine in this way, they would drown. In this manner, their union is formed.

<margin>Manuscript H, folio 21 recto</margin>
### SERPENTS

The serpent is a very large animal. When it sees a bird in the air, it inhales with such vigor that it draws the bird into its mouth. Marcus Regulus, the Consul of the Roman army, was attacked with his forces by such a monster and was almost defeated. After the creature was slain by a catapult, it was found to measure one hundred and twenty-five feet—that is, sixty-four and a half <term>cubits</term> <note>original: braccia; a Renaissance unit of measurement roughly equal to the length of an arm</note>.¹ Its head towered above all the trees in the forest.

<margin>Manuscript H, folio 21 recto and verso</margin>
### THE BOA

This is a massive snake that winds itself around the legs of a cow so that the animal cannot move; it then sucks the cow's milk until the animal is almost dried up. One of this species was killed on the Vatican Hill during the reign of the Emperor Claudius, and it was found to have a whole boy inside whom it had swallowed.

## BONASUS—IT INJURES AS IT FLIES

This animal is a native of Paeonia <note>an ancient region in the Balkans</note>. It has a neck with a mane like a horse, but in all other respects, it resembles a bull—except that its horns curve inward to such an extent that it cannot butt with them. For this reason, its only refuge is in flight. While running, it discharges its waste for a distance of four hundred <term>braccia</term> <note>original: braccia; a Renaissance unit of measurement approximately 23 inches or 58 centimeters</note> along its path; wherever this touches, it burns like fire.

## LIONS, LEOPARDS, PANTHERS, TIGERS

These animals keep their claws retracted in sheaths and never extend them except when they are on the back of their prey or an enemy.

### LIONESS

When the lioness defends her cubs from hunters, she lowers her eyes to the ground so that she will not be terrified by the sight of the spears. She does this so that her cubs are not taken prisoner because of her own flight.
<sig>H 22 r.</sig>

### LION

This animal, which is otherwise so fearsome, fears nothing more than the rattling of empty carts or the crowing of roosters. When it sees a rooster, it is greatly terrified; it gazes at the bird’s comb with a look of fear and is strangely unsettled, even if its own face is covered.

### CAMELS

The Bactrian camel has two humps, while the Arabian has only one. They are swift in battle and very useful for carrying heavy loads. This animal is a great observer of rule and proportion: it will not move at all if its load is heavier than what it is accustomed to, and if it is taken on too long a journey, it does the same and stops suddenly, so that the merchants are forced to make their camp right there. <note>original: H 23 r.</note>

### TIGER

This animal is a native of Hyrcania <note>an ancient region located southeast of the Caspian Sea, in modern-day Iran and Turkmenistan</note>. It bears some resemblance to the panther because of the various spots on its skin, and it is an animal of terrifying speed. When a hunter finds the tiger's cubs, he carries them off instantly. He places mirrors at the spot from which he took them and then immediately flees on a swift horse.

The tigress <note>original: panther; Leonardo or the translator mistakenly switches the name of the animal in this paragraph</note>, when she returns, finds the mirrors fixed to the ground. Looking into them, she thinks she sees her own children; she continues this until, by scratching with her paw, she discovers the fraud. She then follows the scent of her cubs and pursues the hunter. As soon as the hunter sees the tigress approaching, he abandons one of the cubs. She takes the cub and carries it back to her lair, then instantly sets off again after the hunter. This is repeated until the hunter reaches his boat. <note>original: H 23 v. and 24 r.</note>

### CATOBLEPAS

The Catoblepas <note>a legendary creature from Ethiopia, often described in ancient natural histories; it is thought to be based on sightings of the wildebeest</note> is found in Ethiopia, near the primary source of the Niger River. It is not a very large animal. It is sluggish in all its limbs and has a head so large that it carries it awkwardly, so that its head is always tilted toward the ground. This is fortunate, for otherwise it would be a very great plague to mankind: anyone upon whom it fixes its gaze dies instantly. <note>original: H 24 r.</note>

<header>A BESTIARY</header>

<margin>H 24 r. and v.</margin>
### BASILISK

It is found in the province of Cyrenaica <note>original: Cyrenaica; an ancient Greek and Roman province in modern-day eastern Libya</note> and is no more than twelve fingers long <note>approximately 9 inches or 23 centimeters</note>. It has a white spot on its head in the shape of a diadem <note>a crown or royal headband</note>. It drives away every other serpent with its whistling. It resembles a snake but does not move by wriggling; instead, it extends itself straight forward from its center. It is said that on one occasion, when one of these was killed by a horseman’s spear and its venom flowed up the weapon, not only did the man die, but the horse did as well. It ruins the corn—not only the grain it touches, but even that upon which it merely breathes. It scorches the grass and splits stones.

### WEASEL

Upon finding the den of the basilisk, the weasel kills it with the smell of its urine by spreading it around; however, the stench of this urine often kills the weasel itself.

<margin>H 24 v.</margin>
### THE CERASTE

These <note>original: Ceraste; the Horned Viper, likely *Cerastes cerastes*</note> have four small, movable horns. When they wish to feed, they hide their entire body under leaves, leaving only these tiny horns visible. As the snake moves them, it appears to birds that they are little worms wriggling about; consequently, the birds instantly fly down to peck at them. The ceraste then immediately coils itself around the birds in a circle and devours them.

### AMPHISBOENA

This creature has two heads—one in its usual place and the other at its tail—as if it were not enough for it to discharge its poison from only one place. <note>The name Amphisbaena comes from the Greek meaning "to go both ways."</note>

### JACULO

This snake <note>original: Jaculo; likely the "javelin snake" from the Latin *iaculum*, meaning dart or javelin</note> stations itself in trees and hurls itself like a dart, piercing and killing wild animals.

### THE ASP

There is no remedy for the bite of this animal except to instantly cut away the affected part. As deadly <note>original: pestilential</note> as it is, this animal has such a strong affection for its companion that they always travel in pairs. And...

...if by chance one of them should be killed, the other pursues the murderer with incredible speed, and is so alert and eager for vengeance as to overcome every obstacle. It will pass through an entire troop of people seeking only to wound its enemy, traveling any distance; the only ways of avoiding it are by crossing over water or by a very rapid flight. Its eyes turn inwards and it has large ears, and its hearing guides it more than its sight. <margin>H 25 r.</margin>

### ICHNEUMON
<note>original: Ichneumon; the Egyptian mongoose (*Herpestes ichneumon*), famous in antiquity for its supposed battles with snakes and crocodiles.</note>

This animal is the mortal enemy of the asp <note>a venomous snake, likely the Egyptian cobra</note>. It is a native of Egypt, and when it sees an asp near its territory, it runs instantly to the mud or slime of the Nile and covers itself entirely. After drying itself in the sun, it smears itself with mud again, and by drying itself time after time, it covers itself with three or four layers like coats of armor. After this, it attacks the asp and struggles with it determinedly until it seizes its opportunity, flies at the snake's throat, and chokes it. <margin>H 25 v.</margin>

### CROCODILE

This creature is a native of the Nile. It has four feet and is dangerous both on land and in the water. It is the only land animal that is without a tongue, and it bites merely by moving its upper jaw <note>this was a common misconception in ancient natural history, popularized by Aristotle and Pliny the Elder</note>. It grows to a length of forty feet, has claws, and is covered with a hide that will withstand any blow. It remains on land by day and in the water by night. 

When it has finished its meal of fish, it goes to sleep on the bank of the Nile with its mouth open. Then the bird called the *trochilus* <note>likely the Egyptian Plover, which has a symbiotic relationship with crocodiles, cleaning their teeth</note>—a very small bird—runs immediately to its mouth. Hopping in and out among its teeth, the bird proceeds to peck at the remains of the food. This causes the crocodile such entrancing pleasure that it is tempted to open its mouth even wider, and in doing so, it falls asleep. No sooner does the ichneumon perceive this than it flings itself into the crocodile's mouth, pierces its stomach and intestines, and so finally kills it. <margin>H 25 v. and 26 r.</margin>

<header>A BESTIARY</header>

The dolphin knows what puts its enemy at a disadvantage. Consequently, the dolphin understands both the power of a strike from the fins on its back and the vulnerability <note>original: "tenderness"</note> of a crocodile's belly. Therefore, when they fight, the dolphin glides underneath the crocodile, pierces its belly, and so kills it.

<margin>H 26 r.</margin>
The crocodile is terrifying to those who flee from him, but he is an utter coward when he is being pursued.

## HIPPOPOTAMUS

When this animal feels itself becoming physically overloaded <note>This refers to "plethora," a historical medical theory that an excess of bodily fluids, especially blood, caused illness.</note>, it looks for thorns or places where there are fragments of split canes. It then rubs a vein against them so hard that it bursts open. After allowing as much blood to flow as is necessary, it smears itself with mud and so plasters up the wound. It has nearly the shape of a horse, with cloven hoofs, a twisted tail, boar’s tusks, and a neck with a flowing mane. Its hide cannot be pierced except when it is bathing. It feeds on grain <note>original: "corn"; in this context, it refers to cereal crops in general.</note> that grows in the fields and enters them by walking backwards, so that it may appear to have just left rather than entered.

## IBIS

This bird resembles a stork. When it feels ill, it fills its crop with water and gives itself an injection <note>This refers to the ancient belief that the ibis invented the enema by using its long beak to inject water into its rectum.</note> with its beak.

## STAG

<margin>H 26 v.</margin>
When this animal feels itself bitten by the spider called a *phalangium* <note>original: "phalangium"; a name used by ancient naturalists for various types of venomous spiders.</note>, it eats crabs and rids itself of the poison.

## LIZARD

When this animal fights with serpents, it eats sow-thistles and gains its freedom <note>Ancient texts often claimed animals sought out specific plants as antidotes to venom.</note>.

## THE SWALLOW

This bird restores sight to its blind young using the juice of the celandine plant.

## WEASEL

When this animal hunts rats, it eats rue first <note>Rue was believed to be an herb that protected against poison and infection.</note>.

## WILD BOAR

This animal cures its own diseases by eating ivy.

## SERPENT

When the serpent wishes to renew itself, it sheds its old skin <note>original: "slough"</note>, starting from the head. It transforms itself completely within a day and a night.

## PANTHER

<margin>H 27 r.</margin>
The panther will continue to fight with dogs and hunters even after its internal organs <note>original: "entrails"</note> have fallen out.

## CHAMELEON

This creature always takes on the color of the object on which it is resting. As a result, they are often accidentally eaten by elephants along with the leaves they are sitting on.

## CROW

<margin>H 27 v.</margin>
When the crow has killed a chameleon, it detoxifies <note>original: "purges"</note> itself by using laurel.

# XLIV

## Allegory

> *‘Loyalty. To ensure their king does not perish due to poor guarding, cranes stand around him at night holding stones in their feet <note>This refers to the medieval belief that cranes held stones so that if they fell asleep, the stone would drop and wake them.</note>. Love, fear, and reverence—write these upon the three stones of the crane.’*

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 13 r. d</margin>
A man, seeing a large sword at another man’s side, said to him: “Oh, you poor fellow! I have been watching you for a long time now, tied to this weapon. Why don’t you release yourself since your hands are free, and thus regain your liberty?” To this, the other replied: “This is not your business, and in any case, this is an old state of affairs.” The first man, feeling insulted, said: “I see you as having so little knowledge of the world that I supposed anything I could tell you would be new to you.”

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 76 v. a</margin>
Where fortune enters, envy lays siege and fights against it; and when fortune departs, it leaves anguish and remorse behind.

When fortune comes, seize her with a firm hand. I advise you to grab her from the front, for she is bald behind <note>original: "for behind she is bald." This refers to the classical personification of Occasio or Opportunity, who has a long forelock but is bald on the back of her head, meaning she must be seized as she approaches because she cannot be caught once she has passed.</note>.

### A SIMILE OF PATIENCE

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 117 v. b</margin>
Patience serves as a protection against wrongs just as clothes do against the cold. For if you put on more clothes as the cold increases, it will have no power to hurt you. In the same way, you must grow in patience when you meet with great wrongs, and they will then be powerless to trouble your mind.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 299 v. b</margin>
The spider, thinking to find rest within the keyhole, finds death.

# ALLEGORY

### TRUTH

Fire destroys all sophistry <note>original: "sophistry," meaning deceptive arguments or trickery</note>—that is, deceit—and preserves only the truth, which is represented as gold.

Truth cannot be hidden in the end.

Deception achieves nothing; it is useless before such a great judge.

Falsehood puts on a mask.

Nothing remains hidden under the sun.

Fire represents truth because it destroys all trickery and lies, while the mask represents falsehood and lying, through which the truth is concealed.
->Windsor: Drawings 12700 v.<-

[*Sketch: Figures seated on clouds. Rain falling. The ground below is strewn with various tools and implements.*]

> Adam on this side, and Eve on that.
> O human misery! To how many things do you make yourself a slave for the sake of money!
->Windsor: Drawings 12698 r.<-

This figure of Envy is shown making a gesture of contempt toward heaven, because if she were able, she would use her strength against God himself. She is depicted wearing a mask with a beautiful face to hide her true self. Her eyes are shown wounded by palm and olive branches, and her ears are wounded by laurel and myrtle, signifying that victory and truth cause her pain. <note>In Renaissance symbolism, the palm and olive represent victory and peace; the laurel and myrtle represent honor and love. Envy is pained by the success and happiness of others.</note> Bolts of lightning shoot out from her to represent her malicious speech. She is drawn lean and shriveled because she is constantly wasting away from endless longing. A fiery serpent is shown gnawing at her heart. She carries a quiver filled with tongues instead of arrows, because she often causes harm with her speech; and she wears a leopard's skin, based on the belief that the leopard, out of envy, kills the lion through trickery. She holds a vase in her hand filled with flowers, but beneath them, it is packed with scorpions, toads, and other venomous creatures. She is shown riding upon the figure of Death, because envy never dies and thus holds power over him; and Death is depicted with a bridle in his mouth and burdened with various weapons, as these are all the instruments of death.

The moment virtue is born, it gives birth to envy against itself; a body could sooner exist without a shadow than virtue could exist without envy.
->Oxford Drawings, Part ii. No. 6<-

# ALLEGORY

Pleasure and Pain are represented as twins, as if they were joined together, for one never exists without the other. They turn their backs to one another because they are opposites.

If you choose pleasure, know that he has behind him one who will deal out tribulation and repentance to you.

This is pleasure together with pain, and they are represented as twins because the one is never separated from the other.

They are depicted with their backs turned to each other because they are contrary to one another. They are shown growing out of the same trunk because they have one and the same foundation: for the foundation of pleasure is labor and pain, and the foundations of pain are empty <note>original: "vain"; the manuscript uses *vanj* (empty/vain) rather than *varj* (various).</note> and lustful <term>lascivious</term> pleasures.

Accordingly, Pleasure is represented here with a reed in the right hand, which is useless and weak, and the wounds it inflicts are poisoned. In Tuscany, reeds are used to support beds to symbolize that here vain dreams occur, and here a great part of life is wasted. Here, much useful time is squandered—specifically the morning, when the mind is calm and refreshed, and the body is therefore fit to begin new labors. There, many empty pleasures are taken, both by the mind imagining impossible things and by the body indulging in those pleasures that are often the cause of life’s decline; so for this reason, the reed is held as representing such foundations.

->Oxford Drawings, Part 2, No. 7<-

<summary>Leonardo describes an allegory where Pleasure and Pain are joined twins with a shared trunk, symbolizing that pleasure is rooted in labor and pain is rooted in empty indulgence.</summary>
<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, allegory, Pleasure and Pain, Tuscany, symbolism, Oxford Drawings, morality</keywords>

# XLV
## Prophecies

> *“Creatures will be seen on the earth who will constantly fight one another, causing massive losses and frequent deaths on both sides. They will set no limits on their malice . . . O Earth! Why do you hesitate to open up and hurl them headlong into the deep fissures of your vast abysses and caverns, so that you no longer display such a savage and ruthless monster in the sight of heaven?”* <note>original: "Creatures shall be seen upon the earth..." Leonardo is likely describing the destructive nature of humanity.</note>

### COMMON HABIT

Some poor wretch will be flattered, and these same flatterers will always be deceivers, robbers, and assassins to him.

### THE IMPACT OF THE SUN'S DISC

Something will appear that covers the person who tries to cover it. <note>This is a riddle; the answer is likely a shadow.</note>

### ON MONEY AND GOLD

Something shall come out of hollow caves that will cause all the nations of the world to toil and sweat with great agitation, anxiety, and labor in order to obtain its help.

### ON THE FEAR OF POVERTY

This malevolent and terrifying thing will strike such terror into men that, almost like madmen, while trying to escape it, they will rush headlong into its boundless power. <note>Leonardo observes that the fear of poverty often drives people to take risks that lead to their ruin.</note>

### ON ADVICE

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 37 v. c</margin>
The person who is most necessary to those in need will remain unknown; and if he is known, he will be held in low regard.

## ON SNAKES CARRIED BY SWANS

Huge serpents will be seen at a great height in the air, fighting with birds. <note>Leonardo often used "prophecies" as riddles; this likely refers to kites or perhaps a metaphor for human flight and warfare.</note>

## ON CANNONS EMERGING FROM A PIT AND A MOLD

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 129 v. a</margin>
Something will emerge from beneath the ground which, with its terrifying blast, will stun everyone nearby and cause men to drop dead from its "breath." It shall devastate cities and castles. <note>This describes the casting of a cannon in a pit and its subsequent use in siege warfare; the "breath" refers to the toxic and explosive fumes of gunpowder.</note>

## ON CHRISTIANS

There are many who hold the faith of the Son, yet only build temples in the name of the Mother. <note>Leonardo is noting the high number of churches dedicated to the Virgin Mary (the Mother) relative to those dedicated to Jesus Christ (the Son).</note>

## ON FOOD THAT WAS ONCE ALIVE

A large part of the bodies that once had life will pass into the bodies of other animals. That is, houses that are no longer inhabited will pass piece by piece through those that are inhabited, serving their needs and carrying away waste. This is to say that the life of man is sustained by the things he eats, and these things carry away the parts of man that have died. <note>Leonardo describes the cycle of life and digestion: the "uninhabited houses" are the carcasses of animals eaten by the "inhabited houses," which are living people.</note>

## ON MEN WHO SLEEP ON PLANKS MADE FROM TREES

Men will sleep, eat, and make their homes among trees grown in the forests and fields. <note>A riddle referring to wooden furniture and timber-framed houses.</note>

## ON DREAMING

It will seem to men that they see new destructions in the sky, and the flames descending from there will seem to have taken flight and to flee away in terror. They will hear creatures of every kind speaking human language. They will run in a moment, in person, to various <note>The text ends mid-sentence as it moves to the next page.</note>

[...You shall travel to] parts of the world without moving; amidst the darkness, you shall see the most radiant splendors. O marvel of mankind! What frenzy has driven <note>original: "impelled"</note> you to this! You shall hold conversations with animals of every species, and they with you in human language. You shall see yourselves falling from great heights without suffering any injury; the torrents will carry you with them as they mingle in their rapid course. <note>This passage describes the experience of dreaming, where one travels, speaks to animals, and survives impossible falls.</note>

### OF ANTS

There will be many communities that will hide themselves, their young, and their food <note>original: "victuals"</note> within gloomy caverns. There, in dark places, they will support themselves and their families for many months without any light, whether artificial or natural.

### OF BEES

And many others will be robbed of their stored provisions and their food, and will be cruelly submerged and drowned by a thoughtless <note>original: "insensate"</note> people. O justice of God! Why do you not wake to see your creatures abused in this way? <note>This refers to the practice of harvesting honey, which in Leonardo’s time often involved drowning or smoking out the bees.</note>

### OF SHEEP, COWS, GOATS AND THE LIKE

From countless numbers, their little children will be stolen; their throats shall be cut, and they shall be butchered <note>original: "quartered"</note> most barbarously.

### OF NUTS, OLIVES, ACORNS, CHESTNUTS, AND THE LIKE

Many children shall be torn from the very arms of their mothers with pitiless beatings, flung upon the ground, and then crushed <note>original: "maimed"</note>. <note>Leonardo describes the harvesting of nuts and fruits by striking the tree branches with poles to make the "children" (the fruit) fall.</note>

### OF CHILDREN WHO ARE WRAPPED IN SWADDLING BANDS

O cities of the sea, I see in you your citizens—women as well as men—tightly bound around their arms and legs with strong ropes <note>original: "stout bonds"</note> by... <note>Leonardo is comparing the common practice of tightly wrapping infants in swaddling clothes to being bound as a prisoner.</note>

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci presents a series of riddles framed as dark prophecies, describing the mundane realities of dreaming, ant colonies, beekeeping, slaughtering livestock, and harvesting nuts.</summary>

### OF CATS THAT EAT RATS

In you, O cities of Africa! Your own sons shall be seen torn to pieces within their own houses by the most cruel and savage animals of your country. <note>Leonardo uses dramatic language to describe cats hunting rats within homes.</note>

### OF ASSES WHICH ARE BEATEN

O neglectful Nature, why are you so biased <note>original: "partial"</note>, becoming a tender and kind <note>original: "benignant"</note> mother to some of your children, and a most cruel and ruthless stepmother to others? I see your children given into slavery to others without ever receiving any benefit, and instead of <note>original: "in lieu of"</note> any reward for the services they have performed for them, they are repaid with the harshest punishments; they constantly spend their lives in the service of their oppressor.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 145 r. a</margin>
### DIVISION OF THE PROPHECIES

First, of things which relate to rational <note>original: "reasoning"</note> animals; second, those which do not have the power of reason; third, of plants; fourth, of ceremonies; fifth, of customs; sixth, of propositions, decrees, or disputes; seventh, of propositions contrary to Nature (such as speaking of a substance where the more that is taken from it, the more it increases <note>Leonardo is likely referring to a hole or a ditch, which grows larger as more earth is removed.</note>), and reserve the weightier propositions until the end. Begin with those of less importance, and show first the evils and then the punishments; eighth, of philosophical matters.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 145 v. a</margin>
### OF FUNERAL RITES AND PROCESSIONS AND LIGHTS AND BELLS AND FOLLOWERS

The greatest honors and ceremonies shall be paid to men without their knowledge. <note>A riddle referring to the elaborate nature of funerals, which the deceased person cannot witness.</note>

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 367 v. b</margin>
All the astrologers will be castrated—that is, the roosters <note>original: "cockerels"</note>. <note>Roosters "predict" the arrival of the sun, much like an astrologer predicts the stars; they were often castrated to become capons for food.</note>

### CONJECTURE
<note>This appears to be an instruction to organize observations by time and ritual.</note>
Arrange in order the months and the ceremonies which are performed, and do this for both the day and the night.

### OF REAPERS
<note>Leonardo describes the rhythmic movement of harvesters using scythes.</note>
There will be many people moving toward one another, holding sharp iron blades in their hands. They will not harm each other except through exhaustion, for as one leans forward, the other pulls back an equal distance. But woe to anyone who steps between them, for in the end, he will be left chopped to pieces.

### OF SILK-SPINNING
<note>This describes the mechanical process of processing silk cocoons, which Leonardo personifies as victims.</note>
There will be heard mournful cries and loud shrieks—the hoarse, angry voices of those being tortured and plundered <note>original: "despoiled"</note>, and finally left naked and motionless. This will happen because of the driving force <note>original: "motive power"</note> that turns the entire machine.

### OF PLACING BREAD WITHIN THE MOUTH OF THE OVEN AND DRAWING IT OUT AGAIN
<note>A riddle describing the act of baking bread using the "mouth" of the oven as a metaphor.</note>
In every city, land, castle, village, and house, men will be seen who, out of a desire to eat, will pull food right out of each other’s mouths, without the others being able to offer any resistance.

### OF PLOUGHED LAND
The earth will be seen turned upside down, facing the opposite hemispheres, exposing the holes where the fiercest animals hide.

### OF SOWING
<note>Leonardo describes the act of scattering seeds as if it were a wasteful abandonment of food.</note>
Then a large number of the people who remain alive will throw the food <note>original: "victuals"</note> they have saved out of their houses, leaving it as free plunder for the birds and beasts of the field without a second thought.

<page-num>1103</page-num>
<header>PROPHECIES</header>

## OF THE RAINS WHICH CAUSE THE RIVERS TO BECOME MUDDY AND CARRY AWAY THE SOIL
<note>Leonardo describes how heavy rain washes topsoil from one continent into the sea, eventually settling near another.</note>

There will come from out of the sky that which will transport a great part of Africa—which lies beneath that sky—toward Europe, and likewise move parts of Europe toward Africa; and the lands of these provinces will mingle together in a great upheaval <note>original: "revolution"</note>.

## OF BRICK-KILNS AND LIME-KILNS
<note>A description of the industrial process of baking clay into brick and limestone into lime.</note>

In the end, the earth will turn red after being exposed to fire for many days, and stones will be transformed into ashes.

## OF WOOD THAT IS BURNT

The trees and shrubs of the vast forests shall be turned to ashes.

## OF BOILED FISH

Creatures of the water will die in boiling water.

## THE OLIVES WHICH DROP FROM THE OLIVE-TREES GIVE US THE OIL WHICH MAKES LIGHT
<note>This refers to the harvesting of olives, often knocked down with poles, to produce oil for lamps and food.</note>

That which gives us both nourishment and light shall descend with fury from the direction of the sky.

## OF HORNED AND TAWNY OWLS WITH WHICH ONE GOES FOWLING WITH BIRD-LIME
<note>This riddle describes a method of hunting small birds by using a tethered owl as a decoy; the birds attack the owl and get stuck on "bird-lime" (a sticky adhesive) placed on nearby branches.</note>

Many will perish from fractured skulls, and their eyes will almost pop out of their heads because of fearsome creatures that have come forth out of the darkness.

## OF FLAX WHEREBY PAPER IS MADE OUT OF RAGS
<note>Leonardo describes the lifecycle of flax: it is harvested, beaten (mangled) to separate the fibers, worn as linen rags, and finally ground into pulp to make paper for books.</note>

That which was at first despised, mangled, and tortured with many different blows shall eventually be revered and honored, and its lessons <note>original: "precepts"</note> shall be listened to with reverence and love.

<note>The original Italian manuscript reads *si mostra a esso cielo*, meaning "shows itself to that sky."</note>

<header>PROPHECIES</header>

### ABOUT BOOKS WHICH TEACH WISDOM
<note>Leonardo refers to books as "bodies without souls" because they contain the thoughts of the deceased.</note>

Bodies without souls shall, through their sayings, provide instructions <note>original: "precepts"</note> which will help us to die well.

### ABOUT THOSE WHO ARE BEATEN AND WHIPPED
<note>This riddle likely refers to the harvesting or processing of plants for textiles, or perhaps the ringing of bells inside wooden towers, though it is phrased to sound like religious self-flagellation.</note>

Men will hide themselves within the bark of hollow trees, and there, crying aloud, they will make martyrs of themselves by beating their own limbs.

### ABOUT LUST AND SELF-INDULGENCE
<note>original: "Of Wantonness"</note>

And people will go wild after the things that are most beautiful to seek after—to possess and make use of their vilest parts; and afterward, having returned to their senses with a feeling of loss and regret <note>original: "penitence"</note>, they will be filled with great wonder at their own actions.

### ABOUT THE GREEDY
<note>original: "Of the Avaricious." This likely refers to the pursuit of gold or money.</note>

There will be many who, with the utmost zeal and anxiety, will furiously pursue that which has always filled them with dread, not realizing its evil nature.

### ABOUT MEN WHO BECOME MORE STINGY AS THEY AGE, EVEN THOUGH THEY HAVE LITTLE TIME LEFT TO LIVE
<note>original: "Of men who as they grow older become more miserly, whereas, having but a short time to stay, they ought to be more generous."</note>

You will see that those who are considered to have the most experience and judgment will seek and hoard things with more eagerness even as they come to have less need for them.

### ABOUT A DITCH (GIVEN AS AN EXAMPLE OF FRENZY OR MADNESS)
<note>This is a classic riddle: a hole or a ditch is the only thing that grows larger the more you take away from it.</note>

Many will be busy with the practice of taking away from a thing which increases the more they take from it.

### ABOUT THE WEIGHT PLACED ON A FEATHER PILLOW
<note>Leonardo describes the physical behavior of a feather pillow—which compresses under weight and expands when released—as if it were a transforming creature.</note>

And with many bodies, it will be seen that as you raise your head from them, they will increase perceptibly; and when the head that has been lifted returns, their size will immediately diminish.

### ABOUT CATCHING LICE
<note>This is a classic paradox: if you "catch" a parasite, you remove it from your body and kill it, meaning you no longer "have" it.</note>

There will be many hunters of animals who, the more they catch, the fewer they will have; and conversely, they will have more in proportion to how few they catch.

### ABOUT DRAWING WATER WITH TWO BUCKETS ON A SINGLE ROPE
<note>Leonardo refers to a well pulley system where one bucket rises as the other descends.</note>

And many will busy themselves with a thing which, the more they pull it up <note>original: "draw it up"</note>, the more it will tend to escape in the opposite direction.

### ABOUT SIEVES MADE FROM THE SKIN OF ANIMALS
<note>In the Renaissance, sieves were often made from parchment or leather with holes punched in them. Leonardo describes grain or flour passing through the "skin" as if it were a biological process.</note>

We shall see the food of animals pass through their skins in every way except through the mouth, and penetrate through the opposite side until it reaches the level ground.

### ABOUT THE LIGHTS THAT ARE CARRIED BEFORE THE DEAD
<note>This refers to the candles or torches carried in funeral processions.</note>

They will provide light for the dead.

### ABOUT THE LANTERN
<note>Before glass was cheap and common, the "panes" of lanterns were often made of thin, translucent shavings of animal horn to protect the candle flame from the wind.</note>

The fierce horns of powerful bulls will protect the light used at night from the violent <note>original: "impetuous"</note> fury of the winds.

### ABOUT FEATHERS IN BEDS
<note>A simple observation that humans sleep on the plumage of birds.</note>

Flying creatures will support men with their feathers.

## OF MEN WHO PASS ABOVE THE TREES WEARING WOODEN STILTS
<note>Leonardo describes people using stilts to navigate wetlands, making them appear taller than the shrubs and small trees of the marsh.</note>

The swamps will be so vast that men will walk high above the trees of their lands.

## OF THE SOLES OF SHOES WHICH ARE MADE OF LEATHER
<note>This riddle describes the common use of animal hides for footwear.</note>

Across a great part of the country, men shall be seen walking about on the skins of large animals.

## OF SAILING
<note>Leonardo refers to the global trade routes of the Renaissance, where winds carried goods from the East and South to European markets.</note>

There will be great winds through which Eastern goods will be carried to the West; and those from the South, mingled together in great measure by the course of the winds, will follow these through distant lands.

## OF THE WORSHIPPING OF PICTURES OF SAINTS
<note>Leonardo points out the irony of religious devotion directed toward inanimate objects like statues and paintings.</note>

Men shall speak with men who shall not hear them; their eyes shall be open, and yet they shall not see; people will speak to them, and there shall be no reply; they will ask pardon from one who has ears but does not hear; they will offer light to one who is blind, and they will appeal to the deaf with loud cries.¹

## OF DREAMING
<note>This describes the paradoxical nature of dreams, where the mind experiences travel and conversation while the body remains still and silent.</note>

Men shall walk without moving; they shall speak with those who are absent; they shall hear those who do not speak.

## OF THE SHADOW THAT MOVES WITH MAN
<note>Leonardo describes how shadows mimic the movements of living things but change size based on the angle of the light.</note>

Shapes and figures of men and animals shall be seen pursuing these same men and animals wherever they flee. The movements of the one shall be exactly like those of the other, but it shall seem a thing to wonder at because of the different dimensions <note>original: "different dimensions which they assume"</note> they take on.

### OF THE SHADOW CAST BY THE SUN AND OF THE REFLECTION IN THE WATER SEEN AT THE SAME TIME
<note>Leonardo describes how a single person can appear as three entities: the physical body, the shadow on the ground, and the reflection in the water.</note>

Many times a single man will be seen to turn into three, and all will move together; yet often, the one that is most real will leave the others behind.

### OF WOODEN COFFERS WHICH ENCLOSE MANY TREASURES
<note>This riddle refers to walnuts and other nut-bearing trees, where the "treasure" is the edible seed hidden inside the hard shell or "coffer."</note>

Inside walnuts and other trees and plants, great treasures will be found lying hidden within.

### OF EXTINGUISHING THE LIGHT WHEN ONE GOES TO BED
<note>Leonardo describes the act of blowing out a candle; the sudden darkness causes an immediate loss of sight and the sensory awareness of the room's surroundings.</note>

Many people, by blowing their breath out too quickly, will lose their power of sight and, in a short time, all power of sensation.

### OF THE BELLS OF MULES WHICH ARE CLOSE TO THEIR EARS
<note>Pack animals like mules often wore bells on their harnesses. Leonardo notes the annoyance this constant noise must cause the animal.</note>

In many parts of Europe, instruments of various sizes will be heard making different melodies, causing great exhaustion to those who hear them most closely.

### OF DONKEYS
<note>original: "asses"</note>

Their many labors will be repaid only with hunger, thirst, misery, beatings, and proddings.

### OF SOLDIERS ON HORSEBACK
<note>Leonardo reflects on the violence of cavalry charges, where horses carry men into the chaos of battle.</note>

Many will be seen carried at great speed by large animals, leading to the loss of their lives and instant death. In the air <note>likely referring to the dust kicked up by a charge</note> and on the earth, animals of different colors will be seen carrying men furiously toward their own destruction.

### OF STARS ON SPURS
<note>During the Renaissance, spurs used by horsemen often featured a "rowel," a small spiked wheel shaped like a star. These were used to prick the horse to make it run faster.</note>

Because of "stars," you will see men moving as swiftly as any fast animal.

### ON THE HANDLES OF KNIVES MADE FROM RAMS’ HORNS
<note>original: "Hafts" refers to the handles of knives or tools.</note>

In the horns of animals, sharp iron blades shall be seen, which shall take away the lives of many of their own species. <note>Leonardo is pointing out the irony of using an animal's horn to make a handle for a knife used to slaughter that same kind of animal.</note>

### ON THE NIGHT WHEN ONE CANNOT DISTINGUISH ANY COLOR

It shall even come to pass that it will be impossible to tell the difference between colors, for all things will become black in hue.

### ON SWORDS AND SPEARS WHICH, BY THEMSELVES, NEVER DO ANY HARM TO ANYONE

That which is gentle in itself and free from all offense will become terrible and ferocious because of evil companionship, and will take the lives of many people with the utmost cruelty; and it would slay many more if it were not for the fact that these people are protected by bodies which are themselves without life, which have come forth out of pits—that is, by <term>cuirasses</term> of iron. <note>A "cuirass" is a piece of armor consisting of a breastplate and backplate fastened together. Leonardo observes that iron is harmless until held by a violent person, and can only be stopped by other iron (armor) dug from the earth.</note>

### ON TRAPS AND SNARES
<note>original: "Gins" is an archaic term for mechanical traps or engines of war.</note>

Many dead things will move with fury; they will take and bind the living, and will set them before their enemies in order to bring about their death and destruction. <note>This refers to traps made of dead wood or cordage that spring into action to catch live animals.</note>

### ON PRECIOUS METALS

There shall come forth out of dark and gloomy caves that which shall cause the whole human race to undergo great afflictions, perils, and death. To many of those who follow it, it will yield delight after much suffering; but whoever pays it no homage will die in want and misery. It shall bring about an endless number of crimes; it shall prompt and incite wretched men to assassinate, to steal, and to enslave; it shall hold its own followers in suspicion; it shall deprive free cities of their rank; it shall take away life itself from many; it shall make men torment each other with many kinds of trickery, deceit, and betrayal. <note>Leonardo is describing the discovery and influence of gold and silver, which causes both great wealth and great moral corruption.</note>

<note>This first section continues the "Prophecy on Precious Metals" from the previous page. Leonardo is describing the "vile monster" of gold and money.</note>
O vile monster! How much better it would be for men if you would go back to hell! For the sake of this metal, vast forests shall be stripped of their trees; for this, an infinite number of creatures shall lose their lives.

### OF FIRE

From small beginnings shall arise that which shall rapidly become great. It shall have respect for no created thing, but its power shall be such as to enable it to transform almost everything from its natural condition.

### OF SHIPS THAT SINK
<note>original: "founder"</note>

Huge, lifeless bodies shall be seen, carrying great numbers of people with fierce speed to the destruction of their lives.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, page 370, recto a</margin>

### OF WRITING LETTERS FROM ONE COUNTRY TO ANOTHER

Men from the most remote countries shall speak to one another and shall reply.

### OF THE HEMISPHERES WHICH ARE INFINITE AND DIVIDED BY AN INFINITE NUMBER OF LINES, IN SUCH A WAY THAT EVERY MAN ALWAYS HAS ONE OF THESE LINES BETWEEN HIS FEET
<note>Leonardo is likely referring to the concept of the meridian or the center of gravity. As a person moves, they are always "centered" between hemispheres of the globe.</note>

Men shall speak with, touch, and embrace each other while standing in different hemispheres, and they shall understand each other's language.

### OF PRIESTS WHO SAY MASS

There shall be many who, in order to practice their calling, shall put on the richest ceremonial robes, and these shall seem to be made in the style of aprons.

### OF FRIARS WHO HEAR CONFESSION

Unhappy women, of their own accord, shall go to reveal to men all their <term>wantonness</term> and their shameful and most secret acts. <note>"Wantonness" refers to lustful or unrestrained behavior. Leonardo is describing the act of confession, which he frames as a strange social dynamic where women share secrets with male friars.</note>

### OF THE CHURCHES AND DWELLINGS <note>original: "habitations"</note> OF FRIARS

There will be many who will abandon manual labor and a life of poverty and humble possessions to go and live among riches and in magnificent buildings, pretending that this is a way to find favor with God.

### OF THE SELLING OF PARADISE

A countless multitude will publicly and freely sell things of the highest value without permission from the Lord of those things. These items were never theirs, nor were they ever under their control; yet, human justice will take no notice of this. <note>Leonardo is likely referring to the sale of indulgences or the practice of "simony"—selling church offices or spiritual favors.</note>

### OF THE DEAD WHO ARE TAKEN TO BE BURIED

Simple people will carry a great number of lights to illuminate the journeys of those who have completely lost their sight. O human folly! O madness of mankind! These two phrases mark the beginning of this matter. <note>Leonardo is commenting on the irony of carrying candles during a funeral procession to "guide" the dead who can no longer see.</note>

### OF THE DOWRIES OF MAIDENS

In earlier times, young maidens could not be protected from the lust and violence of men, neither by the vigilance of parents nor the strength of walls. However, a time will come when it will be necessary for the fathers and relatives of these maidens to pay a high price to whoever is willing to marry them—even if the women are wealthy, noble, and exceptionally beautiful. In this, it seems certain that Nature wishes to wipe out the human race, as a thing useless to the world and the destroyer of all created things.

### OF THE CRUELTY OF MAN

Creatures will be seen on the earth who will always be fighting one another, resulting in massive losses and frequent deaths on both sides. They will set no limits to their malice; with their violent limbs, they will level a vast number of trees in the world's great forests to the ground. And when they have gorged themselves... <note>Leonardo here describes humanity as a destructive force that not only kills its own kind in war but also devastates the natural environment.</note>

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci presents a series of "prophecies" that serve as biting social commentaries on the corruption of the Church, the absurdity of certain religious customs, and the inherent destructiveness of the human race toward nature and itself.</summary>

...with food, it will satisfy their desire to deal out death, affliction, labor, terror, and exile to every living thing. And because of their boundless pride, they will wish to rise toward heaven, but the excessive weight of their own limbs will hold them down. There will be nothing remaining on the earth, under the earth, or in the waters that will not be pursued, harassed, or destroyed; and what is in one country will be taken away to another. Their own bodies will become the tomb and the means of transit for all the living bodies they have killed. O Earth! Why do you delay in opening up and hurling them headlong into the deep fissures of your huge abysses and caverns? Why do you continue to show such a savage and ruthless monster to the sight of heaven? <note>Leonardo is describing the human race as a "monster" that consumes all other life and destroys the natural world.</note>

### OF SAILING IN SHIPS

The trees from the vast forests of the Taurus Mountains and Sinai, of the Apennines and the Atlas Mountains, will be seen speeding through the air from east to west and from north to south, carrying a great number of men by means of the wind. <note>Leonardo is describing wooden ships; the "trees" are the masts and hulls, and they move "by means of the air" using sails.</note> Oh, how many vows will be made! How many deaths! What partings between friends and relatives there will be! How many will never again see their own lands or their native country, but will die unburied <note>original: "unsepulchred"</note> and have their bones scattered in various parts of the world!

### OF REMOVING ON ALL SAINTS’ DAY

Many will leave their own homes and will carry all their goods with them to go and live in other lands. <note>All Saints' Day (November 1) was traditionally a time for settling debts and moving to new lodgings.</note>

### OF ALL SOULS’ DAY

How many people will there be who mourn for their dead ancestors, carrying candles <note>original: "lights"</note> for them!

### OF FRIARS WHO BY SPENDING ONLY WORDS RECEIVE GREAT RICHES AND BESTOW PARADISE

Invisible money will allow many who spend it to triumph. <note>Leonardo is satirizing the clergy, suggesting that "invisible money"—their prayers and promises of salvation—allows them to live in luxury while giving nothing physical in return.</note>

## ON BOWS MADE FROM THE HORNS OF OXEN

<margin>C.A. 370 v. a</margin>
Many there will be who, by means of the horns of cattle, will die a painful death. <note>This refers to crossbows or composite bows, which were often reinforced with layers of horn. The "painful death" comes from the arrows or bolts shot by these weapons.</note>

<margin>c 19 v.</margin>
Behold a thing which is valued the less the more one has need of it. It is advice.

<margin>F 5 v.</margin>
And many have made a business of deceits and fake miracles, tricking <note>original: "cozening"</note> the foolish crowd; and if no one showed themselves aware of their deceptions, they would impose them upon everyone.

## ON DOING WELL

<margin>G 88 v.</margin>
The branch of the walnut tree, which is struck and beaten just when it has brought its fruit to perfection, represents those who, as a result of their illustrious works, are struck by envy in various ways. <note>It was a common practice to beat walnut trees with poles to knock down the nuts; Leonardo uses this as a metaphor for how society treats successful people.</note>

<margin>I 39 v.</margin>
All these things which in the winter are concealed and hidden beneath the snow will be left bare and exposed in summer—this is said of a lie, which cannot remain hidden.

You will see the lion tribe tearing open the earth with hooked claws and burying themselves in the holes they have made, together with the other animals that are in subjection to them. <note>Leonardo is likely describing the antlion, an insect larva that digs pits in the sand to trap other insects.</note>

Creatures clad in darkness shall come forth from the ground and attack the human race with tremendous onslaughts; their fierce bites will poison the blood even as they devour people. <note>This likely refers to ants or similar ground-dwelling insects viewed through a "prophetic" hyperbolic lens.</note>

<margin>I 63 [15] r.</margin>
A tribe of dreadful winged creatures shall also fly through the air and attack both men and beasts, feeding upon them with loud cries—they shall fill their bellies full of crimson blood. <note>This describes biting insects like mosquitoes, wasps, or horseflies.</note>

You will see blood streaming from the torn flesh of men and wetting the surface of their bodies.

You will see men with a malady so cruel that they will tear their flesh with their own nails—this will be the itch. <note>The "itch" refers to scabies or a similar parasitic skin condition that causes intense scratching.</note>

<header>PROPHECIES</header>

You will see plants continuing without leaves, and rivers standing still in their courses. <note>This likely refers to timber used in buildings and the freezing of rivers or the construction of canals.</note>

The water of the sea will rise above the high summits of the mountains toward the sky, and it will fall down again onto the dwellings of men—this refers to the formation and rain of clouds.

You will see the greatest trees of the forests carried by the fury of the winds from the east to the west—this refers to wooden ships sailing across the sea.

Men will throw away their own food—this refers to the act of sowing grain in the fields.

<margin>1 63 [15] verso</margin>
The human race will reach a point where they cannot understand one another’s speech—as when a German speaks with a Turk.

You will see fathers giving up their daughters to the lust of men, rewarding those men, and abandoning all their former care for their daughters—this occurs when girls are married. <note>Leonardo is referring to the tradition of providing a dowry to the groom.</note>

Men will come forth out of their graves changed into winged creatures, and they will attack other men, taking away their food even from their hands and tables—these are flies. <note>Flies were thought to emerge from the earth or decaying matter, appearing as if rising from graves.</note>

There will be many who will flay <note>original: "flay"; to strip the skin off</note> their own mother and fold back her skin—these are the tillers of the ground who plow the earth. <note>The Earth was traditionally viewed as the "Mother" of all living things.</note>

Happy will be those who listen to the words of the dead—this refers to reading good books and following their teachings.

<margin>1 64 [16] recto</margin>
Feathers will raise men toward heaven just as they do birds—this refers to letters written with quill pens. <note>Writing allows a person's ideas and fame to transcend their physical limits.</note>

The works of men’s hands will become the cause of their death—swords and spears.

Men will pursue the thing they fear most—that is, they live in misery for fear of falling into misery. <note>This describes the irony of people suffering through grueling work or greed just to avoid the possibility of poverty.</note>

Things that have been severed will be joined together and will gain such power that they will restore lost memory to men—these are the papyrus sheets, which are made of cut strips and preserve the memory of the thoughts and deeds of men.

You will see the bones of the dead, by their rapid movement, directing the fortunes of the person who moves them: — The dice. <note>Dice were traditionally carved from animal bone or ivory.</note>

Oxen will protect fire from death by using their horns: — The lantern. <note>In the Renaissance, lantern panes were often made of "horn"—thin, translucent sheets of animal horn—rather than expensive glass.</note>

<margin>1 64 [16] verso</margin>
The forests will give birth to young who will become the cause of their own death: — The handle of the hatchet. <note>The wooden handle of an axe is made from a tree and is used to cut down other trees.</note>

Men will deal violent blows to the very thing that gives them life: — They will thresh the grain. <note>Farmers beat stalks of wheat or barley to separate the edible grain from the husks.</note>

The skins of animals will cause men to break their silence with loud cries and curses: — Balls used for playing games. <note>Refers to leather-bound balls used in sports, where players often shout or swear.</note>

Often, something that is split apart becomes the means of a great joining together: — This is the comb made of split canes, which unites the threads in silk weaving.

<margin>1 65 [17] recto</margin>
Wind passing through the skins of animals will make men leap into the air: — These are bagpipes, which cause men to dance.

## ON NUT TREES THAT ARE BEATEN

Those that have produced the best harvest will be beaten the most; their children will be carried off and stripped of their clothes, and their bones will be broken and crushed. <note>To harvest walnuts, workers beat the branches with poles. The "children" are the nuts, the "clothes" are the husks, and the "bones" are the shells.</note>

## ON SCULPTURE

Alas! Whom do I see? The Savior is crucified once again. <note>Leonardo is likely referring to the act of carving a crucifix out of wood or stone, which involves "cutting" the image of Christ.</note>

## ON THE MOUTH OF MAN, WHICH IS A TOMB

Loud noises will come out of the tombs of those who died by an evil and violent death. <note>Leonardo, who was likely a vegetarian, describes the human mouth as a "tomb" for the animals we eat; the "noises" are the voices or complaints of the people who have consumed them.</note>

## ON THE SKINS OF ANIMALS WHICH RETAIN THE FEELING OF WHAT IS WRITTEN UPON THEM

The more you converse with skins covered in thoughts, the more wisdom you will acquire. <note>Refers to books made of parchment, which is processed animal skin. Leonardo suggests that the "feeling" or wisdom of the author is passed to the reader through the skin.</note>

### PROPHECIES

#### ON PRIESTS WHO CARRY THE HOST WITHIN THEMSELVES

<margin>1 65 [17] verso</margin>
Then almost all the tabernacles where the Body of the Lord <note>original: *Corpus Domini*</note> lives will be plainly visible, walking about by themselves on the different roads of the world. <note>The "tabernacles" are the bodies of the priests who have consumed the Eucharist.</note>

And those who feed the air will turn night into day: — Tallow. <note>Tallow is animal fat used to make candles; as the candle burns, it "feeds the air" and provides light.</note>

And many creatures of the earth and of the water will mount up among the stars: — The Planets. <note>Leonardo refers to the various planets and constellations named after animals, such as Pisces (fish) or Taurus (the bull).</note>

You shall see the dead carrying the living in various parts of the world: — Chariots and ships. <note>Vehicles made of "dead" timber carry living people.</note>

From many, food shall be taken away out of their mouths: — From ovens. <note>Refers to the act of removing bread from the opening, or "mouth," of a baker's oven.</note>

<margin>1 66 [18] recto</margin>
And those who have their mouths filled by the hands of others, shall have the food taken away out of their mouths: — The oven.

#### ON CRUCIFIXES WHICH ARE SOLD

I see Christ sold and crucified again, and his saints suffering martyrdom. <note>Leonardo is critiquing the commercial sale of religious icons and crucifixes as a betrayal of faith.</note>

#### ON DOCTORS WHO LIVE OFF THE SICK

Men will come to such a state of misery that they will be grateful that others should profit from their sufferings, or from the loss of their true riches—that is, their health.

#### On the religious orders of Friars who live by means of the Saints, who have been dead for a long time:

Those who are dead will, after a thousand years, be the ones who provide for many of the living. <note>Refers to how the Catholic Church and its friars were supported by the legacies and veneration of ancient saints.</note>

#### ON STONES TURNED INTO LIME WITH WHICH PRISON WALLS ARE BUILT

<margin>1 66 [18] verso</margin>
Many things which have previously been destroyed by fire will deprive many men of their liberty. <note>Limestone is burned in a kiln (destroyed by fire) to create lime, which is then used as mortar to build the walls of prisons.</note>

<summary>In this collection of riddles, Leonardo da Vinci uses metaphorical language to criticize the commercialization of religion and the medical profession, while observing how natural processes are repurposed for human industry and incarceration.</summary>

<header>PROPHECIES</header>

### OF CHILDREN WHO TAKE THE BREAST

Many Franciscans, Dominicans, and Benedictines will eat that which has recently been eaten by others, and they will remain many months before being able to speak. <note>Leonardo is comparing infants to monks. Babies wear long robes (like habits) and cannot speak, and they "eat" milk produced by the food their mothers have already consumed.</note>

### OF COCKLES AND SEA-SNAILS CAST UP BY THE SEA WHICH ROT WITHIN THEIR SHELLS

<margin>I 67 [19] recto</margin>
How many shall there be who, after they are dead, will lie rotting in their own houses, filling all the air around with their foul stench! <note>The "houses" are the shells of the mollusks.</note>

### PLANT WITH ROOTS UPWARDS

For someone who would be on the point of coming to the end of all possessions and favor. <note>This likely refers to a person whose life or fortune has been "uprooted" or completely overturned.</note>

### OF JACKDAWS AND STARLINGS

<margin>I 138 [90] verso</margin>
Those who trust themselves to inhabit near him—and these will be in great crowds—will almost all die a cruel death; and one will see fathers and mothers, together with their families, being devoured and slain by cruel animals. <note>This riddle likely refers to a fowler's net or a predatory bird used in hunting, where the "animals" are the humans or trained hawks killing the gathered birds.</note>

### OF PEASANTS WHO WORK IN THEIR SHIRTS

Shadows will come from the East which will tinge with much darkness the sky that covers Italy. <note>This is a literal observation of sunset: as the sun sets in the West, shadows grow from the East, eventually covering the land in darkness.</note>

### OF THE BARBERS

<margin>I 139 [91] recto</margin>
All men will take refuge in Africa. <note>In Leonardo’s time, "Africa" was often used as a metaphor for darkness or "the land of the shadows." In the context of a barber, this may refer to the "shady" areas of the face or the shadows cast during the process.</note>

### OF THE SHADOW CAST BY MAN AT NIGHT WITH A LIGHT

<margin>K 50 [1] verso</margin>
There shall appear huge figures in human shape, and the nearer to you they approach, the more will their immense size diminish. <note>An observation of optics: when a light source is behind you, your shadow appears massive on a distant wall, but as you move closer to the wall (and further from the light), the shadow shrinks to your actual size.</note>

## OF MULES WHICH CARRY RICH BURDENS OF SILVER AND GOLD

<margin>Manuscript L, folio 91 recto</margin>
Many treasures and great riches will be loaded onto four-legged animals, which will carry them to various <note>original: "divers"</note> places.

Those who provide light for divine service will be drowned:
The bees that make the wax for candles. <note>In Leonardo’s time, bees were often killed or "drowned" in smoke or liquid to harvest their honey and wax.</note>

The dead will come out from under the earth, and by their fierce movements, they will drive countless human beings out of the world:
The iron that comes from under the earth is "dead," and it is used to make the weapons with which so many men have been killed.

The greatest mountains, even though they are far from the seacoast, will drive the ocean from its place:
This happens because rivers carry down the soil they have taken from the mountains and deposit it on the seashores; where the earth accumulates, the sea must retreat.

The water falling from the clouds will change its nature so much that it will remain for a long time on the slopes of mountains without moving at all. And this will happen in many different regions:
The snow that falls in flakes, which is actually water.

The great rocks of the mountains will spit out fire, so that they will burn the timber of many vast forests and many animals, both wild and tame:
The flint of the tinderbox, which creates a fire that consumes the loads of firewood <note>original: "faggots"</note> cleared from the forests; and with this fire, the meat of animals is cooked.

Oh, how many great buildings will be ruined because of fire:
By the fire of cannons and guns.

Oxen will become a major cause of the destruction of cities, as will horses and buffaloes:
They are the animals that pull the heavy guns and artillery.

Many will grow great through their own destruction:—

### ON GRAIN AND OTHER SEEDS

### ON TREES THAT PROVIDE SAP TO GRAFTED BRANCHES

Fathers and mothers will be seen to pay much more attention to their stepchildren than to their own children. <note>In grafting, the original tree (the "parent") provides nutrients to the new branch (the "stepchild") to ensure it grows.</note>

The time of Herod shall return; for innocent children shall be torn away from their nurses and shall die of terrible wounds at the hands of cruel men. <note>The "children" are young goats (kids) being taken from their mothers to be slaughtered for meat.</note>

### THE MOWING OF GRASS

### THE LIVES OF MEN WHOSE BODILY SUBSTANCE CHANGES EVERY TEN YEARS

Men will pass, when dead, through their own bowels. <note>This likely refers to the biological cycle where the nutrients of the dead are absorbed into the earth and eventually consumed again by the living.</note>

### LEATHER BOTTLES

The goats will carry wine to the cities. <note>In Leonardo's time, wine was frequently transported in bags made from goat skins.</note>

### SHOEMAKERS

<margin>Forster II 61 v.</margin>
Men will take pleasure in seeing their own handiwork worn out and destroyed. <note>Because the wearing out of shoes ensures that the shoemaker will have more work to do.</note>

### BEES

They live together in communities. They are drowned so that their honey may be seized.

<margin>Windsor: Drawings 12587 r.</margin>
Many and very great communities will be drowned in their own dwellings. <note>This refers to the traditional method of harvesting honey by using water or smoke to clear the hive.</note>

<margin>On the Flight of Birds 14 [13] r. <note>original: "Sul Volo"</note></margin>
Snow in summer shall be gathered on the high mountain peaks and carried to warm places, and there it will be allowed to fall when festivals are held in the town squares <note>original: "piazza"</note> during the heat of summer. <note>Ice and snow were harvested from mountains and stored in "ice houses" to provide cooling and treats for the wealthy during the summer months.</note>

# XLVI

## Personal Notes

### *‘O Leonardo, why do you toil so much?’*

<margin>Codex Atlanticus <note>original: "C.A."</note> 66 verso b</margin>
To **WRITE** so clearly about the kite <note>A "kite" here refers to a bird of prey (the Red Kite), not a toy.</note> seems to be my destiny. This is because, in the earliest memories of my infancy, it seemed to me while I was still in the cradle that a kite came down to me, opened my mouth with its tail, and repeatedly struck me inside my lips with its tail.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 71 recto a</margin>
Please do not hold me in contempt! I am not poor! Rather, the man who is truly poor is he who desires too many things. Where will I take my place? In a little while from now, you shall know. Answer for yourself! Very shortly...

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 93 recto a</margin>
If it is claimed that the King loses seventy-two ducats in revenue when this water is diverted from San Cristoforo... <note>San Cristoforo is a canal in Milan where Leonardo was granted water rights by the French King.</note>

This His **Majesty** knows: what he gives to me, he takes from his own resources.

But in this case, nothing will be taken from the King. Instead, it will be taken away from those who have stolen it, because of the regulation of the outlets which the "water-thieves" have enlarged.

If it should be said that this causes a loss to many people, it actually amounts to nothing more than taking back from the thieves what they are required to restore.

And indeed, the magistrate continually reclaims this water without any thought of me; it amounts to more than five hundred "ounces" of water, whereas my portion is fixed at only twelve ounces. <note>An "ounce" (oncia) was a traditional unit used to measure the flow of water in Italian canal systems.</note>

And if it is said that this water right of mine is worth a considerable annual sum: when the canal is low, an ounce here is leased for only seven ducats (valued at four lire each) per year, which totals seventy.

If they claim that this interferes with navigation, it is not true, because the outlets used for this irrigation are located upstream from the shipping routes.

¹ This interpretation is credited to Gerolamo Calvi, who believes this note was written in the final years of Leonardo's life, either just before leaving Rome or while in France. Leonardo thus creates a sharp contrast between this destruction of his hopes and the fact that Lorenzo "the Magnificent" was his first patron. <margin>Manuscript B, 66 recto</margin>
These foundation piles should be between a third and a half <term>braccio</term> <note>original: *braccio*; a Florentine unit of measurement approximately 23 inches (58 cm), literally meaning "an arm."</note> in thickness and about two and a half <term>braccia</term> long. They should be made of oak or alder—that is, a close-grained wood—and, most importantly, the wood should be green <note>In engineering, "green" wood is freshly cut and unseasoned; it is often more durable when driven into wet soil or underwater where it is protected from air.</note>. I have observed the repair of part of the ancient walls of Pavia, which have their foundations in the banks of the Ticino River. The old piles there, which were made of oak, had become as black as charcoal; those made of alder had a red color like <term>Brazil-wood</term> <note>original: *verzino*; a wood used to produce red dye. Leonardo is noting how the underwater environment preserved and colored the timber.</note>. They were very heavy and as hard as iron, showing no signs of decay. When you wish to drive these piles into the ground, you should first start the hole using an iron stake.

### [Dated Note: Thefts of a pupil. Pageant arranged by Leonardo]

On the twenty-third day of April 1490, I began this book and started work again on the horse <note>The Sforza horse; a massive bronze equestrian monument commissioned by Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan.</note>.

Giacomo <note>Giacomo Caprotti, nicknamed Salai ("Little Devil"), who entered Leonardo's service at age ten and remained his companion for decades.</note> came to live with me on St. Mary Magdalene’s Day <note>July 22nd.</note>, 1490, when he was ten years old. He is thievish, lying, stubborn, and greedy.

On the second day, I had two shirts, a pair of <term>hose</term> <note>Tight-fitting garments covering the legs.</note>, and a <term>doublet</term> <note>A man's snug-fitting buttoned jacket.</note> cut out for him. When I set aside money to pay for these things, he stole the money from my wallet, and it was never possible to make him confess, although I was absolutely certain of it. 4 lire.

On the following day, I went to supper with Giacomo Andrea, and the other Giacomo [Salai] ate enough for two and caused trouble enough for four, for he broke three flagons and spilled the wine. After this, he came to the supper where I...

Furthermore <note>original: *Item*; a Latin term used in lists to mean "likewise" or "also".</note>, on the seventh day of September, he stole a <term>style</term> <note>A metal stylus used for drawing on prepared paper.</note> worth twenty-two soldi from Marco, who was with me. It was made of silver, and he took it from Marco's studio. After Marco had searched for it for a long time, he found it hidden in Giacomo’s box. 2 lire 1 soldo.

Furthermore, on the twenty-sixth of the following January, when I was in the house of Lord <note>original: *Messer*.</note> Galeazzo da Sanseverino to organize the pageant for his tournament, some of the pages had taken off their clothes to try on costumes for the "wild men" <note>original: *savages*; performers dressed in leaves or fur, a popular theme for Renaissance festivals.</note> who were to appear in this pageant. Giacomo went to the wallet of one of them as it lay on the bed with his other belongings and took some money he found there. 2 lire 4 soldi.

Furthermore, a Turkish hide <note>A high-quality leather from the Ottoman Empire.</note> had been given to me in that same house by Master Agostino of Pavia to make a pair of boots, and this Giacomo stole it from me within a month and sold it to a cobbler for twenty soldi. With the money—as he has himself confessed to me—he bought aniseed sweets <note>original: *comfits*; sugar-coated seeds or nuts.</note>. 2 lire.

Furthermore, on the second day of April, Giovanni Antonio happened to leave a silver style on one of his drawings, and this Giacomo stole it from him; it was worth twenty-four soldi. 1 lira 4 soldi.

The first year:
*   A cloak: 2 lire
*   6 shirts: 4 lire
*   3 doublets: 6 lire
*   4 pairs of hose: 7 lire 8 soldi
*   A suit of clothes, lined: 5 lire
*   24 pairs of shoes: 6 lire 5 soldi
*   A cap: 1 lira
*   Laces for a belt: 1 lira
