<header># PERSONALIA <note>original: *Personalia*; Latin for "Personal Matters."</note></header>
<page-num>1127</page-num>

<margin>Manuscript reference: Libro A, folio 77 verso.</margin>

When I was at sea, positioned exactly halfway between a flat shore and a mountain, the side with the shore seemed much farther away than the side with the mountain.<sup>1</sup>

Like a swirling wind sweeping through a hollow, sandy valley, driving everything that stands in its way into a vortex with its furious, speeding course . . .

In the same way, the northern blast drives back with its hurricane force . . .

Neither does the stormy sea roar so loudly when the north wind beats it back into foaming waves between Scylla and Charybdis <note>Two legendary sea monsters from Greek mythology located in the Strait of Messina; they personify the dangers of a whirlpool and a rocky shoal.</note>, nor do Stromboli or Mount Etna when the trapped, sulfurous fires burst open and tear the mighty mountain apart. Their force hurls rocks and earth through the air, mingled together in the belching flames. . . .

Nor when Etna’s burning caverns vomit out the uncontrollable element <note>The "element" refers to fire.</note> and thrust it back to its own region in a fury, driving away any obstacle that withstands its violent rage. . . .

Driven by my eager desire, and anxious to see the vast abundance of varied and strange forms created by the master craftsman, Nature, I wandered for some distance among overhanging rocks. Eventually, I came to the mouth of a huge cavern. I stood before it for a time, stunned, as I hadn't known it was there. I stayed there with my back arched, my left hand clutching my knee, and my right hand shading my eyes. I kept bending first one way and then another, trying to see if I could make out anything inside, but the intense darkness made it impossible. After staying there for a while, two emotions were suddenly awakened within me: fear

<sup>1</sup> In the sketch that accompanies this note, a ship is seen traveling from a mountainous shore toward a lower-lying one. This note is labeled by M. Ravaisson-Mollien <note>Jean Paul Pierre Ravaisson-Mollien (1813–1900), a French philosopher and archaeologist who transcribed Leonardo's manuscripts.</note> as an "optical illusion." Its primary interest is the biographical question it raises. Leonardo clearly states here that he was once at sea in a position where both a flat shore and a mountain were visible at the same time. In discussing the interpretation of the "Armenian letters" in the *Codice Atlantico* <note>The largest collection of Leonardo's drawings and writings.</note>, I have shown that this experience is exactly what would happen to a traveler sailing from Khelindreh (the medieval port of Armenia, called "Calindra" in Leonardo’s text) to Cyprus. This is supported by a passage in the Windsor Manuscripts: "Setting out from the coast of Cilicia <note>An ancient region on the south coast of Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey).</note> toward the south, you discover the beauty of the island of Cyprus."

...and desire—fear of the dark, threatening cavern, and the desire to see if there might be any marvelous thing inside.

O powerful and once-living instrument of creative Nature! Your great strength did not save you; you had to abandon your peaceful life to obey the law that God and time ordained for all-procreating Nature! The branching, sturdy dorsal fins did not help you as you pursued your prey, when you used to plow your way, violently tearing open the salty waves with your chest.

O, how many times were schools of frightened dolphins and large tuna seen fleeing before your unthinking fury; and you, lashing with swift, branching fins and a forked tail, created a sudden storm in the sea with a loud roar and the sinking of ships. With a mighty wave, you heaped the open shores with frightened and terrified fish, which, escaping from you, were left high and dry when the sea receded, becoming the plentiful and abundant prize of the neighboring peoples.

<margin>British Museum MS, folio 156 recto.</margin>
O Time, swift destroyer of all created things! How many kings, how many nations have you brought low! How many changes of state and circumstance have followed since the amazing form of this fish died here in this hollow, winding cave? Now, destroyed by Time, it lies patiently within this narrow space; with its bones stripped and bare, it has become a support and a skeleton for the mountain that lies above it. <note>Leonardo is describing a fossilized whale he found while exploring caves in the mountains. He correctly realized that the presence of sea fossils in mountains meant that the land was once under the sea.</note>

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, folio 265 recto a.</margin>
O, how many times were you seen among the waves of the mighty, swelling ocean, towering like a mountain, conquering and overcoming them! And with your black-finned back, plowing through the salt waves with a proud and stately bearing! <sup>1</sup>

*...moving with a heavy motion, turning and twisting through the seawater. And with a bristly and black back, like a mountain, to conquer and overpower them.* <note>original: "grave moto gir volteggiando in fralle marine acque. E con setoluto e nero dosso, a guisa di montagna, quelle vincere e soprafare." This is a draft of the whale passage found on the previous page.</note>

*O, how many times were you seen among the waves of the swollen and great ocean, like a mountain conquering and overpowering them; and with a bristly and black back plowing through the seawater, and with a proud and grave movement.* <note>original: "Oh quante volte fosti tu veduto in fra l’onde del gonfiato e grande occeano, a guisa di montagna quelle vincere e soprafare, e col setoluto e nero dosso solcare le marine acque, e con superbo e grave andamento."</note>

It is the same tireless patience seen in the attempt here, in this "armory of words," to shape the thought into a more exact expression of the mind's purpose. This explains why there are sometimes so many studies for the same figure in Leonardo’s drawings.

On one occasion near Milan, looking in the direction of Lake Maggiore, I saw a cloud shaped like a huge mountain made up of banks of fire. ### Description of Mount Taurus and of the river Euphrates. To the Devatdar <note>original: *Devatdar*; a high-ranking secretary, chancellor, or official in the Mamluk administration</note> of Syria, lieutenant of the sacred Sultan of Babylon <note>In this period, "Babylon" usually referred to the city of Cairo (specifically the fortress of Babylon), the seat of the Mamluk Sultanate, rather than the ancient city in Mesopotamia.</note>:

Finding myself in this part of Armenia in order to discharge with devotion and care the duties of the office to which you have appointed me, and beginning in those areas which seemed to me to be most suitable for our purpose, I entered the city of Calindra, which is near our borders. This city is situated on the seacoast of that part of the Taurus range which is separated from the Euphrates and looks westward toward the peaks of the great Mount Taurus. These peaks are of such a height that they seem to touch the sky; for in the entire world, there is no part of the earth higher than their summit, and they are always struck by the rays of the rising sun four hours before dawn. Because it is made of exceedingly white stone, it shines brightly and performs the same function for the Armenians of these parts as the beautiful light of the moon would in the midst of the darkness. By reason of its great height, it rises above the highest clouds for a distance of four miles in a straight line.

This peak is visible from a great part of the west, illuminated by the sun after its setting during the third part of the night. And it is this which among you, in calm weather, has formerly been thought to be a...

### OF THE SHAPE OF MOUNT TAURUS

I should not be justly accused of idleness, O Devatdar <note>original: *Devatdar*; a title for a high-ranking secretary or official in the Mamluk administration</note>, as your criticisms <note>original: "strictures"</note> seem to suggest. Rather, it is your great affection—which has moved you to grant me these honors—that has compelled me to use the utmost care in seeking out and diligently investigating the cause of such a momentous and startling occurrence. For such a task, time was necessary.

In order to ensure you are well-informed about the cause of so great an effect, it is necessary that I first describe the nature of the region. Then, I will proceed to the event itself; by following this process, I believe you will be fully satisfied.

Do not be distressed, O Devatdar, by my delay in responding to your urgent request. The matters about which you have asked me are of such a nature that they cannot be properly explained without some time passing. This is especially true because, in order to explain the cause of such a massive event, it is necessary to accurately describe the nature of the place. Afterward, you will be able to easily satisfy yourself regarding the request mentioned above.

I will skip any description of the shape of Asia Minor, or which seas and lands define its surface. I know that your own diligence and scholarly care are such that you have already acquired this knowledge. Therefore, I will move on to...

...provide you with an account of the true shape of Mount Taurus, which has been the site of such a surprising and destructive catastrophe; this will help advance our purpose.

Many say this Mount Taurus is part of the Caucasus range. Wishing to be certain about this, I questioned some of the people living on the shores of the Caspian Sea. They informed me that although their mountains share the same name, the ones there are even higher. They confirm that this is the true Mount Caucasus, because "Caucasus" in the Scythian <note>The Scythians were ancient nomadic people of Central Eurasia.</note> language means "supreme height." Indeed, no mountain of such immense height is known to exist anywhere in the East or the West. The proof of this is that those living in countries to the west can see the sun’s rays lighting up part of its summit for a quarter of the longest night; the same is true for those living in countries to the east.

## THE STRUCTURE AND DIMENSIONS OF MOUNT TAURUS

The shadow cast by this ridge of the Taurus is so vast that in mid-June, when the sun is at its highest point in the sky, it reaches the borders of Sarmatia <note>Sarmatia was an ancient region encompassing parts of modern-day Ukraine, Russia, and Poland.</note>, a distance of twelve days' journey. In mid-December, the shadow extends as far as the Hyperborean Mountains <note>In Greek mythology, the Hyperboreans lived in a land "beyond the North Wind"; here Leonardo refers to legendary mountains in the far north.</note>, which are a month’s journey to the north. 

The side facing the wind is covered in clouds and mists. This is because the wind is split in two as it strikes the rock, then closes up again beyond it. In this way, the wind carries clouds from all directions and leaves them where it hits the mountain. Consequently, the area is constantly struck by lightning due to the massive accumulation of clouds. This causes the rock to become completely cracked and filled with massive <term>debris</term> <note>original: *débris*; broken fragments of rock or ruins.</note>.

A very wealthy people lives at the base of this mountain. The area is rich with beautiful springs and rivers; it is fertile and full of every good thing, especially on the southern slopes. After climbing about three miles, you reach the beginning of the forests of great firs, pines, beeches, and other similar trees. Beyond that, for another three miles, you find meadows and vast pastures. The rest of the mountain, leading up to the beginning of the...

The peak of Mount Taurus is covered in eternal snow, for this never melts in any season. This snow cap extends at this height for about fourteen miles in total. From the point where the peak begins, for about a mile upward, the clouds never pass; thus, the clouds extend for about fifteen miles with a height of about five miles in a straight line. Roughly at that distance, we find the actual summit of the peaks of Taurus. Here, from about the halfway point upward, we begin to find the air growing warm; there is no breath of wind to be felt, and nothing can live there for very long. Nothing is produced there except for some birds of prey, which nest in the deep gorges of the Taurus and descend below the clouds to seek their prey upon the grassy hills. Above the cloud line, the mountain is entirely bare rock of a dazzling whiteness. It is impossible to reach the lofty summit because the ascent is both rough and dangerous.

The gleaming of the waves was not visible in the parts that reflected the dark rain and the clouds. However, where they reflect the flashes produced by the thunderbolts, as many gleams were seen—caused by the images of these flashes—as there were waves reflecting them to the eyes of the spectators. The number of these images caused by the lightning flashes upon the waves increased in proportion to the distance from the eyes of the spectators. Similarly, the number of the images diminished the nearer they were to the eyes of those who saw them. This is proved in the definition of the radiance of the moon and of our maritime <note>original: "maritime horizon"</note> horizon, when the sun is reflected there with its rays and the eye receiving this reflection is at a great distance from the sea.

If it is weaker, and the enemy discovers this by means of their spies, they will pass by through treachery . . .

My most illustrious Lords, having closely examined the Isonzo River, and having also been informed by the local people <note>original: "country-folk"</note> how the enemy may arrive from any side...

My most illustrious Lords—As I have carefully examined the conditions of the Isonzo River, and have been given to understand by the local people that whatever mainland route the Turks may take in order to approach this part of Italy, they must finally arrive at this river, I have therefore formed the opinion that even though it may not be possible to build such defenses upon this river as would not ultimately be ruined and destroyed by its floods . . .

My most illustrious Lords—As I have well considered the conditions of the river and recognized that by whatever side of the mainland the Turks may think to approach our Italian lands, they must finally arrive at them by the Isonzo River . . .

### OF CHANGING THE POSITION OF THE RIVER

Regarding what may be said against the permanence of this project, and the concern that logs brought down by the river will break the structures.

To this I reply that all the supports should be equal in height to the lowest depth of the banks. Therefore, if the river should rise to this height, it will not enter the woods near the bank, and not...

# LETTERS

If [the water] enters there, it will not be possible for it to carry away any logs; therefore, the river will flow with only its own water in mere turbulence.

And if it rises above its bank—as was seen this year when it rose about four <term>braccia</term> <note>original: "braccia"; an Italian unit of measurement based on the length of an arm, approximately 23 inches or 58 cm</note> above the lower bank—it carries very large logs with it, bearing them floating along as they accompany its course. It then leaves them resting firmly fixed against the larger trees that are strong enough to offer resistance, and they remain caught in the branches.

If, however, they are borne along on the river, it is because they have few or no branches and float on the surface, and thus do not touch the toothed barrier <note>A defensive hydraulic structure Leonardo designed to snag debris or enemy craft</note> which I have set up.

When the great floods come that carry logs and very large trees, they will pass four or five <term>braccia</term> above the tops of these defenses. The signs of this are visible in the objects left fixed to the branches of the trees after the water has risen.

When the water has no current, it will easily and speedily become choked up with faggots <note>original: "faggots"; bundles of sticks or twigs often used in engineering or as fuel</note>, for those which have fallen into it will always be turning back . . .¹
<margin>Codex Atlanticus, 234 verso c</margin>

I rejoiced so greatly, most illustrious Lord, at your much-wished-for restoration to health that I found my own illness had almost left me upon hearing the news of your Excellency’s recovery. But I am extremely sorry that I have not been able to entirely satisfy your Excellency’s desires because of the malice of this rogue, regarding whom I have never failed to do anything I possibly could that might be of service to him. In the first place, his salary was always paid to him before it was due.

<note>¹ The editor has changed the order of a few of the sentences of this letter as they occur in the edition published by the Accademia dei Lincei <note>original: "Accademia dei Lincei"; the prestigious Italian science academy that published Leonardo's manuscripts</note> in an attempt to improve the sense of continuity.</note>

On the same page is a small drawing or plan of road and river communications with the words **Bridge of Gorizia** <note>original: "ponte di goritia"</note> and **Wippach village, high, high** <note>original: "vil pagho alta alta"</note>. The last word presumably refers to the nature of the land; the first is identical with Wippach (Italian: *Vipacco*), the name of an eastern tributary of the Isonzo and also of a village it flows beneath, which lies on a spur of the hills some twenty kilometers west of Gorizia. From the position of Wippach, it would seem to dominate the road across the mountains from Laibach <note>Modern Ljubljana, Slovenia</note> to Gorizia, which would be the probable route taken by an army advancing from the east to cross the Isonzo at Gorizia. Wippach lies some four kilometers to the south of this road and is connected to it by two roads running northeast and northwest.

...which I believe he would gladly deny if I had not had his signature witnessed by the interpreter. Since I saw that he would only work for me if he could not find work for anyone else—and that he sought such work diligently—I urged him to take his meals with me and to work with his files near me. Besides being economical and good for his productivity, I thought this would help him learn Italian. He always promised to do so, but he was never willing to follow through. 

He acted this way because that German, Giovanni, who makes mirrors, was in his workshop every day. Giovanni wanted to see and understand everything that was being done and then talked about it everywhere, finding fault with what he did not understand. Furthermore, the assistant went to dine with the men of the Pope’s Guard <note>The Swiss Guard, responsible for the Pope's security</note>, and then went out with them with guns to kill birds among the ruins. He continued this routine from lunchtime until evening. 

If I sent Lorenzo <note>Leonardo’s pupil and assistant, Lorenzo behind di Pasqualino</note> to urge him to work, he flew into a rage. He told Lorenzo that he was not going to have so many masters over him and claimed he was busy working for your Excellency’s Wardrobe <note>original: "Wardrobe"; the *Guardaroba*, the department of a princely household in charge of clothing, furniture, and court workshops</note>. Two months passed while this continued, until one day I happened to find Gian Niccolò of the Wardrobe. I asked him whether the German had finished his work for the Magnificent <note>original: "Il Magnifico"; likely referring to Giuliano de’ Medici, Leonardo’s patron in Rome</note>, and he told me it was not true at all—he had only given the man two guns to clean. 

After I confronted him about this, he left the workshop and began to work in his own room. He wasted a great deal of time making another vice, files, and other screw-driven instruments. He also made shuttles there for twisting silk and gold, which he hid whenever any of my people entered. He accompanied all of this with a thousand oaths and insults, so that none of my staff were willing to go there anymore.

The second issue was that, in the room where he slept, he set up another workshop for himself with new bench vices and tools, and there he performed work for others. Afterward, he went to dine with the Swiss of the Guard <note>The Swiss Guard, the military unit responsible for the Pope's security</note>, where there are plenty of idlers, but he surpassed them all in his laziness. Then he used to go out, and more often than not, two or three of them went together with guns to shoot birds among the ruins <note>The ancient Roman ruins, which were then overgrown and used for hunting</note>; this continued until evening.

Finally, I discovered that it was this master Giovanni, the mirror-maker, who had brought all of this about. He did this for two reasons: first, because he said that my arrival here had deprived him of the attention and favor <note>original: "countenance and favour"</note> of your Lordship, which he had always enjoyed. The other reason is that he says the room belonging to this iron-worker would suit him for his own work with mirrors. He has already proven this; for besides setting the assistant against me, he has made him sell all his belongings and leave his workshop to him. Giovanni has now established himself there with a number of assistants, making many mirrors to send to the fairs.

My Lords, Fathers, and Deputies: <note>Leonardo is likely addressing the building committee of a cathedral, such as the one in Milan</note> Just as it is necessary for doctors—who are the tutors and guardians of the sick—to understand what a human being is, what life is, and what health is, and how a balance <note>original: "parity"</note> or harmony of elements maintains this, and similarly how a discord among these elements ruins and destroys it; anyone who has acquired a good knowledge of these conditions will be better able to perform cures than one who lacks it...

You know that medicines, when used correctly, restore health to the sick. They will be used correctly when the doctor, along with his understanding of their nature, also understands what a human being is, what life is, and what the physical makeup and health are. Know these well, and you will know their opposites; when that is the case, you will know well how to devise a remedy—

--- Page 1164 ---
<meta>This page continues Leonardo da Vinci’s draft correspondence and notes. Having previously discussed his frustrations with his assistants in Rome, he now shifts focus to a theoretical and practical defense of his architectural expertise, likely concerning the completion of the crossing tower (tiburio) of Milan Cathedral.</meta>

<page-num>1144</page-num>
<header>LETTERS</header>

You know that medicines, when used well, restore health to the sick; and one who knows them well will use them effectively when they also understand what a human being is, and what life and the physical constitution are, and what health is. Knowing these well, they will also know their opposites, and being thus equipped, they will be closer to devising a remedy than anyone else. In exactly the same way, a cathedral in need of repair requires a "doctor-architect" who understands well what a building is, and upon what rules the correct method of construction is based, where these rules come from, how many parts they are divided into, what causes hold the structure together and make it permanent, what the nature of weight is, and what the "desire for strength" <note>original: "desire of strength"; Leonardo personifies physical forces, referring to the internal tension and resistance of structural materials</note> is, and how these should be interwoven and bound together, and what effect their union produces. Whoever possesses true knowledge of the things mentioned above will satisfy you both by their intelligence and their work.

Therefore, for this reason, I shall strive—without belittling or defaming anyone—to satisfy you partly by arguments and partly by demonstration. Sometimes I will reveal effects from their causes, and sometimes I will confirm my reasoning through experience, fitting them with certain principles of the architects of antiquity and the evidence of the buildings they constructed, showing the reasons for their destruction or their permanence.

I shall show at the same time what the fundamental law of weight is, and what—and how many—causes bring ruin to buildings, and what the conditions are for their stability and permanence.

But in order not to be wordy to your Excellencies, I will speak first of the original design of the first architect of the cathedral <note>likely referring to the original plans for Milan Cathedral, which had been under construction for over a century</note>, and will show you clearly what his purpose was, confirming this by the part of the building that has already been started. Once I have made you understand this, you will be able to clearly recognize that the model which I have constructed possesses in itself that symmetry, that harmony, and that regularity which belongs to the building already begun.

What a building is, and where the rules of sound construction derive their origin, and what and how many parts belong to these. . . .

Either I or some other person who may explain it better than I—choose him, and set aside all bias.
<margin>C.A. 270 r. c <note>Codex Atlanticus, folio 270 recto, column c</note></margin>

When I am established there, I look forward to constructing machines and devices which should be a source of great pleasure to our Most Christian King. Nothing else occurs to me. I am always at your command.

***

# To the Illustrious Commissioners of Buildings

Hearing that your Excellencies have decided to commission certain great works in bronze, I propose to offer you some advice on the subject. First, take care not to act so quickly and hastily in awarding the commission. By rushing, you may lose the opportunity to make a good choice of both the subject matter and the master artist, as Italy has a number of capable men. 

Be careful not to choose some fellow who, through his incompetence, may later give your successors cause to blame both you and your generation. They might judge that this age was poorly equipped with either men of good judgment or talented masters—especially seeing that other cities, and particularly the city of the Florentines, were enriched with such beautiful and great works in bronze at this very same time.

Among these are the gates of their baptistery <note>Leonardo is likely referring to the famous "Gates of Paradise" at the Florence Baptistery, created by Lorenzo Ghiberti</note>. Florence indeed, like Piacenza, is a place of resort where many visitors congregate. When they see its beautiful and stately works of art, they form the impression that the city must have worthy inhabitants, as these works serve as evidence of their character. However, they form quite a different impression if they see a great expenditure of metal wrought so poorly that it would be less of a reproach to the city if the doors were made of plain wood. In that case, the material would have cost little, and therefore would not seem to require a high degree of skill.

Now, the parts principally sought out in cities are their cathedrals; as one approaches these, the first objects that meet the eye are the doors by which one enters the churches.

Beware, gentlemen of the Commission, lest the excessive speed with which you desire to allot the commission for so important a work—with such haste as I perceive you are using—may become the reason why what was intended for the honor of God and men may instead prove a great dishonor to your judgment and to your city. As it is a place of distinction and resort, there is an innumerable concourse of visitors. This disgrace would befall you if, through your negligence, you put your trust in some braggart who—through his subterfuges or by the favor shown to him here—were to be awarded such a commission by you. This would bring great and lasting shame both to him and to you.

I cannot help feeling angry when I reflect upon the sort of men who have made me a confidant of their desire to embark upon such an undertaking, without giving a single thought to their own capacity for it—to say nothing more.

One is a maker of pots, another of <term>cuirasses</term> <note>original: "cuirasses"; pieces of armor covering the torso</note>, a third makes bells and another collars for them, and another even is a <term>bombardier</term> <note>original: "bombardier"; a soldier who operated or manufactured artillery/cannons</note>. Yet another is in the Duke’s household and boasts that he is an intimate acquaintance of Messer Ambrogio Ferrere <note>Ambrogio Ferreri was a high-ranking official and treasurer in the Milanese court</note>, and that he has some influence and has made certain promises to him. If this does not satisfy you, he says he will get on his horse and ride off to the Duke <note>Likely Ludovico Sforza, the Duke of Milan and Leonardo's patron</note>, and will obtain such letters from him that you will never be able to refuse him the work.

But consider to what straits the poor masters—who through study have made themselves competent to execute such works—are reduced, when...

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 335 v. a</margin>

Amid the swirling currents of the winds, a great number of flocks of birds were seen coming from distant lands; these appeared in such a way as to be almost indistinguishable. In their wheeling movements, at one moment all the birds of a single flock were seen edgewise—showing as little as possible of their bodies—and at another moment showing the full extent of their wingspan, facing the viewer directly. At the time of their first appearance, they took the form of an indistinguishable cloud, and then the second and third bands became gradually more clearly defined as they approached nearer to the eye of the beholder.

The nearest of these flocks dropped down low with a slanting movement and settled upon the corpses which were carried along by the waves of this great deluge. They fed upon them and continued to do so until the buoyancy of the bloated bodies failed, and with a slow descent, they sank gradually down to the bottom of the waters.¹

<header>1150 LETTERS</header>

I am writing to remind you of the promise made to me when I last departed: specifically, the grant of <term>twelve ounces of water</term> <note>original: "twelve ounces of water"; a unit of measurement for water flow, usually referring to the right to divert water from a canal for private use or power</note> given to me by the <term>Most Christian King</term> <note>original: "Most Christian King"; the traditional title for the King of France, referring here to Louis XII</note>. Your Lordship knows that I never actually took possession of it. At the time it was granted, there was a shortage of water in the canal, partly because of a great drought and partly because the irrigation outlets had not yet been regulated. However, your Excellency promised me that once this was settled, my expectations would be fulfilled. Consequently, when I was informed that the canal had been regulated, I wrote several times to your Lordship and to Mr. Girolamo da Cusano, who holds the deed of the gift, and I also wrote to Corigero; however, I have never received a reply.

I am now sending my pupil, Salai, as the bearer of this letter. Your Lordship will be able to tell him in person everything that has happened regarding the matter I am petitioning to your Excellency.

I expect to be with you this Easter, as I am almost at the end of my lawsuit. I shall bring with me two paintings of the Madonna which I have begun; considering the time I had available, I have brought them to a very respectable state of completion. I have nothing else to add. . . .

My Illustrious Lord [Antonio Maria], the affection your Excellency has always shown me and the benefits I have received from you are constantly in my thoughts.

I suspect that the small response I have made for the great favors I have received from your Excellency may have made you somewhat angry with me, and that this is the reason I have never had a reply to the many letters I have written to your Excellency. I am now sending Salai to you to explain to your Lordship that I am nearly at the end of my <term>litigation</term> <note>original: "litigation"; a long-running legal dispute Leonardo had with his brothers over their father's estate</note> with my brothers. I hope to be with you this Easter and to bring two paintings of the Madonna of different sizes. I began these for the Most Christian King or for anyone else you might prefer. Upon my return, I would be very glad to know where I am to stay, as I do not wish to cause your Lordship any more trouble. Furthermore, since I have been occupied with work for the Most Christian King, I wish to know whether my salary is to continue or not.

<header>LETTERS</header>

I am writing to the President regarding those water rights which the King granted me. I was not given possession of them because of the scarcity in the canal caused by the great drought, and because the irrigation outlets had not yet been regulated. He promised me, however, that as soon as this was finished, I would be put in possession. Therefore, I ask you—if you happen to meet the President—not to find it troublesome to remind him to grant me possession of this water, now that these outlets are regulated. I am led to understand that the matter rests largely with him. Nothing else comes to mind. I am always at your command.

Good day to you, *Mr. Francesco* <note>original: "Messer Francesco"; likely Francesco Melzi, Leonardo’s devoted pupil and heir, or a high-ranking official</note>. God knows why, after I have written you so many letters, you have never sent a single reply. Just wait until I visit you—by God, I will make you write so much that you might regret it!

<margin>C.A. 372 v. a</margin>
Dear *Mr. Francesco*, I am sending *Salai* <note>Gian Giacomo Caprotti, known as Salai, was Leonardo's long-time assistant and pupil</note> to you to learn from his Excellency the President what decision has been reached regarding the regulation of the water. When I departed, the order for the canal outlets had already been put in motion. The illustrious President promised me that my claim would be settled as soon as this adjustment was made. It has been a considerable time since I learned that the canal and its outlets were in working order. I wrote immediately to the President and to you, and then I wrote again, but I have never had any reply. Would you therefore have the kindness to write and inform me what has taken place? Unless it is actually on the point of settlement, would you please be so kind as to put a little pressure on the President for my sake, and also on *Mr. Girolamo da Cusano*? Please commend me to him, and also offer my respects to his Excellency.

I have encountered someone who expected things from me that he did not deserve. Because his arrogant desires were frustrated, he has tried to turn all my friends against me. Since he found them to be wise and not easily swayed by his will, he has threatened to spread such a report <note>original: *relazione*; here meaning a formal accusation or a damaging rumor intended to ruin someone's reputation</note> about me that it would deprive me of my patrons. For this reason, I have informed your Lordship of this, so...

### [*Draft of a letter to Ludovico Sforza, circa 1482*]

Most Illustrious Lord <note>Ludovico Sforza, also known as "Il Moro," was the Duke of Milan and Leonardo's most significant long-term patron</note>, having now sufficiently seen and considered the proofs of all those who count themselves masters and inventors of instruments of war, and finding that their invention and use of the said instruments does not differ in any respect from those in common practice, I take the liberty—without intending to disparage anyone else—to contact your Excellency in order to acquaint you with my secrets. I then offer myself at your pleasure to effectively demonstrate, at any convenient time, all those matters which are in part briefly recorded below.

1. I have plans for bridges that are very light and strong and suitable for carrying very easily, with which to pursue and at times defeat the enemy; and others that are solid and indestructible by fire or assault, yet easy and convenient to carry away and place in position. I also have plans for burning and destroying those of the enemy.

2. When a place is besieged, I know how to cut off water from the trenches and how to construct an infinite number of bridges, <term>mantlets</term> <note>protective, movable wooden screens or shields used to protect soldiers during a siege</note>, scaling ladders, and other instruments related to such an enterprise.

3. Also, if a place cannot be captured by the method of bombardment—either because of the height of its <term>glacis</term> <note>a defensive slope in front of a fortification</note> or the strength of its position—I have plans for destroying every fortress or other stronghold, unless it has been founded upon solid rock.

4. I have also plans for making cannon that are very convenient and easy to transport, with which to hurl small stones in a manner almost like hail, causing great terror to the enemy from their smoke, and resulting in great loss and confusion.

9. And if it should happen that the engagement is at sea, I have plans for constructing many engines most suitable for either attack or defense, and ships which can resist the fire of all the heaviest cannon, and powder and smoke.

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci offers his services to Ludovico Sforza, detailing his innovative designs for military technology including portable bridges, siege tactics, and naval defenses. This famous letter highlights Leonardo's early focus on engineering and military strategy over the fine arts.</summary>
<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, Ludovico Sforza, military engineering, siegecraft, Renaissance warfare, bridges, cannons, naval defense, Codex Atlanticus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the list of services Leonardo da Vinci offered to Ludovico Sforza in his famous 1482 letter of application, concluding with his skills in art and architecture.</meta>

<page-num>1153</page-num>
<header>LETTERS</header>

5. I also have methods of reaching a specific location through underground caverns and secret, winding passages, built silently even if it is necessary to pass underneath trenches or a river.

6. I can also build <term>armoured cars</term> <note>original: "carri coperti"</note>—safe and indestructible vehicles—which will penetrate the densely packed ranks of the enemy with their artillery. There is no force of armed men so large that these cars will not break through them. Behind these, the infantry will be able to follow completely unharmed and without any opposition.

7. Furthermore, if the need arises, I can make <term>cannon</term>, <term>mortars</term>, and light <term>ordnance</term> <note>general term for artillery and military supplies</note> of very beautiful and functional designs, quite different from those currently in use.

8. Where it is not possible to use cannon, I can provide <term>catapults</term>, <term>mangonels</term> <note>a type of catapult used for throwing heavy stones</note>, <term>trabocchi</term> <note>original: "trabocchi"; counterweight trebuchets used to smash walls</note>, and other engines of wonderful effectiveness that are not commonly used. In short, as the variety of circumstances requires, I can supply an endless number of different engines for both attack and defense.

10. In times of peace, I believe I can give you as complete satisfaction as anyone else in architecture, specifically in the construction of buildings both public and private, and in directing water from one place to another.

I can also perform sculpture in marble, bronze, or clay, as well as painting, in which my work will stand comparison with that of anyone else, whoever they may be.

Moreover, I would undertake the work of the bronze horse, which shall bestow immortal glory and eternal honor upon the blessed memory of the Prince your father and the illustrious House of <term>Sforza</term> <note>The ruling family of Milan; the "bronze horse" refers to the massive monument planned for Francesco Sforza, which Leonardo worked on for years but never cast</note>.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 391 r. a</margin>
And if any of the aforementioned things should seem impossible or impractical to anyone, I offer myself as ready to demonstrate them in your park or in whatever place shall please your Excellency, to whom I commend myself with all possible humility.

Most Illustrious, most Reverend, and my Unique Lord, The Lord Ippolito, Cardinal of Este, My Supreme Lord, at Ferrara.

Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Lord,

A few days ago I arrived from Milan and found that one of my older brothers refuses to fulfill the provisions of a will made three years ago when our father died. Because I do not wish to fail in a matter that I consider most urgent, I must request from your most Reverend Highness a letter of recommendation and support addressed to Ser Raphaello Hieronymo. He is currently a member of our illustrious <term>Signoria</term> <note>original: "Signoria"; the governing body of Florence</note> before whom my case is being tried. More specifically, the case has been referred by his Excellency the <term>Gonfaloniere</term> <note>original: "Gonfaloniere"; the chief magistrate of the Republic of Florence</note> to the aforementioned Ser Raphaello, so that his Lordship may be able to reach a decision and finalize the matter before the upcoming festival of All Saints.

And therefore, my Lord, I beg you as earnestly as I possibly can, that your Highness will write a letter to the said Ser Raphaello in that gracious and persuasive manner that you have mastered.

### [On Squaring the Circle]

->April 28, 1509<-

Having for a long time sought to <term>square the angle</term> <note>To find a square with an area equal to that of a shape with curved sides</note> of two curved sides—that is, the angle *e*, which has two curved sides of equal curvature created by the same circle—I have now solved the proposition in the year 1509, on the eve of the <term>calends</term> <note>original: "calende"; the first day of the month in the Roman calendar</note> of May, at ten o’clock on Sunday evening. I know, therefore (as is shown on the reverse of this page, marked *A*), that if the surface *a b* is taken from its position and given the same value along with portion *c* as the <term>rectilinear</term> <note>consisting of straight lines</note> triangle *d c*, it corresponds exactly to the <term>curvilinear</term> <note>consisting of curved lines</note> triangle *e c*. I would call it the curvilinear triangle *a b d*. Therefore, the square of that triangle *e* will be found in the rectilinear triangle *c d*.

->Windsor MSS. (Beltrami: *Documents and Memoirs*, 201)<-

### DIMENSIONS

The Basilica of Saint Paul <note>San Paolo Fuori le Mura</note> in Rome has five aisles <term>naves</term> and eight <note>The historic basilica actually had 80 columns; this may be an OCR error or a shorthand note by Leonardo.</note> columns. Its interior width across the aisles is 130 <term>braccia</term> <note>an Italian unit of measurement, literally "arms," approximately 23 inches or 58 centimeters</note>. From the steps of the high altar to the main gate is 155 *braccia*; from these steps to the back wall behind the high altar is 70 *braccia*; and the porch is 130 *braccia* long and 17 *braccia* wide.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, 172 v. b</margin>
Made on the . . . day of August, 1516.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, 103 r. b</margin>
Ascension Day at Amboise, at the Château of Cloux <note>now known as Clos Lucé, Leonardo's final residence</note>, May 1517.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus, 249 r. a</margin>
On the twenty-fourth of June—the feast day of St. John—1518, at Amboise, in the palace of Cloux.

---

According to the scholar Calvi, writing about the period between 1504 and 1506, Leonardo refers to the multitude of shells and corals embedded in the rocks which can be seen in the mountains of Parma and Piacenza. This passage seems to be based on first-hand knowledge. If the suggestion of "countryside" <note>original: "campagna"</note> is accepted, it might be that Leonardo was revisiting some of his old haunts. However, the text really only establishes his presence in Parma on the date mentioned. As such, it proves that his stay in Rome was interrupted. Dated references confirm his presence in Rome on the seventh of July 1514, and as late as August 1516. The visit to Parma may possibly have been connected to the fact that Parma was one of the papal cities governed by Giuliano de’ Medici, Leonardo’s patron in Rome.

¹ Louis XII died on the first of January 1515.

## BIBLIOGRAPHICAL NOTES

The presence of this book list on a page of the *Codex Atlanticus* <note>original: "Codice Atlantico"</note> provides strong evidence that Leonardo was listing the specific books he owned. 

Marquis Girolamo d’Adda—whose deep knowledge is shown in his rare pamphlet, *Leonardo da Vinci and His Library: Notes of a Bibliophile* <note>original: "Leonardo da Vinci e la sua Libreria—note di un Bibliofilo"</note> (Milan, 1873)—is the primary source for the following notes. He suggested that because Leonardo used the Italian forms of classical names rather than the original Latin, he might have been using Italian translations. However, I do not believe this conclusion is necessarily true, any more than it would be for a modern writer who uses the names "Virgil" or "Horace" in a list. Nevertheless, Italian translations of all these classical works did exist, and Leonardo may have owned any of them. D’Adda’s extensive bibliographical knowledge makes his descriptions of these works a "master key" <note>original: "open sesame"</note> to understanding Leonardo’s library. By contrast, the following brief notes might face the same criticism Leonardo leveled against those who write summaries—that they diminish the value of the original work:

**BOOK OF ARITHMETIC** — This is perhaps *The Noble Work of Arithmetic, Which Deals with All Matters Pertaining to Merchandise* <note>original: "La nobel opera de arithmetica ne la qual se tracta tutte cosse a mercantia pertinente"</note>, written by Piero Borgi of Venice and published in 1484. The name Master Piero dal Borgo also appears in the Arundel Manuscript (British Museum), folio 190 verso (see page 1181).

The two notes that follow refer to a book, namely: "to have my book bound" and "show the book to Serigatto."

**PLINY**—*Natural History* <note>original: "Historia naturale"</note> by Gaius Plinius Secundus, translated from the Latin language into Florentine by Cristoforo Landino. 1476, Venice <note>original: "Venetiis"</note>.

**BIBLE**—Earliest Italian version: *Illustrated Vernacular Bible* <note>original: "Biblia volgare historiata"</note>. Venice 1471.

**ON MILITARY MATTERS** <note>original: "DE RE MILITARI"</note>—Valturio? Robert Valturio’s *Twelve Books on Military Matters* <note>original: "Roberti Valturii de re militari libri XII"</note>, 1472. Bologna 1483.

**FIRST, THIRD AND FOURTH DECADES [OF LIVY]**—Earliest Italian version: *Livy in the Vernacular* <note>original: "Tito Livio volgarizzato"</note>. Rome 1476.

**GUIDO**—D’Adda suggests Guido da Cauliaco, author of a treatise on surgery:—*Surgery by Guy de Chauliac* <note>original: "Guidonis de Cauliaco Cyrurgia"</note>. Venice <note>original: "Venetiis"</note> 1498.

**PIERO CRESCENTIO**—writer on agriculture: *Twelve Books on Rural Benefits* <note>original: "Ruralium commodorum lib. XII"</note>. Pietro de' Crescenzi, 1471. *The Book of Agriculture by Pietro Crescentio* <note>original: "Il Libro della Agricultura di Pietro Crescentio"</note>. Florence <note>original: "Florentiæ"</note> 1478.

**THE FOUR REALMS** <note>original: "QUADRIREGIO"</note>—the Four Realms:—Love, Satan, Vices, Virtues—a poem composed in imitation of the *Divine Comedy* <note>original: "Divina Commedia"</note> by Federico Frezzi of Foligno. Perugia 1481. Florence, no date.

**DONATUS**—Aelius Donatus, author of a short Latin syntax, *On the Eight Parts of Speech* <note>original: "De Octo Partibus Orationis"</note>. Many editions in the 15th century.

**JUSTINUS**—a Roman historian who made a summary <term>epitome: a brief summary of a larger work</term> of the general history written by Trogus Pompeius.

**GUIDO**—Richter suggests Guido d’Arezzo:—a monk from the tenth century and the inventor of the tonic sol-fa musical system. Many Italian libraries possess manuscript <note>original: "MS."</note> copies of his *Short Treatise on the Discipline of the Musical Art* <note>original: "Micrologus De Disciplina Artis Musicæ"</note>.

**MANUAL OF WISDOM** <note>original: "DOTTRINALE"</note>—perhaps *Manual of Wisdom* <note>original: "Doctrinal de Sapience"</note> by Guy de Roye, Archbishop of Sens. Latin text 1388. French translation, Geneva 1478, and many others.

**MORGANTE**—*The Greater Morgante* <note>original: "Il Morgante Maggiore"</note>. A romantic epic by Luigi Pulci. *The Morgante*, 23 cantos <note>original: "canti"</note>. Printed by Luca the Venetian <note>original: "Per Luca Venetiano stampatore"</note> 1481. *The Greater Morgante*, 28 cantos, Florence 1482, and many others.

**FLOWERS OF VIRTUE** <note>original: "FIORE DI VIRTÙ"</note>—A collection of moral tales and fables composed about 1320. *Flowers of Virtue, which deals with all human vices... and how one ought to acquire virtue.* Venice 1474.

**LIVES OF THE PHILOSOPHERS**—Perhaps *The Book of the Lives of the Philosophers, etc.* <note>original: "El libro de la vita de philosophi"</note> by Diogenes Laertius. Venice 1480.

**LAPIDARY** <note>A book describing the properties of gemstones and minerals.</note>—Perhaps a translation of the Latin poem *On Stones* <note>original: "De Lapidibus"</note> by Marbodeus, or of the *Five Books on Minerals* <note>original: "Mineralium Libri V"</note> by Albertus Magnus, 1476.

**ON THE PRESERVATION OF HEALTH**—Perhaps Arnaldus de Villanova’s *Regimen of Health* <note>original: "Regimen Sanitatis"</note>, 1480, or Ugo Benzo of Siena's *A very useful treatise regarding the preservation of health* <note>original: "Tractato utilissimo circa la conservatione de la sanitade"</note>. Milan 1481.

**CECCO D'ASCOLI**—Francesco Stabili (nicknamed "Cecco," meaning "the blind"), who was burned for heresy in 1347. He was the author of *The Acerba* <note>original: "L’Acerba"</note>, a speculative philosophical poem.
> "In this poem, it is said that the origins of many modern discoveries are outlined, and in particular, the circulation of the blood."

**ALBERTUS MAGNUS**—Perhaps *Work on Animals* <note>original: "Opus De Animalibus"</note>, Rome, 1478; or *The Book of Secrets concerning the virtues of herbs, stones, and animals* <note>original: "Liber secretorum de virtutibus herbarum lapidum et animalium"</note>, Bologna 1478; or *Here begins the book called "Of Life," etc.* <note>original: "Incomenza el libro chiamato della vita"</note>, Naples 1478.

**NEW RHETORIC** <note>original: "RHETORICA NOVA"</note>—Lorenzo Guglielmo of Saona:—*New Rhetoric*. Cambridge 1478. St. Albans 1480.

**CIBALDONE**—*A work by the most excellent physician Master Cibaldone, selected from authentic medical books, which is very useful for keeping oneself healthy.* Published toward the end of the fifteenth century (according to the bibliographer Brunet).

---

¹ In the introduction to his edition of the Leicester Manuscript, Gerolamo Calvi suggests that these two lines refer to Leonardo’s search for and possession of a copy of one of the works of Ramon Lull, the Majorcan philosopher and mystic. This offers a likely explanation for lines that would otherwise be a mystery. An edition of Lull’s *The Ultimate General Art* <note>original: "Ars generalis ultima"</note> was printed in Venice in 1480, and others of his works appeared in Rome and Barcelona. Leonardo may, however, have been looking for one of his manuscripts. The so-called "Lullian method"—an attempt to provide a mechanical aid to the mind for acquiring knowledge through combinations formed by revolving circles—was dismissed in a few sentences by Francis Bacon: "Any superficial student <note>original: "sciolist"</note> may put on a show and display of learning. Such was the art of Lull." The "Enlightened Doctor" <note>original: "doctor illuminatus"</note>, as he was called, is today merely a name in the history of philosophy; any current interest in him centers on his work as a poet and mystic. His most recent biographer, Professor Peers, devotes a chapter each to his romances *Blanquerna* and *Felix*, but only a single page to his intimidating *General Art* <note>original: "Ars Generalis"</note>. However, even though the mechanical devices associated with the "Lullian method" were deservedly discredited, Lull as a thinker broke away from the rigid constraints of the medieval scholars. As the titles of certain chapters in his treatises show, his curiosity regarding the laws of natural forces offers many parallels to Leonardo’s own writings. His scientific activities included geometry, astronomy, physics, chemistry, anthropology, the causes of wind and rain, the laws of navigation, and warfare. He was similar to Roger Bacon in the extraordinary scope of his scientific interests. The two lines in which Leonardo expresses his desire to own a work by Ramon Lull can be compared to another sentence in the Arundel Manuscript: "Roger Bacon, translated into print." Leonardo likely first became interested in the work of both Lull and Bacon through his association with Fra Luca Pacioli. Pacioli belonged to the Franciscan order, as did Lull and Bacon, and was therefore more likely to be familiar with their works.

² Nonius Marcellus and Sextus Pompeius Festus were Roman grammarians from around the fourth century A.D. Brunet, in his *Bookseller's Manual* <note>original: "Manuel du Libraire"</note>, mentions an edition of these three authors printed at Parma in 1480.

->‘*The Duke <note>Likely referring to Ludovico Sforza, Leonardo's patron, who lost Milan to the French in 1499.</note> lost his state, his personal possessions, and his liberty, and none of his enterprises have been completed.*’<-

->So shall ruined hearts yield to hearts.¹ <note>original: "Diruta sic cedent pectora pectoribus."</note><-

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 28 r. b</margin>

The practice of slitting the nostrils of horses is something that deserves to be mocked. These fools follow this custom as if they believe nature failed to provide necessary things, and that men must be her correctors.

Nature has made two holes in the nose, each of which is half the width of the windpipe <note>original: "pipe from the lungs"</note> through which heavy breathing passes. If these holes were not there, the mouth would be sufficient for this great volume of breath.

And if you were to ask me why nature made the nostrils of animals this way, when breathing through the mouth is sufficient, my reply—

---

<note>¹ These lines refer to the Siege of Colle di Val d’Elsa, which was taken by storm from the Florentines in November 1479 by the Duke of Calabria and Federigo, Duke of Urbino. The "Ghibellina" mentioned in the poem is the name of a specific piece of artillery (see Calvi, *Manuscripts of Leonardo*, p. 45).</note>

...dissolved. And when it has all settled, throw away the lemon juice and add fresh juice. Repeat this two or three times so that the paste becomes very fine. Then wash the paste with clear water enough times so that it loses all trace of the lemon juice. After doing this, let the paste dry until it turns into a powder. Then take the white of an egg, beat it well, and leave it to settle; then moisten the powder with this until it becomes a paste again.

From this mixture, you can make pearls as large as you wish and leave them to dry. Then place them in a small turning lathe and polish them—using a dog’s tooth if you like, or if you prefer, a polishing stick made of crystal or chalcedony <note>a translucent variety of quartz</note>.

## HOW A BLOW CAUSES FIRE

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 351 v. b</margin>
If you strike a thick bar of iron between the anvil and the hammer with frequent blows on the same spot, you will be able to light a match <note>In the 1500s, a "match" was a piece of cord or tinder used to carry fire, not a modern friction match.</note> at the spot that has been struck.

<margin>Codex Atlanticus 384 r. a</margin>
I will say one word, or two, or ten, or more, as it pleases me; and I wish that in that same time, more than a thousand people say the same thing, so that they immediately say the same as me. Yet they will not see me, nor perceive what I say.

These will be the hours counted by you; for when you say "one," all those who are counting the hours as you do will say the same number as you at that very same time.

<margin>Codex Trivulziano 18 a</margin>
[*Accompanying a sketch of a flock of birds rising in flight*]
This stratagem was used by the Gauls against the Romans, and it caused such great death that all of Rome was dressed in mourning.

<margin>Codex Trivulziano 44 a</margin>
Sea water filtered through mud or clay deposits leaves all its saltiness behind. Woolen fabrics spread over the sides of ships also absorb fresh water. If it is distilled using a retort <note>a glass or metal vessel used for distilling liquids</note>, sea water becomes of the highest quality. By using a cooking stove in his kitchen, anyone can—with the same wood he uses for cooking—distill a large quantity of water, provided the retort is a large one.

<margin>Manuscript F 2 r.</margin>
One may make thin, grained boards out of wood which will look like camlets <note>a costly fabric with a wavy or "watered" appearance</note> and watered silks, featuring various permanent markings.

When a horse moves through water, it creates less foam the more it is submerged, and more foam when it is less submerged. This happens because the legs are less impeded when they are deeper; consequently, when shallow, they move more rapidly and strike the water more forcefully with their large hooves than they do with their knees and thighs.

### [*Sensibility of the hair of the ox*]

<margin>K 81 [1] r.</margin>
The hair of an ox, when placed in stagnant water during the summer, acquires sensation, life, and movement on its own; it also gains the capacity for fear, flight, and the perception of pain. <note>Leonardo is recording a common folk belief of his time regarding spontaneous generation—the idea that life could arise spontaneously from non-living matter under specific conditions.</note> The proof of this is that if the hair is pressed, it twists and releases itself. If you place it back in the water, it takes flight and moves away from danger, just as it did before.

# SCENTLESS OIL

### To remove the smell from oil:

Take some crude oil and put ten pints of it into a vessel. Mark the height of the oil on the side of the vessel, then add a pint of vinegar and boil the mixture until the oil has dropped back down to the mark you made. By doing this, you can be certain that the oil has returned to its original volume and that all the vinegar has evaporated, carrying the foul smell away with it.

### [Events in Milan in 1500]

Paolo di Vannocco at Siena.
Domenico Chiavaio.
The small hall above for the apostles. <note>Likely a reference to a room designated for a painting or decoration of the twelve apostles.</note>
Buildings by Bramante. <note>Donato Bramante, the renowned Renaissance architect who worked alongside Leonardo in Milan.</note>
The governor of the castle was taken prisoner.
Visconti was dragged away and then his son was killed.
Gian della Rosa <note>identified as Giovanni da Rosate, the Duke's physician and astrologer.</note> was robbed of his money.
Borgonzo <note>identified as Brugonzio Botta, the administrator of the Duke's revenue.</note> began and was unwilling, and so fortune deserted him.
The Duke <note>Ludovico Sforza, known as "Il Moro," Leonardo's primary patron in Milan.</note> lost his state, his personal possessions, and his liberty; none of his enterprises have been completed.¹

---

¹ The note "buildings by Bramante"—given that the following entries relate to the disastrous events following the imprisonment of Ludovico Sforza—possibly refers to the fact that various works designed by Bramante were left unfinished. For example, according to the scholar Amoretti, only one side of the *Canonica di S. Ambrogio* was built, and the columns for the rest lay there for over a century. According to the same authority, the reference to the governor of the castle likely refers to the French governor who, upon the return of the French, was imprisoned for surrendering to Ludovico when his troops briefly reoccupied the city. He cites the names of two members of the Visconti family from Arluno’s chronicle who were taken as captives to France for supporting the Duke. Gian della Rosa is identified as Giovanni da Rosate, a professor at Pavia and the Duke’s physician; and Borgonzo as Brugonzio Botta, the administrator of the ducal revenue, whose house was plundered by French partisans during his flight.

These notes end with Leonardo’s brief, somber reflection on the fallen fortunes of Ludovico Sforza, who at the time of writing was a prisoner at Loches in Touraine, where he remained until his death.

<margin>B.M. 279 v.</margin>
The men at the storming of Syracuse were offered very great rewards by these same Romans. At the sack of Syracuse, a diligent search was made for Archimedes <note>The famous Greek mathematician and inventor who lived c. 287–212 BCE.</note>, and when he was found to be dead, there was a greater lament made in the senate and among the Roman people than if they had lost their entire army; they did not fail to honor him with funeral rites <note>original: "obsequies"</note> and a statue, their leader being Marcus Marcellus.

After the second destruction of Syracuse, the tomb of this same Archimedes was rediscovered by Cato <note>Leonardo likely means Cicero, the Roman orator who famously rediscovered Archimedes' overgrown tomb in 75 BCE, though Leonardo records the name as Cato here.</note> among the ruins of a temple; so Cato caused the temple and tomb to be restored most elaborately. Regarding this, Cato is recorded to have said that he did not glory in any of his actions so much as in having paid this honor to Archimedes.

### HOW TO MAKE ROUGHENED AMBER

<margin>Forster III 33 v.</margin> Take the white of an egg and put it into a sausage skin and boil it; after it has grown hard, paint over the spots, then cover it over with more egg white and put it back into a larger skin.

<margin>Forster III 37 v.</margin> Add pyrites <term>iron disulfide, also known as "fool's gold"</term> to aqua fortis <term>literally "strong water," an archaic term for nitric acid</term>; if it turns green, know that it contains copper. Precipitate this with saltpetre <term>potassium nitrate</term> and soft soap.

<margin>Forster III 45 v.</margin> On the first day of February: twelve hundred lire.

### AQUA FORTIS <note>original: "Aqua Fortis" (Nitric Acid)</note>

One part Roman vitriol <term>likely iron or copper sulfate</term>, one part saltpetre, one part cinnabar <term>mercury sulfide, used as a red pigment</term>, one part verdigris <term>the green pigment or patina that forms on copper</term>.

### TO DISSOLVE COPPER

<margin>Forster III 59 v.</margin> Dissolve the copper with these waters <note>referring to the aqua fortis recipe above</note> and then evaporate it so that it becomes like paste or mustard. Daub it over your figure, polish it well with a brush, and dry it; then cover it with earth out of doors and make a great fire so that the copper between the two layers of earth becomes fused, or else mix this copper with quicksilver <term>mercury</term>.

<page-num>1185</page-num>
<header>MISCELLANEOUS</header>

# MISCELLANEOUS

<margin>Forster III 74 r.</margin>
If lime and orpiment <term>a yellow arsenic mineral used in pigments and depilatories</term> make a hair remover, then lye or a distilled liquid will also make it; it will dissolve hair, horn, bristles, and nails.

<margin>Fogli B 3 r.</margin>
Among Europeans, long fingernails are looked upon as shameful, but among the Indians they are held in great honor. They anoint them with fragrant scents and adorn them with various patterns; they say that long nails are a mark of people of noble birth, and that short nails are a sign of the working class and craftsmen in different trades.

Power reveals itself more strongly when it acts upon a weaker resistance—that is, a lesser resistance.

This conclusion is universal and applies to the ebb and flow of the tides. It proves that the sun or moon exerts a greater influence upon the water where it is shallower; therefore, the shallow waters of the marshes must experience the cause of the tides with greater force than the vast depths of the ocean.

## MEMORANDUM <note>The memorandum is a brief list of personal tasks and books to consult.</note>

To go and make arrangements for my garden.
Giordano’s *On Weights* <note>original: "De Ponderibus," a medieval treatise on statics by Jordanus de Nemore</note>.
The device for balancing <note>original: "The reconciler"</note> the ebb and flow of the sea.
To have two boxes made to fit on a pack saddle.

---

<note>
The fact may perhaps not be without significance that this memorandum, which the order of arrangement of passages from the various manuscripts has caused to come at the end of this book, contains two sentences in which, alongside the record of matters of daily importance, there is a deeper note discernible—one which seems to sound in unison across the centuries. In the words "to go to make arrangements for my garden" (*andare in provitione per il mio giardino*) there is a curious similarity to the words and mood of thought that finds expression in the famous saying in Voltaire's *Candide*: "we must cultivate our garden" <note>original: "il faut cultiver notre jardin"</note>. Each perhaps may contain a formula of renunciation.

So also, in a similar way, the third line of the memorandum, "the reconciler of the flow and ebb of the sea," seems to link itself unforgettably in the memory with two lines by the poet John Keats:

> "The moving waters at their priestlike task
> Of pure ablution round earth’s human shores."

The two present essentially the same image. If you surrender to them, they have the same beauty of suggestion.

With Leonardo, however, the mood changed. Any thought of the movement of water might give way to practical considerations regarding the possibilities of harnessing its power for...
</note>

<summary>This page contains Leonardo's notes on hair-dissolving chemicals, observations on the cultural significance of fingernails, and his theories on why tides are more noticeable in shallow water. It concludes with a personal memorandum that includes a plan to tend his garden and a reference to a book on physics.</summary>

<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, depilatory, orpiment, Indian culture, tides, ebb and flow, memorandum, Giordano de Nemore, On Weights, Candide, Voltaire, John Keats</keywords>

<header>MISCELLANEOUS</header>

See Boltraffio’s <note>Giovanni Antonio Boltraffio (c. 1466–1516), a prominent pupil and assistant in Leonardo’s workshop</note> turning lathe and have a stone removed.
Leave the book for Master <note>original: "Messer"</note> Andrea the German <note>original: "Tedesco"</note>.
Use an arrow as a scale <term>a balance used for weighing</term> and weigh the substance while it is heated, then weigh it again when it is cold.
The mirror belonging to Master Luigi.
Petroleum oil.
[*Figure a b*] The flow and ebb of the waters, tested at the mill of Vanrio <note>likely Vaprio d'Adda</note>.
Cap <note>original: "Cap.", here referring to a "beretta" or hat, listed as a reminder</note>. <note>The following citation is right-aligned in the original</note> Notebooks II 22 v. <note>original: "Quaderni"</note>

---

...public utility. The last line of the memorandum is "*a b* flow and ebb of the waters proved at the mill of Vanrio," with the letters referring to a small drawing of hydraulic machinery placed right at the edge of the page. If "Vanrio" can be interpreted as Vaprio, the reference would be to the waters of the Adda River and to the mill at Vaprio d'Adda. Vaprio was the country home of the Melzi family; Francesco Melzi, a member of that family, became like an adopted son to Leonardo. During his final years in Milan, Leonardo frequently went to Vaprio to conduct his research in peace. If this memorandum is a record of his immediate thoughts, the word "cap" <note>original: "beretta"</note> which ends the list—appearing right after the mention of the mill—might suggest he was thinking about traveling there.
